It decides **which rebase runs**, not **where the replay lands**, and no field, rendering, doc or test may call it the destination. Its directory is the executor's own `gitContext` — `entry.Repo` when non-empty, that entry's worktree otherwise — which is **`base_context` unconditionally, with no carve-out** (round-36 items 1 and 2, narrowed but not disturbed by round-37 item 2): round 35's exception for "the pass-1 row with an empty `Repo` whose worktree stat failed with a non-`IsNotExist` error" named a cell that produces **no rebase row at all**, since `checkSyncWorktreeBranch` stops the run at the shipped rank 4 preflight before the loop's `syncRepoContext` call — and the one place a `syncRepoContext` for that entry *does* run earlier, the new-mode `--no-fetch` I14 preflight, issues **no `GetBranchSHA`**, so it moves no decision read anywhere — so `gitContext` and the base context are the **same directory in every cell that has a decision read at all** and the two can no longer be said to diverge on a pass-1 row with an empty `Repo`. On a **split** row — the external pass-1 row with a non-empty `Repo` — the decision read stays here in `base_context` while the **destination** stays an `execution_context` resolution, which is the whole point of the pair and is unchanged. `deferred`/`depends_on` from the previous draft are deliberately split into `destination.deferred`
and the separate `replay.determinacy` axis: **a deferred destination does not imply an unknown
source range**, and conflating them was the schema's central error (§5.1). Both are derived from the
route's **actual execution order**, not from stack topology: the earlier draft's "an earlier
selected entry's post-rebase tip" is wrong for external, whose pass 1/pass 2 split makes a
materialized child run *before* its non-materialized parent (§5.1 deferral rule, §5.4).

**Skip rule (the fourth determinacy value, and why it is not `unknown`).** A row whose `strategy` is
one of the four skip tokens — `skipped-anchor`, `skipped-archived`, `skipped-updated-ref`,
`skipped-no-base` — runs **no `git rebase` at all** (`argv: []`; `skipped-anchor` additionally runs
**no Git process whatsoever**, being decided by `run.skipsAnchor` above every probe in both loops,
while `skipped-updated-ref` runs **no rebase, no base resolution, no default-branch read, no
`GetBranchSHA` and no `UpdateBaseSHA` *after* the mandatory probes its route issues before the skip**
— round-37 item 1, which withdraws the blanket "no Git process whatsoever" for that arm as false
against the shipped loop, §5.4). There is no replay to be determinate or
indeterminate about, so publishing `determinacy: unknown` would be a false claim of ignorance:
"unknown" means *the plan could not determine a range it will use*, and here **there is no range to
determine**. Such a row therefore publishes, without exception:

- `replay.determinacy = not-applicable` and `replay.reason = not-executed`;
- the candidate facts that are **known because nothing is executed** — `candidate_count: 0`,
  `commits: []`, `commits_listed: 0`, `commits_truncated: false`, and `candidate_digest` = the
  digest of the **empty sequence** (§4.5), none of which costs a probe: the row runs no rebase, so
  "this row replays nothing" is a *counted* fact, not an unknown one (§4.8). The previous draft
  published all of them as `null`, which forced every aggregate over a skip row to be special-cased
  as "unknown but really zero" and made `summary.total_candidates` derivable only by a rule stated
  outside the rows;
- the candidate facts that remain **`null` because there is no range or upstream to name** —
  `range`, `upstream_ref`, `upstream_sha`, `first_candidate`, `may_drop_patch_equivalent` — with
  `replay.upstream_provenance = unknown`. `null` here is not "unknown zero": it is "there is no
  such expression", and inventing an empty-looking range would claim a `<upstream>..<branch>` the
  row never has;
- `collateral_refs: []` **only** because a row that rebases nothing moves nothing: this is a *known*
  empty set, not an unknown one (§4.8). **`collateral_exposed` is not fixed by the skip**: it is
  computed from the *earlier* rows' collateral sets for every row, skip rows included, so it may be
  `true` (a `skipped-updated-ref` row is the paradigm case — its tip is exactly what an earlier
  entry's `--update-refs` is expected to move, §5.4), `false`, or `null` when an earlier row's set
  is unknown. A blanket `false` here would erase the one exposure the plan most needs to publish;
- the skip's cause in the `strategy` token itself (`skipped-no-base` is the base-unset skip,
  `skipped-anchor` the local-only anchor, `skipped-archived` checkout's `Archived` skip,
  `skipped-updated-ref` external pass 2's `markUpdatedAncestors` projection), so no extra cause key
  is needed and none is added.

Consequences that keep the schema total, and they are now **derivations rather than special
cases**: because a skip row publishes `candidate_count: 0`, every aggregate of §4.4 falls out of the
rows themselves — `summary.total_candidates` and `_lower_bound` sum the published counts with no
"skip rows contribute nothing" clause, `summary.max_entry_candidates` is the maximum over published
counts (so an all-skip document publishes `0`, not `null`, because every count is known), and
`summary.entries_with_unknown_candidates` counts `determinacy = unknown` rows only, which a skip row
never is. The §8.3.2a evaluation row for a skip entry reads that same `0` out of the row instead of
substituting one, so the "value: 0 for skip rows" rule and the aggregate rule now have a single
source. None of this is the "treat unknown as zero" lie of §8.3.2: zero really is what these rows
replay, and the document says so as a counted fact rather than as an absence a consumer must
reinterpret. A skip row therefore **never** produces `indeterminate-entry` either: there is nothing
indeterminate about `0`, and a limit is trivially satisfied by a row that replays nothing.
**The one field the skip does not settle is `collateral_exposed`**, which stays
independently computed from the earlier rows (above).
`skipped-no-base` in external does not exist — external has no skip (§5.1 rule 5), so its
unset-base row is a real, blocking `plain`/`plain-explicit-branch` row with
`determinacy = unknown` and `reason = base-unset`.

**Skip-context rule: which context a skip row has, stated arm by arm and closed** (round-36 item 4).
The skip rule above settles what a skip row *replays*; it never said in which context a skip row's
remaining facts are measured, and "the row runs no Git" was left to imply "the row has no context",
which is false on one of the four arms. The mapping is therefore fixed here, exhaustively over the
`strategy` enum's skip tokens, and no other section may restate it loosely:

- **`skipped-updated-ref`** (external pass 2, `markUpdatedAncestors`, §5.4 consequence 2) —
  **the arm is not Git-free, and round-37 item 1 replaces round 36's implied "no context, no
  process" reading with the executor's real order.** Pass 2 runs, in this order:
  `alreadyDone` → `run.selects` → `run.skipsAnchor` → `os.Stat(worktree)` (skip when it *succeeds*)
  → **`internal.IsPrunableWorktree(entry.GitBranch())`** → **only then** the `updatedByRef` skip
  (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:164-190`). So the prunability probe — one cwd-scoped
  `git worktree list --porcelain`, no `-C` (`internal/exec.go:201-221`) — is **issued before the
  skip and gates it**: a prunable entry never becomes a `skipped-updated-ref` row at all, it is the
  blocking `materialization: prunable` row of §5.4 consequence 3, and the planner must evaluate the
  two in that order or it will publish a skip for a run that stops. What the arm does **not** do
  after the skip fires is any of `resolveEntryBase`, `DefaultBranch`/`DefaultBranchIn`,
  `GetBranchSHA`, `git rebase`, `git rebase --abort` or `UpdateBaseSHA` — that, and not "no Git",
  is the claim every section must make.
  `execution_context` **is** established and published, with the ordinary pass-2 rule
  (`entry.Repo`, else the process cwd): it is the store this row's `refs/heads/<git_branch>` lives
  in, and without it the plan cannot *name* the row's ref, cannot publish `head.state`/`head.sha`,
  and cannot evaluate `collateral_exposed`, whose whole content is "an earlier row's collateral set,
  taken in a store, contains **this** ref" — a comparison that is meaningless across stores. This is
  the arm the row exists for, so its ref facts are the point rather than an ornament.
  **`base_context` is published only where the described route's own preflight really resolves this
  entry's base, and is `not-applicable` everywhere else** (round-37 item 1). The rule is stated over
  the route, not over the arm, because exactly one route resolves a base for an entry it will later
  skip: on the **new-mode `--no-fetch`** route `verifySelectedBasesLocally` runs **before** the two
  loops and, for every selected entry that is not a local-only anchor, issues
  `syncRepoContext(layout, entry)` → `resolveEntryBase(stack, entry, repoCtx)` →
  `internal.VerifyGitRef(repoCtx, ref)` (`internal/cli/sync.go:164`, `:239-260`, §9 route order),
  which for a worktree-less entry is the **same directory** the pass-2 arm would use — `entry.Repo`,
  else the process cwd. There, and only there, the row publishes a real `base_context` with
  `source ∈ {entry-repo, process-cwd}` and a real **`base.ref`**, which is the **preflight's**
  resolved ref and **not an execution destination**: nothing rebases onto it on this row. On every
  other route — the legacy external route, and any new-mode route whose effective policy is not
  `--no-fetch`, where `verifySelectedBasesLocally` returns immediately
  (`sel.Policy.Fetch != internal.SyncFetchDisabled`) — no base of this entry is resolved anywhere,
  so all three members are published `{context_id: null, repo_root: null, source: not-applicable}`
  and `base.ref` is `null`. **There is no third, ambiguous context shape**: a `base_context` is
  either the preflight's established directory or `not-applicable`, never "the directory the arm
  would have used".
  **`base.decision_sha` is `null` on this row on every route without exception** — the preflight
  resolves a *ref* and verifies it, and issues no `GetBranchSHA` — and
  **`destination.sha`/`destination.snapshot_sha` are `null` on every route** with the explicit
  not-executed cause, because this row's replay lands nowhere: publishing the peel of a ref the row
  never rebases onto would name a destination the run does not have.
  The rest of the row is fixed and closed, so no consumer has to infer it: `strategy =
  skipped-updated-ref`, `argv = []`, `replay.determinacy = not-applicable`,
  `replay.reason = not-executed`, `replay.candidate_count = 0`, `replay.commits = []`,
  `commits_listed = 0`, `commits_truncated = false`, `candidate_digest` = the empty-sequence digest,
  and `replay.range`/`upstream_ref`/`upstream_sha`/`first_candidate`/`may_drop_patch_equivalent`
  `null` with `upstream_provenance: unknown` (skip rule above). **The holder, working-tree and
  configuration facts are explicitly `null`, not merely unprobed**: `context.dirty`,
  `context.autostash`, `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`,
  `context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`, `context.rebase_in_progress`,
  `context.untracked_present`, `context.overwrite_risk`, `branch_checked_out_at`,
  `collateral_mechanism` and `effective_backend` are all `null` — the row starts no rebase in that
  directory, so every one of them would be a precondition for a command that is never issued — and
  `mutation.will_switch_head`/`head_restored_by_run` are `false` with
  `mutation.will_leave_head_on` `null`.
  **The probes this row really costs are enumerated, and the argv sidecar asserts exactly them**:
  (a) the shared, invocation-cached cwd-scoped `worktree list --porcelain` of §3.7/§13, which the
  executor issues for this row and which the planner mirrors — **no extra process**, since one cwd
  probe answers every pass-2 row; (b) exactly **one** head probe in `execution_context`,
  `git -C <execution_context.repo_root> rev-parse --verify refs/heads/<git_branch>^{commit}`,
  which is what publishes `head.state`/`head.sha` and what makes `collateral_exposed` answerable by
  ref identity; and (c) **only on the new-mode `--no-fetch` route**, the preflight's own reads —
  `DefaultBranchIn`'s **one or two** processes where the base is a literal ref rather than a
  same-repo stack entry (`resolveEntryBase` short-circuits with **no** Git in the stack-entry cell,
  `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:335-356`, §13) plus one `VerifyGitRef` `rev-parse --verify
  <ref>^{commit}`. **Nothing else is issued for this row**, and three absences are asserted rather
  than assumed: **no** `for-each-ref refs/heads/` for this row's own collateral set (it is the
  *known* `[]` of the skip rule, and `collateral_exposed` is read off the **earlier** rows'
  published sets by ref identity), **no** `rev-list` of any shape, and **no cutoff verification**.
  **The cutoff is deliberately not probed**: the arm never reads `LastBaseSHA` (`cutoff.usage:
  not_used`) and runs no rebase whose source boundary it could be, so paying a `rev-parse --verify
  <sha>^{commit}` to verify a boundary nothing will use would be a probe with no consumer.
  `cutoff.recorded_sha` and `cutoff.provenance` stay — they are stack facts — `cutoff.state` is
  `absent` where nothing is recorded (a knowable stack fact) and **`null`** where a SHA is recorded
  but unverified, and `cutoff.resolved_sha` is `null`. `base.name` and `base.kind` stay on every
  route, being stack facts that were never probed.
- **`skipped-anchor`** (external, the local-only anchor), **`skipped-archived`** (checkout's
  `Archived` skip) and **`skipped-no-base`** (checkout's unset base) — these run **no rebase Git and
  no ref Git of their own**, so **both** refs are published `{context_id: null, repo_root: null,
  source: not-applicable}`, the row cites **no** `repositories[]` row through either ref, and **no
  per-row Git process is issued for it at all** (argv sidecar). **The three retain that shape on
  every route, and round-37 item 1's preflight cell does not reach them**: `skipped-anchor` is
  decided by `run.skipsAnchor` above every probe in both external loops
  (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:100-105`, `:171-176`) and is the **one** entry class
  `verifySelectedBasesLocally` skips outright (`entry.Role == SyncRoleAnchor &&
  Policy.Propagation == LocalOnly → continue`, `internal/cli/sync.go:246-248`), so the no-fetch
  preflight resolves no base for it; `skipped-archived` and `skipped-no-base` are **checkout** arms,
  and checkout resolves its bases inside `BuildCheckoutPlan` *after* both skips
  (`internal/checkout_sync.go:473-497`) and never calls `resolveBase`/`DefaultBranchIn` at all. The
  only work that can still cite a context for such an entry is a **push or restore target**, which
  is projected on its own axis by the rule three bullets below. Their probe-dependent facts are
  therefore `null` for the *not-applicable* reason and not for `repo-unavailable`'s: `head.state`,
  `head.sha`, `cutoff.state`, `cutoff.resolved_sha`, `destination.sha`, `destination.snapshot_sha`,
  `base.ref`, `base.decision_sha`, every `context.*`, `branch_checked_out_at`,
  `collateral_mechanism` and `effective_backend`. `collateral_refs` stays the *known* `[]` of the
  skip rule and `collateral_exposed` stays computed from the **earlier rows' published sets by ref
  identity**, which needs no probe of this row and therefore survives having no context.
- **No other skip arm exists**, and a future one may not inherit either shape by analogy: any skip
  token added to `strategy` must name here, explicitly, which of its two refs is established and
  which is `not-applicable`, and a token that needs a probe context must say which probe needs it.
  A `not-applicable` ref is **never** ambiguous with an unestablished one: `source` distinguishes
  them, `repo-unavailable` never fires for it, `blocking` stays `false`, and no `refusal.kind`,
  `blockers[]` row or `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` member may be derived from it.
- **Push and restore work is projected on its own axes, never through these refs.** A skipped entry
  whose branch the route still pushes gets an ordinary `push.targets[]` row carrying its **own**
  `context_id` from the push ladder (§4.4, round-35 item 5), and checkout's `restore` describes
  `opts.RepoDir` through its own `target_*` members; neither reads, nor is derived from, a
  `not-applicable` entry ref. A document whose only remaining work is a push or a restore therefore
  still publishes the `repositories[]` rows those cite, under the emission rule of §4.4.

**Context-pair rule: both contexts are measured, a shared store is proved rather than assumed, and a divergent pair refuses** (round-35 item 2). For **each** of the two refs independently the plan resolves the two raw members of the §4.4 identity — the canonical absolute top level (`git -C <dir> rev-parse --path-format=absolute --show-toplevel`, canonicalized) and the canonical absolute common dir (`git -C <dir> rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, or the plain `--git-common-dir` resolved **against that root** before canonicalization, exactly as §8.6.9 requires; no comparison anywhere in this document is made on an unresolved `.git` string). Neither read is optional and neither may be inferred from the other ref's answer, from the two `source` labels, or from the shipped code's expectations about where a worktree lives:

- **Two different questions, both answered by measurement.** The two refs are *one context* iff their `context_id`s compare byte-equal; they are *one store* iff their measured canonical absolute common dirs compare byte-equal. A linked worktree of `entry.Repo` is a **different context with the same store**, which is the ordinary external pass-1 split, and the document must be able to say so without guessing.
- **Inventory reuse is gated on measured store equality.** `for-each-ref refs/heads/`, `worktree list --porcelain` and the per-detached-worktree `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`/`BISECT_START` hold reads are facts of the **store**, so one process may answer both refs **only** where their common dirs were read and compared equal. Where equality was not established — because the dirs differ, or because either read failed — each ref pays for its own probes and no result crosses between them; a cache keyed by anything other than the measured common dir is forbidden (§13).
- **A divergent pair is a hard blocker.** Where both contexts resolve and their common dirs **differ**, the row publishes `blocking: true` and the rank 5.15 `base-execution-store-divergent` fact of §4.9. The defect is specific rather than hygienic: `base.decision_sha` is read in one store and compared to `LastBaseSHA`, so the **arm** — plain versus `--onto` — is chosen from that store's refs, while `git rebase` peels `base.ref` and the recorded cutoff in the **other** store, so the destination, the replay range and the collateral upper bound are the other store's; the two answers are not comparable, and the executor then records the *decision* SHA as this entry's new cutoff (§2.3), pinning a boundary taken from a store the replay never touched. Guarded execution refuses before any rebase. **No executor changes**: the unguarded run does exactly what it does today, and the document's job is to say so first.
- **The plan shows both contexts and never collapses them.** Such a row publishes both closed `{context_id, repo_root, source}` objects and cites **two** `repositories[]` rows, and the blocker's `detail` names both roots, both canonical common dirs, and which fact each context contributed — the decision SHA on one side, the destination/range/collateral set on the other.
- **The near case is disclosed, and it is not a refusal.** Two contexts sharing one measured store — the ordinary pass-1 split — publishes the `base-execution-context-split` warning of §4.4 instead, whose detail carries the same pair and states that the store is shared (so the inventories are shared) while the *directory* facts are still two answers: the work tree's status, that worktree's own operation markers, the untracked enumeration, and the configuration once `extensions.worktreeConfig` is in play (§4.3, §13).
- **Checkout is exempt by construction**, having one context; a checkout row can be neither split nor divergent, and no fixture may assert either there. **A row with a `not-applicable` ref is exempt for the other reason** (round-36 item 4): there is no second directory to measure, so it can be neither split nor divergent, it raises no `base-execution-context-split` warning and no rank 5.15 blocker, and it forces neither read.

**Probe-failure rule (which failures fail closed, and which publish `null`).** A probe that cannot
answer is not automatically a blocker; only a **replay-critical** one is. The set is closed:

| Probe | Replay-critical? | Failure rendering |
|---|---|---|
| resolving/canonicalizing **either** context ref's raw root — `base_context`'s or `execution_context`'s — **and resolving that context's absolute common dir** — the two raw members of the context identity of §4.4, evaluated once per distinct context (round-34 item 1) | **yes** | `repo-unavailable`, `blocking: true`, that ref's `context_id` **and** `repo_root` both `null` while the other ref keeps whatever it resolved, **no `repositories[]` row and no `config_issues[]` row for that would-be context** — its configuration was never safely probed, so an issue over it would be a parse the plan never performed (round-33 item 2) — and **only the Git-probe-dependent facts `null`** — see the nullability rule below |
| `rev-parse --verify refs/heads/<git_branch>^{commit}` (head), in `execution_context` (round-35 item 3) | **yes** | owned by the more specific `head.state = unresolvable` / `head-ref-missing` |
| `rev-parse <base.ref>` — **twice on a split row** (round-35 item 3): the `base_context` read the executor itself issues as `GetBranchSHA` (`base.decision_sha`) and the `execution_context` read the rebase performs (`destination.sha`/`destination.snapshot_sha`); on a row whose two contexts coincide it is one process | **yes** | owned by `base-ref-missing` |
| `rev-parse --verify <cutoff>^{commit}`, in `execution_context` (round-35 item 3) | **yes** | owned by `cutoff-unresolvable` |
| the candidate `rev-list` count/identity probes, and the `<git_branch>..<upstream>` probe, all in `execution_context` (round-35 item 3), on a row whose upstream **and** tip both resolved | **yes** | `probe-failed`, `blocking: true`, `determinacy = unknown`, `reason = probe-failed`, every candidate field `null` |
| `status --porcelain --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all` in `execution_context` (`context.dirty`) | **yes** | `probe-failed` (the dirty precondition of §5.4.7 cannot be evaluated) |
| `worktree list --porcelain` in `execution_context`, **and the `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply` `head-name` and `BISECT_START` reads that complete it**, for a row whose `mutation.will_switch_head` is `true` | **yes** | `probe-failed` (the switch precondition cannot be evaluated) |
| `rev-parse --show-toplevel` for the row's own `execution_context`, on a row whose `mutation.will_switch_head` is `true` | **yes** | `probe-failed`, `blocking: true`, `branch_checked_out_at` published as observed and the **self-vs-foreign question left unanswered** — without the left-hand side of the comparison the plan cannot say whether the holder is self, and guessing either way is wrong in one direction: guessing *self* authorises a run that dies at Git's `branch … is already used by worktree at …` refusal, guessing *foreign* refuses the ordinary case Git performs happily. This is the one probe whose failure is replay-critical **only** on a switching row; on a non-switching row it is never issued (§4.9 rank 5.9, §5.4.7, §15.8c f5) |
| `worktree list --porcelain` for the collateral exemption only (`will_switch_head: false`) | no | `collateral_refs: null`, `collateral_exposed: null` (§4.8), row not blocking |
| `for-each-ref refs/heads/` (branch inventory), in `execution_context` (round-35 item 3) — it is intersected with the candidate range, which is resolved there, and it is a **store** fact reusable across the two refs only where their common dirs were measured equal (§4.1 context-pair rule) | no | same |
| `ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z` at the canonical work-tree top level containing the row's own execution directory, plus the `rev-parse --show-toplevel` that anchors it (`context.untracked_present`) | no | `context.untracked_present: null`, `context.overwrite_risk: null` (§4.8), row **not** blocking. It is an enrichment probe because nothing depends on its answer: round 18 withdrew the blocker that did, so a failure here — of the enumeration or of the anchor — can only cost a warning (§4.1, §5.4.7, §19.26) |
| the `rebase.*` config reads — the ordered `config --list --show-scope -z` of §4.2/§13 and the typed reads beside it, in `execution_context` | no | `repositories[].config.*` publishes `status: probe-failed` with `value: null` and `source: null` (§4.4, round-31 item 4), `collateral_mechanism: null`, `effective_backend` per §4.1; **never blocking** — the `config-blocking` kind is withdrawn as memberless (§4.9, round-19 item 7), so a failed config read costs facts and warnings, not a refusal — and **no `config_issues[]` row**, since a read that failed parsed nothing (round-33 items 2 and 7) |
| `IsPrunableWorktree`'s cwd probe | no | it is **fail-open in the executor** — `IsPrunableWorktree` returns `false` on any error (`internal/exec.go:199-204`) — so the plan mirrors that answer rather than inventing a failure (§3.7, §5.4.3) |
| `StackEdge` ancestry evaluation, `notes`, commit subjects, and every other enrichment | no | `ancestry: null` / `notes: []` / a `null` subject; never blocking, because none of them describes what will be replayed |

The direction is deliberate: a plan that cannot state a row's replay **refuses**, and a plan that
merely cannot decorate it **publishes `null` and runs**.

**Repo-unavailable nullability: an unusable directory nulls the *probes*, not the *row*.** The
previous draft said a `repo-unavailable` row publishes "every other fact `null`", and that is both
false and harmful: most of a row is derived from `stack.yaml`, the selection and the route, none of
which needs a working directory. The rule is therefore split by **provenance**, not by row:

- **Preserved verbatim, because they are stack-/route-derived and were never probed**: `name`,
  `git_branch`, `repo`, `base_context.source` and `execution_context.source` (the *rule* that chose each context is known even when
  the directory is not), `role`, `materialization`, `base.name`, `base.kind`,
  `cutoff.recorded_sha` (the raw recorded value) and `cutoff.provenance`, `cutoff.usage`,
  `cutoff.write`, `destination.deferred` / `destination.depends_on` (execution-order facts),
  `strategy` and `argv` where the arm fixes them without a probe, `mutation.will_switch_head` /
  `will_leave_head_on` / `head_restored_by_run` (frozen argv facts), `prunability.probe_context`,
  `blocking: true`, the row's `repo-unavailable` kind, and its `blockers[]` entry.
- **`null`, because they are Git-probe-dependent and no probe could run**: the failed ref's
  `context_id` **and** `repo_root` (together, round-33 items 1 and 2, per ref since round-34 item 1),
  `head.sha`, `base.ref`, `base.decision_sha`, `destination.sha`, `destination.snapshot_sha`,
  `cutoff.resolved_sha`,
  `replay.upstream_ref` / `upstream_sha` / `range` / `candidate_count` / `first_candidate` /
  `commits` / `commits_listed` / `commits_truncated` / `candidate_digest` /
  `may_drop_patch_equivalent`, `collateral_refs`, `collateral_exposed`, `collateral_mechanism`,
  `effective_backend`, `context.dirty`, `context.autostash`,
  `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`, `context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`,
  `context.untracked_present`,
  `context.overwrite_risk`, `branch_checked_out_at`, `ancestry`.
- **Two totality axes take their unknown value rather than a fabricated one.** `head.state` is
  **`null`** on this row — the one cell where it is not `present`/`missing`/`unresolvable` — because
  claiming `missing` would assert that `refs/heads/<git_branch>` does not exist when the truth is
  that nothing could look, and it would send the operator to fix a branch when the problem is a
  directory. Consequently **no `head-ref-missing` blocker is emitted** for a `repo-unavailable` row
  at all (it is not that rank 5.2 loses to rank 5.1 — the fact was never established). Likewise
  `cutoff.state` is `absent` when `stack.yaml` recorded nothing (a stack fact) and **`null`** when a
  SHA *is* recorded but could not be verified; `replay.determinacy` is `unknown` with
  `replay.reason = repo-unavailable`, and `replay.upstream_provenance` is `unknown`.
- **The row stays sortable, citable and bindable.** Because `name` survives, the row keeps its place
  in the canonical name sort (§4.7) and its position in the fingerprint's per-entry list; because
  the preserved facts survive, two `repo-unavailable` rows in one document are distinguishable, and
  a token minted over a broken input is stable across processes and **differs** from the token of
  the same stack whose context resolved (§5.3.2, §15.9b(g)). Only the context identity being `null`
  has a
  structural consequence, and it is **total and per ref, never per row** (round-35 item 4): the ref
  whose `context_id` is `null` cites **no** `repositories[]` row — there is no `context_id` to cite
  one by, and the `repo` token is not a join key (round-33 items 1 and 7) —, and **no
  `config_issues[]` row may name that would-be context**, because its configuration was never safely
  probed (round-33 item 2). **The other ref is untouched.** A partial failure — one context
  established, the other not, which is the ordinary shape of a `repo-unavailable` row on an external
  pass-1 split — publishes the surviving ref's `context_id`/`repo_root` and **cites its
  `repositories[]` row exactly as any other row does**, so that row appears in `repositories[]` with
  whatever it was entitled to (its four `rebase.*` slots probed where it is somebody's
  `execution_context`, `not-evaluated` where it is only ever a base context, §4.3), and may carry
  `config_issues[]` rows of its own. Round 34's blanket readings — that such a row cites no
  repository row at all, and that a document whose only would-be contexts are `repo-unavailable`
  rows publishes `repositories: []` — are **withdrawn for the partial case**: `repositories: []` is
  the correct value only where **every** context ref of **every** row failed, and any surviving ref
  anywhere in the document puts its row there (§4.4). The blocker's rank and kind do not change with
  the direction of the failure — one `repo-unavailable` covers both — but its **`detail` names which
  ref failed**, `base_context` or `execution_context`, and which of the two survived (§4.9 rank 5.1),
  and no test, doc or skill may assert an all-`null` row or an empty `repositories[]` for a document
  in which one context resolved.

This is the general form of the §4.8 doctrine — unknown is `null`, known is published — applied to
the one blocker that was previously allowed to erase known facts.

`destination.depends_on` carries a second load: it is the **only** representation of the parent
relation in the document. Row position is not, and must not be read as, execution order (§4.7).

### 4.2 What is knowable, and what must never be claimed

**"Candidate" is defined here and used nowhere else in any other sense.** A candidate is a member of
the **topological source range** `<replay.upstream_sha>..<git_branch>`, merges excluded. It is an
**upper bound on what Git will apply**, evaluated *before* Git's own two filters:

1. **Clean cherry-picks are dropped as a preliminary step — relative to `<upstream>`, not to the
   `--onto` target.** "commits which are clean cherry-picks (as determined by
   `git log --cherry-mark ...`) are detected and dropped as a preliminary step (unless
   `--reapply-cherry-picks` or `--keep-base` is passed)" — `git rebase` manual, `--empty`. Neither
   executor passes those options, so nothing in the argv disables the filter — but the filter has
   **nothing to compare against** when the upstream side of the symmetric difference is empty, which
   is exactly the ordinary `--onto <newbase> <cutoff>` arm whose recorded cutoff is an ancestor of
   the head. The equivalent commit `B'` lives on the **new base**, and the new base is not the
   upstream. See §6.1: the drop the customer saw there is filter 2, not this one.
2. **Commits that become empty after replay are dropped.** `--empty=drop` "is the default
   behavior" — `git rebase` manual. Neither executor overrides it.

Merges are excluded because "by default, a rebase will simply drop merge commits from the todo
list" (`git rebase` manual, `--rebase-merges`), which is why the probe uses `--no-merges`.
**That default is configurable, and the plan must probe it**: `rebase.rebaseMerges` "whether and how
to set the `--rebase-merges` option by default" (`git config` manual, verified present in Git
2.55.0). **"Effectively true" is a *parse*, not a boolean read; round 26 made it total and round 27
makes it exact** (item 1), because the key's value space is wider than `true`/`false` and Git's own
reader — `rebase_config` → `git_parse_maybe_bool`, then `parse_rebase_merges_value`
(`builtin/rebase.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0) — decides three cells that round 26 left as one
"unknown":

- **True — merges are recreated.** Any of Git's boolean-true spellings, which
  `git_parse_maybe_bool_text` accepts **case-insensitively** (`true`, `yes`, `on` and every case
  variant) or, through `git_parse_maybe_bool`'s integer fallback, as **any non-zero integer**
  (`1`, `2`, `-1`; `parse.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0); a **valueless** key (`[rebase]` /
  `rebaseMerges` with no `=`), which Git reads as **true** because `git_parse_maybe_bool_text`
  returns `1` for a `NULL` value — **round 26's "unknown" reading of this spelling is withdrawn**;
  **and** the two mode words **`rebase-cousins`** and **`no-rebase-cousins`**, which
  `parse_rebase_merges_value` compares with `strcmp` and therefore matches **exactly and
  case-sensitively**: both set `rebase_merges = 1` and differ only in cousin handling, so both are
  merge recreation and neither may be read as a non-boolean "off". A row in this cell publishes
  `candidate_count: null`, `replay.determinacy = unknown` and `replay.reason = merge-recreation`.
- **False — merges are dropped.** Any boolean-false spelling (`false`, `no`, `off`, case-insensitive
  again), the integer `0`, the **explicitly empty** value (`rebaseMerges =`), which
  `git_parse_maybe_bool_text` reads as **false** for an empty string — **round 26's "unknown"
  reading of this spelling is withdrawn too** — and the key being **absent** from the whole config
  chain. This is the ordinary cell and the `--no-merges` count is an upper bound as before.
- **Invalid — Git refuses to run at all, so the plan refuses too.** Any other value — a typo, a
  mode word that does not exist, a **case-wrong** `Rebase-Cousins`, a stray quote — is neither a
  boolean nor one of the two `strcmp`-exact words, so `parse_rebase_merges_value`
  **dies**: `Unknown rebase-merges mode: <value>` (`builtin/rebase.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0).
  The die happens while the config is being parsed, *before* the rebase does anything, and it is
  fatal for the whole `git rebase` invocation. That is a **hard configuration failure, not an
  indeterminacy**, and round 27 corrects round 26 here rather than reinterpreting it: the row is not
  "uncountable", the run is *impossible*. The document publishes the document-level, non-waivable
  **rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config`** blocker whose sanitized detail names the key, its sanitized
  value and its context root, publishes the machine-readable evidence in `config_issues[]` (§4.4),
  and `runnable: false` (§4.9 rank 5.07, and the total invalid-value rule below). It is **not** the
  rank 10 `indeterminate-entry` verdict, which describes a *runnable* plan whose limit cannot be
  compared, and the enum member `merge-recreation-unknown` that round 26 added for this cell is
  **withdrawn with it** (§4.1 `replay.reason`).
- **Never false-safe.** No cell may fall back to "assume merges are dropped": that assumption is
  exactly the one that publishes a `--no-merges` number for a run that recreates merges, which is
  the lie this whole subsection exists to prevent. Where the value is true the document publishes
  the unknown count and lets the limit machinery refuse it; where the value is invalid it refuses
  the document.

**The probes are the ordered list read plus a typed one, and both are read** (round-26 item 7,
corrected by round-27 items 1 and 3, **its raw half replaced by round-32 item 4**): the ordered
`git -C <root> config --list --show-scope -z` this context already issues (§13) supplies **every**
occurrence in Git's own parse order, each labelled with the scope it came from, and — because
`--list -z` emits a **valueless** occurrence as the key alone while an **explicitly empty** one
carries the `\n` separator and an empty value — it is the only read that tells those two apart; the
key's absence from that read is the absent cell. `git -C <root> config --type=bool --get
rebase.rebaseMerges` resolves the **last** occurrence — the
one `--get` would print and the one whose effective value the run acts on — through Git's own
boolean parser, printing `true` for a valueless key and `false` for an explicitly empty one, which
is exactly the ambiguity the raw read cannot resolve, and **failing** for a value that is not a
boolean at all. The classification is therefore total: if the typed read succeeds, its answer is the
interpretation; if it fails, the raw last value is matched **case-sensitively** against the two mode
words, and anything else is the invalid cell above. **The ordered `--list --show-scope -z` read
rather than `--get-all` or `--get`, because validity is a property of every occurrence and not of
the last one — and because neither per-key form names the scope an occurrence came from or
separates a valueless occurrence from an empty one** (round-32 item 4): `git_config` hands the
callback each value in order, so an earlier invalid occurrence dies even when a later valid one
would have overwritten it — a repository whose global config says `rebaseMerges = maybe` and whose
local config says `false` still cannot rebase. It is a read this context issues anyway, so the
occurrence scan costs no process of its own (§13). A probe that could not run *at all* is a **failed read**, not a parse, and
keeps its existing meaning (below). The typed read for **this key** costs **one** extra process per repository context, and only where
the key is set at all; the same shape and the same conditionality apply to the two other typed
boolean reads §4.3 requires — `rebase.updateRefs` and `rebase.autoStash` — so the per-context
budget is the ordered list read plus **at most three** typed reads and nothing per key beyond them
(§13, round-33 item 7). Each `repositories[]` row publishes the outcome as
**`config.rebase_merges.interpretation`** — the closed enum `true` / `false` / `unknown` /
**`invalid`**, **never `null`**, whose fourth member round 32 adds (item 3) so the member stays
total on a slot whose `status` is `invalid`: round 27 left **`unknown` with exactly one meaning, the
read failed**, and that meaning is unchanged, so a value Git's own parser rejects — which is not an
interpretation and is a blocker — publishes `interpretation: invalid` in lockstep with
`config.rebase_merges.status: invalid` rather than borrowing `unknown` or breaking the never-`null`
rule. The four members are therefore exhaustive over the slot's five statuses: `valid` publishes
`true`/`false`, `absent` publishes `false` (the key's unset reading), `not-evaluated` and
`probe-failed` publish `unknown`, and `invalid` publishes `invalid`. It sits beside the raw
`config.rebase_merges.value`, and that
interpretation is a **fingerprint member**, because it is not recoverable from the raw value
(§5.3.2, §5.3.2a).

When it is effectively true, merges are *recreated* rather than dropped, so a
`--no-merges` count is **not even an upper bound**, and a conditioned footnote is not enough. The
binding rule: such a row publishes `candidate_count: null`, `replay.determinacy = unknown`,
`replay.reason = merge-recreation`, and the JIT seam cannot rescue it (the config is still true one
entry later). Its `guard.evaluation[]` verdict is `unknown` with
`unknown_kind: not-resolvable` — nothing later resolves a value the config already spelled — and a
guarded run refuses it as the **non-waivable** rank 10 `indeterminate-entry`
(§4.4, §8.3.2a, §4.9 rank 10, §5.3.1). A limit-free `--plan` publishes
the unknown and stays `runnable: true`. **The round-26 second unknown cell is gone rather than
narrowed** (round-27 item 1): the two empty spellings are now decided (true and false respectively)
and an unrecognised value is a rank 5.07 blocker, so `merge-recreation` is once again the *only*
`replay.reason` this key produces. **That reason *outranks* every upstream and cutoff reason, and round 25 states it as a
precedence rather than leaving two true facts to race** (item 3, §4.1 `replay.reason`): a row with a
recorded, resolvable cutoff would otherwise be `exact`, and a row whose destination is deferred
would otherwise be `upstream-deferred` — but neither publishes a count under `rebaseMerges`, so
`merge-recreation` is the reason in both, and the deferred cell is `not-resolvable` at the JIT seam
rather than `deferred-resolvable`. The dominance is conditioned on the *reading*: where the
`rebase.rebaseMerges` probe itself failed, the row is `probe-failed` (or the more specific
`repo-unavailable`) and this rule does not apply, because an unread config is not a true one. A **supplied** limit therefore cannot be evaluated against that row at all, and a
guarded run refuses it with `refusal.kind = indeterminate-entry`; an unguarded or limit-free
`--plan` simply reports the unknown. Silently publishing a `--no-merges` number in this
configuration would be the one lie the count contract exists to prevent.

**A value Git's own parser rejects is a hard failure, and round 27 states the rule once, totally,
for every such key the plan reads** (item 3). **Round 28 keeps the rule and fixes two things about
it: its *scope* — which was unconditional, and refused runs that never touch the key — and its
*domain*, which named four keys where the argv this document publishes parses fatally on the
thirteen of Part 1 — twelve config keys plus the `.gitmodules` context-level key**
(item 2). **Round 29 keeps both corrections and fixes two *scope* facts round 28 got wrong**
(items 1 and 2): `submodule.recurse` was filed as a fetch-only key when Git parses it fatally in
`git checkout` and `git push` as well, and the two sequencer keys were scoped as though the merge
backend were an exception when, since Git 2.26, it is the **default**. The rule is stated in three
parts: the key table, the **route scope** that decides whether a key's invalidity blocks *this* run,
and the binding properties.

**Part 1 — the keys, their parsers and their deaths**, each reproducible without running the
command, all verified against Git 2.55.0. The scope column names **which commands of the described
route read the key**, and it is not one command per key: the **fetch-scope** keys are read by
`git fetch`, the **rebase-scope** keys by `git rebase`, and `submodule.recurse` is read by
`git fetch`, `git checkout` **and** `git push`:

| Scope | Key | Git's parser | What an unrecognised value does | Occurrence rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fetch | `fetch.recurseSubmodules` | `git_fetch_config` → `parse_fetch_recurse_submodules_arg` → `parse_fetch_recurse` (`builtin/fetch.c`, `submodule-config.c`) | boolean spellings **case-insensitively**, else the **exact, case-sensitive** word `on-demand` (`strcmp`), else `die("bad fetch.recursesubmodules argument: <value>")` — so `On-Demand` and `ondemand` are fatal, not defaults | **any occurrence** (`repo_config` callback) |
| fetch, **checkout**, **push** | `submodule.recurse` | three independent readers, each ending in `git_config_bool` (`config.c`): `git_fetch_config` (`builtin/fetch.c`); `git_checkout_config` → `starts_with(var, "submodule.")` → `git_default_submodule_config` (`builtin/checkout.c:1277-1296`, `submodule.c:203-212`); `git_push_config` (`builtin/push.c:519-524`) | booleans **only**: `on-demand` is *not* a legal value of this key, and any non-boolean dies at `bad boolean config value '<value>' for 'submodule.recurse'` — **in all three commands**, while the config is read and before any transfer, checkout or ref update (verified against Git 2.55.0 by running each command in a repository carrying `submodule.recurse = bogus`). `git rebase` does **not** read the key and does not die on it, which is why the key is not rebase-scope | **any occurrence** |
| fetch | `.gitmodules`'s context-level `fetch.recurseSubmodules` | `fetch_config_from_gitmodules` → `gitmodules_fetch_config` → the same `parse_fetch_recurse` (`submodule-config.c`) | the same death — **but only where it is parsed at all**, i.e. where the config chain and `--recurse-submodules` left the mode `RECURSE_SUBMODULES_DEFAULT` (§0.1, §4.4, round-28 item 1) | **any occurrence, in that state only** |
| rebase | `rebase.stat` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_bool` (`builtin/rebase.c`) | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value '<value>' for 'rebase.stat'` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.autoSquash` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_bool` | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value … for 'rebase.autosquash'` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.autoStash` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_bool` | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value … for 'rebase.autostash'` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.updateRefs` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_bool` | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value … for 'rebase.updaterefs'` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.rescheduleFailedExec` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_bool` | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value … for 'rebase.reschedulefailedexec'` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.forkPoint` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_bool` | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value … for 'rebase.forkpoint'` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.rebaseMerges` | `rebase_config` → `git_parse_maybe_bool`, then `parse_rebase_merges_value` (`builtin/rebase.c`) | booleans, then the two `strcmp`-exact mode words, else `die("Unknown rebase-merges mode: <value>")` | **any occurrence** |
| rebase | `rebase.backend` | `rebase_config` → `git_config_string`, and later the `merge`/`apply` test in `cmd_rebase` | **two different deaths**: a **valueless** occurrence is `config_error_nonbool` — `error: missing value for 'rebase.backend'` and then `fatal: bad config …` — on **any occurrence**; and an **effective** value that is neither `merge` nor `apply` dies at `die("Unknown rebase backend: <value>")`, but **only where no argv option already forced a backend** | valueless: **any occurrence**; unknown name: **last occurrence**, argv-conditioned |
| rebase | `rebase.abbreviateCommands` | `repo_config_get_bool` inside `run_sequencer_rebase` (`builtin/rebase.c`) | booleans only; else `bad boolean config value … for 'rebase.abbreviatecommands'` | **last occurrence only** — a config-set lookup, not the ordered callback — and **only on the merge backend**, which is every arm whose `effective_backend` is `merge`, including the **unset-`rebase.backend` default** (Part 2) |
| rebase | `rebase.maxLabelLength` | `repo_config_get_int` in `sequencer.c`'s todo writer | integers only; else `bad numeric config value '<value>' for 'rebase.maxlabellength'` | **last occurrence only**, and **only where the merge backend runs *and* rebase-merges is in effect**, because only the label-emitting todo writer reads it (Part 2) |

**Part 2 — the route scope, which is round 28's correction (item 2) as round 29 repairs it**
(items 1 and 2). Round 27's rule refused a document whenever *any* probed context carried *any*
invalid value of its four keys. That over-refuses in exactly the direction this feature is not for:
it stops a run that never reads the key. Round 28 fixed that but assigned each key a **single**
command, and two of those assignments were wrong. **A key's invalidity is a blocker only where the
route this document describes will really hand that key to Git — and "where" is a set of commands,
not one command**:

- **Fetch-scope keys block only where the described route will attempt a fetch.** A `--no-fetch`
  invocation, a `--plan --continue` (no shipped continuation executor fetches, §0.1, §8.6.4), a
  checkout run under its `no-fetch` default, and any invocation whose fetch is already suppressed
  by causes 1-6 of §8.6.1 are **unaffected**: the value is not parsed, no `config_issues[]` row and
  no blocker are emitted, and — round-30 item 3 — it is **not disclosed** either, these keys having
  no slot in `repositories[].config`. A document that *will* fetch emits the blocker for
  every context it would have fetched in. `fetch.recurseSubmodules` and the `.gitmodules`
  context-level `fetch.recurseSubmodules` are the **only** two members of this fetch-only family;
  `submodule.recurse` left it in round 29 and has its own bullet below.
- **The `.gitmodules` context-level key blocks only where its value would be parsed** — a fetch
  will be attempted **and** the config chain and command line left the mode DEFAULT. Where a valid
  context mode already resolves, Git reads the file with a null member pointer and never parses the
  value, so the plan must not refuse on it either (§0.1, §4.4, round-28 item 1).
- **`submodule.recurse` blocks wherever the described route will run `git fetch`, `git checkout` or
  `git push`** (round-29 item 1). Round 28 filed it with `fetch.recurseSubmodules` and
  thereby published a document as startable for routes that die on it immediately. All three
  commands read the key through `git_config_bool` and die on a non-boolean before doing any work
  (Part 1), so the scope is the **union** of three route facts, and each of them is one this
  document already computes: the fetch of the bullet above; **every `git checkout` the route will
  run** — the standalone `gitCheckout(opts.RepoDir, entry.Branch)` before each checkout-mode row's
  rebase (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1040-1047`) and the `restoreOriginal` checkout of
  `StageRestoring` (`:1202-1219`), both of which run under checkout's `no-fetch` default and on a
  continuation that fetches nothing; and **every `git push` the route will run** — external's
  optional push (`internal/cli/sync.go:118-124`, `:216-229`) and checkout's finalization push
  (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1214-1234`), as projected by `push.targets[]`/`push.executable`
  (§4.4). The practical consequences are the ones the fetch-only filing denied: a **checkout
  `--no-fetch` run**, a **checkout continuation**, a **push-stage continuation** and a
  **`restoring` resume** all carry the blocker when this key is invalid, even though they attempt
  no fetch and, in the last two cases, run no `git rebase` either. Where none of the three commands
  will run — an external `--no-fetch` run whose push is not reached, for one — the value is neither
  parsed, published nor blocked, exactly like any other
  out-of-scope key (round-30 item 3). **`git rebase` is not in the set**: `rebase_config` never reads `submodule.recurse` and a
  rebase over an invalid value completes normally (verified against Git 2.55.0), so a rebase-only
  external row does not make it a blocker.
- **Rebase-scope keys block only where at least one rebase operation will run in that context.** A
  plan whose every row is a `skipped-*` non-executing row, a push-stage continuation, a `restoring`
  resume and a rows-less document all run no `git rebase`, so an invalid `rebase.*` value in the
  probed context is neither parsed nor published and blocks nothing — and **round 31 makes the slot
  say so instead of publishing a value the route never evaluated** (item 4): where the key is one of
  the four `repositories[].config` carries, that member publishes `status: not-evaluated` with
  `value: null` and `source: null`, which is a fact about this route and **not** a claim that the key
  is unset; round 30's "its *valid* effective value is published exactly as before" is withdrawn as
  the same over-claim on the disclosure side that "out-of-scope values are published" was on the
  evidence side. Where at least one row of that repository context
  really executes `git rebase` the key **is** parsed, its slot publishes `valid`/`absent`/
  `probe-failed`/`invalid` accordingly, and the blocker — where the value is invalid — is emitted
  once for the context, not once per row. **Round 34 adds the context axis to the same rule**
  (item 2): "that repository context" means the context a row uses as its **`execution_context`**,
  since that is where `git rebase` starts and therefore the only place these keys are read. A
  context that every row uses only as its **`base_context`** — the `entry.Repo` of an external
  pass-1 row, whose rebase runs in the worktree — is out of scope for all four keys, publishes
  `not-evaluated` in all four slots, produces no `config_issues[]` row and costs no configuration
  process (§4.3, §13).
- **Scope is a property of the *described underlying route*, never of the describing invocation, and
  round 31 corrects the wording that confused the two** (item 1). Earlier drafts wrote "a plan-only
  route that executes nothing" as though `--plan` were itself an out-of-scope cell. It is not:
  `plan-only` is the **projection wrapper** (§0.2, §4.4 `invocation`), not a route, and every
  document projects an underlying run — legacy or new-mode, fetching or not, rebasing or not — whose
  commands decide the scope. The rule, stated once and read the same way in every bullet above:
  **a key is in scope for this document exactly when the run the document describes would hand that
  key to Git**, i.e. when the described route would really execute the `git fetch`, `git checkout`,
  `git push` or `git rebase` that reads it. So a `--plan` over a fetching external run is
  fetch-scope, a `--plan` over a checkout run is checkout- and push-scope, a `--plan` over an
  executing external row is rebase-scope, and the *only* cell in which every key of Part 1 is out of
  scope is one whose **described route would execute none of the four commands** — never merely
  "because `--plan` mutates nothing". The corollary binds in both directions: `--plan` never
  narrows the scope below its guarded twin's, so a plan document and the guarded run it authorises
  parse exactly the same keys and publish exactly the same `config_issues[]` rows (§4.4, §8.7.2).
  (These same routes are **not** exempt from `submodule.recurse`, whose scope is the checkout and
  push they do run.)
- **The two sequencer cells and `rebase.backend`'s unknown-name death are scoped further, by the
  row's `effective_backend` and its own argv** (§2.1, §2.2, §4.1). The backend is derived, not
  assumed, and the derivation is the one §4.1 publishes: **`effective_backend` is `merge` when the
  argv carries a merge-forcing option *or* when `rebase.backend` is absent or `merge`, and `apply`
  only when the effective `rebase.backend` is exactly `apply` and no merge-forcing option is
  present.** Since
  Git 2.26 the merge backend is the **built-in default** — "'git rebase' has learned to use the
  merge backend … by default, while allowing '--apply' option to use the 'apply' backend" (Git 2.26
  release notes), which the `git config` manual does **not** restate ("Default backend to use for
  rebasing. Possible choices are `apply` or `merge`", Git 2.55.0), so this document proves it by
  running the command rather than by quoting a default the manual omits (Part 2's verified cells) —
  so an unset key is a *merge* arm, not an
  exempt one, and `rebase.backend = merge` is the same arm spelled out. On that footing:
  - `rebase.backend`'s *unknown-name* death is reachable only where the argv forces no backend —
    the **scoped** external arms (`git rebase [--onto …] <base>`) and **both** checkout arms
    (`git rebase --no-fork-point …`) — and is unreachable on the `scope=all` external arms, whose
    `--update-refs` calls `imply_merge` and fixes the backend before the test runs (verified:
    `git -c rebase.backend=bogus rebase --update-refs <base>` rebases normally, while the same
    config without `--update-refs` dies at `fatal: Unknown rebase backend: bogus`). Its *valueless*
    death is unconditional on every arm. The name test is **case-sensitive**: `APPLY` dies like any
    other unknown name.
  - **`rebase.abbreviateCommands` is read on *every* merge-backend arm**, which is every arm of
    both modes whose `effective_backend` is `merge` — the `--update-refs` external arms, and the
    scoped external arms and both checkout arms whenever `rebase.backend` is unset or `merge`.
    **Round 28's "the `--update-refs` arms, or an arm whose effective
    `rebase.backend`/`rebaseMerges`/`autoSquash` selects merge" is withdrawn on both halves**: it
    omitted the unset default, which is the overwhelming majority of repositories, and it credited
    *configured* `rebase.rebaseMerges`/`rebase.autoSquash` with selecting the backend, which they
    do not — only the command-line `--rebase-merges`/`--autosquash`/`--update-refs`/`-i` family
    calls `imply_merge`, and a configured `rebase.backend = apply` beats both config keys
    (verified: `-c rebase.backend=apply -c rebase.rebaseMerges=true -c
    rebase.abbreviateCommands=bogus rebase <base>` runs the apply backend and never reads the key,
    while the same argv without the backend config dies at
    `fatal: bad boolean config value 'bogus' for 'rebase.abbreviatecommands'`).
  - **`rebase.maxLabelLength` is read only where a merge-backend arm *emits labels***, i.e. where
    rebase-merges is in effect — from the argv (which neither executor passes) or from an effective
    `rebase.rebaseMerges` on a merge arm. A merge-backend rebase without rebase-merges never reads
    it, `--update-refs` alone does not make it reachable, and an apply arm cannot reach it at all
    (verified in all four combinations against Git 2.55.0).
  Each blocker is emitted **only** where the arm that will run really reaches it, and its detail
  names the arm, the derived `effective_backend` and the argv or config that made it reachable.
- **Scope narrows the parsing *and* the evidence, and round 30 withdraws the "never the disclosure"
  guarantee as impossible** (item 3). The previous bullet promised that a key whose invalidity is out
  of scope for this route "is still published in `repositories[].config.*.value` with the same
  sanitization". That promise cannot be kept and must not be restated: `repositories[].config` is a
  **four-member** object — `update_refs`, `rebase_merges`, `backend`, `auto_stash` (§4.4) — so nine
  of Part 1's thirteen keys have no value slot in it, **in scope or out**, and this feature does not
  add a general per-key slot. The rule that replaces it: **only the invalid values of keys the
  described route will really hand to Git are parsed, and every one of those is published as
  structured evidence in the top-level `config_issues[]` array** (§4.4, round-30 item 2 as round-31
  items 2 and 3 reshape it) — **one row per published issue, identified by its `issue_id`** and
  one-to-one with the rank 5.07 blocker it causes. An
  **out-of-scope** invalid value blocks nothing **and is not disclosed** — neither raw nor
  effective — and no consumer may read its absence from `config_issues[]` as a claim that the value
  is valid; the array states what the route parses, never what the repository contains. **Round 31
  makes the disclosure rule *total* rather than merely negative** (item 4), **and round 32 makes the
  trio's `source` member total with it** (item 3): "not disclosed" is not
  an absent key, because an absent key is unreadable evidence. **Three** of the four members of
  `repositories[].config` — `update_refs`, `backend` and `auto_stash` — are **closed per-field objects
  `{status, value, source}`**, and **`rebase_merges` is the one declared exception: it extends that
  shape with a fourth member, `interpretation`, and is closed at `{status, value, source,
  interpretation}`** (round-33 item 5, making the arity difference a stated exception rather than a
  claim that all four slots have the same members). Every slot's `status`
  is the closed enum **`valid` / `absent` / `not-evaluated` / `probe-failed` / `invalid`**, and the
  four statuses that are not `valid` are exactly the four ways a slot can carry no effective value:
  the key was read and is unset (`absent`, `value: null`, `source: null`), the described route never
  parses that key so nothing was
  read (`not-evaluated`, `value: null`, `source: null` — the **out-of-scope** cell), the read itself
  failed (`probe-failed`, `value: null`, `source: null`), and a **route-applicable** read found a
  **fatal effective occurrence** (`invalid`, `value: null`, `source` **the scope of that
  occurrence** and therefore **never `null`**, with the evidence in `config_issues[]` and
  the rank 5.07 blocker beside it). So `source` is `null` in exactly the three statuses `absent`,
  `not-evaluated` and `probe-failed`; it is `probed` where `status` is `valid`; and it is the
  offending occurrence's scope member — the same value that row's `config_issues[].source` carries —
  where `status` is `invalid`. Round 31's `unset` member is **withdrawn** (round-32 item 3): it said
  nothing `status: absent` did not already say, and it occupied the one member that now has to carry
  a scope. **`status: invalid` holds for a `repositories[].config` member iff a `config_issues[]`
  row exists whose `context_id` equals that repository row's
  `context_id` and whose `key` maps to that slot** (round-32 items 1 and 3), and the mapping is
  **explicit and closed**, from Git's own lower-cased key name to the slot name:
  `rebase.updaterefs` → `update_refs`, `rebase.rebasemerges` → `rebase_merges`,
  `rebase.backend` → `backend`, `rebase.autostash` → `auto_stash`; every other key of Part 1 maps to
  **no slot**, which is why an invalid `submodule.recurse` publishes a row and a blocker and changes
  no slot at all. The join is on `context_id` and **never** on the rendered `repo_root`, which §11
  makes lossy and which two distinct contexts may share. So the slot and the array can
  never disagree, and no consumer has to read "no value" as either "valid and empty" or "we did not
  look". The **nine** keys of Part 1 that have no slot at all keep having none — this feature adds
  no general per-key slot, and a partial enumeration of Git's config surface presented as total is
  the false completeness §4.8 forbids — so for those nine the *only* published fact is a
  `config_issues[]` row where the route parses them and finds them fatal, and **nothing at all**
  otherwise. A **route-irrelevant** key is therefore never parsed into `config_issues[]` and its
  raw value need never be revealed anywhere in the document. What is
  unchanged is that every **route-relevant** valid fact keeps its own real schema location: the four
  effective config values in `repositories[].config` (§4.4), the submodule recursion mode, its
  provenance and its effect in `fetch.repos[].fetch_effect.submodule_recursion` (§4.4), and the
  per-row derivations that read them (`effective_backend`, `collateral_mechanism`,
  `context.autostash`, §4.1) — **and no universal thirteen-key value table is promised anywhere**,
  in this document, in the docs or in the skills. This is a narrowing of a *promise*, not of a refusal: the blocker set
  is exactly the one round 29 left.

**Part 3 — the properties that bind, and what identifies a blocker:**

1. **Within scope, the predicate is "any occurrence", not "the effective value" — except for the
   three cells the table marks otherwise — and round 31 states *which* occurrence becomes the
   issue** (item 3). `repo_config` hands the ordered callback every
   occurrence of the key in parse order, and `git_config_bool`/`parse_fetch_recurse`/
   `parse_rebase_merges_value`/`git_config_string` die on the occurrence they are handed, so a
   later valid occurrence never rescues an earlier invalid one. The plan therefore reads those keys
   out of **one ordered `git -C <context_root> config --list --show-scope -z` per repository
   context** — the read §13 already budgets — and **never** with `--get-all`, and never with an
   **untyped** per-key `--get`
   (round-32 item 4, made exact by round-34 item 4 — the three typed `--type=bool --get`
   interpretations of `rebase.rebaseMerges`/`rebase.updateRefs`/`rebase.autoStash` answer a
   *different* question, the effective boolean parse, and are the **only** `--get` invocations this
   document issues at all): only the ordered list carries the scope each occurrence came from, which is
   what `config_issues[].source` publishes, and only its `-z` framing distinguishes a **valueless**
   occurrence (the key alone) from an **explicitly empty** one (the key, the separator and an empty
   value), which is the distinction `raw_value_present`'s biconditional is built on (§4.4). It
   applies **Git's own parser** — case-insensitive booleans with the integer fallback,
   case-sensitive `on-demand`/`rebase-cousins`/`no-rebase-cousins` — to every occurrence, **in
   Git's real parse order and not in scope-name order**: the scan walks the occurrences exactly as
   the ordered read delivers them, `command` scope included where the described route inherits one
   (§4.4 `config_issues[]`), and
   **exactly one issue is produced per `(context_id, key)` — the *first* occurrence that would make
   the described command die**. Every occurrence after it is never parsed by that command, because
   the command is already dead, so publishing a second row for it would claim a parse that cannot
   happen — the **row-survival rule**, stated once here and restated nowhere in weaker form. The three
   exceptions are **`rebase.backend`'s unknown-name death**, **`rebase.abbreviateCommands`** and
   **`rebase.maxLabelLength`**, which Git resolves through the **config set** (`repo_config_get_*`)
   and therefore evaluates on the **last** occurrence alone: for those the plan evaluates the
   **final effective value** and nothing else, so an earlier invalid value **overridden by a later
   valid one produces no issue and no blocker at all**, and only a final effective value Git
   rejects produces one.
   Publishing "any occurrence" for them would refuse runs Git performs, which is the same class of
   error as round 27's missing scope; publishing an *earlier* occurrence for the callback keys, or
   a *later* one, would name a value Git never reaches. Both halves are asserted against the real
   command in §15.16e (vi).
2. **The consequence is a document-level, non-waivable rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config` blocker**,
   **exactly one per published config issue, joined to it by `issue_id`** (round-30 item 2 as round
   31 restructures it, item 2, **the join stated as the only one by round-32 item 4**, §4.4), whose
   detail names the context root, the key in Git's own
   lower-cased spelling, the offending value **sanitized** through the §11 renderer, the Git message
   the run would die with, and — round 28, widened by round 29 — **the scope that made it apply**:
   the fetch this route will attempt, the `git checkout` or `git push` it will run, or the rebase
   arm that will run with the `effective_backend` that reaches the key. Where more than one command
   of the route reads the same key — `submodule.recurse` under a checkout run that also pushes —
   there is still **one** issue and therefore one blocker, and its detail names the **first**
   command of the route that would die, in execution order, with the others listed after it.
   **The detail is a sanitized string and nothing more**: the machine-readable facts — including the
   base64 and SHA-256 of the raw bytes, which no `detail` may carry — live in `config_issues[]`, and
   the two are joined by the row's `issue_id` (item 3 below). **The generic blocker detail carries
   that join in a fixed, greppable shape** (round-32 item 4): every rank 5.07 `detail` contains the
   sanitized substring `config issue <issue_id> (<key>, <route_command>)`, and everything else it
   may say — the context root, the scope, the death message, the sanitized value where the row has
   one — is additional prose around it. The **value and source evidence lives on the issue row, not
   in the sentence**. Because item 1 leaves exactly one
   issue per `(context_id, key)`, "one blocker per issue" and "one row per issue" are the same
   statement counted twice, and **no document may publish a blocker without its row or a row without
   its blocker**.
   `runnable` is **`false`**, no plan is presented as
   executable, and no token can cover it (§4.9, §5.3.1). It is not a *guard introduction* in the
   §8.6.2 sense — the unguarded run dies too, at Git, having done nothing — and the detail says so.
3. **Identity is a stable digest, never the rendered detail and never a tuple a reader has to
   reassemble** (round-28 item 2, restructured by round-30 item 2, **made a single opaque member by
   round-31 item 2**, **and made the *only* identity by round-32 item 4**). Two blockers of this
   kind are the same blocker **iff their `issue_id`s are equal**, and nothing else: the surviving
   raw `(kind, repo_root, key)` triple of round 28 is **withdrawn** as an identity and as a
   de-duplication key, because `repo_root` is the sanitized display path (§4.4) and two distinct
   contexts may legitimately render to one, which is exactly the collision `context_id` exists to
   prevent — and because a second key over the same rows can only ever disagree with the first. The
   sanitized `detail` participates in **neither** identity nor de-duplication. This matters:
   §11's renderer is lossy by design (control bytes, invalid UTF-8 and over-long values all collapse),
   so two genuinely different invalid values in two different contexts can render to one string, and
   the generic `blockers[]` de-duplication on the whole `(kind, entry, detail)` tuple (§4.7) would
   silently drop one of them. For this kind the sort key stays `(rank, entry, detail)` so the
   canonical order is unchanged, and the **tie-break** is the row's `issue_id`, which is
   total and byte-stable; the de-duplication is over that id alone. **The evidence a consumer needs is a
   structured array, not fields bolted onto a blocker** (round-30 item 2): round 28 said "each
   blocker of this kind carries `repo_root`, `key` and the sanitized `value` as members of its own
   detail object", which contradicted `blockers[]`'s own closed `{kind, entry, detail}` tuple (§4.4)
   and made one kind's rows structurally unlike every other kind's. That is **withdrawn**. The
   per-key facts are published once, in the top-level closed-row **`config_issues[]`** array of §4.4
   — `{issue_id, context_id, repo_root, key, source, route_command, error_kind, raw_value_present,
   raw_value_base64, raw_value_sha256, sanitized_value}` — and `blockers[].detail` stays a
   **sanitized string** carrying the fixed substring `config issue <issue_id> (<key>,
   <route_command>)` (and possibly the
   context root, the scope and the death message), which points at the matching
   `config_issues[]` row by that id. **A `detail` never *requires* the raw value to be legible, and
   never carries it.** **No raw or unsafe bytes ever
   appear in a `detail`**, here or anywhere else, exactly as `encoding_issues[]` established for
   rank 5.08 (§4.4, §4.9 rank 5.08, round-28 item 4). A machine consumer reads the array; a human
   reads the sentence and the id; neither parses the other.
4. **It is a different fact from the withdrawn `config-blocking` kind** (§4.9): that kind was about
   *valid* values whose effect the plan disliked, and it stays withdrawn. This one is about values
   Git refuses to parse, where the plan's alternative would be to publish a run that cannot start.
   A **valid** value of any key in the table still blocks nothing, and where that key is one of the
   four `repositories[].config` carries, the corresponding
   member publishes `status: valid` with its `value` and `source: probed` exactly as before; the other nine have no such slot
   and never had one (round-30 item 3, round-31 item 4).

The domain is **closed at the twelve config keys plus the one `.gitmodules` key of Part 1 in v1** —
thirteen members in all,
and the closure rule is stated so the list can be checked rather than trusted. **Round 30 replaces
its first half, which the schema could never satisfy** (item 3): the rule used to read "a key is a
member when *the document itself resolves and publishes an effective value for it* **and** Git parses
it fatally", and only **four** of the thirteen have a published value slot at all
(`repositories[].config`, §4.4), with two more surfacing only through
`fetch_effect.submodule_recursion` — so a membership test written that way excluded nine members the
table plainly contains. The rule as it stands: **a key is a member when it lies in a
command-specific configuration namespace this feature models — `rebase.*` as `rebase_config` and the
sequencer read it, and the submodule-recursion keys `git fetch`, `git checkout` and `git push` read —
**and** Git parses it fatally while executing the argv of §2.1/§2.2.** Both halves are load-bearing.
Dropping the first
would open the domain to the whole of `git_default_config` — `core.*`, `i18n.*`, `commit.gpgsign`
(which `rebase_config` really does parse with `git_config_bool` on every rebase) and every other key
Git reads — which the plan cannot enumerate and must not pretend to; a partial enumeration presented
as total would be exactly the false completeness §4.8 forbids. Dropping the second would admit keys
Git merely `warning()`s about or returns an error for, which stop nothing. Publication is a separate
question from membership and is answered by Part 2's route scope plus `config_issues[]` (§4.4): the
document parses and publishes the **route-applicable** members and says nothing at all about the
rest. So the general Git config surface is
**deliberately outside v1**, stated here rather than implied, and no rendering may say the plan
validates a run's configuration. Two near neighbours are named rather than left implicit:
`submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` is parsed by the same `parse_fetch_recurse` and dies too
when it is read from config or from `.gitmodules` (`gitmodules_cb` passes a null
`gitmodules_oid`, so `die_on_error` is set, `submodule-config.c`); and `rebase.instructionFormat`
and `rebase.missingCommitsCheck` are **not** members for reasons of Git's behaviour rather than of
policy — `repo_config_get_string` returns an error for a valueless `instructionFormat` instead of
dying, and `missingCommitsCheck` only `warning()`s on an unrecognised setting and is reached only
under `--edit-todo`, which neither executor issues. v1 does not publish the blocker for
`submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules`, and §19 records that one extension as a deliberate
deferral rather than an oversight.

**The cherry-pick drop, and why its boolean is arm-aware rather than constant.** The full `rebase.*`
key set in Git 2.55.0 is `abbreviateCommands, autoSquash, autoStash, backend, forkPoint,
instructionFormat, maxLabelLength, missingCommitsCheck, rebaseMerges, rescheduleFailedExec, stat,
updateRefs` (verified this round with `git help -c` and the `git config` manual). **There is no
`rebase.reapplyCherryPicks` key and no `rebase.empty` key**, so the earlier draft's "defensive
probe" of a non-existent key is removed: probing it would always read unset, could never flip the
boolean, and would document a knob Git does not have. On 2.55.0 only `--reapply-cherry-picks` or
`--keep-base` on the command line disables the preliminary drop, and neither executor passes either
(frozen argv, §4.3).

`replay.may_drop_patch_equivalent` is therefore derived from the **arm and the range**, not from a
config probe (§4.1):

| Effective replay upstream | `<git_branch>..<upstream>` | value |
|---|---|---|
| recorded cutoff that is an ancestor of the head (the ordinary `--onto` arm, §6.1) | empty | `false` — no upstream-only commit exists for `--cherry-mark` to match |
| base ref holding commits the head lacks (the plain arm onto an advanced base, §6.2) | non-empty | `true` — the filter can fire, and in §6.2 it did |
| recorded cutoff that has diverged from the head | non-empty | `true` |
| deferred, unresolvable, unset, or probe failure | unknown | `null` (§4.8) |

The probe is one `git rev-list --count <git_branch>..<upstream>`, and the value is recomputed at the
JIT seam for any row whose upstream only resolves there (§5.2).

The `--empty=drop` filter has no config knob and neither executor passes `-i`/`--exec` (which would
imply `keep`/`stop`), so `may_drop_becomes_empty` stays `true` unconditionally — and it is the
filter that produced the customer's `dropping … patch contents already upstream` line (§6.1).

**`rebase.backend` is a *default*, not a constraint — and its own default is `merge`.** It "sets the
default backend to use for rebasing. Possible choices are `apply` or `merge`" (`git config` manual,
verified against Git 2.55.0) — **which does not name the default, so the default is established from
Git's own behaviour and its release notes rather than from that page**: the merge backend has been
Git's built-in default since **2.26** ("'git rebase' has learned to use the merge backend … by
default", Git 2.26 release notes), and a repository with no `rebase.backend` at all really does run
the merge backend on 2.55.0 (verified: a plain `git rebase <base>` there dies on an invalid
`rebase.abbreviateCommands`, which only the sequencer reads, and prints the merge backend's
`Rebasing (n/m)` progress rather than the apply backend's `First, rewinding head…`). **Round 29
states the built-in default and the derived capability explicitly, because two round-28 scope
sentences silently assumed the opposite** (item 2). The binding derivation, published per row as
`effective_backend` (§4.1) and used by every scope rule in this document:

- `effective_backend = merge` when the row's argv carries a **merge-forcing option** — the
  `imply_merge` family: `--update-refs` (the only one either shipped executor passes), and
  `--rebase-merges`/`-r`, `-i`/`--interactive`, `--exec`, `--autosquash`, `--keep-base` — **or**
  when the effective `rebase.backend` is **absent** or `merge`;
- `effective_backend = apply` **only** when the effective `rebase.backend` is exactly `apply`
  (case-sensitive, last occurrence) **and** the argv carries no merge-forcing option;
- `effective_backend = null` when the `rebase.backend` probe failed **and** the argv forces
