That is **withdrawn**: `cmd_fetch` reads the config chain **first** — `repo_config(the_repository, git_fetch_config, &config)` — then `parse_options`, then the `--recurse-submodules` override, and only then reaches `.gitmodules`, behind **two** guards (`builtin/fetch.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0): `if (config.recurse_submodules != RECURSE_SUBMODULES_OFF)` gates the *call* to `fetch_config_from_gitmodules(sfjc, rs)`, and `int *rs = config.recurse_submodules == RECURSE_SUBMODULES_DEFAULT ? &config.recurse_submodules : NULL` gates the *member*. So the **context-level `[fetch] recurseSubmodules` in `.gitmodules`** is still a **context mode** binding every submodule of the context, and still the lowest of the context-mode sources — it decides `mode` **only where neither `fetch.recurseSubmodules` nor `submodule.recurse` occurs in the config chain at all and no `--recurse-submodules` was given** — but the precedence is achieved by **not consulting the file**, not by being overwritten. **The three arms are materially different and the document publishes them as such**: (a) the chain/CLI resolved `no` ⇒ `fetch_config_from_gitmodules` is **never called**, so the file is not opened for this purpose at all; (b) the chain/CLI resolved `yes`/`on-demand` ⇒ the file *is* read, but `gitmodules_fetch_config` guards `parse_fetch_recurse_submodules_arg` behind `if (config->recurse_submodules)` (`submodule-config.c`), so with `rs == NULL` the value is **read and never parsed**; (c) the chain/CLI left it DEFAULT ⇒ the value is parsed by Git's own parser. **Therefore an invalid `.gitmodules` `[fetch] recurseSubmodules` value is *ignored* in arms (a) and (b) and is a *hard fetch-config failure* in arm (c) alone** — `die("bad fetch.recursesubmodules argument: <value>")`, raised while the fetch is reading its configuration and before any transfer — which is exactly how §4.2's route-scoped invalid-value rule and §4.9 rank 5.07 scope it: a `.gitmodules` recurse value blocks only where a fetch will be attempted **and** no valid context mode already resolves. **The two `.gitmodules` rungs are consumed at two different moments, through two different reads, and round 28 states that too** (item 1): rung 2 in `cmd_fetch`, before the walk, through `config_from_gitmodules(gitmodules_fetch_config, …)`; every per-submodule value of rung 4 later, during the walk, through `repo_read_gitmodules` → `gitmodules_cb` → the submodule-config cache. Round 26's "the same single read supplies both rungs" is **withdrawn as a claim about Git**, while the plan's own probe is unchanged and still costs one read per context (§13): the two rungs come out of the **same three-source ladder** and may never be resolved from two different sources, which is the property the probe preserves. It sits **above** every per-submodule key, which `get_fetch_recurse_config` never reaches while a context mode is set. **`.gitmodules` is read through Git's own three-source fallback, and round 27 states it exactly** (item 2). `config_from_gitmodules` (`submodule-config.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0) is guarded by `if (repo->worktree)` and then takes the **first** source that exists, in this order: the **working-tree `.gitmodules` file** (`GITMODULES_FILE`, `if (file_exists(file))`), else the **index blob `:.gitmodules`** (`GITMODULES_INDEX`), else the **`HEAD:.gitmodules` blob** (`GITMODULES_HEAD`), else nothing at all. **The fallback is not a bare-repository special case — it runs in an ordinary non-bare repository too**, which is exactly the case round 26 got wrong: a repository whose `.gitmodules` has been deleted from the working tree but is still staged reads the **index** blob, and one whose index entry is gone too reads **`HEAD`**, so "the file is missing" is not the same fact as "the key is unset". The two round-26 claims that are **withdrawn** are the ones this replaces: that the worktree file is the only source in a non-bare context, and that a bare context reads `HEAD:.gitmodules` — a bare repository has no `repo->worktree`, so `config_from_gitmodules` reads **nothing**, and a bare context contributes no `.gitmodules` rung at either level. Two properties survive unchanged: an **uncommitted** edit to a present working-tree file counts, because that file is what the fetch about to run will read; and the ladder is Git's, not the plan's. **What round 28 corrects is the *unmerged* cell, which round 26 made the fail-closed arm and round 27 kept** (item 1): `is_gitmodules_unmerged` guards **`repo_read_gitmodules`** — the per-submodule read of rung 4 — and **not** `config_from_gitmodules`, so the context-level read of rung 2 has no unmerged gate at all; and where the working-tree file is absent, `repo_get_oid(repo, ":.gitmodules")` **fails** on an unmerged path, so the disjunction in `config_from_gitmodules` falls straight through to `repo_get_oid(repo, "HEAD:.gitmodules")`. The ladder under an unmerged index is therefore **working-tree file → index-read failure → `HEAD` blob → nothing**, and it **resolves**: an unmerged `.gitmodules` is not an unknown mode, does not null `mode`/`mode_source`, and does not reach rank 5.05 on that account. For rung 4 the unmerged index means Git reads **no** per-submodule `.gitmodules` values at all — which is "unset", falling to rung 5's `on-demand`, not "unknown". Both prior spellings ("unmerged is the one state `repo_read_gitmodules` declines to parse", offered as a *context-mode* failure) are **withdrawn**. **The two `.gitmodules` rungs come from the same three-source ladder, and no context may resolve them from two different sources** — the context-level `[fetch] recurseSubmodules` of rung 2 and every per-submodule `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` of rung 4 — even though Git consumes them through two separate reads at two separate moments (above). The plan mirrors the ladder with the same one process per context: `config --file <work-tree top level>/.gitmodules --list -z` where the file exists, else `config --blob :.gitmodules --list -z`, else `config --blob HEAD:.gitmodules --list -z`, else no read at all (§13) — and, because Git's own index read fails rather than refuses on an unmerged entry, the plan's blob probe failing for that reason is the **same** signal and falls to the `HEAD` probe rather than nulling the mode. Where neither key occurs anywhere the value is Git's default **`on-demand`** (“When set to on-demand, only changed submodules are fetched. When set to yes, all populated submodules are fetched… When set to no, submodules are never fetched”, `git fetch` manual, verified against Git 2.55.0). **The two keys are not interchangeable in *value* space, which is why the resolution must be published rather than assumed**: `submodule.recurse` is parsed as a **boolean** (`git_config_bool` → on/off), so its occurrences can only produce `yes` or `no`, while `fetch.recurseSubmodules` takes the full `yes`/`on-demand`/`no` — a last occurrence of `submodule.recurse` can therefore never restore `on-demand`, and a context that reads `fetch.recurseSubmodules=on-demand` followed by `submodule.recurse=true` really is `yes`. `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` overrides the context value **only where no context value is set at all**, and **round 25 corrects the direction rounds 23 and 24 stated backwards** (item 1). `get_fetch_recurse_config` (`submodule.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0) begins `if (spf->command_line_option != RECURSE_SUBMODULES_DEFAULT) return spf->command_line_option;` — and that field is **not** the command line alone: `builtin/fetch.c` passes its `recurse_submodules` variable, which `git_fetch_config` has already filled from the last occurrence of `fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse` and which `--recurse-submodules` overwrites only when given. So a **set context mode overrides every per-submodule value**. Only when the context mode is unset does the function look at the submodule at all, and then in this order: it takes `submodule->fetch_recurse` — the `.gitmodules` value, read through the submodule-config cache — overrides it with `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` from the **superproject's own config** when that key is set, returns the result **if it is not itself unset**, and otherwise returns `spf->default_option`, Git's `on-demand`. **The effective per-submodule ladder is therefore exactly five rungs, in this order** (round-26 item 6 inserting the second; rounds 23-25 counted four): (1) the **context mode from the config chain** — `--recurse-submodules` (never passed by the shipped call, §0.1) else the last-occurrence value of `fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse` — whenever it is set at all; (2) the **context mode from `.gitmodules`**, its `[fetch] recurseSubmodules`, which binds every submodule of the context exactly as rung 1 does and applies only where rung 1 is absent; (3) `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` in the superproject's config; (4) the same key in `.gitmodules`; (5) `on-demand`. **The two `.gitmodules` rungs are different keys with different scopes and must never be merged**: rung 2 is `fetch.recurseSubmodules` at the top of the file and binds everything; rung 4 is `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` inside one submodule's section and binds only it — and rung 2 outranks rungs 3 and 4, so a `.gitmodules` that carries both a context-level `yes` and a per-submodule `no` recurses into that submodule. Each `submodules[]` row republishes the outcome as its own **`effective_mode`** with an **`effective_mode_source`** naming the rung that produced it — the closed enum `context-mode` / `config-per-submodule` / `gitmodules-per-submodule` / `default-on-demand`, where **`context-mode` covers rungs 1 and 2 alike** and the row's own `mode_source` says which of the two supplied it, so no new `effective_mode_source` member is minted — so no reader re-derives the direction, and **every row of a context whose `mode` is set publishes `effective_mode` equal to that `mode` and `effective_mode_source: context-mode`, whatever `.gitmodules`'s per-submodule sections or the per-submodule config keys say**. Round 24's ladder sentence ("command line, then `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules`, then the context mode") is **withdrawn**: it inverted rungs 1 and 2, so it would have published `mode: yes` beside a row claiming a `no` override that Git never reads, and `mode: no` beside a row a `fetch.recurseSubmodules=yes` really fetches — both in the under-reporting direction this feature exists to prevent. Like `mode_source`, **`effective_mode_source` is provenance and is excluded from the candidate-equivalence comparison of §8.6.9**, while `effective_mode` itself is compared. **`mode_source` is a closed enum of exactly four values plus `null`, and this is the authoritative statement of it** (round-29 item 6; any three-value restatement elsewhere is either round-24 history or a fixture-scoped subset, never the enum) — `fetch.recurseSubmodules` / `submodule.recurse` / **`gitmodules-fetch.recurseSubmodules`** (round-26 item 6, the rung-2 source) / `default-on-demand`, plus `null` in the one nullable cell below — naming the key whose *last writing occurrence* produced `mode`, and `default-on-demand` exactly where none of the three occurred at all** (round-24 item 1, replacing round 23's unconstrained “names which key answered”; extended by round-26 item 6): it is the only field that distinguishes a configured `on-demand` from an unconfigured one — and now also a config-chain mode from a `.gitmodules` one — and it is **provenance, not effect** — two contexts that resolve the same `mode` from different keys fetch identically, so `mode_source` is deliberately **excluded** from the candidate-equivalence comparison below while every other member of the object is in it. **`mode` and `mode_source` are nullable together, and only for one reason** (round-26 item 6, **narrowed by round-28 item 1**): where rung 1 is absent and **every** source of the rung-2 ladder that the plan can still try **fails to read** — an existing working-tree `.gitmodules` the probe cannot open or parse, or a `HEAD` blob probe that fails after the index probe already failed — the context mode is *not established*, so both members are `null`, `reach` is `unknown`, and a context with at least one **present gitlink** fails closed at rank 5.05 exactly as an unconditional `yes` over an unknown reach does, because a mode nobody could read may be `yes` (§4.9 rank 5.05, §8.6.1 cause 5). **An *unmerged* index entry is no longer one of those cells** (round-28 item 1): Git's own ladder treats the failed index read as a fall-through to `HEAD:.gitmodules`, so the plan does too, and the mode resolves; round 26's "unmerged in the index, which is the one state `repo_read_gitmodules` itself declines to parse" named the wrong function and the wrong path and is **withdrawn**. **An *invalid* rung-2 value is not one of those cells either, and never was an unknown**: where the value is parsed at all it is a hard fetch-config failure the previewed run dies on, published as rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config`, and where a valid context mode already resolved it is ignored by Git and therefore by the plan (§4.2, §4.9 rank 5.07). **Where `mode` is `null` the route does not fetch** (round-28 item 7): the effect mode is the thing that decides whether and how far the fetch reaches, so an unresolvable mode over a present gitlink takes suppression cause 5 and publishes `fetch.attempted: false` — there is no alternative cell in which such a context is fetched and described afterwards as `unknown-fetch-effect` (§8.6.1 cause 5 and the ninth cell). A **missing** `.gitmodules` is not a failure: it contributes nothing **once all three sources have been tried and none exists** — the working-tree file, the index blob and the `HEAD` blob (round-27 item 2) — and the ladder falls to rung 3, and a context with no present gitlink publishes `may_recurse: false`/`reach: none` and fetches whatever its mode says. It costs one read beyond the config chain: the single ordered `.gitmodules` read that supplies rung 2 supplies every per-submodule value of rung 4 as well (§13), while the last-occurrence resolution of rung 1 stays inside the ordered `config --list -z` this row already issues, exactly as it already resolves `skipFetchAll`/`skipDefaultUpdate`. No flag participates: the shipped call passes no `--recurse-submodules` (`internal/cli/sync.go:604-635`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:616-625`), which is precisely why the **default** matters — an ordinary superproject recurses on demand without anyone configuring anything. `may_recurse` is `false` only where recursion is impossible: every candidate submodule's `effective_mode` is `no`, **or** the context has no submodule that is both a **gitlink** (a `160000` index entry, which is what `git fetch` iterates — `submodule.c` `get_fetch_task_from_index`) and *present* — a `.git` file or directory at the gitlink path (Git's “populated”), **or** a store for it under `$GIT_DIR/modules/`, since “a changed submodule can be fetched as long as it is present locally e.g. in `$GIT_DIR/modules/`” and `yes` fetches “all populated submodules … and submodules that are both unpopulated and changed” (`git fetch` manual, verified against Git 2.55.0), so presence and population are not the same test and the narrower one would under-report the reach. **Round 24 removes submodule *activity* from that gate** (item 2). Round 23 required each candidate to be “active” (`submodule.<name>.active`, else `submodule.active` pathspecs, else the presence of `submodule.<name>.url`, per `gitsubmodules(7)`), and the fetch path does not apply that test to a populated gitlink: `get_fetch_task_from_index` walks the index gitlinks, `fetch_task_create` decides on `get_fetch_recurse_config` — the **context mode** where one is set, else the per-submodule value from config and then `.gitmodules`, else `on-demand` (the exact ladder above, as round 25 corrects it) — and opens the submodule repository, with **no `is_submodule_active` call anywhere on that path** (`submodule.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0). So an **inactive but populated** submodule is recursed into under `yes` exactly like an active one, and gating the reach on activity under-reported it in precisely the direction this feature exists to prevent. Activity keeps **one narrow, published role**: the second arm — submodules that are *not* in the index and are reached only through the changed-submodule scan (`get_fetch_task_from_changed`) — does consult `is_tree_submodule_active`, so `active` stays in `submodules[]` as an **informational** member describing that arm, and no predicate in this document (`may_recurse`, `reach`, the rank 5.05 refusal, the caps) reads it. The gitlink-and-presence clause is what keeps the ordinary submodule-free repository exactly where round 22 left it: no gitlinks means no reach, and `submodules: []` with `may_recurse: false`. `reach` is the closed enum **`none`** (`may_recurse: false`), **`bounded`** (every submodule that could be recursed into is enumerated in `submodules[]`, with its own effect resolved, at every level that could be reached) and **`unknown`** (it is not — a candidate submodule whose store or config could not be read, a gitlink whose enumeration exceeded the cap, or an enumerated submodule that itself may recurse further into a level that could not be established). `submodules[]` is the **bounded** publication this feature prefers to a shrug: `{path, name, active, present, effective_mode, effective_mode_source, repo_root, common_dir, fetch_effect, may_recurse_further}` rows sorted by `path` (bytewise) — `active` informational per the paragraph above — each `fetch_effect` resolved by *this same* ladder in that submodule's own directory — so a reader can see which stores a bare fetch may contact and which refs it may move there — capped at **50 submodules per context and depth 3**, with either cap making `reach: unknown` rather than a truncated list that reads as complete. **The consequences are graded by how certain the recursion is, and stated here rather than left to the emitter**: `mode: on-demand` recurses only “when its superproject retrieves a commit that updates the submodule's reference” (`git config` manual), which is a fact that does not exist until the fetch has run, so a bounded reach is published, the fetch proceeds, and the uncertainty lands in `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs` (below) rather than in a refusal; an **`on-demand`** context whose reach is `unknown` still fetches — refusing there would refuse the default configuration of every superproject whose submodule store is merely unreadable — but its document publishes `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect`; and a context in which **some present gitlink submodule's `effective_mode` is `yes`** — unconditional recursion, whether it came from the context-level `mode` or from a per-submodule override, and whether or not that submodule is *active* (round-24 item 2) — while `reach` is `unknown` **fails closed**: the fetch is not performed, the document carries the non-waivable rank 5.05 `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` blocker (`runnable: false`, §4.9) and `freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate` (§8.6.1 cause 5). The asymmetry is deliberate and is the strong recommendation this document makes: under `yes` the recursion is **certain** for every populated submodule, so performing it while unable to name the stores it writes would be the very “read-only” lie §0.1 exists to prevent, while under `on-demand` it is conditional and usually does not happen at all. **The resolved effect is published on the row and on every candidate**, and the effect is **unknown** — `fetch_effect: null` — only where the *reads* behind it fail: `HEAD` cannot be read where the single-remote ladder needs it, or the effective `fetch.all`/`skipFetchAll`/prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`/`insteadOf`/remote enumeration or the config read itself fails, **or — from round 23 — a legacy `$GIT_DIR/remotes/<name>`/`branches/<name>` file exists for the resolved name and cannot be read or parsed (item 5), or the submodule recursion `mode` itself cannot be resolved (item 3)** (round-22 items 2 and 3 and round-23 items 3 and 5 add keys and two bounded file reads to that read, not a second config read). **The last of those causes carries a consequence round 28 makes explicit, because two cells of this document described it two ways** (item 7): an unresolvable `mode` over a context with at least one **present gitlink** is a *fail-closed* fact — suppression cause 5, `fetch.attempted: false`, rank 5.05, `freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate` — **not** an attempted fetch described afterwards as `unknown-fetch-effect`. Over a context with **no** present gitlink an unresolvable mode changes nothing that can be reached (`may_recurse: false`, `reach: none`), so it is not a suppression and the effect's other reads decide the row as usual. **An `unknown` submodule *reach* is deliberately not in that list**: the top-level effect is still fully resolved, so it is published, and the uncertainty is carried by `submodule_recursion.reach` and by `freshness`/`fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs` rather than by nulling an effect the plan does know. **`fetch_effect: null` does not by itself refuse anything** (round-21 item 7): on a token with a single candidate context the row stays determinate — the route knows exactly where its `git fetch` will run — so it attempts the fetch and reports what happened; the rank 5.0 `fetch-context-indeterminate` blocker belongs to the *choice* between **two or more** candidates that cannot be shown materially the same, where an unresolved effect is what makes the choice unprovable (below, §8.6.9, §4.9 rank 5.0). **A multi-remote effect adds no per-remote outcome axis**: `ok` stays the exit status of that context's one `git fetch` process (`fetchQuiet`, `internal/cli/sync.go:604-635`), which is aggregate over the remotes it contacted, so a fetch that refreshed one remote and failed another publishes `ok: false` and `freshness: possibly-stale` for the whole row — the honest reading of a status the shipped call site discards — and no field claims per-remote success. It exists because the common dir alone does not determine what a fetch *does*: two worktrees of one repository share a store yet can sit on branches configured to different remotes, or differ in `fetch.all`/`skipFetchAll`, or — through `extensions.worktreeConfig` and `config.worktree`, which the ordered read already sees last — differ in **prune, pruneTags or `tagOpt`**, so one worktree's fetch **deletes** refs or tags the other's fetch only adds to (round-22 item 2), and their fetches refresh different refs (§8.6.9); `context_source` is the closed enum `worktree` / `entry-repo` / `process-cwd` / **`workspace-repo-root`**. **`context_candidates[]` is the deterministic, sorted enumeration of every context the route's own first-entry rule could resolve for that token** — `{context_root, context_common_dir, fetch_effect, context_source, first_entry}` tuples sorted by `(context_root, context_source, first_entry)` — and it exists because the new-mode external route's map-building order is `TopoSort`-derived and therefore unspecified between processes (§4.7, §8.6.9). **The enumeration is one candidate per *root component*, not one per minimum-depth entry** (round-22 item 5): `TopoSort` randomizes only the zero-in-degree **root seed**, so a token's first entry can vary only across the components that could supply it, and its within-component first entry is fixed. It has exactly one member wherever the order cannot matter (checkout, the legacy route, and any token whose selected entries can be first from only one root component — which includes same-root siblings and same-root entries under different parents), and **candidates collapse to one materially distinct context — however their roots are spelled — only when their canonical absolute `context_common_dir` values *and* their `fetch_effect` values are all equal**, the effect compared **whole**: the `all` flag, `contacted`, `may_delete_refs`/`may_delete_tags`/`may_clobber_tags`, the full `name`-sorted `remotes[]` row set, every row's `source`, its `url_configured` **and** `url_effective` **and** `url_source`, every row's **ordered** refspec list, every row's `prune`/`prune_tags`/`tag_opt`, **and the whole `submodule_recursion` value — `mode`, `may_recurse`, `reach` and the `path`-sorted `submodules[]` rows with their own effects, but *not* `mode_source`, which is provenance and cannot change what a fetch does (round-24 item 1)** (round-23 items 1, 3 and 5: a member added to the effect is a member of the comparison, by the same construction round 22 relied on, so two worktrees that differ only in `submodule.recurse`, or only in which legacy file supplies a URL, do not collapse — while two that resolve the same `yes` from different keys **do**) — never a single remote name (round-20 items 1 and 3, round-22 items 2 and 3: a member added to the effect is a member of the comparison, by construction and not by a second rule). The ordinary multi-worktree stack is the collapsing shape: every worktree of one repository shares one common dir and one `origin`, so one `git fetch` in any of them refreshes the same refs (§8.6.9). Where two or more **materially different** members remain — different canonical common dirs, different fetch effects (a different `all`, a different `contacted`, a different remote row set, a different configured or effective URL, a different refspec sequence, or a different `prune`/`prune_tags`/`tag_opt`), or a candidate whose common dir or fetch effect could not be resolved and therefore cannot be **shown** to agree with another — the document publishes **`context_root: null`, `context_common_dir: null`, `context_source: null`, `fetch_effect: null`, `attempted: false`, `ok: null`** plus the `fetch-context-indeterminate` blocker rather than a value that would differ between two runs of the same command. **That four-`null` shape is the *indeterminate* shape and belongs to multi-candidate rows alone** (round-21 item 7). A row with a **single** candidate is determinate by construction — there is nothing to choose between — so it publishes its `context_root` and `context_source` and **attempts the fetch** even when the context is broken: an unresolvable common dir (a directory that is not a work tree) or an unresolvable effect publishes `context_common_dir: null`/`fetch_effect: null` **beside a non-null `context_root`**, with `attempted: true` and `ok: false` when the fetch then fails. "I cannot describe this fetch" and "I cannot decide which of two fetches this route performs" are different facts, and only the second is a refusal. **In external** the rows mirror `UniqueRepos` + `fetchQuiet` exactly (§8.6.9): the legacy route's token set is every unique repo of the whole stack, the new-mode route's is the selected repos (R1), and the context is fixed by the **first entry of that token** in the map-building order, never by the row that later cites the token. **In checkout the array is at most one row, and its shape is fixed** (§8.6.9): checkout fetches with a single `RunSilentDir(opts.RepoDir, "git", "fetch")` labelled `default repo` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:616-625`), so the row is `{repo_token: "" (default), context_root: <canonical ws.RepoRoot/opts.RepoDir>, context_common_dir: <its canonical absolute common dir>, context_source: workspace-repo-root, fetch_effect: <that context's effective bare-fetch effect>, context_candidates: [that one context], attempted: true, ok: <exit status>}` — the full canonical eight-key shape, with a **single-member** candidate list, so `fetch-context-indeterminate` is unreachable in checkout by construction (§8.6.9). Checkout **ignores `entry.Repo` entirely** when fetching — there is no per-entry fetch and no cross-repo fetch — and because that block sits inside `if opts.NewMode`, a **legacy checkout route never fetches at all** and publishes `[]`. **A checkout `--fetch` document publishes this row even when its plan turns out to be empty** (round-21 item 7): the shipped fetch runs after the lock and *before* the stack load, the plan build and the `len(plan) == 0` return (`internal/checkout_sync.go:611-654`), so an empty-stack or empty-selection checkout run really does fetch, and its rows-less document publishes the attempted row with **whichever of the four attempted-row verdicts its own fetch earned — `fetched`, `possibly-stale`, `unknown-fetch-effect` or `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`** (round-23 item 1: the previous two-value list predated both the round-22 no-contact cell and round 23's unknown one, and a checkout context can reach either — its single default remote may resolve to nothing, and its submodule reach may be unknown) — never `not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets`, which is the *external* zero-context cell | `[]` when the route resolved **no context to fetch**, **including every legacy-checkout route**. Note the one cell where rows exist and nothing was attempted: an indeterminate context publishes its known tokens with `attempted: false` and a `null` chosen context (above), so "`attempted: false`" and "`fetch.repos: []`" are not the same statement |
| `fetch.outcome` | `skipped` / `ok` / `failed` / `partial`, decided by a **closed predicate over the `attempted: true` rows of `fetch.repos[]`** and by nothing else: **`ok` iff every attempted row has `ok: true`**; **`failed` iff every attempted row has `ok: false`**; **`partial` iff at least one attempted row succeeded *and* at least one failed** — which is reachable only on a **multi-context** fetch, since one attempted row is `ok` or `failed` by construction (a **multi-remote** `fetch_effect` does not change that: one context still runs one `git fetch` whose exit status is one bit, so a fetch that refreshed one remote and failed another is a `failed` row, §4.4 `fetch.repos[]`, round-20 item 1), and is therefore unreachable in checkout, whose array is at most one row (§8.6.9); and **`skipped` iff no row was attempted at all**. Zero attempted rows are never `ok`: "every attempt succeeded" over an empty set is the vacuous truth `freshness` also refuses to publish as `fetched`. `partial` and `failed` both carry `freshness: possibly-stale`, because both leave at least one context unrefreshed. `skipped` covers **eight** distinct causes (round-23 item 3 added the seventh; **round-27 item 5 adds the eighth to *this* restatement, which had been left behind when round-25 item 2 added suppression cause 6 everywhere else**), disambiguated by `freshness`: policy `no-fetch`, a `--continue` invocation, **no plannable subject** (the rows-less refusal was established before the fetch step, §8.6.1), the **live-owner suppression** of §8.6.1 step 6 (an *actually live* checkout-lock or sync-run-guard owner, whether or not it owns this run's payload, and never a stale, dead or undecodable one), the **indeterminate fetch context** of §8.6.9 (the route's own first-entry rule does not determine one object store, so the plan/guard route declines the fetch rather than guess), the **unbounded submodule reach** of §8.6.1 cause 5 (an effective `fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse` of `yes` whose `submodule_recursion.reach` is `unknown`, so the route fails closed rather than recursively contact and rewrite refs in stores it cannot name, round-23 item 3), the **checked-out fetch destination** of §8.6.1 cause 6 (a positive refspec covering `refs/heads/**` over a held — or unestablishable — local-branch destination, so the route declines a fetch Git would either refuse outright or use to move a branch out from under a working tree, round-25 item 2, §4.9 rank 5.06), and **zero fetch targets** (the policy said fetch, nothing suppressed it, and the route's resolved context set was empty, §8.6.1) | never |

`absent` — the key was parsed and is unset (`value: null`, `source: null`); **`not-evaluated`** — the described route never hands this key to Git, so nothing was read and nothing may be inferred (`value: null`, `source: null`, the **out-of-scope** cell of §4.2 Part 2); `source` is `probed` under `valid`, **`null` in exactly the three no-read statuses** `not-evaluated`, `probe-failed` and `absent`, and the occurrence's scope under `invalid` (§4.2, §4.3). **Round 31's `unset` source member is withdrawn** (round-32 item 3): `status: absent` already carried that fact, and the member is needed to name a scope. A rows-less document that resolved a directory but that **nothing** cites — the ordinary checkout `plan-unavailable` cell, where `ws.RepoRoot` is a §8.6.6 hard precondition and is therefore *resolvable* — still publishes `[]`: resolvability is not citation, and the row appears only where a push target or a restore context requires one. The previous draft's "`[]` is impossible" is withdrawn: it forced a document that never resolved a repository to invent one. A probe failure inside an established context yields `status: probe-failed` with `value: null` and `source: null` for that key, never a default |

It is the *boolean*; **what** would be pushed is `push.targets[]` below, and both are bound into the fingerprint (§5.3.2) | never (boolean) |
| `intent.push_source` | `flag` / `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` / `flag-legacy-continuation` — which of the four rules above produced `intent.push` | never |
| `push.targets[]` | the **canonical projection of what the described run would push**, and the reason a push-only run is approvable at all (§4.4 `approval.fingerprint`, §8.6.4a). One row per branch the route would push, `{repo, context_id, repo_root, git_branch, remote, ref, force, lease, scope}`, sorted by **`(context_id, git_branch)`** — **round-35 item 5 gives the push axis the same stable identity the entry and repository axes already have**, for the same reason and with the same consequences: `repo_root` is a §11 rendering, two distinct push contexts may render to one string, and a sort key ending in a rendering was not total and could reorder between processes. `context_id` is the **64-lowercase-hex identity of the context this push runs in**, computed by the §4.4 rule from that context's raw canonical root, its `root_source` label and its raw canonical common dir, and it is the **only** key by which the row cites `repositories[]` — never the `repo` token, never `repo_root`, and never the pair. **It is never empty and has no fallback**: a target whose push context could not be established is not published as a row at all, exactly as an unestablished context yields no `repositories[]` row (§4.1, §4.4 `repositories[]`); the array is a projection of contexts the document really resolved, so "unknown identity" is not reachable here. `repo` is the `StackEntry.Repo` token, kept because it is what an operator reads and what the shipped output prints, and it stays **descriptive**: it is not a key, not a sort member and not a join. `repo_root` is the **canonical** directory the push command runs in as §11 renders it, exactly as the shipped code resolves it (`entry.Repo` when non-empty, else the entry's worktree, in external; `opts.RepoDir` in checkout) — **display-only, a fingerprint non-member, and never a join, sort or de-duplication key** (§5.3.2). The push context stays its **own** projection and is never derived from, or read as, either of an entry row's two context refs (§4.1): the push ladder is `entry.Repo` **else the worktree**, which is neither `base_context`'s rule nor `execution_context`'s, and a row whose entry contexts split may still push from one directory; `git_branch` is `GitBranch()`; `remote` is `origin` and `ref` is `refs/heads/<git_branch>`, the local ref pushed to `origin/<git_branch>`; `force` is the constant `with-lease`, because every shipped push is `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>` (`pushScoped`, `internal/cli/push.go:103`; `gitPush`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:438-446`); `lease` is the object of the `push.targets[].lease` row below. `scope` is the closed enum naming **which shipped rule produced the row**: `stack-all`, `selected-rebased`, `transaction-plan`, each derived exactly as the "**Deriving `push.targets[]`**" rules under this table specify. **The array is a *conditional projection*, not a report of completed work**: every row states what the route would push **if the rebase and validation this same document describes succeed**, so on a fresh run it is derived from the plan's own rows rather than from any `completed`/`Completed` list, which at plan time is empty by construction. On a continuation it is derived from the persisted `Completed`/`Pushed` state **plus** the remaining rows the resume would still rebase, for exactly the same reason. Like every other plan fact it describes intent, and `--plan` pushes nothing (§0.1, §8.3.1). **Whether the run can reach the push at all is a separate, explicitly published pair of fields** — `push.executable` and `push.blocked_by[]` below — never an inference a consumer has to make from `blockers[]` (§8.6.4a) | **`[]` whenever `intent.push` is `false`** — a run that does not push has no targets. **The converse does not hold, and the previous draft's biconditional is withdrawn**: `intent.push: true` legitimately yields `[]` when the route has no eligible target — every selected entry archived or worktree-less on the external arms, every branch already recorded in `payload.Pushed` on a scoped resume, an empty `tx.Plan`, and the checkout `restoring` resume, whose shipped arm reaches `finalizeCleanup` with `tx.Stage != completed` and therefore **drops the persisted push entirely** (§8.6.4a, §18.20). Such a document publishes `intent.push: true` with `push.targets: []`; whether it is *workless* then depends on `entries` **and** the `restore` object below, not on this array alone (§4.4 `approval.fingerprint`). `null` is never used here: the set is derived from the same selection/plan the rows come from, so "unknown" is not reachable while `intent.push` is known |
| `push.targets[].lease` | the **force-with-lease baseline**, published as an object because "force-push" and "force-push if the remote is where I last saw it" are different blast radii and the shipped argv passes no explicit lease: `{mode, expectation, expected_ref, expected_sha, expected_sha_freshness}`. `mode` is the constant **`implicit-remote-tracking`** — `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>` with no `=<expect>` protects the ref it is about to update "by requiring their current value to be the same as the remote-tracking branch we have for them" (`git push` manual, `--force-with-lease`). **Which remote-tracking ref that is follows the remote's own fetch refspecs, and this document resolves it that way rather than assuming a name** (round-19 item 3): the baseline ref is the result of applying `remote.<remote>.fetch` — read in **that push context**, `remote` being the row's `remote` operand — to the pushed ref `refs/heads/<git_branch>`, exactly as Git maps it before reading the value. **The mapping is first-match in configured order, and negative refspecs take no part in it** (round-20 item 3) — **the *lease query* alone is first-match; the fetch itself applies every matching positive refspec, so the two read the same list for different purposes** (round-21 item 6): the refspec list is consumed **in the order the configuration sets it**, never byte-sorted, and the baseline is the destination of the **first matching non-negative** refspec — a negative refspec (`^<pattern>`, which "may only contain a `<src>` and do not specify a `<dst>`", `git fetch` manual) has no destination to map to, so it can neither supply nor shadow a lease baseline. `refs/remotes/origin/<git_branch>` is merely what the *default* refspec `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*` produces; a remote configured `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/upstream/*`, a **single-branch** clone whose only refspec is `+refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main`, or any narrowed refspec set maps differently or not at all, and a document that printed `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` there would name a ref the lease never reads. Two refspec sets that differ only in order can map one branch to two different tracking refs, which is why the sequence is published and compared as a sequence everywhere (§4.4 `fetch.repos[]`, §4.7). `expected_ref` is therefore the **mapped** ref name, or `null` when the refspecs map this branch nowhere. **`expectation` is the closed enum `sha` / `absent`, and it is the field that corrects the previous draft's central error**: where the mapping exists **and** the mapped ref resolves in `repo_root`, `expectation` is `sha` and `expected_sha` is its value **as resolved at plan time in `repo_root`**; where the refspecs provide **no mapping**, or the mapped ref **does not exist**, Git does not degenerate to an unprotected force — it leases against the **null OID**, i.e. it requires the ref to be **absent on the remote** and rejects the push as stale info if the remote already has that branch. Both of those cells are `expectation: absent` with `expected_sha: null`, and they are *stricter* than the ordinary case, not weaker: the push succeeds only against a remote that has never seen the branch. `expected_sha_freshness` is the document's own `freshness` **scoped to this target's context**: `fetched` only when a fetch really succeeded in the context whose common dir backs `repo_root` (§8.6.9), otherwise the same non-`fetched` cause the document publishes; **and `possibly-stale` regardless of that fetch whenever a *negative* fetch refspec of that remote excludes the pushed branch from being fetched at all** (round-20 item 3): the lease baseline is a ref no fetch of this remote updates, so "the fetch succeeded" says nothing about it, and labelling it `fetched` would claim a currency the run cannot have. It is the honest statement that the plan may be describing a remote state nobody refreshed, and `push.executable` is **not** downgraded for it — an unrefreshed lease baseline is a knowability fact, not a projected gate failure, and the two must not be conflated. **The plan never claims an explicit lease SHA**: it does not pass `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<sha>`, does not promise the push will use the value published here, and says so — a fetch (or another process) between plan and push moves the baseline, and the honest statement is "this is the ref the lease will read, this is what it held when I looked, and this is how stale that reading may be". **A fetch can also *delete* that ref, and the plan's own fetch is one of them** (round-22 item 2): where the effective `prune` of the row's remote is true, the very `git fetch` this document performs at step 5 may remove the mapped remote-tracking ref when the branch is gone upstream — and where the remote's refspecs reach tags — `prune_tags`, or any positive destination pattern covering `refs/tags/**` (round-24 item 3) — `refs/tags/**` is **pruned** on the same terms — pruned, not clobbered: an unforced tag update is rejected, and only a **forced** tag-covering refspec updates an existing tag, which is the separate `may_clobber_tags` member (round-23 item 2). So `expectation` is read **after** that fetch and can legitimately be `absent` where a pre-fetch reading would have said `sha` (and, symmetrically, `sha` where the fetch created the ref); a later prune between plan and push moves it again. The published `fetch_effect.may_delete_refs`/`may_delete_tags` of that context is what makes this legible rather than surprising, and nothing here downgrades `push.executable`: a lease baseline that moved is a knowability fact, exactly like an unrefreshed one | `expected_sha` is `null` exactly when `expectation` is `absent` or the mapped ref could not be resolved in `repo_root`; **`expected_ref` is `null` exactly when the remote's fetch refspecs map `refs/heads/<git_branch>` nowhere** — the unmapped cell, which is `expectation: absent` — and `null` too when the refspec read itself failed, which is likewise `absent` rather than a guessed name; `mode`, `expectation` and `expected_sha_freshness` are never `null` |

That frame is the one an operator is about to act on, and it is the same frame `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` and the four-conjunct plan→execute predicate already use; nothing about the **unguarded** route changes, and the shipped gates it really has are published as blockers regardless. It is a **derived** field — every input is already published as a blocker or as a named reason — and it exists because the previous draft asked consumers to *infer* non-executability from a rank 4 blocker plus prose, which is exactly the inference an agent gets wrong on the one operation that force-pushes branches. `false` never empties `push.targets[]` where targets exist: "what would be pushed" and "will the run get there" are two facts, and collapsing them hides either the blast radius or the gate. **The checkout `restoring` resume is `false`, never `true`**: `intent.push` is `true`, `push.targets` is `[]`, and `finalizeCleanup`'s `tx.Stage == StageCompleted && opts.Push` guard is false, so the requested push never happens (§8.6.4a, §18.20). The condition is the built plan, not the stack file: a non-empty `stack.yaml` whose selection or plan reduces to zero steps is the same cell. | `restore.executable` / `restore.blocked_by[]` | the same totality pair as `push.executable`/`push.blocked_by[]`, for the restoring mutation, evaluated over the **same corresponding controlled invocation** (round-20 item 6). `executable` is `true` when every projected precondition of `restoreOriginal` holds, `false` when any is projected to fail, `null` **only** where the question could not be established (`plannability: unavailable`, or `applies: false` on external — an inapplicable restore publishes `executable: null` with `blocked_by: []`, never a `false` that would read as "your restore will fail"). `blocked_by[]` is the sorted, deduplicated list of **reason tokens** from a closed set, built on the **same** membership predicate as `push.blocked_by[]` and not on a rank range (round-20 item 6): a kind is a member iff it is **effective and unwaived** in this document *and* its fact makes `restoreOriginal` unreachable — or fails it — **in the corresponding controlled invocation**. Two consequences follow from the shipped order and are stated here rather than left to inference. First, the run-stopping state and selection facts of ranks 1-4 qualify, because they stop the invocation before the transaction advances to `StageRestoring` at all; **so does rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config` where the offending key is `submodule.recurse`**, and it qualifies twice over (round-29 item 1) — it stops the invocation, and `restoreOriginal`'s own `gitCheckout` is one of the commands that dies on it — while an invalid rebase-scope key on a `restoring` resume runs no `git rebase`, is out of scope, and is **not** a member. Publishing both fields is what lets one document state the shipped per-entry-dynamic execution *and* the guarded freeze without either claim contradicting the other (§8.8) | never |
| `intent.validation.command_digest` | the **full 64-character lowercase-hex SHA-256** of the exact command string — **the command itself is never published**, because a plan document is pasted into issues and CI logs far more often than the executor's own `validating <name>: <cmd>` line is, and a validation command routinely carries tokens or internal hostnames. The digest is enough to prove two invocations validate identically, which is all the fingerprint needs. It is the **one** validation value the fingerprint binds, together with `applies` (§5.3): the labels above are descriptive, so a token minted by a `--plan` document is not invalidated by the guarded invocation's freeze. Under `stability: per-entry-dynamic` it is the digest of the command **as read at plan time** — a snapshot of the unguarded route, and the exact value a guarded invocation freezes and consumes (§8.8) | `null` when no command applies |
| `intent.validation.cli_test_ignored` | `true` when `--test` was supplied on a route that ignores it — external, where the flag reaches only `CheckoutSyncOpts` (`internal/cli/sync.go:50-58`). The plan mirrors the executor exactly and says so rather than pretending the flag took effect | never (boolean) |
| `state` | the **single** top-level observed-state object, and it is a **pre-acquisition snapshot**: every member is read **before this invocation creates, acquires or reclaims any guard, lock or transaction** — before `setupSyncRunState`, before `AcquireCheckoutLock`/`forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, before `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, and before any sentinel write — and that one snapshot is the value carried unchanged through plan derivation, blocker projection and the guard seam (§8.6.1 step 2, §9). Nothing observed *after* an acquisition may be substituted for it: re-reading `.sync-run.lock` at the guard seam of a fresh new-mode external run, or at the checkout continuation seam that sits below `forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, would read **this process's own** artefact and refuse the invocation against itself. **The snapshot is the value the *document* publishes and the *plan facts and fingerprint* are computed from, and that is the whole of its job.** It is **not** a licence to answer a *native shipped precondition* from a stale read: the scoped-continuation seam re-evaluates `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s own conditions through the **shared `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable` predicate extracted from that function**, from a **fresh read taken immediately before the seam** — still before any acquisition or reclaim and still before this invocation has written any artefact of its own, so it cannot read itself. **There is exactly one such carve-out in this document, and §8.7.5 step 1 is its single normative statement**; every other mention of it — this row, §9, §15.15f4 (vi-b), §15.16c e3 and §19.24 — is a cross-reference to that rule and neither restates nor extends it. That native read is deliberately **not** the safe inspector below: it keeps the shipped `os.ReadFile` behaviour, symlink-following and all, because its job is to reproduce a shipped refusal byte-for-byte, while the inspector's job is to describe the file (§8.7.5 step 1). The two reads answer two different questions ("what does this document describe?" versus "would the shipped function refuse right now?"), and §8.7.5 fixes which fields come from which. **Its key domain is fixed, and it is two-layered, because the object holds two kinds of fact that were previously flattened into one**: `{snapshot, files, external_cell, worktree, git_op, head}`, where **`state.files` is the map of *runtime-file artefacts*** and its own key domain is closed at **five**: `{checkout_transaction, checkout_lock, external_legacy_state, external_payload, external_run_guard}`. Every member at both levels is always an object — **`null` is not a member value of either map**. The round-14 flat domain `{snapshot, checkout_transaction, checkout_lock, sync_run_guard, external_state, worktree, git_op, head}` is **withdrawn for two independent defects**, and this round fixes both. First, it applied the `{applicable, presence}` totality pair to **all** members, including `snapshot`, `worktree`, `git_op` and `head`, none of which is a file: there is no `Lstat` behind "the working tree is dirty", so `presence: absent` on `state.worktree` was a token with no meaning, and a schema test asserting the pair over every member could only have been satisfied by inventing one. Second, `external_state` was a **composite** — one object standing for two independent files (`.sync-state.yaml` and `.sync-state.v2.yaml`) plus a joint classification — so a single `presence` had to answer for two paths that can be absent, readable, corrupt or symlinked **independently**, which is exactly the conflation the totality pair exists to prevent. **There is no `state.external_state` path anywhere in this document**: the legacy file is `state.files.external_legacy_state`, the v2 payload is `state.files.external_payload`, and the shipped joint classification is `state.external_cell` (below). The renames are total and mechanical: `state.checkout_transaction` → `state.files.checkout_transaction`, `state.checkout_lock` → `state.files.checkout_lock`, `state.sync_run_guard` → **`state.files.external_run_guard`**; no consumer, prose line, skill string, fixture or test may use the old spelling. Each **`state.files.*`** member therefore carries the closed **totality pair** `{applicable, presence}` before anything else: **`applicable`** is `false` on the routes where the artefact cannot exist (the checkout transaction and checkout lock in external mode; the external legacy state, v2 payload and run guard in checkout mode) and `true` everywhere else, and **`presence`** is the closed enum **`absent`** (the `Lstat` returned `ErrNotExist`) / **`readable`** (a regular file that decoded under **that artefact's own** shipped loader) / **`unreadable`** (the path exists but is not a decodable regular file: a non-regular file, an I/O failure, or a decode failure **by that file's own rule**, §8.6.1 step 2a) / **`symlink`** (the `Lstat` reported a symlink, which is recorded and **never followed**, §11), plus **`not-applicable`** where `applicable` is `false`. The round-13 encoding "each member is either `null` (the artefact does not exist / was not applicable in this mode) or an object" stays **withdrawn**: it spelled *absent*, *not applicable on this route* and *present but unreadable* with one token, so a consumer could not tell a feature with no guard from a feature whose guard is a corrupt or symlinked file — the exact cell in which the most dangerous answer, "nothing is running", must never be inferred. **`presence: unreadable` is not one fact but a family, and the family member is published**: every `state.files.*` row carries **`unreadable_reason`**, a closed enum — `not-regular-file` (a directory, socket, device or FIFO at the path), `io-error` (the `Lstat` succeeded on a regular file and the read failed), `decode-error` (the bytes were read and **that artefact's own shipped loader refused them**), `empty-document` (retained in the enum, emitted by no artefact under the per-file decode table of §8.6.1 step 2a) — `null` on every row whose `presence` is not `unreadable`. **What counts as a decode failure is a property of each file, not one rule for all five** (§8.6.1 step 2a, round-16 item 4): `.sync-state.yaml` has no version field and its shipped loader is permissive, so an **empty** legacy document is `readable` as the zero state and the classifier's semantics are preserved; `.sync-state.v2.yaml`'s loader validates its `state_version` as shipped, so a version it rejects is `decode-error`; the **checkout transaction**'s loader validates nothing, so an absent, pre-v2 **or future** `state_version` is `readable` — a future one is then projected as the *shipped continuation refusal* naming the number (§8.6.4), never as a decode error; and the two lock artefacts use their own permissive YAML-structure decode, where `pid: 0` is a readable value and not an unreadable file. Unreadable and malformed are therefore **distinguishable answers, not one bucket**: an operator whose guard file is a directory and an operator whose guard file is truncated YAML need different remedies, and a test that could not tell them apart could not assert either. `unreadable_reason` never changes a verdict: every rank, refusal and `execute_blocked_by` member below treats all four the same way, because none of them can be shown to be dead. Every other member of that artefact — `pid`, `alive`, `self`, `stage`, `token_matches_payload`, … — is `null` unless `presence` is `readable`, and that nullity is a *known unknown* (§4.8), never a `false`. **The consequence is the reason the axis exists: an `unreadable` or `symlink` guard is not an absent guard.** Its liveness is unknown, so `alive` is `null` and never `false`; it can never make the live-owner fact of §8.6.1 cause 3 evaluate to "no owner"; and no document, prose line or test may render that cell as clean, stale or reclaimable. What the two routes then do with it is deliberately different and is fixed in §8.6.1: the plan-only route **projects** the cell as state (with whatever `state-refused` blocker the shipped ladder implies for it, and none where the shipped ladder implies none), while the guarded controlled route **fails closed** — an `unreadable` or `symlink` **owner-signalling** artefact at the guard seam is its own non-waivable `state-refused` blocker, because an owner artefact that cannot be decoded cannot be shown to be dead. **Because the shipped ladder often implies no blocker there, that divergence is published as a field and not only as prose**: every document whose snapshot holds an `unreadable` or `symlink` owner-signalling artefact carries **`owner-artefact-undecodable`** in `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` (§4.4 that row, §4.9 rank 3, §8.6.1 step 2a), so the four-conjunct plan→execute predicate stays exact in exactly the cell where the plan-only document would otherwise read "this will run" over a guarded twin that refuses. The plan-only rendering is allowed to say plainly that the **underlying legacy/unguarded route would ignore the file** — a bare `tws sync <f>` over a corrupt `.sync-run.lock` on a legacy route behaves exactly as it does on `main` (§18.12) — and the controlled-execution block is stated **explicitly** beside it rather than being inferred from that sentence. **`state.snapshot` is `{taken_before_acquisition: true, self_pid}` and holds *probe metadata only***: it describes *when* and *by whom* the observation was made and carries no artefact, no path, no liveness and no verdict — `self_pid` is `os.Getpid()`, and `taken_before_acquisition` is the invariant every other member depends on. It is the one member of `state` that is neither a file row nor a Git probe, which is why it carries neither `{applicable, presence}` nor `applies`. The round-13 `self_artefacts[]` member is **withdrawn**: the snapshot is by construction taken before this invocation creates, acquires or reclaims anything, so the list is `[]` in every document that can exist — the plan-only route acquires nothing, and a guarded execution publishes no document at all (§8.7.6) — which made it a field whose only non-`[]` value was unobservable and whose assertions required a guarded document that does not exist (§15.15f4, §15.20, §15.21). Self-exclusion is published where it is observable, as the per-artefact `self` flag, and is proved by the unit/helper tests of §15.15f4 rather than by a CLI field. Every artefact that names a PID carries `{pid, alive, self}`, where **`alive` is the *independent* signal-probe answer for that recorded PID and nothing else** — `pid > 0 && isProcessAlive(pid)` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:302`) evaluated on the raw PID the artefact records, and `null` whenever `presence` is not `readable` — and **`self` is `pid == state.snapshot.self_pid`**, the shipped self-exclusion conjunct spelled as a published field (`forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:281`; `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, `internal/sync_run_state.go:226`, both of which read `pid != os.Getpid() && isProcessAlive(pid)`). **`alive` must be read, named and documented for exactly what the shipped predicate computes, and no more.** `isProcessAlive` is `os.FindProcess` followed by `Signal(syscall.Signal(0))` and reports `err == nil`, so `alive: true` means precisely *"a process with this PID exists **and this user may signal it**"* — a **signalable PID**, not "the process that wrote this artefact is still running" and not "every live process is detected". Two residuals follow directly and are published as prose in the document's own vocabulary rather than papered over: a live process owned by **another user** answers `EPERM`, so the probe reports `alive: false` for a process that is genuinely running (a **false-dead**, which makes the guard *less* conservative, never more); and a PID the operating system has **reused** answers `nil` for an unrelated process, so `alive: true` can outlive the writer (a **false-live**, which makes the guard more conservative and can, on the guarded route, refuse a run whose real owner exited). Neither is fixable with a PID alone — no shipped artefact records a process **birth identity** (start time, boot id, or a held file descriptor), so nothing on disk can distinguish "PID 4242, still the guard's owner" from "PID 4242, recycled" — and the residual window is therefore **stated, bounded and deliberately left open in v1**: portable birth-identity stamping of `.sync-run.lock`/`.checkout-sync.lock` (and the reclaim predicates that would consume it) is its **own follow-up feature**, not a silent widening of this one (§18, §19.21). Every claim in this document is written against that predicate: no sentence, field description, refusal detail, skill string or test may say "the owner is alive", "the process is running" or "identity is verified" where the evidence is a signal probe — the honest form is "a signalable PID owns this artefact", which is exactly what `alive` is asserted to mean in §15.15f/f2/f3. `alive` is deliberately **not** `SyncExternalState.GuardLive` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:415-418`), which folds an ownership test into liveness and reports `false` for a guard whose PID is alive whenever its token does not match `payload.OwnerToken`: that conflation is correct for the shipped "is *this run* still running?" question and wrong for ours, because another process's guard is a live process that can be moving refs (§8.6.1 cause 3, §9 D3). Ownership is published **beside** liveness, never inside it: `state.files.external_run_guard` is populated by the **dedicated safe artefact inspector** of §8.6.1 step 2a — never by widening the shipped `classifySyncState`'s `AlwaysReadGuard` flag, which would change unguarded behaviour (§8.6.1 step 2, §8.6.7) — and it adds `{token_matches_payload}`, which means exactly what it says — **the guard's `token` equals `payload.OwnerToken`** — and is therefore the **negation** of the shipped `SyncExternalState.GuardForeign()` predicate (`internal/sync_run_state.go:434-436`), never an alias for it. Written out: `token_matches_payload = (guard.Token == payload.OwnerToken)`, so **`GuardForeign() == true` publishes `token_matches_payload: false`** and a payload-owned guard publishes `true`. It is `null` — a known unknown, never `false` — whenever the comparison cannot be made at all: no readable guard, no readable payload, or an empty `payload.OwnerToken`, which are precisely the three cases `GuardForeign()` collapses onto `false` for its own purposes (`s.Guard != nil && s.Payload != nil && s.Payload.OwnerToken != "" && …`). The previous draft called this field "the shipped `GuardForeign()` predicate", which inverted it: it would have published `token_matches_payload: true` for the *foreign* guard and `false` for the run's own, turning every ownership assertion in §8.6.1, §9 and §15.15f2 upside down. The polarity is fixed here, once, and every consumer of the field reads equality — so a consumer can distinguish "our run is live", "someone else's run is live" and "nothing is live" without either fact standing in for the other. **The exact shape of every member — the five file rows and the five non-file ones — is fixed in the two blocks immediately below this table, and no other spelling of them exists.** **`state.files.checkout_transaction.lock_pid` is informational and is *not* a PID-bearing artefact in the sense above**: it carries no `alive` and no `self` member, and nothing in this document may derive liveness, ownership or a refusal from it (see the transaction rule below). **`state.git_op` publishes two different questions and keeps them apart** (§8.6.2, §8.6.8): `in_progress` is the **blocking** answer and mirrors the shipped `gitOperationInProgress` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:396-406`) exactly — the four markers `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply` (either directory), `MERGE_HEAD`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, `REVERT_HEAD`, each resolved through `git rev-parse --git-path <name>` and `os.Stat`, with **any** resolution or stat failure answering `false` just as `gitPathExists` does — while `kind` is the **non-blocking descriptive label** from the broader `probeActiveGitOp` inventory (`internal/stack_status.go:339-401`), whose marker list additionally contains **`BISECT_LOG`**. `kind_source` names which of the two produced the label (`git-operation-in-progress` / `active-op-probe`), so a reader can never mistake a `kind: bisect` for a refusal (§8.6.2). The `state.observed` spelling of the previous draft is **withdrawn** — it named the same object twice (`state` in the top-level key set, `state.observed` in this table) and no consumer could tell whether `state.observed.checkout_lock` or `state.checkout_lock` was the contract. There is one object, it is `state`, and observation is what the whole object *is* (§9): the plan **reports** these facts and never acquires, steals or clears any of them. **The live-owner fact of §8.6.1 cause 3 is derived from this snapshot and has exactly four conjuncts** — the artefact is an **owner-signalling artefact** (see immediately below), it is **present in the snapshot** with `presence: readable` (pre-existing, not created by this invocation), `alive` is `true`, and `self` is `false` — i.e. a **pre-existing foreign PID that answers the signal probe**. **The owner-signalling set is closed at two members, and they are both *lock files*: `state.files.checkout_lock` and `state.files.external_run_guard`.** `state.files.checkout_transaction` is **not** a member, and the round-13 wording "or a checkout transaction whose lock PID does" is **withdrawn**. The reason is a property of the artefact, not a policy preference: `.checkout-sync.lock` and `.sync-run.lock` are **acquired and released around a run** (`writeLockExclusive`/`ReleaseCheckoutLock`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:222-253`; `writeSyncGuardExclusive`/`ReleaseSyncRunGuard`), so their existence is itself the concurrency claim, whereas `tx.LockPID` is a **persisted field of a recovery record that deliberately outlives its process** — written once at `internal/checkout_sync.go:660` and rewritten at `:743` on every `--continue` — and the transaction survives precisely so an operator can resume after that process is gone (§12). Treating it as an owner signal makes a stale transaction whose PID the OS has since **reused** a permanently unresumable feature: the `--continue` that is supposed to clear it would refuse itself on the strength of its own recovery file, with no command that could ever succeed. So `lock_pid` is published as an informational, `alive`-less field, it never suppresses a fetch and never contributes a blocker, and a transaction's concurrency question is answered **only** by the checkout lock beside it — which is exactly what the shipped code does, since `AcquireCheckoutLock`/`forceAcquireCheckoutLock` consult `LockInfo.PID` from the lock file and never `tx.LockPID` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:185-220`, `:262-285`). The transaction still refuses runs, loudly, but as the shipped **transaction-exists** state fact (`:564-566`), which needs no liveness at all. Token ownership stays irrelevant to it, and "foreign" here means a different process, never `token_matches_payload: false`. That derived fact is what decides the fetch suppression of §8.6.1 and, on the guarded execution route, the non-waivable `state-refused` concurrency refusal, so both its inputs and its exclusions are published facts, not internal ones | never (object; individual members null) |
| `summary.plannability` | the **rows-less discriminator**, a closed enum: `rows` (`entries` is non-empty), `empty` (`entries` is `[]` and row derivation **succeeded** — the stack loaded, sorted and selected, and the described run simply has no entry: an empty `stack.yaml`, a selection that legitimately matches nothing, or a continuation whose `RemainingRebaseEntries` is empty, §8.6.4a), `unavailable` (`entries` is `[]` because row derivation was **prevented** — `plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable`, `selection-refused`, or a `state-refused` cell that leaves no run to describe, such as `nothing to continue — no sync in progress` or `no transaction to continue`). It exists because "zero rows because there is no work" and "zero rows because I could not look" are opposite facts that were previously distinguishable only by enumerating refusal kinds, and it is what selects the aggregate profile below | never |
| `summary.entries` / `summary.deferred_destinations` / `summary.conditional_strategies` | counts over the **published rows** | never |
| `summary.max_entry_candidates` | the largest per-entry `candidate_count` among entries with a non-null count | `null` when every count is null, **including both rows-less profiles** |
| `summary.total_candidates` | sum over entries **only when every countable entry is countable** — `determinacy = not-applicable` rows contribute a real `0` and never make the total `null` (§4.1 skip rule) | `null` when any entry is `unknown`, and `null` on a `plannability: unavailable` document |
| `summary.total_candidates_lower_bound` | sum over the countable entries | `null` on a `plannability: unavailable` document; otherwise never |
| `summary.entries_with_unknown_candidates` | how many rows are `determinacy = unknown` — **`not-applicable` rows are excluded**, because they are known to replay nothing (§4.1 skip rule) | never (it counts published rows, so it is `0` on both rows-less profiles) |
| `summary.collateral_exposed_entries` | how many selected rows are **known** to risk having their own tip rewritten by an earlier entry (§4.3) | never (counts published rows) |
| `summary.entries_with_unknown_collateral` | how many rows publish `collateral_refs: null` / `collateral_exposed: null`, i.e. how many rows the two facts above exclude (§4.8) | never (counts published rows) |
| `summary.collateral_refs` | union of the local branch refs **at risk** across rows with a **known** set — an **upper bound**, exactly like the per-row sets (§4.3) — each element the same repo-qualified `{repo, ref, sha, stack_owned}` tuple as the row-level field and **sorted by `(repo, ref)`** | `null` when no selected row has a known set **and** on a `plannability: unavailable` document; `[]` when every known set is empty, **including a `plannability: empty` document**, whose run demonstrably moves no ref |
