This is the one constant the schema makes nullable, and it is nullable for the same reason every other unknown is (§4.8) |
| `summary.collateral_refs_unowned` | how many of those refs are `stack_owned: false` — the count that makes an unowned blast radius visible without reading every row | `null` exactly when `summary.collateral_refs` is `null` |

| `guard.limits` | the **single, total encoding of the effective guard**, and the *only* one: a per-key object `{max_replay_per_entry, max_replay_total}` whose every member is itself the object **`{value, origin}`**. `value` is a non-negative integer **or `null`** when that key has no effective limit; `origin` is the closed enum `none` (unguarded — no flag, nothing persisted for that key) / `flags` (fresh run, command line) / `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` (a continuation inheriting the interrupted run's guard from a v2 payload or from **any** checkout transaction, v2 or pre-v2, whether or not an identical flag was repeated) / `flags-persisted-continuation` (a continuation whose persisted state exists but held **no** value for this key, armed by this invocation's flag — the member the earlier draft spelled `flags-v2-continuation`, renamed because a **pre-v2 checkout transaction is also persistable state**, §8.7.4, §10.3) / `flags-legacy-continuation` (**legacy external only**: `.sync-state.yaml` has nowhere to persist a limit, so the flag must be repeated on every invocation). The keys resolve **independently**, by the total rule of §8.7.4: flags on a fresh invocation; for each key on a continuation, the persisted value when the key is not supplied, the supplied value when nothing was persisted for it, and the (identical) value when both agree. **`0` is a legal, meaningful limit** — "refuse if any selected entry replays anything at all" — so the schema, the persistence and every comparison distinguish *absent* from *zero* (§8.3.2a, §8.7.4, §10.3), and the absent case is spelled **`{value: null, origin: "none"}`** — never a `null` member, never an omitted key, and never a second parallel field. A per-key conflict between a supplied flag and a persisted value is not resolved silently: it is `refusal.kind = guard-limit-mismatch` **naming the key** (§4.9, §8.7.4). The fingerprint binds each key's **effective `value`** as published; `origin` is a **descriptive source label and is not a tuple member** (§5.3.2). There is deliberately **no config source** (§8.3.4), so a fresh no-flag run is unguarded by construction | **never `null`, at any level**: the object is always present, both keys are always present, and each carries `{value, origin}` — an unguarded run publishes `{value: null, origin: "none"}` twice |
| `guard.limit_conflicts[]` | the **per-key record of a rejected limit change**, published exactly when a continuation supplies a limit that disagrees with the one its interrupted run persisted (§8.7.4, §4.9 rank 7): one object per conflicting key, `{key, effective_value, effective_origin, supplied_value}`, sorted by `key`. `effective_value`/`effective_origin` repeat what `guard.limits.<key>` already publishes — **the persisted value stays the effective one**, because a resume is guarded by the run that created its state and a flag cannot loosen or tighten it behind that run's back — and `supplied_value` is the number this invocation *attempted*, which appears **nowhere else in the document**: without it the operator is told "your flag disagrees" and cannot see with what, and a consumer cannot tell a `50`-against-`10` conflict from a `0`-against-`10` one. It is a **derived, non-fingerprint** field (§5.3.2): the effective limits are bound, an attempted-and-rejected value is not part of the work being authorised. Keys that agree, keys that inherit and keys this invocation arms produce **no** row here | `[]` — the ordinary case, on every fresh run and every non-conflicting continuation |
| ~~`guard.limits_source`~~ | **withdrawn this round.** The previous draft published the values in `guard.limits` and their origins in a parallel `guard.limits_source` object, so every consumer had to join two maps and reconcile two spellings of "absent" (`guard.limits.<key>: null` versus `guard.limits_source.<key>: null` versus the enum member `none`). Three encodings of one fact is two too many, and the dual shape made the fingerprint row (`{value, origin}`) look like a third. The origin is now a member of each key's object in `guard.limits`, the enum is unchanged, and **no document, test, skill or example may emit or read a `guard.limits_source` key** | — |
| `guard.evaluation[]` | per evaluated limit: `{id, limit, value, basis, entry, verdict, unknown_kind, unknown_entries}` — **eight members, all eight always present on every row**, with the per-member contract of §8.3.2a and never an omitted key. `id` is a stable, canonical identifier for the evaluation row (`<limit>:<entry>` for a per-entry row, `<limit>` for an aggregate one) so `approval.covers` can reference it exactly, and it is **unique within the array by construction** — one row per `(limit key, entry)` pair, one aggregate row per limit key — which is what makes the canonical sort below total. **`limit` is the numeric effective threshold this row was compared against**, i.e. the `guard.limits.<key>.value` of the key the row's `id` names — a non-negative integer, **never `null` on an emitted row** (a key with `{value: null}` is not in force and emits no rows at all, §8.3.2a) and never the `{value, origin}` object, never the key's *name* (the `id` carries that) and never a second copy of `value`. **`entry` is the row's logical entry name on a `per-entry` row and `null` on every `total` and `lower-bound` row**, because an aggregate row is about the run, not about an entry; it is the same logical name `entries[].name` publishes, never a Git branch (§4.5). `basis` is a **closed enum** — `per-entry` (this row's own `candidate_count`), `total` (the exact sum, every entry countable) or `lower-bound` (the sum over countable entries only, because some row is `unknown`, §8.3.2); `verdict` is a **closed enum** — `within-limit` / `exceeded` / `waived` (exceeded **and** covered by a matching token, §5.3.1) / `unknown` (the limit could not be compared against this row's value at all). `unknown_kind` is `null` unless `verdict` is `unknown`, and then it is `deferred-resolvable` (the JIT seam of §5.2 will resolve the value one entry later) or `not-resolvable` (nothing later resolves it — the `merge-recreation` row of §4.2, whose config is still true at the seam — round-26's second source, the withdrawn `merge-recreation-unknown` row, is gone with round-27 item 1 — and a `probe-failed` row). `unknown_entries` is `null` on every `per-entry` row and on every exact `total` row, and, on a `lower-bound` aggregate row, the **count of rows contributing an unknown remainder** — the number that makes "at least this many, plus N rows nobody could count" machine-readable. Emission, comparison, verdict assignment, the per-member nullability table and the array's canonical sort are total and are fixed in §8.3.2a. **The array is sorted by `id`, bytewise, ascending** — the ids embed the entry name deterministically, so this is a stable total order over a set that is unique by construction, and it is the same order §4.7 canonicalizes every other list with (§4.7; the array itself is a fingerprint **non-member**, §5.3.2). A `waived` row stays in the array with its `limit`, `value` and `entry` intact: waiving is a change of verdict, never a deletion of evidence | `[]` when no limit applies. **On a rows-less document it is not blanket `[]`** (§4.4 profile table, §8.3.2a): a `plannability: empty` document with a supplied `max_replay_total` emits exactly one `total` row with `value: 0` and `verdict: within-limit`, because the described run really does replay nothing; a supplied `max_replay_per_entry` emits nothing there, because there is no entry; and a `plannability: unavailable` document emits `[]` under **either** limit, because no plan was established and nothing was measured |
| `guard.indeterminacy_policy` | which policy the invocation applied to `verdict: unknown` rows with `unknown_kind: deferred-resolvable` — `jit-deferred` (recommended and the v1 default: they do **not** refuse up front and are re-evaluated at the JIT seam, §5.2, §8.3.2) or `refuse-up-front` (the alternative §19.9 keeps open). A `not-resolvable` unknown refuses under **both** policies, because no later seam can rescue it. The field is published so a consumer never has to infer the policy from `would_refuse` | never |
| `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` | the **raw** guard verdict, computed as if no token had been supplied: `true` when any `guard.evaluation[]` row is `exceeded`, or is `unknown` with `unknown_kind: not-resolvable`, or is `unknown` with `unknown_kind: deferred-resolvable` **and** `guard.indeterminacy_policy` is `refuse-up-front`. Under the recommended `jit-deferred` policy a `deferred-resolvable` unknown therefore leaves it `false` — the row is visible in `guard.evaluation[]` and counted in `summary.entries_with_unknown_candidates`, and it is re-checked before its own rebase (§5.2, §8.3.2a). This is the number-only question — "is this run bigger or less determinate than my limits allow?" — and it is what an operator compares against a re-plan | never (boolean); `false` when no limit applies |

With no token supplied, or a non-matching one, it equals `guard.would_refuse_without_approval`. Those are the only two escapes, and they are the same window §9 already bounds; the predicate is exact over everything the document could see. `guard.would_refuse` never implies `runnable: false`; a document exists only on the plan-only route, so both fields are always **projections** (§8.7.6) | never (boolean); `false` when no limit applies |

Every member is **non-waivable**: a matching token never empties this array (§5.3.1). The v1 domain is **closed at five** (round-23 item 3 added the fourth; round-25 item 2 adds the fifth) — **`live-owner-concurrency`** (the pre-existing live foreign owner of §8.6.1 cause 3, which on the plan-only route suppresses the fetch and, where the shipped ladder refuses nothing, leaves `runnable: true` while the guarded twin refuses at rank 3), **`owner-artefact-undecodable`** (added this round: the snapshot holds an **owner-signalling** artefact — `state.files.checkout_lock` or `state.files.external_run_guard` — whose `presence` is **`unreadable`** or **`symlink`**, so its liveness is `null` and the guarded controlled route fails closed at rank 3, while the shipped ladder for that cell frequently refuses nothing at all — **narrowed in round 17 to exactly the cells the two native acquisition ladders would not already refuse**, since a corrupt or unreadable *regular* guard/lock file is rejected by `ClaimSyncRunGuard`/`AcquireCheckoutLock` in their own words and is therefore a shipped rank 3 refusal with no divergence to publish, leaving the member to the symlink-that-decodes cell and to an **applicable** artefact on a path the running route never consults — the legacy not-applicable`, which is not an undecodable presence, carries no `unreadable_reason` and can never emit the token — so the cross-mode cell earlier drafts named, `state.files.checkout_lock` under an sets `runnable: false`, so it is listed here for totality rather than to add information), **`fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate`** (§4.9 rank 5.05, round-23 item 3 — likewise `runnable: false`, share: that run still issues the fetch, which either dies at `refusing to fetch into branch '<ref>' checked out at '<path>'` and carries on against stale refs, or prunes a covered local branch out from under a worktree's HEAD). **The second member exists for exactly the reason the first does**: without it, a legacy-route document over a corrupt or symlinked `.sync-run.lock` publishes `runnable: true`, `guard.would_refuse: false`, `refusal.kind: null` and `execute_blocked_by: []` — four fields that together promise a run its guarded twin refuses — and the four-conjunct predicate would be *wrong* rather than merely incomplete. It is derived from the same step 2 snapshot, so it is total over `plannability` in the same way; it is published **whether or not** the shipped ladder also refuses that cell; it is **non-waivable**; and it is independent of `live-owner-concurrency` — a document may carry both (a live foreign checkout lock beside an unreadable guard), in which case the array holds both members, sorted. **The plan-only rendering says both things plainly**: the guarded route will refuse, *and* the underlying unguarded route would ignore the file and behave exactly as it does on `main` (§18.12). The two sentences are not in tension and neither may be dropped: one describes the controlled path, the other the frozen one. Which artefacts the rule ranges over — every owner-signalling artefact **within that narrowed set**, or only the one the route about to run would consult — is the single open sub-question of §19.22; **the token, its rank, its non-waivability and its publication are settled here regardless of that choice**, and only the *set of cells* that emit it moves. It exists because the previous draft published a plan whose `runnable`, `would_refuse` and `refusal.kind` all said "this will run" over a cell the guarded run refuses; that counterexample is eliminated by publishing the fact rather than by redefining `runnable` (§8.6.1 cause 3, §8.7.1, §9). A member is published **whether or not** the same observation also produced a `blockers[]` row: where the shipped ladder refuses the cell too, the kind appears in both, and the two agree by construction. It is a **derived answer, not work**, so it is a fingerprint non-member (§5.3.2), and it is never `null` (§4.8). **It is also total over `plannability`, and round 25 states which members a rows-less document can really carry** (item 7): `live-owner-concurrency` and `owner-artefact-undecodable` are derived from the step 2 snapshot, which precedes the stack load and the sort, so they are published identically on a rows-bearing document, on a `plannability: empty` one and on a `plannability: unavailable` one; **`fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` and `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` are reachable on a rows-less document too** — on the checkout `--fetch` route, whose single `workspace-repo-root` context is resolved and decided **before** the stack load and the `len(plan) == 0` return (`internal/checkout_sync.go:611-654`, §4.9 rank 5.05/5.06, §15.18b b2) — so **`fetch-context-indeterminate` is the only member that stays rows-less-unreachable**, needing two or more candidate contexts whose entries would themselves be rows. The earlier two-member reading of this sentence is withdrawn as stale rather than narrowed — the profile table defers to §8.6.1 cause 3 and step 2a rather than zeroing this array where no plan was derived | `[]` |
| `refusal.kind` | stable enum: `plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable`, `selection-refused`, `state-refused`, `preflight-refused`, `restore-blocked`, `fetch-context-indeterminate`, `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate`, `fetch-local-branch-checked-out`, **`invalid-git-config`** (round-27 item 3), **`identity-not-utf8`** (round-27 item 7), `repo-unavailable`, **`base-execution-store-divergent`** (round-35 item 2), `head-ref-missing`, `prunable-worktree`, `branch-checked-out-elsewhere`, `external-rebase-in-progress`, `context-dirty`, `base-unset`, `base-ref-missing`, `cutoff-unresolvable`, `probe-failed`, `selection-hazard`, `guard-limit-mismatch`, `approval-without-limits`, `approval-mismatch`, `revalidation-mismatch`, `indeterminate-entry`, `limit-per-entry`, `limit-total`. **Exactly one** value is published, chosen by the closed precedence of §4.9 over the **effective** verdicts: a limit violation covered by a matching token has verdict `waived` and is therefore **not** a candidate for `refusal.kind` at all, which is what lets `--plan --approve-plan <fp>` publish `refusal.kind: null` for a run that will really execute (§5.3.1, §4.9). The same token is the machine-readable kind on a guard-generated refusal's marker line (§8.7.6) | `null` when nothing would refuse |
| `refusal.detail` | the sanitized human sentence that accompanies `kind`, naming the entry and field | `null` when `kind` is `null` |
| `approval.fingerprint` | the cross-invocation approval token of §5.3, published by **every document that satisfies all three clauses of the usable-token predicate — it describes approvable work, it carries at least one effective replay limit, and its `encoding_issues` is `[]`** — in JSON as this field, and in the human rendering as the labelled final line (§8.3.5) — and by **no other invocation**: an executing guarded run never prints, echoes or otherwise yields a token (§8.7.6, §8.7.7). **Lexical form, fixed and binding**: exactly **64 characters** matching `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` — the full lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the canonical invariant tuple (§5.3), with no prefix, no separator and no truncation. Comparison is **byte-exact and case-sensitive** after trimming leading/trailing whitespace on the supplied value **only**; an uppercase or abbreviated token is `approval-mismatch`, never a near-match. On a `--continue` invocation it is a **continuation-scoped** token over the remaining work (§8.7.4) | **non-`null` exactly when all three clauses of the usable-token predicate hold — (a) the document describes approvable work: `entries` is non-empty **or** `push.targets` is non-empty **or** `restore.applies` is `true`; **and** (b) at least one key of `guard.limits` has a non-`null` `value`; **and** (c) `encoding_issues` is `[]`.** The predicate is exactly these three clauses, here and in every restatement; the two-clause form of earlier drafts is **withdrawn** wherever it survived (round-29 item 3). Otherwise `null`, and the human final line is the literal `none` (§8.3.5). Clause (a) is the work predicate refined over three drafts (`entries == []`, then `&& push.targets == []`, then `&& restore.applies == false`): a run interrupted at `stage: pushing` (external, §8.6.4a) or at `stage: completed` with a pending push (checkout) has **no** remaining rebase entry and **does** have remaining work — a `git push --force-with-lease` per branch, the most consequential thing a sync does — and a checkout transaction resumed at `stage: restoring` has neither rebase rows nor push targets, yet its resume still **switches HEAD in the operator's one physical checkout**, deletes the transaction and releases the lock (§8.6.4a). So a rows-less document with a non-empty `push.targets[]`, **or with `restore.applies: true`**, still mints a **real 64-hex token** over the tuple of §5.3.2 (whose `entries[]` is legitimately empty and whose `push_targets[]`/`restore` are not). Clause (b) is added this round and follows from a rule that was already binding: **`--approve-plan` requires at least one effective limit** (§8.5.1) — a flag error on a fresh run, rank 7.5 `approval-without-limits` on a resume — so a token minted where no limit is in force could never be supplied to anything, in any invocation, and would be a receipt for an operation that cannot exist. **A limitless plan is not a degraded plan**: its rows, aggregates, collateral, blockers, fetch block and `state` are all real and complete, and it is the ordinary `--plan` an operator runs to look; it simply cannot authorise a guarded run, and the exit is to re-run the plan with the limits the operator intends to guard with (`--max-replay-per-entry` / `--max-replay-total`), which is what `approval.usable` and the three clause booleans of `approval.covers` — `has_work`, `requires_limits`, `encoding_safe` (round-30 item 4) — say in fields. `null` therefore covers the three clause failures and every combination of them: every genuinely workless document (`plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable`, `selection-refused`, a `state-refused` `nothing to continue`, a stack with no entries, and any continuation whose remaining set, push set **and** restoring work are all empty) fails (a); every **limitless** document however much work it describes fails (b); every document with a non-empty `encoding_issues[]` fails (c); and their intersections fail more than one. Conversely the token is **never** null when work exists, a limit is in force and `encoding_issues` is `[]` — not because `guard.would_refuse` is `true`, not because a blocker exists, and not because `runnable` is `false`. **Round 27 adds the one exception, and states it as a third precondition rather than as a caveat** (item 7), **which round 28 restates in the field the schema now carries** (item 4): (c) **`encoding_issues` is `[]`** — equivalently, every bound identity string of the tuple is valid UTF-8. The predicate is therefore exactly three clauses, and **every restatement of it in this document, in §8.3.6, in §8.5.1, in §8.6.3, in the profile table, in the docs, in the skills and in the tests carries all three**: (a) approvable work, (b) at least one effective limit, (c) no encoding issues. Where clause (c) fails the document publishes `approval.fingerprint: null` and `approval.usable: false` and mints nothing — because a token whose plan cannot be *shown* to the operator without loss is a receipt for a run nobody read (§5.3.2a, §4.9 rank 5.08, §11) — and the evidence is the top-level `encoding_issues[]` array, never prose. **The rank 5.08 blocker and `runnable: false` are the *narrower* consequence, and round 28 separates the two** (item 4): they attach only to a document that **would otherwise mint** — one satisfying (a) and (b), or one on which `--approve-plan` was supplied — because that is the only cell in which the loss has an effect worth stopping. A **limitless** plan over the same repository fails (b) already, mints nothing for that reason, publishes `encoding_issues[]` so the operator sees the fact, and publishes **no** rank 5.08 blocker and **no** `runnable: false`: the underlying `tws sync` really does run those branches, and a document that called it unrunnable would be lying about the command. The exception is otherwise deliberately narrow: it is a property of the bound strings, not of the document's rendering, and every other document mints exactly as before |
| `approval.usable` | the **single boolean a consumer branches on before trying to use a token**: `true` **iff** `approval.fingerprint` is non-`null`, i.e. iff all **three** preconditions above hold — approvable work, an effective limit, and `encoding_issues == []`. It is published rather than inferred because "the token is `null`" has **three** materially different causes with three different operator actions (round-27 item 7 adds the third), and a consumer that only sees `null` cannot tell them apart: no work (nothing to approve — act on `summary.plannability`, `entries`, `push.targets`, `restore.applies`), no effective limit (something to approve, nothing to guard it with — re-run the plan with a limit flag, `approval.covers.requires_limits`), and a bound identity that is **not valid UTF-8** (something to approve, no way to show it faithfully — act on `encoding_issues[]`, whose rows name the field id, the byte length, the base64 and the digest, §5.3.2a). **The third cause is legible with or without the rank 5.08 blocker** (round-28 item 4): on a document that would otherwise mint, the blocker is there too and `runnable` is `false`; on a limitless one, `encoding_issues[]` is non-empty while `runnable` stays `true` and no blocker is published, and a consumer distinguishes the two by reading the array rather than by inferring from `runnable`. It is a **derived, non-fingerprint** field (§5.3.2): it answers a question *about* a token, exactly like `supplied` and `accepted`. **Round 30 makes the diagnosis machine-total rather than leaving it to prose** (item 4): the three causes are published as the three clause booleans `approval.covers.has_work`, `approval.covers.requires_limits` and `approval.covers.encoding_safe`, so `(usable, has_work, requires_limits, encoding_safe)` separates no work, no limits and an encoding issue — and every combination of them — without a consumer inferring anything from `runnable`, from a blocker's presence or from the count of `encoding_issues[]` | never (boolean) |
| `approval.scope` | `full-run` / `remaining-work` — which plan the token authorises. A `--plan --continue` always mints `remaining-work`, and an initial full-run token can never match a continuation, because the remaining plan is not the plan that was approved (§8.7.4) | never |
| `approval.covers` | an **object**, not prose, so a consumer can compute the waiver rather than parse a sentence: `{scope, waived_evaluation_ids[], waived_kinds[], hard_blockers_waived, has_work, requires_limits, encoding_safe, note}` — **eight members since round-30 item 4, which makes the token's cause machine-total**. `scope` mirrors `approval.scope` (`full-run` / `remaining-work`); `waived_evaluation_ids[]` lists the **`guard.evaluation[].id` values** a matching token would move from `exceeded` to `waived`, sorted bytewise; `waived_kinds[]` is the derived, sorted subset of `{limit-per-entry, limit-total}` those ids imply; `hard_blockers_waived` is the constant **`false`** — published as a field rather than stated in prose, because "an approval never waives a hard blocker" is the property most likely to be assumed away by a consumer (§5.3.1). **The next three are the three clauses of the usable-token predicate, one boolean each, published in the polarity that reads as the answer to "is this clause satisfied?"** — and each is a fact about *this document*, computable with or without a supplied token: **`has_work` is clause (a)**, `true` iff `entries` is non-empty **or** `push.targets` is non-empty **or** `restore.applies` is `true`; **`requires_limits` is clause (b) *inverted*, and keeps its round-12 name and polarity so no consumer or test breaks**: `true` **iff** *no* key of `guard.limits` has a non-`null` `value`, i.e. iff this document has no effective limit for an approval to cover and therefore mints no token however much work it describes (§8.5.1, `approval.fingerprint` above); **`encoding_safe` is clause (c)**, `true` iff `encoding_issues` is `[]`. **The quadruple `(usable, has_work, requires_limits, encoding_safe)` is therefore total over the three clauses and their every combination, and round 30 withdraws the pair-only reading** (item 4): `(usable, requires_limits)` alone could not distinguish "no work" from "an encoding issue", both of which it reported as `(false, false)`, so the sentence "`(false, false)` means a limit is in force but there is nothing to approve" was wrong in exactly the cell round 27 added. `usable` is the conjunction — `has_work && !requires_limits && encoding_safe` — and is published anyway, so a consumer branches on one boolean and diagnoses on three. The eight reachable cells, all of them legal documents: `(true, true, false, true)` a usable token; `(false, false, false, true)` nothing to approve (act on `summary.plannability`/`entries`/`push.targets`/`restore.applies`); `(false, true, true, true)` work but no guard — re-plan with `--max-replay-per-entry`/`--max-replay-total`; `(false, true, false, false)` work and a guard but an unshowable identity — act on `encoding_issues[]`; and the four multi-clause failures `(false, false, true, true)`, `(false, false, false, false)`, `(false, true, true, false)`, `(false, false, true, false)`, each of which fails exactly the clauses its booleans name. `(true, …)` with any clause boolean unsatisfied is unreachable by construction and a schema test asserts it. `note` is a fixed sanitized sentence naming §5.3.1. When no limit is exceeded, `waived_evaluation_ids` and `waived_kinds` are `[]` — a token that waives nothing is still a valid identity check | never (object; the two lists may be empty) |
| `approval.supplied` | `true` when `--approve-plan <token>` was given on this invocation, including `--plan --approve-plan` | never (boolean) |
| `approval.accepted` | whether the supplied token matched this document's fingerprint bytewise. Under `--plan --approve-plan` the document still exits 0 and carries `refusal.kind = approval-mismatch` when it did not (§8.3.5). Against a document whose `approval.fingerprint` is `null` — **no approvable work, or no effective limit** — it is **`false`** and `refusal.kind` stays whatever the document's own top-ranked kind is: a token can never match "no plan", and reporting `approval-mismatch` there would tell the operator to re-plan when the real problem is that no plan exists or that nothing is being guarded (§4.9). On the limitless cell the document's own kind is `approval-without-limits` on a resume (rank 7.5) and the invocation is a flag error on a fresh run, so the operator is told the actionable fact rather than a mismatch. A rows-less document that **does** carry `push.targets[]`, **or `restore.applies: true`**, and has an effective limit, is not such a case: it has a real token, so a supplied token is compared against it and a mismatch is a genuine `approval-mismatch` | `null` when `approval.supplied` is `false` |

**The exact shape of every member, stated once.** The five **file** rows all carry `{applicable, presence, unreadable_reason}` and then their own decoded fields, every one of which is `null` unless `presence` is `readable`. **The totality triple is not uniformly non-null, and this document states the rule rather than a slogan** (round-18 item 5): **`applicable` and `presence` are never `null`** — presence in particular is always one of `absent`/`readable`/`unreadable`/`symlink`/`not-applicable`, which is what makes "not measured" unrepresentable here — while **`unreadable_reason` is `null` on every `presence` other than `unreadable`**, because a reason without an unreadable presence is a contradiction and an unreadable presence without one is an unfinished inspector (§8.6.1 step 2a, §15.20, §15.21). Round 15's "no member of the triple is ever `null`" is withdrawn: it was never implementable against the inspector this document specifies.

The **non-file** members carry no `presence` and no `unreadable_reason`, because there is no path to `Lstat` behind any of them; each carries `applies`, which is the *route* question the file rows answer with `applicable`:

- **`state.snapshot` = `{taken_before_acquisition, self_pid}`** — probe metadata only, as fixed above. No `applies`: it is true of every route.
- **`state.external_cell` = `{applies, cell}`** — the shipped joint classification `ClassifyExternalSyncState` returns (`internal/sync_run_state.go:343-425`), which is a **function of two file rows** (`external_legacy_state` × `external_payload`) and therefore belongs to neither. `applies` is `true` in external mode and `false` in checkout, where `cell` is `null`. It is the home of the `cell` member the withdrawn composite carried; `marker_present` moved to the legacy row and `payload_version` to the payload row's `state_version`, because each is a property of one file. It is **derived, never probed twice**: the same classification the shipped ladder consumes (§8.6.7).
- **`state.worktree` = `{applies, dirty, probe_ok}`** — checkout's shipped whole-repo gate `gitWorkingTreeDirty` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:420-426`, refused at `:570-577`), full `status --porcelain`, untracked files and submodules **included**. `applies: true` in checkout only; in external the shipped route has no whole-repo dirty gate at all, so `applies: false`, `dirty`/`probe_ok` are `null`, and the tracked-dirty question is answered **per row** by `context.dirty` (§4.1, §5.4.7), which is a different predicate for a different reason.
- **`state.git_op` = `{applies, in_progress, kind, kind_source}`** — **checkout-only**, per the mode rule below, and **round 25 closes its two value domains** (item 6), which earlier rounds described only by example and left `null` doing two different jobs. **`kind` is the closed enum `none` / `rebase` / `merge` / `cherry-pick` / `revert` / `bisect` / `probe-failed`, plus the `null` sentinel used *only* where `applies` is `false`.** The first six are `probeActiveGitOp`'s own labels, byte-for-byte and in its own marker order — `rebase-merge` and `rebase-apply` both report `rebase`, then `MERGE_HEAD`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, `REVERT_HEAD`, `BISECT_LOG`, else `StackStatusOpNone` = `"none"` (`internal/stack_status.go:34,339-351,391-399`) — so the plan invents no vocabulary and a consumer can compare the two surfaces directly. **`probe-failed` is the seventh, and it replaces the previous draft's second use of `null`**: where `probeActiveGitOp` returns an error (a missing `.git`, an unreadable or malformed `gitdir:` pointer, a vanished or non-directory target, a non-`ENOENT` marker stat), the label is `probe-failed` — an answer, not an absence — while `null` now means one thing only, "this route has no such fact". **`kind_source` is the closed enum `executor-markers` / `active-op-probe` / `null`**, naming *which* inventory produced `kind`: `executor-markers` for the four the executor's own `gitOperationInProgress` consults (`rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`, `MERGE_HEAD`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, `REVERT_HEAD`, resolved through `gitPathExists`), `active-op-probe` for a label only the wider status probe can produce — `bisect`, `none` and `probe-failed` — and `null` exactly where `applies` is `false`. **`in_progress` follows the executor and nothing else**: `true` iff one of the four executor markers exists, `false` otherwise — including a `bisect`-only repository and including a `probe-failed` cell, where `gitPathExists`'s `false`-on-any-error bias is the executor's own answer and the plan mirrors it rather than fabricating a refusal (§8.6.2). **The four cells are therefore total and mutually exclusive**: external → `{applies: false, in_progress: null, kind: null, kind_source: null}`; checkout with an executor marker → `{true, true, rebase|merge|cherry-pick|revert, executor-markers}`; checkout clean or mid-bisect → `{true, false, none|bisect, active-op-probe}`; checkout with a failed probe → `{true, false, probe-failed, active-op-probe}`.
- **`state.head` = `{applies, detached, branch}`** — checkout's shipped detached-HEAD gate (`gitCurrentBranch`, refused at `internal/checkout_sync.go:578-583`). `applies: false` in external, where no shipped check reads a repository-wide HEAD, and the per-row HEAD facts are `mutation.*`/`branch_checked_out_at` instead.

**`state.git_op` is a checkout fact, and this round scopes it explicitly.** It mirrors `gitOperationInProgress(opts.RepoDir)` and its **four** markers, evaluated through the same `gitPathExists` (§8.6.2 exactness rule), and it exists because **checkout has a repository-wide Git-operation refusal**. **External has none**: no external arm calls `gitOperationInProgress`, there is no single repository the external route would run it in, and a stack's entries live in *N* worktrees whose operation state is independent. So on every external document `state.git_op` is `{applies: false, in_progress: null, kind: null, kind_source: null}`, and it **contributes no top-level blocker on that route** — the external Git-operation facts are **per row and per context** (§4.1 `context.rebase_in_progress`, §4.9 rank 5.45) and per continuation gate (§8.6.4, the shipped `isRebaseInProgress` on the failed branch's worktree). Publishing a broad top-level external Git-op blocker would refuse a run over an unrelated worktree the executor never looks at, which is the over-refusal direction this document forbids everywhere else. **Bisect is unchanged and stays a non-blocking label** in checkout (`kind: bisect`, `in_progress: false`, `kind_source: active-op-probe`, §8.6.2, §19.23). **And `applies` is the route axis, not a probe outcome**: it is `true` on every checkout document — including one whose probe failed, which publishes `kind: probe-failed` rather than `applies: false` — and `false` on every external document, where all three companions are `null` and no probe is issued at all.

`freshness = possibly-stale` is not cosmetic: it is the difference between "this is what
`origin/master` is" and "this is what `origin/master` was the last time a fetch succeeded, which may
predate the merge you are syncing for". Because both executors ignore fetch failure, a plan that
omitted it would silently inherit the same defect it exists to expose.

**Deriving `push.targets[]`: the three shipped rules, stated exactly.** "The branches this run would
push" was an unstated primitive in every earlier draft, and the plausible readings — the selection,
the rebased set, the `completed` list — disagree in real cells. The derivation is fixed here, per
arm, and it is a **projection conditional on the rebase and validation this same document
describes succeeding**, never a reading of a `completed` list that is empty at plan time by
construction:

- **External `scope=all`, and every legacy run — `pushFeature` → `pushEntries`**
  (`internal/cli/push.go:57-63`, `:118-152`; `internal/cli/sync.go:216-229`). The loop iterates
  **`stack.Branches`** — the whole stack, in file order, *not* the selection and *not* `TopoSort` —
  and pushes every entry whose worktree directory exists, printing `(archived, skipped)` for the
  rest. So the target set is **every materialized entry of the stack**, `scope: stack-all`:
  it includes entries this run never rebased, and it includes a **local-only anchor**, which
  `--local-only` skipped in the rebase loop and which `pushEntries` neither knows about nor
  excludes. It is bounded only by the archived skip. Two consequences follow and both are stated on
  the document rather than left to be discovered: a `scope=all --push` run force-pushes branches
  outside anything the operator selected, and it does so even for entries whose rows are
  `skipped-anchor`.
- **External `only`/`subtree` — `pushScoped`** (`internal/cli/push.go:70-108`). The loop iterates
  `sel.Entries` and pushes an entry **iff** it is in the run's `completed` set, is **not** in
  `payload.Pushed`, and has a worktree. The plan therefore projects, as `scope: selected-rebased`,
  exactly the **selected entries this document expects to rebase and validate successfully**:
  every selected row whose plan is executable, **excluding** local-only anchors (`skipsAnchor`
  marks them done without appending to `completed`, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:100-105`,
  `:171-176`), **excluding** non-materialized rows (they reach `completed` through pass 2 or
  `markUpdatedAncestors`, and are then dropped by `pushScoped`'s own worktree check), and
  **excluding** any row this document already marks `blocking` — a row that will not rebase will not
  be pushed. On a **continuation** the same rule reads the frozen state instead of guessing:
  the target set is (persisted `Completed` ∪ the remaining rows this resume would still rebase)
  minus `payload.Pushed`, intersected with the selection and the materialized set. That is why a
  push-stage resume — every entry already in `Completed`, none in `Pushed` — projects a full,
  non-empty set with no rebase rows at all (§8.6.4a).
- **Checkout — `finalizeTransaction`/`finalizeCleanup`** (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1221-1247`).
  Both push **every entry of `tx.Plan`** from `opts.RepoDir`, and `tx.Plan` is what
  `BuildCheckoutPlan` already filtered: archived entries skipped, selection applied, cross-repo
  entries refused upstream. So the projection is `scope: transaction-plan` over the planned
  entries, **subject to the stage**: `completed` publishes them (the retry really runs),
  `restoring` publishes **none** (the shipped guard drops the push, §8.6.4a, §18.20), and a fresh
  run publishes them conditionally on reaching finalization.

**The push context of each row, and where its `context_id` comes from** (round-35 item 5). The
directory is the shipped push ladder and nothing else — `entry.Repo` when non-empty, else that
entry's worktree, in external; `opts.RepoDir` in checkout (`pushScoped`/`pushEntries`,
`internal/cli/push.go:70-108`, `:118-152`; `gitPush`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:438-446`) — and its
`context_id` is the §4.4 identity of **that** directory: the same function, the same three raw
members, and therefore the same value wherever another axis resolved the same directory. Three
consequences follow and each is stated rather than left to be inferred. **It is not derivable from
the entry row's contexts**: the push ladder is `entry.Repo` **else the worktree**, which coincides
with `execution_context` on a pass-2 or checkout row, with `base_context` on a pass-1 row whose
`Repo` is set, and with **both** on a pass-1 row whose `Repo` is empty — so a consumer that reads
either entry ref as the push context is right two cells out of three and silently wrong in the
others. **It shares `repositories[]` rows rather than adding new ones**: where the push directory is
already somebody's base or execution context, the target's `context_id` names that existing row, and
where it is not, one more row appears there with four `not-evaluated` config slots (§4.3, §4.4).
**And it is why the array is a projection over established contexts**: a target whose push directory
could not be established has no id, so it is not published as a row at all, and the array never
carries a `null` identity.

**The conditionality is the point, and it is what the fingerprint binds.** `push.targets[]` is not
"what has been pushed" and not "what is complete": it is the identity of the force-push this
approval would authorise, computed from the plan. So a token minted over a `--only pr2` push set
cannot authorise a `scope=all` resume even though both publish `intent.push: true`; a token minted
before an entry was archived does not authorise the smaller set that follows; and a token minted
while a branch was still absent from `payload.Pushed` does not authorise a resume that has since
recorded it. Whether the run *reaches* the push is the separate `push.executable`/`push.blocked_by[]`
pair, which no token waives (§4.9 rank 4, §8.6.4a).

**The two rows-less profiles, stated exactly once.** Every rows-less document — whatever its
`refusal.kind` — takes one of these two column values, and no other combination is legal. This
replaces §5.5's earlier "every aggregate `null`", which was false for every count-of-published-rows
field, and §8.6.3's silence about the repository axis. §5.5 and §8.6.3 are readings of this table
and state nothing that contradicts it:

| Field | `plannability: empty` (derivation succeeded, no work) | `plannability: unavailable` (derivation prevented) |
|---|---|---|

| `summary.entries_with_unknown_candidates` / `collateral_exposed_entries` / `entries_with_unknown_collateral` | `0` | `0` |
| `summary.max_entry_candidates` | `null` | `null` |
| `summary.total_candidates` | **`0`** — every countable entry is countable, vacuously | **`null`** — no candidate fact was established |
| `summary.total_candidates_lower_bound` | **`0`** | **`null`** |
| `summary.collateral_refs` | **`[]`** — the described run rebases nothing, so it moves nothing | **`null`** |
| `summary.collateral_bound` | `upper` | **`null`** |
| `summary.collateral_refs_unowned` | **`0`** | **`null`** |

That last cell is the ordinary empty-stack/empty-selection checkout document, and it is why this profile's token rule and its restore row must be read together: with `entries: []`, `push.targets: []` **and** `restore.applies: false`, the token follows the actual work and is `null` | **`applies: false`**, every other member `null`/`false`/`[]` — no transaction context was established |

Emitting a `within-limit` total here would claim a measurement over a stack nobody could read (§8.3.2a) |

Two of them are snapshot-derived and reachable on any profile — `live-owner-concurrency` where the step 2 snapshot holds a pre-existing signalable foreign owner in an owner-signalling artefact (an empty run under a live neighbour still refuses when guarded, and the fetch block is then the live-run one) and `owner-artefact-undecodable` where an owner-signalling artefact's `presence` is `unreadable`/`symlink`, on exactly the same footing (both appear, sorted, when both facts hold). **Two more are fetch-decided and are reachable here too**, on the checkout `--fetch` route alone, whose single `workspace-repo-root` context is resolved and whose fetch is decided *before* the stack load and the `len(plan) == 0` return (`internal/checkout_sync.go:611-654`): `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` (rank 5.05) and `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` (rank 5.06), each published together with `runnable: false`, `fetch.attempted: false` and its own `freshness` value. **`fetch-context-indeterminate` is the only member that stays unreachable on this profile**, needing two or more candidate contexts whose entries would themselves be rows. The two fetch-decided members are absent here **for a reason, not by fiat**: this profile's refusal is established at step 3 or step 5, *before* the fetch step, so suppression cause 2 (`not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`) applies, no context is ever resolved and neither 5.05 nor 5.06 can have been decided (§8.6.1). The round-13 wording "`[]` — no controlled-path execution was projected" is **withdrawn**: the snapshot is taken at step 2, *before* the stack load of step 3 and the sort/selection of step 5, so a `plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable` or `selection-refused` document has looked at the neighbour even though it never derived a plan, and publishing `[]` there would assert "the guarded twin will not refuse for concurrency" from evidence the document never gathered. The document's own `refusal.kind` (rank 1-3) is unaffected and the two facts ride on separate axes (§8.6.1 cause 3, §15.18b) |

subject.
