the previous draft listed rank 5.0 in this cell and that stays withdrawn as impossible, here, in §8.6.3 and in §15.18b. **5.05 `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` and 5.06 `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` are different and are reachable**, on the checkout route alone: that route's single `workspace-repo-root` context is resolved and its fetch decided *before* the stack load and the `len(plan) == 0` return, so an empty checkout `--fetch` document over a superproject whose unconditional submodule recursion cannot be bounded publishes the first with `runnable: false` and `freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate`, and one whose mirror refspec meets a checked-out local branch publishes the second with `runnable: false` and `freshness: not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out` (§8.6.1 causes 5 and 6, §8.6.3, §15.18b b2 (v3)/(v4)). **5.07 `invalid-git-config` is reachable here too, and on either route** (round-27 item 3, **route-scoped by round-28 item 2 and rescoped by round-29 item 1**): it attaches to a *repository context* rather than to a row or a fetch context, so any document that probed one at all can carry it — subject to the scope, which on this profile means a fetch-only key needs the fetching route, a rebase-scope key is unreachable (no rows, no rebase), and `submodule.recurse` is reachable on the fetchless push-stage and `restoring` cells because they run `git push` and `git checkout` —, with `runnable: false`. **5.08 `identity-not-utf8` is reachable only where this profile still mints a token** — the push-stage continuation and the `restoring` resume, whose `push.targets[]`/`restore` members are the bound strings — and is unreachable on a profile that mints none (§4.9 ranks 5.07/5.08). In the reachable cells this column is **`false`**, exactly as it would be with rows | **`false`** — a rank 1-3 fact stops it |
| `refusal.kind` | `null`, unless an independent rank 3, rank 4, **rank 4.5**, **rank 5.05** (checkout only, round-23 item 3: an unbounded submodule reach in the single `workspace-repo-root` context, whose fetch is decided before the empty-plan return), **rank 5.06** (checkout only, round-25 item 2: a covering positive refspec over a held local branch in that same context, decided at the same point), **rank 5.07** (round-27 item 3 as route-scoped by round-28 item 2 **and rescoped by round-29 item 1**: an invalid value of one of §4.2's thirteen keys in *any* context this document probed **that this route will really hand to Git** — reachable here because a probed context needs no rows, unreachable for a *fetch-only* or *rebase-scope* key where the route attempts no fetch and runs no rebase, and **reachable for `submodule.recurse` on exactly those routes**, since a rows-less push-stage continuation runs `git push` and a rows-less `restoring` resume runs `git checkout`), **rank 5.08** *conditionally* (round-27 item 7 as scoped by round-28 item 4: only on the rows-less cells that **would otherwise mint** — the push-stage continuation and the `restoring` resume under an effective limit — and never on a rows-less cell that mints no token, which publishes `encoding_issues[]` alone with `runnable: true`) or (under the blocking rendering) rank 6 fact applies (a dirty tree still refuses an empty run; a `restoring` resume whose projected `restoreOriginal` would fail publishes `restore-blocked`, §4.4 `restore.executable`) — **and, on the rows-less cells that carry approvable work (a non-empty `push.targets[]` or `restore.applies: true`) under an effective limit, unless a guard verdict of ranks 7, 7.5 or 8 applies**, which this column publishes on a `runnable: true` document exactly as a rows-bearing one would (round-20 item 5, bounded by round-21 item 4): `guard-limit-mismatch`, `approval-without-limits` and `approval-mismatch` against the real token those cells mint are reachable in a **published** document, and `revalidation-mismatch` (rank 9) is reachable at the guarded seam of the same cells (where the refusal is a marker line, §8.7.6). **Ranks 10, 11 and 12 are not reachable on this profile at all**, and the previous draft's `indeterminate-entry`/`limit-total` cells are withdrawn: this profile's own `guard.evaluation[]` row above fixes the measurement — a supplied `max_replay_total` emits exactly one `total` row with `value: 0` and `verdict: within-limit`, and a supplied `max_replay_per_entry` emits none — so there is no `unknown` row for `indeterminate-entry` (10) to refuse on, no entry for `limit-per-entry` (11) to exceed, and no total for `limit-total` (12) to exceed, since `0 > L` is false for every non-negative `L`. A rows-less document's remaining push or restore work is not replay work and is never counted into a replay limit (§8.3.2a). This column is therefore **total over ranks 3, 4, 4.5, 6, 7, 7.5 and 8** here; the `runnable` column stays total over the **hard** ranks 1-6 alone | its own top-ranked kind |

The asymmetry in `runnable` is the reason the discriminator exists: `tws sync <f>` over a feature
whose stack legitimately holds no entry **succeeds today**, so a document reporting it unrunnable
would describe a different command; while a document that could not read, sort or select the stack
describes no command at all. **The asymmetry is about the emptiness alone.** It says only that "no
rows" is not itself a blocker; it never suppresses one. A `plannability: empty` document that also
carries an independent non-waivable fact — a rank 3 `state-refused` dirty tree or live guard, a
rank 4 I19 containment failure or push-stage completion-gate failure, a **rank 4.5
`restore-blocked`** fact wherever restore work exists (the checkout `restoring` resume whose
projected `restoreOriginal` cannot succeed, §4.4 `restore.executable`/`restore.blocked_by[]`), or a
rank 6
`selection-hazard` under the blocking rendering — publishes `runnable: false` and that fact's
`refusal.kind`, because the empty run
really would refuse. **The `runnable` and `refusal.kind` rows of the table are total over the same
set of *hard* facts, and `refusal.kind` is total over the guard verdicts besides**
(round-19 item 6, extended by round-20 item 5): every rank reachable in the `runnable` column is
reachable in the
`refusal.kind` column — the previous draft's omission of rank 4.5 from the second, which would
have published `runnable: false` with `refusal.kind: null` on the one rows-less cell whose *whole*
remaining work is the restore, is corrected here, in §8.6.3 and in §15.18b alike — **and the
`refusal.kind` column additionally covers ranks 7, 7.5 and 8 on the rows-less cells that carry approvable
work under an effective limit** (the push-stage continuation and the checkout `restoring` resume),
where a limit conflict or a token mismatch
is the honest refusal of a document whose plan is perfectly runnable — with
rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` reachable at the guarded seam of those same cells, which emits a
marker line and no document (§8.7.6), and **ranks 10, 11 and 12 unreachable together**: the
profile's evaluation set is one `total` row of `value: 0`/`within-limit` or no row at all, so
nothing is unevaluable, no entry exists to exceed a per-entry limit and `0` exceeds no total
(round-21 item 4). `runnable`
does not move for any of them, by the standing rule of §4.9 that guard verdicts are not execution
blockers. The earlier draft's unconditional "`runnable` stays `true` on an empty
document" is **withdrawn** here, in §8.6.3 and in §15.18b alike; the two statements were already
inconsistent with the `refusal.kind` row directly above. What is **also** withdrawn is the previous
round's inclusion of the rank 5.0 `fetch-context-indeterminate` cell on this profile: it cannot
occur without rows, and asserting it would have required a fixture that does not exist. **The
rows-less rank-5 set is exactly four members, and round 28 states all four here, in §4.9, in §8.6.3
and in §15.18b in the same words** (round-23 item 3, round-25 item 2, round-27 items 3 and 7,
round-28 item 6): `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` (5.05) and `fetch-local-branch-checked-out`
(5.06) are each decided
from a fetch context rather than from a row, and checkout resolves and decides its one context
before the empty-plan return, so both are reachable on a rows-less checkout `--fetch` document and
on nothing else; **`invalid-git-config` (5.07)** attaches to a *repository context*, so it is
reachable on either route wherever one was probed **and** this route will really hand the offending
key to Git (§4.2's route scope); and **`identity-not-utf8` (5.08)** is reachable **conditionally** —
only where the rows-less document **would otherwise mint** a token, i.e. the push-stage continuation
and the `restoring` resume under an effective limit, and never where it mints none, in which case
the document publishes `encoding_issues[]` with `runnable: true` and no blocker at all. No
restatement of this set anywhere in the document may list fewer than the four, or list 5.08
unconditionally (§4.9 ranks 5.05-5.08, §8.6.1 causes 5 and 6, §8.6.3,
§15.18b b2 (v3)/(v4)/(v5)/(v6)).

**`plannability` is about rebase rows, and remaining work is not.** The discriminator answers "were
rows derivable?", so a push-stage continuation is `plannability: empty` — derivation succeeded and
produced no rebase entry — while its **remaining work is not empty**. The fields that carry
that distinction are `push.targets[]` (what would be pushed) with its `push.executable` pair,
**`restore`** (the HEAD switch, transaction deletion and lock release a checkout resume still owes),
`approval.fingerprint` (which is
non-`null` exactly because something is left to approve) and `intent.push`/`intent.push_source`
(why). A consumer asking "is there anything left?" reads `entries`, `push.targets` **and**
`restore.applies`; a
consumer asking "could the plan look?" reads `plannability`. Neither question is answerable from the
other, which is why both fields exist and why the token rule is stated over the triple.

### 4.5 Candidate identity, bounded

A count answers "how much"; the customer's request asks "**which**": *"expose old cutoff B, new
base D, and replay C before mutation"* (`request.md`). The schema therefore publishes identity,
bounded so a wide range cannot turn a plan into a `git log`:

- `replay.range` — the range expression with resolved values, e.g.
  `pr2: 9f1c2ab..feat/pr2 (upstream = recorded cutoff)`. This is what makes the number auditable:
  the operator can paste it into `git rev-list`/`git log` and get the same set.
- `replay.first_candidate` — `{sha, short, subject}` for the **oldest** candidate: the first commit
  Git puts in its todo list, i.e. `C1` in replay order. `git rev-list` lists newest-first, and
  commit **limiting happens before ordering** ("these are applied before commit ordering and
  formatting options, such as `--reverse`", `git rev-list` manual), so `--reverse --max-count=1`
  returns the *newest* candidate — the wrong end, and the previous draft's error. The correct probe
  is count-derived: `git rev-list --count --no-merges <upstream>..<branch>` → `N`, then
  `git rev-list --skip=<N-1> --max-count=1 --no-merges --topo-order --format=… <upstream>..<branch>`.
  Two bounded probes, and the second one is skipped entirely when `N == 0`.
- `replay.commits[]` — the deterministic ordered SHA list in **replay order (oldest-first)**,
  emitted in `--json` and under a verbosity flag, bounded by a documented cap (recommend 50,
  spec-fixed) with `commits_listed`, `commits_truncated`, and the full `candidate_count` alongside,
  so a truncated list can never be mistaken for the whole set. **`--reverse --max-count=<cap>` is
  forbidden**: it lists the newest `cap` commits reversed, which is the opposite end of the todo
  list from the one the operator needs. Two correct shapes, and the spec picks one:
  1. consume the **whole** `git rev-list --reverse --topo-order --no-merges <upstream>..<branch>`
     stream to EOF and cap **implementation-side** by *retaining* only the first `cap` lines —
     simplest, and exact for any `N`. **The pipe is never closed early**: every SHA must reach the
     digest (property 3 below), so the cap is a retention bound, not a consumption bound, and
     memory stays O(cap) while the read stays O(N). The earlier draft's "closing the pipe early"
     is **withdrawn** — it contradicted the digest it appears beside, and would have hashed a
     prefix while claiming to bind the range;
  2. count first, then `git rev-list --skip=<max(0, N-cap)> --max-count=<min(N, cap)> --reverse
     --topo-order --no-merges <upstream>..<branch>` — the oldest `cap` commits, emitted oldest-first,
     i.e. `C1..Ccap`.
  Shape 2 costs one extra probe and never materialises more than `cap` lines; shape 1 costs one
  probe and streams. Either way the listed prefix is `C1..Ccap`, `commits_truncated` is `N > cap`,
  and the order is asserted against a rebase todo list in the tests (§15.5). (Git 2.55 adds
  `--max-count-oldest`, which would do this in one probe; the spec may adopt it only if it also
  fixes a minimum Git version, which this feature does not.)
- `replay.candidate_digest` — **the identity that survives the cap, and the only candidate identity
  the fingerprint binds** (§4.6, §5.3.2). It is the full 64-hex SHA-256 of the **complete, uncapped,
  oldest-first** candidate SHA sequence of that row: each full 40-character lowercase-hex SHA in
  `--topo-order --reverse --no-merges` order followed by a single `\n`, hashed in that order, with
  the empty sequence hashing to the ordinary SHA-256 of zero bytes. Three properties are binding:
  1. **It is computed from the plan object's own full sequence, never from the rendered list.** The
     digest input is the whole range Git will consider; `replay.commits` is a *rendering* of the
     first `cap` of them. Digesting the rendered list would make the approval token a function of a
     presentation choice — two invocations of the same run with different caps, or one in `--json`
     and one in the human form, would mint different tokens for the same replay, and a stack whose
     tail changed beyond the cap would mint the *same* token for a different replay. Both directions
     are wrong, and the second is a safety hole: it is exactly the "same count, different commits"
     failure of Finding 4, moved from the count to the list.
  2. **`replay.commits` may stay capped, or be omitted entirely, without changing the token.** The
     human default prints no list at all; `--json` prints at most `cap`; both publish the same
     `candidate_digest`, and the fingerprint therefore does not depend on which rendering minted it
     (§15.5a).
  3. **It costs no extra `git` process, but it does constrain the probe shape.** Shape 1 above
     streams the *whole* `rev-list` already: the implementation hashes every line as it arrives and
     retains only the first `cap` for `replay.commits`, so one probe yields the capped list, the
     truncation flag and the digest — provided the stream is read to **EOF**, which is why shape 1
     forbids an early close. **Shape 2 cannot produce the digest at all** — a
     `--skip`/`--max-count` window never sees the tail — so a spec that picks shape 2 must add a
     second, full-stream probe whose output is hashed and discarded. That is the one real cost of
     binding identity rather than rendering, and §19.12 now decides the probe shape with it in view.
  The digest is a fact about the range, so it is `null` exactly when `replay.commits` is `null`
  (§4.8), and the count it accompanies is bound beside it: the fingerprint binds
  **`candidate_count` *and* `candidate_digest`**, so neither a re-ordered same-length range nor a
  same-prefix longer range can pass as the approved one.
- `--topo-order` is part of the contract, not decoration: it is the order Git's own todo list uses,
  so the published list is the list the operator will see in the rebase.
- **Human default**: `count + range + first candidate`, in the **bound two-line row grammar of
  §8.3.5** (round-37 item 4), which fixes the field set, its order and every absent-value spelling
  so the customer's headline — configured base, resolved base ref, **destination short SHA**,
  recorded cutoff, **effective replay upstream**, strategy, count, range and **first candidate with
  its sanitized subject** — is answered on the default rendering with no flag. It is two lines per
  entry rather than the one line the earlier drafts assumed, because the eleven fields do not fit one
  readable line and the alternative was leaving half of them to `--json`; the full list stays one
  flag away and every compressed field stays complete in the JSON twin.
- Subjects are attacker-influenceable metadata: sanitize every rendered subject through
  `ancestrySanitize` (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:551-570`) with a spec-fixed limit, one line only,
  and never interpolate one into a suggested command (`ancestryCommandToken`, `:578-580`).
- Nothing in this section may be rendered with a verb that implies application. The bound line reads
  `candidates 1 range <B-short>..feat/pr2 first <C-short> "C"` (§8.3.5), never `applies C` and never
  `1 commit will be applied`. The earlier drafts' illustrative spellings `replays (candidate): C`
  and `candidates: 1 (9f1c2ab "C")` are **withdrawn as renderings** — they were examples of the
  banned-verb rule, and round-37 item 4 replaces them with the one grammar the rendering may use —
  while the rule they illustrated is unchanged and applies to every surface, JSON key, help string,
  skill and test name included.

### 4.6 Fingerprint content follows from §4.5

Because identity is published, the approval fingerprint binds identity — **`replay.candidate_count`
together with `replay.candidate_digest`, the digest over the complete, uncapped, oldest-first
candidate SHA sequence** (§4.5) — and not the count alone, and **never** the rendered or capped
`replay.commits`. Two plans that both say `candidates: 1` but name
different commits must produce different fingerprints, or the approval token would authorise a run
the operator never saw; and two renderings of the *same* plan — human without a list, `--json` with
a capped one — must produce the *identical* fingerprint, or the token would depend on how it was
printed. **What the hash is computed over is stated once, in §5.3: a canonical
*invariant tuple projected from* the canonical document, never the rendered document itself, whose
membership is the exhaustive whitelist of §5.3.2, and whose **byte encoding is the typed,
length-prefixed binary (TLV) encoding of §5.3.2a** — over raw bytes, so a name Git accepts but UTF-8
does not is bound as the bytes it is (round-26 item 2, replacing round 25's canonical JSON) — any
field of the document not in that table is
excluded, including fields added later, and no implementation may choose its own serialization for
the fields that are in it (round-25 item 4).** §5.3
states the tuple, its whitelist, its explicit non-member list, and the two distinct jobs it has to do
(cross-invocation approval identity vs intra-run revalidation); §8.7 states the CLI contract.

### 4.7 Canonical ordering: what the document guarantees, and what it must not

`TopoSort` seeds Kahn's algorithm by iterating a **Go map** (`for name, deg := range inDegree`,
`internal/stack.go:157-163`). Go randomises map iteration, so the relative order of **independent
roots** — and therefore the interleaving of their whole subtrees — is *unspecified and varies
between processes*. **That map range is the *only* source of variation** (round-22 item 5): each
parent's children are appended while iterating `s.Branches` in `stack.yaml` file order
(`internal/stack.go:141-155`) and the FIFO queue preserves what is already in it, so **within one
root component the sequence is fully determined**, and the earlier "any two entries that become
ready at the same time" phrasing — which read a level tie as a draw — is withdrawn. Every consumer of `TopoSort` inherits this: `syncWithStackScoped`'s loops,
`BuildCheckoutPlan`'s row order, `SyncSelection.Entries`, and therefore `SyncRunState.Selected`,
`CheckoutTransaction.Selected` — **and, on the new-mode external route, the fetch context itself**,
because `syncFeatureScoped` builds `UniqueRepos` over `selectedRealEntries(stack, run.Sel)`
(`internal/cli/sync.go:559-566`) and `UniqueRepos` records the *first* entry it sees for each token
(`internal/stack.go:37-52`). Two runs of the identical command can therefore fetch a token in two
different directories. That is a shipped, unguarded behaviour this feature does not change, and
§8.6.9 states exactly how the document handles it: it enumerates the candidates deterministically
instead of publishing a value it cannot reproduce.

Three consequences, and they are load-bearing for a fingerprint:

1. **The global order must not be changed.** Making `TopoSort` deterministic would alter the
   execution order of existing runs, the persisted `Selected` lists, and the checkout plan array
   that `--continue` indexes by position (`tx.CurrentIndex`) — a cross-cutting behaviour change no
   plan feature is entitled to make. It stays exactly as shipped, unspecified sibling order and all.
2. **The document is canonicalized instead.** Rows are emitted sorted by logical `Name`;
   **`fetch.repos[]` sorted by `(repo_token, context_root)`** — the authoritative key, spelled
   identically in §4.4, §8.6.9 and §15.15h5, and **not** this section's previous "sorted by repo"
   (round-40 item 5), which under-specified the array: one token legitimately has more than one
   context root (`entry-repo` vs the `process-cwd` fallback, §8.6.9), so a single-member key leaves
   those rows tied and the byte-stability §15.15h5 asserts unreachable. The single-key precedent
   exists (`sel.Repos` is `sort.Strings`-ed, `internal/sync_selection.go:241-244`) but decides only
   the first member, never the tiebreak. Each row's `context_candidates[]` is sorted by
   `(context_root, context_source, first_entry)` so the *set* of possible contexts is byte-stable
   even where the shipped choice among them is not (§8.6.9);
   `collateral_refs`, `summary.collateral_refs`,
   `route_triggers`, `blockers`, `warnings` and the selected-name list sorted by their natural key —
   `blockers` by the rank-bearing tuple of §4.9 and **`warnings` by its own rankless tuple
   `(kind, entry, detail)`** (§4.4; a warning has no rank, so it cannot borrow the blocker one),
   **`guard.evaluation[]` and
   `guard.limit_conflicts[]` bytewise by their own `id`/key** (§4.4, §8.3.2a), `approval.covers`'s
   two id lists bytewise, the nullable collateral lists
   whenever they are non-null (§4.8) — **and the two evidence arrays are named here explicitly
   rather than left to "their natural key"** (round-31 item 2), because each has a key that is
   neither obvious nor recoverable from a rendering: **`config_issues[]` is sorted bytewise
   ascending by `issue_id` and de-duplicated on `issue_id` alone** — one opaque, total, byte-stable
   digest over the raw identity tuple, so two invalid values whose §11 renderings collide never
   collapse and no sort key reaches into a lossy member (§4.4, §4.2 Part 3) — and
   **`encoding_issues[]` is sorted by `(field_id, path_label_ascii` bytewise`, owner_entry_ascii_or_null`
   — `null` first, then bytewise —`, sha256` bytewise`)` with exact whole-row duplicates removed**
   (§4.4, §5.3.2a rule 10). **`repositories[]` is sorted by `(repo, context_id)`** for the same
   reason and is named here for the same reason (round-32 item 1): its previous `(repo, repo_root)`
   key ended in a §11 rendering, which is lossy and therefore not a total order — two contexts that
   render to one path would have tied with nothing left to break the tie — while `context_id` is a
   total, byte-stable digest over the raw identity. Both are sets, both are canonicalized, and neither may be emitted in
   discovery order — and nothing is emitted from a map range. **Canonicalization
   sorts sets and preserves sequences, and `fetch_effect` is both at once** (round-20 item 3): its
   `remotes[]` rows are a *set* and are sorted by `name`, while each row's `refspecs[]` is a
   *sequence* whose configured order is a Git fact — a fetch applies **every** matching positive
   refspec in that order, writing each mapped destination, and the implicit-lease baseline of §4.4
   is separately read off the **first matching non-negative** one (round-21 item 6) — so sorting it
   would publish a configuration Git does not have and would move that baseline with it. **The scalar members round 22 adds — `contacted`, `may_delete_refs`, `may_delete_tags` on the effect and `prune`/`prune_tags`/`tag_opt` on each remote row — are neither set nor sequence and need no canonicalization; they are compared by value, which is all the collapse rule ever asked of them** (round-22 items 2 and 3). **The members round 23 adds are canonicalized by the same two rules and no third one** (items 1, 3 and 5): `may_clobber_tags` on the effect and `source`/`url_source` on each remote row are scalars compared by value; `submodule_recursion` is an object whose own scalars (`mode`, `mode_source`, `may_recurse`, `reach`) are compared by value — **except `mode_source`, which round-24 item 1 removes from the equivalence comparison as provenance that cannot change a fetch, while it is still canonicalized and published like any other scalar** — and whose `submodules[]` is a **set sorted bytewise by `path`**, each member's nested `fetch_effect` canonicalized recursively by these same rules; a row's `active` member **stays in the comparison** even though round-24 item 2 makes it informational for the reach, because it still gates the unpopulated-but-changed arm and so can change what a fetch does — so a submodule list is order-independent while every refspec sequence inside it stays in configured order. **The members round 25 added were left unclassified, and round 26 classifies them by the same two rules** (item 3): `may_update_local_branches` and `may_delete_local_branches` are scalars compared by value; `local_branch_destinations` is an object whose `truncated` is such a scalar and whose three arrays split across both rules. **`patterns[]` is a *sequence*, not a set** — its rows are `{remote, dst, forced}`, one per positive refspec whose destination pattern covers `refs/heads/**`, and they are emitted **in each remote's configured refspec order, with the remotes themselves in the `name`-sorted order `remotes[]` already uses**: the order inside a remote is the same Git fact `refspecs[]` carries — later matching refspecs still apply, and the *first* matching one is what the lease baseline of §4.4 reads — so sorting the patterns of one remote would publish a configuration Git does not have, exactly as sorting `refspecs[]` would. The remote-level ordering is a tws choice and is therefore the canonical sorted one, which makes the whole array byte-stable without inventing an order inside any remote. **`branches[]` and `held[]` are *sets* and are canonically sorted**: `branches[]` bytewise by the published branch name — which §4.4 strips of its `refs/heads/` prefix — and capped at 200, `truncated` recording the cut (§4.4), `held[]` by the tuple `(branch bytewise, worktree path bytewise, hold bytewise)` — never truncated — because both are enumerations of what a store *contains*, with no Git-fixed order to preserve, and a `held[]` sorted by discovery order would vary with the worktree inventory's own listing. Both are **nullable**, and `null` is not an empty set: an enumeration that failed publishes `null` beside known booleans (§4.8), and canonicalization applies only where they are non-null. **`submodules[].effective_mode_source` is classified with `mode_source`, not against it** (round-25 item 1, classified here): it is a scalar, canonicalized and published like any other, and it is **excluded from the candidate-equivalence comparison** as provenance that cannot change what a fetch does — two candidates whose submodule reaches the same `effective_mode` by way of a context mode and by way of a per-submodule key fetch identically, and treating the label as material would publish a `fetch-context-indeterminate` (rank 5.0) over a difference Git does not have. `effective_mode` itself **stays in** the comparison, as do `mode`, `may_recurse` and `reach`. The other deliberately
   unsorted list is `replay.commits[]`, whose order is a **Git fact** (documented oldest-first
   replay order within one row, §4.5), not a
   tws choice. **Canonicalization is not permitted to invent a value the run does not fix**: where
   the unspecified order really would change a published fact — the new-mode fetch context — the
   document publishes `null` plus the sorted candidate set and a blocker, never a sorted-first
   guess (§8.6.9).
3. **Row position carries no meaning.** Parent relationships travel in `destination.depends_on`, so
   a consumer reconstructs the dependency graph without relying on order. The human rendering may
   print rows in the canonical order and must not label it "execution order"; if execution order is
   shown at all, it is shown as a **nonbinding** projection with that word in the output.

The fingerprint is computed over the canonical **invariant tuple projected from** the canonical
document — not over the document's bytes (§5.3) — so **independent-row order is not fingerprint
material** for two reasons at once: the tuple's per-entry list is name-sorted, and the document the
projection reads is itself canonical. Two processes planning the same two-root stack therefore
produce byte-identical JSON **and** the same token (§15.6 test). Execution keeps whatever order
`TopoSort` produces.

### 4.8 Unknown is `null` — never an empty list and never `false`

The count contract of §4.2 has a schema-wide corollary the previous draft applied only to
`candidate_count`: **a fact the plan could not determine is `null`, whatever its type**. An empty
list means "this set was computed and is empty"; `false` means "this was evaluated and is false";
`0` means "this was counted and is zero". None of them may stand in for "not known".

**Scope, stated before the table because the previous round got it wrong.** This section is **not**
the document's field contract and is **not** exhaustive over nullable fields: **§4.4's field table is
the authoritative, complete field and nullability contract** (with §8.3.6 authoritative for the
top-level key set). What follows is the **hazard subset** — the fields where an unknown could
plausibly be published as a known `[]`, `false` or `0`, and where getting it wrong silently
under-states a blast radius or over-states a certainty. Many fields are legitimately nullable without
appearing here (`requested_route`, `policy.selector`, `refusal.detail`, `push.executable`,
`restore.executable`, `approval.fingerprint`, `approval.accepted`), and their absence from this table
means nothing about them; §4.4 governs. The tri-directional "these three tables name the same fields"
invariant of the previous round is **withdrawn** as impossible (§8.3.6): the enforceable relation is
top-level key-set agreement between §4 (§4.1 for `entries`, §4.4 for everything else) and §8.3.6,
and **containment** of this table in §4.4 (§15.21).

| Field | `null` (unknown) | `[]` / `false` / `0` (known) |
|---|---|---|
| `replay.commits` | `determinacy = unknown` — deferred, unresolvable, unset base, missing head, `merge-recreation` (round-26's `merge-recreation-unknown` is withdrawn by round-27 item 1) | the range resolved and contains no candidate, **and every `determinacy = not-applicable` skip row**, whose empty sequence is known without a probe (§4.1 skip rule) |
| `replay.commits_listed` / `replay.commits_truncated` | exactly when `replay.commits` is `null` | a listed (possibly empty, possibly complete) range |
| `replay.candidate_digest` | exactly when `replay.commits` is `null` | a resolved range — **including a known-empty one**, which digests the empty sequence rather than publishing `null` (§4.5) |
| `replay.candidate_count` | as §4.1 — `determinacy = unknown` only | a counted range, **including every `not-applicable` skip row, which publishes `0`** (§4.1 skip rule) |
| `collateral_refs` | the range is unknown, or the `repositories[].config`/branch-inventory/worktree probe failed | the mechanism and range are known and no ref qualifies — **including every `not-applicable` skip row**, which replays nothing and therefore has a known-empty set (§4.1 skip rule) |
| `collateral_exposed` | any earlier row's collateral set is unknown | every earlier set is known and this tip is not in one |
| `collateral_mechanism` | the `rebase.updateRefs` probe failed | `argv` / `config` / `none`, each verified |
| `effective_backend` | the `rebase.backend` probe failed **and** the argv forces no backend | `merge` whenever the argv forces it, and `merge` whenever the probe read the key as absent — Git's built-in default since 2.26 (§4.2); `apply` only on a read `apply` with no merge-forcing option |
| `replay.may_drop_patch_equivalent` | the effective upstream is deferred/unresolvable, or the upstream-side count probe failed | `true`/`false` from the arm-aware rule of §4.2 |
| `repositories[].config.*.value` | the slot's `status` is anything other than `valid` — `absent` (parsed and unset), `not-evaluated` (this route never parses the key), `probe-failed` (the read failed) or `invalid` (a route-applicable read found a fatal effective occurrence, evidenced by a `config_issues[]` row matched on `context_id` + the key→slot map); the four are distinguished by `status`, never by the `null` itself, and **`source` is `null` in exactly the first three and names the offending occurrence's scope under `invalid`** (§4.4 `repositories[]`, round-31 item 4, round-32 items 1 and 3) | `status: valid` with the probed value and `source: probed`; `status: absent` with `source: null` (round 31's `unset` member withdrawn) |
| `context.dirty` / `context.autostash` / `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm` | the tracked-dirty probe (§4.1, §5.4.7) or the config read failed — the ordered `config --list --show-scope -z` or the typed boolean read beside it (§4.1 probe-failure rule, §4.3, §13); the derived arm fact is `null` exactly when one of its two inputs is (round-26 item 8) | a probed answer, and a derived one for the third |
| `context.untracked_present` / `context.overwrite_risk` | the untracked **enumeration** failed, or its work-tree **anchor** did not resolve — an **enrichment** failure, so the pair is `null`, the row is **not** `probe-failed` and nothing is blocked on that account (§4.1). **Those are the only two `null` causes, on every route** (round-21 item 2): the round-18 "fresh checkout rows are `null`, because the shipped whole-repo gate owns the question at rank 3" clause is **withdrawn here as it already was in §4.1** (round-20 item 2) — that gate is `git status --porcelain` and is silent under `status.showUntrackedFiles=no`, so a fresh checkout row is probed like any other and is warning-capable, and leaving the clause in this table would have made the schema's own hazard list contradict the field it describes | the enumeration ran: `false`/`none-known` when the row's **work tree** holds no untracked non-ignored file, `true`/`unknown` when it holds at least one — **fresh checkout rows included**. **Neither value is a prediction**, so neither may be read as "this run is safe" or "this run will fail": `none-known` says only that there is nothing present for Git to refuse to overwrite, and `unknown` says the planner cannot decide (§4.1, §5.4.7, §19.26) |
| `branch_checked_out_at` | the worktree inventory failed on a `will_switch_head` row | `null` also means "no worktree holds this branch" when the inventory succeeded — the one place the table's rule is ambiguous, so the row publishes the inventory's own success through `probe-failed`/blocking rather than through this field alone. A **non-null** value is likewise not by itself a blocker: only a **foreign** holder is (§4.1, §5.4.7) |
| `summary.collateral_bound` | `summary.collateral_refs` is `null` | `upper` |
| `summary.collateral_refs` | no selected row has a known set, or `plannability: unavailable` | the union over known sets; `[]` on `plannability: empty` |

Three consequences the spec must carry:

1. **`summary.entries_with_unknown_collateral` is mandatory** (§4.4). Without it, a document whose
   rows are all `null` and whose `summary.collateral_exposed_entries` is `0` reads as "no collateral
   anywhere", which is the exact misreading this rule exists to prevent.
2. **Revalidation compares known sets only** (§5.2, §5.3.1). The "new collateral appeared" refusal is
   defined over a row whose approved collateral was **known**; a row approved with `null` collateral
   was never approved as collateral-free, so it is resolved at the JIT seam like any other deferred
   fact and re-checked there — it is never silently waived, and never treated as an approved empty
   set.
3. **The fingerprint distinguishes the two** (§5.3): `null` and `[]` are different tuple values, so a
   token minted while collateral was unknown does not match a run whose collateral resolved.

This narrows §8.3.6's "lists are never `null`" to what it always meant: **lists of published rows**
(`entries`, `blockers`, `warnings`, **`encoding_issues`**, **`config_issues`**, `route_triggers`, `repositories`,
`fetch.repos`, each row's
`fetch.repos[].context_candidates`, `push.targets`, `push.blocked_by`, `restore.blocked_by`,
`guard.evaluation`, `guard.limit_conflicts`, **`guard.execute_blocked_by`**,
`approval.covers.waived_evaluation_ids` and
`approval.covers.waived_kinds`)
are never
`null`; the unknown-bearing per-entry facts in the table above are nullable by design. The list is
**closed at seventeen members and identical** to the one §8.3.6 publishes **and to the one §15.21
asserts** — round-28 item 4 added `encoding_issues`, which is `[]` on every document that resolved no
invalid bound identity and is never `null` even where the whole question was moot, and **round-30
item 2 adds `config_issues`**, which is `[]` on every document that parsed no route-applicable
invalid config value and is likewise never `null` —; the three are edited together or not at all, and §15.21 asserts them equal as sets so a
silent omission — as happened to `guard.execute_blocked_by` in the round-14 test text — fails the
suite instead of surviving a review. **`context.untracked_present` and `context.overwrite_risk` are deliberately not seventeenth and
eighteenth members** (round-18 item 1, renumbered by round-30 item 6): they are nullable *per-entry facts* of the table above, not
lists of published rows, and their `null` carries the whole point of the pair — "this directory was
not enumerated" versus "it was, and here is the residual". Neither is a list at all any more: round
17's `context.untracked_overwrite_paths[]` is **withdrawn** with the rank 5.55 blocker it fed, so
the never-null list is unaffected in both membership and count (§4.1, §5.4.7, §19.26). Note the
distinction the indeterminate fetch row makes concrete (§8.6.9): the *list* is never `null`, while
the **chosen** `context_root`/`context_common_dir`/`context_source`/`fetch_effect` values taken from it are
`null`
exactly when the route does
not determine one — an unknown value inside a known set, which is the same rule, not an exception.
The one deliberate scalar exception on a list-bearing object is `restore.executable`, which is `null`
where the question was never established (§4.4) while its `blocked_by[]` stays `[]`.

### 4.9 Refusal precedence and blocker ordering

`blockers[]` is a set of facts; `refusal.kind` is **one** token. The mapping between them is a fixed,
closed precedence — not "the first one found", which would vary with probe order, row order and
mode.

**Scope of this precedence.** The full ladder below is the **plan document's** collapse rule: a
`--plan` invocation observes every fact — state, selection, rows, guard verdicts — in one pass, so
it can rank all of them. A **guarded execution** does not, and the analysis does not pretend
otherwise: it reaches the guard seam only after the shipped ladder has already refused everything it
refuses (§8.7.1), so at the seam it ranks exactly the facts that are available there — the row
blockers it can still see, and the guard verdicts it owns — and emits the marker line for the
top-ranked one (§8.7.6). **The marker is decided by *origin*, not by rank** (§8.7.6): any refusal the
guard itself generates at its own seam or at a JIT seam carries it, whatever its rank; any refusal a
shipped check already owns keeps its shipped text and carries none — including the rank 5
`head-ref-missing` that checkout raises inside `BuildCheckoutPlan` (`resolve branch %q`,
`internal/checkout_sync.go:500-503`), which fires **before** the guard seam and is therefore a
shipped refusal despite sitting at a rank the guard usually owns. Ranking and marking are two
independent questions and the previous draft conflated them. The two renderings agree on **every
kind the guard itself produces**, which is what an operator who plans and then executes actually
compares.

**Precedence is evaluated over *effective* verdicts.** A limit violation that a matching
`--approve-plan` token covers has `guard.evaluation[].verdict = waived` and is **not** ranked at all:
it never enters `blockers[]` and never becomes `refusal.kind` (§4.4, §5.3.1). So a document whose
only fact was `limit-per-entry`, replayed with its own token, publishes `refusal.kind: null`,
`guard.would_refuse: false` and `guard.would_refuse_without_approval: true` — three fields that
together say "the guard would have refused this, you approved it, and it will now run". Ranking the
waived violation anyway would make `--plan --approve-plan` unable to answer the only question it
exists to answer.

**Precedence, highest first:**

| Rank | `refusal.kind` | Why it outranks the next |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable` | no rows exist at all — the stack could not be read (§8.5.5) or could not be sorted (§5.5). Nothing below is computable. The two are mutually exclusive by construction (a stack that did not load is never sorted); if both were ever recorded, `plan-unavailable` wins, so the order stays total |
| 2 | `selection-refused` | *which* entries participate is undecided, so no row is trustworthy (I10-I13, R6, R7) |
| 3 | `state-refused` | the run cannot start or resume at all: state cells, transaction, lock, live guard, dirty tree, detached HEAD, Git operation in progress, **every arm of the two native acquisition ladders — `ClaimSyncRunGuard` on a fresh new-mode external run and `AcquireCheckoutLock` on a fresh checkout run, each projected verbatim with its own shipped sentence (§8.6.2)** — and every continuation gate of §8.6.4. **On the guarded execution route this rank additionally carries the live-owner concurrency refusal of §8.6.1 cause 3** — a **checkout lock or sync-run guard** (never a checkout transaction, whose `lock_pid` is a persisted recovery field) that was **already present and readable in the pre-acquisition snapshot** and whose recorded PID is **another, signalable** PID, whatever the shipped ladder made of that cell and whoever owns the payload — because a guarded run that merely declined the fetch would execute on refs it knowingly left stale. An artefact **this** invocation created, acquired or reclaimed is never that fact, however alive its PID, and an artefact whose `presence` is `unreadable` or `symlink` is not "no owner" either: its liveness is unknown, so — **in the cells where the native acquisition ladder would not already refuse the run this invocation is about to perform** — the guarded route fails closed on it under its own rank 3 blocker, which the plan publishes as the **`owner-artefact-undecodable`** member of `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`. **That qualifier is the whole membership rule, and it is narrower than the round-15 wording it replaces** (round-17 item 3): a **corrupt or unreadable regular** guard or lock file is already rejected *natively*, with `invalid sync guard; inspect %s and use --abort to recover: %w` / `read existing sync guard: %w` and their checkout twins, so that cell is a **shipped** rank 3 refusal the plan projects with the shipped sentence and there is no controlled-path divergence left to publish; the member is reserved for the cells the native ladder reads straight through or never reads at all — the archetype being a **symlink whose target decodes to a valid artefact**, which `os.ReadFile` follows and accepts while the `Lstat`-first inspector records `presence: symlink`, and an **applicable** owner-signalling artefact sitting on a path **this route never consults** (a `.sync-run.lock` under a legacy external route). **Applicability bounds it** (round-19 item 5): a `not-applicable` artefact — `state.files.checkout_lock` on any external route, the three external artefacts in checkout — has no undecodable presence to fail closed on, so the cross-mode cell earlier drafts listed here is impossible and is removed. It is published separately from `live-owner-concurrency`, because "someone else is running" and "I cannot tell whether someone else is running" are different facts with the same verdict, and a document may carry both (§4.4 `state`, §4.4 `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`, §8.6.1 cause 3 and step 2a, §19.22). It is **non-waivable** (an approval covers limit violations only, §5.3.1) and, in the cells where no shipped check refuses first, it is guard-generated and therefore marked (§8.7.6). The **plan-only** route projects the same observation as a blocker only where the shipped ladder implies one, and otherwise reports it through the `state` object and `freshness: not-refreshed-live-run` — but in **both** cells it publishes the matching `guard.execute_blocked_by` member — `live-owner-concurrency` for the live foreign owner, `owner-artefact-undecodable` for the undecodable one — so a document whose `runnable` stays `true` still predicts its guarded twin's refusal (§4.4, §8.6.1, §9) |
| 4 | `preflight-refused` | a shipped pre-mutation preflight refuses this run: I19 containment, wrong-branch worktree, and the external **completion gate** (`staleStackEdgesFiltered` plus the failed-branch ancestry check) that a push-stage resume must pass **before** its push (§8.6.4a) |
| 4.5 | `restore-blocked` | **checkout only, document-level** (`entry: null`): the projected `restoreOriginal` cannot succeed — the restore target does not resolve, a **foreign** worktree holds it, or the `OriginalHEAD` consistency rule will fail because the recorded original branch is **not** in `tx.Plan` and its tip has moved (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1258-1284`, §4.4 `restore.blocked_by[]`). It is a **guard introduction** in the §8.6.2 sense — no shipped check runs before the mutation — so a guarded refusal carries the marker line (§8.7.6). It ranks below the shipped preflights, because those refuse earlier and for reasons that are not about restoration, and above rank 5, because a run whose restore is already known to fail would rebase the whole stack and then strand the operator mid-transaction with the lock still held and HEAD on the wrong branch. **Non-waivable**: an approval authorises work, not a failing checkout. On the `restoring` resume it is the *only* possible refusal of the invocation's whole content; on a fresh run and on any earlier stage it refuses before the first `git checkout` |
| 5 | hard blockers, in the fixed suborder below — two document-level facts at 5.0 and 5.05 (round-23 item 3), then the row blockers | the run would start and then fail at Git, or the guard cannot name the context the run would fetch in |
| 6 | `selection-hazard` | the selection is legal on this route but structurally hazardous — a duplicate `GitBranch` or a checkout cross-repo entry that the **legacy** route does not itself reject (§8.5.6). It ranks below the facts that stop the run and above every guard verdict, because it describes *what will be replayed*, not *how much* |
| 7 | `guard-limit-mismatch` | the supplied limits disagree with the limits the interrupted run persisted, so this invocation asked for a guard the frozen state does not describe (§8.7.4). **The document is still a full document, and it describes exactly one plan**: the **persisted** limits stay effective and stay published in `guard.limits.<key>` with their `persisted-*` origin, the rejected attempt is published beside them in `guard.limit_conflicts[]` (§4.4), and the plan, its rows, its evaluations against the **persisted** limits and its `approval.fingerprint` are all computed as if the flag had not been given. `runnable` stays **`true`** — nothing about the work is broken; it is the invocation's flag set that is inconsistent — and `refusal.kind` is this kind unless something rank 1-6 outranks it. **A token cannot waive it**: the fingerprint is minted over the persisted plan (whose effective limit values the tuple binds, §5.3.2), so a matching token proves only that the *plan* is the one that was approved, and the mismatch is a fact about the command line, not a limit violation an approval can cover (§5.3.1). The operator's two exits are to drop the conflicting flag or to repeat the persisted value; both are named in `refusal.detail` |
| 7.5 | `approval-without-limits` | `--approve-plan` was supplied on a `--continue` whose **effective** limits both resolve to `{value: null, origin: none}` (§8.7.4), so the token can waive nothing: an approval covers limit violations and nothing else (§5.3.1), and an unguarded resume carrying one would look protected while being exactly as unguarded as it was before. The same condition on a **fresh** invocation is decided earlier and harder — a flag error in `resolvePlanGuardOptions`, no document at all (§8.5.1, §8.6.6) — because nothing but a flag could have supplied a limit there. Like rank 7 it is a fact about the *command line*: the document is complete, its rows and aggregates are real, `runnable` stays **`true`**, and — the correction this round makes — **no token is minted**, because the same missing precondition that makes the approval meaningless makes a token unusable: the document publishes `approval.fingerprint: null`, `approval.usable: false` and `approval.covers.requires_limits: true` (§4.4 usable-token rule). The two exits are to add a limit flag — which makes the *next* `--plan --continue` mint a real, usable token over the same remaining work — or to drop `--approve-plan` |
| 8 | `approval-mismatch` | the plan is executable, but this token does not authorise it |
| 9 | `revalidation-mismatch` | the token matched at the seam, but a JIT re-resolution found the approved identity, base, candidate set or collateral had drifted (§5.2, §5.3). It outranks the limit verdicts because "the plan you approved is no longer the plan" is a stronger fact than "the number is too big" |
| 10 | `indeterminate-entry` | executable and authorised, but an effective limit **cannot be compared** against a value: a `guard.evaluation[]` row with `verdict: unknown` that refuses under the invocation's `guard.indeterminacy_policy` — always the `unknown_kind: not-resolvable` rows (§4.2 `merge-recreation`; **round-26's second source `merge-recreation-unknown` is withdrawn by round-27 item 1, its two empty spellings now resolving to `true`/`false` and its invalid value refusing at rank 5.07 instead**), and additionally the `deferred-resolvable` ones only under the non-recommended `refuse-up-front` policy (§8.3.2a, §19.9). **Non-waivable**: an approval clears only ranks 11-12, so a token can never turn "there is no number to compare" into "approved" (§5.3.1). It is nevertheless a *guard* verdict, not a blocker: `runnable` stays `true`, because the plan itself is perfectly executable — it is the limit that cannot be evaluated (§4.4) |
| 11 | `limit-per-entry` | an effective per-entry limit is exceeded and **not waived** |
| 12 | `limit-total` | only the aggregate limit is exceeded and **not waived** |

**Documents that mint no token never publish `approval-mismatch`.** The rule is stated over the
*work* and the *limits*, not over ranks and not over `entries` alone: **`approval.fingerprint` is
`null` whenever `entries` is `[]`, `push.targets` is `[]` *and* `restore.applies` is `false`, and
equally whenever no key of `guard.limits` carries an effective value** (§4.4 usable-token rule)
and a supplied
token cannot match, because there is nothing to match against. Ranks 1-2 are the three kinds that
produce such a document by construction (`plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable`,
`selection-refused`, §8.6.3), but they are not the only cells: a rank 3 `state-refused` with
`nothing to continue — no sync in progress`, a continuation whose remaining rebase, push **and**
restoring work are all empty, and a
stack that legitimately holds no entry are workless too — and a fully populated plan run **without a
limit flag** mints no token either, for the separate reason that there is nothing for an approval to
cover (§8.5.1). In every one of them the honest answer is
the document's **own** top-ranked kind, not rank 8: "no plan exists", or "nothing is guarded", is the
fact the operator must
act on, and `approval-mismatch` would send them to re-plan something that cannot be planned. Such a
document therefore publishes `approval.supplied: true`, `approval.accepted: false`,
`approval.fingerprint: null`, `approval.usable: false` and `refusal.kind` = its own top-ranked kind.
This is not an exception
to the ladder; it is the ladder, stated for the cases where rank 8 has no object.

**A rows-less *push-stage* or *restoring* document is not one of them.** With `entries: []` and a
non-empty `push.targets[]` — or with `restore.applies: true` — and at least one effective limit,
there **is** an object for rank 8:
the document publishes a real token, a supplied
token is compared against it bytewise, and a mismatch is an ordinary `approval-mismatch` at rank 8
(§4.4, §8.6.4a). Silently ignoring a supplied approval there — the previous drafts' behaviour, which
followed from the `entries == []` and then the `entries == [] && push.targets == []` rules — would
have made the single most consequential remaining
operation a sync performs, a force-push of every synced branch, and the one resume that switches
HEAD in the operator's checkout without rebasing anything, the two operations no token could
ever bind. Without a limit the same document mints no token, but that cell is not silence either: it
is rank 7.5 `approval-without-limits`, which names the missing precondition (§8.5.1).

Ranks 1-5 are the **non-waivable execution blockers** and are exactly the set that sets
`runnable: false` (§4.4); rank 6 sets it only under the blocking rendering (§8.5.6, §19.13); ranks
7-12 never do. **Rank 5 always needs an object to attach to, and that object is a row for most of
its members, a *fetch context* for three of them and a *repository context* or the *document's own
bound identity* for the two round 27 adds** (round-26 item 1, restating round-23 item 3 and
round-25 item 2 in this paragraph, which still counted only the row members; round-27 items 3 and 7
add 5.07 and 5.08; round-35 item 2 adds 5.15): 5.1-5.9 (5.15 and 5.45
included) are row blockers, and 5.0
needs a `fetch.repos[]` token with two or more materially different candidate contexts, which needs
two or more selected entries of that token — so **those** are the members that cannot occur on a
rows-less document. **5.05 `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` and 5.06
`fetch-local-branch-checked-out` are decided from a single resolved fetch context and are therefore
reachable with no rows at all**, on the checkout `--fetch` route whose one `workspace-repo-root`
context is resolved before the stack load and the `len(plan) == 0` return
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:611-654`) — which is why §4.4's profile table lists ranks 3, 4, **4.5**,
**5.05**, **5.06**, **5.07**, conditionally **5.08**, and 6 in its `runnable` column. **The two new
members split on the same question**
(round-27 items 3 and 7, **both refined by round 28**): **5.07 `invalid-git-config` is reachable with
no rows** wherever a
repository context was probed at all — the checkout `--fetch` route's single `workspace-repo-root`
context is the archetype — **and, from round-28 item 2, only where that route will really hand the
offending key to Git**, which round-29 item 1 makes a per-key question rather than a per-route one:
a rows-less `--no-fetch` or `--continue` document that runs no rebase publishes an invalid
*rebase-scope* value with no blocker, and still **carries** the blocker for an invalid
`submodule.recurse`, because the push-stage continuation runs `git push` and the `restoring` resume
runs `git checkout`, both of which die on it (§4.2 Part 2); while **5.08 `identity-not-utf8` needs something bound**, so it is
reachable on a rows-less document exactly when that document **would otherwise mint** a token, i.e. on the
push-stage continuation and the `restoring` resume whose `push.targets[]`/`restore` members carry
the offending bytes **under an effective limit**, and is unreachable on a document that mints none —
which, from round-28 item 4, publishes the top-level `encoding_issues[]` array with `runnable: true`
and no blocker rather than nothing at all. **The rows-less rank-5 set is therefore exactly
`{5.05, 5.06, 5.07, conditional 5.08}`, and every restatement of it — here, in §4.4's profile table,
in §8.6.3 and in §15.18b — names all four with 5.08's condition attached** (round-28 item 6). Rank 4.5 `restore-blocked` is
the one non-waivable kind that is *more* likely without rows than with them, since the
`restoring` resume has none. The earlier "neither is reachable on a rows-less document … only ranks
3, 4, 4.5 and 6" reading of this paragraph is **withdrawn as stale**, not re-decided: it contradicted
the profile table's own `runnable`/`refusal.kind` rows and §15.18b b2 (v3)/(v4), which already assert
both cells. **Ranks 7, 7.5 and 8 are a different question and are reachable there**
(round-20 item 5, bounded by round-21 item 4): they attach to the *invocation*, not to a row, so wherever a rows-less document
carries approvable work under an effective limit **with `encoding_issues == []`** — all three
clauses of §4.4's usable-token predicate (round-33 item 15) — the push-stage continuation and the
`restoring`
resume, the two cells that mint real tokens — a limit conflict, a limitless approval or an approval
mismatch ranks and becomes that
document's `refusal.kind` while `runnable` stays `true`; rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` joins them
at the guarded seam, where the refusal is a marker line rather than a document (§8.7.6). **Ranks 10, 11 and 12 are structurally out of
reach without rows**, and the round-20 wording that admitted `indeterminate-entry` and `limit-total`
here is withdrawn: a rows-less document's replay measurement is fixed by §4.4's profile table — one
`total` row with `value: 0` and `verdict: within-limit` under `max_replay_total`, and **no** row at
all under `max_replay_per_entry` — so no evaluation row can be `unknown` (10), no entry exists to
exceed a per-entry limit (11), and `0` exceeds no non-negative total limit (12). The remaining push
or restore work is not replay work and is never counted into either limit (§8.3.2a). §4.4's
profile table states this as the asymmetry between its two columns, and §8.6.3 and §15.18b assert
it.

**Hard blockers (rank 5), fixed suborder** — 5.0, **5.05**, **5.06**, **5.07** and **5.08** are the **document-level** members (`entry: null`,
so the canonical sort already places them first among rank 5, in that suborder; 5.07 and 5.08 are round 27's, items 3 and 7), and 5.1-5.9 (5.15 and 5.45 included) are the row blockers:

| Sub-rank | `refusal.kind` | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| 5.0 | `fetch-context-indeterminate` | a `fetch.repos[]` row whose `context_candidates[]` holds **two or more contexts that differ in their canonical absolute common dir or in their effective bare-fetch effect** (`git -C … rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, and the `{all, contacted, may_delete_refs, may_delete_tags, may_clobber_tags, may_update_local_branches, may_delete_local_branches, local_branch_destinations, remotes[], submodule_recursion}` effect an argument-less `git fetch` would resolve there — the `fetch.all`/`skipFetchAll` remote set with each remote's `source`, its configured and effective URL with `url_source`, its **ordered** fetch refspecs and its effective prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`, plus the effective submodule recursion, round-20 items 1 and 3, round-22 items 2 and 3, round-23 items 1, 3 and 5), or among which one candidate's common dir or fetch effect **will not resolve and therefore cannot be shown equal to the others**, so the route's own first-entry rule does not determine **which object store its `git fetch` refreshes, or what it would fetch into it** (§8.6.9). **Two or more candidates require two or more *root components*, and round 22 states that as the rank's real precondition** (item 5): `TopoSort` randomizes only its zero-in-degree root seed, so a token whose selected entries can be first from a single root component has exactly one candidate and can never reach this rank — same-root siblings, and same-root entries under different parents, included. **The rank is about a nondeterministic *choice*, and needs two or more candidates to have one** (round-21 item 7): a token with a **single** candidate is determinate however broken that context is — a missing, misconfigured or unresolvable remote, a `process-cwd` fallback outside any repository, a `HEAD` or config read that failed — because the route still knows exactly where its one `git fetch` runs. Those cells **attempt** the fetch, publish `context_root`/`context_source` with `context_common_dir`/`fetch_effect` `null` where the probe did not resolve, and report the outcome as `ok: false` / `fetch.outcome: failed` / `freshness: possibly-stale`; the earlier "or one whose common dir or fetch effect will not resolve" reading refused a run the executor performs without complaint, and is withdrawn. Candidates that agree on both — every worktree of one repository tracking one remote, and the `entry.Repo` those worktrees came from — collapse instead, so the ordinary multi-worktree stack never reaches this rank. It is document-level and **non-waivable in v1**: an approval covers limit violations only (§5.3.1), and no token can bind a fetch context the document could not name, so `--approve-plan` neither clears this blocker nor changes `runnable`. **The detail is required to name the operator's real exits, and to name them honestly**, because "re-run the command" is not one — the ambiguity is decided by the candidate **set**, which is order-independent, while `TopoSort`'s own order is **unstable and unspecified between processes** (Go randomises map iteration, §4.7 consequence 1) — so a rerun re-rolls the order and still produces the same refusal, forever (§4.7, §18.21). The three exits, all of which the detail states: (1) **narrow the selection to a determinate one** — a `--only`/`--from` selection under which the token can be first from a **single root component**, which the candidate list makes checkable because it names each candidate's `first_entry` (round-22 item 5); (2) **make the candidates agree** — fix the workspace so the missing worktree exists, correct the `entry.Repo` value or the process working directory that fell back to another clone, or align `branch.<name>.remote`/`fetch.all`/refspecs/prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`/legacy `remotes/`-`branches/` files/submodule recursion so every candidate resolves the same `(absolute common dir, effective fetch effect)` pair, after which they collapse and the plan fetches; or (3) **deliberately take the `--no-fetch` route** — `--plan --no-fetch` and a `--no-fetch` run need no fetch context at all, and the detail says plainly that this is **a different route** (new-mode, local-only refs, §5.3, §0.2), not a workaround for the same run. The **unguarded** command is unchanged — it still fetches wherever the shipped map order lands — which the detail also states explicitly, so the operator is never told a working command is broken, only that the guard will not authorise it |
| 5.05 | `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` | **document-level, new in round 23** (item 3): a `fetch.repos[]` row in which some present gitlink submodule's effective recursion is **`yes`** — unconditional, so “all populated submodules are fetched” (`git fetch` manual, verified against Git 2.55.0), whether that `yes` is the context `mode` (which, being set, binds every submodule of the context — **from the config chain or, where that sets nothing, from `.gitmodules`'s context-level `[fetch] recurseSubmodules`**, round-26 item 6) or, **only where no context mode is set at all**, a per-submodule `fetchRecurseSubmodules` from config or `.gitmodules` (round-25 item 1 correcting the override direction) — while its `fetch_effect.submodule_recursion.reach` is **`unknown`**: a candidate submodule whose store, config or gitlink could not be read, an enumeration over the 50-submodule/depth-3 cap, or an enumerated submodule that may itself recurse into a level that could not be established (§4.4 `fetch.repos[]`). **The rank has one further arm from round 26** (item 6, **narrowed by round-28 items 1 and 7**): a context whose mode could not be established at all — rung 1 absent and **every remaining source of the rung-2 `.gitmodules` ladder failing to read**, so `mode`/`mode_source` are `null` — fails closed here too wherever a **present gitlink** exists, because a mode nobody could read may be `yes`; a context with no present gitlink publishes `may_recurse: false`/`reach: none` and fetches. **An index-unmerged `.gitmodules` is not that cell** (round-28 item 1): `is_gitmodules_unmerged` guards `repo_read_gitmodules`, not `config_from_gitmodules`, and a failed `:.gitmodules` read falls through to `HEAD:.gitmodules`, so the mode resolves and this rank does not apply. **An *invalid* `.gitmodules` recurse value is not that cell either**: it is either ignored by Git — because a valid context mode already resolved — or a hard fetch-config failure published at rank 5.07, never an unknown mode (§4.2, §4.9 rank 5.07). **And where the mode is `null` over a present gitlink this rank is the *only* outcome** (round-28 item 7): the route does not fetch, the row publishes `attempted: false`, and no cell of §8.6.1 fetches such a context and describes it afterwards as `unknown-fetch-effect`. **Round 24 removes activity from that predicate** (item 2): the fetch path decides on the index gitlink, the submodule store and the effective mode, with no `is_submodule_active` call (`submodule.c` `get_fetch_task_from_index` → `fetch_task_create` → `get_fetch_recurse_config`), so an inactive-but-populated submodule reaches this rank exactly as an active one does. The fact it states is narrow and provable: **this fetch will recursively contact remotes and move `refs/remotes/**` and tags in repositories this document cannot name**. It therefore **fails closed** — the route skips the fetch entirely (§8.6.1 cause 5), publishes `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.outcome: skipped`, `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: false` and `freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate`, and sets `runnable: false`. It is **non-waivable in v1** for the same reason as 5.0: an approval covers limit violations only (§5.3.1), and no token can bind a set of repositories the document could not enumerate. **The detail names the operator's real exits**, and “re-run it” is not one: (1) make the reach establishable — initialise or repair the submodule whose store could not be read; (2) set the recursion the run should really have — `fetch.recurseSubmodules=no` (or `on-demand`) in that context, which as a **context mode** binds every submodule and overrides every per-submodule key (round-25 item 1) — **and, where the `yes` came from `.gitmodules`'s own context-level `[fetch] recurseSubmodules`, a repository-config key of either name overrides it without editing a tracked file** (round-26 item 6) —, or, **where no context mode is set at all**, `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules=no` for the one submodule, remembering that the two context-level keys resolve by **last occurrence** and not by precedence between them (round-24 item 1) and that a per-submodule `no` is simply never read while a context mode exists; either way a configuration change with effects beyond this feature, and stated as such; or (3) take the `--no-fetch` route, which needs no reach at all (§5.3, §0.2). The **unguarded** command is unchanged — it still fetches, still recurses, and still moves those refs — which the detail states explicitly (§8.6.1, §8.6.9, §11, §14) |
| 5.06 | `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` | **document-level, new in round 25** (item 2): a `fetch.repos[]` row whose resolved `fetch_effect` has at least one **positive** fetch refspec whose destination pattern **covers `refs/heads/**`** — the mirror `+refs/*:refs/*`, `refs/heads/*:refs/heads/*`, `refs/h*`, or a legacy `branches/<name>` file's synthesised `refs/heads/<branch>:refs/heads/<name>` (§0.1, §4.4) — while that context's `fetch_effect.local_branch_destinations.held[]` is **non-empty**: some covered local branch is held by a worktree of that store, by Git's own fetch-side predicate `branch_checked_out()` (`branch.c` `prepare_checked_out_branches`; `builtin/fetch.c` `check_not_current_branch`) and by its **four** kinds of hold — HEAD on the branch, a recorded in-progress rebase, a bisect's origin, and a branch in a running rebase's `--update-refs` state. It is one kind wider than rank 5.4's `git checkout` holder rule, and the document keeps the two predicates separate rather than merging them (round-25 item 2). **The predicate has a second, fail-closed arm, and round 26 states it here rather than leaving the cell to fetch** (item 4): the same covering refspec with `local_branch_destinations.branches`/`held` **`null`** — the store's `for-each-ref refs/heads/` or its worktree inventory did not read — ranks here too, because "no worktree holds a covered destination" and "I could not establish whether one does" have the same consequence for a fetch about to write `refs/heads/**`. The two arms differ only in the detail they publish (named branch/worktree/hold rows versus the named failed probe and an explicit "holds unknown"), never in kind, rank, suppression, `freshness` or `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` member. **`held[]` is a store-wide fact**, enumerated over every non-bare worktree registered against the canonical common dir and therefore identical from every worktree of that store (§4.4, §8.6.9). The fact it states is provable from config and the worktree inventory alone: **this fetch writes `refs/heads/**` in a store where a working tree is standing on one of the destinations.** Git resolves that meeting in one of two ways, and the plan names both because they fail differently. For a held branch the remote **advertises**, `check_not_current_branch` **dies** — `refusing to fetch into branch '<ref>' checked out at '<path>'` — *before* `prune_refs` and before any ref is updated, so nothing moves; but the shipped `fetchQuiet` discards that status (§0.1), so the **unguarded** run simply continues against **stale** refs, which is the silent-staleness failure `freshness` exists to prevent. For a held branch the remote **no longer has**, the die never applies — it is evaluated over the ref map, and a branch with no remote counterpart has no entry there — so an effective prune **deletes it**, leaving that worktree's HEAD dangling (`prune_refs` → `refs_warn_dangling_symrefs`, `   (HEAD has become dangling)`, also discarded). **The plan therefore fails closed**: the route skips the fetch entirely (§8.6.1 cause 6), publishes `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.outcome: skipped`, `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: false` and `freshness: not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out`, and sets `runnable: false`. **Under the guard, therefore, no covered deletion ever reaches a held branch and no HEAD is ever left dangling** — the dangling cell exists only on the unguarded route. It ranks **below** 5.05 because an unnamable *reach* is the broader fact (that fetch writes stores this document cannot even list, while this one writes refs it can name exactly), and above every row blocker because it is a property of a fetch context rather than of a row. **The refusal is deliberately conservative in one direction, and the detail says so rather than overclaiming**: whether the die fires depends on what the remote advertises, which no local read can settle — the plan will not contact a remote to find out, because contacting it *is* the fetch — so a covered, held branch that the remote happens not to have and that no prune would remove is refused too. Both the over-refusal and its reason are published, and the honest alternative (fetch anyway, then report a failure whose refs may already be gone) is worse in exactly the direction this feature exists to close. It is **non-waivable in v1**, for the same reason as 5.0 and 5.05: an approval covers limit violations only (§5.3.1). **The detail names the operator's real exits**, and “re-run it” is not one: (1) move the working tree off the covered branch — check out another branch, finish or abort the rebase or bisect that holds it, or remove the worktree — which the `held[]` rows name with their `worktree` paths and `hold` kinds; (2) narrow the refspec so it stops covering `refs/heads/**` (the ordinary `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/<r>/*` covers nothing local), or turn off the prune that makes the deletion possible, remembering that a **mirror** refspec is what usually puts a non-bare clone in this cell at all; or (3) take the `--no-fetch` route, which needs no fetch context (§5.3, §0.2). The **unguarded** command is unchanged — it still issues the fetch, still dies or still prunes — which the detail states explicitly (§0.1, §8.6.1 cause 6, §11, §14) |
| 5.07 | `invalid-git-config` | **document-level, new in round 27** (item 3), **route-scoped and widened by round 28** (item 2), **its scope corrected again by round 29** (items 1 and 2): some repository context this document probed carries a value of one of the thirteen keys of §4.2's table — the fetch-scope `fetch.recurseSubmodules` and `.gitmodules`'s context-level `fetch.recurseSubmodules`, the fetch/**checkout**/**push**-scope `submodule.recurse`, and the rebase-scope `rebase.stat`, `rebase.autoSquash`, `rebase.autoStash`, `rebase.updateRefs`, `rebase.rescheduleFailedExec`, `rebase.forkPoint`, `rebase.rebaseMerges`, `rebase.backend`, `rebase.abbreviateCommands` and `rebase.maxLabelLength` — that **Git's own parser rejects**, **and the route this document describes will really hand that key to Git**, so the command this document is previewing dies while reading its configuration, before it fetches or replays anything: `die("bad fetch.recursesubmodules argument: <value>")` (`parse_fetch_recurse`, `submodule-config.c`), `bad boolean config value '<value>' for '<key>'` (`git_config_bool`, `config.c`, which is how `submodule.recurse` and six of the `rebase.*` keys are read), `Unknown rebase-merges mode: <value>` (`parse_rebase_merges_value`, `builtin/rebase.c`), `missing value for 'rebase.backend'`/`Unknown rebase backend: <value>` or `bad numeric config value … for 'rebase.maxlabellength'` — all verified against Git 2.55.0 (§4.2). **The scope clause is round 28's correction and is not decoration** (item 2), **and round 29 fixes the two assignments round 28 got wrong** (items 1 and 2): the two fetch-only keys block **only** where the described route will attempt a fetch — never on `--no-fetch`, never on a `--continue`, never on a checkout run under its `no-fetch` default and never where a §8.6.1 suppression already declined the fetch — the `.gitmodules` key blocks only in the one state where Git parses it at all; **`submodule.recurse` blocks wherever the route will run `git fetch`, `git checkout` *or* `git push`**, because all three commands read it through `git_config_bool` and die on a non-boolean, so a checkout `--no-fetch` run, a checkout continuation, a push-stage continuation and a `restoring` resume all carry it while `git rebase`, which never reads the key, never does; and rebase-scope keys block **only** where at least one `git rebase` will really run in that context, with `rebase.backend`'s unknown-name arm narrowed by the arm's own argv and the two sequencer keys narrowed by the row's derived `effective_backend` — `rebase.abbreviateCommands` on **every** merge-backend arm, **including the unset-`rebase.backend` default**, which is Git's built-in default since 2.26, and `rebase.maxLabelLength` only where such an arm also has rebase-merges in effect. Out of scope the value is neither parsed nor published, and its absence from `config_issues[]` is not a claim that it is valid — **round 30 withdraws the "still published in `repositories[].config.*`" guarantee as impossible** (item 3): that object has four members and nine of the thirteen keys have no slot in it (§4.2 Part 2, §4.4). **Round 31 makes the four slots that do exist total rather than silent** (item 4), **and round 32 makes their `source` total with them** (item 3): each publishes `{status, value, source}` with `status` in the closed enum `valid`/`absent`/`not-evaluated`/`probe-failed`/`invalid`, so an out-of-scope key reads `not-evaluated` and an invalid one reads `invalid` beside its `config_issues[]` row — matched by `context_id` plus the explicit key→slot mapping of §4.4, never by the rendered `repo_root` — with `source` naming that occurrence's scope rather than `null`, and neither is mistakable for `absent`. | 5.08 | `identity-not-utf8` | **document-level, new in round 27** (item 7): at least one **bound identity string** — a `BYTES` member of the fingerprint tuple of §5.3.2, such as a branch name, a base ref, a push ref or a config value, and **never a display-only rendering: since round-33 item 4 the entry and repository roots are not bound and cannot raise this rank, their raw bytes being carried inside `context_id`'s digest instead, and since round-35 item 5 the *push target's* root is not bound either, which round-36 item 6 removes from this list — `push.targets[].repo_root` is an explicit fingerprint non-member (§5.3.2) and the member that replaced it, `push_targets[].context_id`, is 64 lowercase hex and therefore ASCII by construction, so no push-context path can reach this rank and no fixture may build one that does** — is **not valid UTF-8**. Round 27 closes the remaining gap on the controlled path by refusing to mint at all. **Round 28 makes two corrections that narrow the rank without weakening the rule** (item 4). First, **the evidence moves out of the prose**: the per-member facts are published as the top-level, closed-row **`encoding_issues[]`** array of §4.4 — `{field_id, path_label_ascii, owner_entry_ascii_or_null, byte_length, raw_base64, sha256}`, deterministically sorted — and this blocker's `detail` names only the count and points at that array. **No raw invalid text appears in any `detail`, ever**, which round 27's "in its detail, one encoding issue per offending member" left open to an implementation that would have inlined it.
