On a **limitless** plan over the same repository the array is published, the token is `null` for the limit reason it was already `null` for, and **no** blocker and **no** `runnable: false` are published: the run really is runnable, `tws sync` really does replay those branches, and claiming otherwise would make the document wrong about the command it describes. The exits the detail names: rename the offending branch, ref or directory, or run the sync unguarded and without `--approve-plan`. **The `identity-not-utf8` *kind* stays exactly one fact with exactly one rank**: the limitless cell is not a second, softer member of the enum — it publishes no blocker at all, only `encoding_issues[]` and a `null` token — so no consumer switch gains an arm and `refusal.kind` gains no value |
| 5.1 | `repo-unavailable` | **either** of the row's two contexts could not be **established**: the canonical absolute top level of its `base_context` or of its `execution_context` could not be resolved or canonicalized, or that context's absolute common dir could not be resolved, so the context identity of §4.4 has no pre-image and **that ref's** `context_id` and `repo_root` are both `null` while the other ref keeps whatever it resolved (§4.1, round-33 items 1 and 2, round-34 item 1). **One kind covers both**, because the consequences are the same in either direction — a row whose base cannot be resolved states no destination, and a row whose rebase has nowhere to run states no run — and the blocker's `detail` names which ref failed rather than minting a second kind. It outranks everything below because **no Git fact of the row could be probed at all** — publishing `head-ref-missing` for a row whose repository directory is unusable would send the operator to fix a branch when the problem is a directory, and it outranks 5.15 for the same shape of reason: a comparison between two stores presupposes that both were established. **The `detail` names which ref failed and which survived** (round-35 item 4), and a *partial* failure changes nothing else about the surviving ref: it keeps its `context_id`/`repo_root`, cites its `repositories[]` row and may carry `config_issues[]` rows, so no assertion may require an all-`null` row or an empty `repositories[]` here (§4.1). Such a row cites **no** `repositories[]` row for the failed ref and can produce **no** `config_issues[]` row for it, because nothing about that context's configuration was safely probed. The row is not blank, though: every stack- and route-derived fact survives, and precisely because the head was never probed, such a row emits **no** `head-ref-missing` blocker to outrank (§4.1 repo-unavailable nullability rule) |
| 5.15 | `base-execution-store-divergent` | **new in round 35** (item 2), external only: **both** of the row's contexts were established, and their **measured** canonical absolute Git common dirs differ (`git -C … rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, resolved and canonicalized exactly as §8.6.9 requires, compared bytewise — never inferred from the two `source` labels and never from the roots). The row is then incoherent by construction and not merely unusual: `base.decision_sha` is `GetBranchSHA` in the **base** store and is what the executor compares to `LastBaseSHA` to choose between the plain and `--onto` arms, while `git rebase` peels `base.ref` and the recorded cutoff in the **execution** store, so the destination, the replay range, `head.sha` and the collateral upper bound are facts of a store the strategy decision never looked at — and, on success, the executor records the *decision* SHA as this entry's new cutoff (§2.3), pinning a boundary the replay never used. A guarded run therefore **refuses before any rebase**; the shipped unguarded run performs it exactly as it does today and **no executor changes** (§4.1 context-pair rule). It ranks **below** `repo-unavailable`, because both contexts must resolve before the comparison can be made at all, and **above** `head-ref-missing` and everything under it, because those facts are drawn from one of the two stores and reporting them first would send the operator to fix a branch, a cutoff or a dirty tree when the problem is that the row names two repositories. The `detail` names **both** contexts — each `{context_id, repo_root, source}` and its canonical common dir — and which fact each contributed; the row publishes both `repositories[]` rows and both context refs, and no rendering may collapse them. **Checkout can never produce it** (one context), and the near case — two contexts, one measured store — is the `base-execution-context-split` **warning** of §4.4, not this blocker |
| 5.2 | `head-ref-missing` | `head.state != present` (§5.1 rule 6) — without the row's own tip nothing else about the row is computable |
| 5.3 | `prunable-worktree` | `materialization = prunable`; external pass 2 stops the run (§5.4.3) |
| 5.4 | `branch-checked-out-elsewhere` | `mutation.will_switch_head` is `true` and `branch_checked_out_at` names a **foreign** worktree — a canonical worktree other than the one containing the directory this row's own `git` call runs in, both resolved through `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` before canonicalization (§4.1, §5.4.7): the arm's implicit `git checkout <branch>` cannot happen, so `git rebase <base> <branch>` (external pass 2) or `gitCheckout` (checkout) fails before any replay. A holder counts whether it has the branch **checked out** or is **mid-operation on it while detached** — `rebase-merge/head-name`, `rebase-apply/head-name` or `BISECT_START` — because Git refuses the checkout in all four cases and the porcelain's `branch` lines name only the first (§4.1, §5.4.7). A **self** hold (HEAD already on `<git_branch>` in that same worktree, including when the command runs in a **subdirectory** of it) is not a blocker at any rank |
| 5.45 | `external-rebase-in-progress` | **external only** — the directory this row’s own `git rebase` would run in already has a rebase in progress: a `rebase-merge` **or** `rebase-apply` directory exists in its `$GIT_DIR` (§4.1 `context.rebase_in_progress`), so the executor’s next rebase in that directory dies at `It seems that there is already a rebase-merge directory` before replaying anything. **It covers both arms**: the pass-1 row’s own worktree *and* the pass-2 row’s `execution_context.repo_root` (`entry.Repo`, else the process cwd). It ranks **above** `context-dirty` because it is the stronger and more specific fact — an interrupted rebase is usually *why* the tree looks dirty, and unlike a dirty tree it is **never** rescued by `rebase.autoStash`: Git refuses the invocation before it would stash, so the settled `autostash-across-switch` warning of §19.18 does not reach this rank either. On **pass 2** it is also the one blocker that prevents *destruction rather than mere failure*: the shipped failure handler answers that refusal with `git rebase --abort` in the very same directory (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:200-206`), which aborts the **foreign** rebase that was already there and resets its HEAD — so blocking before `git rebase` is what keeps a `tws sync` from discarding an unrelated in-progress rebase (§5.4 consequence 7, §11, §12). It is a **guard introduction**, not a projection of a shipped fresh-run preflight: **no external arm probes this before a fresh rebase on either arm** — `isRebaseInProgress` is called only on the `--abort` cleanup paths and on the two `--continue` failed-branch gates (`internal/cli/sync.go:270`, `:302`, `:317`, `:373`) — so a fresh guarded run refusing here carries the marker line (§8.7.6), and the plan-only document is the *only* place an operator is told, before the fact, why the next `git rebase` will fail. It must never be described as “the shipped fresh preflight”, because there is none; and it must never be computed with the shipped `isRebaseInProgress`, whose `false` bias at a `break` stop and on an unreadable context would let exactly the destructive pass-2 cell through (§4.1). On a **continuation** the different question — "is the *recorded failed branch's* worktree still mid-rebase?" — **is** a shipped gate, is computed with `isRebaseInProgress` verbatim, and is projected as a rank 3 `state-refused` carrying the shipped sentence instead (§8.6.4); the two must not be merged, in either direction |
| 5.5 | `context-dirty` | `context.dirty` is `true` — **tracked** unstaged or staged changes as `status --porcelain --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all` reports them after its in-memory index refresh, Git's own clean-work-tree precondition, untracked files and submodule gitlinks excluded (§4.1, §5.4.7) — **and this row's `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm` is not `true`**. **Round 26 makes the autostash escape arm-specific, because it was never a property of the config alone** (item 8): `rebase.autoStash` is an option of `git rebase`, so it applies to exactly the arms whose *only* working-tree-touching command is that rebase — **external pass 1** (the rebase runs in the worktree that already has the branch checked out, and the stash is taken and reapplied in place) and **external pass 2** (`git rebase <base> <git_branch>`, whose implicit checkout is Git's own, inside the rebase, so the stash is carried **across** that switch — the `autostash-across-switch` warning). It applies to **nothing on the checkout arm**, and the two checkout cells differ: a **fresh** checkout run never reaches this rank at all, because `RunCheckoutSync`'s whole-repo `gitWorkingTreeDirty` gate refuses first and harder — untracked files and submodules included — as a rank 3 `state-refused` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:565-577`), and **that shipped gate is unchanged by round 28**: a fresh checkout run over any dirty tree still refuses, at rank 3, exactly as it ships. A checkout **continuation** never re-runs that gate (`gitWorkingTreeDirty` is called only from `RunCheckoutSync`), so it can legitimately resume dirty, and each of its entries begins with a **standalone `gitCheckout(opts.RepoDir, entry.Branch)`** *before* the rebase (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1040-1047`) — a command `rebase.autoStash` does not reach, since the option belongs to `git rebase` and the rebase runs only **after** that checkout has already succeeded. **Round 26 concluded from that pair that a tracked-dirty checkout continuation is a blocker at this rank whatever `rebase.autoStash` says. Round 28 withdraws that unconditional blocker** (item 3), because it is wrong about `git checkout`: a standalone `git checkout <branch>` does **not** refuse on tracked dirt as such. It performs a two-way merge and **carries unrelated local modifications across the switch**, succeeding whenever the dirty paths do not differ between the two commits; it refuses — `error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:` — only where a dirty path **overlaps** the difference between HEAD and the target. Refusing every tracked-dirty continuation therefore stopped a large class of runs Git performs without complaint, in the over-refusal direction, and rank 5.5 no longer has a checkout arm at all: **`context-dirty` is an external-arm rank**, and a checkout continuation is never published under it on account of tracked dirt. **What replaces it is a residual, and it is non-blocking by construction** (round-28 item 3): the plan cannot decide the overlap question, because the answer depends on the diff between HEAD and each entry's branch at the moment that entry's checkout runs — after every earlier entry has already rewritten history — so a row-time verdict would be a guess. The document publishes the **`checkout-dirty-present` warning** instead (§4.4 `warnings[]`), one row per checkout-continuation entry row whose context is tracked-dirty, whose detail names the dirty state, states plainly that **Git may refuse the standalone checkout** with that message, and says that `rebase.autoStash` does not reach it because the option applies only after the checkout. `runnable` stays **`true`**, no `refusal.kind` is produced, and **the admission guarantee excludes this cell exactly as it excludes `untracked-present`**. **The unknown arm follows the fact, not the old rank** (round-28 item 3): on an **external** row a `context.dirty` of `null` still fails closed here, because the fact still feeds a blocker there; on a **checkout-continuation** row it no longer can, since this rank has no checkout arm — so an unknown dirty probe publishes the same `checkout-dirty-present` warning with a detail saying the state could not be established, and `runnable` stays `true`: the four-conjunct predicate of §4.4/§14 promises *admission*, not Git success, and a checkout the arm's own `git checkout` refuses is one of the named things it does not cover (§14, round-18 item 1). The alternatives were both worse: the unconditional blocker refused runs that work, and a silent `runnable: true` with no warning would have hidden a real, arm-specific failure mode behind a green document. Where the escape *does* apply this stays **not** a blocker but the `autostash-across-switch` warning — **settled, not pending** (round-25 item 5, §19.18): the warning leaves `runnable: true` in v1 and no rank is reserved for the alternative. **Round 27 renames the field this rank reads and narrows what it promises** (item 4): the predicate is `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`, and "applies" means only that Git will **start** — it stashes the tracked changes and *attempts* to reapply them, and where that reapply conflicts the rebase can still exit 0 with a conflicted tree and the stash retained (`context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`, §4.1, §5.4.7). That residual never moves this rank in either direction — a row Git will start is not `context-dirty` — but no rendering of this rank, its warning or its absence may describe the outcome as a rescue. An untracked-only context is not dirty at this rank at all; neither is a **stat-dirty, content-identical** file, which the refresh clears exactly as rebase's own check does; and neither is a context whose only change is a **moved or dirty submodule**, which `git rebase`'s own `require_clean_work_tree` ignores. Checkout's shipped whole-repo refusal, which *does* count untracked files and submodules, is a separate rank 3 `state-refused` fact |
| 5.6 | `base-unset` | `base.kind = none` in external (§5.1 rule 5) |
| 5.7 | `base-ref-missing` | `base.ref` does not resolve, including the I14 rows (§8.6.5) |
| 5.8 | `cutoff-unresolvable` | recorded cutoff does not resolve; the run dies at `fatal: invalid upstream` (§6.5) |
| 5.9 | `probe-failed` | a **replay-critical** probe failed and no more specific kind above owns it (§4.1 probe-failure rule) — the candidate `rev-list` probes on a row whose upstream and tip both resolved, the dirty probe, the worktree inventory on a `will_switch_head` row, or the **`rev-parse --show-toplevel`** that resolves that row's own command context, without which the self-vs-foreign comparison at 5.4 has no left-hand side (§5.4.7). It ranks below the specific facts because "I could not measure this row" is weaker evidence than "this row is broken", and it is now the **last** sub-rank of rank 5 |

**Sub-rank 5.10 `config-blocking` is withdrawn, and the kind is removed from the schema**
(round-19 item 7). It never had a member. **Round 27's `invalid-git-config` (5.07) does not revive
it, and the two must not be conflated** (item 3): `config-blocking` was to have refused *valid*
configuration whose effects the plan disliked — which is what the rest of this paragraph rejects,
and which stays rejected — while 5.07 refuses only values Git's own parser **rejects**, where the
previewed command dies during config parsing and the alternative is to publish a run that cannot
start. Every sentence below is therefore still binding for valid values: `rebase.backend` is a default any merge-forcing option
overrides (§4.2); an effectively-true `rebase.rebaseMerges` produces the rank 10 `indeterminate-entry` guard verdict on
a `runnable: true` plan, not a row blocker (§4.2, §4.4) — **an *invalid* one is the separate rank
5.07 fact, not this one** (round-27 item 3); `rebase.autoStash` acts through the rank
5.5 `context-dirty` decision, which is a working-tree fact; and the last candidate — an effective
`rebase.updateRefs` re-enabling collateral movement on a scoped run — is settled in this round as
the **`collateral-update-refs-config` warning**, not a refusal (§4.3, §4.4 `warnings[]`). A kind
whose membership is empty is not a reserved slot but an invitation to invent one, so it is deleted
from `refusal.kind`, from the rank order, from `runnable`'s blocker set and from the hard-blocker
table of §5.3.1, and §19.4's sub-question about its v1 membership goes with it. The rank-5 suborder
is otherwise unchanged and nothing is renumbered.

**Sub-rank 5.55 `untracked-would-be-overwritten` is withdrawn** (round-18 item 1). Round 17 added
it on the claim that `context.untracked_overwrite_paths` was an **exact** set — the untracked
enumeration of a directory intersected with the additions of the trees the arm would write. It is
not exact, and the gap is structural rather than a matter of a missing residual: Git chooses
between an **up-to-date** path (nothing is replayed), a **fast-forward** path (the ref moves and
*that* tree is checked out) and a **replay** path (a sequential cherry-pick whose first working-tree
write is onto the `--onto` commit) at runtime, so the tree the refusal would come from is not the
union the planner computed; and the refusal's own predicate is `unpack_trees`' absent-entry check
over the entries the checkout **actually writes**, under `core.ignorecase`, sparse-checkout patterns
and that path's ignore rules, which a `diff-tree --diff-filter=A` name list does not model. A
**checkout continuation** compounds it: `ContinueCheckoutSync` never re-runs the fresh whole-repo
dirty gate (`gitWorkingTreeDirty` is called only from `RunCheckoutSync`,
`internal/checkout_sync.go:570-577`), so untracked files present at resume time are gated by
nothing at all. The blocker is therefore removed rather than narrowed: what remains is the
**non-blocking** pair `context.untracked_present`/`context.overwrite_risk` and the
`untracked-present` warning (§4.1, §4.4, §5.4.7). No rank is renumbered — 5.5 and 5.6 keep their
values, the suborder is otherwise unchanged, and `untracked-would-be-overwritten` is removed from
the `refusal.kind` enum, so no consumer switch has a dead arm.

**Canonical sort of `blockers[]`** — the array is sorted by the tuple

```
(precedence rank incl. sub-rank, logical entry name, sanitized detail)
```

with a document-level blocker (`entry: null`) sorting before any entry-bearing blocker of the same
rank, string comparison bytewise on the sanitized values (§11), and exact duplicates of the whole
tuple removed. **`warnings[]` is sorted by its own rankless tuple**

```
(kind, logical entry name, sanitized detail)
```

with the same document-level-first, bytewise and duplicate rules (§4.4). The previous draft's
"`warnings[]` is sorted by the identical tuple" is **withdrawn**: warnings carry no rank, so that
tuple's first member was undefined for them and the array had no total order at all (round-19
item 7). The sort is total on both arrays, so two processes
over the same facts emit the same arrays — which is what lets `blockers[]`/`warnings[]` be part of
the canonical, byte-stable document (§4.7). Neither array is fingerprint material: their contents
are derived from the observed-state and row facts the fingerprint already binds or deliberately
excludes (§5.3).

**Rules.**

- Every detected **unwaived** blocker stays in `blockers[]`; precedence chooses only `refusal.kind`.
  A waived limit violation is not a blocker (it is a `waived` row in `guard.evaluation[]`), which is
  the only way `blockers[]` and `refusal.kind` can stay consistent with each other.
- Co-occurrence never changes the array: a run with a dirty tree *and* an unresolvable cutoff *and*
  a per-entry limit violation publishes three blockers and `refusal.kind = state-refused`.
- Ranks 7-12 are guard verdicts, so they are published only when a limit or a token applies; ranks
  1-6 exist whether or not the invocation is guarded.
- `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` is independent of the rank: it stays `true` when a limit is
  exceeded even though a higher-ranked blocker owns `refusal.kind`, so an approval can never be read
  as covering the higher-ranked fact (§5.3.1). `guard.would_refuse` differs from it only by the
  waivers a **matching** token applies, and a token never touches ranks 1-10.
- `runnable` is independent of `refusal.kind` in the other direction: a document may carry
  `refusal.kind = limit-per-entry` and `runnable: true`, because the plan is executable and the
  guard is what is refusing (§4.4).
- **`runnable` is also independent of the controlled-path axis, and that is why the axis exists.**
  `runnable` is computed over the ranks the *unguarded* route's own ladder produces, so the one
  rank 3 fact the shipped ladder may not produce — the pre-existing live foreign owner of §8.6.1
  cause 3 — can leave `runnable: true` on a document whose guarded twin refuses. That is published
  in `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`, never by moving `runnable` (§4.4), which keeps
  "can this plan execute at all?" answering the same question in every document.
- A guarded execution refuses on the top-ranked kind **available at its seam**, and marks it by
  **origin**: a refusal a shipped check owns keeps its shipped text and carries no marker whatever
  its rank (including checkout's in-`BuildCheckoutPlan` `head-ref-missing`); a refusal the guard
  generates at its own seam or a JIT seam carries the marker whatever its rank (including the
  legacy-external `plan-unavailable` interception the guard introduces) (§8.7.1, §8.7.6).
