## 5. The whole-stack dependency challenge

### 5.1 Source range, destination commit, and strategy are three separate determinacy questions

The previous draft asserted that "source ranges are knowable for the whole stack". That is true only
under a condition the draft never stated, and false without it. The corrected rules, derived
directly from the argv predicates of §2.1/§2.2 and from the loops that run them:

**Rule (destination deferral) — executor order, not stack topology.** A destination is deferred
**iff the entry's executor-resolved `base.ref` will be rewritten by an entry this route actually
executes *earlier***. Three inputs decide it, and the topology edge alone is none of them:

1. the route's **real execution order** — external: pass 1 over the *materialized* entries in
   `TopoSort` order, then pass 2 over the *non-materialized* ones in `TopoSort` order (two separate
   loops over the same `sorted` slice, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:93-163` then `:165-211`);
   checkout: its single plan-array order, i.e. `TopoSort` minus archived, unselected,
   anchor-under-local-only and empty-base rows (`BuildCheckoutPlan`,
   `internal/checkout_sync.go:464-517`);
2. the **materialization of the base provider** — which loop it lands in, and whether it is in the
   run at all;
3. the base provider's **planned arm and outcome** — a row planned as `skipped-updated-ref`,
   `skipped-anchor`, `skipped-archived`, `skipped-no-base`, unselected or blocking rewrites nothing.

| child row | base provider | deferred? | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| materialized | materialized parent that will rebase | **yes** | both in pass 1, parent first in `TopoSort` order |
| materialized | **non-materialized** parent | **no** — destination is the current snapshot | the parent runs in **pass 2, after the child**. On an unscoped external run the child's own `--update-refs` then feeds `markUpdatedAncestors`, so that parent's own row becomes `skipped-updated-ref` later (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:151-154`, `:358-379`) — the reverse of a deferral |
| non-materialized | materialized parent that will rebase | **yes** | every pass-1 entry precedes every pass-2 entry |
| non-materialized | non-materialized parent | **only if that parent will actually rebase earlier** | both are in pass 2 in `TopoSort` order; **not** deferred when the parent's planned arm is `skipped-updated-ref`, an anchor skipped under local-only, unselected, or blocking |
| any | a topology parent that is **not** the resolved `base.ref` — the cross-repo case, where `resolveEntryBase` returns the parent's logical name literally (§3.3) | **never** | the run never rebases onto that parent's branch, so claiming a dependency would invent one the executor does not have |
| checkout, any | a parent excluded from the plan array (archived, unselected, anchor under local-only, empty base) | **no** | nothing in the plan rewrites this row's base before it runs |

`destination.depends_on` names the base provider **only** in the deferred cells, and it names the
row that really executes earlier — never merely `entry.Base`.

**Rule (effective replay upstream).** For a selected entry — and **every ref in the rules below is
resolved in `execution_context`, because `git rebase` resolves them there** (round-35 item 3): the
plain arm's upstream `base.ref`, the `--onto` arm's destination, the recorded cutoff it passes as the
source boundary, `head.sha` at the other end of the range, and the branch inventory the collateral
upper bound intersects. The **one** ref this rule does *not* take from that context is
`base.decision_sha`, which is `GetBranchSHA` in `base_context` and which decides only **which arm is
selected**, never what the arm replays or where it lands (§4.1). On every coincident row the two are
one read; where they are two stores, the row is refused at §4.9 rank 5.15 before any of this matters:

1. **Recorded cutoff present and resolvable** → the effective upstream commit is the **recorded
   cutoff**, in *both* argv arms. The `--onto` arm passes the cutoff as the literal upstream; the
   plain arm is only ever selected when the cutoff **equals** the post-parent base SHA, in which
   case the base ref resolves to that same commit. The source range is therefore
   `cutoff..<git_branch>` **regardless of whether the destination is deferred** —
   `replay.determinacy = exact`, `replay.upstream_provenance = recorded-cutoff`.
   *Exact* here means "both ends are pinned at plan time": the upstream is an immovable SHA and the
   other end is `head.sha`. It is not a claim that the range survives anything that moves the
   **tip** — a `--update-refs` collateral rewrite of a not-yet-processed entry (§4.3) or a foreign
   writer does. Such an entry is flagged `collateral_exposed` and is recomputed at the JIT seam;
   exactness is a statement about the plan's inputs, not a promise about the future.
   External carries one degenerate sub-case: when `GetBranchSHA(base)` returns empty **in
   `base_context`** — i.e. when `base.decision_sha` is `null` — external
   downgrades to the plain arm *and* skips the cutoff update (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:122-135,
   158-162`). That is a **decision-context** fact and the plan must model it as one: the arm changes
   because the *decision* read came back empty, whether or not `base.ref` resolves in
   `execution_context`. In the ordinary cell it does not resolve there either, the run fails at
   `git rebase`, and the row is `determinacy = unknown`, `reason = base-ref-missing`; the cell in
   which it resolves in one store and not the other is exactly the divergence §4.9 rank 5.15 refuses
   (round-35 item 3).
2. **No recorded cutoff (`cutoff.state = absent`) and destination not deferred** → the
   upstream is `base.ref` resolved now. Countable, but it is a **current snapshot**: the ref can
   move (a concurrent process, a later fetch, a foreign push).
   `replay.determinacy = snapshot`, `replay.upstream_provenance = base-ref-snapshot`.
3. **No recorded cutoff and destination deferred** → the plain-rebase upstream is the base ref
   resolved **at rebase time**, i.e. the **unknown post-rebase parent**. The source range is
   unknown; any count is at best a current-snapshot estimate over a boundary the run will not use.
   `replay.determinacy = unknown`, `replay.upstream_provenance = base-ref-deferred`,
   `replay.reason = upstream-deferred`, `candidate_count = null`. The *strategy* is nevertheless the
   determinate `plain` (strategy rule below). The plan may additionally publish a clearly-labelled
   `snapshot_candidate_count` (from the pre-rebase parent), but it must never be
   the value a threshold is evaluated against and must never be labelled exact.
4. **Cutoff recorded but unresolvable** → **both** executors still select the `--onto` arm whenever
   the destination SHA reads (neither verifies the recorded SHA:
   `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:123-135`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:1116-1122`), so the run fails
   with `fatal: invalid upstream <sha>` (§6.5). Strategy is `onto`; the range is `unknown` with
   `reason = cutoff-unresolvable`. This is the case the guard converts
   from a mid-run bogus "conflict" into a pre-rebase refusal.
5. **Base unset (`base.kind = none`)** → the modes diverge, and the plan is total here too.
   *Checkout* **skips the entry**: `base := entry.Base; if base == "" { continue }`
   (`internal/checkout_sync.go:485-488`). The row is `strategy = skipped-no-base`, `argv = []`,
   `replay.determinacy = not-applicable`, `replay.reason = not-executed`, `blocking = false` — an
   intentional skip, but published **explicitly**, with the cause carried by the `skipped-no-base`
   strategy token and `base.kind = none` rather than by a replay reason (§4.1 skip rule), because
   the shipped run omits the entry
   silently and an operator reading "nothing happened to pr3" is owed the reason.
   *External* has no such skip. `resolveEntryBase` finds no in-stack parent for the empty name and
   `resolveBase("", ctx)` returns the **empty string**: the `origin/<default>` rewrite fires only
   when `base == defaultBranch`, and the shipped default-branch resolver never yields an empty
   name — `DefaultBranchIn` falls back to `"main"` on every failure path and `DefaultBranch()`
   returns `"main"` on error (`internal/exec.go:59-88`). The previous draft's "or literally
   `origin/`" alternative is therefore **unreachable** and is removed. The single token external
   passes is `""`, which `git rev-parse` cannot read, so `currentBaseSHA` is empty, the plain arm is
   selected, and `git rebase --update-refs ''` (pass 1) or `git rebase '' <branch>` (pass 2) fails
   at Git. The row is `strategy = plain` / `plain-explicit-branch` with the empty token **printed
   verbatim and quoted** so it is visible at all, `replay.determinacy = unknown`,
   `replay.reason = base-unset`, `blocking = true`, and `blockers[]` carries
   `{kind: base-unset, entry}`. A guarded external run refuses **before** mutation; plan-only
   returns the document and exits 0 (§8.3.5).
6. **Head ref missing or unresolvable (`head.state != present`)** → the row has no tip, so it has no
   range, no identity and no count, in either mode. `head.state` is therefore a **totality axis of
   its own**, not a footnote of `materialization`: a branch can be absent, or present and
   unpeelable, independently of whether a worktree exists. The row is
   `replay.determinacy = unknown`, `replay.reason = head-ref-missing`, `candidate_count = null`,
   `replay.range = null`, `replay.commits = null` (§4.8), `blocking = true`, with
   `{kind: head-ref-missing, entry}` in `blockers[]`. Both executors are modelled explicitly:
   *Checkout* fails **while building the plan** — `preSHA, err := gitResolveRef(repoDir, branch)` →
   `resolve branch %q: %w` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:500-503`) — which aborts the whole
   `BuildCheckoutPlan` call before the transaction and before the first `git checkout`, so **no**
   entry of that run executes. The planner must **not** inherit that abort: plan-only publishes the
   offending row plus every other row it could build and reports the run unrunnable, while the
   guarded run keeps the shipped whole-plan failure.
   *External* has no eager resolution. On **pass 2** the missing branch is the rebase operand, so
   `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` fails at Git and the run stops with the archived-conflict line
   (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:196-207`). On **pass 1** the branch is normally implied by the
   materialized worktree, so this cell arises when the ref was deleted or detached under a live
   worktree, and the shipped `checkSyncWorktreeBranch` preflight owns the message
   (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:111-116`) — the row still publishes `head.state` and its own
   blocker, and §4.9 ranks the shipped `preflight-refused` above it.

**Rule (strategy determinacy).** The arm is chosen by a predicate over the recorded cutoff and the
base SHA **read at the moment the entry is reached** — `currentBaseSHA` in external
(`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:122-135`), the re-resolved `NewBaseSHA` in checkout
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:1024-1030,1116-1122`). Written out literally:

```
external : onto  ⟺  LastBaseSHA != "" && currentBaseSHA != "" && LastBaseSHA != currentBaseSHA
checkout : onto  ⟺  LastBaseSHA != ""                        && LastBaseSHA != NewBaseSHA
```

The previous draft read "deferred destination ⇒ `conditional`" off these predicates. That is wrong,
and the correction is mechanical:

- **Cutoff absent ⇒ `plain`, always, and determinately.** With `LastBaseSHA == ""` the left conjunct
  is false in both modes, so no unknown value can flip the arm. The strategy is `plain`, the argv
  tokens are fully knowable (`git rebase [--update-refs] <base.ref>` / `git rebase --no-fork-point
  <Base>`) — **even when the destination SHA is deferred**, because the token is a *ref name*, not
  the SHA. What stays unknown is the replay range and count (rule 3), not the strategy or the argv.
  A row may therefore hold `strategy = plain`, non-null `argv`, and `determinacy = unknown`
  simultaneously; the schema must permit exactly that combination.
- **`conditional` requires a recorded cutoff *and* a deferred destination SHA.** Only then is the
  right-hand comparison unevaluable at plan time. External adds a third conjunct that must appear in
  the published predicate: `currentBaseSHA != ""`. So external's condition reads
  `onto unless post-rebase(<parent>) == <cutoff> or post-rebase(<parent>) is unreadable`, and
  checkout's reads `onto unless post-rebase(<parent>) == <cutoff>`. `strategy_condition` publishes
  the mode's real predicate, not a shared approximation.
- **Unresolvable recorded cutoff + resolvable destination ⇒ `onto` in both modes**, determinately —
  neither executor verifies the cutoff before choosing (external:
  `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:123-135`; checkout: `internal/checkout_sync.go:1116-1122`) — and the
  run then **fails** at `git rebase` with `fatal: invalid upstream <sha>` (§6.5). The row is
  `strategy = onto`, `argv` non-null, `determinacy = unknown`, `reason = cutoff-unresolvable`,
  `blocking = true`.
- **Unresolvable destination (`base.ref` missing) diverges by mode.** External's `GetBranchSHA`
  returns `""`, the second conjunct fails, and it falls back to **`plain`** — passing the
  unresolvable ref to `git rebase`, which fails there — *and* silently skips the cutoff update
  (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:122,158-162`). Checkout never reaches a rebase at all: the base is
  resolved eagerly, first in `BuildCheckoutPlan` ("resolve base %q for %q",
  `internal/checkout_sync.go:495-498`) and again per entry in `processBranch` ("re-resolve base
  %q", `internal/checkout_sync.go:1024-1029`), so the failure is a plan/preflight error. Both rows
  are `determinacy = unknown`, `reason = base-ref-missing`, `blocking = true`, but the modelled
  strategy is `plain` for external and `unknown` for checkout, and the modelled failure point
  differs — the plan must state which.

Under rule 1 the *range* is unaffected by which arm wins, which is why a `conditional` strategy and
an `exact` range coexist without contradiction; under rule 3 the *strategy* is unaffected by the
deferred destination, which is why a determinate `plain` and an `unknown` range coexist too. The
`RebaseStrategy` function of §7.3 must be total over this whole product — mode × materialization ×
cutoff state × destination state × **head state** — and return `conditional` in exactly one cell of
it.

For the customer's stack (`master`, `pr1`, `pr2` with `pr2.base = pr1`), with cutoffs recorded:

- **PR1**: destination `master`, resolvable now; upstream = `cutoff(pr1)`; range exact; strategy
  determinate.
- **PR2**: destination = `post-rebase(pr1)`, **deferred**; upstream = `cutoff(pr2)` (recorded,
  immovable) so the range `cutoff(pr2)..pr2` is **exact**; strategy `conditional` — `onto` unless
  `post-rebase(pr1) == cutoff(pr2)`, in which case `plain` over the identical boundary.

And the same stack **without** recorded cutoffs (the normal state after `tws new`, §2.3):

- **PR1**: upstream = `origin/master` (or `master`), snapshot; countable, labelled `snapshot`;
  strategy `plain`, argv known.
- **PR2**: upstream = `pr1` **after** PR1 runs → range `unknown`; strategy still **`plain`** and its
  argv still known, because no cutoff exists to compare. Nothing honest can be counted, and the
  §6.2 cold-squash transcript shows why the number would mislead: the boundary the run uses simply
  does not exist yet.

**Just-in-time resolution.** Every `deferred`/`conditional`/`unknown` field has exactly one moment
at which it becomes determinate: the per-entry re-resolution both executors already perform
(external `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:117-135`, checkout `internal/checkout_sync.go:1024-1030`).
At that point the parent has moved, the base ref resolves to its final value, the arm predicate can
be evaluated, and the range can be counted and identified. The guard therefore *resolves* the
deferred row there — filling `base.decision_sha`/`destination.sha`, `strategy`, `argv`, `replay.*` — and re-checks the
thresholds and the approval against the now-exact facts (§5.2). A deferred row is not a permanent
apology; it is a promise to be resolved one entry later, before that entry's own rebase.

Checkout mode already behaves this way at execution time — it re-resolves `NewBaseSHA` per entry
inside `processBranch` precisely because the plan's value went stale.

Note the second-order effect: if Git drops PR1's only candidate (the exact-squash case),
`post-rebase(pr1) == master`, and PR2's destination lands where the plan's snapshot said it would.
If PR1 conflicts, PR2 is never reached. Neither outcome is predictable, which is why deferral must
be a first-class state and not a best-effort guess.

### 5.2 Per-edge just-in-time guard vs fully precomputed run plan

| | Precomputed whole-run plan | Per-edge JIT guard |
|---|---|---|
| Shows the operator the whole blast radius up front | yes | no (one edge at a time) |
| Destination SHAs | frontier exact; deferred rows carry a labelled snapshot | always exact |
| Candidate ranges | `exact` with a resolvable recorded cutoff (even when deferred); `snapshot` at the frontier without one; `unknown` for a deferred entry without one (§5.1) | always exact |
| Strategy / argv | determinate everywhere except the one `conditional` cell — a recorded cutoff **and** a deferred destination together (§5.1) | always determinate |
| Can stop before the *first* rebase | yes | yes |
| Can stop before the *third* entry with fresh facts | no | yes |
| Interaction cost in CI/agents | one decision | N decisions unless approval is run-scoped |
| Implementation cost | moderate | low (it is where checkout already re-resolves) |

**Recommendation: both, with one approval — and an approval that waives exactly one thing.** Compute
the whole-run plan after the fetch and before the first rebase; that is what is printed and what the
thresholds are evaluated against. A matching `approval.fingerprint` waives **only the limit
violations that were already known and shown in the approved document** (§5.3.1): it never waives a
hard blocker, and it never pre-authorises a violation the document did not contain. Then, at each
entry, re-evaluate that entry's row with fresh facts (the parent has just moved) and **stop** —
refusing with a fresh-plan instruction, not waiving — if:

- a fact the approved row declared deferred or unknown resolves to a value that **newly exceeds**
  an effective limit (the approval could not have covered a number nobody saw) — refused with that
  limit's own kind;
- the candidate identity changed, the upstream changed, or the tip moved on a row approved as
  `exact` — `revalidation-mismatch` (§4.9 rank 9);
- new collateral appears **where the approved row's collateral was known** — a ref enters a known
  `collateral_refs`, or a row known to be unexposed becomes `collateral_exposed`; also
  `revalidation-mismatch`. A row approved
  with `null` collateral (§4.8) was never approved as collateral-free: it resolves at this seam like
  any other deferred fact and is re-checked against the same blocking and limit rules;
- the cutoff became unresolvable, the base ref stopped resolving, or the strategy resolved outside
  the approved shapes — the first two are rank 5 hard blockers even at this seam, the third is
  `revalidation-mismatch`.

**Which unknowns this seam can rescue is decided by `replay.reason`, and by nothing else**
(round-25 item 3, §4.1). The seam re-measures a row whose reason is **`upstream-deferred`** — the
one member whose fact really does resolve when the parent moves — and it can rescue nothing else:
`merge-recreation` is still true one entry later, so a row carrying it is `not-resolvable` up front
and is refused with `indeterminate-entry` under **both** indeterminacy policies (§4.4
`guard.indeterminacy_policy`, §8.3.2a), and the hard reasons are rank 5 blockers before the seam is
reached. Because the reason ladder puts `merge-recreation` **above** `upstream-deferred`, a row that
is both never reaches the seam under a deferral it cannot honour, which is the concrete defect the
missing precedence allowed: the same row could be published as deferred, deferred past the guard,
and then produce no number at the seam either.

Approval is granted once per **plan**, and a plan is either the full run or the remaining work: an
uninterrupted run keeps its approval in process, and any interruption invalidates it by
construction, because the remaining plan is not the plan that was approved. A guarded continuation
that needs a waiver therefore mints a **continuation-scoped** token from `--plan --continue`
(§8.7.4). What the route persists is the *guard*, not the *approval*: v2 external payloads and
**every** checkout transaction — v2-shaped or legacy-shaped — carry the two **pointer-backed limit
values** and nothing else (§10.3): their *presence* is the durable "this run was guarded" signal, so
no `guard_enabled` boolean exists to disagree with them. Only the
legacy external route persists neither and repeats its flags, and a continuation of a run that
was never guarded may arm one from flags without writing anything back
(`guard.limits.<key>.origin: flags-persisted-continuation`, §8.7.4). Agents and CI answer once per plan,
not once per entry. Every refusal raised at this seam is **guard-generated by origin**, so it
carries the `plan-guard:` marker line (§8.7.6).

**What the seam re-measures, and what it may reuse** (round-34 item 5). "Re-evaluate that entry's
row with fresh facts" is a statement about **every mutable precondition of the row**, not only about
its ranges: the **decision** SHA as the executor resolves it in `base_context` (`base.decision_sha`)
and the **destination**, the head, the candidate count and the full-sequence digest wherever identity
is revalidated, all in `execution_context`, where `git rebase` resolves them (round-35 item 3); the
`rebase-merge`/
`rebase-apply` operation-directory pair, the tracked-dirty status, the branch/worktree holds and
untracked presence in `execution_context`; and any further mutable fact the row's own action reads.
Reusing a plan-time value for any of them would let a guarded run start a rebase against a tree, a
holder set or an in-progress operation that has since changed — including changes **this same run**
caused one entry earlier, which is exactly the case the seam exists for. What the seam may reuse is
the run-invariant half: the context identity of §4.4 and the ordered configuration inventory of
§4.3, cached per context for the invocation (§13). The conservative ceiling is **twelve** Git
processes per external JIT row — the ten of the re-probe set plus the **one or two**
`DefaultBranchIn` costs when the seam re-resolves a **literal** base (§5.4 consequence 4, round-37
item 3), falling back to **ten** only in the identified subcase where the row's base names a
**same-repo stack entry** and `resolveEntryBase` short-circuits with no default-branch read — and
**eight** per checkout row, which resolves no default branch anywhere (§13, §9, §15.16 (d2)).

The JIT step is also the only place a `determinacy = unknown` row can be evaluated at all. A guard
that refused every unknown row up front would refuse every un-synced stack's second entry; a guard
that ignored them would leave the broadest possible replay unguarded. Resolving at the JIT seam and
enforcing the same thresholds there is the only option that is both honest and useful — and it means
a run **can** stop at entry 3 for a reason that did not exist at entry 1.

### 5.3 TOCTOU and revalidation

A plan is inherently racy: another process can move `master` between plan and rebase, and
external's `--onto <ref-name>` re-resolves the base *inside* `git rebase` (D3), so external can
rebase onto a different commit than the plan printed even within one process. The plan being
non-mutating (§0.1) does not make it a snapshot of the future.

Options, in increasing strength:

1. **Print-only** — document the race, change nothing. Cheapest, weakest.
2. **Plan fingerprint, split into two distinct jobs** — see the split below. Compute it per
   invocation and re-validate per entry just before mutation (§5.2). It is deliberately **not**
   persisted: a token authorises one plan, and the only plan a continuation can execute is the
   remaining one (§8.7.4).
3. **Pin the destination** — pass a resolved SHA to `git rebase --onto <sha>` in external, matching
   checkout (D3). This *eliminates* the intra-process race but is a behaviour change to the frozen
   external argv and would break `internal/cli/testdata/sync_noflag/external-clean/argv.log`. It
   must therefore be restricted to guarded runs if it is done at all.

**The split (this is the correction).** One hash cannot do both jobs, and the previous draft's
single tuple quietly conflated them.

**Fingerprint domain — stated once, and binding everywhere else.** `approval.fingerprint` is the
SHA-256 of a **canonical invariant tuple projected from the canonical document**, and **not** of the
rendered document. Every other section that mentions the fingerprint refers to this rule and states
no other: §4.6, §4.7, §8.3.3 and §8.7.7 are readings of it, not competing definitions. The
projection is what makes `--plan` and `--plan --approve-plan <fp>` publish the **same** token for
the same facts (§15.16f), which is the property the whole `--approve-plan` workflow rests on.

**The membership rule is a whitelist, not a pair of prose lists.** The previous draft described the
tuple as "closed in both directions" and then gave two paragraphs; two paragraphs cannot be closed,
because a field mentioned in neither had no defined status and every schema addition reopened the
question. §5.3.2 replaces them with an **exhaustive inclusion table**, plus one rule:

> **Any field of the document that is not listed in §5.3.2 is excluded from the tuple — including
> every field added to the schema after this analysis.** Adding a field to the fingerprint is
> therefore an explicit edit to that table and to nothing else.

Letting an excluded fact invalidate a token would train users to re-approve reflexively, which is
the worst possible outcome for a safety control; letting an included one slip out would authorise a
run nobody previewed.

**5.3.2 The fingerprint whitelist (exhaustive).** (This block and §5.3.3 were added by a later
round; §5.3.1, which states what a matching token *waives*, keeps its number and follows them —
the citations `§5.3.1`, `§5.3.2` and `§5.3.3` all keep their referents.)

**Document-level members.** Every row is a fact about *which run* is authorised:

| Tuple member | Source field | Why it must invalidate a token |
|---|---|---|
| `scope` | `approval.scope` (`full-run` / `remaining-work`) | a full-run token must never authorise a resume, and vice versa (§8.7.4) |
| `workspace_mode`, `workspace_stable_id`, `workspace_repo_root` | `workspace.*` | the same feature name in another workspace is another run. **`workspace_stable_id` is nullable and is bound as `BYTES\|NULL`** (§5.3.2a top-level id 3, §4.4): where workspace resolution could not establish an id, the canonical `NULL` sentinel is bound rather than an empty string, so a document with an id and one without never collapse onto one token (round-34 item 8) |
| `feature` | `feature` | — |
| `route` | `route` — the **effective**, state-derived one on a continuation (§0.2) | a legacy and a new-mode run of the same stack differ in fetch set, selection refusals, state and argv (R1-R11) |
| `policy_fetch`, `policy_propagation`, `policy_scope_kind`, `policy_selector` | `policy.*` — the persisted policy on a v2 continuation | this is the **effective** operand set the trigger flags resolved to. It is bound *instead of* `route_triggers[]`: two spellings that resolve to one policy describe one run, and binding the raw flag list would make a redundant, legal flag repeat on a continuation mint a different token (§8.7.4) |
| `limits[key] = value` for each of `max_replay_per_entry`, `max_replay_total` | `guard.limits.<key>.value` — the **effective** value of the **single** per-key `{value, origin}` encoding of §4.4/§8.7.4, read straight out of the document with no second field to reconcile | **a token minted under one guard must not authorise a run guarded differently** (§8.7.4): a token minted with `--max-replay-per-entry 10` does not authorise `--max-replay-per-entry 20`, and a token minted with `--max-replay-per-entry 10` alone does not authorise `--max-replay-per-entry 10 --max-replay-total 10`, because the *other* key's value moved from the absent sentinel to a number. **Round 30 withdraws the "a token minted with no limit must not authorise a limit-bearing run or vice versa" justification as unreachable** (item 1): a document with no effective limit on either key fails clause (b) of §4.4's usable-token predicate and publishes `approval.fingerprint: null`, so there is no such token to be mismatched, and the pairs a test can actually build are the ones named above (§4.4, §8.5.1, §15.16g). `value` is a number **or the explicit absent sentinel** — `0` and "no limit" are different tuple values, and the sentinel is what makes the per-entry-only and per-entry-plus-total tokens differ (§8.3.2a, §10.3). **`origin` is deliberately *not* a member** (see the non-member table): it is a source label describing *how* the same effective value was reached — `flags` on a fresh run, `persisted-payload`/`persisted-transaction` on a resume that inherited it, `flags-persisted-continuation`/`flags-legacy-continuation` where the invocation armed or repeated it — and binding a label would invalidate a token for a run that guards identically, so a persisted `10` and an identically repeated `--max-replay-per-entry 10` mint the **same** token. The label stays published, so an operator still sees where the guard came from; the token binds what the guard *is*. The earlier draft bound the pair and then justified it as "not the source label", which was self-contradictory; the pair-binding is **withdrawn** |
| `intent_push` | `intent.push` | "and then force-push every synced branch" is the most consequential thing a sync does after the rebase (§3.11) |
| `push_targets[]` — the canonical, **`(context_id, git_branch)`**-sorted list of `{repo, context_id, git_branch, remote, ref, force, lease.expectation, lease.expected_ref, lease.expected_sha, scope}` tuples (**round-35 item 5**: the rendered `repo_root` is replaced by the pushing context's **stable identity** as both the sort key and the bound member, exactly as round-33 item 4 did for the entry and repository structs — a §11 rendering is lossy, two distinct push contexts may render to one string, and a sort that ended in a rendering was not total; the descriptive `repo` token stays a member but is **not** a key) | `push.targets[]` | binding `intent.push` alone would authorise "and then force-push" without saying **what**: a token minted for a scoped push of one branch would authorise a `scope=all` push of the whole feature, in another repository, with the same boolean. **The lease baseline is bound with the target** — `lease.expected_ref` and `lease.expected_sha`, the remote-tracking ref the implicit `--force-with-lease` will read (as the remote's own fetch refspecs map it, §4.4) and the value it held at plan time (§4.4): approving a force-push over a remote tip you were shown is a different authorisation from approving one over a tip that has since moved, and **`expectation: absent`** — the lease that requires the remote branch *not to exist* (§4.4) — must never be authorised by a token minted when a SHA expectation existed, or the reverse: the two are different authorisations over the same argv, which is why `expectation` is bound alongside `expected_sha` rather than being inferred from its nullness. `lease.mode` and `lease.expected_sha_freshness` are **not** members — the mode is a constant and the freshness label is a fetch fact (see the non-member table). It is also what makes a **push-only** document approvable at all — with `entries[]` empty, the push set is the entire work being authorised (§4.4, §8.6.4a) |
| `restore` → `{applies, will_switch_head, target_branch, target_sha, push_dropped}`, in that fixed order | `restore` | the checkout restoring mutation is real work and, on a `restoring` resume, the **only** work: a token must bind *which* branch HEAD will be put back on and *which* commit that branch was when the operator approved it, or an approval minted over `restore → main@<sha1>` would authorise a resume that switches to a `main` someone has since moved. `deletes_transaction`, `releases_lock`, `target_source`, `executable` and `blocked_by[]` are **not** members: the first two are on-success effects derived from `executable` (§4.4), `target_source` is a label describing *how* the same branch/tip pair was reached (probed on a fresh run, recorded on a resume — and `scope` already distinguishes those two runs), and the executability pair is a derived answer of exactly the kind `push.executable` is. `applies: false` is a legal tuple value, not an absence, and is what every external document binds (§4.4, §8.6.4a) |
| `validation_applies`, `validation_command_digest` | `intent.validation.applies`, `intent.validation.command_digest` | a token must not authorise a run that validates with a different command, or with none (§8.8) |
| `repositories[]` → `{repo, context_id, config.update_refs.{status, value}, config.rebase_merges.{status, value}, **config.rebase_merges.interpretation**, config.backend.{status, value}, config.auto_stash.{status, value}}`, in canonical `(repo, context_id)` order | `repositories[]` | those values decide collateral movement, merge recreation, the backend and the dirty-tree precondition; one flat object could not distinguish two repositories, and two arms of one `repo` token can resolve to two directories (§4.3, §4.4, §5.4). **It is the `.value` that is bound, spelled out here so no reader has to infer it** (round-18 item 4): each `config.*` is the object `{status, value, source}` (§4.4, round-31 item 4), the **`.value`** is the effective answer the run will act on — including the canonical `null` sentinel wherever the status is not `valid`, which is a different tuple value from any string (§4.8) — the **`.status`** is the closed enum that says *which* of the four no-value cells a `null` is, and each **`.source`** is a *descriptive label* of how that answer was reached, listed as an explicit non-member below. There is no third reading: the tuple contains the four `.value` scalars of each row and, since round-31 item 4, their four `.status` scalars beside them, **plus the one derived scalar round 26 adds — `config.rebase_merges.interpretation`, the closed `true`/`false`/`unknown`/`invalid` reading of §4.2** (item 7, its fourth member added by round-32 item 3), which is a member because it is the **effective answer the run acts on** and because recovering it from `.value` means reimplementing Git's own boolean parser — `2` is true to Git, `rebase-cousins` is true and is not a boolean at all, and `git config --get` prints the same empty line for a valueless key and an explicitly empty one — so a consumer verifying a token must be given the answer rather than asked to re-derive it — and no part of any `.source`. **Round 31 adds each slot's `.status` to the tuple, and only because `.value` alone is no longer discriminating** (item 4): the slot is now `{status, value, source}` with `value: null` under **four** different statuses — `absent`, `not-evaluated`, `probe-failed` and `invalid` (§4.4 `repositories[]`) — so a token minted over a repository whose `rebase.updateRefs` was *unset* would otherwise match a run whose probe *failed* and one whose route never evaluated the key, which are three materially different runs. `.status` is bound; `.source` stays a non-member, because it is a label over an answer the pair already carries — including under `invalid`, where round-32 item 3 makes it the occurrence's scope, which the `.status` and the row's `config_issues[]` evidence already determine; and nothing beyond these — no out-of-scope value, no `config_issues[]` row (§5.3.2 non-members) — enters the tuple. **The projected identity is `context_id`, not `repo_root`** (round-32 item 1): the rendered root is lossy, so binding it would have let two materially different contexts project one tuple member and would have left the projection's own ordering non-total |
| `entries[]` — the canonical, name-sorted list of the per-entry tuples below | `entries[]`, which on a continuation is exactly `RemainingRebaseEntries` (§8.6.4a) | the set of work being authorised. The continuation stage that produced that set is **not** a member: its entire effect is the resulting list and the per-entry facts derived from it. **An empty list is a legal tuple value**, not an absence: a push-only document binds `entries[]: []` together with a non-empty `push_targets[]`, a checkout `restoring` document binds `entries[]: []` and `push_targets[]: []` together with `restore.applies: true`, and in each case the combination is what its token authorises |

**Per-entry members**, one sub-tuple per row, in `name` order:

| Tuple member | Source field |
|---|---|
| identity | `name`, `git_branch`, `repo`, **`base_context.context_id`** and **`execution_context.context_id`** (round-33 item 4 replaced the display root with the id; **round-34 item 3 binds both context ids and both `source` labels**, because a row whose base resolves in one repository and whose rebase runs in another is different work from a row where the two coincide, and the single member could not say so: the id is a digest over the *raw* canonical root, the root source and the raw common dir and therefore binds those bytes exactly — §4.1, §4.4), `base_context.source`, `execution_context.source`, `role`, `materialization` |
| head | `head.state`, **`head.sha`** |
| base | `base.name`, `base.ref`, **the strategy-decision SHA** (`base.decision_sha`, read in `base_context`) **and the destination SHA** (`destination.sha`, or `destination.snapshot_sha` when deferred, read in `execution_context`) — **two members since round-35 item 3**, because a row that chooses its arm from one store and replays in another is different work from one whose two contexts coincide, and the single member could not say so; on a coincident row the two carry the same value and the plan issues one `rev-parse` |
| cutoff | `cutoff.recorded_sha`, `cutoff.state` |
| deferral | `destination.deferred`, `destination.depends_on` |
| replay | `replay.determinacy`, **`replay.reason`**, `replay.upstream_provenance`, **`replay.upstream_sha`**, **`replay.candidate_count`** and **`replay.candidate_digest`** — the digest over the *complete, uncapped* oldest-first candidate sequence (§4.5), so neither truncation nor the choice of rendering can weaken or move it. **`replay.reason` is an explicit member, not an oversight and not a label** (round-18 item 4): it is the field that distinguishes *why* a row replays nothing or replays indeterminately — `not-executed` on a skip row, `head-ref-missing`, **`upstream-deferred`** (the §4.1 spelling of the enum member; the bare `deferred` of the previous draft named no member of it and is corrected here, round-19 item 4), `merge-recreation` — and two rows that agree on `determinacy` and on a `null`/`0` count while disagreeing on the reason are **different work**, so a token minted over one must not authorise the other. `replay.commits`, `commits_listed` and `commits_truncated` are **not** members: they are the capped rendering of the same fact |
| execution shape | `strategy` (or `conditional` **plus both** `argv_alternatives`), `effective_backend` |
| mutation | `mutation.will_switch_head`, `mutation.will_leave_head_on`, `mutation.head_restored_by_run` — a row that switches HEAD and leaves it there authorises a different thing from one that does not (§5.4.7) |
| preconditions | `context.dirty`, `context.autostash`, **`context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`** (round-26 item 8, renamed by round-27 item 4 — the derived, arm-aware fact rank 5.5 actually reads; two rows agreeing on the first two while disagreeing on it are different work, since one refuses and the other does not. **`context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict` is *not* a second member**: it is a total function of this one, so binding it would bind the same bit twice, and it is listed as an explicit non-member below), `branch_checked_out_at` — the facts that decide rank 5.4/5.5, so a token minted over a clean context cannot authorise a dirty one. **`context.untracked_present` and `context.overwrite_risk` are deliberately *not* members** and are listed as non-members below: they decide nothing, and binding them would invalidate a token because an unrelated scratch file appeared in the directory between plan and run (round-18 item 1, §4.1, §5.4.7) |
| collateral | `collateral_mechanism`, `collateral_exposed`, and `collateral_refs` **including its known/unknown state** and each element's `{repo, ref, sha, stack_owned}` tuple (`null` ≠ `[]`, §4.8) |

Every unknown enters the tuple as a **canonical `null` sentinel** distinct from every string, number
and empty list, so a token minted while a fact was unknown does not match a run in which it
resolved — and a `repo-unavailable` row, whose failed context ref carries `context_id` and
`repo_root` both
`null` and which cites no
`repositories[]` row for it (§4.1, §4.4), is encoded by that sentinel rather than by omission — the
sentinel standing in for the **bound** member, which since round-33 item 4 is the `context_id` and
since round-34 item 3 is one such member per context ref, so a row whose *base* context broke
projects a different tuple from one whose *execution* context did. Note what
that row still contributes: its `name`, `git_branch`, `repo`, both `source` labels, `role`,
`materialization`, `cutoff.recorded_sha`, the deferral facts and the `mutation.*` facts are all
**preserved** and bound (§4.1 repo-unavailable nullability rule), so the tuple stays discriminating
— two different broken rows never collapse onto one another — and the token stays stable across
processes for the same broken input.

**Explicit non-members.** These are excluded by the whitelist rule; they are listed only because
each has been proposed at least once and each would break a real workflow:

| Excluded | Why binding it would be wrong |
|---|---|
| `invocation` (`plan-only` vs `guarded-execution`) | it differs **by construction** between the `--plan` document and the guarded run it authorises; binding it would make every token self-invalidating |
| `requested_route` | it records what the command line asked for, not what will run; the **effective** `route` is bound |
| `route_triggers[]` | superseded by the effective policy above — see that row |
| `policy.fetch_default_applied` | a label on how the bound policy value was reached |
| **`context.untracked_present`, `context.overwrite_risk`** | ambient observations of the working tree that decide **nothing**: neither is a blocker, neither moves `runnable`, and `overwrite_risk` is a declared *residual* the planner cannot settle (§4.1, §5.4.7). Binding them would invalidate a perfectly good token because an unrelated scratch file was written into the directory between the `--plan` invocation and the guarded one — the same self-invalidation the `state` exclusion below exists to prevent. Round 17 bound the withdrawn `context.untracked_overwrite_paths`; round 18 removes the field and the binding together |
| `intent.push_source`, `intent.validation.source`, `.stability`, `.guarded_stability`, `.cli_test_ignored`, **`guard.limits.<key>.origin`**, **`repositories[].config.update_refs.source`, `repositories[].config.rebase_merges.source`, `repositories[].config.backend.source`, `repositories[].config.auto_stash.source`** | descriptive labels of the shipped route or of how an effective value was reached. A `--plan` document describes the route (`config-per-entry`, `per-entry-dynamic`) while the guarded invocation freezes it, so binding a label guarantees a mismatch (§8.8); and a resume that inherits `--max-replay-total 20` guards exactly as one that repeats the flag, so `persisted-payload` versus `flags-persisted-continuation` must not mint two tokens (§8.7.4). Note the contrast with `push.targets[]`, which is **not** a label: it is the projected work itself, and it is a member |
| `approval.fingerprint`, `approval.supplied`, `approval.accepted`, `approval.usable`, `approval.covers` | the fingerprint cannot contain itself, and `supplied`/`accepted`/`usable`/`covers` are answers *about* a token, not facts about the work — `usable` and `covers`'s three clause booleans `has_work`/`requires_limits`/`encoding_safe` (round-30 item 4) restate the mint preconditions of §4.4, which are already decided by the work, the limit values and the identity bytes the tuple *does* bind. **`approval.scope` is the one `approval.*` field that is a member** (see the document-level table): it names *which plan* — full run or remaining work — the token authorises, which is a property of the work, not an answer about a token. The previous draft's blanket "`approval.*` in its entirety" contradicted that member row and is withdrawn; the exclusion is exactly these five subfields |
| `push.executable`, `push.blocked_by[]`, `restore.executable`, `restore.blocked_by[]`, `restore.target_source`, `restore.deletes_transaction`, `restore.releases_lock`, `guard.limit_conflicts[]` | derived answers, not work: executability is computed from blockers the tuple already binds or deliberately excludes (§4.9), and a limit conflict records a flag this invocation *attempted* and the document rejected — the **effective** limits are bound, and binding a rejected attempt would mint a different token for the same guarded plan (§4.4, §8.7.4) |
| `guard.would_refuse`, `guard.would_refuse_without_approval`, `guard.indeterminacy_policy`, **`guard.execute_blocked_by[]`**, and **every** `guard.evaluation[]` field including `verdict`, `value`, `basis` and `unknown_kind` | a waiver is a verdict change; binding verdicts would make an approved replay mint a different token than the document that authorised it. The *inputs* to those verdicts — the limits and the candidate identities — are bound instead |
| `blockers[]`, `warnings[]`, `refusal.*`, `runnable` | derived from facts the tuple already binds or deliberately excludes (§4.9) |
| **`encoding_issues[]`** (round-28 item 4) | it is a statement *about* the pre-image — which `BYTES` members failed `utf8.Valid`, with their base64 and digests — computed from the tuple rather than added to it, so binding it would be circular; and every document that publishes a non-empty one mints no token at all (§4.4 usable-token clause (c), §5.3.2a rule 10) |
| **`config_issues[]`** (round-30 item 2, **eleven**-member rows since round-32 item 1 added `context_id` to round-31 item 2's ten) | it is a statement about the *repository's configuration as this route will parse it*, not about the work, and every one of its rows carries a non-waivable rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config` blocker with `runnable: false` — so the resulting document authorises nothing whatever a token said, and binding the array would only mint a second, equally unusable token. **`issue_id` is a non-member with the array that carries it**, and for the same reason: it is a digest *of* evidence about a refused document, not a fact about the work. The **effective** config values that do decide work are bound where they belong: the four `repositories[].config.*.{status, value}` pairs and `config.rebase_merges.interpretation` in the document-level table above — the status members being exactly what keeps `absent`, `not-evaluated`, `probe-failed` and `invalid` from collapsing into one `null` (round-31 item 4, §4.4, §4.9 rank 5.07) |
| `state` in its entirety — including `state.snapshot`, every `applicable`/`presence` pair, every PID, every `alive`/`self` flag, `state.files.external_run_guard.token_matches_payload` and `state.files.checkout_transaction.lock_pid` | observation of a concurrent process, and of whether a neighbour's artefact happened to be readable at snapshot time, is not a property of the work. The **totality** encoding does not change this: an artefact that reads `presence: unreadable` in one run and `readable` in the next describes the same plan, so binding `presence` would invalidate a token for a fact about someone else's file. The round-13 gloss "or of which artefacts this invocation will later create" is dropped with the `self_artefacts[]` field it described (§4.4) |
| `fetch.attempted`, `fetch.repos[]` (including every `context_root`/`context_common_dir`/`context_source` label, every `context_candidates[]` member, and — from round 23, and from round 25 with its `may_update_local_branches`/`may_delete_local_branches`/`local_branch_destinations` members and its `submodules[].effective_mode_source` — **every** member of `fetch_effect`, its `submodule_recursion` object and its `submodules[]` rows, with no exception), `fetch.outcome`, `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs` (**including its `null`**), `freshness`, and `push.targets[].lease.expected_sha_freshness` | a fetch that succeeded this time and failed last time, with every resolved SHA unchanged, must not invalidate a token; a fetch that *moved* a base invalidates it through `base.decision_sha`/`destination.sha`, and one that moved a remote tip invalidates it through `lease.expected_sha`. **The context labels are incidental unless material**, and where they are material they are already bound through the resolved identities the probes produced (§8.6.9). A context set that is *undecidable* is not handled by binding it either: it is `fetch-context-indeterminate`, a rank 5.0 blocker on a `runnable: false` document, and it is **non-waivable in v1** (§4.9 rank 5.0, §5.3.1) — the document still mints its ordinary token wherever work and an effective limit exist (§4.4), and that token authorises nothing here, because no approval can clear a fetch context the document could not name. The previous draft's "no token is minted over an ambiguous fetch in the first place" contradicted §4.4's token rule and §15.15h4″'s assertion, and is withdrawn. **The round-23 members ride this same exclusion, and the whitelist stays exhaustive by naming them** (items 1, 3 and 5): a submodule store that was readable on Monday and unreadable on Tuesday describes the same replay, so binding `submodule_recursion` would invalidate a token for someone else's checkout; where a submodule reach is material it is material as a **refusal** — rank 5.05, non-waivable, on a `runnable: false` document — exactly as an undecidable context is, and no approval can clear either. **Round 25's members ride the same exclusion** (item 2): which local branches a fetch context could write, and which of them a neighbouring worktree happens to be standing on, is a fact about someone else's checkout and about a fetch, not about the replay this token authorises — and where it *is* material it is material as the non-waivable rank 5.06 refusal on a `runnable: false` document, exactly as 5.0 and 5.05 are |
| `summary.*` in its entirety, including `plannability` | every member is derived from per-entry facts already bound; binding both would double-count and could invalidate a token for a rounding of its own inputs |
| `schema_version`, `snapshot_candidate_count`, `prunability.probe_context`, `ancestry`, `notes`, commit subjects, `replay.range` prose, human ordering, row position, timestamps, and every rendering choice | none of them changes what will be replayed. **`schema_version` is a non-member here and stays one** (round-27 item 6): the 2-byte version field inside §5.3.2a's header is the *tuple encoding's own* schema version and is not this document key — the two are versioned independently, and no reader may infer that publishing `schema_version: 1` binds it |
| `context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict` (round-27 item 4) | it is `true` exactly where `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm` is `true`, which the tuple already binds; a derived restatement is not a second fact, and binding it would only make the pre-image longer |
| **`entries[].base_context.repo_root`, `entries[].execution_context.repo_root`, `repositories[].repo_root` and — round-35 item 5 — `push.targets[].repo_root`** (round-33 item 4, extended to both entry refs by round-34 item 3 and to the push target by round-35 item 5, which retires the push struct's field 2) | all four are **display-only §11 renderings** of a context whose *identity* the tuple already binds — as `base_context.context_id` and `execution_context.context_id` per entry, as `repositories[].context_id` per repository row and as `push_targets[].context_id` per push target — and the renderer is lossy by design, so binding a rendered root would let two materially different contexts project one member while adding nothing the ids do not already carry. The **raw** canonical root bytes are inside the tuple exactly once per distinct context, hashed into `context_id` together with the root source and the raw common dir (§4.4), which is why removing the rendered members weakens no token and why no `encoding_issues[]` row may name any of those paths (§5.3.2a rule 10) |

**5.3.2a The tuple's byte encoding, chosen here rather than left to the implementation**
(round-25 item 4; **the encoding itself is replaced in round 26, item 2**). A whitelist fixes *what*
is hashed; it does not fix *what bytes* are hashed, and
until round 25 the document said only "SHA-256 of a canonical invariant tuple", which two honest
implementations can spell differently — and two spellings mean two tokens for one plan, or, worse,
one token for two plans. Round 25 fixed that gap with **canonical JSON**. **That choice is withdrawn
here, for a correctness reason and not a taste one**: JSON strings are sequences of Unicode code
points, and the values this tuple binds are **not** — a Git ref name, a repository path, a config
value and a branch name are *byte* strings, and Git accepts bytes that are not valid UTF-8 in all of
them. Every JSON encoder must therefore do something with an invalid sequence, and Go's
`encoding/json` replaces each one with U+FFFD, so two materially different plans — two branches
whose names differ only in invalid bytes, two repositories whose paths do — produce the **same**
pre-image and the **same** token. That is a token minted over one plan authorising another, which is
precisely the failure `approval.fingerprint` exists to make impossible; it cannot be repaired by
tightening the JSON rules, because the collision is in the value space, not in the formatting. The
encoding is therefore fixed, normatively, as an **unambiguous typed, length-prefixed binary
(TLV) encoding over raw bytes, hashed with SHA-256**:

1. **The pre-image is a single self-delimiting byte string, and it begins with a domain-separation
   header**: the 11 ASCII bytes `tws-plan-fp` followed by one `0x00` — 12 bytes — then a 2-byte big-endian
   **encoding version** (`0x0001`, this encoding) and a 2-byte big-endian **tuple schema version**
   (**`0x0004`**), which is the version of the **field-id tables below** and of nothing else.
   **Round 33 bumped that second number from `0x0001` to `0x0002`, round 34 to `0x0003`, and round 35
   bumps it to `0x0004`; every one of the three is mandatory rather than cosmetic** (round-33 item 4,
   round-34 item 3, round-35 items 3 and 5):
   round 33 re-pointed the entry struct's id 4 from the rendered `repo_context.repo_root` to that
   context's `context_id`; round 34 split that member in two — id 4 and id 5 now carry
   **`execution_context.context_id`/`execution_context.source`** and the ids 36 and 37 carry
   **`base_context.context_id`/`base_context.source`** —; and round 35 **retires the push struct's
   id 2** (the rendered `repo_root`), **adds the push struct's id 11** (`context_id`), **re-points
   the entry struct's id 12** at the *execution-context* destination SHA and **adds the entry
   struct's id 38** for `base.decision_sha`. Rule 3 requires a bound-member change,
   an added member, a retirement and a re-pointing alike to move every token, so a new binary must
   not verify an old token as if the two field 4s, or the two field 12s, named the same fact. The encoding version is **unchanged**,
   because the framing, the tags and the rules
   below are the same. The header
   is inside the hash, so a future encoding or tuple revision can never mint a token that collides
   with one minted under this one, and an old binary handed a new pre-image mismatches rather than
   mis-verifies. The header is **16 bytes** in total and is followed by exactly one value: the
   top-level tuple `STRUCT` of the field-id tables below.
   **Both header versions belong to the tuple encoding, and neither is the document's
   `schema_version`** (round-27 item 6, correcting round-26 item 2's parenthesis, which said the
   second field *was* the document's key). The three numbers are **not** the same number, and since
   round-33 item 4 they do not even share a value: `schema_version` versions the `--json` document — its top-level key set,
   its member names, its nullability — and is an explicit fingerprint **non-member** (§5.3.2), while
   these two bytes version the pre-image's framing and its field-id assignments. The consequences
   are exactly the ones a reader would otherwise get wrong: adding a *rendered-only* key bumps
   `schema_version` and **must not** change any token; adding, retiring or renumbering a *bound*
   member bumps the tuple schema version and **must** change every token; and a verifier may not
   read either number out of the document to decide what the other should be. The tests assert the
   independence in both directions (§15.6a). **Round 28 restates the header as a constant and checks
   the document for contradictions rather than repeating the correction** (item 5): the 16 bytes are
   the **encoding magic** `tws-plan-fp\0`, the **encoding version** and the **tuple schema version**,
   three compile-time constants of the fingerprint encoder and **nothing about the `--json`
   document's schema**. `schema_version` is a fingerprint **non-member** (§5.3.2), it is not read
   into the header, the header is not read out of it, and **no sentence anywhere in this document,
   the docs, the skills or the tests may bind the two** — round 28 audited every restatement of the
   header (§5.3.2, §8.3.6, §15.6a, §19, §20) and found none that still does, so this is a standing
   prohibition rather than a repair. A `schema_version` bump with no bound-member change must leave
   every token byte-identical, and a bound-member change must move every token even if
   `schema_version` does not budge; §15.6a asserts exactly those two directions.
2. **Every value is `<type tag><payload>`, and there are six tags and no others**:
   `0x00 NULL` (empty payload), `0x01 BOOL` (exactly one byte, `0x00` or `0x01`),
   `0x02 UINT` (8 bytes, big-endian, unsigned), `0x03 BYTES` (an 8-byte big-endian byte **length**,
   then exactly that many raw bytes), `0x04 STRUCT` (an 8-byte big-endian byte length of the
   member block, then the members of rule 3) and `0x05 ARRAY` (an 8-byte big-endian byte length of
   the element block, then an 8-byte big-endian **element count**, then that many bare values).
   Lengths and counts are redundant with self-delimitation on purpose: a decoder can validate them,
   and a test can assert them.
3. **Every struct member is `<field id><value>`, where the field id is a 2-byte big-endian integer
   fixed by the tables below**, and members are emitted in **ascending field-id order**, each
   exactly once. **No member is ever omitted**: an unknown, an absent limit and an unresolved probe
   are the `NULL` tag, which is distinct from `0x00`-payload `BOOL`, from `UINT` zero, from a
   zero-length `BYTES` and from a zero-count `ARRAY` (§4.8). Field ids are **retired, never reused
   *within a tuple schema version***:
   a member deleted by a later round leaves a hole, and a renamed member keeps its id. **Re-pointing
   an existing id at a different fact is legal only together with a bump of the tuple schema
   version; round-33 item 4 was the first such bump, round-34 item 3 the second and round-35
   items 3 and 5 the third**
   (`0x0001` → `0x0002` → `0x0003` → `0x0004`, rule 1): round 33's two re-pointings were the entry struct's
   id 4 (the display `repo_context.repo_root` becomes that context's `context_id`) and the
   repositories struct's id 2 (round-32 item 1's identical
   substitution, which shipped in no released encoding and is versioned by the same bump); round 34
   re-points the entry struct's ids 4 and 5 at the **execution** context's `context_id`/`source`
   and **adds** ids 36 and 37 for the **base** context's, so the two contexts are separate bound
   members rather than one flattened one; round 35 re-points the entry struct's id 12 from "the
   destination SHA as `base.sha` names it" to `destination.sha`/`destination.snapshot_sha` **as
   resolved in `execution_context`**, appends id 38 for `base.decision_sha`, **retires** the push
   struct's id 2 and appends the push struct's id 11 for that target's `context_id` — a retirement
   leaves a hole that is never refilled within this schema version, and the id may not be reused by
   a later round either (rule 3's "retired, never reused"). **Adding a member is a bump for the same
   reason a re-pointing is**: an old binary that walked the entry struct would find two ids it does not know
   and could not decide whether the difference was a new fact or a corrupted pre-image. The
   version byte is what makes an old token mismatch rather than mis-verify against the new table.
4. **The dotted paths of §5.3.2 are names, not structure — and this rule is what removes the
   flat/nested ambiguity** (round-26 item 2). A whitelist row spelled with dots
   (`execution_context.context_id`, `base_context.context_id`, `head.sha`, `config.update_refs.value`, `lease.expected_sha`,
   `mutation.will_switch_head`, …) names a **leaf scalar of the struct in whose table the row
   appears**, and is encoded as a leaf member of that struct with the id assigned below. The dots
   produce **no** nested struct, so `{"head": {"sha": X}}` and `{"head.sha": X}` are not two legal
   spellings of one tuple: there is one spelling, the leaf id. The **only** composite values in the
   whole pre-image are the ones named here: the top-level tuple struct, the `restore` struct, the
   four arrays `push_targets[]`, `repositories[]`, `entries[]` and each entry's `collateral_refs[]`
   with their element structs, and the one array-of-arrays `argv_alternatives`. Nothing else nests.
5. **Array order is the canonical order the document already guarantees, and the element count is
   bound with it** — `entries[]` by `name`, `push_targets[]` by **`(context_id, git_branch)`**
   (round-35 item 5; the rendered root is neither a key nor a member),
   `repositories[]` by `(repo, context_id)`, `collateral_refs[]` by its own canonical sort,
   `argv_alternatives` in the fixed order stated at its field id, `replay.candidate_digest` standing
   in for the candidate sequence so no commit list is serialized here at all (§4.5, §4.7). An array
   element is a **bare value** (`<type tag><payload>`), never a `<field id><value>` pair: its
   identity is its position, which the canonical sort fixes.
6. **Strings are raw bytes, and are never validated, transformed or normalized** — this is the rule
   the JSON encoding could not state. A `BYTES` payload is the **exact byte sequence of the Go
   string** as it was read from Git, from config, from `stack.yaml` or from the filesystem: no UTF-8
   validation, no replacement of invalid sequences with U+FFFD, no NFC/NFD normalization, no case
   folding, no trimming, no escaping of any kind, and no separator anywhere — the length prefix
   delimits the value, so no member can impersonate a separator and no escape can make two distinct
   values collide. A branch whose name holds a lone `0x80`, a repository path holding `0xC0 0x80`
   (which reaches the pre-image as the raw member of that context's `context_id` digest rather than
   as a bound `BYTES` member of its own, round-33 item 4),
   and a name holding the literal bytes of U+FFFD are three different values with three different
   tokens.
7. **Integers are unsigned 64-bit big-endian.** Every numeric member of the whitelist is a
   non-negative integer — the two `limits.<key>` values and `replay.candidate_count`, plus any
   future count — and so are the structural lengths and element counts of rule 2. A negative or
   non-integral value is a schema error rather than a formatting question. **`unknown_entries` is
   not among them**: it is a `guard.evaluation[]` member and an explicit fingerprint **non-member**
   (§5.3.2 non-member table), and round 25's rule listing "`unknown_entries`-like counts" as
   whitelist numbers is corrected here rather than reinterpreted (round-26 item 2). **`NULL` is the
   only spelling of unknown**, and the absent-limit sentinel is `NULL` rather than an omitted member
   (§4.8, §8.3.2a).
8. **Booleans are one byte**, `0x00` or `0x01`, and an unknown boolean is `NULL` — never `0x00`
   (§4.8: `false` and "not known" are different answers, and `context.dirty`, `collateral_exposed`
   and `context.autostash` each have both).
9. **The digest is `SHA-256` over the entire pre-image, header included**, rendered as 64 lowercase
   hex characters (§8.7.7's lexical form).
10. **The encoding defines those bytes; *approval* additionally requires them to be valid UTF-8, and
    round 27 separates the two questions** (item 7). Rule 6 stays exactly as written — the pre-image
    binds raw bytes, validates nothing and normalizes nothing, and two names differing only in
    invalid bytes have two different digests — because that is what makes the *encoding* honest. It
    is not enough to make the *workflow* honest, and this is the gap round 26 left open: the
    `--json` document, the human rendering and every consumer between them are **UTF-8 surfaces**,
    and Go's `encoding/json` rewrites each invalid sequence to U+FFFD, so the plan an operator reads
    and approves can be a lossy image of the plan the token binds — two different runs that look
    identical on screen, one of which the operator authorised. The controlled path therefore
    **detects the condition losslessly and refuses to mint**: before the digest is taken, every
    `BYTES` member of the tuple is checked with `utf8.Valid` **on the raw bytes**, never on the
    marshalled output — **"of the tuple" is exact, and round-33 item 4 narrows the checked set by
    narrowing the tuple**: the entry and repository roots are no longer bound members, so an invalid
    byte in a *rendered* root raises nothing here, while the same bytes still move the token through
    the `context_id` they are hashed into (§4.4, §5.3.2). Every member that **is** bound keeps the
    check unchanged. If any member fails, the document publishes one row of the top-level,
    closed-shape **`encoding_issues[]`** array per offending member — `field_id`,
    `path_label_ascii`, `owner_entry_ascii_or_null`, `byte_length`, `raw_base64`, `sha256`,
    deterministically sorted (§4.4, round-28 item 4) — and publishes `approval.fingerprint: null`
    and `approval.usable: false`. **Round 28 separates the evidence from the refusal, and both from
    the prose** (item 4): the evidence is that array and **never** a `detail` string, which may not
    carry raw invalid text under any circumstance; and the non-waivable rank 5.08
    `identity-not-utf8` blocker with `runnable: false` is published **only where the document would
    otherwise mint** — approvable work under an effective limit, or a supplied `--approve-plan`. A
    **limitless** plan over the same bytes publishes the array and the `null` token and stops there:
    it does not claim the underlying run is unrunnable, because it is not. **The JSON stays valid,
    complete and auditable**: the lossy U+FFFD spellings remain in
    their fields (removing them would break the schema), and the base64/digest evidence beside them
    is what an auditor compares against the repository. **Nothing about the encoding is relaxed**:
    the raw-TLV rules still define the bytes, the debug accessor still dumps them, and the
    adversarial fixtures still assert that two invalid-byte plans produce two different pre-images
    and two different digests — what round 27 removes is the claim that either of them yields a
    *usable, approvable* token.

**The field-id tables.** Ids are per-struct, start at 1, and are fixed here. Types are the tag of
rule 2; `|NULL` marks a member that may carry the null tag.

**Why this and not the canonical JSON of round 25.** The JSON form is *readable*, and that was its
case: one marshalling discipline shared with the `--json` surface, and a pre-image an operator can
print and diff. Both arguments survive; neither answers the defect. **JSON cannot represent the
values this tuple binds** — invalid UTF-8 in a ref name, a path or a config value is silently
rewritten to U+FFFD by every conforming Go encoder, which collapses distinct plans onto one token
(above), and the failure is *silent*, at mint time, in the direction that authorises work the
operator never saw. Two further defects follow the same shape and are worth naming because prose was
holding them shut: JSON's escaping, number and member-order freedoms are **encoder options** that had
to be pinned by four paragraphs of prose (`SetEscapeHTML(false)`, no exponent, no reordering), and
every one of them is a place an implementation can silently differ, whereas TLV has no options to
pin; and JSON's structure invites the flat/nested ambiguity rule 4 has to forbid, since a dotted
whitelist path reads as a nested object to one implementer and a flat key to another. **The
debuggability argument is answered rather than dismissed**: the implementation must expose the
pre-image through the same debug accessor §15.6a already requires, plus an **annotated dump**
rendering (one line per member: offset, field id, tag, length, value as hex **and** as a
lossy-but-labelled text preview), so a token-mismatch investigation diffs two dumps exactly as it
would have diffed two JSON documents — and, unlike the JSON pre-image, the dump never lies about the
bytes. The **single-marshalling** argument is answered by scope: the tuple is a projection with its
own whitelist, its own order and its own null discipline (§5.3.2), so it was never the `--json`
marshaller's output in the first place; sharing the *encoder* would have coupled the token to a
rendering surface that is explicitly allowed to change (`replay.commits` caps, human vs JSON).

**The adversarial cases are named, and are tests, not assurances** (§15.6a). They fall into three
families, and the third is new this round. **Separator injection**: a branch named `a","b` or
`a\",\"b`, a repository path containing `","`, a detail string containing `}{`, a ref name containing
a raw newline or tab, and two entries whose names differ only after a JSON escape (`a"b` vs `a\"b`)
— all of which are now settled *structurally*, since a length-prefixed value cannot contain a
separator that does not exist, and the tests assert the property rather than the escaping.
**Unicode**: a non-ASCII name and its percent-escaped spelling, a precomposed `é` (U+00E9) against a
decomposed `e`+U+0301 — different bytes, different tokens, no NFC/NFD normalization anywhere — and an
ASCII `a` against a Cyrillic `а` (U+0430). **Invalid UTF-8, which the JSON pre-image could not
distinguish at all** (round-26 item 2): a branch name holding a lone continuation byte `0x80` against
one holding `0x81`; a name holding the overlong `0xC0 0x80` against one holding a real `0x00`-free
truncated sequence `0xE2 0x82`; and either of them against the same name holding the three bytes of
U+FFFD (`0xEF 0xBF 0xBD`) — the spelling a JSON encoder would have produced for **all** of them.
Each pair must produce **different pre-images and different digests**, and each single value must
produce the **same** digest across processes, machines and renderings. **Round 27 corrects what that
family proves** (item 7): it is a property of the *encoding*, asserted over the pre-image and the
computed digest, and it is **not** a claim that those plans mint two approvable tokens — they mint
none at all, because the invalid bytes are a bound identity and rule 10 refuses (`identity-not-utf8`,
§4.9 rank 5.08). The round-26 wording "each pair must mint different fingerprints" is therefore
withdrawn as a statement about `approval.fingerprint` and kept as one about the digest; the U+FFFD
member of each triple is the one spelling that is valid UTF-8, so it is also the one whose document
still mints and publishes a token — which is exactly the pair a test should compare (§15.6a, §15.21).

**This whitelist is exactly what lets the plan token equal the guard-seam token.** The guard seam
computes the same tuple from the same planner (§8.7.2), and every field that *must* differ between a
`--plan` invocation and its guarded twin — `invocation`, `approval.*`, the guard verdicts, `state`,
the fetch outcome, timestamps — is on the non-member list. If any of them were members, the
`--approve-plan` workflow could not exist.

**5.3.3 The two jobs, restated over that tuple.**

- **`approval.fingerprint` — cross-invocation approval identity.** It answers "is the run I am about
  to authorise the run I was shown?", over exactly the §5.3.2 tuple. The consequences worth stating
  in prose: because the **effective limit values** are inside it, a token
  minted under
  `--max-replay-per-entry 10` does not authorise a run guarded at `20`, and one minted under a
  per-entry limit alone does not authorise a run that also carries `--max-replay-total`, because the
  second key's value moved from the absent sentinel to a number
  (§8.7.7) — while their `origin` labels are outside it, so a resume that inherits a persisted limit
  and one that repeats the identical flag mint the **same** token for the **same** guard (§8.7.4).
  **Round 30 withdraws the "a token minted by a `--plan` invocation that carried no limits does not
  authorise a limit-bearing run, and vice versa" reading of this member** (item 1): a limitless plan
  fails clause (b) of §4.4's usable-token predicate and mints **no** fingerprint at all, so that
  token never exists and cannot mismatch anything. What survives is the binding above, between two
  documents that both mint. Because `intent.push` is inside it, **a token minted for a non-pushing run can never
  authorise a force-pushing one** — the single most consequential thing a sync does after the
  rebase — and because the **push targets with their lease baselines** are inside it, a token
  minted over one branch set, or over a remote tip the operator was shown, cannot authorise a push
  of a different set or over a tip that has since moved (§4.4). Because the **`restore` identity**
  is inside it, a checkout resume that would put HEAD back on a different branch, or on the same
  branch at a different commit, mints a different token — which is what makes the one resume that
  rebases nothing and pushes nothing approvable rather than unbindable (§8.6.4a). And because the validation **digest** is inside it, a token cannot authorise a run that
  validates with a different command, or with none. Because **`head.sha`, the destination SHA,
  `replay.upstream_sha`, `replay.candidate_count` and `replay.candidate_digest`** are inside it,
  `candidates: 1` before
  and `candidates: 1` after cannot authorise each other when they name different commits: a
  materially changed base or candidate set is exactly what must invalidate an approval, and an
  approval that bound only counts would authorise a run the operator never saw. And because the
  digest covers the **complete, uncapped** sequence while `replay.commits` is excluded, two ranges
  that share their oldest `cap` commits but differ in the tail mint **different** tokens, while the
  same range rendered with a list, without one, or with a different cap mints the **same** one
  (§4.5, §4.6).
  **What the validation claim does and does not cover**: the
  digest binds the command *as resolved at plan time*, and on a guarded invocation §8.8 makes that
  binding real by freezing and consuming exactly that digest, so a config edit between plan and
  execute changes the digest and is refused rather than silently obeyed. The shipped **unguarded**
  legacy external route stays `per-entry-dynamic` and is not covered by any identity claim; the
  document publishes both `stability` and `guarded_stability` so the two statements are separable
  and neither has to be softened (§4.4, §8.8).
- **What is deliberately *outside* the fingerprint** is the non-member table of §5.3.2, and the
  whitelist rule makes it complete: anything not listed as a member is outside. Restated for the
  case that matters most: if every
  resolved identity is unchanged, a fetch that
  succeeded this time and failed last time does not change what will be replayed; and a guard
  verdict, a waiver and a supplied token change no fact about the work, which is why
  `--plan` and `--plan --approve-plan <fp>` over identical inputs publish the identical token.
- **`revalidation.digest` — intra-run/JIT identity.** Recomputed per entry at the seam of §5.2 over
  that entry's *now-resolved* facts and compared against the approved row. It exists because a
  deferred row legitimately changes shape between approval and execution: `conditional` becomes
  `onto` or `plain`, a `null` count becomes a number. The rule is not "nothing changed" but
  "nothing changed **beyond what the approval declared deferred**": a row approved as
  `deferred + conditional + unknown` may resolve; a row approved as `exact` may not acquire a
  different upstream, a different candidate identity, or a moved tip. A mismatch is
  `refusal.kind = revalidation-mismatch` (§4.9 rank 9) with a precise "the plan changed" detail
  naming the entry and the field — identity drift, base drift, candidate drift and newly appearing
  collateral on a row whose approved set was known all collapse to that one kind, and the marker
  line carries it, because a JIT refusal is guard-generated by origin (§8.7.6). Permitted resolution
  is an *identity* allowance only: the effective
  limits are re-evaluated against the resolved values, and a newly exceeded limit stops the run with
  its own limit kind even though the shape change itself was expected (§5.2, §5.3.1). On a guarded
  route the seam also **confirms the frozen validation intent** rather than re-reading config: the
  digest it compares is the one frozen at plan time (§8.8).

**Fetch and approval — the honest consequence.** A `--plan` under an effective `fetch` policy
resolves identities *after* moving remote-tracking refs. If the operator then runs the approved
command and it fetches again, and upstream moved in between, `destination.sha` changes, the fingerprint no
longer matches, and the run is refused. That is deliberate: the alternative — excluding the
destination SHA to make the token stable — would authorise a rebase onto a commit nobody previewed.
