**This applies to the *verification* invocation exactly as it applies to the executing one**
(round-34 item 6). The human three-step flow's step 2 (`--plan` + the same flags + the token) is a
second plan, not a replay of the first document: on a fetch-enabled route it fetches again, and a
`refusal.kind: approval-mismatch` there means the **plan drifted between the two previews**, not
that the token failed to waive anything. The recovery is the initial preview again — read it, take
the new receipt — and the same is true one step later: step 3 re-resolves and may refuse before it
rebases anything. **Both windows are TOCTOU windows this design narrows and does not close**, and no
part of this document, the docs, the skills or the tests may describe the round trip as atomic, may
attribute such a refusal to the limit flags, or may resolve it by re-supplying the stale token. The
stable, fully-local workflow is the **explicit new-mode `--no-fetch` route** below — a *different*
route, chosen on both invocations, with `route` asserted — and it is never to be added silently to a
legacy round trip to make the race go away.

**The round trip is per underlying route, and there is no single recommended pair.** The previous
draft recommended `--plan --no-fetch` → `--no-fetch --approve-plan` generically. That is wrong,
because `--no-fetch` is a **mode trigger** (§0.2): adding it does not make a *legacy* preview local,
it changes which run is being previewed. **The invariant that makes any pair valid** is flag
identity, and it is stated once here and enforced in §8.7.7: the executing invocation carries the
**same trigger flags, the same limit flags, the same `--push` intent and the same validation
intent** as the `--plan` invocation that minted the token; it drops only `--plan`/`--json` and adds
`--approve-plan <fp>`. Adding, dropping or changing any of them changes the fingerprint tuple and
the token is refused. The two honest round trips:

```
# legacy external route — the run a bare `tws sync <f>` performs
tws sync <f> --plan --json --max-replay-per-entry 10   # fetches, as the legacy run does; route: legacy
tws sync <f> --approve-plan <fp> --max-replay-per-entry 10   # same limits, same route, now guarded
```

The second invocation succeeds **only if the guarded identities are unchanged after the second
fetch** — base/destination SHAs, tips, upstreams, candidate identity, collateral. If upstream moved
in between, it refuses with `approval-mismatch` and the operator (or agent) re-plans and re-approves.
That is a deliberate cost of previewing a route that fetches; it is not a bug to be engineered away
with a stability exclusion.

```
# explicit new-mode no-fetch route — stable and fully local
tws sync <f> --plan --no-fetch --json         # route: new-mode, fetch.attempted: false
tws sync <f> --no-fetch --approve-plan <fp>   # same route, same (absent) limits, deterministic
```

Both invocations here describe the **new-mode** run (restricted fetch set, header, v2 state, the
new-mode-only selection refusals, R1-R11), so a consumer **must assert `route`** in the document
before trusting the pair. Automation that wants determinism should choose this route deliberately,
not stumble into it.

**There is intentionally no fully-local preview of the legacy external route.** Adding `--no-fetch`
to a legacy preview changes the run it previews; not adding it means the preview fetches. No
document, flag help, skill, or agent instruction may claim otherwise, and §14 states the same thing
in the user-facing wording.

A fetch-enabled approval is a *snapshot-of-the-network* approval and requires reapproval whenever
the fetched refs move. **The `define` decision (§19.3) this paragraph used to name is withdrawn**
(round-40 item 4): §19.3 was **closed** by round-34 item 9 and struck from the open list in
round 35, so there is nothing here for `define` to ratify. The split, the excluded set and the two
per-route round trips above are **settled** by the exhaustive whitelist and non-member table of
§5.3.2 and the field-id/encoding contract of §5.3.2a, at tuple schema version **`0x0004`** — the
same closure §19.3 itself states. `define` may not add, retire, re-point or reorder a tuple member
on the strength of this paragraph or any other prose: a membership change is an **amendment**, made
only by moving §5.3.2, §5.3.2a, the §15.6a/§15.21 assertions and the version constant **together**,
in one change, and a `define` that wants a different membership is writing the **successor** of the
version in force and must say so. A membership edit without that coordinated amendment is a silent
token break, not a decision.

**Recommendation: option 2, split as above, in both modes; option 3 only behind the guard flag, if
the spec wants it.** No option should be described as atomicity: nothing here is atomic, and the
spec must say so. Deferred rows participate in the fingerprint by their *deferral facts*
(`depends_on`, determinacy, reason), not by a guessed SHA.

**Nothing approval-shaped is persisted, and that is a decision, not a gap.** `SyncRunState`
(new-mode external) and `CheckoutTransaction` (both checkout routes, since a legacy checkout run
still writes a transaction, `internal/checkout_sync.go:656-690`) *could* carry a token as additive
`omitempty` keys — and must not, because the only plan such a token could authorise is the one the
interruption destroyed. What they carry instead is the **guard**, encoded once: the effective
limit values as `*int` pointers (§10.3), whose presence *is* "guarded" — so a resume stays as
guarded as the run that started it even when the flags are dropped, and there is no second boolean
that could claim otherwise. The **legacy external route carries neither**: `.sync-state.yaml` holds only
`started_at/failed_branch/pending/completed/skipped` (`internal/syncstate.go:11-17`) and is written
only on failure, so a guarded legacy external run repeats its limit flags on every invocation
(§8.7.4). Every guarded continuation that needs a waiver mints a fresh **remaining-work** token from
`--plan --continue`; `approval.covers` and `approval.scope` say so on the document itself.

### 5.3.1 What a matching fingerprint waives — and what it never waives

An approval is a **narrow waiver**, not an override switch. Stated exactly:

**It waives exactly this:** the limit violations that the approved document already contained — the
`guard.evaluation[]` rows whose verdict was `exceeded` at approval time, i.e. exactly the rows
`approval.covers.waived_evaluation_ids[]` names (§4.4). Waiving is expressed as a **verdict change,
not a deletion**: each covered row stays in `guard.evaluation[]` with `verdict: waived` and its
`limit`, `value` and `entry` intact, leaves `blockers[]`, and stops being a candidate for
`refusal.kind` (§4.9). Consequently a run that was `guard.would_refuse_without_approval: true` and
is approved publishes `guard.would_refuse: false` and `refusal.kind: null` — *and executes*. That
combination, not the previous draft's "`would_refuse: true` + `accepted: true`", is the legal
executing shape: the old pairing forced every consumer to special-case a `true` that meant `false`,
and made `--plan --approve-plan` unable to state whether the command would run. The operator was
shown "pr2 replays 40 candidates, over your limit of 10", said yes to that, and gets that — with the
40 and the limit still visible in the `waived` row.

**It never waives a hard blocker**, whatever the token says:

| Hard blocker | Why an approval cannot cover it |
|---|---|
| an unresolvable `base_context` or `execution_context` (`repo-unavailable`, §4.1) | no probe of that row ever ran, so the approved identity was never established |
| a **replay-critical** probe failure (`probe-failed`, §4.1 probe-failure rule) | the token would authorise a replay the document could not measure |
| `head.state != present` (§5.1 rule 6) | the row has no tip, so the approved identity never existed |
| prunable worktree (§5.4.3) | the shipped external pass 2 stops the run at that row |
| the row's branch is already checked out in **another** worktree of its context (`branch-checked-out-elsewhere`, §5.4.7) | the arm's implicit `git checkout` cannot happen; the run fails before replaying. (A **self** hold is not a blocker and needs no waiver) |
| an `execution_context` with **tracked** uncommitted changes and `rebase.autoStash` false/unset (`context-dirty`, §5.4.7) | `git rebase` refuses to start; approving the replay does not clean the tree |
| missing or unresolvable `base.ref`, `base.kind = none` in external (§5.1 rule 5) | the run cannot perform the rebase it describes; `git rebase` fails at the ref |
| unresolvable recorded cutoff | the run fails with `fatal: invalid upstream <sha>` (§6.5) |
| unsafe state: existing checkout transaction, held lock, live scoped-sync guard, `previous sync incomplete` cell | the shipped ladder owns these and the guard never softens a shipped refusal (§8.7.1) |
| a **pre-existing live foreign owner** at the guard seam (`state-refused`, §8.6.1 cause 3, §4.9 rank 3) — published on the plan side as `guard.execute_blocked_by`'s `live-owner-concurrency` member | another process is moving `refs/remotes/**` under this run's `--onto` re-resolution (D3); an approval authorises a *replay count*, not concurrency, and no token minted before the neighbour started could have described it. It is the one member of this table that the **unguarded** route ignores, which is why the plan publishes it as its own axis rather than through `runnable` (§4.4) |
| an **undecodable owner artefact** at the guard seam (`state-refused`, §4.4 `state`, §8.6.1 step 2a, §4.9 rank 3) — published on the plan side as `guard.execute_blocked_by`'s `owner-artefact-undecodable` member | the artefact exists and cannot be decoded, so its owner’s liveness is **unknown**; a token proves the plan was approved, not that nobody else is running, and “approved” over an unreadable lock would mean “unchecked” |
| dirty working tree, detached HEAD, another Git operation in progress | same |
| every continuation gate of §8.6.4 (mismatch, nothing to continue, rebase still active, failed branch missing, parent not contained, unreadable state, missing selection, I20) | same: the shipped resume ladder owns them, and an approval authorises work, not resumption |
| a fresh **external** row whose own **execution directory** already has a rebase in progress (`external-rebase-in-progress`, §4.1 `context.rebase_in_progress`, §4.9 rank 5.45) | `git rebase` refuses before replaying anything (`already a rebase-merge directory`); approving the replay does not finish or abort the other rebase, `rebase.autoStash` does not rescue it either, and on pass 2 an approval would hand the run to a failure path that **aborts** the other rebase (§5.4 consequence 7) |
| *(withdrawn)* the round-17 row for a fresh **external** row whose execution directory held an **untracked** file at a path the row's own Git call would create (`untracked-would-be-overwritten`, rank 5.55) | **Round 18 removes the row because it removes the blocker, not because approval now covers it.** The fact the planner can honestly publish is *presence*, not collision (`context.untracked_present`, `context.overwrite_risk: unknown`, §4.1), and a residual warning is not a blocker, so there is nothing here to waive in either direction. The general rule this table exists for is unchanged and is the reason the row cannot come back as a waivable one: **an approval waives limit violations only**, and no token has ever authorised Git to destroy untracked work — the honest statement is that the guard does not know whether Git will refuse, and that `rebase.autoStash` would not help if it did, because it stashes tracked changes only (§4.1, §5.4.7, §19.26) |
| an indeterminate fetch context (`fetch-context-indeterminate`, §4.9 rank 5.0) | the document could not name the directory the run's own `git fetch` would run in, so there is no fetch context the token could have bound |
| an unbounded submodule reach (`fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate`, §4.9 rank 5.05, round-23 item 3) | the document could not enumerate the repositories the run's own `git fetch` would recursively contact and rewrite, so there is no reach the token could have bound |
| a checked-out fetch destination (`fetch-local-branch-checked-out`, §4.9 rank 5.06, round-25 item 2) | the run's own `git fetch` would write a local branch a worktree is standing on: no token authorises Git to move or delete a branch under a working tree, the plan declined the fetch rather than performing it, and the fact is a property of that context's refspecs and worktrees rather than a limit anyone approved |
| a **configuration value Git's own parser rejects** (`invalid-git-config`, §4.9 rank 5.07, round-27 item 3, scoped by round-28 item 2 and round-29 item 1) | the previewed command — `git fetch`, `git checkout`, `git push` or `git rebase`, whichever of them the route's scope names for that key — dies while reading its config, before it does anything; approving a replay does not make an unparsable value parse, and the token would authorise a run that cannot start |
| a **bound identity string that is not valid UTF-8** (`identity-not-utf8`, §4.9 rank 5.08, round-27 item 7) | the document the operator approved is a lossy rendering of the plan the token would bind — JSON rewrites the bytes to U+FFFD — so "approved" would mean "approved something you were never shown"; no token is minted at all, and the supplied one is recorded as `accepted: false` |
| `plan-unavailable` (unreadable/missing `stack.yaml`), `stack-unsortable` (§5.5), `selection-refused` | there is no plan to have approved |
| a limit set that disagrees with the persisted one (`guard-limit-mismatch`, §8.7.4) | the token was minted against one limit set; executing under another would waive a violation nobody evaluated |
| a token supplied on a resume with **no effective limit at all** (`approval-without-limits`, §8.5.1, §4.9 rank 7.5) | there is no violation for it to waive, so honouring it would mean "approved" where nothing was ever checked |

**And one non-waivable verdict that is *not* a hard blocker**: an effective limit against a
`merge-recreation` row is `indeterminate-entry` at **rank 10** (§4.2, §4.9) — round-26's second source `merge-recreation-unknown` is withdrawn with round-27 item 1, and an *invalid* `rebase.rebaseMerges` value is now the rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config` blocker instead (§4.9) — on a plan whose
`runnable` stays `true`. A token cannot clear it either — a waiver moves a verdict from `exceeded`
to `waived`, and this verdict is `unknown`: there is no number to compare the limit against, so
"approved" would mean "unchecked". It is listed here rather than in the table above because
conflating it with a hard blocker was the previous draft's error: the plan is executable, and
dropping the limit (or the `rebase.rebaseMerges` configuration) is what makes it runnable *and*
guardable, not an approval.

In precedence terms (§4.9): a token can only ever clear ranks 11-12, and only for the violations the
approved document already showed. Ranks 1-10 refuse with a token supplied exactly as they refuse
without one, and **`guard.execute_blocked_by[]` is unchanged by any token**, matching or not: it is
the projection of a refusal no approval can reach, so a document may legitimately publish a real
64-hex fingerprint, `approval.accepted: true` and a non-empty `execute_blocked_by` at once — the
plan was approved, and the guarded run still refuses while the neighbour lives, or while the lock
that would have named it cannot be decoded (§4.4, §8.6.1 cause 3 and step 2a), and `refusal.kind`
names the higher-ranked fact rather than `approval-mismatch` — and
for **every document that minted no token**, by the **usable-token predicate of §4.4** (approvable
work — `entries` non-empty **or** `push.targets` non-empty **or** `restore.applies` true — **and** at
least one effective limit **and** `encoding_issues == []`), whose
`approval.fingerprint` is `null`, the supplied token
is recorded as `approval.accepted: false` without ever displacing that document's own top-ranked
kind (§4.9); a rows-less document that still carries `push.targets[]` — or `restore.applies: true` —
and has a limit in force
has a real token and is
compared like any other. No section, test or example may state the predicate in its withdrawn
two-clause form, or state the work clause without the limit and encoding clauses (round-28 item 6:
the predicate is three clauses in every restatement). Note
the asymmetry that follows from §4.4: clearing ranks 11-12 is *waiving a guard verdict on a runnable
plan*, which is why those ranks never set `runnable: false` in the first place, and why a waiver
never changes `runnable`.

**It never silently absorbs new facts.** A JIT fact that was unknown or deferred at approval time
and, once resolved, **newly exceeds** a limit stops the run with its limit kind; a changed candidate
identity, a changed upstream, a moved tip on a row approved as `exact`, or collateral appearing on a
row whose approved collateral set was **known** (§4.8, §5.2) stops it with
`revalidation-mismatch` (§4.9 rank 9) — while a row approved with `null` collateral is
re-evaluated at the seam rather than treated as approved-empty. The refusal names the entry and the
field and instructs a fresh
`--plan` + re-approval. Treating "approved" as "approved for whatever it turns into" would make the
guard strictly worse than no guard, because the operator would believe they had seen the run.

### 5.4 The third arm: external pass 2 (non-materialized entries)

Pass 2 is not "pass 1 without a worktree". It is a distinct executor arm with distinct inputs, and
the planner's strategy/upstream derivation must be **total over
`(mode, materialization, cutoff state, destination deferral)`** — this cell included.

For an external entry whose worktree directory is absent (§2.1 step 7):

| Fact | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `strategy` | `plain-explicit-branch` | the argv is `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` — a plain rebase with an **explicit branch operand**, which is a shape pass 1 never produces |
| `argv` | `["rebase", <base.ref>, <git_branch>]` | `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:196-201`; no `--update-refs`, no `--onto`, no `--no-fork-point` |
| repo context | `entry.Repo`, else the **process cwd** — **one directory, so this arm's `base_context` and `execution_context` are the same context and carry the identical `context_id`** — published as `base_context` = `execution_context` = `{context_id, repo_root, source}` with `source ∈ {entry-repo, process-cwd}` (§4.1, round-33 item 1, round-34 item 1) | `resolveEntryBase(stack, entry, entry.Repo)` and `RunSilentDir(entry.Repo, …)` / `RunSilent(…)`; **not** `syncRepoContext`, because there is no worktree |
| `cutoff.usage` | `not_used` | `entry.LastBaseSHA` is never read on this arm — the recorded cutoff cannot select `--onto` here, whatever its state |
| `cutoff.write` | `never` | `UpdateBaseSHA` is not called on this arm |
| `replay.upstream_provenance` | `base-ref-snapshot` (nothing rewrites this base earlier) or `base-ref-deferred` (an entry executed earlier does) | the upstream is always `<base>` as Git resolves it at rebase time |
| `replay.determinacy` | `snapshot` or `unknown` — **never `exact`** | there is no pinned upstream available on this arm |
| `replay.reason` | `cutoff-not-used-on-arm` when a cutoff **is** recorded (whatever its state) and the base ref is countable; `no-recorded-cutoff` only when `cutoff.state = absent`; `upstream-deferred` when the destination is deferred; `head-ref-missing`/`base-ref-missing`/`base-unset` as their cells dictate | the reason must state *why this arm's upstream is the base ref*; claiming `no-recorded-cutoff` on a row that has one would be a false fact about `stack.yaml`, and `cutoff-unresolvable` would be a false fact about the run, since this arm never resolves it |
| `cutoff.recorded_sha` | still published, verbatim | it is a real recorded fact; it is simply `not_used` here |
| `mutation.will_switch_head` | **`true`** | the argv carries an explicit branch operand, and "`git rebase master topic` is a shortcut for `git checkout topic && git rebase master`" (`git rebase` manual, DESCRIPTION) |
| `mutation.will_leave_head_on` | `<git_branch>` | on success HEAD stays there; and on this arm's own failure path `git rebase --abort` "reset[s] HEAD to the original branch. If `<branch>` was provided when the rebase operation was started, then HEAD will be reset to `<branch>`" (`git rebase` manual, `--abort`) — so both outcomes leave HEAD on the rebased branch |
| `mutation.head_restored_by_run` | **`false`** | external has no restoration path at all: `restoreOriginal` exists only in checkout (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1257`), and nothing in `syncWithStackScoped`'s pass-2 loop puts HEAD back (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:190-211`) |

Seven consequences the spec must state (they are numbered 1-7 because later rounds added three; the
citations `§5.4.3`, `§5.4.4`, `§5.4.6` and `§5.4.7` keep their referents):

1. **A recorded cutoff must not be used to compute this row's count, and the reason must say so.**
   Using `cutoff..branch` for a
   pass-2 entry would publish a range the executor will not replay. The count comes from the base
   ref (snapshot) or is `null` (deferred). The row's `replay.reason` is then
   **`cutoff-not-used-on-arm`**, never `no-recorded-cutoff`: the cutoff exists, it is published
   verbatim in `cutoff.recorded_sha`, and the honest statement is "this arm does not read it", not
   "there is none". The distinction is load-bearing for the operator who is about to `tws sync` a
   stack whose cutoffs they carefully maintained.
2. **`updatedByRef` is a dynamic outcome, not a strategy — and it is *not* Git-free.** When an
   earlier pass-1 entry marks this entry through `markUpdatedAncestors`, pass 2 prints
   `[+] <name> (archived)` and runs **no rebase, no `resolveEntryBase`, no
   `DefaultBranch`/`DefaultBranchIn`, no `GetBranchSHA` and no `UpdateBaseSHA`** — but the loop
   reaches that print only **after** the unconditional `IsPrunableWorktree(entry.GitBranch())`
   probe of consequence 3, which is a real `git worktree list --porcelain` in the process cwd and
   which **gates** the skip (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:164-190`). Round-37 item 1 withdraws the
   earlier "no Git process at all" wording as false against the shipped loop and fixes the order the
   planner must reproduce: `stat` → **prunability** → `updatedByRef`, so a prunable entry is the
   blocking row of consequence 3 and never a skip row. **One further route-dependent read may
   already have happened before either loop**: on the new-mode `--no-fetch` route
   `verifySelectedBasesLocally` resolved and verified this entry's base in the same directory this
   arm would use, which is the *only* cell where a `skipped-updated-ref` row carries a real
   `base_context` and `base.ref` (§4.1 skip-context rule, §9 route order). The plan models the row
   as `strategy = skipped-updated-ref` with
   `argv = []`, `replay.determinacy = not-applicable` and `replay.reason = not-executed` (§4.1 skip
   rule), and must label it a *projection*: the mark is derived from topology plus
   worktree-directory absence, never from a verification that the ref actually moved — and per §4.3
   it only really moves when the ref points into the replayed range **and survives Git's two
   filters** and is not checked out
   anywhere. So the honest row says "expected to be advanced by the parent's `--update-refs`; tws
   does not verify this". Note the direction: a pass-1 **child** marking its non-materialized
   **parent** is why that parent is *not* a deferral source for the child (§5.1 deferral rule).
3. **Prunable is blocking, not a note — and the verdict is cwd-scoped.**
   `IsPrunableWorktree(entry.GitBranch())` ⇒ the run stops with
   `[?] <name> (missing — run: tws archive …)` and `syncFailure`
   (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:181-184`). The row is `materialization = prunable`,
   `blocking = true`, and it appears in `blockers[]` with `runnable: false`. A guard must never
   report such a run as ready. The planner **runs the same probe the executor runs** — `git worktree
   list --porcelain` in the **process cwd**, no `-C`, evaluated *before* the arm switches to
   `entry.Repo` — and publishes `prunability.probe_context = cwd` (§3.7). Substituting a
   `-C repoRoot` inventory here would answer a different question and desynchronise the plan from
   the run in exactly the multi-repo/divergent-cwd case the guard exists for; the cwd scoping is a
   recorded follow-up defect (§18.16), not something this feature silently repairs.
4. **Pass 2 has its own JIT seam.** Pass 1's seam (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:117-135`) does not
   cover this loop: pass 2 resolves its base at `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:196` and calls
   `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` immediately after. A guarded run must recompute and re-check
   the row — resolved base ref, count, identity, limits, approval scope, **and the §5.4.7
   preconditions (`context.rebase_in_progress`, `context.dirty` and `branch_checked_out_at`, all
   three re-probed in that row's real context, since another process may have started a rebase,
   dirtied it, or checked the branch out since the plan)** — and re-enumerate the non-blocking
   `context.untracked_present`/`context.overwrite_risk` pair in the same pass, so the residual
   warning describes the directory as it is *now* rather than as it was at plan time (it refreshes a
   warning; it gates nothing, §4.1) —
   **between those two statements**, before the Git call, for every pass-2 row it executes (§8.7.5).
   Without it, every
   non-materialized entry of a guarded run would be unguarded.
5. **This is the arm where a missing head ref is fatal.** The branch is a rebase *operand* here, so
   `head.state != present` means `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` fails at Git and the run stops
   (§5.1 rule 6). The row publishes `head.state`, `replay.reason = head-ref-missing` and
   `blocking = true`; the count is `null`, never `0`.
6. **Every probe for this row runs in this row's *actual* context, and the process cwd is one of
   them.** `entry.Repo` is the Git context when it is non-empty; when it is empty the executor runs
   `RunSilent`/`resolveEntryBase(stack, entry, "")` with **no `-C` at all**, i.e. in the **process
   cwd**. The plan mirrors that exactly and publishes it as **both** context refs of §4.1 — on this
   arm `base_context` and `execution_context` name one directory and therefore carry one
   `context_id`, which is why the split of round-34 item 1 changes nothing here and everything on
   pass 1: base resolution,
   `rev-parse`, the candidate `rev-list` probes, the branch-ref and worktree inventories and the
   ordered `rebase.*` config read for that row are issued in **that** directory, and the
   `repositories[]` row the entry cites through both refs is the one whose `repo_root` is that
   directory, with
   `root_source: process-cwd` (§4.4). Probing a pass-2 row against the workspace repo root instead
   would answer a different repository's question — the same class of desynchronisation the
   prunability mirror avoids (§5.4.3) — so **prunability is not the only cwd-scoped part of the
   plan**, and no section may claim it is (§11). Note the consequence for the repository axis: one
   `repo` token can legitimately produce two `repositories[]` rows when the cwd and the token's
   worktree/root differ — and, since round 34, also when one **pass-1** row's base context is
   `entry.Repo` while its execution context is that entry's worktree; round 35's third source, a
   pass-1 row with an **empty** `Repo` reaching the executor through a non-`IsNotExist` stat error,
   produces **no rebase row and therefore no strategy-row context pair** — `checkSyncWorktreeBranch`
   stops that run at the shipped rank 4 preflight before the loop's `syncRepoContext` call
   (round-36 item 1) — while the one earlier caller that does answer for it, the new-mode
   `--no-fetch` I14 preflight, yields a **`preflight-refused` row with a process-cwd base context and
   no execution context**, not a pass-1 strategy row, so it is a repository-axis source for that
   refusal row alone (round-37 item 2, §4.1 `base_context`, §8.6.5) — and the fingerprint binds
   every one of them context-qualified (§5.3). Two rows of one token can also be **two stores**, in
   which case the row does not merely publish two repository rows: it refuses at §4.9 rank 5.15
   (round-35 item 2).
7. **This arm *mutates HEAD in a repository the operator is standing in*, and its preconditions are
   therefore first-class.** Pass 2 is the only tws code path that rebases a branch **it did not check
   out into a worktree of its own**, and the consequences were missing from every earlier draft:
   - **It switches HEAD, and leaves it switched.** `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` in `entry.Repo`
     — or, when `Repo` is empty, in the **process cwd** — performs the implicit
     `git checkout <git_branch>` the manual documents, replays, and returns with HEAD **on that
     branch** and the working tree checked out there. On failure the shipped handler runs
     `git rebase --abort` in the same context (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:200-206`), which per
     the manual resets HEAD to `<git_branch>` as well. **There is no `restoreOriginal` in external**:
     whatever branch the operator had checked out in that repository before running `tws sync` is
     not restored on success, on conflict, or on abort. The plan publishes this as
     `mutation.will_switch_head`, `mutation.will_leave_head_on` and
     `mutation.head_restored_by_run: false`, per row and with the row's `execution_context` beside it, so
     "this command will leave you on `pr3` in `~/work/api`" is a **plan fact** rather than a
     discovery. `--plan` itself performs none of it (§0.1).
   - **Dirty state is probed in the arm's *actual* context, with Git's *own* predicate, and blocks
     by default.** `git rebase` refuses to start on a work tree with **tracked** modifications
     unless autostash is in effect — `cannot rebase: You have unstaged changes` /
     `cannot rebase: Your index contains uncommitted changes` — and it is **indifferent to untracked
     files**. The plan therefore probes the tracked predicate in `execution_context` with **exactly one
     command**, `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 git -C <repo_root> status --porcelain --untracked-files=no
     --ignore-submodules=all`,
     reusing `probeDirty`'s environment (`internal/stack_status.go:326-337`) but not its argv, and
     publishes `context.dirty` from **that**. **`--ignore-submodules=all` is not a convenience
     flag**: `git rebase`'s clean-work-tree precondition ignores submodules, so a repository whose
     only modification is a moved gitlink or a dirty submodule work tree rebases without complaint,
     and a probe that counted it would refuse a run Git performs — the same one-directional error as
     the diff pair below, on the topology (a stack over repositories with submodules) where it is
     most likely to fire. Checkout's whole-repo gate is **unchanged**: `gitWorkingTreeDirty` keeps
     its full `status --porcelain`, submodules and untracked files included, because that is the
     precondition checkout really has. The **`diff-files --quiet` + `diff-index --quiet
     --cached HEAD` alternative of the previous draft is withdrawn, not merely deprecated**: those
     plumbing commands read the recorded stat data, so a file whose mtime/inode changed while its
     content did not — `touch`, a checkout by another tool, a build that rewrites a file byte-for-byte
     — is reported as modified by `diff-files` and **not** by `git status`, which refreshes the index
     first. `git rebase`'s own clean-work-tree check performs that refresh too, so `status
     --porcelain --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all` is the read-only in-memory-refresh
     equivalent of the executor's
     precondition and the diff pair is strictly stricter than Git. Under `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` the
     refresh stays in memory and no index is written, so the probe is still read-only (§0.1).
     When the probe reports dirt **and the effective `rebase.autoStash` of that context is `false` or
     unset** (the documented default, §4.3), the row is a **blocking preflight**:
     `refusal.kind = context-dirty` at §4.9 rank 5.5, `blocking: true`, `runnable: false`. This is a
     guard-introduced preflight, not a shipped one — external has no dirty check anywhere — so a
     guarded refusal here carries the marker (§8.7.6). Note the probe is per **row context**, not
     per repository: two rows of one token can resolve to two directories (consequence 6), and one
     of them can be dirty while the other is clean.
   - **Untracked-only is deliberately *not* a `context-dirty` blocker, and that asymmetry with
     checkout is stated rather than smoothed.** A context whose only changes are untracked files
     publishes
     `context.dirty: false`, no rank 5.5 blocker, and a run that really does start — the plan must
     predict Git, not a stricter policy of its own; blocking there would refuse a run that works
     today,
     which is the one direction a preflight introduced by this feature must never take. Checkout is
     the opposite case and keeps its shipped behaviour **unchanged**: `RunCheckoutSync` refuses on
     full `status --porcelain`, untracked files included **wherever `status.showUntrackedFiles`
     leaves them visible** — the key's `no` value silences them and the shipped gate then does not
     refuse, which is a shipped fact the plan mirrors rather than corrects (round-20 item 2)
     (`gitWorkingTreeDirty`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:420-426`, `:570-577`), and the plan projects
     that refusal verbatim as a rank 3 `state-refused` blocker from the top-level
     `state.worktree.dirty` fact (§8.6.2). So the *same* untracked-only repository legitimately
     blocks a checkout run and does not block an external pass-2 row: two different predicates,
     because there are two different shipped preconditions, and the document publishes both facts
     separately (`state.worktree.dirty` vs the row's `context.dirty`) rather than one blended one —
     with the presence pair below published on **both**, precisely because the checkout gate's
     coverage is configurable and a presence fact must not be.
   - **Untracked files can still stop an external row at the checkout Git performs next — and the
     planner cannot decide *whether* they will, so this document publishes presence and calls the
     rest unknown** (round-18 item 1, withdrawing round-17 item 2).
     `require_clean_work_tree` ignores untracked files, so `git rebase` starts; but the very next
     thing the arm does is **write the working tree**, and Git refuses to clobber an untracked file
     with a tracked one, aborting with
     `The following untracked working tree files would be overwritten by checkout` (Git's wording,
     which this document does not pin and no test may byte-compare, §15.8c d5). That is a real
     failure of a real run, and no shipped external check predicts it. Round 17 answered it with a
     hard rank 5.55 blocker over `context.untracked_overwrite_paths[]` — the directory's untracked
     enumeration intersected with the additions of the trees the arm would write — and claimed that
     set was **exact** up to four named residuals. **That claim is withdrawn: the set is not exact,
     and the reason is structural rather than a missing residual.**
     - **Git chooses the writing path at runtime, and the three paths write different trees.** With
       `git rebase <upstream> <branch>` the branch may already be current, in which case Git
       reports it up to date and replays nothing at all; it may be a strict ancestor of the new
       base, in which case Git **fast-forwards** the ref and checks out *that* tree instead of
       replaying a range; or it may replay, which is a **sequential** cherry-pick whose first
       working-tree write is onto the `--onto` commit and whose later writes are one commit at a
       time. A union over "HEAD tree → new base tree" plus "the candidate range's additions" plus,
       on pass 2, "HEAD tree → the branch operand's tree" is therefore not the tree any of the three
       paths actually writes: it is too large on the up-to-date and fast-forward paths, and on the
       replay path it names paths that are created and deleted **inside** the range and never land.
     - **The refusal's own predicate is not a diff.** Git decides it in `unpack_trees`, over the
       entries the checkout is **actually writing**, under `core.ignorecase`, sparse-checkout
       patterns and that code path's own treatment of ignored files. `diff-tree -r --name-only
       --diff-filter=A` models none of that, so even over the right tree pair the intersection is a
       different question from the one Git asks.
     - **Checkout continuation has no gate to fall back on.** `gitWorkingTreeDirty` runs only in
       `RunCheckoutSync` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:570-577`); `ContinueCheckoutSync` resumes
       straight into `resumeTransaction` (`:718-754`) with **no** dirty check and no untracked
       check, so a `--continue` writes the working tree with whatever untracked files have appeared
       since the run started. A guard that claimed exactness here would be claiming it in precisely
       the cell that has no shipped gate at all.
     What the plan publishes instead is the fact it can actually stand behind:
     - **Enumerate presence**, once per distinct **work tree**, anchored at its canonical top level:
       `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 git -C <toplevel> ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z`, where
       `<toplevel>` is `git -C <dir> rev-parse --path-format=absolute --show-toplevel` canonicalized.
       **That `-C <toplevel>` form is the only one this document ships** (round-20 item 2): round
       19's "equivalently the `-- :(top)` pathspec" alternative is withdrawn, because one probe with
       two legal spellings is two argv assertions that can drift, and the pathspec form needs
       pathspec magic the `-C` form does not. **The anchor is part
       of the predicate** (round-19 item 1): `ls-files` is cwd-relative, so the same command run in
       a subdirectory enumerates that subtree and nothing above it, and an external pass-2 row whose
       context is the **process cwd** may legitimately be standing in a subdirectory of the work
       tree the arm is about to write. A cwd-anchored probe would then publish
       `untracked_present: false`/`overwrite_risk: none-known` over a work tree holding a top-level
       untracked file — the one direction this pair must never get wrong, since `none-known` is the
       only value it states positively. Anchoring costs nothing extra where §13 already resolves
       `--show-toplevel` per context, it collapses two rows of one work tree onto one probe, and it
       makes the answer identical on **every route and from every subdirectory**.
       `-z` because
       paths may contain newlines (§11); `--exclude-standard` because Git's checkout overwrites
       **ignored** files silently, so counting them would inflate a warning that already declares
       its own uncertainty. The document says so plainly rather than claiming safety it does not
       provide: ignored files really can be overwritten, and that is shipped Git behaviour this
       feature neither changes nor hides.
     - **Publish `context.untracked_present` and `context.overwrite_risk`** (§4.1) on **every row
       with an execution directory** — external rows, checkout continuation rows **and fresh
       checkout rows** (round-20 item 2): `false`/`none-known` when the row's **work tree**
       holds no
       untracked non-ignored file — the one direction a presence probe really does settle, because
       with nothing there Git has nothing to refuse to overwrite — and `true`/`unknown` otherwise,
       with **`unknown` meaning exactly what it says**: the arm is about to write this working tree,
       an untracked file is present, and **Git may still refuse**. It is one `warnings[]` row of
       kind `untracked-present` (§4.4), it is **never** a blocker, it **never** sets
       `runnable: false`, it is not a `refusal.kind`, and it is not fingerprint material (§5.3.2).
       No rendering may turn it into "this run will fail", and none may turn `none-known` into "this
       run is safe" — the second is a statement about untracked files and about nothing else.
     - **A fresh checkout run is in this fact's domain after all, and round 20 corrects round 18 on
       exactly this point.** The earlier text excused the cell on the ground that the shipped
       whole-repo gate refuses such a run "for **any** untracked file"
       (`gitWorkingTreeDirty`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:420-426`, `:570-577`). It does not: the
       gate is `git status --porcelain`, and `git status` honours **`status.showUntrackedFiles`**,
       whose `no` value means "Show no untracked files" (`git config` manual) — so in a repository
       (or a user configuration) carrying that key, an untracked-only tree passes the gate and the
       run proceeds. Deriving a **presence** fact from a **display** preference is precisely the
       kind of configurable oracle §4.2 refuses elsewhere, so the probe runs on fresh checkout rows
       independently, with the same argv, the same anchor and the same warning-only status; it can
       only *add* an advisory to a run the shipped gate already allows, never refuse one. **The
       shipped gate itself is untouched**: `state.worktree.dirty` still mirrors `gitWorkingTreeDirty`
       byte for byte, including its `showUntrackedFiles` sensitivity, and still projects a rank 3
       `state-refused` blocker where the shipped run refuses — the two facts sit side by side and
       neither is derived from the other (§4.4 `state`, §8.6.2).
     Three properties bound the replacement, and each is a rule about *direction*. **It never widens
     `context.dirty`**: an untracked file leaves the tracked predicate untouched and the run
     authorised, so §5.4.7's untracked-only allowance above is preserved exactly. **It never
     refuses**: an over-refusal on an undecidable fact is the one direction a preflight introduced
     by this feature must not take, and the withdrawn blocker took it — every cell where the
     intersection was too *large* was a run Git performs and the guard would have stopped. And **it
     never pretends**: a failed enumeration publishes `null`/`null` as an ordinary **enrichment**
     failure, not a replay-critical `probe-failed`, because nothing depends on the answer (§4.1,
     §4.8). An **exact** verdict is still reachable — by asking Git itself with a dry-run two-way
     `read-tree`, or by the executor probing at the moment it writes — but it is a **simulation**,
     not a static prediction, and §19.26 records it as out of scope for v1 and a candidate
     follow-up rather than a residual of the shipped design. **`rebase.autoStash` is irrelevant in
     both directions**: it stashes tracked changes only (`git stash` without `-u`), so it neither
     creates nor clears an untracked collision, and no configuration turns this warning into a
     blocker or a blocker into this warning.
   - **When `rebase.autoStash` is effectively `true`, the plan says what Git will really do — and
     what it will not.** It will "automatically create a temporary stash entry before the operation
     begins, and apply it after the operation ends" (`git config` manual, `rebase.autoStash`) — i.e.
     it will carry the
     operator's uncommitted **tracked** work **across a HEAD switch onto another branch** and
     reapply it there,
     which the same manual warns "might result in non-trivial conflicts". It does **not** cover
     untracked files: autostash is a plain `git stash`, and untracked files are stashed only under
     `-u`/`--include-untracked` (`git stash` manual), which rebase never passes — so untracked work
     simply stays in the working tree across the switch, where it may now sit beside a different
     branch's checkout. The plan publishes
     `context.dirty: true` with `context.autostash: true` and the `autostash-across-switch` fact;
     **that fact is a `warnings[]` entry with `runnable: true`, settled in round-25 item 5** —
     the blocker rendering §19.18 previously left open is withdrawn, and no `refusal.kind` member
     exists for it (§4.4, §4.9, §19.18). What was never open: it is never silent, and no text may
     claim autostash protects untracked work.
   - **What the option does *not* promise, published as its own fact rather than left in a manual
     quotation** (round-27 item 4, `context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`). "Apply it after the
     operation ends" is an *attempt*, and Git's own handling of a failed attempt is the reason this
     document may never call the option a rescue: `apply_save_autostash_oid` runs
     `git stash apply` with `no_stdout`/`no_stderr`, and where that apply conflicts it **stores the
     entry** (`git stash store -m autostash`), prints
     `Your local changes are stashed, however applying them resulted in conflicts.…` on stderr and
     returns an error — which `finish_rebase` **discards** (`sequencer.c`, `builtin/rebase.c`,
     verified against Git 2.55.0). Three consequences bind every rendering: the rebase can **exit
     0** while the working tree carries conflict markers and an unmerged index from the partial
     apply; the stash entry **survives** in `refs/stash` and must be popped or dropped by hand; and
     the `git stash apply` diagnostics that would have explained which paths conflicted are
     **suppressed** by rebase itself, so the operator sees only the five-line summary — and, under
     the shipped `RunSilentDir` external call, may not even see that. The plan therefore publishes
     the residual on every row where the option applies and says it in the warning's detail; it does
     **not** predict the conflict, because that is a content question no static plan can answer
     (§4.1, §18.2). **"Autostash is on, so your changes are safe" is a sentence this feature must
     never emit**, in the document, the flag help, the docs or the skills (§11, §14).
   - **Whether the option *applies* is a property of the *arm*, not of the config, and round 26
     states the three cells separately** (item 8, §4.1 `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`,
     §4.9 rank 5.5; round-27 item 4 renames the field and replaces the word "rescue" with what the
     option actually buys — that Git **starts** instead of refusing at `cannot rebase: You have
     unstaged changes`). **External
     pass 2** is the cell the paragraph above describes: one `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` whose
     checkout is Git's own, inside the rebase, so an effective `autoStash` carries tracked work
     across that implicit switch and the row is a warning rather than a blocker. **External pass 1**
     applies too, and more simply: the rebase runs in the worktree that already has the branch
     checked out, so the stash is taken and reapplied **in place** with no switch at all — the same
     warning kind, whose detail says so rather than describing a switch that does not happen. **On
     both arms the reapply may conflict, and both details say so** (`context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`
     above): "in place" describes where the stash lands, not that it lands cleanly.
     **Checkout is neither.** A **fresh** checkout run cannot reach the question: `RunCheckoutSync`
     refuses any dirty repository up front with its whole-repo `gitWorkingTreeDirty` gate — untracked
     files and submodules included, stricter than rebase's own precondition — as a rank 3
     `state-refused` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:565-577`). A checkout **continuation** can and does
     resume dirty, because `ContinueCheckoutSync` never re-runs that gate, and its per-entry sequence
     begins with a **standalone `gitCheckout(opts.RepoDir, entry.Branch)`** before the rebase
     (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1040-1047`). `rebase.autoStash` is an option of `git rebase` and
     applies only **after** that checkout has succeeded, so it reaches nothing before it.
     **Round 28 corrects what round 26 concluded from that** (item 3). Round 26 made a tracked-dirty
     checkout continuation a blocker regardless of the config; that is **withdrawn**, because the
     standalone `git checkout <branch>` does **not** refuse on tracked dirt as such. Git performs a
     two-way merge and **carries unrelated local modifications across the switch**, succeeding
     whenever the dirty paths do not differ between the two commits, and refuses — `error: Your
     local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:` — **only where a dirty
     path overlaps the difference between HEAD and the target**. Whether that overlap exists is not
     decidable at plan time: each entry's checkout runs after every earlier entry has already
     rewritten history, so the diff the overlap is measured against does not exist yet. The document
     therefore publishes the fact and refuses nothing: the non-blocking
     **`checkout-dirty-present`** warning (§4.4 `warnings[]`), one row per tracked-dirty checkout
     **continuation** entry row, whose detail names the dirt, says Git **may** refuse that checkout
     with that message, and says `rebase.autoStash` does not reach it. `runnable` stays `true`,
     `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm` stays `false`, and **no** `autostash-across-switch`
     warning is emitted — that kind would tell an operator their work is about to be carried safely
     across a switch the option has nothing to do with. **The residual is excluded from the
     admission guarantee exactly as `untracked-present` is** (§14): the four-conjunct predicate
     promises admission, not Git success, and a checkout Git refuses is one of the outcomes it
     explicitly does not cover. **The fresh-checkout gate is untouched**: `RunCheckoutSync`'s
     whole-repo `gitWorkingTreeDirty` refusal still stops any dirty fresh run at rank 3, untracked
     files and submodules included, exactly as it ships.
   - **A rebase already in progress in that directory blocks before pass 2 runs, and this is the one
     precondition whose absence is *destructive* rather than merely fatal.** Pass 2 rebases in a
     directory it does not own, and `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` refuses outright when that
     directory's `$GIT_DIR` already holds a `rebase-merge` or `rebase-apply` directory
     (`It seems that there is already a rebase-merge directory`). The shipped handler's answer to
     that refusal is `git rebase --abort` **in the same directory**
     (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:200-206`) — so an unguarded `tws sync` that meets a colleague's,
     or the operator's own, in-progress rebase in `entry.Repo` **aborts it**: the manual's `--abort`
     resets HEAD to the original branch and discards the conflict resolution already done there.
     Every other pass-2 precondition predicts a run that *fails*; this one predicts a run that
     *destroys work while failing*. The plan therefore probes the **operation directory** in the
     row's real context — `rebase-merge` or `rebase-apply` via `rev-parse --git-path` + `os.Stat`,
     the shipped `gitRebaseInProgress` shape (§4.1 `context.rebase_in_progress`) — and blocks at
     §4.9 rank 5.45 **before** the Git call, on the JIT seam of consequence 4 as well as at plan
     time. Three properties bind: it is **not** the shipped `isRebaseInProgress`, whose `false` at a
     `break` stop and on an unreadable context is exactly the answer that would let this cell
     through (§8.6.4); `rebase.autoStash` never rescues it, because Git refuses before it would
     stash; and it is a **guard introduction**, so a guarded refusal carries the marker line while
     the unguarded run keeps its shipped behaviour, abort and all (§8.7.6, §18.12). Pass 1 has the
     same blocker over its own worktree, but not the same stakes: its failure path is `syncFailure`,
     which never runs `--abort`.
   - **A branch already checked out in a *foreign* worktree blocks before pass 2 runs; a self hold
     does not.** The implicit checkout cannot happen if **some other** worktree of that context
     already holds `refs/heads/<git_branch>`, so the run fails at Git
     (Git's holder refusal, `branch … is already used by worktree at …`) before replaying anything. **"Holds" is
     wider than "has it checked out", and the inventory must say so.** Git refuses the checkout
     for a worktree that is *detached* but mid-operation on the branch: an interrupted rebase
     records the branch in `rebase-merge/head-name` (interactive/merge backend) or
     `rebase-apply/head-name` (apply backend), and an in-progress bisect records the original
     branch in `BISECT_START` — none of which appears as a `branch refs/heads/<x>` line in
     `git worktree list --porcelain`, which reports those worktrees as `detached`. So the plan
     builds the holder set from the porcelain **plus** those three per-detached-worktree reads, in
     the same `execution_context`, and a holder found either way is a holder. Reading only the porcelain
     branch lines would publish `branch_checked_out_at: null` for precisely the case a stacked
     workflow produces most often — a colleague's, or the operator's own, interrupted rebase on a
     stack branch — and then authorise a run that dies at Git.
     The plan probes it
     with the **same** `BuildWorktreeInventory(repo_root)` call §4.3 already makes for the
     `--update-refs` exemption — one `worktree list --porcelain` process, extended with those cheap
     file reads — and **always publishes `branch_checked_out_at`**,
     including when the holder is the row's own execution context. It blocks with
     `refusal.kind = branch-checked-out-elsewhere` at §4.9 rank 5.4 **only in the foreign case**.
     **The command context is unchanged and the comparison is between worktrees, not between
     command directories**: the row's `git` call still runs exactly where the executor runs it
     (`execution_context.repo_root` — `entry.Repo` or the process cwd — for pass 2, `opts.RepoDir` for
     checkout), and the plan resolves *that* directory to its containing worktree with
     `git -C <dir> rev-parse --show-toplevel` before comparing it against the holding path. Both
     sides are canonicalized after that resolution, because a symlinked, `/private`-prefixed or
     trailing-slash spelling of the same directory is the same worktree and must not be read as a
     foreign one. Resolving first is what makes the rule correct in the common case the previous
     draft got wrong: when the process cwd (or `entry.Repo`) is a **subdirectory** of the worktree
     that holds the branch, a raw directory comparison reads `…/repo/src` ≠ `…/repo` and refuses a
     run Git performs happily. A subdirectory of the row's own worktree is **self**, and self is
     allowed. **When that `rev-parse --show-toplevel` itself fails on a `will_switch_head` row —
     the context is not a work tree, is a bare repository, or is unreadable — the comparison has no
     left-hand side and the row is a replay-critical `probe-failed`** (§4.1, §4.9 rank 5.9): the
     plan publishes the holder it observed and refuses to guess a side, because guessing *self*
     authorises a run that dies at Git and guessing *foreign* refuses a run that works. On a
     non-switching row the probe is never issued at all.
     **The self case is explicitly allowed**: `git rebase <base> <branch>` in the very worktree that
     already has `<branch>` checked out is the ordinary shape — the implicit `git checkout <branch>`
     is a no-op — and it is exactly what a **checkout-mode** row does on the second and every later
     entry once `gitCheckout` has already put HEAD there, and what a pass-2 row does in a repository
     the operator happens to have on that branch. Blocking it would refuse the most common shape of
     a switching row and would make the guard stricter than Git. The rule is stated over
     `mutation.will_switch_head` plus the foreign-path test, not over the arm, so it covers
     **checkout mode's `gitCheckout` rows too** (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1040-1047`, whose failure
     is the shipped `FailSwitch`) and correctly exempts every external **pass-1** row, whose branch
     is checked out in its own worktree *by construction* and which passes no operand at all.
   - **`rebase.autoStash` therefore joins the per-repository effective config** (§4.3 correction 3,
     §4.4 `repositories[]`, §13's per-context probe table) and the fingerprint's repository facts
     (§5.3.2), because it decides whether a tracked-dirty context refuses or is silently stashed across a
     switch — two materially different runs.
Checkout has no analogue: `BuildCheckoutPlan` skips `entry.Archived` outright
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:474-475`), so the cell is `skipped-archived` with no argv; an entry with
an empty base is skipped the same way as `skipped-no-base` (§5.1 rule 5). Both are §4.1 skip-rule
rows: `determinacy = not-applicable`, `reason = not-executed`, and — the correction the skip rule
already made everywhere else — **counted, not unknown**: `replay.candidate_count: 0`,
`replay.commits: []` and `replay.candidate_digest` = the digest of the **empty sequence**, never
`null` (§4.1 skip rule, §4.8). The row replays nothing, and "replays nothing" is a fact the plan
knows without probing; publishing `null` would make it indistinguishable from a range nobody could
measure and would drag the row into `summary.entries_with_unknown_candidates` and into
`verdict: unknown` at the guard seam (§8.3.2a). §15 adds a
pass-2 matrix (materialized × archived-metadata × worktree-missing × prunable × updated-by-ref,
crossed with cutoff absent/present/unresolvable) so this arm is covered by tests rather than prose.

### 5.5 The stack that cannot be sorted

Every ordering fact this document publishes — execution order, the deferral rule, the pass split,
row canonicalization — is defined over `TopoSort`'s output. When the entry set does not linearise,
`TopoSort` returns `cycle detected in stack.yaml` (`internal/stack.go:177-180`) and there is no
output to define them over. The shipped executors already treat it as fatal: external prints
`Error: %v\n` and returns an incomplete result, i.e. `sync incomplete` at exit 1
(`internal/cli/sync.go:548-551`, `:568-571`), external continuations return the error directly
(`:343`, `:411`), `ResolveSyncSelection` propagates it on the new-mode route
(`internal/sync_selection.go:166`), and checkout fails inside `BuildCheckoutPlan`
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:465-468`), after the lock but before the transaction.

The plan mirrors that as a **rows-less refusal document**:

- `refusal.kind = stack-unsortable`, `refusal.detail` carrying the shipped literal verbatim,
  `runnable: false`, `entries: []`, `push.targets: []`, `restore.applies: false` and
  `approval.fingerprint: null` — there is nothing to approve, by the rows-less rule of §4.4 — with
  `blockers[]` holding the single document-level blocker. Its
  aggregates are **not** "every aggregate `null`", which the previous draft claimed and which was
  false for every count-of-published-rows field: it is the `plannability: unavailable` column of the
  profile table in §4.4, exactly — `summary.plannability: unavailable`, `summary.entries: 0`,
  the three "how many rows" counters `0`, the candidate and collateral aggregates `null`,
  `summary.collateral_bound: null`, and `repositories[]` `[]` unless the route had already
  established a safe workspace context (checkout's `ws.RepoRoot`).
- **Plan-only exits 0** (a complete refusal document is a successful description, §8.3.5);
  a **guarded execution exits 1** and rebases nothing, because the sort precedes the first rebase on
  every route.
- **The fetch facts are total and route-independent, because the plan sorts before it fetches.** The
  plan/guard route runs `TopoSort` (and, on the new-mode route, `ResolveSyncSelection`) at step 5 of
  §8.6.1 — **before** the fetch, on **every** route. On the **new-mode** route that is where the
  shipped executor sorts anyway (`internal/sync_selection.go:166`); on the **legacy checkout** route
  nothing fetches at all and the sort inside `BuildCheckoutPlan` is reached without one; and on the
  **legacy external** route, where the shipped executor fetches and *then* sorts, the plan route
  deliberately hoists the sort above the fetch (§8.6.1, "early structural validation"), because it
  is a pure read and moving it can only prevent a network write, never cause one. So the document
  publishes `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.repos: []`, `fetch.outcome: skipped` and
  `freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` **on all four route × mode cells**, never `local-only`
  and never `fetched` — the one variation being a `--continue` over the same unsortable stack, which
  reports `not-refreshed-continuation` by the suppression precedence of §8.6.1 rather than because
  anything about the sort differs. The previous draft's legacy-external exception — "the document reports the
  fetch it really performed" — is **withdrawn**: it was the only cell in which a rows-less document
  could carry a fetch, it forced every consumer to branch on the route before trusting the fetch
  block, and after the hoist it is unreachable. The **unguarded** legacy external run is unchanged:
  it still fetches and then dies at the sort, with its shipped message and its shipped argv
  sequence (§10.1).

This **widens `plan-unavailable`'s meaning** from "the stack could not be read" to the general class
"no rows can be derived at all", with `stack-unsortable` as its named sibling so a consumer can tell
an unreadable stack from an unsortable one. Both sit at rank 1 of §4.9, above every other kind: with
no rows there is nothing for a selection, a state cell, a limit or a token to be about.

---

## 6. Customer topologies, verified against real Git 2.55.0

All transcripts below were produced in throwaway repositories during this analysis (scratch fixtures
removed afterwards) and are reproducible with the argv the executors actually use.

### 6.1 Exact squash, with recorded cutoffs — succeeds, and hides the drop

Topology: `master = A-B'` (B' a distinct commit with identical patch), `pr1 = A-B`, `pr2 = A-B-C`;
recorded cutoffs `cutoff(pr1) = A`, `cutoff(pr2) = B`.

```
git rev-list --count A..pr1  = 1        # PR1 candidate replay
git rev-list --count B..pr2  = 1        # PR2 candidate replay

$ git rebase --no-fork-point --onto master A pr1
Rebasing (1/1)dropping 78ee96a… B -- patch contents already upstream
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/pr1.
# pr1 == master : 1 candidate, 0 applied

$ git rebase --no-fork-point --onto pr1 B pr2
Rebasing (1/1)Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/pr2.
# 1 candidate, 1 applied
```

This is exactly the reported smoke result (checkout and external): PR1 replayed candidate B, Git
dropped it, PR2 replayed candidate C only. The reason external "literally
reported dropping B" and checkout did not is D9, and the mechanism is **stderr, not stdout**:
`Rebasing (n/m)`, `dropping <sha> … -- patch contents already upstream` and
`warning: skipped previously applied commit` are all written by `git rebase` to **stderr**.
`RunDirClean` pipes that stream through `runWithFilteredStderr`'s read loop and re-emits every
surviving line to `os.Stderr` (`internal/exec.go:142-185`) — which is also where the
`skipped previously applied commit` → `    (skipped duplicate commit)` rewrite happens
(`:172-176`); its `cmd.Stdout = os.Stdout` assignment is incidental, because git puts none of these
lines on stdout. Checkout instead captures the merged stream with `CombinedOutput()` and discards it
whenever the rebase succeeds (`gitRebaseOnto`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:350-362`). Any test or
doc that asserts these lines on **stdout** is asserting the wrong stream (§15.3).

**Which filter dropped B, exactly.** The `dropping … -- patch contents already upstream` line is the
**becomes-empty** filter (`--empty=drop`), not the preliminary clean-cherry-pick drop. The upstream
here is the recorded cutoff `A`, and `A` is an ancestor of `pr1`, so `A...pr1` has **no upstream-only
commit** for `--cherry-mark` to match B against: `B'` lives on `master`, which is the `--onto`
target, not the upstream. B is therefore put on the todo list, replayed onto `master`, found to
change nothing, and dropped (§4.2 filter 2). The contrast with §6.2 — where the *same* topology is
rebased with `master` as the **upstream** and Git reports `skipped previously applied commit`, the
preliminary drop's wording — is what makes the distinction concrete. The plan's row therefore
publishes `may_drop_patch_equivalent: false` and `may_drop_becomes_empty: true` for `pr1` here, and
the arm-aware rule of §4.2 is exactly what produces that pair.

**What the guard must show** (the bound two-line row grammar of §8.3.5 — count, range and first
candidate per §4.5; the pre-round-37 table sketch this section carried is **withdrawn as a
rendering**, exactly as §4.5's illustrative spellings were). **Both rows print all eleven fields,
including the deferred one** (round-39 item 1): a deferred destination fills the `<destination>`
half of `<resolved>@<destination>` and never elides the `<resolved>@` half, so `pr2`'s cell is
`pr1@post-rebase(pr1)` — and it reads `pr1` in **both** modes here, but by **two different routes,
one per mode, that happen to meet on this fixture** (round-40 item 1). External resolves it:
a base naming a **same-repo stack entry** short-circuits to that parent's **Git branch** in
`resolveEntryBase` (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:335-340`), before `resolveBase`'s default-branch
rewrite can see it. Checkout **does not call that helper at all** — `BuildCheckoutPlan` carries
`entry.Base`, a **logical name**, verbatim, its only substitution being the scoped local-only one
that swaps in `parent.GitBranch()` for a propagated row (`internal/checkout_sync.go:484-493`, D1),
which this unscoped run does not take. The two agree here because this fixture's parent has
`Name == GitBranch == pr1`, so the logical name checkout prints and the Git branch external
resolves are the **same string**; that is a property of the fixture, not a shared code path, and no
text, rendering, skill or test may state or imply that checkout reaches the external helper.
Where a parent's `branch:` is **decoupled** the two routes visibly part — external prints the
parent's Git branch, checkout prints the logical name and, resolving it as a ref, fails the whole
plan — which is D1 and the §15 item 12 gap, documented there and unchanged by this round
(§2.4, §4.1 `<git_branch>`).
**Every SHA on these lines is the first 12 lowercase hex characters** of the `--json` twin's full
SHA (§8.3.5), never Git's own 7-character abbreviation from the transcript above — `78ee96a` is a
`git rebase` stderr spelling and may not appear in a row (round-39 item 2):

```
# checkout mode; external prints `origin/master` as `<resolved>` where `master` is the default branch
Entries:
  - pr1 [pr1] base master → master@<B'-short> cutoff <A-short> upstream <A-short> strategy onto
    candidates 1 range <A-short>..pr1 first <B-short> "B"
  - pr2 [pr2] base pr1 → pr1@post-rebase(pr1) cutoff <B-short> upstream <B-short> strategy conditional
    candidates 1 range <B-short>..pr2 first <C-short> "C"
```

Everything the withdrawn sketch put on continuation lines — `deferred`/`depends_on`, the arm-aware
drop pair and "destination resolved before pr2 rebases" — stays a `--json` fact and, where a
rendering shows it at all, a **verbose** line *below* the two bound lines, which it may never alter
(§8.3.5).

`pr2`'s range is `exact` even though its destination is deferred (§5.1 rule 1: the recorded cutoff
`B` pins the upstream), and its strategy is `conditional` because a recorded cutoff **and** a
deferred destination are both present — `post-rebase(pr1)` might equal `B`, in which case the plain
arm replays the identical range. In external the published predicate carries the third conjunct as
well (`onto unless post-rebase(pr1) == B or post-rebase(pr1) is unreadable`, §5.1). Neither row may
say "applies".

### 6.2 Cold exact squash, no recorded cutoff — succeeds for a different reason

Same topology, `LastBaseSHA` absent (the normal state after `tws new`, §2.3):

```
git rev-list --count master..pr1 = 1
$ git rebase --update-refs master          # external plain-rebase argv
warning: skipped previously applied commit 46621b8
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/pr1.
# pr1 fast-forwards onto master : 1 candidate, 0 applied
```

The save is **Git's preliminary duplicate-patch detection**, not a tws cutoff — and it is available
here precisely because the upstream is `master`, which holds `B'`, a commit `pr1` does not have
(§4.2 filter 1; contrast §6.1, where the upstream is the cutoff and the filter cannot fire).
`tws new` never initialises
`LastBaseSHA` (`internal/cli/new.go:133-138,221-231`), so this outcome is not a deterministic tws
guarantee and the plan must not present it as one: `cutoff.recorded_sha = null`,
`cutoff.state = absent`, `cutoff.provenance = none`, `strategy = plain`, the upstream taken from
the base ref with `replay.upstream_provenance = base-ref-snapshot`,
`replay.determinacy = snapshot` — **not** `exact`, and under no circumstances a `cutoff.*` value —
and `may_drop_patch_equivalent: true`, because `pr1..master` is non-empty.
(Note tws already rewrites this specific warning to `    (skipped duplicate commit)` **on stderr**,
`internal/exec.go:172-176`.)

**And the row this topology makes unknowable.** In the same cold stack, `pr2` has no recorded cutoff
*and* a deferred destination, so its plain-rebase upstream is `pr1` **after** PR1 runs
(§5.1 rule 3).
Its row is `replay.determinacy = unknown`, `replay.reason = upstream-deferred`,
`candidate_count = null` — and, correcting the previous draft, **`strategy = plain`, not
`conditional`**: with no recorded cutoff the `--onto` predicate's first conjunct is false in both
modes, so the arm cannot depend on the deferred SHA. The argv is therefore printed in full
(`git rebase --update-refs pr1` in an unscoped external run; `git rebase --no-fork-point pr1` in
checkout) beside a `null` count. A plan that printed `1` for the count — the value the pre-rebase
`pr1` would suggest — would be describing a boundary the run never uses. The number
becomes real at the JIT seam, one entry later, and the guard's thresholds are applied to it there.

### 6.3 Materially edited merge — stops at PR1, never reaches PR2

Topology: `master = A-B''` where B'' touches the same file with different content.

```
$ git rebase --no-fork-point --onto master A pr1
Auto-merging b.txt
CONFLICT (add/add): Merge conflict in b.txt
error: could not apply edbcf5e… B
# rebase-merge in progress; pr1 unchanged; pr2 never attempted
```

This matches the reported checkout behaviour exactly. **What the guard must show, before touching
anything:** identical plan rows to §6.1 — the same two-line rows in the bound grammar of §8.3.5
(round-37 item 4), i.e. 1 candidate for `pr1` named by SHA and subject, and 1 candidate for `pr2`
with an exact range and the deferred `post-rebase(pr1)` destination. The guard cannot predict the
conflict, and must not imply it can. Its value here is
different and still real: the operator sees *before* the stop that PR1 is about to replay a commit
whose content the maintainer already changed — and, because §4.5 publishes identity rather than a
bare `1`, *which* commit that is — alongside the shipped `StackEdge` verdict
(`divergent` / `base-rewritten` or `stale` / `parent-advanced`) that says why.

### 6.4 Desired future reparent — the case the guard must preview but not perform

Topology: `master = A-B'-D`, `pr2 = A-B-C`, base explicitly changed to `master` while the old cutoff
`B` is preserved:

```
git rev-list --count B..pr2 = 1
$ git rebase --no-fork-point --onto master B pr2
Rebasing (1/1)Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/pr2.
# pr2 = A-B'-D-C : exactly C was selected
```

The plan for this run is fully determinate (`base.ref = master`, `destination.sha = D`,
`cutoff.recorded_sha = B` with `provenance = recorded-by-sync`,
`replay.upstream_sha = B` with `provenance = recorded-cutoff`, `replay.determinacy = exact`,
`strategy = onto`, `candidate_count = 1`, `replay.range = B..pr2`,
`replay.first_candidate = {C}`, destination not deferred) — which is precisely why it is worth
previewing, and precisely what the request asks for: "expose old cutoff B, new base D, and replay C
before mutation". Note that `replay C` is satisfied by §4.5's identity fields, not by the count.
**And on the default human rendering it is satisfied *visibly*, not only in `--json`** (round-37
item 4): this topology is the acceptance criterion for the bound two-line row grammar of §8.3.5,
which prints — in the mode-correct variant, since `<resolved>` is a mode fact (round-38 item 3):

```
# checkout: the base is resolved literally by BuildCheckoutPlan
Entries:
  - pr2 [feat/pr2] base master → master@<D-short> cutoff <B-short> upstream <B-short> strategy onto
    candidates 1 range <B-short>..feat/pr2 first <C-short> "C"

# external: `master` is this repository's default branch, so resolveBase rewrites it
Entries:
  - pr2 [feat/pr2] base master → origin/master@<D-short> cutoff <B-short> upstream <B-short> strategy onto
    candidates 1 range <B-short>..feat/pr2 first <C-short> "C"
```

— in both, the new base **D** beside the ref that names it, the preserved cutoff **B** as both the
recorded and the effective boundary, and **C** as the first candidate with its sanitized subject.
The document's `base.ref` for the external run is therefore `origin/master` and its `destination.sha`
is still `D`, so the exposure the request asks for is unchanged by the rewrite; only an external
fixture that deliberately configures a **non-default** literal base prints `master` as `<resolved>`.
A rendering that shows `master` without its destination SHA, that shows the external row's
`<resolved>` as `master` where the base is the default branch, or that omits the first candidate,
does not answer this section and is non-conforming (§8.3.5, §15.2a).
**Out of scope for this feature:** performing the reparent (changing
`base` while preserving the cutoff) and inferring that `B ≡ B'`. Those belong to
`safe reparent/restack` (`docs/roadmap.md`, P1 backlog) and to the tesserapatch contract
(`docs/roadmap.md`, "Tool collaboration contracts").

### 6.5 Two failure modes the plan can catch that the executors currently cannot

- **Unresolvable cutoff.** `git rebase --no-fork-point --onto master <missing-sha> pr1` →
  `fatal: invalid upstream '<missing-sha>'`, exit 128. External reports this as a *conflict* with
  "Resolve conflicts in: …" (D10, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:140-146`); checkout classifies it
  `FailSwitch`. A pre-rebase `git rev-parse --verify <cutoff>^{commit}` turns this into an exact,
  actionable refusal. `VerifyGitRef` already exists for it (`internal/exec.go:90-97`), and
  `StackEdge` already models the verdict as `base-record-unresolvable`
  (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:88,410-414`).
- **Multi-commit partial drop.** Candidate 2 → `dropping <sha> B1 -- patch contents already
  upstream` → 1 applied. Confirms the upper-bound contract of §4.2 in the general case, not just the
  1-commit case: the candidate count was 2, the applied count was 1, and nothing available before
  the rebase could have distinguished them.

---

## 7. Reuse versus a dedicated planner

### 7.1 Reuse without hesitation

- `SyncSelection` / `ResolveSyncSelection` for *which* entries participate, roles, and every
  selection refusal (`internal/sync_selection.go:165-247`). The plan must never re-derive scope —
  and must never call it on the **legacy route**, where the executor does not: there the
  participating set is "every entry `TopoSort` returns", exactly as `run == nil` means today
  (`syncRunContext.selects`, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:31-36`; zero-value `sel` in
  `BuildCheckoutPlan`). Calling it there would invent refusals the run does not perform (R6, R7).
- `StackEdge` for the ancestry verdict, heads, merge base, recorded-base verdict, guidance and
  identity notes (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:147-181,371-540`). Consume it verbatim, exactly as
  `stack-status` does (`internal/stack_status.go:709-764`) — the roadmap makes this binding: any
  surface that shows ancestry "must consume the shipped `StackEdge` projection rather than compute
  its own".
- `StackStatusReport`'s **documentation style**: versioned schema (`schema_version` from a
  document-scoped constant), `null` for "not established", no
  map iteration, sanitised display (`internal/stack_status.go:24,86-95,977-995`;
  `internal/stack_ancestry.go:551-624`).
- `probeDirty` for materialization and dirty facts, and `probeActiveGitOp` for the **descriptive**
  Git-operation label only — the blocking predicate is the executor's `gitOperationInProgress`
  (`internal/stack_status.go:326-401`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:396-406`; §8.6.2 exactness rule); **`BuildBranchRefInventory`
  (`internal/stack_status.go:424-447`) for the full `refs/heads/*` set the collateral rule of §4.3
  computes over** — it is one `for-each-ref` per repository context and already fail-closed, which
  is exactly the shape "every local branch, or nothing" needs; and `BuildWorktreeInventory`
  (`internal/agent_status.go:527-536`) for the checked-out-branch set that exempts refs from
  `--update-refs`
  (§4.3) — **and `IsPrunableWorktree` itself, cwd scoping and all**
  (`internal/exec.go:199-221`), for the prunable verdict, because that is the call the executor
  makes and the planner's job here is to mirror it, not to improve it (§3.7, §5.4.3).

### 7.2 What must **not** be reused as the plan's base

`stackBaseRef` resolves an in-stack parent to `refs/heads/<parent.GitBranch()>` and otherwise
returns `se.Base` verbatim (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:318-329`). That is a **third** rule,
matching neither executor: it never performs external's `origin/<default>` mapping (D2) and never
performs checkout's literal-name resolution (D1). The evaluator knows this and models it as
*informational notes* rather than as truth (`identityNotes`, `internal/stack_ancestry.go:482-540`;
`StackBasePolicyForMode`, `:64-70`). A plan guard that used `StackEdge.BaseRef` as the rebase
destination would print a ref the run will not use — the single worst failure mode a guard can
have.

### 7.3 Recommendation: one shared decision function, no third truth

Introduce, in `internal/`, a **rebase planner** that is the *single* producer of the per-entry
decision, and make both executors consume it:

1. `ResolveSyncBase(mode, route, stack, entry, sel, baseCtx) (baseName, baseKind, baseRef)` —
   extracted from `resolveEntryBase`/`resolveBase` and `BuildCheckoutPlan`'s base rule, preserving
   each mode's behaviour **exactly** (including D1, D2, and pass 2's context rule — `entry.Repo`
   when it is non-empty and the **process cwd** when it is empty, §5.4 consequence 6; the earlier
