   "pass 2's `entry.Repo`-only context" phrasing was wrong and is withdrawn). **Its context argument
   is the row's `base_context` and never its `execution_context`** (round-34 items 1 and 2): on
   external **pass 1** that is `syncRepoContext(layout, entry)` — `entry.Repo` when non-empty, else
   the entry's worktree, **two cells and not three** (round-36 item 1, which withdraws round-35
   item 1: the `""`/process-cwd fall-through needs a stat error that is not `os.IsNotExist`, and
   `checkSyncWorktreeBranch` fails the run at the shipped rank 4 preflight before
   `syncRepoContext` is ever reached, so that cell cannot occur) — and it is therefore
   **always** the same directory `GetBranchSHA` is handed; the rebase
   itself always runs in the worktree; on pass 2 and in checkout the two coincide. A planner that passed
   one context to both would answer a different repository's question on every pass-1 row with a
   non-empty `Repo`, which is exactly the class of desynchronisation this function exists to
   prevent. Verified by the existing argv goldens.
2. `RebaseStrategy(mode, materialization, scoped, cutoff, cutoffState, baseState, headState)
   (strategy, argv, condition)` — the single owner of the four external pass-1 shapes, the external
   pass-2 shape, and the two checkout shapes of §2.1/§2.2/§5.4, where `baseState` ranges over
   `resolved | deferred | unresolvable | unset` and `headState` over
   `present | missing | unresolvable` (§5.1 rule 6). On a v2 continuation its `scoped` argument
   comes from the **persisted** policy, never from the invocation's flags (§0.2, §8.6.4) — that is
   what keeps a continuation's projected argv equal to the argv the resume really passes. This is
   provably argv-identical and
   is the change that stops the guard from ever drifting from the executor. It must be **total over
   the whole product** `(mode, materialization, cutoff state, destination deferral, head state)` —
   every cell returns a value, and exactly one cell returns `conditional`:

   | materialization | cutoff | destination SHA | external | checkout |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   | materialized | absent | known or **deferred** | `plain` (argv known) | `plain` (argv known) |
   | materialized | present | known, `==` base SHA | `plain` | `plain` |
   | materialized | present | known, `!=` base SHA | `onto` | `onto` |
   | materialized | present | **deferred** | `conditional` (+ `currentBaseSHA != ""` conjunct) | `conditional` |
   | materialized | present | unresolvable | `plain` (external falls back, then fails) | `unknown` (fails resolving the base first) |
   | materialized | unresolvable | known | `onto` (then `fatal: invalid upstream`) | `onto` (then `FailSwitch`) |
   | any | any | **base unset** (`base.kind = none`, §5.1 rule 5) | `plain` / `plain-explicit-branch` over the empty `""` token — the only token `resolveBase("", ctx)` can return (§5.1 rule 5) — `blocking` | `skipped-no-base`, `argv = []`, not blocking |
   | any | any | any, with **`headState != present`** (§5.1 rule 6) | the arm's normal shape, `blocking` — pass 2 fails at the branch operand | `unknown`, `blocking` — `BuildCheckoutPlan` fails at `resolve branch %q` |
   | non-materialized | any | any | `plain-explicit-branch`, or `skipped-updated-ref` when an earlier pass-1 entry marked it | n/a — `skipped-archived` |
   | anchor under local-only | any | any | `skipped-anchor` | excluded from the plan |

   `argv` is `null` **only** in the `conditional` cell; `skipped-*` cells carry `[]`.
2a. `EntryContexts(mode, route, layout, entry) (baseCtx, execCtx Context)` — the **one** producer of
   the two context refs of §4.1, so no caller re-derives either from `entry.Repo` (round-34
   item 1). It reproduces the shipped rules verbatim: external pass 1 → `baseCtx =
   syncRepoContext(layout, entry)` — **`entry.Repo` when non-empty, else the worktree**, which is
   **two** cells and not three (round-36 item 1, withdrawing round-35 item 1's unreachable
   process-cwd *strategy-row* cell: the pass-1 loop's non-`os.IsNotExist` stat error is answered by
   `checkSyncWorktreeBranch`'s wrong-branch refusal before the loop's `syncRepoContext` runs;
   round-37 item 2 keeps that mapping and adds only that the **route's own I14 preflight** may have
   answered `""` for the same entry earlier, which produces a `preflight-refused` row rather than a
   pass-1 strategy row and is therefore not a cell of *this* function's strategy-row mapping) — and
   `execCtx = layout.WorktreePath(entry.Name)`; external
   pass 2 → both `entry.Repo`, else the **process cwd**; checkout → both `opts.RepoDir`. It also
   owns the identity of §4.4 — the canonical absolute root, the root source and the absolute common
   dir hashed into `context_id` — so two refs naming one directory provably produce one id and one
   `repositories[]` row, **and it returns both contexts' measured canonical common dirs beside the
   ids**, since §4.1's context-pair rule forbids sharing an inventory or refusing for divergence on
   anything less than a measurement (round-35 item 2). Every probe helper takes a `Context`, never a
   bare path string, which is
   what makes "was this probe issued in the right context?" a type question rather than a review
   question; the `rebase.*` configuration inventory hangs off the **execution** context (§4.3), and
   so — since round-35 item 3 — does every ref, range and inventory probe `git rebase` resolves,
   leaving `baseCtx` with the default-branch read, the `base.ref` resolution and the `GetBranchSHA`
   behind `base.decision_sha` and nothing else. **It also produces the skip-row shapes of §4.1's
   skip-context rule, rather than leaving a caller to decide them** (round-36 item 4, made
   route-aware by round-37 item 1): on a
   `skipped-updated-ref` row it returns the ordinary pass-2 `execCtx`, and a `baseCtx` that is the
   **preflight's** context (`entry.Repo`, else the process cwd) **only on the new-mode `--no-fetch`
   route, where `verifySelectedBasesLocally` really resolved that entry's base**, and `source:
   not-applicable` on every other route; on `skipped-anchor`/`skipped-archived`/`skipped-no-base` it
   returns `not-applicable` for **both** on every route, so no probe helper can be handed a
   directory for a row the route never touches. It takes the resolved **route** for exactly that
   reason: the base-context cell of a skip row is a fact about the route, not about the arm. The **push** context is *not* produced here: it has
   its own ladder and its own `context_id` on the `push.targets[]` row (§4.4, round-35 item 5).
3. `ExecutionOrder(mode, route, stack, sel, materialization) []name` **and**
   `DestinationDeferred(order, entry, baseRef, providerArm) (deferred bool, dependsOn string)` —
   the §5.1 deferral rule as code, so "deferred" is computed from the route's real order (external
   pass 1 then pass 2; checkout plan order), the base provider's materialization, and that
   provider's planned arm. Deferral must never be re-derived from `entry.Base` by a caller; the
   external pass-1-child/pass-2-parent cell is the one every topology-based implementation gets
   wrong.
4. `ReplayUpstream(cutoff, cutoffState, baseRef, baseSHA, deferred, materialization)
   (upstreamRef, upstreamSHA, provenance, determinacy, reason)` — the §5.1 rule plus §5.4's arm as
   one function, so the "is this range exact,
   a snapshot, or unknown?" question has exactly one implementation and cannot be re-derived
   differently by the human renderer, the JSON encoder, and the threshold check. Its `deferred`
   argument comes from step 3 and from nowhere else.
4a. `RemainingRebaseEntries(route, state, stack, sel) []name` — the §8.6.4a derivation as one
   function, so "which entries does this `--continue` still have to do?" has exactly one
   implementation shared by the plan document, the guard seam and the fingerprint tuple. It is
   **state-derived, never flag-derived** (§0.2), it re-derives its universe from the *current*
   stack exactly as the shipped resumes do, and it is total over
   `(route × persisted state × stage)`. Nothing else in the planner may compute a remaining set.
4b. `PushTargets(mode, route, stack, sel, remaining, state) []PushTarget` — the §4.4
   `push.targets[]` projection as one function, mirroring `pushFeature`/`pushEntries` for
   `scope=all`, `pushScoped` (selected ∩ rebased ∖ `payload.Pushed`, worktree-bearing only) for
   `only`/`subtree`, and `finalizeTransaction`/`finalizeCleanup` over `tx.Plan` for checkout. Like
   4a it is **state-derived on a continuation** and is shared by the document, the guard seam and
   the fingerprint tuple, so a push-stage resume with no remaining rebase entry still has exactly
   one definition of its remaining work (§8.6.4a). It issues **no** Git process and performs no
   push.
5. `BuildRebasePlan(...) (RebasePlan, error)` — a projection layered on 1-4b (non-mutating in the
   §0.1 sense; read-only when the resolved fetch policy is `no-fetch`), adding cutoff verification,
   candidate counts, bounded identity **and the full-sequence `candidate_digest`** (§4.5),
   collateral refs, deferral, push targets with their executability pair, **the checkout `restore`
   projection** — target branch and tip from the transaction on a continuation and from the same
   pre-mutation `gitCurrentBranch`/`gitResolveRef` probe `RunCheckoutSync` performs on a fresh run,
   plus its own `executable`/`blocked_by[]` preconditions (§4.4, §8.6.4a) — fetch/freshness facts,
   and the
   `StackEdge` verdict. It runs `TopoSort` and the selection **before** the route's fetch on every
   route (§8.6.1), so a `TopoSort` failure produces a rows-less `stack-unsortable`
   document — with no fetch performed — rather than an error (§5.5), and a per-row probe failure
   produces a `null` fact rather
   than a zero or an empty list (§4.8). `BuildCheckoutPlan` becomes an adapter that produces
   `CheckoutPlanEntry` from `RebasePlan` (or gains the fields), so checkout keeps one plan, not two.
6. `RefusalKind(blockers) (kind, orderedBlockers)` — the §4.9 precedence and canonical sort as one
   function, consumed by the JSON encoder, the human renderer **and** the guarded refusal's stderr
   line, so the three cannot disagree about which fact refused a run.

Only step 5 issues extra Git processes, and only when a plan is actually requested — which is what
keeps the no-flag budget frozen (§10, §13).

---

## 8. CLI and API options

### 8.1 Fixed points (non-negotiable)

- `tws sync <feature>` with no flags must remain byte-identical on stdout/stderr **and**
  argv-identical, in both modes. Evidence: `internal/cli/testdata/sync_noflag/**` plus the harness
  contract at `internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go:19-31` ("a regeneration that alters a committed
  output golden … IS the regression this criterion exists to catch").
- **`syncTriggerFlags` is frozen at its six members** (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:31`). No control
  flag joins it, so no control flag changes `newMode`, the I8 operand list
  (`syncChangedTriggerList`, `:143-152`), or the I20 gate (§8.5).
- Errors stay Cobra `RunE`; the process has exactly two exit codes today, 0 and 1
  (`internal/cli/root.go:53-57`).
- Flag names must not collide with the eleven existing ones (§1.1), and any entry-valued flag should
  register completion like `--only`/`--from` (`internal/cli/sync.go:144-145`, `internal/cli/sync_modes.go:520-543`).
- Non-TTY convention already exists: gate on `isTerminal()` and require an explicit flag otherwise
  (`internal/cli/registry.go:296,317,322-328`).

### 8.2 Options considered

| Option | Shape | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. explicit `--plan` | non-mutating preview (§0.1), prints and exits 0 | zero risk to existing runs; perfect for agents with `--json`; trivially testable | does not stop anything by itself; requires the operator to look; under an effective `fetch` policy it still writes remote-tracking refs |
| B. automatic preflight on every run | always print the plan before mutating | maximal safety | breaks the no-flag goldens by construction; adds Git probes to every run; noisy |
| C. threshold guard | refuse when candidates > N or plan indeterminate | stops exactly the surprising runs; cheap to reason about | any *default* > 0 changes the no-flag path, which is why v1 ships the limits as **flags only, no config** (§8.3.4); "N" is ambiguous until per-entry vs aggregate is decided (§8.3.2) |
| D. TTY prompt | ask for confirmation | familiar | tws sync is routinely driven by agents/CI; a prompt inside a locked, state-writing transaction with an unbounded stdin wait is a hang risk; the repo has no confirm prompt anywhere except `pick` (`internal/cli/picker.go:11-25`) |
| E. approval token | `--approve-plan <fingerprint>`, where the token is only ever read out of a `--plan` document — human or `--json` — and never printed by an executing invocation (§8.7.7) | deterministic in TTY and non-TTY alike; naturally plan-scoped (§5.2); the waiver is narrow by construction — it covers the limit violations shown in the approved document and never a hard blocker or a newly-resolved excess (§5.3.1) | two invocations proactively and three reactively (§8.7.7), and the pair's shape depends on the underlying route (§5.3); fingerprint must be stable, documented, and must bind the whole run including its push and validation intent |

### 8.3 Recommendation

**A + C + E, with B and D rejected.**

1. `tws sync <feature> --plan [--json]` — the **plan-only inspection route** (§8.6).
   **Non-mutating in the §0.1 sense**: no worktree, no local
   branch, no `stack.yaml`, no state file, no lock, no sentinel, no transaction, no push; **fully
   read-only under `--no-fetch`**; and, under an effective `fetch` policy, it **runs the run's fetch
   and therefore updates remote-tracking refs** before projecting. It computes and prints the plan
   for exactly the run the same flags would perform — **including which route** that is: bare
   `--plan` describes the legacy path, `--plan` plus any trigger flag describes the new-mode path
   (§0.2, §8.5), and `route`/`route_triggers` say which. `--plan` composes with `--only`,
   `--from`, `--fetch`/`--no-fetch`, `--full`/`--local-only`, and with `--continue`, where it
   describes the *remaining* entries of whatever the state holds — v2 payload, legacy
   `.sync-state.yaml`, or checkout transaction — under the **state-derived** effective route, and
   where I20, like every other continuation gate, is **projected into the document** rather than
   raised (§8.5.3, §8.6.4). **`--plan --push` is legal**: `--push` is part of the run being
   described, so the document publishes `intent.push: true`, **projects the branch set it would push
   as `push.targets[]`**, binds both into the fingerprint (§5.3)
   and pushes **nothing** — refusing the combination would make it impossible to preview, or
   approve, the runs whose blast radius extends to a remote, which are precisely the runs worth
   previewing. `--plan --abort` stays refused by the plan surface's own validation, not by I8,
   because `--abort` describes no run at all — that cell, and every other control-flag
   combination, is fixed once in the compatibility matrix of §8.5.1.
   **`--plan` obeys the fetch axis** rather than forcing `--no-fetch`: a preview that shows a
   different new base than the run would use is worse than a preview that touches the network. The
   consequence must be documented in the flag help, not
   buried: in **external** mode the effective default is `fetch`, so a bare `tws sync <f> --plan`
   fetches; in **checkout** mode the effective default is `no-fetch`, so it does not
   (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:107-116`). **`--plan --no-fetch` is not a local variant of the same
   preview**: `--no-fetch` is a mode trigger, so it previews the *new-mode* run instead (§0.2,
   §5.3), and there is deliberately no fully-local preview of the legacy external route. A
   `--plan --continue` never fetches on any route, because no continuation executor does (§8.6.4).
   The already-shipped header states the resolved decision
   (`Sync mode: fetch=… propagation=… scope=…`, `internal/cli/sync_modes.go:502-504`,
   `internal/checkout_sync.go:519-521`), and §4.4's `fetch.*`/`freshness` fields state its outcome —
   including the **non-fatal failure** case, where the plan is a projection over stale refs.
2. **Thresholds — `--max-replay` is ambiguous and must not ship as one number.** For a broad stack,
   "max replay 5" can mean "no entry replays more than 5", "the run replays no more than 5 in
   total", or both, and the three refuse different runs: a 12-entry stack replaying one commit each
   passes the first and fails the second. **Decision required in `define`; recommendation: ship both
   limits with unambiguous names and publish both facts unconditionally.**
   - Facts (always in the plan, guard or no guard): `summary.max_entry_candidates`,
     `summary.total_candidates`, `summary.total_candidates_lower_bound`,
     `summary.entries_with_unknown_candidates` (§4.4).
   - Limits: `--max-replay-per-entry <n>` and `--max-replay-total <n>`, independently settable,
     both opt-in. If the spec insists on the single name `--max-replay`, it must bind it to exactly
     one meaning in the flag help and the docs, and the recommended binding is **per-entry**
     (the surprising run is usually one entry replaying far more than expected).
   - **Unknown rows are not zero.** `total_candidates` is `null` whenever any selected entry is
     `determinacy = unknown`. The aggregate limit is then evaluated against
     `total_candidates_lower_bound`, the refusal (or the pass) states that the true total is at
     least that, and every unknown row is re-checked against **both** limits when the JIT seam makes
     it countable (§5.2). Summing over unknowns as if they were zero would be the same lie the count
     contract exists to prevent. §8.3.2a makes the comparison and the emission total.
   - **Indeterminacy rule.** Refuse before the first rebase when any selected entry has
     `cutoff.state = unresolvable`, an unresolvable `base.ref`, `base.kind = none` in external
     (§5.1 rule 5), or `strategy = unknown`. A
     `determinacy = unknown` *source range* (§5.1 rule 3) is common and benign in cold stacks, so it
     must not be a hard refusal by default; it is re-evaluated at the JIT seam against the same
     limits (§5.2), and the plan says so — its evaluation row is
     `verdict: unknown, unknown_kind: deferred-resolvable`, and under the recommended
     `guard.indeterminacy_policy: jit-deferred` it does **not** set `guard.would_refuse*` up front
     (§8.3.2a, §4.4). The one unknown the JIT seam cannot rescue is
     `reason = merge-recreation` (§4.2): with a limit in effect, that row refuses up front with
     `indeterminate-entry`, because no honest number exists to compare — a **rank 10, non-waivable
     guard verdict**, not a hard blocker and not a configuration refusal — the `config-blocking`
     kind no longer exists (§4.9, §5.3.1) — and, per §4.4,
     that
     refusal leaves `runnable: true`, because the plan itself is executable; it is the *limit* that
     cannot be evaluated. Whether a flag may make
     other unknowns a hard refusal up front is an open decision (§19.9), and the document publishes
     which policy it applied rather than leaving it inferable.
   - **Limits are per invocation, over *this* invocation's work — never cumulative.** A limit is
     compared against what the command about to run would replay: the whole selected plan on a fresh
     invocation, and **only the remaining work** on a `--continue` (§8.6.4a, §8.7.4). Nothing is
     carried forward: a run that replayed 30 candidates before an interruption and would replay 5
     after it is compared as **5** on the resume, not 35, and the guard keeps no counter across
     invocations because no route persists one (only the limit *values* persist, §10.3). This is
     stated here, in the **flag help** for both limits, and in the docs and skills (§14), because
     the opposite reading — "a budget for the whole stack over time" — is the natural one for a flag
     called `--max-replay-total`, and an operator who believes it would over-trust a resume. The
     name means "the total of this invocation", and the document's `approval.scope`
     (`full-run` / `remaining-work`) is what says which invocation that is.
   - Because every limit is opt-in **and flag-only on a fresh run** (item 4), the no-flag path is
     untouched; on a continuation the limits come from the total resolution table of §8.7.4 —
     persisted values, or this invocation's flags where nothing was persisted — never from a config.

3. `--approve-plan <fingerprint>` — the **guarded execution route** (§8.7): it re-computes the same
   plan non-interactively and executes it if the token still matches. The token is exactly 64
   lowercase hex characters and is compared bytewise (§4.4). The fingerprint is the
   `approval.fingerprint` half of the §5.3 split — approval scope, workspace mode, stable id and
   repo root, feature,
   **effective route and trigger set**, fetch/propagation/scope policy, **the effective limit
   `value` per key** (the published `origin` label is a non-member, §5.3.2), **push intent *and the projected `push.targets[]`***, the
   validation intent (`applies` + `command_digest`, §8.8), the context-qualified
   `repositories[]` config facts,
   the
   canonical selected-name list, and per entry the base/cutoff/head/upstream identities, **the
   candidate count and the full-sequence `candidate_digest`** (§4.5), deferral facts
   (`depends_on`), strategy (or conditional shapes), effective backend and
   collateral mechanism — computed over a **canonical invariant tuple projected from the document**,
   never over the rendered document (§5.3), and **published only by `--plan` documents that describe
   an approvable plan *and* carry at least one effective limit**
   (`approval.fingerprint`, §4.4; `null` **exactly** when `entries` is `[]`, `push.targets` is `[]`
   **and** `restore.applies` is `false`, **or** when neither `guard.limits` key has an effective
   value, **or** when `encoding_issues` is non-empty — the single **three-clause** usable-token
   predicate of §4.4, stated identically
   here, in §4.9, in §5.3.1, in §8.6.3 and in every test (round-28 item 6: no restatement carries
   fewer than three clauses), with `approval.usable` and the **three** clause booleans of
   `approval.covers` — `has_work`, `requires_limits`, `encoding_safe` — published so the three
   `null` causes are distinguishable **from published fields alone** (round-30 item 4: the
   `(usable, requires_limits)` pair could not separate "no work" from "encoding issue")),
   never persisted, and re-validated per entry through `revalidation.digest`. An
   approval
   that bound only `(entry, count)` would authorise a different run than the one shown: a different
   repository, a different route, a different scope, a different commit, a different blast
   radius — or the same replay followed by a force-push nobody previewed. **No executing invocation
   emits a token**; the acquisition workflows — proactive and
   reactive — are fixed in §8.7.7.
   - **What it waives is narrow and fixed** (§5.3.1): the limit violations already shown in the
     approved document, and nothing else. Hard blockers, JIT facts that newly exceed a limit,
     changed candidate identity and new collateral all still stop the run.
   - **The round trip depends on the underlying route** (§5.3) and always repeats the **same trigger
     flags, limit flags, `--push` and validation intent**: bare `--plan` (human or `--json`) → bare
     `--approve-plan <fp>` for the legacy external
     run (both fetch; it succeeds only while the guarded identities hold), and
     `--plan --no-fetch --json` → `--no-fetch --approve-plan <fp>` for the explicit new-mode
     no-fetch run (stable, fully local, and the consumer must assert `route: new-mode`).
   - **`--plan --approve-plan` is legal, executes nothing, and is the precise "will this run?"
     probe**: it prints the document with
     `approval.supplied: true`, `approval.accepted: true|false`, the covered violations moved to
     `verdict: waived`, and, on a mismatch,
     `refusal.kind = approval-mismatch` — still exit 0, because a document was produced (item 5).
     On a match, `guard.would_refuse` is the **effective** verdict and
     `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` the raw one, so
     `runnable && !guard.would_refuse && guard.execute_blocked_by == [] && refusal.kind == null`
     answers whether the exact command
     line — same `T`, `L`, `P`, `V`, minus `--plan`, plus the token — will be **admitted** and
     execute (§4.4, §5.3.1). **"Admitted" is the whole claim** (§0.2): the four conjuncts cover the
     guard, the projected shipped gates and this document's declared blockers, and cover nothing
     Git decides after the first process starts — a conflict, a checkout Git refuses, a failing
     validation command or a rejected push leaves the predicate correct and the run failed.
     **The `execute_blocked_by` conjunct is not decoration**: it is the term that covers the
     controlled-path refusals the *unguarded* route ignores — a pre-existing live foreign owner
     above all — which `runnable` deliberately does not move (§4.4, §8.6.1 cause 3).
4. **No config-armed guard in v1: limits are flags only.** The previous draft proposed
   `sync.plan_guard.max_replay_per_entry` / `sync.plan_guard.max_replay_total` defaults in
   `internal/config.go`. Dropped. A config default would arm the guard on a **bare no-flag run**,
   which is exactly the path §8.1 freezes byte- and argv-identically, and it would make "is this run
   guarded?" depend on ambient state that the goldens do not capture. The only non-flag source that
   exists is a run's **own persisted limits on `--continue`** (§8.7.4, §10.3), which cannot arm a
   fresh run at all; each key's `guard.limits.<key>.origin` names it explicitly rather than leaving it ambient
   (§4.4). Config defaults remain a plausible **follow-up feature**, with their own
   analysis of the no-flag interaction; they are not part of this one.
5. **Exit codes**: keep the shipped 0/1 alphabet (`internal/cli/root.go:53-57`), and bind it to the
   route, not to the verdict:
   - **Plan-only (`--plan`) exits 0 whenever a complete document was produced** — including a
     document whose `runnable` is `false`, whose `guard.would_refuse` is `true`, whose
     `refusal.kind` is `plan-unavailable`, or whose `approval.accepted` is `false`. Describing a run
     that cannot proceed *is* the successful execution of a description command, and an agent must
     be able to read the document rather than guess from a status code.
   - **Every document that describes an approvable plan under an effective limit publishes its
     token, in both renderings.**
     `--json` carries `approval.fingerprint` as a **string or `null`** — 64 lowercase hex characters
     (`^[0-9a-f]{64}$`, §4.4) whenever **all three clauses** of §4.4's usable-token predicate hold:
     the document describes work to approve — `entries` is non-empty, **or** `push.targets` is
     non-empty, **or** `restore.applies` is `true` —, **and** at least one `guard.limits` key has an
     effective value, **and** `encoding_issues` is `[]`;
     `null` when the work triple is all empty/false, **or** no limit is in force, **or**
     `encoding_issues` is non-empty,
     whatever the refusal kind (§4.4, §8.6.3). A limitless plan is a complete, useful document that
     deliberately mints nothing, and it says which precondition is missing through
     `approval.usable: false` + `approval.covers.requires_limits: true`, with
     `approval.covers.has_work: true` and `approval.covers.encoding_safe: true` naming the two
     clauses that *are* satisfied (round-30 item 4, replacing the round-29 reading that inferred the
     third clause from a non-empty `encoding_issues[]`); the operator re-runs the
     same plan with the limits they intend to guard with. The
     **human** rendering prints, after the rows and any refusal prose, a **fixed four-part tail on
     every document without exception** (round-32 items 5 and 6, replacing round 31's two-part
     tail): the **status lines**, then the **configuration-issue block**, then the
     **guarded-execution blocker block**, then the fingerprint line.

     **The default human *entry row* is a bound grammar too, and round 37 closes the last place the
     document left the customer's headline to a presentation choice** (item 4). Until now the tail
     was byte-exact while the rows above it were "count + range + first candidate" (§4.5) with the
     field set, the order and the absent-value spellings unstated — so two conforming
     implementations could print the same plan differently and neither would name the **new base**
     or the **first candidate** in a form the operator could quote. The request the whole feature
     exists for is explicit — *"expose old cutoff B, new base D, and replay C before mutation"*
     (`request.md`, §6.4) — so the row that answers it is fixed here, **on the default human
     rendering, with no flag and no verbosity level required**, as exactly **two lines per entry**
     under one `Entries:` header, in the document's canonical row order (§4.7):

     ```
     Entries:
       - <name> [<git_branch>] base <configured> → <resolved>@<destination> cutoff <recorded> upstream <effective> strategy <strategy>
         candidates <count> range <range> first <first>
     ```

     with the **eleven** fields of the table below **total** — every one printed on every row, never
     omitted, never reordered, and every absent cell carrying a fixed literal rather than a blank, for the same
     reason the `Configuration issues:` block's value field is total (round-33 item 8): an optional
     field makes two documents with different facts print the same line and makes the block
     unparsable by position.

     | Field | Value | Absent / unknown spelling |
     |---|---|---|
     | `<name>` | `name`, sanitized (§11) | never absent |
     | `<git_branch>` | `git_branch`, sanitized | never absent; printed **always**, even where it equals `name`, so a decoupled `branch:` is visible without a second command (§4.1, D1) |
     | `<configured>` | `base.name` verbatim, sanitized — the base **as `stack.yaml` configures it** | `<none>` when `base.kind: none` |
     | `<resolved>` | `base.ref` — the ref the executor really passes to Git | `<unresolved>` when `base.ref` is `null` |
     | `<destination>` | the **destination commit**: the first 12 characters of `destination.sha` | `post-rebase(<logical-parent-name>)` when `destination.deferred` — the literal `post-rebase(`, the parent's **logical name** taken from `destination.depends_on`, and `)`, e.g. `post-rebase(pr1)`, and that spelling is the only one any surface, test or skill may use; `<not-executed>` on every `skipped-*` row; `<unresolved>` when the peel failed or the ref is missing |
     | `<recorded>` | the **recorded** cutoff: the first 12 characters of `cutoff.recorded_sha`, with ` (unresolvable)` appended when `cutoff.state: unresolvable` and ` (unverified)` when `cutoff.state` is `null` | `<none>` when nothing is recorded (`cutoff.state: absent`) |
     | `<effective>` | the **effective replay upstream**: the first 12 characters of `replay.upstream_sha` — the boundary the run will really replay from, which is *not* the recorded cutoff on a pass-2 arm (§5.4 consequence 1) | `<not-executed>` on every `skipped-*` row, whose `replay.upstream_sha` is `null` for the *not-applicable* reason and which therefore takes precedence; `<unknown>` for any other `null` |
     | `<strategy>` | the `strategy` enum member, ASCII, verbatim | never absent — `unknown` and the four `skipped-*` tokens are members |
     | `<count>` | decimal `replay.candidate_count` | `<unknown>` when `null`; a skip row prints the counted `0` (§4.1 skip rule) |
     | `<range>` | `replay.range`, sanitized | `<none>` when `null`, **including every `skipped-*` row**, which has no range expression (§4.1 skip rule) |
     | `<first>` | `<12-char sha> "<sanitized subject>"` from `replay.first_candidate` | `<none>` when the count is a known `0`; `<unknown>` when the range is unknown |

     **Every SHA on these two lines is the first 12 lowercase hex characters of the full SHA the
     `--json` twin publishes** — a pure display truncation that costs **no** probe and cannot vary
     with repository size, unlike `rev-parse --short`. The published `head.short` and
     `first_candidate.short` members stay `--json` facts and are not re-spelled here, so there is
     exactly one abbreviation rule in the human surface. `→` is the literal U+2192 arrow, emitted as UTF-8 on a
     surface this document already fixes as UTF-8 (§5.3.2a, §11), and every interpolated value passes
     through §11's renderer; subjects are sanitized through `ancestrySanitize`, one line, and never interpolated
     into a suggested command (§4.5). **No verb implying application may appear on either line**:
     the header is `candidates`, never `applies` or `will be applied` (§4.5, §4.2).
     **`post-rebase(…)`'s operand is the parent's logical name wherever the document writes it**
     (round-38 item 3) — here, in `strategy_condition`'s predicate and in every worked example — so
     the human destination cell and the predicate can never name the parent two different ways, and
     `destination.depends_on` is that literal's **source field**, never a spelling of it.

     **What the two lines say for the customer's own topology** (§6.4, `master = A-B'-D`,
     `pr2 = A-B-C`, base changed to `master` with cutoff `B` preserved) is the acceptance criterion
     for this grammar, and it must be readable without the JSON. **It has two honest variants,
     because `<resolved>` is a *mode* fact and not a spelling choice** (round-38 item 3): checkout
     resolves the base literally inside `BuildCheckoutPlan` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:485-489`),
     while external rewrites a base that names the repository's **default** branch to its
     remote-tracking form through `resolveBase` (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:335-356`). Both must
     be rendered and asserted; neither may be printed for the other mode:

     ```
     # checkout mode
     Entries:
       - pr2 [feat/pr2] base master → master@<D-short> cutoff <B-short> upstream <B-short> strategy onto
         candidates 1 range <B-short>..feat/pr2 first <C-short> "C"

     # external mode, where `master` is the repository's default branch
     Entries:
       - pr2 [feat/pr2] base master → origin/master@<D-short> cutoff <B-short> upstream <B-short> strategy onto
         candidates 1 range <B-short>..feat/pr2 first <C-short> "C"
     ```

     — in **both**, the **new base D** is visible as the destination beside the ref that names it,
     the **old cutoff B** is visible as both the recorded and the effective boundary, and **C** is
     visible as the first candidate with its subject. `<configured>` stays `master` in both, because
     it is `stack.yaml`'s own token; only `<resolved>` differs, and an external fixture that
     deliberately configures a **non-default** literal base resolves it unchanged and prints
     `master@<D-short>` there too. A rendering that prints `master` without `@<D-short>`, that
     prints the external row's `<resolved>` as `master` where the base *is* the default branch, or
     that omits `first`, does not answer the request and is non-conforming.
     **A rows-less document prints the header and the literal `none`** — `Entries: none`, on one
     line, with no row lines at all — on the same `none`-or-every-member rule the two tail blocks
     already use, so a reader never has to tell "no rows" from "the rows were not printed"
     (§8.6.3).
     **`--json` is unchanged and remains the complete surface**: every field these two lines
     compress — the full 40-character SHAs, `base.decision_sha`, `destination.snapshot_sha`,
     `replay.commits`, `candidate_digest`, `collateral_refs`, every `context.*` and both context
     refs — stays exactly as §4.4 defines it, and no field is removed from the document because the
     human row summarises it (§8.3.6). The **verbose** human form may add lines **below** a row and
     may never alter these two, and the four-part tail below the rows is untouched: this block adds
     a fixed shape *above* it and reorders, rewords and omits nothing in it (§15.16a2).

     **The status lines are explicit, labelled and byte-stable, and round 32 stops the human form
     inferring them from prose** (item 6). Three of the four conjuncts an agent reads off the JSON
     had no labelled human surface at all — a reader had to infer `runnable` and the refusal from
     free prose that varies by kind. The rendering is fixed, in this order, one line each, on
     **every** document:

     ```
     Plan runnable: yes
     Guard would refuse: no
     Refusal kind: none
     ```

     `Plan runnable:` is `yes`/`no` from `runnable`; `Guard would refuse:` is `yes`/`no` from
     `guard.would_refuse` (the **post**-waiver verdict, so a matching token that waived a limit
     shows `no`); `Refusal kind:` is the `refusal.kind` enum member, or the literal `none` where it
     is `null`. The ordinary refusal prose stays exactly as it is and is printed above these lines —
     these are a machine-legible restatement, not a replacement, and no kind is spelled differently
     here than in `refusal.kind`.

     **The configuration-issue block is deterministic and comes before the blockers** (round-32
     item 5). A rank 5.07 document could previously say only "this run's configuration is invalid"
     in one blocker sentence; the array behind it was `--json`-only. The rendering is fixed:

     ```
     Configuration issues: none
     ```

     when `config_issues[]` is empty, and otherwise the labelled header followed by **one line per
     row, in the array's own canonical `issue_id` order** (§4.4, §4.7), each line in **exactly** this
     grammar — two spaces, `- `, the full id, one space, the key, one space, the bracketed pair, a
     colon, one space, the value field (round-33 item 8, which fixes the grammar the round-32 draft
     left as a sketch with an optional value):

     ```
     Configuration issues:
       - <64-hex issue_id> <key> [<source>, <route_command>]: <value-field>
       - <64-hex issue_id> rebase.autostash [global, rebase]: sometimes
       - <64-hex issue_id> rebase.backend [local, rebase]: <valueless>
       - <64-hex issue_id> submodule.recurse [command, checkout]: ""
     ```

     **Every row is rendered and every line carries a value field** — the round-32 wording "may show
     `sanitized_value` only where it is non-`null`" is withdrawn, because an optional field makes two
     documents with different evidence print the same line and makes the block unparsable by
     position. The field is total, over three cells and no others: a **valueless** occurrence
     (`raw_value_present: false`) prints the literal `<valueless>`; an **explicitly empty** value
     (`sanitized_value: ""`) prints the two characters `""`; and every other row prints
     `sanitized_value` itself. The two literals are fixed spellings rather than examples. **They are
     display literals and are not claimed to be unambiguous against a repository value that
     sanitizes to the same characters**: the human line is a rendering, and the authoritative
     answer to "was there a value at all" is `raw_value_present` in the `--json` twin, which the
     block's own `issue_id` points at — the same division of labour every other human/JSON pair in
     this document has (§4.4, §11). `key` is Git's own
     lower-cased spelling, `source` is the eight-member scope enum and `route_command` is the
     four-member command enum, both printed as the ASCII enum member — so the line is byte-exact and
     the suite asserts it as such (§15.16a2).

     The id is printed as all **64 lowercase hex characters** and is never abbreviated: it is the
     join key a reader carries to the `--json` array, and a truncated id is not one (§4.4).
     **No raw or unsafe bytes are printed here or anywhere else** — every value goes through §11's
     renderer, and the
     base64 and the digest stay `--json`-only evidence (§4.4 `config_issues[]`, §11). Every row is
     printed, never a count and never a sample, and the block is byte-stable across processes
     because the array is canonically ordered. It is printed **immediately above** the
     guarded-execution blocker block, so the two blocks and the fingerprint line are a fixed tail
     that byte-stability tests assert as a whole.

     **`guard.execute_blocked_by[]` is rendered explicitly, and round 31 makes that mandatory rather
     than optional** (item 6). Until now the human form published `runnable`, the refusal and the
     fingerprint, and left the **controlled-path execution axis** — the one field that can report a
     refusal the *unguarded* ladder does not perform (§8.6.1 cause 3, §4.4
     `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`) — visible only under `--json`. A human reading a document with
     `runnable: true`, no refusal and a real token therefore had no way to see that the guarded twin
     will refuse. The rendering is fixed:

     ```
     Guarded execution blockers: none
     ```

     when the array is empty, and otherwise the labelled header followed by **one line per member,
     in the array's own canonical (sorted, deduplicated) order**, each carrying the reason token and
     its sanitized detail:

     ```
     Guarded execution blockers:
       fetch-context-indeterminate: <sanitized detail>
       live-owner-concurrency: <sanitized detail>
     ```

     — the two members in the array's own bytewise order, which the example follows rather than
     inventing one.

     **Every** member is printed — never a count, never "and 2 more", never a sample — because the
     array is the admission predicate's third conjunct and a truncated list is a false one. The
     block is byte-stable across processes (the array is canonically ordered, §4.4, §4.7), its
     details go through §11's renderer like every other human string, and it is printed
     **immediately before** the fingerprint line so that `tail -1` keeps its defined answer.
     Where a rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config` blocker is published its own `detail` carries the fixed
     `config issue <issue_id> (<key>, <route_command>)` substring and the `Configuration issues:`
     block above carries the evidence, so the human form points at the offending row **by its
     `issue_id`** and the value lives on that block's line in the total three-cell field of
     round-33 item 8 — `<valueless>`, `""` or the sanitized value — never as an optional suffix on
     the sentence (round-31 item 2, round-32 item 5, §4.4 `config_issues[]`).

     Then the final line, unchanged:

     ```
     Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>
     Approval fingerprint: none
     ```

     The literal `none` is what a `null` fingerprint renders as, so the line is always present and
     `tail -1` always has a defined answer. **The line is not the token**: it is a labelled line
     *containing* the token, and no document, skill, test or example may treat `tail -1`'s output as
     something that can be passed to `--approve-plan` directly. **The extraction and the admission
     check are two different reads, and round 32 makes the second one read the whole output**
     (item 6): `tail -1` answers only "which token did this document mint", while the four-conjunct
     admission question is answered by the labelled **status lines**, the **configuration-issue
     block** and the **guarded-execution blocker block** — all of which are above the final line.
     A snippet that inspects only the last line cannot see three of the four conjuncts.
     **Round 33 replaces the snippet that stood here, because it demanded the four conjuncts of the
     *first* preview and therefore contradicted the workflow it was written for** (item 11): the
     preview that mints the token is, by construction, the one whose plan exceeds a limit the
     operator has chosen to accept, so `Guard would refuse: yes` with `Refusal kind: limit-per-entry`
     is the **normal, correct** reading there and a check that rejects it rejects every run worth
     approving. The three invocations are three different questions, and each asks its own
     (§8.7.7 Workflow A′):

     ```
     # 1. preview, without a token: check the HARD ADMISSION facts only, and take the receipt.
     out1=$(tws sync <f> --plan --max-replay-per-entry 10) || exit 1
     fp=$(printf '%s\n' "$out1" | tail -1 | sed -n 's/^Approval fingerprint: //p')
     [ -n "$fp" ] && [ "$fp" != none ] || { echo "no usable plan token (no work, no effective limit, or a non-empty encoding_issues)"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out1" | grep -qx 'Plan runnable: yes'               || { echo "plan is not runnable"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out1" | grep -qx 'Configuration issues: none'       || { echo "invalid git configuration; no token can help"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out1" | grep -qx 'Guarded execution blockers: none' || { echo "guarded execution is blocked"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out1" | grep -qxE 'Refusal kind: (none|limit-per-entry|limit-total)' || { echo "refusal is not waivable"; exit 1; }
     # NOTE: 'Guard would refuse: yes' is legitimate here and is NOT checked.

     # 2. re-plan with the SAME trigger and limit flags PLUS the token: now require all four conjuncts.
     #    NOTE: on a fetch-enabled route this invocation FETCHES AGAIN. If upstream moved since
     #    step 1, this document is a different plan and legitimately refuses; that is plan drift,
     #    not a defect in the token. Go back to step 1 and take a fresh receipt.
     out2=$(tws sync <f> --plan --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan "$fp") || exit 1
     if printf '%s\n' "$out2" | grep -qx 'Refusal kind: approval-mismatch'; then
       echo "plan drift: the plan changed between step 1 and step 2 (a fetch-enabled re-plan may refetch); re-run step 1"; exit 1
     fi
     printf '%s\n' "$out2" | grep -qx 'Plan runnable: yes'               || { echo "plan is not runnable"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out2" | grep -qx 'Guard would refuse: no'           || { echo "the limit verdicts are not waived: see 'Refusal kind:' — plan drift, or a verdict this token cannot waive"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out2" | grep -qx 'Guarded execution blockers: none' || { echo "guarded execution is blocked"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out2" | grep -qx 'Refusal kind: none'               || { echo "document still carries a refusal"; exit 1; }
     printf '%s\n' "$out2" | grep -qx 'Configuration issues: none'       || { echo "invalid git configuration"; exit 1; }

     # 3. execute, with the same flags and the same token. This one fetches again too, and may
     #    refuse with approval-mismatch if the refs moved between step 2 and now. A refusal here
     #    is the guard working: nothing has been rebased. Re-run step 1.
     tws sync <f> --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan "$fp"
     ```

     **The three invocations are three points in time, and on a fetch-enabled route each of them
     refetches — so the drift window is real and is documented rather than engineered away**
     (round-34 item 6). Step 2 is a *second plan*, not a replay of the first document: under an
     effective `fetch` policy it performs the route's fetch again, and if upstream moved in between,
     `destination.sha`, the tips, the ranges and therefore the fingerprint move with it, so the token minted
     over step 1's document no longer matches and the document publishes
     `refusal.kind: approval-mismatch`. **That is a correct answer, and the diagnostic must say
     so**: the round-33 snippet's `token did not waive the limit verdicts` message named the wrong
     cause and sent operators looking at their limit flags for a network fact, so it is replaced by
     an explicit `approval-mismatch` arm that names **plan drift** and by a fallback message that
     points at the published `Refusal kind:` instead of guessing. The recovery is **step 1 again** —
     a fresh preview over the refreshed refs, read again, minting a fresh token — never a re-run of
     step 2 with the stale token, and never a loop that retries until it happens to win the race.
     **Step 3 may refuse for the same reason**, between step 2's validation and its own execution,
     and that refusal is the guard doing its job: it happens **before** any rebase, so nothing is
     half-done (§5.2, §5.3, §8.7.6). **The stable, fully-local workflow is a different route, and
     the snippet may never quietly become it**: `--no-fetch` is a **mode trigger** (§0.2), so
     `tws sync <f> --plan --no-fetch …` previews the **new-mode** run — different fetch set,
     different selection refusals, different state and header — and adding it to make the round trip
     deterministic silently changes which run was approved. An operator who wants determinism must
     choose that route **on both invocations and deliberately**, with `route` asserted in the
     document (§5.3, §8.7.7); no doc, skill, snippet or test may insert `--no-fetch` into a legacy
     round trip on the operator's behalf.

     — the token extraction by `sed` (or `awk '{print $3}'`, or `jq -r .approval.fingerprint` under
     `--json`, which yields the JSON `null` for the same case and must be tested for). **Step 1's
     admission check is the hard-fact set and nothing more**: `Plan runnable: yes`,
     `Configuration issues: none`, `Guarded execution blockers: none`, and a `Refusal kind:` that is
     `none` or one of the **two waivable limit kinds**; any other kind means no token can help
     (§5.3.1, §4.9). **Step 2 is where all four conjuncts are required**, on the **displayed values
     of the second document** — `Plan runnable: yes`, `Guard would refuse: no`,
     `Guarded execution blockers: none`, `Refusal kind: none` —, because that is the first document
     in which a matching token has actually moved the limit verdicts to `waived`, and reading them
     there is reading the answer rather than predicting it (round-33 item 12).
     **`Guarded execution blockers: none` is the third-listed conjunct of the JSON predicate** —
     `guard.execute_blocked_by == []`, the one
     field that can report a controlled-path refusal the unguarded route would ignore (§8.6.1
     cause 3). **Step 2's flags must be byte-identical to step 1's apart from `--approve-plan`, and
     step 3's to step 2's**: a changed trigger, scope or limit *value* yields `approval-mismatch`,
     while **dropping the limit flags entirely** is not a mismatch at all — on a fresh run it is a
     flag error before any document exists, and on a resume it is rank 7.5
     `approval-without-limits` (§8.5.1, §8.7.4, §15.16g, round-33 item 13). That is the whole reason
     the fingerprint is a
     *final* line: a human who previews and then approves should not
     have to re-run the command with `--json` to obtain the receipt of what they just read. It is
     printed on `--plan` and on nothing else (§8.7.6, §8.7.7).
   - **Plan-only exits non-zero only when no valid document can be produced**: the workspace or
     feature cannot be resolved, flags are invalid, the repository context is unusable, or the
     encoder itself fails. In `--json` these emit no partial document on stdout; the message goes to
     stderr.
   - **Guarded *executing* invocations exit 1 on refusal**, exactly like any other `RunE` failure,
     and emit **no document and no token at all** — `--json` is valid only with `--plan` in v1.
     Their machine contract is exactly one **anchored, guard-written** `^plan-guard: <kind>: ` line
     on stderr carrying the
     `refusal.kind` token chosen at the guard seam (§8.7.6); an agent that needs the
     structured detail, or a token, runs `--plan` with the same flags (§8.7.7).
   Human implication: `--plan` is safe in a `set -e` script and never masks "this run is broken" as
   a shell error; the operator reads `runnable: false` / `guard.would_refuse: true`. JSON
   implication: consumers branch on `runnable`, `guard.would_refuse` (and
   `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` when they want the pre-waiver number),
   **`guard.execute_blocked_by[]`** and `refusal.kind`,
   never on the exit status. **The guarded-refusal exit code is 1, and that is settled** (round-36
   item 9): a distinct code (e.g. 2 for "refused by plan guard") would be useful for CI but is a
   cross-cutting convention change to `Execute()` that this feature does not make, so it is **not**
   an option `define` may pick up — §19.2 is closed, not deferred.
6. **JSON**: one versioned document, **`schema_version: 1`** from a document-scoped constant — the
   shipped spelling everywhere in this repository (`internal/stack_status.go:24,87`,
   `internal/agent_status.go:376`, `internal/session.go:33`) — absent facts `null`; the **row
   lists**, which are the **closed seventeen-member** set §4.8 states in identical words —
   `entries`, `blockers`, `warnings`, **`encoding_issues`**, **`config_issues`**, `route_triggers`, `repositories`,
   `fetch.repos`, each row's
   **`fetch.repos[].context_candidates`**, **`push.targets`**, **`push.blocked_by`**,
   **`restore.blocked_by`**, `guard.evaluation`, **`guard.limit_conflicts`**,
   **`guard.execute_blocked_by`**,
   `approval.covers.waived_evaluation_ids` and `approval.covers.waived_kinds` —
   never
   `null` (round-29 item 5 restored `encoding_issues` here: it was added to §4.8's and §15.21's
   copies of the list by round-28 item 4 and silently omitted from this one, and the three copies are
   the same set or the suite fails; **round-30 item 2 adds `config_issues` to all three at once**,
   for the same reason), while the unknown-bearing per-entry facts of §4.8, the settled nullable scalars
   (`fetch.repos[].context_root`/`context_common_dir`/`context_source`/`fetch_effect` on an
   indeterminate row, `push.executable`, `restore.executable`, `restore.target_branch`,
   `restore.target_sha`) and the deliberately nullable
   `approval.fingerprint` of §8.6.3 are nullable **by design**; keys stable
   and canonically ordered (§4.7, §4.9). `--json` **requires `--plan`** (§8.5.1), so
   the document is a plan-only artefact and no executing invocation ever emits one. The complete
   top-level key set is
   `schema_version, route, requested_route, route_triggers, invocation, workspace, feature, policy,
   intent, push, restore, fetch, freshness, repositories, state, runnable, blockers, warnings,
   encoding_issues, config_issues, entries, summary, guard, refusal, approval` (§4.1, §4.4) — **`encoding_issues` is
   the top-level array added in round 28** (item 4), carrying the closed-shape machine evidence for
   invalid-UTF-8 bound identities that round 27 had left inside a blocker sentence (§4.4,
   §5.3.2a rule 10), and **`config_issues` is the top-level array added in round 30** (item 2),
   carrying the closed-shape, route-filtered machine evidence for the rank 5.07 `invalid-git-config`
   fact that rounds 27-29 had left inside that blocker's `detail` (§4.2, §4.9 rank 5.07); **`restore` is the top-level object
   added in round 21**, holding the checkout restoring mutation with its own `executable`/`blocked_by[]`
   pair (§4.4, §8.6.4a), `push` holds `targets[]` with `executable`/`blocked_by[]`, and `guard`
   carries `limits` as its **single** per-key `{value, origin}`
   encoding with **no** `limits_source` sibling and **no** `guard_enabled` sibling anywhere in the
   document or on disk (§8.7.4, §10.3) plus the **`execute_blocked_by[]`** controlled-path
   execution axis, whose member domain is closed at **five** — `live-owner-concurrency`,
   **`owner-artefact-undecodable`**, `fetch-context-indeterminate`, `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` and `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` (round-25 item 2) — **the count corrected by round-27 item 5**, which found this restatement still saying "three" while listing five and while §4.4, §15.21 and §20 had all moved on; the two kinds round 27 adds (`invalid-git-config`, `identity-not-utf8`) are deliberately **not** members, because both set `runnable: false` on the unguarded route too and this axis exists only for facts `runnable` cannot express (§4.4, §4.9 ranks 5.07/5.08);
   `entries[]` carries the §4.1 rows, defined in §4.1 and referenced here and by §4.4 rather than
   duplicated as a §4.4 field row (§15.21) — **each row's `base_context` and `execution_context` being the closed
   three-member object `{context_id, repo_root, source}` whose `context_id` is the *only* key by
   which that ref joins `repositories[]`, its `repo_root` being a display-only §11 rendering that no
   consumer may join, sort or de-duplicate on** (round-33 item 1, round-34 item 1, §4.1, §4.4), and
   each row carrying **`base.decision_sha` beside `destination.sha`/`destination.snapshot_sha`** —
   the strategy-decision read and the actual destination, two keys since round-35 item 3, with
   `base.sha` removed from the key set entirely so no consumer may keep reading a base-context SHA
   as the destination. **`push.targets[]` rows carry `context_id`** and are ordered by
   `(context_id, git_branch)`, their `repo_root` being display-only exactly as the entry and
   repository roots are (round-35 item 5, §4.4, §5.3.2). **`state` is two-layered and no member of either layer
   is ever `null`**: its key domain is exactly
   `{snapshot, files, external_cell, worktree, git_op, head}`, and `state.files`' key domain is
   exactly `{checkout_transaction, checkout_lock, external_legacy_state, external_payload,
   external_run_guard}`. **The `{applicable, presence, unreadable_reason}` triple belongs to the
   five `state.files` members and to nothing else** — there is no path to `Lstat` behind
   `worktree`, `git_op`, `head`, `external_cell` or `snapshot`, so requiring a `presence` of them
   was a schema defect, not a strictness — with nullity pushed down to the members inside each row,
   so "absent",
   "not applicable on this route", "present but unreadable" (with its reason) and "present and
   decoded" are four distinguishable answers
   rather than one `null` (§4.4 `state`). **Which bytes count as "decoded" is fixed per file, not
   per schema**: each row's `presence`/`unreadable_reason` mirrors that artefact's own shipped
   loader — permissive and version-less for `.sync-state.yaml` (an empty document is `readable`),
   version-validating for `.sync-state.v2.yaml`, permissive-including-future-`state_version` for the
   checkout transaction (whose too-new case is a shipped **continuation refusal** carrying the
   number, not a decode error), and structural-YAML-only for the two lock artefacts (§8.6.1 step 2a,
   §8.6.4). A schema test may therefore not assert one decode rule across the five rows.
   `state.snapshot` holds exactly
   `{taken_before_acquisition, self_pid}` and is probe metadata only; `external_cell`, `worktree`,
   `git_op` and `head` each carry `applies` plus their own members, and `git_op`/`worktree`/`head`

   `state.external_cell`. **The three statements
   are not three copies of one contract, and this round fixes the invariant that said they were**:
   **§4.4's field table is authoritative** — it is the complete field-by-field meaning and
   nullability contract for the document; **this key set is authoritative for the top level** and
   must name exactly the keys §4.4 publishes there, so an edit to either is an edit to both; and
   **§4.8 is a deliberate *subset*** — the fields where "unknown" could be mistaken for a known
   zero, empty list or `false` — never an enumeration of every nullable field. **"Names exactly the
   keys §4.4 publishes" is read against §4 as a whole, not against §4.4's field table alone**: some
   top-level keys are defined elsewhere in §4 and merely referenced in §4.4 — `entries` is §4.1's —
   and demanding a duplicate §4.4 row for them would put one contract in two places. The
   mechanically enforceable form, which §15.21 asserts, is emitted-key ⊆ this key set, this key set
   ⊆ keys defined or referenced in §4, and every member of this key set emitted by some document. The previous round's

   between §4 (§4.1 for `entries`, §4.4 for the rest)
   and §8.3.6, **containment** of §4.8 in §4.4 with matching nullability, and one shared never-null
   row-list enumeration of **seventeen** members (round-28 item 4 added `encoding_issues`,
   round-30 item 2 adds `config_issues`), stated
   identically in this item, in §4.8 and in
   §15.21, and edited in all three or in none.
   This is the agent/CI
   contract.
7. **`--plan --json` stdout purity is not free today, and the spec must say how it is achieved.**
   The existing operational prose is written with bare `fmt.Printf`/`fmt.Println` to **process
   stdout**, not through `cmd.OutOrStdout()`:
   - the sync-modes header `Sync mode: fetch=… propagation=… scope=…`
     (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:502-504`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:517-522`);
   - `fetchQuiet`'s `Fetching <label>... ` + `done`/`failed` (`internal/cli/sync.go:604-635`) and
     checkout's inline equivalent (`internal/checkout_sync.go:617-625`);
   - under `--verbose`, `internal.RunDir` wires **git fetch's own stdout and stderr** to the
     process's (`internal/exec.go:126-134`);
   - the local-only no-op block and every `[+]`/`[-]`/`[?]` status line.
   Any of these emitted during a `--plan --json` invocation would put non-JSON bytes on stdout and
   break every consumer that pipes to `jq`. **Rule: under `--plan --json`, the JSON document is the
   only thing written to stdout.** The plan path must therefore route its header, fetch progress and
   verbose fetch output to **stderr** (or suppress them), which is safe because that path is new
   code — but it must be implemented *without* touching the byte stream of the non-plan paths, whose
   goldens are frozen (§10.1). Concretely: the plan path gets its own printer that writes prose to
   `cmd.ErrOrStderr()` and the document to `cmd.OutOrStdout()`, and it invokes a fetch variant whose
   child stdout is redirected to stderr; the existing `fetchQuiet`/`printSyncModeHeader`/status-line
   calls on the executing paths are left untouched. `--plan` **without** `--json` keeps prose on
   stdout, as every other human surface does — **including the final `Approval fingerprint:` line**
   (item 5), which is part of the human document and therefore belongs on stdout with the rows, not
   on stderr with the progress prose. Tests must assert byte-exact stdout for
   `--plan --json` (schema keys stable, `null` never conflated with zero/clean, deterministic
   ordering, nothing else on the stream) in both modes and under both fetch policies, including a
   failed fetch, and must assert that the human form's **last** stdout line is the fingerprint line,
   with the fixed tail above it in order (round-32 items 5 and 6): the three labelled status lines
   (`Plan runnable:`, `Guard would refuse:`, `Refusal kind:`), then the **`Configuration issues:`**
   block, then the **`Guarded execution blockers:`** block (round-31 item 6) immediately above the
   fingerprint line — each block `none` on an empty array, otherwise every member on its own line in
   canonical order, the configuration-issue lines in the **fixed grammar** of §8.3.5
   (`  - <issue_id> <key> [<source>, <route_command>]: <value-field>`, whose value field is total,
   round-33 item 8), the whole tail byte-stable
   across processes (§8.3.5, §15.16a, §15.16a2).

**8.3.2a Threshold comparison and evaluation, made total.** The previous draft fixed the two limit
*names* and left the comparison, the emission and the unknown handling to the implementation, which
is exactly where a guard becomes unpredictable. All three are fixed here.

**Comparison.** For every limit, on every seam, the predicate is:

```
exceeded  ⟺  value > limit          # strict; equality passes
```

`candidate_count == limit` is **`within-limit`**, in the document, at the guard seam and at the JIT
seam. This is the reading an operator assumes from "max", it makes `--max-replay-per-entry 1` mean
"one commit is fine, two is not", and it makes the boundary testable rather than folklore. It also
makes **`0` a meaningful, legal limit** — "refuse if any selected entry replays anything at all" —
which is why `0` must survive persistence as a value rather than as an absence (§10.3), and why
§8.5.1 accepts a non-negative integer rather than a positive one.

**Emission.** For **every supplied limit**, the document emits evaluation rows — always, whether or
not anything is exceeded, so `guard.evaluation[]` is a complete record of what was checked and not a
list of complaints:

| Limit | Rows emitted | `basis` | `value` | `verdict` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_replay_per_entry` | **one row per published entry**, `id = max_replay_per_entry:<name>` | `per-entry` | that row's `candidate_count` | `within-limit` / `exceeded` by the predicate above |
| `max_replay_per_entry`, against a row whose `determinacy` is `not-applicable` (§4.1 skip rule) | one row, as above | `per-entry` | **`0`**, read straight out of the row's published `replay.candidate_count` — the row replays nothing, and that is a counted fact, not an unknown, so this rule is a *reading* rather than a substitution (§4.1 skip rule) | `within-limit` (`0 > limit` is false for every non-negative limit) |
| `max_replay_per_entry`, against a row whose `determinacy` is `unknown` | one row, as above | `per-entry` | **`null`** | `unknown`, with `unknown_kind` read **off the row's published `replay.reason`** and from nothing else — `deferred-resolvable` exactly for **`upstream-deferred`** (the reason §5.2 re-checks) and `not-resolvable` for every other member of the unknown set, `merge-recreation` first among them (its round-26 twin `merge-recreation-unknown` is **withdrawn** by round-27 item 1: the two empty spellings are decided by the typed probe and an unrecognised value refuses the whole document at rank 5.07, so no row reaches a limit carrying it). **Round 25 makes that derivation total by fixing the reason's own precedence** (item 3, §4.1): because `merge-recreation` outranks `upstream-deferred`, a row that is *both* merge-recreating and deferred publishes `merge-recreation` and is therefore **`not-resolvable`** — the classification is a lookup on one published field, never a second evaluation that could disagree with it. A `probe-failed`, `repo-unavailable`, `head-ref-missing`, `base-unset`, `base-ref-missing` or `cutoff-unresolvable` row is already a rank 5 blocker and outranks the verdict, and is likewise `not-resolvable` here |
| `max_replay_total`, every entry countable | **exactly one** row, `id = max_replay_total` | `total` | `summary.total_candidates` (the exact sum) | `within-limit` / `exceeded` |
| `max_replay_total`, some entry uncountable | **exactly one** row, `id = max_replay_total` | `lower-bound` | `summary.total_candidates_lower_bound` | see the three-way rule below |

**The aggregate row under an unknown remainder** is the case the previous draft left undefined, and
it is three-way, not two-way. With `L` the limit, `B` the lower bound and `U > 0` the number of
uncountable rows (published as `unknown_entries`):
| Condition | `verdict` | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `B > L` | **`exceeded`** | certain: the true total is at least `B`, so no resolution of the unknowns can bring it under the limit |
| `B <= L` and `U > 0` | **`unknown`** | *not* `within-limit`: the countable part fits, but `U` rows could add any amount. Reporting "within limit" here would be the aggregate form of treating unknown as zero. `unknown_kind` is `not-resolvable` if **any** contributing unknown is, else `deferred-resolvable` |
| `B <= L` and `U == 0` (`basis: total`) | **`within-limit`** | the exact sum fits |

**The member contract, made total.** The previous rounds fixed `basis`, `verdict`, `unknown_kind`
and `unknown_entries` and left `limit` and `entry` to be inferred from the tables, which is how a
consumer ends up parsing an `id` to recover a threshold. All eight members are fixed here, and
**every row carries all eight keys** — a member that does not apply is an explicit `null`, never an
omitted key and never a `0`/`""` stand-in (§4.8):

| Member | Type and meaning | `null` when |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | the row's canonical identity — `<limit key>` on an aggregate row, `<limit key>:<entry>` on a per-entry row. Unique within the array by construction (one row per limit key per entry, one aggregate row per limit key) | **never** |
| `limit` | the **numeric effective threshold this row was compared against**: the `guard.limits.<key>.value` of the key the row's `id` names, a non-negative integer, `0` included. It is the number, never the `{value, origin}` object, never the key name, and never the key's `origin` label (§4.4, §5.3.2) | **never on an emitted row.** A key whose `guard.limits.<key>.value` is `null` is not in force and emits **no rows at all**, so `limit: null` is unreachable rather than merely unusual |
| `value` | the measured quantity: the row's own `replay.candidate_count` on `per-entry`, `summary.total_candidates` on `total`, `summary.total_candidates_lower_bound` on `lower-bound` | exactly when `verdict` is `unknown` **on a `per-entry` row** — there was no number to compare (§4.8). It is **never** `null` on a `total` or `lower-bound` row, whose value is a sum over the countable rows and therefore always exists, even when the verdict over it is `unknown` |
| `basis` | the closed enum `per-entry` / `total` / `lower-bound` | **never** |
| `entry` | the **logical** entry name (`entries[].name`), never a Git branch (§4.5) | **always on a `total` or `lower-bound` row** — an aggregate is about the run, not an entry — and never on a `per-entry` row |
| `verdict` | the closed enum `within-limit` / `exceeded` / `waived` / `unknown` | **never** |
| `unknown_kind` | `deferred-resolvable` / `not-resolvable` | exactly when `verdict` is **not** `unknown` |
| `unknown_entries` | the count of rows contributing an unknown remainder | on every `per-entry` row and on every exact `total` row; **non-`null` (and `> 0`) exactly on a `lower-bound` row** |

**Canonical sort: `id`, bytewise, ascending, and nothing else.** The ids embed the entry name
deterministically — `max_replay_per_entry:<name>`, with `<name>` the same logical name the sorted
`entries[]` uses — so sorting by `id` is a **stable total order over a set with no duplicate keys**,
it needs no tuple and no tie-break, and it puts every per-entry row of one limit in entry order with
that limit's aggregate row beside them. It is deliberately *not* `entries[]` order, execution order
or emission order: `TopoSort`'s **root-component** order is unspecified between processes, so any
order derived from it inherits that (§4.7 consequence 1; siblings within one component are file-
ordered, round-22 item 5),
so any order derived from it would make two runs of the same command emit different bytes. Two
consequences bind the schema: `approval.covers.waived_evaluation_ids[]` is a **sorted subset of the
same key space**, comparable to the array by a merge rather than a scan (§4.4); and the sort exists
for **document byte-stability**, not for the token — `guard.evaluation[]` is an explicit
**non-member** of the fingerprint tuple, because a waiver is a verdict change and binding verdicts
would make an approved replay mint a different token than the document that authorised it; what the
tuple binds instead are that array's *inputs*, the effective limits and the candidate identities
(§5.3.2).

**Emission on a rows-less document, which the emission table above cannot express because it is
written per published entry.** The two profiles of §4.4 differ, and the difference is not cosmetic:

| Document | `max_replay_per_entry` supplied | `max_replay_total` supplied |
|---|---|---|
| `plannability: empty` — a valid, sorted, selected stack with **no** entry (empty `stack.yaml`, a legitimately empty selection, an empty `RemainingRebaseEntries`) | **no rows.** There is no entry to compare against, and a synthetic row would have no `entry` to name. The absence is a *known* fact — the run has no per-entry work — not an unknown, so it never yields `verdict: unknown` and never contributes to `would_refuse*` | **exactly one row**: `id = max_replay_total`, `basis: total`, `value: **0**`, `verdict: within-limit`, `unknown_entries: null`. The total is the exact sum over zero countable rows, which is `0`, and `0 > L` is false for every non-negative `L` — including `L = 0`, so even the strictest legal limit passes a run that replays nothing |
| `plannability: unavailable` — `plan-unavailable`, `stack-unsortable`, `selection-refused`, or a `state-refused` cell that left no run to describe | **`[]`** | **`[]`**. Not a `within-limit` `0`: no plan was established, so the `0` would be a measurement nobody took. `summary.total_candidates` is `null` there for the same reason (§4.4), and an evaluation row whose `value` contradicted its own summary would be the aggregate form of "treat unknown as zero" (§8.3.2) |

Two consequences follow and are binding. **A limit never refuses an empty run**: with `[]` or a
single `within-limit` row, `guard.would_refuse` and `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` are
`false` on both profiles, and `refusal.kind` stays whatever the document's own top-ranked fact is.
And **a push-only document is evaluated as the empty rebase it is**: an interrupted run resuming at
`stage: pushing` has `entries: []`, so a supplied `max_replay_total` yields the same single
`value: 0` `within-limit` row, while the work it actually has left is described **separately** by
`intent.push` and `push.targets[]` (§4.4, §8.6.4a). The replay limits are limits on *replay*; v1
defines no limit over push targets, no evaluation row may imply one, and the document must not be
readable as "the guard checked the push".

**Verdicts drive `would_refuse` through §4.4's rule and nothing else**: `exceeded` always refuses;
`unknown` refuses when `unknown_kind` is `not-resolvable`, or when the invocation's
`guard.indeterminacy_policy` is `refuse-up-front`; a `deferred-resolvable` unknown under the
recommended `jit-deferred` policy does not refuse now and **is re-evaluated at the JIT seam against
the same limit and the same strict predicate**, where a newly resolved value that exceeds stops the
run with that limit's own kind (§5.2, §5.3.1). The alternate policy stays in §19.9; the *field* that
records which one was applied is not open, because a consumer must never have to infer it from a
boolean.

### 8.4 Why no prompt

Agents and CI are first-class users here (`docs/roadmap.md`, agent integration section; the shipped
`tws status`/`tws stack status --json` surfaces). A prompt is a hang in every non-interactive
context unless it is TTY-gated, and TTY-gating produces two different behaviours for the same
command — the exact non-determinism the request asks to avoid. Refusal + `--approve-plan` gives one
behaviour everywhere. A `--interactive` prompt can be added later as pure sugar over the same
fingerprint.

### 8.5 Routing: the control flags are orthogonal to the mode triggers

**Recommendation: `--plan`, `--json`, `--max-replay-per-entry`, `--max-replay-total` and
`--approve-plan` do NOT join `syncTriggerFlags`.** They are parsed and validated separately, and
they describe or guard whichever underlying path the six shipped triggers select (§0.2). The
alternative — a seventh trigger — is rejected in §17 and by Finding 5.

**8.5.1 Presence membership is explicit, and it lives outside the shipped presence map.**
`resolveSyncPolicy` reads a *closed* key set: `syncPresenceFlags` = the six triggers plus `push`
(`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:34`), and `newMode` is computed over `syncTriggerFlags` alone
(`:47-53`). **Neither `syncPresenceFlags` nor `CheckoutSyncOpts.Changed` is extended.** The previous
draft proposed adding `changed["plan"]`, `changed["approve-plan"]` and the limits to the presence
map; that is rejected, because `Changed` is consumed by the continuation mismatch checkers
(`syncContinueMismatches`, `internal/cli/sync.go:435-460`; `checkoutContinueMismatches`,
`internal/checkout_sync.go:767-789`), and a control key inside that map is one `range` away from
turning "you passed `--plan` last time" into a frozen-axis mismatch refusal. The control flags live
in their own value instead:

- a dedicated resolver `resolvePlanGuardOptions(cmd) (planGuardOptions, error)` builds a
  `planGuardOptions{Plan, JSON, MaxPerEntry, MaxTotal, Approve, present map[string]bool}` from the
  command's own `Changed` inspection, and runs **after** `resolveSyncPolicy` and **before** the mode
  dispatch, so both workspace modes reject identically and identically early, exactly as the
  sync-modes contract requires;
- checkout receives it as its own field on `CheckoutSyncOpts` (e.g. `PlanGuard`), never merged into
  `Changed`, so `checkoutContinueMismatches` keeps iterating exactly the seven shipped keys;
- **every mismatch checker ignores plan-guard presence.** The only code allowed to read it is the
  dedicated approval/limit logic of §8.7 — which compares tokens and thresholds, never axes.

Its rules are stated **once**, as a closed compatibility matrix, and every other section — the
hard-error set of §8.6.6, the I8 note of §8.5.2, the guarded route of §8.7, the skills of §14 and
the tests of §15.17a —
**cites this table rather than restating it**. Rows are the four control flags; the first three
columns are the shipped verbs/modifiers they can be combined with; the last column is the
requirement a control flag places on the *other* control flags. Every cell is closed: a combination
not named here does not exist, and no cell may be softened or hardened elsewhere in this document.

| Control flag | with `--abort` | with `--continue` | with `--push` | requires |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--plan` | **refused** — hard flag error, no document, exit 1 (§8.6.6). `--abort` describes no run: there is no plan to project, and the abort verb's own state ladder is a mutation, not a subject | **allowed** — describes the *remaining* work of whatever state exists, under the **state-derived** effective route, with every continuation gate projected as a blocker rather than raised (§8.5.3, §8.6.4). Never fetches (§8.6.4) | **allowed and described** — `intent.push: true`, `push.targets[]` projected, `push.executable`/`push.blocked_by[]` published, and **nothing pushed** (§8.3.1, §4.4). Refusing it would make the runs with the largest blast radius the only unpreviewable ones | — |
| `--json` | **refused**, by the `--plan` rule above: `--json` cannot appear without `--plan`, and `--plan --abort` is already refused | **allowed** (with `--plan`) | **allowed** (with `--plan`) | **`--plan`.** `--json` alone is a hard flag error: the document is a plan-only artefact and no executing invocation emits one (§8.3.6, §8.7.6) |
| `--max-replay-per-entry` / `--max-replay-total` | **refused** — hard flag error, exit 1.
