An abort replays nothing, so a replay limit has no object; accepting it would imply the guard inspected an abort | **allowed**, subject to the **state** rules of §8.7.4: a value that disagrees with the one the interrupted run persisted is `guard-limit-mismatch` (rank 7), an equal one is redundant-and-accepted, and a key nothing persisted is *armed* by the flag for the remaining work | **allowed** — orthogonal axes; the limits bound replay, never push (v1 defines no push limit, §8.3.2a) | a **non-negative integer** value; `0` is legal and distinct from absent (§8.3.2a, §10.3) |
| `--approve-plan <fp>` | **refused** — hard flag error, exit 1. There is no plan to approve, and an approval waives only limit violations (§5.3.1) | **allowed**, subject to the same **state** rules: the token must be a *continuation-scoped* one minted by `--plan --continue` (`approval.scope: remaining-work`), and the full-run token of the interrupted run is an `approval-mismatch` (§8.7.4) | **allowed**, and **bound**: the token binds `intent.push` *and* `push.targets[]`, so a token minted without `--push` never authorises a pushing run (§5.3.2, §8.7.7) | a **non-empty** token, and **at least one effective replay limit** (below). With `--plan` it is **accepted and non-mutating**: it executes nothing and answers "would this exact command run?" through `approval.accepted`, the waived verdicts and `refusal.kind` (§8.3.3) |

**`--approve-plan` requires at least one effective replay limit**, because an approval waives limit
violations and nothing else (§5.3.1): with no limit in force there is no violation to waive, so the
token would be a safety control that provably does nothing while looking like one. The requirement
is over the **effective** limits of §8.7.4, so it has exactly two decidable renderings and no third:

- on a **fresh** invocation the effective limits can only come from flags, so `--approve-plan` with
  neither limit flag is decided by `resolvePlanGuardOptions` as a **hard flag error** — no document,
  exit 1, §8.6.6 — naming both limit flags in its message;
- on a **`--continue`** the effective limits may be persisted, so the check runs **after** the
  per-key resolution of §8.7.4: if both keys resolve to `{value: null, origin: none}` the invocation
  refuses with `refusal.kind = approval-without-limits` (§4.9 rank 7.5), projected as a blocker
  under `--plan` and raised at exit 1 when executing, with `runnable` staying `true` — the plan is
  fine; the flag set is not. Requiring the flag to be *repeated* on a continuation instead would
  contradict the inherit cell of §8.7.4, where dropping the limit flag is the normal, documented
  workflow.

This is also why **no `guard_enabled` key exists** anywhere (§8.7.4, §10.3): "is this invocation
guarded?" is exactly "does any key of `guard.limits` have a non-`null` `value`?", and a persisted
per-key limit *pointer* is the only durable signal of it.

**And it is why a limitless `--plan` mints no token** (§4.4 usable-token rule, added in round 12).
**It is also why a limitless plan over an invalid-UTF-8 identity is a *complete* document and not a
refused one** (round-28 item 4): it already mints nothing for the limit reason, so the encoding
clause adds no consequence there — the document publishes `encoding_issues[]`, keeps `runnable: true`
and publishes no rank 5.08 blocker, because the run it describes really is runnable.
The requirement above makes a token minted without an effective limit unusable in **every**
invocation that could consume it — a fresh guarded run rejects it as a flag error before reading it,
and a continuation refuses it as `approval-without-limits` — so publishing one would hand the
operator a receipt no command accepts. A `--plan` with no limit flag therefore describes the run in
full and publishes `approval.fingerprint: null`, `approval.usable: false` and
`approval.covers.requires_limits: true`; the operator who wants a token re-runs the same plan with
the limits they intend to guard with, which is also the flag set the executing invocation must
repeat (§8.7.7). Nothing else about the document changes, and no blocker is added: wanting to look
is not an error.

**8.5.2 I8 is untouched.** `syncChangedTriggerList` enumerates `syncTriggerFlags`
(`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:143-152`), so `--abort cannot be combined with %s` keeps exactly its
current operand set and no shipped message or golden moves. `--plan --abort` and
`--max-replay-total 5 --abort` are refused by the plan-guard resolver with their own message, not by
widening I8 — the `--abort` column of the §8.5.1 matrix is where those cells are decided, and this
section only records that deciding them does not touch I8's operand list.

**8.5.3 I20 keeps its gate; the plan-only route projects it.** The gate is
`newMode && (cell 1 || cell 7)` in external
(`internal/cli/sync.go:96-99`, cells from `syncStateCell`, `internal/sync_run_state.go:428-431`) and
`opts.NewMode && (no transaction || StateVersion < 2)` in checkout
(`internal/cli/checkout_sync.go:44-51`). Since no control flag sets `newMode`:

- `tws sync <f> --plan --continue` alone → **no I20**. It describes the legacy continuation the
  same command without `--plan` would perform: `handleSyncContinue` over `.sync-state.yaml`
  (`internal/cli/sync.go:311-334`), or the cell-5 scoped continuation when a v2 payload exists, or
  checkout's `ContinueCheckoutSync`. If there is nothing to continue, the document says so
  (`refusal.kind = state-refused`, mirroring `nothing to continue — no sync in progress`) rather
  than inventing a plan.
- `tws sync <f> --plan --continue --only pr2` → a trigger *is* present and `newMode` is true, so I20
  applies. The two routes handle it differently **by design, and identically in substance**: a
  guarded or unguarded **executing** invocation fires the shipped I20 literal at exit 1, unchanged;
  the **plan-only** route *projects* it — `runnable: false`, `refusal.kind = state-refused`,
  `detail` carrying `cannot use sync mode flags on --continue without v2 state; continue without
  them or abort and start a new run` verbatim (`errSyncModeFlagsNeedV2`,
  `internal/cli/sync_modes.go:24-26`) — and exits 0 with the document, exactly as it projects every
  other continuation gate (§8.6.4). Inheriting the early return here would be the one place where
  `--plan` stopped describing and started refusing. Against v2 state the document describes the
  remaining entries, reconciled against the frozen payload (§3.10, §12), and the sync-modes
  `--continue` mismatch rules (`.tpatch/features/sync-modes/spec.md`, §10.5) apply to the trigger
  flags exactly as they do today — projected on the plan route, enforced on the executing one.
- **A continuation's effective route is the state's, not the flags'** (§0.2): with a v2 payload or
  a v2 transaction the document publishes `route: new-mode` even when no trigger flag was given,
  and `requested_route` records a conflicting request. That is what makes the projected argv and the
  fingerprint match the resume that will really run.
- **Control flags are legal on `--continue`** — `--plan`, the two limits and `--approve-plan` all
  compose with it (§8.7.5) — and they neither set `newMode` nor enter the mismatch checkers
  (§8.5.1). `--no-fetch` on a continuation is a different matter: it is a **trigger**, so it can
  raise I20 against legacy state — enforced when executing, projected as a `state-refused` blocker
  under `--plan` — and it does not make the continuation more local: no
  continuation executor fetches in the first place (§0.1, §8.6.4).

**8.5.4 The frozen axis decision is not touched by the guard.** A persisted guard limit is
*additional* state (§10.3): it never re-opens the fetch/propagation/scope decision a run froze, and
`--continue` continues to reject a changed axis before it ever looks at a limit or a token. Limits
are persisted **where the route has somewhere to persist them** — `SyncRunState` for
new-mode external, `CheckoutTransaction` for both checkout routes; the legacy external route has no
v2 payload and repeats its limit flags instead. **No route persists an approval**: every guarded
continuation that needs a waiver mints a continuation-scoped token from `--plan --continue`
(§5.3, §8.7.4, §8.7.5).

**8.5.5 Missing or unreadable `stack.yaml`: intercept, never fall through.** On the legacy external
route `syncFeature` answers a `LoadStack` failure with `fetchQuiet` + `syncFallback` — an
unconditional `git rebase --update-refs origin/main` in **every** directory under the worktrees
root, wrapped in `internal.Must` (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:390-399`, §2.1 step 3). Because the
control flags are not triggers, that path **is reachable** under `--plan` and under a guarded
legacy run, and the earlier claim that trigger routing makes it unreachable was false. The
requirement is therefore behavioural, not incidental:

> Both the plan-only and the guarded-execution seams load the stack themselves **before** any
> fetch or rebase on the legacy route. If it cannot be loaded, the invocation returns a structured
> `plan-unavailable` result — `runnable: false`, `refusal.kind = plan-unavailable`,
> `entries: []`, `approval.fingerprint: null`, `fetch.attempted: false`,
> `fetch.outcome: skipped`, `freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` (§4.4, §8.6.1) — and runs
> **no** `git rebase`, in particular not `syncFallback`.

Exit codes follow §8.3.5: `--plan` prints that document and exits **0** (a complete refusal document
is a successful description); a guarded execution invocation exits **1** and mutates nothing in the scoped sense of §0.1 — a
refusal that happens *after* the route's fetch has run leaves that fetch's remote-ref, `FETCH_HEAD`
and tag writes in place, and no text may promise otherwise (round-35 item 9). On the
new-mode route the shipped literal `sync modes require a stack; feature %q has no readable
stack.yaml` (`internal/cli/sync.go:151-155`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:594-597`) is kept exactly as
is and is reported as the same `plan-unavailable` kind — so a guarded new-mode refusal here prints
the shipped sentence with **no** marker line, while the guarded **legacy external** refusal, which
this feature introduces where the shipped behaviour was `syncFallback`, does carry the marker
(§8.7.6). A test asserts, for every route × mode
combination, that no `git rebase` process is started and no worktree ref moves (§15.18).

**8.5.6 New-mode-only refusals stay new-mode-only, and become a named hazard.** The
duplicate-`GitBranch` refusal
(`internal/sync_selection.go:231-239`) and checkout's cross-repo refusal (`:223-229`) fire only when
`ResolveSyncSelection` runs with `NewMode`/`ModeCheckout`, i.e. only on the new-mode route (R6, R7).
A bare `--plan` over the legacy path must therefore **not** claim the run would be rejected, and it
must not stay silent either. It publishes a **`selection-hazard`** fact (§4.4 enum, §4.9 rank 6):
a duplicate `GitBranch` becomes two rows that will rebase the
same Git branch twice, carrying that kind and the exact
`--only` remedy; a checkout cross-repo entry becomes a row planned literally in the single repo, as
the legacy run really would, carrying the same kind and the `StackEdge` `cross-repo-unsupported`
status alongside. Adding
a trigger flag flips the same stack to the shipped `selection-refused` refusal — and the plan says
which of the two it is describing, because `route` and `route_triggers` are in the document.

**Loudness is the only open part, and the schema is representable either way** (§19.13). Under the
**blocking** rendering the fact lands in `blockers[]`, sets `runnable: false`, and — with no
higher-ranked blocker — becomes `refusal.kind = selection-hazard`, so a guarded legacy run refuses
at the seam with that kind on its marker line. Under the **warning** rendering the identical tuple
lands in `warnings[]`, `runnable` stays `true`, `refusal.kind` is unaffected, and a guarded run
proceeds after emitting the warning. What is **not** open, and is fixed here: the kind exists, its
rank is 6, its tuple shape and canonical sort are the same as every other blocker's (§4.9), and it
is never re-derived as `selection-refused` on a route that does not refuse.

### 8.6 The plan-only inspection route

`--plan` does **not** enter the executor's fresh-run refusal ladder. It has its own inspection
route, and that resolves a contradiction the previous draft carried: its §3.8 said "report
dirty/Git-op as blocking facts without refusing", while its §8.5 made `--plan` a trigger flag and
therefore inherited every fresh-run refusal wholesale. Only one of those can be true; this is the
one.

**8.6.1 Order of operations** (identical in both workspace modes, both routes):

1. resolve workspace, feature, layout/repo dir — the hard errors of §8.6.6, and the only non-zero
   exits;
2. take the **pre-acquisition state snapshot** — observe live state **without taking it**, and
   **before this invocation creates, acquires or reclaims anything**:
   the **five dedicated safe file inspectors of step 2a** (checkout transaction, checkout lock,
   external legacy state, external v2 payload, external run guard) →
   `state.files.*`; `ClassifyExternalSyncState` → `state.external_cell` (the shipped joint
   classification, called with the **shipped** `AlwaysReadGuard: newMode`, §8.6.7); `probeDirty` →
   `state.worktree`; the shipped `gitOperationInProgress` predicate **plus** `probeActiveGitOp` as a
   label → `state.git_op`, **in checkout mode only** (§4.4 `state.git_op`, §8.6.2);
   `gitCurrentBranch` (detached?) → `state.head`, likewise checkout-only → the top-level `state`
   object of §4.4, **including the `alive`
   and `self` flags of every PID any owner-signalling artefact names**, and project every fresh-run
   gate the observed
   facts imply as a blocker (§8.6.2).
   **`HasCheckoutTransaction` and `ReadCheckoutLock` are *not* the plan's inspectors and must not be
   called here.** `HasCheckoutTransaction` is `os.Stat(path); return err == nil`
   (`internal/checkout_sync.go:173-176`) and `ReadCheckoutLock` is `os.ReadFile` + `yaml.Unmarshal`
   with every failure collapsed into one `error` (`:290-300`). Both **follow symlinks**, and both
   answer *absent* and *unreadable* with the same value — a `false` for the transaction, a non-`nil`
   error for the lock — which is precisely the conflation §4.4's totality triple exists to remove:
   a checkout lock that is a symlink into another feature's state directory, or a directory, or
   truncated YAML, would be published as "no lock" and the guarded route would take it. They remain
   the **executor's** predicates, unchanged and uncalled by this feature on the shipped paths
   (§10.1); the plan reads the same two paths through its own inspectors and derives its own facts. **This one snapshot is the value carried through steps 3-7,
   through the guarded route's own seams, and through every later evaluation of a state fact
   (§4.4 `state`, §9): nothing read after an acquisition may replace it.** On the plan-only route
   that is trivially satisfied — it acquires nothing ever — and on the guarded route it is the rule
   that keeps an invocation from refusing against its own `.sync-run.lock`, its own checkout lock or
   its own reclaimed guard;

   **2a — every runtime file is inspected through its own dedicated safe inspector, the guard is
   inspected on *every* route, and the shipped classifier's flag is left exactly where it is.**
   The shipped `classifySyncState` passes `AlwaysReadGuard: newMode`
   (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:272-278`), so `ClassifyExternalSyncState` opens `.sync-run.lock`
   only when the run is a new-mode run, when the legacy file decoded to a sentinel, or when a
   payload was found (`internal/sync_run_state.go:401-421`). On a **legacy** route with no sentinel
   and no payload the guard is therefore never looked at — and that is precisely the cell in which
   **guard-only residue** lives: a `.sync-run.lock` left by a crashed or still-running scoped run
   whose payload and sentinel are gone, absent, or were never written. A plan that cannot see it
   publishes `presence: absent` for an artefact that exists, and the guarded route would fetch and
   rebase under a neighbour it never looked for. So the snapshot **always** inspects the guard path,
   on every route and in both modes, and the inspection is its own function:

   > **One inspector per runtime file, all five with the same shape — and each with its *own file's*
   > decode rule.**
   > `inspect<Artefact>(featurePath) → {presence, unreadable_reason, …decoded fields}`, over the
   > five paths of §4.4 `state.files`: `CheckoutTransactionPath`, `CheckoutLockPath`,
   > `SyncStatePath`, `SyncRunStatePath`, `SyncRunGuardPath`. Each performs **one `os.Lstat`
   > first**. `ErrNotExist` ⇒ `presence: absent`. A
   > symlink ⇒ `presence: symlink`, **recorded and never followed, never opened, never decoded** —
   > the same I18 answer the classifier gives for the same bytes, reached without a second `Lstat`
   > and without a read (§11). A non-regular file (directory, socket, device, FIFO) ⇒
   > `presence: unreadable`, `unreadable_reason: not-regular-file`, with the mode recorded. A
   > regular file ⇒ exactly one read through that artefact's shipped loader
   > (`LoadCheckoutTransaction`, the `LockInfo` decode, `LoadSyncState`, `LoadSyncRunState`,
   > `ReadSyncRunGuard`), and an I/O failure on that read ⇒ `presence: unreadable`,
   > `unreadable_reason: io-error`. Every one
   > refuses nothing, mutates nothing, and returns no policy — together they are the `state.files`
   > half of §4.4 and nothing else. **`presence` is never `null` and `unreadable_reason` is `null`
   > on every presence but `unreadable`** — the `absent`, `readable` and `symlink` arms above set no
   > reason, by construction, and that is the two-part rule §4.4 and §15.21 assert rather than the
   > withdrawn "no member is ever `null`" (round-18 item 5).
   >
   > **What "decoded" means is a property of the file, not of the inspector, and round-16 fixes the
   > round-15 blanket rule.** The previous draft said "a YAML failure **or an unsupported
   > `state_version`** ⇒ `decode-error`; an empty document ⇒ `empty-document`" for all five paths.
   > That is one rule applied to five formats that do not share it, and it misreports at least three
   > cells. The inspectors mirror each artefact's **shipped** loader exactly:
   >
   > | Artefact | Shipped decode | Inspector verdict |
   > |---|---|---|
   > | `external_legacy_state` (`.sync-state.yaml`) | `LoadSyncState` — `os.ReadFile` + `yaml.Unmarshal` into `SyncState`, which has **no version field at all** (`internal/syncstate.go:11-32`) | permissive. YAML that does not parse ⇒ `decode-error`. **An empty document is `presence: readable`**, decoding to the zero `SyncState` — no `failed_branch`, empty lists — because that is exactly what the shipped loader returns and what `ClassifyExternalSyncState` then classifies. Publishing `empty-document`/`unreadable` here would contradict `state.external_cell`, which is computed from the shipped classifier over the same bytes, and would make the two halves of the same document disagree about one file. `marker_present` is the shipped `isSyncMarker` test over the decoded `FailedBranch`, i.e. `false` on the zero value |
   > | `external_payload` (`.sync-state.v2.yaml`) | `LoadSyncRunState` — read, unmarshal, **then** `s.StateVersion != SyncRunStateVersion` ⇒ `unsupported scoped sync state version %d` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:105-118`) | version-validating, **as shipped**. A YAML failure ⇒ `decode-error`; a `state_version` the shipped loader rejects — **any** value other than the current one, including an absent/zero one on this path — ⇒ `decode-error` too, because the shipped loader really does refuse to produce a payload. An empty document is therefore *also* `decode-error` here (it decodes to `state_version: 0`), not `empty-document`: the inspector reports the loader's answer, not an independent opinion. **The version number is still shown to the operator** — not by this row, whose `state_version` is `null` like every other decoded field, but by the shipped cell sentence the document already projects: cells 3/6/9/12 embed `syncErrText(st.PayloadErr)`, i.e. `unsupported scoped sync state version %d` (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:334-336`), so the remedy is as legible here as in the transaction row below, and neither path invents its own wording |
   > | `checkout_transaction` (`<feature>-checkout-sync.yaml`) | `LoadCheckoutTransaction` — read + unmarshal, **no version check anywhere** (`internal/checkout_sync.go:121-131`); the version gate lives in `ContinueCheckoutSync` (`:722-726`) | permissive. A YAML failure ⇒ `decode-error`. **An absent or pre-v2 `state_version` is `readable`** — that is a legitimate, still-resumable transaction (§8.7.4, §10.3) — and, the cell the blanket rule got backwards, **a `state_version` newer than `CheckoutTransactionVersion` is also `readable`**: the file decoded, its fields are published, and its consequence is projected as the **shipped continuation refusal** `checkout sync transaction state version %d is newer than %d; upgrade tws or remove %s` at rank 3 (§8.6.4), *with the number*, not as an inspector `decode-error`. The distinction is operationally load-bearing: "your tws is too old, here is the version" and "this file is corrupt" send an operator to two different remedies, and only one of them is true |
   > | `checkout_lock` (`<feature>-checkout-sync.lock`) | `ReadCheckoutLock` — read + unmarshal into `LockInfo`, no version field (`internal/checkout_sync.go:290-300`) | permissive YAML-structure rule only: parses ⇒ `readable`; does not parse ⇒ `decode-error`. A structurally valid document with `pid: 0` is **readable** with `pid: 0`; its liveness question is answered by `alive`, not by `presence` |
   > | `external_run_guard` (`.sync-run.lock`) | `ReadSyncRunGuard` — read + unmarshal into `SyncRunGuard`, no version validation (`internal/sync_run_state.go:236-247`) | same permissive YAML-structure rule. `state_version` is published as a decoded field and **never** gates `presence`. An empty document decodes to the zero guard and is `readable` with `pid: 0` — which is also exactly the input the native reclaim arm `sync guard is being initialized or is invalid` fires on, so the diagnostic and the native answer agree about the *facts* while remaining separate mechanisms (§8.7.5 step 1) |
   >
   > **`empty-document` therefore survives as an `unreadable_reason` only where an artefact's own
   > loader treats emptiness as a failure** — it is emitted by no inspector under the table above,
   > and is retained in the closed enum for the artefacts a later round may add rather than being
   > removed from a published enum that consumers already switch on. No inspector may invent it for
   > a file whose shipped loader accepts empty bytes.
   >
   > **`Lstat`-first is the property, not an implementation detail.** The shipped readers reach for
   > the bytes directly (`os.Stat`/`os.ReadFile`), so a symlink is followed and an existing-but-
   > unreadable path is indistinguishable from an absent one. The inspectors invert that order once,
   > for every file, so `absent`, `symlink`, `unreadable` (with its reason) and `readable` are four
   > distinct answers on all five paths — including the two that the round-14 draft covered only
   > through the shipped classifier (`.sync-state.yaml`, `.sync-state.v2.yaml`) and the two it read
   > through `HasCheckoutTransaction`/`ReadCheckoutLock`, which cannot express any of the
   > distinctions at all.

   **The separation from the shipped refusal path is the whole point of the dedicated function, and
   it is exact.** `AlwaysReadGuard: true` must **not** be handed to the call whose result reaches
   `syncSymlinkRefusal`, because that predicate is not a pure function of the guard file: it
   computes `handlingV2 := st.Marker != "" || st.Payload != nil || st.PayloadErr != nil ||
   st.HasGuardFile()` and refuses a **legacy-path symlink** whenever `newMode || handlingV2` holds
   (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:281-293`), while `HasGuardFile()` is true for a guard that is
   present-and-readable, present-and-unreadable **or** a symlink
   (`internal/sync_run_state.go:440-441`). Widening the flag would therefore make guard-only residue
   flip `handlingV2` to `true` on the legacy route and turn a `.sync-state.yaml` symlink that the
   shipped `tws sync <f>` accepts today into a hard refusal — a behaviour change on the **unguarded**
   path, produced by a preview feature, in the one area where the shipped rule is a deliberate
   security compromise. The binding separation is therefore:
   - the value passed to `syncSymlinkRefusal`/`handlingV2` is the **shipped** classification, called
     with the **shipped** `AlwaysReadGuard: newMode` and nothing else. The plan/guard route does not
     change the flag, does not re-derive `handlingV2`, and does not add a fourth disjunct to it;
   - the snapshot's guard facts come **only** from the guard inspector, are published **only**
     under `state.files.external_run_guard`, and feed **only** this document's own derivations — the
     live-owner fact of cause 3, the `owner-artefact-undecodable` fact of §4.4, the `state-refused`
     projections of §8.6.2, and the guarded seam of §8.7.1. The same separation holds for the other
     four inspectors: `state.files.checkout_transaction` and `state.files.checkout_lock` never feed
     `AcquireCheckoutLock`/`forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, and `state.files.external_legacy_state`/
     `state.files.external_payload` never feed `syncCellRefusal` — the shipped cell still comes from
     `ClassifyExternalSyncState` and is published as `state.external_cell` (§8.6.7);
   - **no unguarded behaviour changes**: a bare `tws sync <f>` never calls the inspector, its cell
     selection, its refusal sentences, its argv and its `sync_noflag` goldens are untouched
     (§10.1, §18.12);
   - **plan-only projects, guarded may refuse — and the plan says so in a field.** On `--plan` a
     guard-only residue is *state*: it is
     published with its `presence`, it contributes the live-owner fact when `presence: readable`
     with a foreign signalable PID, and it carries a `state-refused` blocker only where the shipped
     ladder implies one for that cell. On the **guarded controlled route** the same observation may
     **fail closed** with its own non-waivable rank 3 blocker — a `readable` foreign live guard by
     cause 3, and an `unreadable`/`symlink` **owner-signalling** artefact because an owner artefact
     that cannot be decoded cannot be
     shown to be dead (§4.4 `state`). Both are guard **introductions** by origin, so both carry the
     marker line where no shipped check refuses first (§8.7.6). **Both are also published on the
     plan-only document** — `live-owner-concurrency` and **`owner-artefact-undecodable`** in
     `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` respectively — so the four-conjunct plan→execute predicate is
     exact in the undecodable cell as well as the live one; the plan-only rendering may add that the
     *unguarded* route would ignore the file entirely, which is true and is not a contradiction
     (§4.4 `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`, §19.22). Which owner-signalling artefacts the refusal
     ranges over — all of them, or only the one the route would consult — is §19.22's remaining
     choice; the token, its rank and its publication are settled here either way;
   - **the cell is asserted in both directions** (§15.15f5): a legacy-route fixture carrying only
     `.sync-run.lock` (no payload, no sentinel) whose PID is a live helper ⇒ the `--plan` document
     publishes `state.files.external_run_guard: {presence: readable, alive: true, self: false,
     token_matches_payload: null}`, suppresses the fetch and carries
     `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]`, while the guarded twin exits 1 at
     rank 3 and the **unguarded** `tws sync <f>` over the same fixture fetches and rebases exactly
     as today; the same fixture with the helper killed publishes `alive: false` and fetches; a
     `.sync-run.lock` **symlink** on the legacy route publishes `presence: symlink`,
     `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["owner-artefact-undecodable"]` **and leaves the
     shipped legacy-path symlink behaviour unchanged** — asserted directly, by pointing
     `.sync-state.yaml` at a symlink in the same fixture and checking that the unguarded run still
     behaves as it does on `main`; and an **unreadable** guard publishes `presence: unreadable` with
     its `unreadable_reason`, `alive: null`, never `absent` and never `alive: false`, and the same
     `execute_blocked_by` member;

3. load the stack (→ rows-less `plan-unavailable` on failure, §8.5.5) — **this is before the fetch,
   so a `plan-unavailable` document never fetched**;
4. on a `--continue` invocation, derive the **effective route and policy from the state** and
   project every continuation gate as a blocker (§8.6.4); on a fresh invocation the route is
   trigger-derived (§0.2);
5. run the **structural validation of the entry set — `TopoSort`, and the selection on the new-mode
   route — on every route, before the fetch**. On the new-mode route this is exactly where the
   shipped executor does it (`ResolveSyncSelection`, `internal/sync_selection.go:166`), so
   `selection-refused` and `stack-unsortable` are established there anyway; on the **legacy** route
   the shipped executors sort *later* (legacy external fetches and then sorts; legacy checkout sorts
   inside `BuildCheckoutPlan`), and the plan/guard route **deliberately hoists the sort above the
   fetch**. See the "early structural validation" rule below — it is a divergence in *order only*,
   between two pure reads, and it is what makes `stack-unsortable` a rows-less
   `not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` document on **every** route. On the legacy route the selection is
   "the whole stack", exactly as `run == nil` means today;

   **5a — enumerate the fetch contexts before deciding to fetch, on the plan and guard paths
   alike.**
   The `context_candidates[]` of §8.6.9 — the first-entry candidate set per `repo_token`, each
   resolved through the `fetchQuiet` ladder, canonicalized, and reduced by `git rev-parse
   --git-common-dir` equivalence — is computed **here**, between the sort and step 6, and never
   after the fetch it describes. Two properties follow and both are the point of the hoist: on the
   **new-mode external** route an indeterminate token is discovered **before any network call**, so
   the rank 5.0 `fetch-context-indeterminate` refusal happens with `refs/remotes/**` untouched
   rather than after the plan has already refreshed one of the candidate repositories it could not
   choose between; and the enumeration itself is pure — `stat` on candidate worktree directories
   plus one `rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir` and one remote/refspec resolution
   per candidate root — so hoisting it adds no mutation. The
   legacy external route and both checkout routes have a single candidate per token by construction
   (§8.6.9), so for them this step is a confirmation, not a decision. **The same order binds the
   guarded execution seams** (§9), including the new-mode external route where the invocation has
   already written its own state: the enumeration and its refusal run before the fetch, and the
   refusal tears down **only the artefacts that invocation created** (§8.7.5, §12). This is a
   deliberate ordering divergence on the **controlled paths only** — the plan seam and the guard
   seam — and it is stated rather than implied: an unguarded `tws sync <f> --only …` still builds
   the map and fetches in whatever directory the shipped order lands in, with its argv and its
   goldens unchanged (§18.12, §18.21);
6. run the route's own fetch, if its policy says so, at the same point the run does — subject to the
   closed suppression set below;
7. build the plan over the already-sorted entry set, evaluate any effective limits and
   any supplied token, rank the blockers and pick the single `refusal.kind` (§4.9), canonicalize,
   publish, exit 0.

It takes **no lock**, writes **no state**, and never touches a local branch, worktree, `stack.yaml`,
or metadata file. Step 2 is *reporting*, never acquiring, stealing, or clearing.

**Early structural validation is deliberate, and it is stated rather than hidden.** Step 5 runs
`TopoSort` (and, on the new-mode route, `ResolveSyncSelection`) **before** step 6 on every route,
including the legacy external one where the shipped executor fetches first and sorts afterwards
(`syncFeature`: fetch loop, then `TopoSort`). Four things make that safe and one makes it necessary:

- **It moves a pure read, not a mutation.** `TopoSort` and the selection resolution touch no file,
  no ref and no process; reordering them relative to the fetch cannot change what the run does,
  only what the *preview* had to touch before it could refuse.
- **It can only remove a mutation, never add one.** The reordering's entire observable effect is
  that a cycle (or a selection refusal) is discovered **before** `git fetch` moves
  `refs/remotes/**`. A preview that refuses without touching the network is strictly safer than one
  that fetches and then refuses, and a *guarded* run that refuses `stack-unsortable` before fetching
  mutates strictly less than the unguarded run it guards. Nothing downstream depends on the fetch
  having happened, because there is no plan to compute.
- **The unguarded no-flag path keeps the shipped order exactly.** This rule governs the plan-only
  and guarded seams only. A bare `tws sync <f>` still fetches and then fails at the sort, its
  message and its argv sequence unchanged, and the `internal/cli/testdata/sync_noflag/**` goldens
  are untouched (§10.1).
- **It removes an unreachable freshness cell rather than creating one.** The previous draft carved
  out "the legacy external route is the one cell where a cycle is found *after* the executor's own
  fetch, and there the document reports the fetch it really performed". With step 5 hoisted, that
  cell does not exist: **no `stack-unsortable` or `selection-refused` document ever reports
  `fetched`/`possibly-stale` on any route**, and the carve-out, its aggregate footnote in §4.4 and
  its assertions in §5.5, §8.6.3, §15.15g and §15.18a are withdrawn. Every remaining `freshness`
  value stays reachable — `fetched`/`possibly-stale`/`unknown-fetch-effect`/
  `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`, the **four attempted-row verdicts**, from any rows-bearing
  fetching route **and from a rows-less checkout `--fetch` document too**, whose single
  `workspace-repo-root` row is attempted before the plan build (§8.6.9, round-23 item 1 correcting
  the two-value list this bullet and §4.4's rows-less profile previously carried),
  `local-only` from a `no-fetch` policy, `not-refreshed-continuation` from any `--continue`,
  `not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` from any of the three no-subject kinds,
  `not-refreshed-live-run` from a live owner, `not-refreshed-context-indeterminate` from a
  new-mode token whose candidate contexts disagree (§8.6.9),
  `not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate` from an unconditional submodule recursion whose
  reach cannot be bounded (§8.6.1 cause 5, round-23 item 3),
  **`not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out`** from a covering positive refspec whose covered local
  branches are held — or whose holds could not be established (§8.6.1 cause 6, round-25 item 2,
  round-26 items 4 and 5) — and
  `not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets` from an empty
  context set — so the enum has no dead members and no cell without a value.
- **The necessity**: without it, "a rows-less document never fetched" would be true on three routes
  and false on the fourth, and every consumer, skill and test would have to special-case which
  route produced the refusal in order to know whether its base SHAs meant anything. One rule that
  holds everywhere is worth one deliberate, non-mutating reordering.

**The step 2 → step 6 ordering is load-bearing, not incidental.** The plan observes state *before*
it fetches precisely so it can decline to fetch. The suppression set is **closed at six causes**
(round-23 item 3 added the fifth, §8.6.1 cause 5; round-25 item 2 adds the sixth, §8.6.1 cause 6),
they are mutually exclusive by the precedence given, and every other cell fetches per route policy:

> **Step 6 is skipped in exactly six cases** (round-23 item 3 added the fifth; round-24 item 4
> corrected this header, which still said "four" while the list below it, §9, §18.5 and §20 said
> five; round-25 item 2 adds the sixth, and every restatement in §4.4, §8.6.3, §9, §11, §18.5 and
> §20 is updated with it rather than left to drift again).
>
> 1. **Continuation** — any `--continue` invocation, because no shipped continuation executor
>    fetches (§8.6.4). `freshness: not-refreshed-continuation`.
> 2. **No plannable subject** — the document is rows-less because `plan-unavailable` (step 3),
>    `selection-refused` or `stack-unsortable` (step 5) was established **before** step 6, so there
>    is no subject to fetch for. `freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`. **This now holds on
>    every route**, legacy external included, because step 5 sorts before step 6 (the early
>    structural validation rule above).
> 3. **Pre-existing foreign owner with a signalable PID** — the **step 2 snapshot** holds an
>    **owner-signalling artefact** that already
>    existed before this invocation touched anything, that decoded (`presence: readable`), and whose
>    recorded PID satisfies
>    `pid > 0 && pid != os.Getpid() && isProcessAlive(pid)`
>    (`internal/checkout_sync.go:302`; the self conjunct is the shipped one, `forceAcquireCheckoutLock`
>    `internal/checkout_sync.go:281` and `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` `internal/sync_run_state.go:226`).
>    **The owner-signalling set is closed at two, and both are lock files: the checkout lock
>    `.checkout-sync.lock` and the sync-run guard `.sync-run.lock`.** **That is the whole predicate,
>    and it has exactly four
>    conjuncts: an owner-signalling artefact, pre-existing and readable in the snapshot, signalable,
>    and not this process.** Two conjuncts the
>    round-10 draft additionally required are withdrawn, and one artefact the round-13 draft
>    additionally admitted is withdrawn with them, each for a reason that is a defect in the
>    draft rather than a change of policy:
>    - **The checkout transaction is not an owner signal, and `tx.LockPID` never blocks or
>      suppresses anything.** The round-13 clause "or a checkout transaction whose lock PID does" is
>      **withdrawn**. A lock file is *acquired and released around a run*, so its presence is the
>      concurrency claim itself; `tx.LockPID` is a **persisted field of a recovery record that is
>      designed to outlive its process** (written at `internal/checkout_sync.go:660`, rewritten on
>      each `--continue` at `:743`), and the transaction exists precisely so a *later* process can
>      resume after the writer is gone. Deriving liveness from it makes PID **reuse** permanent: a
>      transaction whose recorded PID the OS has handed to an unrelated process would suppress every
>      fetch and refuse every guarded run — including the `--continue` whose whole purpose is to
>      clear it — with no invocation that could ever succeed. The shipped code agrees: both
>      `AcquireCheckoutLock` and `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` decide liveness from `LockInfo.PID` in
>      the **lock file** and never read `tx.LockPID` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:185-220`,
>      `:262-285`). So `state.files.checkout_transaction.lock_pid` is published informationally, with no
>      `alive` and no `self`, and a transaction's concurrency question is answered by the checkout
>      lock beside it or not at all. The transaction still refuses runs — as the shipped
>      **transaction-exists** state fact (`:564-566`), which requires no liveness — and that refusal
>      is unchanged (§4.4 `state`, §8.6.2).
>    - **"Alive" is a signal probe, not a proof of a running owner.** `isProcessAlive` is
>      `Signal(0)`, so the conjunct means *a PID exists that this user may signal*: a live process
>      owned by another user reads as **dead** (`EPERM`), and a **reused** PID reads as alive. The
>      predicate is written and asserted in exactly those terms (§4.4 `state`, §15.15f/f3); the
>      residual window is bounded, documented, and closed only by a portable **birth-identity**
>      follow-up, never by rewording this clause (§19.21).

>    - **Token ownership is irrelevant.** The suppression must not be read off
>      `SyncExternalState.GuardLive` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:415-418`), which sets itself to
>      `false` for a guard whose PID is alive whenever `guard.Token != payload.OwnerToken`. That is
>      the right answer to "is *this run* still running?" and the wrong answer to ours: a
>      token-mismatched guard is still a **live process**, and a live process is exactly what the D3
>      hazard is about (§2.4, §9). The plan therefore computes liveness itself, from the raw PID,
>      and publishes ownership **separately** as `state.files.external_run_guard.token_matches_payload`
>      (`SyncExternalState.GuardForeign()`, `:434-436`) so the two facts can be read without either
>      standing in for the other. **"Foreign" in this cause means a different *process*, never a
>      mismatched token**, and the two words must not be swapped anywhere in this document.
>    - **"And it blocks the run" is not required either.** Whether the observation happens to land
>      in a cell that refuses this verb is a property of the shipped state ladder, not of the other
>      process's ability to move `refs/remotes/**` while we fetch. A live owner in a cell that would
>      have let this invocation proceed is precisely the case where fetching under it is most
>      damaging.
>
>    **What the conjuncts exclude is as binding as what they admit.** An artefact this
>    invocation **created, acquired or reclaimed** is never a live-owner fact, however alive its PID
>    is, because that PID is ours: the `.sync-state.v2.yaml` + `.sync-run.lock` + sentinel a fresh
>    new-mode external run writes before its guard seam, the checkout lock `AcquireCheckoutLock`
>    takes before `BuildCheckoutPlan`, the lock `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` re-takes on a checkout
>    `--continue`, and the guard `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` rewrites on a scoped resume are all excluded
>    twice over — they are absent from the pre-acquisition snapshot **and** they carry `self: true`
>    (§4.4 `state.snapshot`). Without that exclusion every guarded fresh new-mode external run and
>    every checkout continuation would refuse itself at rank 3, which is the shipped code's own
>    reason for writing `pid != os.Getpid() && isProcessAlive(pid)` rather than liveness alone. The
>    exclusion is *not* a liveness weakening: a genuinely concurrent process is a different PID and
>    is still caught, and an artefact that was in the snapshot with another live PID stays a blocker
>    even if this invocation later reclaims it — the snapshot, not the post-reclaim file, is the
>    evidence.
>
>    `freshness: not-refreshed-live-run`, with the observed artefact, its PID and its ownership
>    named in the document. **Stale, dead and self-owned owners follow route policy**, unchanged: a
>    guard whose PID is gone, a dead lock PID, **a transaction with no live lock — including one
>    whose own `lock_pid` looks signalable, which is now irrelevant by construction** — every
>    ownerless state
>    cell and every artefact this invocation created itself fetch exactly as they would with no state
>    at all (see the "not suppressed" cells below). **The one cell that is not "no owner" is
>    `presence: unreadable` or `presence: symlink`**: an owner-signalling artefact that exists but
>    cannot be decoded has **unknown** liveness (`alive: null`), so it is neither a live-owner fact
>    nor a clean cell. The plan-only route publishes it as state and follows route policy for the
>    fetch, saying so through `presence` and its `unreadable_reason`; the **guarded** route fails
>    closed on it with its own
>    non-waivable rank 3 blocker **in the cells the native acquisition ladder would not already
>    refuse**, because an owner artefact that cannot be read cannot be shown to
>    be dead (§4.4 `state`, step 2a above). **That qualifier is a round-17 narrowing of this clause
>    rather than a rule beside it**: `ClaimSyncRunGuard` and `AcquireCheckoutLock` already reject a
>    corrupt or unreadable **regular** guard/lock file on a fresh run, in their own words
>    (`invalid sync guard; inspect %s and use --abort to recover: %w`, `read existing sync guard:
>    %w`, and their checkout twins), so those cells are **shipped** rank 3 refusals the plan
>    projects verbatim (§8.6.2) and leave no divergence between the two routes to publish. The
>    member is reserved for what the native ladder reads straight **through** or never reads at
>    all — a symlink whose target decodes, and an **applicable** owner-signalling artefact on a path this route
>    does not consult (`.sync-run.lock` under a
>    legacy external route). **Applicability bounds the member** (round-19 item 5): the token is
>    emitted only for an artefact whose `applicable` is `true` on this route, because a
>    `not-applicable` artefact has `presence: not-applicable` — not an undecodable presence — and the
>    cross-mode cell earlier drafts named, `.checkout-sync.lock` under an external route, is
>    therefore impossible and is removed, not narrowed (§4.4 `state`). **Where the two routes do then differ, the plan-only
>    document publishes the divergence as `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["owner-artefact-undecodable"]`**
>    — the second member of that closed array, added this round, on exactly the same footing as
>    `live-owner-concurrency`: derived from the step 2 snapshot, total over `plannability`,
>    non-waivable, a fingerprint non-member, and published whether or not the shipped ladder also
>    refuses that cell. It does **not** suppress the fetch (nothing is known to be running) and it
>    does **not** set `runnable: false` by itself (the shipped ladder is what `runnable` is computed
>    over), which is precisely why it needs its own field: without it the undecodable cell publishes
>    four fields that all read "this will run" over a guarded twin that refuses (§4.4
>    `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`, §4.9 rank 3, §19.22).
>
>    **The predicate has one definition and two consequences, and this is the single place both are
>    stated.** On the **plan-only** route a pre-existing live foreign owner suppresses the fetch —
>    regardless of token ownership and of whether this cell refuses the verb — and the document
>    additionally projects whatever `state-refused` blocker the shipped ladder implies for that cell,
>    where it implies one (§8.6.2). Describing a run over refs nobody refreshed is honest, because
>    `--plan` executes nothing. A **guarded executing** invocation cannot stop at the suppression:
>    having declined the fetch it would rebase against refs it deliberately left stale, while the
>    other process keeps moving `refs/remotes/**` under it — the D3 hazard pointed at the guard
>    rather than at the neighbour. So **at the guard seam any pre-existing live foreign owner is
>    itself a non-waivable `state-refused` concurrency blocker** (§4.9 rank 3), whatever
>    the shipped ladder made of that cell and whether or not the guard's own payload owns it, and the
>    invocation refuses instead of executing. Where no shipped check refuses first, that refusal is a
>    **guard introduction** and carries the marker line (§8.6.2, §8.7.6); where a shipped cell already
>    refuses, the shipped sentence and its marker-free output win, exactly as §8.7.1 requires. **The
>    unguarded run is untouched**: a bare `tws sync <f>` under another process's live guard fetches
>    and rebases exactly as it does today, argv and goldens unmoved (§18.12). This is a deliberate
>    **controlled-path safety divergence**, of the same family as the step 5a hoist and stated rather
>    than implied: the guarded run mutates strictly *less* than the unguarded one in this cell, never
>    more.
>
>    **The plan document states the second consequence in a field, not only in this prose.** Because
>    the divergence exists, the *plan-only* document of a cell the shipped ladder lets through would
>    otherwise publish `runnable: true`, `guard.would_refuse: false` and `refusal.kind: null` over a
>    command its guarded twin refuses — a counterexample to the whole plan→execute contract, and one
>    the round-12 draft carried in §15.15f2/f3 as a matched pair of assertions. It is eliminated by
>    publishing the fact: **every document whose snapshot holds a pre-existing live foreign owner
>    carries `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]`** (§4.4), whatever its `runnable`
>    value, whatever its **`plannability`**, and whether or not a limit is in force, and the
>    plan→execute predicate everywhere in this
>    document is
>    `runnable && !guard.would_refuse && guard.execute_blocked_by == [] && refusal.kind == null`
>    (§8.3.3, §8.7.7).
>
>    **"Every document" is total over `plannability`, and the profile table of §4.4 defers to this
>    rule rather than restating it.** The array is derived from the **step 2 snapshot**, which is
>    taken *before* the stack is loaded (step 3) and *before* the sort and selection (step 5), so the
>    observation that produces `live-owner-concurrency` is complete on every route and in every cell
>    that can publish a document at all — including the rows-less ones. That includes
>    `plannability: unavailable`: an unreadable `stack.yaml`, an unsortable stack and a refused
>    selection each say "this plan could not be derived", and none of them says "no neighbour is
>    running". Publishing `[]` there — as the round-13 profile table did, with the reasoning "no
>    controlled-path execution was projected" — asserted the strongest possible fact (the guarded
>    twin will not refuse for concurrency) from the weakest possible evidence (we never got far
>    enough to look at the plan), and it contradicted this rule two paragraphs above it. **The
>    precedence is one-directional and is stated here:** where the snapshot detects a pre-existing
>    signalable foreign owner, `guard.execute_blocked_by` carries `live-owner-concurrency` in the
>    `empty` column, in the `unavailable` column and in every rows-bearing document alike; where it
>    does not, the array is `[]`. `plannability` never adds, removes or overrides a member. The
>    `refusal.kind` of a rows-less document is unaffected — a `plan-unavailable` document still
>    refuses as `plan-unavailable` at rank 1, and the concurrency fact rides beside it on its own
>    axis, exactly as it does when the shipped ladder refuses a rows-bearing cell.
>
>    **Continuation-freshness precedence is a separate ordering and is not touched by this.** The
>    rule that a `--continue` reports `not-refreshed-continuation` rather than
>    `not-refreshed-live-run` (and rather than `not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`) orders the **fetch**
>    causes only, because it answers "why did this invocation not fetch?" and the executor's own
>    never-fetch behaviour outranks this route's precaution. It says nothing about whether a
>    neighbour exists. So a rows-less guarded `--continue` under a pre-existing signalable foreign
>    owner publishes `freshness: not-refreshed-continuation` **and**
>    `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]` together, and its guarded twin still
>    refuses at rank 3. The two orderings share an input and decide different fields; conflating them
>    would either hide the neighbour or misreport the fetch cause.
>
>    The two cells then project consistently and neither is silent:
>    - where the shipped ladder **does** refuse that cell, the document carries the rank 3
>      `state-refused` blocker, `runnable: false`, `refusal.kind: state-refused` **and** the
>      `execute_blocked_by` member — the guarded refusal is the shipped one, marker-free;
>    - where the shipped ladder refuses **nothing**, the document keeps `runnable: true` and
>      `refusal.kind: null` — `runnable` answers "can this plan be executed at all?" over the shipped
>      ladder and an approval never moves it, which is a prior contract this round does not touch
>      (§4.4, §19) — and the non-empty `execute_blocked_by` is the *only* field that says the guarded
>      twin refuses. A plan carrying effective limits therefore still mints its ordinary token there
>      (the work and limit clauses of §4.4 are both satisfied), and that token authorises nothing in
>      this cell, because the refusal is non-waivable (§5.3.1): the honest reading is "the plan is
>      approvable, and the guarded run will still refuse while the neighbour lives", which is exactly
>      what the four-conjunct predicate computes.
>
>    A consumer that reads only `runnable`/`would_refuse`/`refusal.kind` is therefore reading an
>    incomplete predicate, and every consumer, skill, doc and test in this document is taught the
>    four-conjunct form (§8.3.5, §14, §15.16j).
> 4. **Indeterminate fetch context** — the route's own first-entry rule resolves **two or more
>    materially different** contexts for some token, where "materially different" is decided by the
>    canonical **absolute common dir** of each candidate **and its effective bare-fetch effect**
>    — the `{all, contacted, may_delete_refs, may_delete_tags, may_clobber_tags, may_update_local_branches, may_delete_local_branches, local_branch_destinations, remotes[], submodule_recursion}` value of §4.4, compared
>    whole — rather than by its worktree
>    root (§8.6.9): candidates sharing one store *and* one resolved fetch effect refresh
>    the same refs and collapse, candidates differing in either — or among which one will not
>    resolve, and so cannot be shown to agree — do not. **Two or more candidates are required**
>    (round-21 item 7): a token with a single candidate is determinate even where its context or its
>    remote is broken, so it fetches and reports the failure (`ok: false`, `fetch.outcome: failed`,
>    `freshness: possibly-stale`) instead of suppressing anything. The ambiguity
>    exists because the new-mode external map is built over
>    a `TopoSort`-ordered selection whose **root-component interleaving** is unspecified — the one
>    thing `TopoSort` randomizes (§4.7, §8.6.9, round-22 item 5).
>    The plan will not fetch in a store it cannot reproduce, so it fetches in none of them:
>    `freshness: not-refreshed-context-indeterminate`, with the rank 5.0
>    `fetch-context-indeterminate` blocker naming the token and its sorted `context_candidates[]`.
>    The enumeration runs at step 5a, **before** any network call, on the plan and guard paths
>    alike. It is one of **four** suppressions that are **not** shared with the unguarded run
>    (round-23 item 3 added the third, round-25 item 2 the fourth) — the
>    others are cause 3's pre-existing live foreign owner, which the guarded seam turns into a refusal
>    (above), cause 5's unbounded submodule reach and cause 6's checked-out fetch destination (both
>    below) — so all four are members of
>    `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` (§4.4), whose remaining member,
>    `owner-artefact-undecodable`, is **not** a suppression at all: an undecodable owner artefact
>    blocks controlled execution while leaving the fetch to route policy, because nothing is known
>    to be running (§8.6.1 step 2a). **All four** suppressions
>    say so in the blocker detail rather than implying the shipped command is broken (round-27
>    item 5 repairs the count, which had been left at "three" when round 25 added cause 6 to the
>    sentence above it): a bare
>    `tws sync <f> --only …` still fetches wherever the shipped map order lands, still fetches
>    and rebases under another process's live guard, and still recurses into every populated
>    submodule its configuration tells it to, unchanged (§4.9, §8.6.9, §18.12). It still issues the
>    fetch that dies at a checked-out destination, too, and carries on against stale refs (cause 6).
> 5. **Unbounded submodule reach** — the context is determinate and its own effect resolves, but the
>    fetch would not stop there: some **present gitlink** submodule's effective recursion — the
>    **context mode** (`fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse`, resolved by **last occurrence
>    in the ordered config** rather than by precedence between the two keys, round-24 item 1, **or,
>    where that chain sets nothing, the context-level `[fetch] recurseSubmodules` of `.gitmodules`**,
>    round-26 item 6), which
>    binds every submodule of that context whenever it is set at all, or — **only where no context
>    mode is set by either source** — that submodule's own `fetchRecurseSubmodules` from config and then
>    `.gitmodules` (round-25 item 1 correcting the direction round 24 stated backwards)
>    — is **`yes`**, so "all populated submodules are fetched"
>    (`git fetch` manual, verified
>    against Git 2.55.0), while `fetch_effect.submodule_recursion.reach` is **`unknown`** — a
>    candidate
>    submodule whose store or config could not be read, an enumeration over the 50-submodule/depth-3
>    cap, or an enumerated submodule that may itself recurse into a level that could not be
>    established (§4.4 `fetch.repos[]`, round-23 item 3). **Submodule *activity* is not part of this
>    cause** (round-24 item 2): `git fetch` recurses into a populated gitlink on the strength of the
>    index entry, the submodule store and the effective mode alone (`submodule.c`
>    `get_fetch_task_from_index` → `fetch_task_create` → `get_fetch_recurse_config`), so an
>    inactive-but-populated submodule triggers this cause exactly as an active one does, and `active`
>    survives only as an informational member of `submodules[]` (§4.4). The plan will not contact remotes and
>    rewrite `refs/remotes/**` and tags in repositories it cannot name, so it fetches in none of
>    them: `freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate`, with the rank 5.05
>    **`fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate`** blocker (`runnable: false`, §4.9) naming the context,
>    the resolved `mode`/`mode_source` and the bounded part of `submodules[]` it did establish.
>    **It is a fail-closed rule with a deliberately narrow domain**: `mode: no` cannot reach it,
>    and `on-demand` — Git's **default**, where recursion depends on what the fetch turns out to
>    bring down — never reaches it either, publishing `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect` and fetching
>    (the ninth cell below). **The one arm round 26 adds is an *unreadable* mode, not a lax one**
>    (item 6, **narrowed by round-28 item 1 and tightened by round-28 item 7**): where the config
>    chain sets no context mode and **every remaining source of the rung-2 `.gitmodules` ladder fails
>    to read**, the mode itself is unknown (`mode`/`mode_source` `null`,
>    `reach: unknown`) and a context with at least one **present gitlink** takes this cause and this
>    rank, because an unread mode may be `yes`; a context with no present gitlink cannot recurse and
>    fetches. **An index-unmerged `.gitmodules` is no longer such a cell** (round-28 item 1): Git's
>    own loader falls from the failed index read through to `HEAD:.gitmodules`, so the mode resolves
>    and this cause does not apply. **And this cause is the *only* treatment of an unresolvable
>    mode** (round-28 item 7): there is no alternative cell in which the same context is fetched and
>    then described as `unknown-fetch-effect` — where the mode is `null` over a present gitlink the
>    fetch is skipped and the row publishes `attempted: false`. Like cause 4 it skips *all* fetches of
>    that invocation, for the same reason:
>    a partially-fetched preview would mix refreshed and stale identities with nothing in the
>    document to tell them apart.
> 6. **A checked-out fetch destination** — new in round 25 (item 2). The context is determinate, its
>    effect resolves, its reach is fine, and the fetch would nevertheless write `refs/heads/**` in a
>    store where a working tree is standing on one of the destinations: the resolved effect has a
>    **positive** refspec whose destination pattern **covers `refs/heads/**`** (the mirror
>    `+refs/*:refs/*`, `refs/heads/*:refs/heads/*`, `refs/h*`, or a legacy `branches/<name>` file's
>    synthesised `refs/heads/<branch>:refs/heads/<name>`, §0.1) and
>    `fetch_effect.local_branch_destinations.held[]` is **non-empty** — some covered branch is held
>    as HEAD, by a recorded in-progress rebase, by a bisect, or by a running rebase's
>    `--update-refs` state, in a non-bare worktree of that store, which is exactly what Git's own
>    `branch_checked_out()` reports (`branch.c` `prepare_checked_out_branches`) and is **one kind
>    wider** than §4.9 rank 5.4's `git checkout` holder rule (§4.4, round-25 item 2) — **or the
>    enumeration that would answer that question did not resolve**: `branches` or `held` is `null`,
>    because the store's `for-each-ref refs/heads/` or its worktree inventory could not be read
>    (round-26 item 4). **The unknown cell fails closed with the known one, and that is the whole
>    point of the cause**: "no worktree holds a covered destination" and "I could not find out
>    whether one does" have the same consequence for a fetch that is about to write `refs/heads/**`,
>    and treating the second as the first would fetch precisely where the evidence was missing. The
>    document distinguishes them where it matters — a refusal over a non-empty `held[]` names the
>    branch, the worktree and the hold kind; a refusal over `held: null` names the probe that failed
>    and says the holds are **unknown**, in `refusal.detail` and in the published effect — while the
>    kind, the rank, the suppression, the `freshness` value and the
>    `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` member are the same in both, because the action is the same. No new
>    enum member is minted for the unknown cell (§4.4 `freshness`, §4.9 rank 5.06). Git resolves that meeting in one of two ways and neither is acceptable under a preview:
>    for a held branch the remote **advertises**, `check_not_current_branch` (`builtin/fetch.c`)
>    **dies** with `refusing to fetch into branch '<ref>' checked out at '<path>'` before
>    `prune_refs` and before any update, and the shipped `fetchQuiet` discards that status, so the
>    run continues against **stale** refs; for a held branch the remote no longer has, the die never
>    applies — it is evaluated over the ref map — and an effective prune **deletes** the branch,
>    leaving that worktree's HEAD dangling. The route therefore declines the fetch:
>    `freshness: not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out`, with the rank 5.06
>    **`fetch-local-branch-checked-out`** blocker (`runnable: false`, §4.9) naming the context, the
>    covering `patterns[]` and every `held[]` row with its worktree and hold kind. **Its domain is
>    deliberately narrow in one direction and deliberately conservative in the other**: no covering
>    positive refspec means no cause at all — the ordinary
>    `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/<r>/*` clone can never reach it, which is why this cause is invisible
>    to every non-mirror workspace — while a covered *held* branch refuses even though the die itself
>    depends on what the remote advertises, because settling that question means performing the
>    fetch. Like causes 4 and 5 it skips *all* fetches of that invocation, for the same reason. And
>    like them it is **not** shared with the unguarded run, which still issues the fetch and still
>    dies or prunes (§0.1, §4.9 rank 5.06, `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`).
>
> In all six the document publishes `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.repos[]` with no attempted
> row, `fetch.outcome: skipped` and `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: false`; only `freshness`
> distinguishes them, in that precedence order when more than one applies (a `--continue` against a
> live-owned artefact reports the continuation cause, because that is the executor's own behaviour
> rather than this route's precaution — **and, for the same reason, so does a `--continue` whose
> stack cannot be read or sorted: `not-refreshed-continuation` outranks
> `not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` on every rows-less continuation**, which is the precedence §4.4's
> profile table now states instead of its withdrawn "always no-plan-subject" wording). Cause 4 is
> the one that still publishes **rows** in
> `fetch.repos[]` — with `context_root: null`, `context_common_dir: null`, `context_source: null`,
> `fetch_effect: null`,
> `attempted: false`,
> `ok: null` and a populated `context_candidates[]` — because the tokens are known even though
> their contexts are not. **Causes 5 and 6 publish rows too, and of the opposite kind** (round-23
> item 3; round-25 item 2): their context is fully resolved, so the row keeps its `context_root`,
> `context_common_dir`, `context_source` and its **resolved** `fetch_effect` — including, for
> cause 5, the `submodule_recursion` object whose `reach: unknown` is the reason for the refusal,
> and, for cause 6, the `local_branch_destinations` object whose covering `patterns[]` and non-empty
> `held[]` — **or whose `null` `branches`/`held`, on the fail-closed unknown arm** (round-26 item 4) —
> are — with `attempted: false` and `ok: null`. A reader must be able to see exactly which
> context was declined and why, and nulling an effect the plan did resolve would hide the evidence.
>
> **A seventh cell publishes the same fetch block without being a suppression at all: zero fetch
> targets.** (Round 23 renumbered the non-suppression cells when cause 5 became a suppression of its
> own; round 25 renumbers them once more for cause 6; the ladder below is otherwise unchanged.) When
> the policy *is* `fetch`, none of the six causes applies, and the route resolves
> an **empty** context set — external `UniqueRepos` over a stack with no branches, or
> `selectedRealEntries` over a selection with no repo — no `git fetch` process is invoked, because
> there is nothing to invoke it on. **It is an external-only cell** (round-21 item 7): checkout's
> context is `ws.RepoRoot`, resolved as a hard precondition, and its single fetch runs *before* the
> stack load and the empty-plan return (`internal/checkout_sync.go:611-654`), so an empty checkout
> `--fetch` document reports a **real attempt** instead — and, because the attempted-row table below
> is total, **any of its four verdicts**: `fetched`, `possibly-stale`, `unknown-fetch-effect` or
> `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`, decided exactly as they are for any other attempted row.
> **Round 24 withdraws the stale "`fetched`/`possibly-stale`" pair this sentence carried** (item 4),
> which predated round 23's two new attempted-row verdicts, and states the one exception with it:
> where a suppression applies *before* that fetch — on this route, cause 5's unbounded submodule
> reach and cause 6's checked-out fetch destination, and causes 1 and 3 as on every route — the
> empty checkout `--fetch` document has **no** attempted row and reports that suppression's own
> value instead (§4.4 profile table). The
> zero-target cell itself is not a decision the plan made; it is the shipped loop
> iterating an empty map. The document publishes `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.repos: []`,
> `fetch.outcome: skipped`, `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: false` and
> `freshness: not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets` (§4.4). It ranks **below** the six suppressions and
> **above** the policy value, so a `--continue`, a pre-existing live foreign owner, an
> indeterminate context, an unbounded submodule reach or a checked-out fetch destination still
> wins, and it is never reported
> as `local-only` (the policy was `fetch`) nor as `fetched` (nothing was refreshed). The ordinary
> cell that produces it is a `plannability: empty` document on a fetching external route.
>
> **An eighth cell runs the fetch, succeeds, and still refreshes nothing** (round-22 item 3). The
> policy is `fetch`, a context resolves, `git fetch` really runs — and it contacts **no remote**,
> because the **default** remote resolution resolved to nothing (Git gives a *given* name its
> URL-alias fallback and a defaulted one none, so `remote_get` returns nothing and the command falls
> through to an empty multi-remote list) **and no legacy `$GIT_DIR/remotes/<name>` or
> `$GIT_DIR/branches/<name>` file supplies one either** (round-23 item 5: Git consults both before
> the URL-alias fallback, `remote.c` `remotes_remote_get_1`, so a default resolution is only
> contact-free once those two file reads have come back empty), or because `fetch.all` is on with
> every remote `skipFetchAll`-suppressed. The process **exits 0**, so the row is honest with `attempted: true`,
> `ok: true` and `fetch.outcome: ok`, its `fetch_effect` is **resolved** with `contacted: false` and
> `remotes: []`, and the document reports `freshness: not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` — never
> `fetched`, which would read as "your refs are current" over a fetch that touched nothing but
> `FETCH_HEAD`. It is **not** a suppression: nothing was declined, so it sits below the six
> suppressions and below the zero-target cell in precedence, and — by the attempted-row decision
> table of §4.4, which round 23 makes total — **`possibly-stale` outranks it** whenever any
> attempted context also failed, **`unknown-fetch-effect` outranks it** whenever any attempted
> context's effect or submodule reach could not be established, and it **itself outranks
> `fetched`**, so a run whose contexts split between contacting and not-contacting publishes this
> value and not `fetched` (§4.4 `freshness` rules 1-4, §8.6.9). It applies on **both**
> routes, checkout included, since checkout's one context can resolve a default remote that is not
> there.
>
> **A ninth cell attempts, succeeds, and cannot say what it did** (round-23 items 1 and 3, **narrowed
> by round-28 item 7**): the
> policy is `fetch`, the route fetched, no attempted row failed, and at least one attempted row's
> `fetch_effect` is `null` — a single-candidate context whose `HEAD`, config or legacy remote file
> would not read (§4.4, §8.6.9) — or its `submodule_recursion.reach` is `unknown`
> under an `on-demand` mode that may have recursed into stores this document cannot enumerate. The
> row is honest — `attempted: true`, `ok: true` — the document publishes
> **`freshness: unknown-fetch-effect`** and `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: null`, and it is
> **not** a refusal: the fetch this route ran is the fetch the unguarded run performs, the context
> was determinate, and only the *description* is incomplete. **The recursion *mode* is no longer one
> of the `fetch_effect: null` causes this cell admits** (round-28 item 7): round 23 listed
> "the recursion mode would not read" here *and* made the same condition a fail-closed cause 5,
> so one context could be described as both fetched-with-an-unknown-effect and not-fetched. The
> conflict is resolved in the fail-closed direction, because the mode is precisely what decides how
> far the fetch reaches: **where `submodule_recursion.mode` is `null` over a context with a present
> gitlink the route does not fetch at all** (cause 5, `attempted: false`, rank 5.05), and where the
> context has no present gitlink the unresolvable mode reaches nothing and is not a suppression.
> **`unknown-fetch-effect` is therefore reserved for rows that really were attempted** — a context
> whose *other* effect reads failed, and a **resolved** mode whose reach became or stayed `unknown`
> under `on-demand`, including a reach that only became unknown once the transfer had started (a
> submodule store that opened and then would not read, an enumeration that hit the 50-submodule or
> depth-3 cap mid-walk). It exists because the alternatives are
> both lies: `fetched` would claim a refresh the plan cannot vouch for, and
> `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` would claim a *known* absence of contact where nothing is
> known. It sits directly below `possibly-stale` and above `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` in
> the attempted-row table, and — unlike cause 5 — it never suppresses a fetch.
>
> **The attempted-row table itself, stated once and normatively** (round-23 item 1, §4.4
> `freshness`). Rules are evaluated in order over the `attempted: true` rows of `fetch.repos[]`; the
> first whose predicate holds decides the document, and no later rule can revise it:
>
> | Rule | Predicate over the attempted rows | `freshness` | `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 0 | there are **no** attempted rows | the §8.6.1 suppression ladder, in full and in this order: continuation → no-plan-subject → live-run → context-indeterminate → submodule-reach-indeterminate → **local-branch-checked-out** → no-fetch-targets → policy (`local-only`) | `false` — **never `null`**, on every rung, because a suppressed fetch runs no process (§4.4 tri-state, round-25 item 7) |
> | 1 | some row has `ok: false` | `possibly-stale` | `true` if some row already wrote refs; else `null` **only where the failure could have written something or nothing is known** — a row that **contacted** a remote and then failed may have updated some refs and not others, and an unresolved effect (`fetch_effect: null`) or an `unknown` reach hides the question; else **`false`**, which round 24 makes explicit (item 5): a failed row whose effect **resolved** with `contacted: false`, whose reach is `none`/`bounded` and whose bounded members could write nothing, provably moved no ref, and `null` would misreport a known zero as unknown |
> | 2 | else some row has `fetch_effect: null`, or `submodule_recursion.reach: unknown` | `unknown-fetch-effect` | `true` where some resolved row wrote refs, else `null` |
> | 3 | else some row has `fetch_effect.contacted: false` | `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` | `true` where some contacted row can write a ref; `null` where none can but a submodule recursion may have written unobservably; else `false` |
> | 4 | else (every row resolved, succeeded and contacted) | `fetched` | `true` where any contacted remote row can write a ref (positive refspec, effective prune, or tag auto-following/`tags`); `null` where none can but a recursion may have; else `false` |
>
> Rule 3 firing **before** rule 4 is the round-23 correction that matters most in practice: a
> two-context run whose fetches both succeed, one contacting a remote and one contacting none,
> publishes `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` — never `fetched`, and never both. The mutation
> column is the tri-state of §4.4 restated against the same rows, so the two fields can never
> disagree about the same run.
>
> **In every other cell step 6 follows the route's fetch policy exactly**, whatever the document's
> `refusal.kind` turns out to be. A `state-refused` blocker with **no pre-existing live foreign
> owner** — a stale guard, a
> dead lock PID, a `previous sync incomplete` sentinel, a transaction with no live lock, an
> unreadable or too-new payload, any `syncCellRefusal` cell, **and any artefact this invocation
> created, acquired or reclaimed itself** — does **not** suppress the fetch: no *other*
> process is moving refs, so the D3 hazard below does not exist, and declining to fetch there would
> publish base SHAs staler than the run's own would be. The symmetric cell is equally binding: a
> pre-existing **live** foreign owner suppresses the fetch even where the document carries **no**
> `state-refused` blocker
> at all — another process's live guard whose cell lets this verb proceed is still a running
> process. On the
> **guarded** seam that same cell does not merely decline the fetch: it refuses, as the non-waivable
> `state-refused` concurrency blocker of cause 3, published as `guard.execute_blocked_by`'s
> `live-owner-concurrency` member on the plan side, so no guarded run ever executes over refs it
> chose not to refresh.

The reason for the rule is the **D3 concurrency hazard**. External passes `--onto <ref-name>`, not a
SHA, and
re-resolves it *inside* `git rebase` at the moment each entry is reached (§2.4 D3, §5.3). A live
external run that has rebased `pr1` and not yet reached `pr3` will resolve `origin/master` for
`pr3` **after** our fetch would have moved it — so a preview that fetches can silently change the
destination of an entry another process is about to rebase. A "read-only" preview would have caused
a different rebase in someone else's run; nothing in the document is worth that. That hazard is
**entirely a property of liveness**, which is why the rule is scoped to it and to nothing else.

**Precisely what is *not* suppressed**, restated as cells because a test asserted the opposite in an
earlier draft (§15.20b):

- a **stale** guard, a **dead** lock PID, `previous sync incomplete`, a checkout transaction with
  no live lock, and every state-cell refusal that names no live *other* process — the interrupted
  run is not
  running, no ref is moving under anyone, so step 6 follows
  the route's policy exactly as it would with no state at all, and freshness is reported normally
  (`fetched`, `possibly-stale` or `local-only`). The document still carries its
  `refusal.kind: state-refused`; the two facts are independent. **A guard whose *token* is foreign
  but whose PID is alive is the opposite cell and belongs to cause 3**: `GuardLive` reports it as not
  live, the plan does not, and the fetch is suppressed with the ownership published beside the
  liveness (§4.4 `state`);
- **an artefact this invocation created, acquired or reclaimed** — the fresh new-mode external run's
  own `.sync-state.v2.yaml`/`.sync-run.lock`/sentinel, the checkout lock this run acquired, the lock
  a checkout `--continue` force-acquired and the guard a scoped resume reclaimed. Its PID is alive
  because it is *ours*; it is absent from the pre-acquisition snapshot and carries `self: true`, so
  it is neither a suppression nor a refusal, exactly as the shipped
  `pid != os.Getpid() && isProcessAlive(pid)` conjunct decides (§4.4 `state`, §8.6.1 cause 3, §9);
- a **dirty tree**, a **detached HEAD**, an **in-progress Git operation**, an I19 containment
  failure or any **row** blocker — none of them implies a concurrent tws process, and all of them
  are established over rows that exist, so none of them suppresses the fetch;
- note the one boundary the earlier draft blurred: a **selection refusal** — and, equally, an
  **unsortable stack** — is *not* in this list. Neither
  is suppressed because of liveness — nothing is running — but because both are decided at step 5,
  before the fetch, and leave no subject to fetch for (cause 2 above,
  `freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`). "Nothing is running" and "there is nothing to plan"
  are two different reasons and the document distinguishes them;
- an **empty context set** is not in this list either: a fetching route with zero resolved contexts
  runs no `git fetch` because there is none to run, not because the plan declined one, and it
