| I19 containment mismatch (cwd belongs to another working tree) | `internal/cli/checkout_sync.go:22-31` | `preflight-refused` blocker, with both paths in the detail. The document is still computable because every plan probe is `-C ws.RepoRoot`-scoped — with the single deliberate exception of the cwd-scoped prunability mirror, which is external-only (§3.7) |
| I20 on `--continue` with trigger flags against a pre-v2/absent transaction | `:44-51` | `state-refused` with `errSyncModeFlagsNeedV2` verbatim — the plan route evaluates the projected I20 itself rather than reaching the CLI check (§8.5.3) |
| previous checkout-sync incomplete (transaction exists) | `:59-62` | `state-refused`, with the transaction's stage, current index and failed entry, read from `state.files.checkout_transaction` (the plan's own inspector, not `HasCheckoutTransaction`, §8.6.1 step 2a) |
| dirty tree / detached HEAD / another Git operation in progress / lock held | `internal/checkout_sync.go:564-583`, `:185-220` | `state-refused` (§8.6.2), observed with `probeDirty`/**`gitOperationInProgress`**/`gitCurrentBranch` and, for the lock and the transaction, with the plan's **own** `Lstat`-first safe inspectors — never `ReadCheckoutLock`/`HasCheckoutTransaction`, which follow symlinks and cannot tell *absent* from *unreadable* (§8.6.1 step 2/2a) — and never taken. The Git-operation blocker is the shipped four-marker predicate exactly; `probeActiveGitOp` contributes the descriptive `state.git_op.kind` label only, and a bisect-only or malformed-`.git` repository yields **no** blocker here because the executor raises none (§8.6.2 exactness rule) |
| every continuation gate of `ContinueCheckoutSync`/`resumeTransaction` | §8.6.4 | `state-refused` with the shipped sentence |

**Guarded execution keeps the normal ladder**: I19, `--abort`/`--continue` dispatch, I20 and the
previous-transaction refusal all run first and unchanged, and the guard seam sits where §9 puts it
(after `BuildCheckoutPlan`, before `SaveCheckoutTransaction`). The plan-unavailable interception is
unaffected by the reordering: plan-only loads the stack itself (§8.6.1 step 3), and the guarded path
reaches `BuildCheckoutPlan` — and therefore its own missing-stack/missing-base/missing-branch
refusal — **before** the transaction is persisted and before the first `git checkout`
(stack load `:628-637`, plan `:640-645`, persist `:683-688`), so no mutation can precede it.

**8.6.9 The fetch context is mirrored exactly: `UniqueRepos` + `fetchQuiet` in external, a single
`RunSilentDir(opts.RepoDir, …)` in checkout.** `fetch.repos[]` was
`{repo, attempted, ok}` in every earlier draft, which quietly asserted that a fetch happens *in the
repository the token names*. It does not. **In external**, the shipped pair resolves a **context**
per token, and the
plan publishes that context because `freshness` is a statement about it:

**The fetch context is its own projection and is neither of the two per-entry context refs of §4.1**
(round-34 item 1). `fetch.repos[]` resolves one context per **`repo_token`** through the
`UniqueRepos` + `fetchQuiet` ladder below, which is a different ladder from either
`base_context` or `execution_context`: it is keyed on the token rather than on the row, it prefers
the **first** entry's worktree even for rows that resolve elsewhere, and it falls back to the
process cwd on a rule of its own. No consumer may derive one from the other in either direction, and
the `fetch-context-divergent` warning exists precisely because the fetch context and the entry
contexts can legitimately be different directories. The same independence holds for
`push.targets[].repo_root` (§4.4) and `prunability.probe_context` (§3.7).

- **`UniqueRepos(stack, featurePath)`** (`internal/stack.go:37-52`) iterates `stack.Branches` **in
  slice order** and records each `Repo` token **once**, the first time it is seen. The value it
  records is `<featurePath>/worktrees/<thatFirstEntry.Name>` **if that directory exists**, and the
  empty string otherwise. It never falls back to a *later* entry's worktree, and it never
  substitutes the `Repo` token at this stage. **Which slice it iterates depends on the route**: the
  legacy route passes the loaded stack, so the order is `stack.yaml`'s file order; the new-mode
  route passes `internal.Stack{Branches: selectedRealEntries(stack, run.Sel)}`, so the order is the
  selection's — i.e. `TopoSort`'s, which is unspecified among independent roots (consequence 1).
- **`fetchQuiet(repo, wtPath, verbose)`** (`internal/cli/sync.go:604-635`) then picks the directory
  in one fixed order: `-C wtPath` when `wtPath != ""`; else `-C repo` when `repo != ""`; else
  **no `-C` at all** — `internal.Run`/`internal.RunSilent`, i.e. the **process cwd**.

So each row of `fetch.repos[]` publishes
`{repo_token, context_root, context_common_dir, context_source, fetch_effect, context_candidates[], attempted, ok}`
with `context_source` taken from that ladder — **and that is the only shape this document
publishes** (round-18 item 2). The row keys here, the row keys in §4.4 and the row keys §15.21
asserts are one list, in one order, edited together or not at all; the same rule binds
`context_candidates[]`, whose member is
`{context_root, context_common_dir, fetch_effect, context_source, first_entry}` in all three
places. `fetch_effect` is a **member of both**, not of the chosen row alone: a candidate list that
omitted it could not express the collapse rule below, which is defined over the *pair*
`(context_common_dir, fetch_effect)` of each candidate. Any prose elsewhere that abbreviates either
tuple is a citation of these keys and never a second schema:

| First entry of the token | `Repo` token | `context_source` | `context_root` |
|---|---|---|---|
| its worktree directory exists | anything | `worktree` | that worktree path |
| its worktree directory is **absent** | non-empty | `entry-repo` | the `Repo` token's directory |
| its worktree directory is **absent** | empty | **`process-cwd`** | the process working directory, with no `-C` |

Three consequences the document must carry rather than smooth over:

1. **"First entry" means first in the map-building order, not first in any sorted order — and on the
   new-mode route that order is not determinate.** On the
   legacy route the order is `stack.Branches` as written in `stack.yaml`: a file order, stable
   across processes, so the first entry of each token is a fact and the plan publishes the resolved
   `context_root` for it. On the **new-mode** route the map is built over
   `selectedRealEntries(stack, run.Sel)` (`internal/cli/sync.go:559-566`), whose slice is
   `sel.Entries` — built in `TopoSort` order (`internal/sync_selection.go:166`), whose
   **independent-root order is unspecified and varies between processes** — and **only** that
   order, since within one root component the sequence is fixed (round-22 item 5, below)
   (§4.7). Two invocations of the identical command can therefore hand `UniqueRepos` a different
   first entry for the same token, and `fetchQuiet` can then run in a different directory. **The
   document must not promise a byte-identical chosen value it cannot reproduce**, so the rule is:

   > For every `repo_token`, the plan enumerates **`context_candidates[]`**: one
   > `{context_root, context_common_dir, fetch_effect, context_source, first_entry}` tuple per
   > selected entry of
   > that token that
   > `TopoSort` could legally place first, each resolved through the `fetchQuiet` ladder above,
   > **canonicalized**, and annotated with the canonical
   > absolute common dir and effective bare-fetch effect of that context (`git -C <context_root>
   > rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, plus the `fetch.all`/remote/refspec
   > resolution of the
   > "materially the same" rule below), then sorted by
   > `(context_root, context_source, first_entry)` — a
   > deterministic, byte-stable list on every route. The enumeration runs **before** the fetch, at
   > step 5a of §8.6.1, on the plan seam and the guard seam alike.
   >
   > **"Could legally place first" is decided by the *root component*, not by depth alone and not by
   > ancestry** (round-22 item 5, which narrows round 21's minimum-depth rule without reopening its
   > purpose). `TopoSort` is
   > Kahn's algorithm over a **FIFO** queue seeded from the zero-in-degree set
   > (`internal/stack.go:157-175`), and every entry has at most one base, so the graph is a
   > **forest**. Exactly **one** thing in it is randomized: the **root seed**, which is built by
   > ranging a Go map (`for name, deg := range inDegree`). Everything after that is deterministic —
   > `children[e.Base] = append(children[e.Base], e.Name)` is built by iterating `s.Branches` in
   > **`stack.yaml` file order**, so each parent's children are appended in file order, and a FIFO
   > queue preserves the relative order of everything already in it. Two consequences, and the rule
   > follows from their conjunction:
   >
   > - **Globally the output is strict BFS level order** — every entry at depth *d* is dequeued
   >   before any entry at depth *d+1*, because the deeper one is enqueued only while its parent is
   >   being processed and the remaining depth-*d* entries are already ahead of it in the queue.
   > - **Within one root component the order is fully determined** — level by level, children in
   >   file order — so a component's own first selected entry of token *t* is a **fact**, not a
   >   draw. Only the interleaving *between* components varies, and it varies exactly as the root
   >   permutation does.
   >
   > Therefore, for token *t*, the candidate set is: **for each root component whose subtree
   > contains a selected entry of *t*, the deterministically first such entry in that component's
   > own order, keeping only the components whose first such entry sits at the *minimum depth*
   > across components** (a component whose shallowest *t*-entry is deeper can never win a level-
   > ordered race, whatever the root permutation), **each resolved through the `fetchQuiet` ladder
   > and then deduplicated on the resolved context tuple**
   > `(context_root, context_common_dir, context_source, fetch_effect)`, the surviving member
   > keeping the bytewise-least `first_entry` so the list stays reproducible. "Selected entries of
   > *t*" means exactly the slice `UniqueRepos` is handed — `selectedRealEntries(stack, sel)`, i.e.
   > `sel.Entries` in `TopoSort` order, membership-filtered by the scope and mapped back to real
   > stack entries, archived rows included exactly as the shipped code includes them
   > (`internal/cli/sync.go:579-589`, `internal/sync_selection.go:166-221`) — so the enumeration
   > respects the run's real selection, filter and order rather than a re-derived stack.
   >
   > **Two entries of one root component never produce two candidates**, however they sit: siblings
   > under one parent are ordered by `stack.yaml`, and two entries under *different* parents of the
   > same component are ordered by their parents, which are themselves ordered by that component's
   > own deterministic sequence. Round 21's "every minimal-depth entry is a candidate" over-
   > enumerated exactly there — it read the tie at a level as a draw when only the **root** seed is
   > drawn — and over-enumeration manufactures ambiguity, and with it rank 5.0 refusals, that the
   > shipped code does not have. A **deeper** entry of the same token is still never a candidate,
   > even when it is not a descendant of the shallower one, for the level-order reason above. On the
   > legacy route the same rule is applied to the file-ordered slice, where there is no draw at all,
   > and yields exactly one candidate.
   >
   > **The rank 5.0 consequence follows directly** (§4.9): a token can be indeterminate **only when
   > its selected entries span two or more root components** that can each supply the first entry
   > *and* whose resolved contexts are not materially the same. One component ⇒ one candidate ⇒ a
   > determinate row that fetches, whatever its context turns out to be (round-21 item 7).
   >
   > **Two candidates are *materially* the same iff they write the same store *and* would perform
   > the same fetch — the pair `(context_common_dir, fetch_effect)`.** `git fetch` writes
   > `refs/remotes/**` and fetched tags into the
   > repository's **common directory**, which every linked worktree of one repository shares
   > (`--git-common-dir` resolves to the same store from each, and `refs`, `objects` and
   > `packed-refs` are all members of Git's `common_list`). **`FETCH_HEAD` is not, and round 22
   > corrects the earlier wording that put it there** (item 4): it is a **per-worktree pseudo-ref**,
   > absent from `common_list`, written into the context's own `$GIT_DIR` — `.git/worktrees/<wt>/
   > FETCH_HEAD` for a linked worktree — and truncated even by a fetch that contacts nothing. The
   > correction removes it from the *equivalence argument*, not from the mutation inventory (§0.1
   > still lists it as a write): **collapse rests only on the shared `refs/**`, `refs/tags/**` and
   > `objects/` the common dir names, plus equivalent remote effects**, which is exactly the claim
   > the rule needs — two worktrees of one repository collapse because the refs a later probe reads
   > are shared, not because their `FETCH_HEAD` files are. **The planner never reads `FETCH_HEAD`
   > anywhere** — not for freshness, not for the lease baseline, not for candidate equivalence, and
   > no probe in §13 names it — so its per-worktree-ness costs the document nothing and must not be
   > used to argue that two worktrees fetch differently. A fetch also
   > fetches whatever an
   > argument-less `git fetch` resolves **in the directory it runs in**, which is **not always one
   > remote** (round-20 item 1): with an effective **`fetch.all`** — configuration `git fetch` has
   > honoured since **Git 2.44**, which "pretends as if `--all` was passed from the command line
   > when no remote parameter was given" (2.44 release notes) — it updates *every* configured
   > remote except those carrying `remote.<name>.skipFetchAll` (or its deprecated synonym
   > `remote.<name>.skipDefaultUpdate`, last occurrence winning), **including a remote configured
   > with no URL**, which the iteration still attempts — as an **explicitly named** sub-fetch, so
   > `url.<base>.insteadOf` may rewrite the name into something reachable and the member may
   > succeed, and where it does not, that one remote fails while the others still move
   > (round-21 item 5 as corrected by round-22 item 3); and otherwise the current branch's
   > `branch.<name>.remote` when HEAD is attached and that key is set, else **the sole configured
   > remote when the context has exactly one — a step that exists only from Git 2.37, added by
   > commit `8a649be7` to `remotes_remote_for_branch`, below which the ladder falls straight to
   > `origin`** (round-22 item 1), else Git's documented default
   > **`origin`** — "when no remote is specified, by default the `origin` remote will be used, unless
   > there's an upstream branch configured for the current branch" (`git fetch` manual, verified
   > against Git 2.55.0), with the same sole-remote-then-`origin` fallback on a **detached** HEAD,
   > which carries no `branch.<name>.remote` to consult (round-21 item 5; Git's own
   > `remote_for_branch` order — the branch's remote, then the single configured remote, then
   > `origin`) — **and a default-resolved name that resolves to nothing contacts nothing and exits
   > 0**, because Git applies its URL-alias fallback only to a name that was *given*
   > (round-22 item 3): that context publishes a **resolved** effect with `remotes: []`,
   > `contacted: false`, and the document's `freshness` is `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`
   > (§4.4). **"Resolves to nothing" is decided only after Git's two legacy files, which round 23
   > adds to this ladder and the previous drafts omitted entirely** (item 5): `remotes_remote_get_1`
   > consults `$GIT_DIR/remotes/<name>` and then `$GIT_DIR/branches/<name>` whenever the config
   > remote has no URL — `valid_remote()` is `!!remote->url.nr` — and only then falls through
   > (`remote.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0). Both files can make an apparently
   > unresolvable name into a real, contacting fetch: `remotes/<name>` supplies `URL:` plus `Pull:`
   > refspecs that **append** to the configured ones, and `branches/<name>` supplies a URL and the
   > synthesised **`refs/heads/<branch>:refs/heads/<name>`** refspec, whose destination is a *local
   > branch* (§0.1, §4.3). Both go through `add_url_alias`, so `insteadOf` applies to them exactly
   > as it does elsewhere; both are skipped for a name that is not a valid nick (empty, `.`/`..`, or
   > containing a slash — so a URL-valued `branch.<name>.remote` never reaches them); neither is
   > reachable from the `fetch.all` ladder, whose `for_each_remote` iterates the **config** remote
   > list alone; and each row records which of them answered in `remotes[].source`. **The read costs
   > no process**: `remotes` and `branches` are `is_common` members of Git's `common_list`
   > (`path.c`, verified against Git 2.55.0), so both resolve to the **common** directory this rule
   > already canonicalizes as `context_common_dir`, and the probe is two `os.Stat`/reads for the
   > resolved name — never a directory walk (§13). The per-worktree caveat is therefore about
   > *resolution*, not about the files: two worktrees of one store share these files but can resolve
   > **different names** into them (different `HEAD`, different `branch.<name>.remote`, different
   > worktree config), so the legacy effect is still part of the equivalence key below, and a
   > legacy file that exists but will not read or parse makes the effect `null`, never `contacted:
   > false`. **A bare fetch may also recurse into submodules and move refs in *their* stores**
   > (round-23 item 3): the effect therefore carries `submodule_recursion`
   > `{mode, mode_source, may_recurse, reach, submodules[]}`, resolved — from round 24 (item 1) — by
   > the **last occurrence** of `fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse` in this context's own
   > ordered config, whichever key that is, else Git's default **`on-demand`**, with per-submodule
   > `submodule.<name>.fetchRecurseSubmodules` overrides, a **gitlink-and-presence** test — a
   > `160000` index entry with a `.git` file/directory at its path or a store under
   > `$GIT_DIR/modules/`, and **not** an activity test, since the fetch path consults no
   > `is_submodule_active` for a populated gitlink (round-24 item 2; `submodule.<name>.active` and
   > `submodule.active` are still read, but only to publish the informational `active` member) —
   > and a bounded enumeration (50 submodules, depth 3) whose members carry their own resolved
   > effects (§4.4). It is part of this equivalence key like every other member **except
   > `mode_source`, which is provenance and excluded** (round-24 item 1), it is what
   > `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect` and the rank 5.05 fail-closed refusal are computed from, and
   > it is the reason no text here may describe the listed contexts as the fetch's full reach. Each resolved remote carries
   > its configured URL — **`null` where it is configured without one** — its **effective** URL
   > after `insteadOf` rewriting, its configured fetch refspecs
   > **in configured order**. **`remote.pushDefault` is not part of this ladder** (round-19
   > item 2): it selects the *push* remote and no fetch consults it, so the previous draft's
   > `branch.<name>.remote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `origin` chain described a command Git does not
   > run; `remotes.default` is `git remote update`'s group key, not a fetch fallback. **The
   > "no single-configured-remote rule" claim that stood beside them is withdrawn** (round-21
   > item 5): that rule is Git's, it sits between the branch remote and `origin`, and omitting it
   > published `origin` for every single-remote clone whose remote is named anything else. Both halves are load-bearing, and the previous draft published
   > only the first:
   >
   > - **The common dir must be compared as an absolute path.** `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`
   >   legitimately answers the **relative** `.git`, so comparing raw outputs would collapse every
   >   pair of unrelated repositories onto one another — the worst possible direction for this
   >   check, since it turns "two independent clones" into "one store" and authorises a fetch in
   >   whichever one the map order picked. The plan therefore obtains it as
   >   **`git -C <context_root> rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`**, or, where that
   >   option is unavailable, resolves the plain output **against `context_root`** before
   >   canonicalizing. **No comparison anywhere in this feature is made on an unresolved `.git`
   >   string**, and a candidate whose common dir cannot be made absolute is unresolvable, not
   >   equal.
   > - **The effective fetch effect must match too, and it is compared whole.** Two worktrees of one
   >   repository share a common
   >   dir and can still be on branches whose `branch.<name>.remote` differs — one tracking
   >   `origin`, one tracking a fork — so `git fetch` in one refreshes refs the other never touches;
   >   one worktree may carry `fetch.all` (or a `skipFetchAll` the other does not) so that one
   >   bare fetch contacts three remotes where the other contacts one; and, under
   >   `extensions.worktreeConfig`, one may carry `remote.<name>.prune`/`pruneTags` or a
   >   `tagOpt` the other does not, so one fetch **deletes** remote-tracking refs and local tags
   >   that the other only adds to (round-22 item 2).
   >   Collapsing them on the store alone would publish "the fetch happened" for a set of refs that
   >   was never fetched — or hide a deletion behind an addition — which is precisely the misreading
   >   `freshness` exists to prevent. The plan
   >   therefore resolves the `fetch_effect` value
   >   `{all, contacted, may_delete_refs, may_delete_tags, may_clobber_tags, may_update_local_branches, may_delete_local_branches, local_branch_destinations, remotes[], submodule_recursion}` — `remotes[]` being
   >   `{name, source, url_configured, url_effective, url_source, refspecs[], prune, prune_tags,
   >   tag_opt}` rows, sorted
   >   by `name`, each refspec list left in **configured
   >   order**, and `submodule_recursion` the bounded recursion value of §4.4 (round-23 items 1,
   >   3 and 5) — per
   >   candidate, exactly as an argument-less `git fetch` would in that directory — the `fetch.all`
   >   remote set when that key is effectively true, else the attached
   >   branch's `branch.<name>.remote`, else the sole configured remote (Git ≥ 2.37), else `origin`,
   >   and never
   >   `remote.pushDefault` — publishes it on
   >   the row and on every candidate, and requires the **whole** value — the flag, `contacted`,
   >   both tag deletion facts and `may_clobber_tags`, **both local-branch facts and the whole
   >   `local_branch_destinations` object with its `patterns[]`, its capped `branches[]` and its
   >   complete `held[]`** (round-25 item 2, **with its rationale corrected in round 26, item 4**:
   >   `branches[]` and `held[]` are properties of the **object/ref store**, not of a working tree —
   >   Git's own `branch_checked_out()` walks *every* worktree of the store
   >   (`branch.c` `prepare_checked_out_branches`) — so two candidates that resolve to the same
   >   canonical absolute common dir have **identical** `held[]` by construction, whichever of them
   >   is standing on a covered branch, and the round-25 claim that "two worktrees of one store
   >   differ in exactly this member" is **withdrawn as wrong about Git**: it would have refused the
   >   ordinary multi-worktree stack at rank 5.0 for a difference that cannot exist. The member stays
   >   in the comparison for the case where it really can differ — candidates that resolve to
   >   *different* stores — and the store-wide result is computed once per common dir and reused for
   >   every candidate and context that resolves to it, which is also how §13 budgets it), the row set, each row's `source`,
   >   each configured
   >   and effective URL with its `url_source`, each ordered refspec
   >   list, each row's prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`, and the whole `submodule_recursion` object with
   >   its `path`-sorted `submodules[]` — its `effective_mode_source` members excepted, exactly as
   >   `mode_source` is (round-25 item 1) — to be **equal across candidates** before it
   >   collapses them. **Every one of those members comes from the same ordered
   >   `config --list -z` this rule already issues per context** (§13), including
   >   `fetch.prune`/`fetch.pruneTags`, the per-remote overrides, `remote.<name>.tagOpt` and the
   >   `url.<base>.insteadOf` rewrite rules — no extra process, no per-key ladder, and no second
   >   read (round-22 items 2 and 3). **A remote that is configured without a URL, or a selected
   >   remote name that is
   >   neither configured nor a URL, is a *resolved* effect, not an unknown one** (round-21 item 5):
   >   it is published with `url_configured: null` and its rewritten `url_effective`, the fetch is
   >   attempted, and the outcome — success where an `insteadOf` rule makes it reachable, otherwise
   >   `ok: false`/`possibly-stale` — is reported rather than being converted into an unresolvable
   >   effect (round-22 item 3). **A resolved effect that contacts nothing is likewise not unknown**:
   >   `contacted: false` with `remotes: []`, `attempted: true`, `ok: true`, and
   >   `freshness: not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`. Only the **reads** can be unknown — a candidate whose
   >   `fetch.all`/`skipFetchAll`/prune/`tagOpt`/`insteadOf`/remote-enumeration or `HEAD` read fails
   >   — or, from round 23, whose legacy `remotes/`/`branches/` file for the resolved name exists and
   >   will not read or parse, or whose recursion `mode` will not resolve —
   >   has effect `null`, which is
   >   **unknown, not equal**: among two or more candidates that is enough to prevent the collapse
   >   and the token refuses (below), while a single candidate carries it and fetches anyway
   >   (round-21 item 7).
   >
   > So a token whose candidates are two
   > worktrees of one repository on branches with the same effective fetch effect — the ordinary
   > multi-worktree external stack, and the exact shape
   > this feature exists to preview — produces **one material effect** however the map order lands,
   > and the row **collapses safely**: it publishes the chosen `context_root`/`context_source`
   > (canonically first among the collapsed candidates, so the value is reproducible), the shared
   > `context_common_dir` and `fetch_effect`, the full candidate list so a consumer can see the
   > collapse was checked,
   > fetches, and carries **no** blocker. Equality is compared on the canonicalized absolute common
   > dir, so a
   > symlinked or `/private`-prefixed spelling never splits one store into two.
   >
   > - **Collapse** whenever every candidate's common dir **and** `fetch_effect` resolve and all of
   >   them are equal — the effect compared over its whole value (`all`, `contacted`, both tag
   >   deletion facts and `may_clobber_tags`, both local-branch facts and the whole
   >   `local_branch_destinations` value, the `name`-sorted
   >   `remotes[]` rows, each row's `source`, each configured and effective URL with its
   >   `url_source`, each ordered refspec list, each row's
   >   prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`, and the whole `submodule_recursion` value, provenance labels
   >   `mode_source`/`effective_mode_source` excepted) —
   >   including checkout and the legacy route.
   > - **Publish and fetch, without collapsing anything, when there is exactly one candidate.**
   >   A single-candidate token is determinate by construction: the route has one directory to run
   >   `git fetch` in and nothing to choose between (round-21 item 7) — and, from round 22, **that
   >   is the ordinary case for a single-rooted stack, including one whose sibling's worktree is
   >   missing**, because siblings of one root component never split the candidate set (item 5). It publishes its
   >   `context_root`/`context_source` and attempts the fetch **even when the context is broken** —
   >   a directory that is not a work tree, an unreadable `entry.Repo`, a `process-cwd` fallback
   >   outside any repository, a remote that is missing, misconfigured or URL-less — with
   >   `context_common_dir`/`fetch_effect` `null` wherever those probes did not resolve, and the
   >   outcome reported where outcomes belong: `attempted: true` with `ok: false`,
   >   `fetch.outcome: failed`, `freshness: possibly-stale` where the process failed, and
   >   `ok: true` with `contacted: false` and `freshness: not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` where it
   >   succeeded without reaching a remote (round-22 item 3), and `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect`
   >   where it succeeded but its effect was `null` or its submodule reach `unknown` under an
   >   `on-demand` mode (round-23 items 1 and 3). The shipped `fetchQuiet`/`RunSilentDir`
   >   call ignores that error and the run continues (§0.1), so refusing here would refuse a run the
   >   executor performs. **`fetch_effect: null` is therefore not a refusal trigger on its own.**
   >   **The one reach that *is* a refusal is cause 5's**, and it is not a property of the candidate
   >   set at all: an effective recursion `mode` of **`yes`** over an `unknown` reach declines the
   >   fetch on a single-candidate row too, at rank 5.05, because there the recursion is certain and
   >   the stores it will contact and rewrite cannot be named (§4.9 rank 5.05, §8.6.1 cause 5). An
   >   `on-demand` mode never reaches that rank.
   > - **Refuse** when **two or more** candidates — which, by the enumeration above, means **two or
   >   more root components** (round-22 item 5) — have **different** canonical absolute common dirs,
   >   **different `fetch_effect` values** (including a differing `all`, a differing `contacted`, a remote present for one
   >   candidate and `skipFetchAll`-suppressed for the other, the same remotes in a different
   >   refspec order, one candidate pruning where the other does not, one candidate resolving its
   >   URL from a legacy `remotes/`/`branches/` file where the other resolves it from config, or a
   >   differing `submodule_recursion` — round-23 items 3 and 5), or when
   >   **any** of those two-or-more candidates' common dir or fetch effect cannot be resolved
   >   (a directory that is not a work tree, an
   >   unreadable `entry.Repo`, a `process-cwd` fallback outside any repository, or a context
   >   whose `HEAD`/config reads failed) and it therefore cannot be **shown** materially the same as
   >   its siblings: the row publishes
   >   **`context_root: null`, `context_common_dir: null`, `context_source: null`,
   >   `fetch_effect: null`,
   >   `attempted: false`, `ok: null`** with the full sorted candidate list, the document carries
   >   the rank 5.0 **`fetch-context-indeterminate`** blocker naming the token, its candidates and
   >   **which of the two axes disagreed**
   >   (`runnable: false`, §4.9), and the plan/guard route **skips the fetch entirely** with
   >   `fetch.outcome: skipped` and `freshness: not-refreshed-context-indeterminate` (§8.6.1
   >   cause 4). An unresolvable candidate refuses rather than being dropped, because "I could not
   >   tell whether these are the same store, or whether they would fetch the same thing" is not
   >   "they are the same". It skips *all*
   >   fetches of that invocation, not just the ambiguous token, because
   >   a partially-fetched preview would publish some refreshed identities and some stale ones with
   >   nothing in the document to tell them apart.
   >
   > **The refusal is required to carry its exits, and they are these three** (§4.9 rank 5.0), so no
   > text anywhere may tell an operator to "try again". The reason is not that a rerun would land the
   > same way — Go randomises map iteration, so the map order is **unstable and unspecified between
   > processes** (§4.7 consequence 1) and a rerun may well pick a different first entry. It is that
   > the refusal is decided by the candidate **set**, which is order-independent and therefore
   > identical on every rerun: "try again" would be advice to gamble on an ordering the refusal does
   > not read. The previous draft's "stable-but-unspecified" wording is **withdrawn** — it named the
   > opposite property of the one §4.7 establishes — and no text in this document, the docs or the
   > skills may call `TopoSort`'s or `UniqueRepos`'s order stable.
   > (1) **Narrow to a determinate selection** — a `--only`/`--from` selection under which the token
   > can be first from exactly one **root component**; the published `context_candidates[]` names
   > each candidate's `first_entry`, so the operator can read which selection collapses it
   > (round-22 item 5).
   > (2) **Make the candidates agree on both axes** — restore the missing worktree, correct the
   > `entry.Repo` (or the process working directory the empty token fell back to), or align
   > `fetch.all`/`skipFetchAll`, `branch.<name>.remote`, the fetch refspecs, the effective
   > prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`, any legacy `remotes/`/`branches/` definition and the effective
   > submodule recursion (round-23 items 3 and 5) so every candidate
   > resolves the same
   > `(absolute common dir, effective fetch effect)` pair; the row then collapses and the plan
   > fetches normally.
   > (3) **Deliberately take the `--no-fetch` route** — `--plan --no-fetch`, and a `--no-fetch` run,
   > need no fetch context at all. The detail must say what that is: **a different route**
   > (new-mode, local refs only, §5.3, §0.2), chosen on purpose, not a synonym for the run that
   > refused.
   > **An approval is not among the exits**: this blocker is non-waivable in v1, and a supplied token
   > leaves it exactly where it was (§5.3.1). The detail also states that the **unguarded** command
   > still fetches, unchanged, so the operator is never told a working command is broken.
   >
   > The practical effect of stating equivalence this way is that the refusal fires **only where the
   > ambiguity is material**: a stack whose worktrees all live under one repository never sees it,
   > a **single-rooted** stack never sees it at all — its one component fixes the first entry, so a
   > missing sibling worktree changes the *context*, never the number of candidates (round-22
   > item 5) — while a selection whose token spans **two root components** that resolve to genuinely
   > independent repositories — an
   > absent-worktree root falling back to `entry.Repo`, or to the process cwd — always does.

   **The unguarded route is unchanged.** A bare `tws sync <f> --only …` still builds the same map in
   whatever order `TopoSort` produced and still fetches wherever `fetchQuiet` lands — this feature
   does not sort `selectedRealEntries`, does not touch `UniqueRepos`, and does not make `TopoSort`
   deterministic (§4.7 consequence 1, §18.12). What it declines to do is *claim* a context, or
   authorise a run whose fetch it cannot name. **Legacy external stays determinate** (file order),
   **checkout stays determinate** (one `RunSilentDir(opts.RepoDir, …)`, one candidate), and neither
   can ever carry this blocker.
2. **`freshness` is about exactly those contexts.** `fetched` means every fetch this route performed
   succeeded *in the directory it really ran in*. It does **not** mean the repository a given entry
   row probes was refreshed, and no text, skill or test may read it that way. The first-entry rule
   makes the divergence concrete: **archive the first entry of a token and the token's fetch moves**
   — to the `Repo` directory, or, when the token is the empty default repo, to the **process cwd**,
   which may be an unrelated repository the operator happens to be standing in. The refs the run
   then rebases against were never refreshed, and the plan says so with the
   `fetch-context-divergent` warning (§4.4) — under a predicate that is **closed in both
   directions**:

   > `fetch-context-divergent` is emitted for a `fetch.repos[]` row **if and only if** (i) the
   > document has **at least one entry row** citing that `repo_token`, and (ii) the row's canonical
   > **`context_common_dir`** differs from the canonical common dir of **every** such entry row's
   > context — the **raw** canonical root the row was probed in, which is also the `context_id`
   > pre-image's first member, never the display `repo_root` §11 renders (round-33
   > items 1 and 2). **The comparison is on the common dir, not on the worktree root**,
   > for the same reason the candidate collapse is (consequence 1): a fetch in one worktree, or in
   > the `entry.Repo` root the worktrees were created from, refreshes the very
   > `refs/remotes/**` the rows read, so calling it "divergent" would warn about a fetch that did
   > exactly what the operator expected. **This predicate is on the store axis only**, deliberately:
   > the `fetch_effect` axis governs *candidate collapse*, where two possible contexts of one token
   > must be interchangeable before the plan may pick either, while this warning asks the weaker
   > question of whether the store the rows read was written at all. What survives the change is the case the warning exists
   > for: a fetch that landed in a **different repository** — the `process-cwd` fallback in an
   > unrelated checkout, or an `entry-repo` value pointing at another clone.
   > One warning per diverging `(repo_token, context_root)` pair, **published with `entry: null`**
   > — it is a document/repository-level fact about a fetch context, not a fact about one row, and
   > the previous draft's "one example entry context" named an **arbitrary** row, which is exactly
   > the kind of unspecified choice §4.7 forbids in a byte-stable document (round-20 item 7). The
   > detail is derived **canonically** instead: the token, the fetch `context_root` and its common
   > dir, plus the **sorted, deduplicated** list of the diverging entry contexts' canonical
   > context roots — the `base_context.repo_root`/`execution_context.repo_root` pair of each diverging row, deduplicated (bounded and explicitly truncated with a count when it is
   > long, never sampled). A row whose `context_root` is
   > **`null`** — the
   > indeterminate cell of consequence 1 — is **never** divergent: there is no context to compare,
   > and the document already carries the stronger `fetch-context-indeterminate` blocker. A row
   > whose own **common dir** is `null` is not divergent either, in **both** of the cells that can
   > produce that (round-21 item 7): the multi-candidate indeterminate row, and a *determinate*
   > single-candidate row whose `--git-common-dir` probe failed while the fetch was still attempted.
   > The predicate needs two comparable common dirs; without one it is unsatisfiable, and a warning
   > there would assert a divergence nobody measured.

   Both conjuncts are load-bearing. Without (i) the warning fires on **rows-less** documents, where
   it is meaningless: a `plannability: unavailable` document has no entry row for the fetch to
   diverge *from* — there is no repository the operator was led to believe was refreshed — and a
   `plannability: empty` document describes a run that rebases nothing, so no context is material.
   Neither ever carries the warning, whatever their `fetch.repos[]` holds (and by §8.6.1 a
   no-plan-subject document holds `[]` anyway). Without (ii) a token whose entry rows probe
   *several* directories — the divergent-cwd case of §5.4, where one arm resolves the worktree and
   another the cwd — would warn even though the fetch really ran in one of the contexts the rows
   use; the warning is about a fetch that refreshed **none** of them. A row whose `repo_token` has
   entry rows in two contexts and whose fetch matches one of them — or shares its common dir with
   one of them — is **not** divergent, and the plan
   states the split through `repositories[]` (two rows) rather than through a warning. The checkout
   `workspace-repo-root` row is likewise never divergent, by construction (see below).
3. **Fetch *order* is unspecified and is not published as one.** `syncFeature` iterates the
   resulting map with `for repo, wtPath := range repos` (`internal/cli/sync.go:543-546`) — a Go map
   range, so the order varies between processes exactly as `TopoSort`'s does (§4.7). `fetch.repos[]`
   is therefore sorted by `(repo_token, context_root)` and the document never claims an order.

**Checkout's fetch context is a different, simpler shipped fact, and is stated here rather than
inferred from the external ladder.** Checkout does not use `UniqueRepos` or `fetchQuiet` at all. Its
whole fetch is one call inside the new-mode block:

```go
if opts.NewMode {
    printSyncModeHeader(opts.Policy)
    if opts.Policy.Fetch == SyncFetchEnabled {
        fmt.Printf("Fetching %s... ", "default repo")
        if fetchErr := RunSilentDir(opts.RepoDir, "git", "fetch"); fetchErr != nil { … }
    }
}
```

(`internal/checkout_sync.go:616-625`). Five consequences, all binding:

- **Exactly one row, with a fixed shape.** A checkout `--fetch` document publishes
  `fetch.repos: [{repo_token: "", context_root: <canonical opts.RepoDir>, context_common_dir:
  <its canonical common dir>, context_source:
  workspace-repo-root, fetch_effect: <that context's effective bare-fetch effect,
  `{all, contacted, may_delete_refs, may_delete_tags, may_clobber_tags, may_update_local_branches, may_delete_local_branches, local_branch_destinations, remotes[], submodule_recursion}`
  resolved by the same ladder as any other context>, context_candidates: [<that one context, with
  its own `context_common_dir` and `fetch_effect`>], attempted: true, ok: …}]` — one
  row, the **default** token, the `workspace-repo-root` context source, which is the same
  `root_source` every checkout entry row's
  `base_context` and `execution_context` carry — in checkout the two always name one context, the workspace repository root (§4.1, §4.4) — and a **single-member** candidate list, so
  `fetch-context-indeterminate` is unreachable here by construction (§8.6.9 consequence 1) —
  **including when that context's own remote is missing or misconfigured**, which makes the fetch
  fail (`ok: false`, `freshness: possibly-stale`) and never makes it indeterminate (round-21
  item 7). The row carries the **full canonical eight-key shape** of §4.4 and §15.21; earlier drafts
  omitted `fetch_effect` from this cell and from its test, which would have made checkout the one
  place a row and its schema disagreed.
  `context_root` is `opts.RepoDir`, which is `ws.RepoRoot`, so
  it matches `RunSilentDir`'s directory byte-for-byte after canonicalization.
- **The fetch happens before the plan exists, so an *empty* checkout plan still fetches**
  (round-21 item 7). The shipped order is lock → `printSyncModeHeader` + `git fetch` → stack load →
  `BuildCheckoutPlan` → `if len(plan) == 0 { ReleaseCheckoutLock(...); return nil }`
  (`internal/checkout_sync.go:611-654`), so an empty stack, a selection that matches nothing and a
  plan that reduces to zero steps all fetch first and exit 0 afterwards. Their rows-less
  `plannability: empty` document therefore publishes this row with `attempted: true` and
  **whichever of the four attempted-row verdicts §4.4's decision table awards it** — `fetched`,
  `possibly-stale` when the fetch failed and the run continued past it, `unknown-fetch-effect` when
  its effect or reach could not be established, or `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` when it
  succeeded contacting nothing — and **never** `not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets`, which is external's zero-context cell (§4.4
  profile table, §8.6.1). **The `attempted: true` premise carries the suppression exceptions with
  it** (round-23 item 3, round-25 item 2, restated here by round-26 item 5): where a suppression
  applies *before* the fetch, this same empty document publishes `attempted: false` with
  `not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate` (cause 5) or
  `not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out` (cause 6), as it already does for a `--continue`
  (cause 1) and a live foreign owner (cause 3). It is the one place where a document with no entries still reports a real
  network effect, and the profile table models it rather than treating "no rows" as "no fetch".
- **`entry.Repo` is ignored, and the plan says so rather than projecting a per-repo fetch.**
  Checkout is single-repository by construction; a multi-repo `stack.yaml` produces **no** extra
  fetch row, because no extra fetch happens. Publishing one per token would describe a fetch the
  route never performs — the mirror-image of the external divergence this section exists to expose.
- **`fetch-context-divergent` does not apply to this row, ever** (§4.4, and the guard rule below).
  There is nothing for it to diverge from: every checkout entry row probes `ws.RepoRoot`, which is
  the fetch context, so the warning's predicate is unsatisfiable here. The cross-repo entry that
  *could* have created a divergence is already refused upstream — `ResolveSyncSelection` rejects it
  on the new-mode route (`internal/sync_selection.go:223-229`), and the fetch block only runs on
  that route — so a checkout document can never carry both a fetching row and a foreign-repo entry.
- **A fetching checkout document is always `route: new-mode`.** `--fetch` is a trigger, the mode
  default is `no-fetch` (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:107-116`), and the fetch block is gated on
  `opts.NewMode`, so `policy.fetch = fetch` and `route: legacy` cannot co-occur in checkout. A
  legacy checkout document therefore publishes `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.repos: []` and
  `freshness: local-only` (or a more specific cause, §8.6.1) — never a fetch row.

The fingerprint binds none of this (§5.3.2): it binds the **resolved input refs** the fetch produced
— `base.decision_sha`, `destination.sha`, `head.sha`, `replay.upstream_sha` — so a fetch that moved a base invalidates a token
through the identity it moved, while a context label that changed without moving any resolved ref
does not. Where a context difference *is* material it has already changed one of those identities,
and where it is not, it is incidental and must not force a re-approval.

### 8.7 The guarded execution route

A limit or an approval **without** `--plan` is a real run. Its four defining properties are fixed in
§8.7.1-§8.7.4, its seam inventory in §8.7.5, its machine contract in §8.7.6 and its token workflows
in §8.7.7. The subsections are numbered because other sections cite them.

**8.7.1 The shipped ladder runs first, unchanged.** A guarded run enters the route's **normal
preflight and refusal ladder** — the checkout ladder of §2.2 and §8.6.8, the external state cells of
§2.1, every continuation gate of §8.6.4, and I10-I14 on the new-mode route — and that ladder refuses
exactly as it does today, with its own sentences and exit 1. The guard never softens, re-words,
re-orders or re-implements a shipped refusal. This is the reason §4.9's ranks 1-4 are described as
"the shipped ladder's": by the time the guard seam is reached, none of them can still be pending.
**The one place where "by the time the seam is reached" is not automatic is a seam this feature
deliberately hoists, and the rule is enforced there by hand.** The scoped external `--continue` seam
sits **above** `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, so that a limit refusal cannot rewrite `.sync-run.lock`
(§8.7.5) — which also puts it above `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s **own** refusal ladder, whose live-guard
arm (`sync guard held by live process %d; cannot reclaim`,
`internal/sync_run_state.go:226-228`) is a shipped check like any other. So that seam evaluates the
native conditions *first*, emits their sentences verbatim and marker-free when they fire, and only
then computes the plan and the limits — before the actual reclaim (§8.7.5, steps 1-3). Hoisting a
seam never licenses skipping, re-wording or out-ranking the shipped refusal it hoisted past; where
this document hoists, it re-evaluates.
It is also why those refusals carry **no marker line** — but the rule that decides the marker is
**origin, not rank** (§4.9, §8.7.6): *every* refusal a shipped check owns is marker-free, including
the rank 5 head/base failures checkout raises inside `BuildCheckoutPlan`, and the only pre-seam-rank
refusals that *do* carry a marker are the ones the guard introduces where no shipped refusal exists
to run first — the legacy-external `plan-unavailable`
interception that replaces `syncFallback` (§8.5.5, §8.7.6), and the **live-owner concurrency
refusal** of §8.6.1 cause 3 in the cells the shipped ladder lets through. That second introduction is
the route's one deliberate addition to the ladder, and it only ever *adds* a refusal: a **checkout
lock or sync-run guard** that was **already present in the pre-acquisition snapshot** with
`presence: readable` (§8.6.1 step 2, §4.4
`state`) and whose recorded PID is **another, signalable** PID stops a guarded run at
rank 3
rather than letting it rebase against refs the same invocation declined to refresh, while the
unguarded run keeps fetching and rebasing through that cell exactly as shipped (§9, §11, §18.12).
**A checkout transaction is not one of those artefacts** — its `lock_pid` is a persisted recovery
field, never an owner signal (§8.6.1 cause 3) — and the **fail-closed** arm for an `unreadable` or
`symlink` guard is the same introduction seen from the other side: unknown liveness refuses on the
guarded route and is published as state on the plan-only one (§4.4 `state`, §8.6.1 step 2a).
**It never fires against the invocation's own artefacts**: the state and guard a fresh new-mode
external run writes before this seam, the checkout lock it acquired, and the lock or guard a
continuation force-acquired or reclaimed are excluded by the snapshot and by the `self` flag alike
(§8.6.1 cause 3), which is what keeps the introduction from turning every guarded run into a
self-refusal. The plan-only twin of the same cell publishes it as
`guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]` (§4.4), so the ladder addition is visible in
the document that authorises the run rather than only at exit 1.

**8.7.2 The same plan object, at the seam.** It computes **the same plan object** the plan-only
route would compute, from the same shared planner, **after the route's fetch and before the first
rebase** (§9). Same planner, same rules, same `refusal.kind` vocabulary — so "what `--plan` showed
me" and "what the run enforced" cannot drift apart by construction.

**8.7.3 A refusal is clean, and clean means scope-correct, not scorched** (§9). If a limit is
exceeded, an approval does not match, or a blocking row exists, it refuses with `refusal.kind`
chosen by §4.9 and exit 1: a *fresh* refusal before the first rebase removes only the state and
locks **this invocation created**; a *continuation* refusal removes nothing and preserves the
interrupted payload/legacy state/transaction byte-for-byte; and a refusal that happens after some
entry of this invocation has already rebased persists progress exactly as the shipped failure
path does, because refs have moved and the operator needs the recovery record.

**8.7.4 What persists across an interruption: the guard, never the approval.** If the run proceeds,
it re-validates per entry at the JIT seam (§5.2, §5.3) — and it persists **no token**. The rule, its
three consequences, and the total limit-source table that follows them:

> An approval authorises **one plan**. An interruption replaces the full-run plan with a
> remaining-work plan, and the two cannot share a fingerprint, because the entry set, the tips and
> the destinations all differ. Therefore **any interrupted run needs a new token**, minted by
> `--plan --continue` (human or `--json`, §8.3.5) and carrying `approval.scope: remaining-work`.
> The initial full-run token is not "still valid but narrower"; it is invalid, and presenting it is
> an `approval-mismatch`.

1. **Every route that has somewhere to persist, persists the *guard*, additively — and that
   includes a legacy checkout run.** `SyncRunState` and `CheckoutTransaction` gain **exactly two
   keys**, the effective `max_replay_per_entry` / `max_replay_total` (§10.3), so a resume is as
   guarded as the run that started it even when the operator drops the flags. They do **not** gain
   an approval key, and — the correction this round makes — they do **not** gain a `guard_enabled`
   boolean either: the previous draft's third encoding of one fact is **withdrawn**. "Guarded" is
   `any key has a value`, on disk exactly as in `guard.limits` and in the fingerprint tuple, and a
   separate boolean could only ever disagree with the values beside it (`guard_enabled: true` with
   no limit, or `false` with one) and would need its own rule for which side wins. **The presence of
   a per-key limit pointer is the sole durable guard-enabled signal**, and `--approve-plan` requires
   at least one effective limit (§8.5.1), so an approval can never be carried by a run that nothing
   guards. Two details are not optional:
   - **The limit values are persisted as pointers (or with explicit presence booleans), never as
     scalars with `omitempty`.** `0` is a legal limit meaning "refuse any entry that replays
     anything" (§8.3.2a), and an `int` with `omitempty` serialises `0` to *nothing*, so a resume
     would read the strictest possible guard as **no guard at all** — a silent, safety-inverting
     downgrade. A `*int` with `omitempty` omits only `nil`, which is exactly the additive behaviour
     boundary §10.3 requires, and keeps `absent` and `zero` distinguishable everywhere: on disk, in
     `guard.limits`'s per-key `{value, origin}` object, and in the fingerprint tuple, which binds
     that `value` — `0` and the absent sentinel being two different tuple values (§5.3.2).
   - **A legacy (no-trigger) checkout run creates a transaction, so it persists them too.**
     `RunCheckoutSync` writes a `CheckoutTransaction` **before the first `git checkout`** on *both*
     routes and sets `StateVersion` only under `opts.NewMode`
     (`internal/checkout_sync.go:652-681`). The guard keys are additive and do **not** bump
     `state_version` (§10.3), so a **newly started guarded checkout run persists its guard whether or
     not the run is new-mode**, and a pre-v2-shaped transaction written by this tws carries them.
     The previous draft's "pre-v2 checkout persists nothing" was a claim about the *shape* of the
     transaction mistaken for a claim about its *existence*; it is withdrawn.
2. **Only the legacy external route has nowhere to persist.** `.sync-state.yaml` holds exactly
   `started_at/failed_branch/pending/completed/skipped` (`internal/syncstate.go:11-17`), is written
   only by `saveIncompleteSync` on failure, and has no guard keys and no version to grow them under.
   A guarded run on that route
   therefore **repeats its limit flags on every invocation** — on the
   `--plan --continue` that mints the continuation token *and* on the approving `--continue` that
   consumes it. Dropping the flags
   there does not "inherit" the guard; it produces an unguarded continuation, which the document
   states plainly rather than implying otherwise. The other rows-less-of-persistence cell is a
   **pre-existing transaction that carries no guard keys** — one written by an older tws, or by a
   run that was simply unguarded: nothing was persisted for either key, so a continuation's flags
   **arm** it (`flags-persisted-continuation`), exactly as they do for an unguarded v2 payload.
3. **Conflicting limits are a refusal, not a merge — and the comparison is per key.** When a
   continuation supplies a limit flag that disagrees with the persisted value **for that key**,
   there is no honest answer — the persisted value describes
   the run that was approved, the supplied one describes a different guard — so the invocation
   refuses with `refusal.kind = guard-limit-mismatch` (§4.9 rank 7) **naming the key** and both
   values, in the
   shape the axis-mismatch sentences already use. A disagreement on one key refuses the invocation
   even when the other key agrees or is absent; there is no partial acceptance. **`0` participates
   like any other value**: persisted `0` versus supplied `5` is a conflict, and persisted `0` versus
   supplied `0` is the ordinary redundant-and-accepted cell.

**The per-key rule, and the total resolution table it drives.** The previous draft treated "supplied
limit flags" as an all-or-nothing operand, which left the ordinary mixed case undefined: an
operator who persisted both limits and now supplies only `--max-replay-total`, or who persisted only
one of them. Limits resolve **independently, one key at a time**, over
`{max_replay_per_entry, max_replay_total}`:

| For one key, on a `--continue` | Persisted value for that key | Supplied flag for that key | Effective value for that key (`guard.limits.<key>.value`, bound into the fingerprint) | `guard.limits.<key>.origin` (published label, **not** bound) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| inherit | present (**including `0`**) | absent | the persisted value | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` |
| confirm | present | present and **equal** | the persisted value (the flag is redundant, and accepted) | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` |
| conflict | present | present and **different** | — | refusal: `guard-limit-mismatch` naming this key |
| arm | absent | present (**including `0`**) | the supplied value — this invocation arms that key for the remaining work | `flags-persisted-continuation`, or `flags-legacy-continuation` on legacy external |
| unguarded | absent | absent | none for that key — published as `value: null` | `none` |

**There is exactly one origin domain, and it is the published enum of §4.4**: `none` / `flags` /
`persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` / `flags-persisted-continuation` /
`flags-legacy-continuation`. The previous draft's parallel `persisted` / `supplied` / `null`
spelling in this table was a second, undeclared domain for the same fact — three names for
"inherited", two for "absent" — and it is **withdrawn**: no table, document, test, skill or example
may use it.

"Present" means the persisted state carries a **value** for that key, which for a pointer-backed
`0` it does; the previous draft's scalar `omitempty` shape would have mapped persisted `0` onto the
`unguarded` row and silently dropped the strictest guard the CLI can express (§10.3).

So a continuation whose state persisted **no** limits accepts whatever is supplied (the `arm`
row applied to both keys), and a continuation that inherits one key while arming the other is
representable exactly — which is why `guard.limits` is a **per-key `{value, origin}` object** rather
than a value map beside a single label (§4.4). The document-level rule is total over
(invocation kind × persisted guard × supplied flags), and every cell names the `origin`
value each key takes:

| Invocation | Persisted guard | Supplied limit flags | Effective limits (`guard.limits.<key>.value`) | `guard.limits.<key>.origin` (per key) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fresh (any route) | — (nothing is read on a fresh run) | none | none — **unguarded by construction** | both `none` |
| fresh (any route) | — | present | the flags | `flags` for each supplied key, `none` for an absent one |
| `--continue`, v2 payload / **any** checkout transaction | **present** | none | the **persisted** values | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` |
| `--continue`, v2 payload / **any** checkout transaction | **present** | present and **identical** | the persisted values (the flags are redundant, and accepted) | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` |
| `--continue`, v2 payload / **any** checkout transaction | **present** | present and **different** for any key | the **persisted** values stay effective (see the conflict rule below) | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction`, with the rejected attempt in `guard.limit_conflicts[]` and `refusal.kind = guard-limit-mismatch` (rank 7) |
| `--continue`, v2 payload / **any** checkout transaction | **present for one key only** | present for the other key | per key: the persisted one inherits, the supplied one arms | `persisted-*` for the inherited key, `flags-persisted-continuation` for the armed one |
| `--continue`, v2 payload / **any** checkout transaction | **absent** (the interrupted run was unguarded, or its transaction predates this feature) | none | none — the continuation stays unguarded | both `none` |
| `--continue`, v2 payload / **any** checkout transaction | **absent** | present | the flags — **this invocation arms the guard for the remaining work** | `flags-persisted-continuation` |
| `--continue`, legacy external `.sync-state.yaml` | impossible (no place to persist, and no version to grow one under) | none | none — unguarded continuation, stated in the document | both `none` |
| `--continue`, legacy external `.sync-state.yaml` | impossible | present | the flags, **on this invocation only**; nothing is written | `flags-legacy-continuation` |

**An unguarded continuation cannot be approved.** The two `absent` + `none` rows above describe a
resume with no effective limit in either key. A `--approve-plan` supplied there waives nothing —
there is no violation to waive — so the invocation refuses with `refusal.kind =
approval-without-limits` (§4.9 rank 7.5, §8.5.1) rather than running as if the token had done
something: `runnable` stays `true`, the document is complete, **no token is minted** (§4.4
usable-token rule — the document publishes `approval.fingerprint: null`, `approval.usable: false`
and `approval.covers.requires_limits: true`, because a token no invocation could ever supply is not
a token), and the two exits are to add a limit flag (the `arm` row, after which the next
`--plan --continue` mints a real one) or to drop `--approve-plan`. The fresh-run form of the
same condition never reaches a document at all, because only a flag could have supplied a limit
there (§8.5.1).

**What a `guard-limit-mismatch` document actually contains.** The earlier drafts named the refusal
and left its document undefined — a dash in the "effective limits" column — which made three
questions unanswerable: what the plan evaluates against, whether a token is minted, and whether one
could clear the mismatch. All three are fixed here:

- **The persisted limits remain the effective ones**, published in `guard.limits.<key>` with their
  `persisted-payload`/`persisted-transaction` origin exactly as an agreeing resume publishes them.
  A resume is guarded by the run that created its state; a flag that disagrees does not
  half-apply, and there is no cell in which a supplied value silently wins.
- **The attempted value is published beside them, not lost**, as one `guard.limit_conflicts[]` row
  per conflicting key — `{key, effective_value, effective_origin, supplied_value}`, sorted by `key`
  (§4.4). Without
  it the operator reads "your `--max-replay-total` disagrees with the persisted one" and cannot see
  with what, and a consumer cannot distinguish a stricter attempt from a looser one. **The array is
  the fixed schema, and the shape is no longer `define`'s to pick**: the previous draft offered
  per-key fields on `guard.limits` as an equal alternative and left the choice open, which meant two
  possible documents for one fact and a `null`-vs-absent question on every non-conflicting run. The
  array is chosen because it is `[]` in the overwhelmingly common case, because it sorts and diffs
  cleanly, because it keeps `guard.limits` a clean two-key `{value, origin}` object whose members
  never change shape, and because §4.4 already fixes it as a never-`null` published row list
  (§8.3.6, §4.8). No document, test, skill or example may publish the attempted value anywhere else.
- **The document is otherwise complete and the plan is real.** Rows, aggregates, `push.targets[]`,
  `restore`, the fetch block and `guard.evaluation[]` are all computed against the **persisted**
  limits, `runnable` stays **`true`** — nothing about the work is broken — and `refusal.kind` is
  `guard-limit-mismatch` unless a rank 1-6 fact outranks it (§4.9). The invocation is refused
  because its *flag set* is inconsistent with the state it is resuming, not because the plan cannot
  be described.
- **A token is minted, and it cannot clear the mismatch.** `approval.fingerprint` is computed over
  the persisted plan like any other document (the tuple binds the **effective** limit values,
  §5.3.2) — and the persisted limit is itself what satisfies the limit precondition of §4.4, so this
  cell is `approval.usable: true` with `approval.covers.requires_limits: false` — so
  `--plan --continue` in this cell yields a usable token — but supplying it *with the
  same conflicting flag* refuses again: an approval waives only limit **violations** it was shown
  (§5.3.1), and a mismatch is a fact about the command line. The two ways forward are to drop the
  conflicting flag or to repeat the persisted value, and `refusal.detail` names both, with the key
  and both values.

**Arming a previously-unguarded continuation is deliberately
allowed**, per key, because refusing it would leave an operator who has just been surprised by a
mid-run
conflict unable to add the very limit the surprise argues for, and because it can only ever make the
resume *more* refusing, never less. **Nothing in the table can un-guard a guarded run**: omitting
a flag inherits the persisted value for that key, and disagreeing with it refuses. **A redundant,
equal flag changes nothing** — not the effective value, not the published origin, and not the
token. And **the fingerprint binds each key's effective `value`, not its `origin`** (§5.3.2):
`origin` answers *how* this invocation arrived at the same guard — inherited from persistence,
supplied on the command line, or armed on a previously-unguarded resume — and two invocations that
guard the remaining work identically must mint the identical token, or a resume that legitimately
repeats its flags would be told to re-plan. The earlier draft bound `{value, origin}` and then
argued in the same sentence that the source label was immaterial; that contradiction is resolved
here in favour of the value, and §5.3.2 lists `origin` among the explicit non-members. The label
stays **published**, so the operator still sees where the guard came from. When a continuation arms
the guard this way,
the values are **not** written back into the payload or transaction — v1 persists a guard only where
the run that *created* the state chose one, and adding a write here would turn a resume into a state
mutation the frozen-axis doctrine never contemplated (§8.5.4, §10.3).

**The continuation token binds the continuation.** Its tuple (§5.3) is computed over the
**remaining** entries, **the remaining `push.targets[]`**, the **effective persisted route and
policy** (state-derived, §0.2), the
**effective limit values per key** from the tables above, and the run's
`intent.push` and
validation identity as the resume
will really use them — persisted on v2, off the invocation on legacy external (§3.11). So a token
minted for the remaining work of a scoped v2 run cannot authorise a legacy continuation, a different
remaining set, a differently-armed guard, or a resume whose push intent or push set differs.

**And the limits themselves are re-evaluated against the remaining work, not accumulated.** A
persisted `--max-replay-total 20` inherited by a resume constrains the **remaining** entries of that
resume; the candidates the interrupted run already replayed are gone, and nothing anywhere counts
them again. Two consequences worth stating because both have been assumed the other way: a resume
can pass a total limit the original run failed (that is correct — less work is left), and a
long-running stack resumed five times is never refused merely for the sum of its parts. The flag
help says so in one sentence (§8.3.2, §14), and `approval.scope: remaining-work` on the document is
the machine-readable form of the same fact.

**Exact workflows.** With `<f>` interrupted at `pr2` and a per-entry limit of 10:

```
# v2 external or any checkout transaction, guarded run: limits persist, the token does not
tws sync <f> --plan --continue --json                  # exit 0; guard.limits.*.origin: persisted-*;
                                                       # approval.scope: remaining-work; read fp
tws sync <f> --continue --approve-plan <fp>            # guarded resume of the remaining entries

# legacy external only: nothing persists, so both invocations repeat the limits
tws sync <f> --plan --continue --max-replay-per-entry 10 --json
tws sync <f> --continue --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan <fp>

# continuation of a run that was NOT guarded (or a transaction predating this feature):
# the flags arm it for the remaining work
tws sync <f> --plan --continue --max-replay-per-entry 10 --json   # guard.limits.<key>.origin:
                                                                  #   flags-persisted-continuation
tws sync <f> --continue --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan <fp>

# conflicting limits on a guarded continuation
tws sync <f> --continue --max-replay-per-entry 50      # exit 1: guard-limit-mismatch on
                                                       #   max_replay_per_entry (persisted 10)

# partial: the state persisted only max_replay_per_entry; this invocation arms the other key
tws sync <f> --plan --continue --max-replay-total 40 --json
                                                       # per-entry: persisted-payload (persisted)
                                                       # total:     flags-persisted-continuation
                                                       #            (supplied)
```

**8.7.5 Seams: every underlying path, and every continuation.** The guard must have a seam on
**every** underlying path — external legacy (`syncFeature`, after the fetch loop and before
`syncWithStack`'s first rebase), external new-mode (`syncFeatureScoped`, same position), checkout
legacy and checkout new-mode (after `BuildCheckoutPlan`, before `SaveCheckoutTransaction`), **and
every continuation path below** — so that **no guarded invocation can fall through to an unguarded
rebase**, including the `syncFallback` path of §8.5.5. Control flags are legal on `--continue`
(§8.5.3),
so every continuation path needs a seam of its own; none of them is covered by the fresh-run seams
above, and each recomputes the plan for the *remaining* work before any remaining rebase:

| Continuation path | Guard seam | JIT seam |
|---|---|---|
| external legacy `handleSyncContinue` (`internal/cli/sync.go:311-360`) | after the state load, rebase-in-progress check, stack load and the `done` map, **before** `syncWithStackFiltered` (`:348`) | pass 1 at `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:117-135`; pass 2 before its Git call at `:196-201` (§5.4.4) |
| external scoped `handleScopedSyncContinue` (`:363-431`) | after `syncContinueMismatches`, the selection rebuild, the failed-branch checks and the foreign-guard refusal, but **before `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` (`:400-403`)** — and **below a re-evaluation of `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s own live-guard condition**, see below | same two seams |
| checkout `ContinueCheckoutSync` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:718-754`) | after the v2 mismatch/selection checks and the forced lock reclaim, **before** `resumeTransaction` | `processBranch`'s re-resolution (`:1024-1030`) for every entry `executeTransaction` still runs |
| checkout `resumeTransaction` (`:866-931`) | its `StagePlanned`/`StageRebasing` and post-conflict arms funnel into `executeTransaction`, so the `ContinueCheckoutSync` seam covers them | per entry, as above |
| checkout `resumeFromSwitched` (`:933-939`) | **a seam of its own**: it calls `doRebase` immediately, bypassing `processBranch`'s re-resolution | the check must run between entry load and `doRebase` |
| external pass 2 rows on any route | — | each row is re-checked immediately before `git rebase <base> <git_branch>` (§5.4.4) |

**Every seam in that table evaluates *published state facts* from the *pre-acquisition snapshot*,
never from a
re-read — with exactly one carve-out, whose normative statement is step 1 below and which is stated
there and nowhere else: the scoped-continuation seam
re-evaluates `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s **native** conditions from a fresh read taken immediately
before the reclaim it gates, through the shared `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable` predicate, because
that function's refusal is a claim about *now* and a stale read
would fabricate a live owner that has already exited. The carve-out is narrow by construction: it
feeds only the native arms, never a published field, never the fingerprint, and never
`guard.execute_blocked_by[]`, and it runs before this invocation has written anything, so it cannot
read this process's own guard.** The snapshot is taken at §8.6.1 step 2, at the top of the route and **before**
`setupSyncRunState`, `AcquireCheckoutLock`, `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` and `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`
(§4.4 `state`, §9). Two seams in the table would otherwise be unsound, and they are the reason the
rule is stated here rather than left to §8.6.1:

- **checkout `ContinueCheckoutSync`** — its seam sits *after* the forced lock reclaim, so a re-read
  of `.checkout-sync.lock` there returns **this process's own PID**, alive by definition. Under a
  re-read every guarded checkout `--continue` would refuse itself at rank 3; under the snapshot it
  refuses only when the lock was already held by another live process before the reclaim — which is
  precisely the case `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` itself refuses first, with its own sentence
  (`lock held by live process %d; cannot reclaim`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:281-283`), so the
  guard adds nothing there and introduces nothing.
- **external new-mode fresh runs** — the seam sits after this invocation wrote
  `.sync-state.v2.yaml`, `.sync-run.lock` and the sentinel, so the same self-refusal would follow
  from a re-read (§9). The snapshot predates all three.

The scoped-continuation seam is the one case where the ordering *and* the snapshot both matter, and
the ordering requirement below is unchanged and independent: the snapshot keeps the seam from
misreading a reclaimed guard as a foreign one, while the seam's position keeps a refusal from
rewriting the guard at all. **It is also the one seam that re-reads**, and the two facts do not
conflict: the snapshot answers "what does this document describe?", while step 1 below answers
"would the shipped `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` refuse *now*?" — a question about the present that a stale
read can only answer by inventing a live owner that has exited (step 1, below).

**The scoped-continuation seam moves above the guard reclaim, and this is a requirement, not a
preference.** `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` rewrites `.sync-run.lock` with this process's PID
(`internal/sync_run_state.go:207-232`). A limit or approval refusal that fired *after* it would have
rewritten a recovery artefact on its way to doing nothing — leaving a guard whose PID names a
process that has already exited, for a run that never resumed. Placing the seam **before** the
reclaim keeps a pre-resume refusal completely inert. It costs nothing: the seam needs only the
payload, the stack, the rebuilt selection and its own `TopoSort` + `done` map, all of which are pure
reads, and the shipped `TopoSort`/header/reclaim order below it is otherwise untouched.

**Hoisting the seam creates one hazard, and closing it is part of the requirement: the native
live-guard refusal must still fire first, in its own words.** `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` is not only an
acquisition; it is a **refusal ladder**, and the refusal that matters here is
`if guard.PID != os.Getpid() && syncProcessAlive(guard.PID) { return fmt.Errorf("sync guard held by
live process %d; cannot reclaim", guard.PID) }` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:226-228`). It is a
shipped check, so by §8.7.1 it owns its cell: its sentence is byte-fixed and its output is
**marker-free**. Moving the guard seam above the reclaim moves it above that check too, so a
guarded `--continue` under a genuinely live neighbour would hit a plan/limit/approval refusal
*first* and print the guard's words instead of the shipped ones — a rewording of a shipped refusal,
which §8.7.1 forbids, and a change in `refusal.kind` for an operator who is simply being told to
wait. The ordering at this seam is therefore **three steps, in this order**:

1. **Evaluate `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s own conditions, exactly as written, without reclaiming — from
   a *fresh* read taken here, not from the step 2 snapshot, and through the **same code** the
   shipped function runs.** In
   the shipped order: guard file absent ⇒ nothing refuses (the reclaim would simply create it); read
   error ⇒ `read sync guard: %w`; YAML error ⇒ `invalid sync guard %s: %w`; `guard.PID <= 0` ⇒
   `sync guard is being initialized or is invalid; retry or inspect %s`; and
   `guard.PID != os.Getpid() && syncProcessAlive(guard.PID)` ⇒
   `sync guard held by live process %d; cannot reclaim`. Each is emitted **verbatim**, at exit 1,
   **with no marker line**, and with `refusal.kind: state-refused` — because the **origin** is the
   shipped function, not the guard (§4.9, §8.7.6 origin rule). The evaluation is a pure read; it
   must not call `removeLockIfUnchanged` or `writeSyncGuardExclusive`, and it must not reorder or
   merge the five conditions. This also keeps the pre-existing `state.GuardForeign()` refusal above
   it (`internal/cli/sync.go:397-399`) exactly where it is.

   **How that is guaranteed, rather than asserted: one extracted predicate, two callers, and a
   return type that carries the evidence.** A second
   hand-written implementation of those five conditions is exactly the kind of duplication that
   drifts on the first edit, and a re-derivation from the plan inspector's `unreadable_reason` would
   not even start equal (see the next paragraph). The recommendation is therefore a **pure
   refactor**: extract
   ```go
   // syncGuardReclaimCheck is the evidence checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable judged:
   // absent reports the os.IsNotExist arm, and originalBytes are the exact bytes
   // the verdict was reached over — the bytes removeLockIfUnchanged must compare.
   type syncGuardReclaimCheck struct {
       absent        bool
       originalBytes []byte
       guard         SyncRunGuard // zero value when absent
   }

   // checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable returns the error ReclaimSyncRunGuard would
   // return before it writes anything, and — when the reclaim may proceed — the
   // evidence it reached that verdict over. It performs exactly one os.ReadFile
   // and writes nothing.
   func checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable(featurePath, ownerToken string) (syncGuardReclaimCheck, error)
   ```
   containing the shipped body **verbatim** — the same `os.ReadFile(SyncRunGuardPath(featurePath))`,
   the same `os.IsNotExist` early success, the same `yaml.Unmarshal` into `SyncRunGuard`, the same
