   `guard.PID <= 0` test, the same `guard.PID != os.Getpid() && syncProcessAlive(guard.PID)`
   conjunct, and the same four `fmt.Errorf` format strings (`internal/sync_run_state.go:207-232`).
   The caller becomes, exactly:
   ```go
   func ReclaimSyncRunGuard(featurePath, token string) error {
       path := SyncRunGuardPath(featurePath)
       if err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(path), 0700); err != nil {
           return fmt.Errorf("create sync guard directory: %w", err)
       }
       check, err := checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable(featurePath, token)
       if err != nil {
           return err
       }
       if check.absent {
           return writeSyncGuardExclusive(path, token)
       }
       if err := removeLockIfUnchanged(path, check.originalBytes); err != nil {
           return fmt.Errorf("reclaim sync guard: %w", err)
       }
       return writeSyncGuardExclusive(path, token)
   }
   ```
   and the hoisted precheck calls the **same function** and nothing else, discarding the check
   value. **The return contract is the correction this round makes, and it is a correctness fix,
   not a style one** (round-17 item 1). An `error`-only predicate cannot express the two facts the
   reclaim needs after it: *which* arm succeeded, and *over which bytes*. Round 16's
   "`MkdirAll` → predicate → the two writes it already performs" therefore left the caller with
   only one way to obtain either — a **second `os.ReadFile`** — and that second read is unsound in
   both directions. It loses the `absent`/`present` distinction, so the caller either calls
   `removeLockIfUnchanged` on a guard that never existed (a `%w`-wrapped `ENOENT` where `main`
   simply creates the file) or re-derives absence from a different read than the one it judged. And
   it **destroys the compare-and-swap**: `removeLockIfUnchanged(path, data)` is only a CAS because
   `data` are the bytes the decision was made over, so anchoring it to a *fresh* read compares the
   file against itself, always succeeds, and silently removes a guard another process wrote inside
   the window — turning the one mechanism that makes the hoisted precheck safe into a no-op.
   Returning `{absent, originalBytes}` makes the CAS **anchored to the judged bytes** by
   construction and keeps the whole function at **one** `os.ReadFile`, which is also what `main`
   does. The refactor is then behaviour-preserving **byte-for-byte**: same syscall count, same
   order, same errors, same wrapped `%w` chains — which is what makes "the plan-guard never re-words
   a shipped refusal" a property of the code instead of a promise in a document. Three details are
   part of the extraction and are stated so they are not "tidied" away: the `os.MkdirAll` stays in
   `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, **outside** the extracted predicate, because the precheck must write
   nothing (§8.7.5 step 3, §9); the `reclaim sync guard: %w` wrapper stays in the caller too,
   because it reports a **write** that failed and is not one of the five refusal arms; and
   `ownerToken` is accepted **for call-shape parity with `ReclaimSyncRunGuard(featurePath, token)`**
   and is consulted by **no arm** — ownership is not part of any reclaim condition
   (`internal/sync_run_state.go:207-232`), and §15 asserts that passing a different token changes
   no verdict, so the parameter can never become a silent second predicate. §15 asserts the
   equivalence directly rather than trusting the diff (§15.16c e3a).

   **The same design principle governs the optional checkout hoist, if `define` takes it** (§19.24):
   `checkForceAcquireCheckoutLockReclaimable(featurePath string) (checkoutLockReclaimCheck, error)`
   with `{absent, originalBytes, info}`, one `os.ReadFile`, `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` reduced to
   `MkdirAll` → check → (`absent` ⇒ `writeLockExclusive`) / (`removeLockIfUnchanged(lockPath,
   check.originalBytes)` → `writeLockExclusive`), and no token parameter at all because the shipped
   function takes none (`internal/checkout_sync.go:262-288`). The shape is the requirement; the
   hoist itself remains the open choice.

   **The plan inspector is *not* the source of these arms, and must never be mapped onto them.**
   §8.6.1 step 2a's guard inspector is `Lstat`-first, refuses to follow symlinks, and classifies a
   path into `{absent, readable, unreadable, symlink}` with an `unreadable_reason`. The shipped
   reclaim does none of that: `os.ReadFile` **follows** a symlink and reads its target, a directory
   at the guard path yields a *read* error (`read sync guard: %w`, not `not-regular-file`), and an
   empty or structurally-odd YAML document decodes to a zero `SyncRunGuard` and lands on the
   `guard.PID <= 0` arm rather than on any "unreadable" one. Translating `unreadable_reason` into
   these messages would therefore change *which* sentence an operator sees, and in the symlink case
   would change the *answer*: the plan's `presence: symlink` says "not decoded", while the shipped
   reclaim happily reads through it. **So the two live side by side with fixed, non-overlapping
   jobs**: `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable` decides the native arms and their sentences, keeping the
   shipped directory/symlink/`os.ReadFile`-follow behaviour exactly as it is today at this step; the
   inspector remains **diagnostic only**, feeding `state.files.external_run_guard`, the live-owner
   fact and `owner-artefact-undecodable`, and never a native message. The two can legitimately
   disagree about the same file — a symlinked guard is `presence: symlink` in the document *and*
   readable to the reclaim — and that is a published fact, not a defect. Ordering closes the one
   hazard it creates: the guard's **own** `owner-artefact-undecodable` blocker is a controlled-route
   refusal that may, where §19.22 puts it, fire **earlier** than step 1 and stop the invocation
   before the native arms are ever evaluated. That is allowed, because it is the guard's own
   marker-carrying refusal in its own words; what is forbidden in every ordering is the reverse —
   the guard **never** emits a native sentence it did not obtain from
   `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable`, and never fabricates `sync guard held by live process %d` from an
   artefact it could not decode.

   **Why this one read is fresh, and why that does not weaken the snapshot rule.** The step 2
   snapshot exists so that *plan facts* and the *fingerprint* describe one coherent moment, and so
   that no seam refuses an invocation against an artefact **this** invocation created (§4.4 `state`,
   §9). Neither purpose is served by answering a **native shipped precondition** from it. The
   `sync guard held by live process %d; cannot reclaim` sentence is a claim about **now**: it tells
   an operator that another run is in progress and that they should wait. If the owner exited in the
   window between step 2 and this seam — a window that spans the stack load, `TopoSort`, the
   selection rebuild and the whole plan computation, and that is *longest* on exactly the large
   stacks where a neighbour is most likely to finish — a snapshot-sourced evaluation would print a
   **fabricated live refusal** naming a PID that is already gone, and would keep printing it for as
   long as the operator retried, because every retry re-reads the same dead guard and re-derives the
   same stale answer only if it, too, reads stale. Emitting a shipped sentence about a state that no
   longer holds is a **re-wording of a shipped refusal by another means**, which §8.7.1 forbids as
   firmly as changing its text.

   **The fresh read is safe in exactly the way the snapshot is, and for a checkable reason.** It is
   performed **before** any acquisition or reclaim on this route and **before this invocation has
   written any artefact of its own** — the scoped continuation writes nothing until step 3 — so it
   cannot read this process's own guard, which is the failure mode the snapshot rule exists to
   prevent. The self conjunct `guard.PID != os.Getpid()` is still evaluated, exactly as the shipped
   function does, as a second line of defence.

   **The race is bounded, named, and deliberately left where the shipped code already leaves it.**
   Between step 1's read and step 3's reclaim there is a window in which the guard can change: an
   owner can exit (the guard goes stale), a new owner can appear, or the file can be replaced.
   Three things follow, and none of them is a new hazard this feature introduces. First, the window
   is **smaller than the shipped one**, not larger: `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` itself already reads,
   decides, and only then calls `removeLockIfUnchanged` + `writeSyncGuardExclusive`, so the same
   read-decide-write gap exists on `main`; hoisting a precheck above the plan adds a second read,
   never a second write. Second, the **authoritative** check is still the reclaim's own: step 1 is a
   *precheck*, and step 3 re-runs the identical conditions inside `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` immediately
   before writing — so a new live owner that appears inside the window is caught there, with the
   same sentence, and the operator sees no difference. Third, the shipped
   `removeLockIfUnchanged(path, data)` compares the bytes **the reclaim's own verdict was reached
   over** — `check.originalBytes`, never a re-read (see the return contract above) — against the
   bytes on disk before
   removing them, so a guard replaced inside the window is not silently clobbered; that
   compare-and-swap is untouched by this feature and is the reason the second read is safe to
   perform at all. What the precheck is *for* is the opposite direction — an owner that has
   **exited** — which is why it must be fresh rather than snapshot-sourced, and why a disagreement
   between the document's `state.files.external_run_guard` and the guarded twin's behaviour is
   expected rather than a bug.

   **The division of labour is fixed and total**: the **snapshot** supplies every published
   `state.*` field, every plan fact, every blocker projection, `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` and the
   fingerprint; the **fresh read** supplies the answer to "would `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` refuse right
   now?" and nothing else. It is never published as `state.files.external_run_guard`, never
   substituted into the fingerprint, and never used to derive `live-owner-concurrency` or
   `owner-artefact-undecodable` — those stay snapshot-derived, so a document and its guarded twin
   still describe one moment. The two can therefore legitimately disagree, and the disagreement is
   the honest one: the document says "when I looked, PID 4242 held the guard", and the invocation
   proceeds because PID 4242 has since exited. This is the **only** carve-out from the
   snapshot-substitution rule in the whole document (§4.4 `state`, §9).
2. **Only if step 1 passes, compute (or revalidate) the plan and evaluate the limits and the
   approval** — still
   above the reclaim, so a `limit-total`, `limit-per-entry`, `approval-mismatch`,
   `guard-limit-mismatch` or `revalidation-mismatch` refusal leaves `.sync-run.lock` **byte-identical**
   (§8.7.3, §12). This is the property the hoist exists for, and it survives step 1 because step 1
   writes nothing either.
3. **Only if step 2 passes, call `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`** and continue into the shipped
   `TopoSort`/header/resume order, unchanged. The reclaim is the **first** write of the invocation,
   and it happens strictly after step 1's fresh read and step 2's verdict — so the ordering is
   *read (snapshot) → read (native precheck, fresh) → decide → **the reclaim's own single
   authoritative read** → compare-and-swap over exactly those bytes → write*, with no write between
   any of the reads. The reclaim's internal read count is **unchanged from `main`**: one
   `os.ReadFile`, whose bytes are carried to `removeLockIfUnchanged` through the check value rather
   than fetched again (step 1's return contract). This feature therefore adds exactly one read — the
   hoisted precheck — and no write anywhere.

Two consequences are binding. **The plan-guard never re-words the native refusal**: it does not
translate "held by live process" into `live-owner-concurrency` prose, does not attach the marker
line to it, and does not let a limit refusal pre-empt it — the operator under a live neighbour gets
the same sentence and the same exit code as on `main`. And **the guard is never rewritten on a
limit refusal**: because step 2 sits above the reclaim, and step 1 wrote nothing, the refusal is
inert on disk in every one of its cells. There is no ordering that satisfies both properties other
than this one, which is why it is stated as a requirement.

**The plan-only route projects step 1 as state, and projects nothing else.** A `--plan --continue`
against a live foreign guard publishes the same observation as a rank 3 `state-refused` blocker
carrying that shipped sentence in `refusal.detail` (§8.6.2, §8.6.4), `runnable: false`, and — where
the snapshot's owner-signalling fact also holds — `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]`
(§8.6.1 cause 3). It reclaims nothing, refuses nothing and exits 0, exactly as every other
projection does. **It performs no fresh read**, because it has no seam and reclaims nothing: the
document is a snapshot document end to end, and the fresh read of step 1 exists only on the
**guarded** continuation, immediately before the reclaim it gates. A plan-only document may
therefore name an owner that has since exited — which is what "observed at snapshot time" means
everywhere else in this document — and the guarded twin run a moment later may proceed. That is not
a contradiction between the two routes; it is the same TOCTOU window §5.3/§9 already bound, and it
is why the guarded route re-reads the one predicate whose whole content is a claim about *now*. **§8.7.1's marker rule is unchanged by this subsection and is restated for the one
cell it touches**: the live-guard reclaim refusal is a *shipped* refusal, so it is marker-free on
the guarded route; the live-owner concurrency refusal the guard **introduces** in cells where no
shipped check refuses first still carries its marker line (§8.7.6). The two must not be collapsed
into one message, and §15's scoped-continuation tests assert the sentence, the marker's absence,
the exit code and the byte-identical guard file together.

Behaviour at those seams:

- **Plan-only continuation** describes the remaining work and nothing else (§8.6.4); it takes no
  lock, reclaims no guard, and never fetches.
- **Guarded continuation recomputes and re-validates before any remaining rebase.** The remaining
  rows are re-planned from live facts — the earlier entries have already moved refs — and the
  effective limits are evaluated against those, not against the numbers of the interrupted run.
- **Every guarded continuation that needs a waiver uses a continuation-scoped token** minted by
  `--plan --continue` (§8.7.4). No route persists an approval, so a v2 continuation and a legacy
  external one differ only in where the *limits* come from — persisted state versus repeated
  flags — never in whether the token has to be fresh. A supplied full-run token is refused as
  `approval-mismatch`, and a supplied limit that contradicts a persisted one as
  `guard-limit-mismatch` (§4.9 ranks 7-8).
- **A continuation never fetches**, so its plan carries `fetch.attempted: false` and
  `freshness: not-refreshed-continuation` (§8.6.4).
- **A continuation refusal preserves the interrupted state exactly.** The fresh-run teardown of §9
  never runs on a continuation: the v2 payload, the legacy `.sync-state.yaml` and the checkout
  transaction are the operator's only recovery record, and this invocation did not create any of
  them. A pre-resume refusal (the seams above) leaves them byte-identical, leaves the scoped guard
  untouched because it refuses before the reclaim, and — in checkout — releases only the lock this
  invocation force-acquired (`forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, `internal/checkout_sync.go:740`) per
  the existing safe semantics, while the transaction survives for the next `--continue`/`--abort`.
- **A JIT refusal after ownership has been reclaimed keeps the recovery state and does not
  hand-edit the guard.** Once the scoped resume has reclaimed the guard and rebased at least one
  remaining entry, refs have moved, so the refusal takes the route's **shipped failure path** for
  the entries completed so far (`syncFailure`, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:256-262`, dispatching to
  `saveScopedSyncFailure` on the v2 route, `internal/cli/sync_modes.go:453-472`, and to
  `saveIncompleteSync` on the legacy one, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:264-281`) and stops before
  the refused entry's rebase. The guard file is left exactly as a shipped mid-run failure leaves
  it — owned by this PID, and therefore **stale** the moment the process exits, which is precisely
  the state `ClassifyExternalSyncState`'s liveness check and `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` are built to
  handle (`internal/sync_run_state.go:223-232`, `:343-431`). The refusal **never** deletes the
  payload, the legacy state, the transaction or the guard, and never calls `clearSyncRunState`: a
  live guard belongs to another process and is a shipped refusal (§8.6.2), a stale one is reclaimed
  by the next `--continue`, and deleting either would destroy the record of the work that already
  happened. **And it says so**: this is exactly the cell whose refusal states that the recovery state
  is preserved and prints the `--plan --continue` → guarded `--continue` workflow, with the
  `state-preserved: ` detail token on the marker line (§12, §8.7.6) — unlike a pre-resume refusal at
  the seams above, which suggests no `--continue` at all because it changed nothing. **The token's
  meaning is "this invocation advanced or took ownership of something, and the record of that is
  intact", not "state exists on disk"**, and the distinction is the whole reason a pre-resume
  refusal omits it: the interrupted payload/legacy state/transaction it found is byte-identical
  afterwards, so there *is* preserved state — this invocation simply did not create, advance or
  reclaim any of it, and printing the token would tell an operator that the refusing invocation
  produced the recovery record it is looking at. A pre-resume refusal must still say, in prose, that
  the interrupted run's recovery record is untouched and that the remedy is to fix the named fact
  and re-issue the **same** invocation; what it must not do is print `state-preserved: ` or imply
  that `--continue` would resume something this invocation started (§12).

**8.7.6 The machine contract for guarded execution.** A guarded *executing* invocation produces
**no JSON**: `--json` is valid only with `--plan` in v1 (§8.5.1, §8.3.6), and no
"guarded-execution refusal document" exists in this design.

- **Refusal — one anchored, guard-written marker line, at any position on stderr.** Exit 1, and
  exactly one **line the guard wrote**, matching

  ```
  ^plan-guard: <kind>: <sanitized-detail>$
  ```

  where `<kind>` is the `refusal.kind` token chosen at the guard seam (§4.9) and `<sanitized-detail>`
  names the entry and the fact, e.g.
  `plan-guard: limit-per-entry: pr2 replays 40 candidates (limit 10)`. **One part of the detail is
  fixed rather than free prose**: a refusal taken at or after the **JIT seam**, once this invocation
  has rebased at least one entry or has reclaimed an interrupted run's guard, begins its detail with
  the literal token `state-preserved: ` and ends it with the resume workflow, e.g.
  `plan-guard: revalidation-mismatch: state-preserved: pr2 base moved (approved <sha>, now <sha>); continue with --plan --continue`
  (§12). A **pre-mutation** refusal never emits that token, so the marker alone distinguishes
  "nothing moved" from "something moved and the recovery record is intact"; it is a prefix of the
  single detail, never a second line, and it goes through the same sanitation as the rest. The **previous draft promised
  this as the "first stderr line", and that promise is impossible**: by the time the guard seam runs,
  Cobra, the root command, the mode header's error paths and — on a fetching route — `git fetch`'s
  own stderr under `--verbose` (`internal.RunDir`, `internal/exec.go:126-134`) may all have written
  to stderr already, and Cobra additionally re-prints a returned `RunE` error, so a "first line"
  contract would be both unachievable and duplicated. The contract is therefore **anchoring and
  guard authorship, not position — and it is scoped to what the guard controls**:
  - the guard writes **exactly one** line matching `^plan-guard: ` per invocation, and it is
    structurally incapable of writing a second (the mechanism below);
  - **passthrough output is uncontrolled and the contract does not pretend otherwise.** Git's own
    stderr, a `--verbose` fetch, Cobra's usage block and a shipped refusal's sentence all flow to
    the same stream, and a branch name, a commit subject or a path may contain the literal
    `plan-guard: ` anywhere in them. The document therefore promises **one guard-written line**, not
    "the substring occurs once in the stream". Consumers parse the **anchored** line — start of
    line, then the prefix, then a `<kind>` from the closed enum of §4.9 — which is what makes a
    mid-line occurrence in passthrough text harmless, and it is the only parse any doc, skill or
    test may teach;
  - **it is decided by origin, not by rank.** It is emitted **exactly** for refusals the guard
    itself generates: every verdict ranked at the **guard seam** (§8.7.5) — the row blockers it can
    still see and its own rank 6-12 kinds — every **JIT seam** refusal, which is where
    `revalidation-mismatch` (§4.9 rank 9) and any newly-exceeded limit fire, and the kinds the guard
    *introduces* rather than inherits, for which no shipped check exists to run first: the
    legacy-external `plan-unavailable` interception
    of §8.5.5, where the shipped behaviour is `syncFallback` and there is no sentence to preserve,
    the first four §8.6.2 introductions — `repo-unavailable`, `probe-failed`,
    `branch-checked-out-elsewhere` and `context-dirty` — each of which refuses *before* a `git`
    invocation that would have failed anyway, the rank 4.5 `restore-blocked` of §4.4/§8.6.4a, which
    refuses before a `restoreOriginal` the shipped arm attempts only after rebasing everything,
    and the rank 5.0 `fetch-context-indeterminate` of
    §8.6.9, which the guard introduces over a fetch the shipped route performs without complaint, so
    there is likewise no shipped sentence to keep, and the rank 3 **live-owner concurrency refusal**
    of §8.6.1 cause 3 **in the cells the shipped ladder lets through** — a live foreign guard, or any
    live owner in a cell that does not refuse this verb — where the guard is again the only thing
    refusing; where a shipped state cell already refuses the same observation, that sentence and its
    marker-free output win (§8.7.1). **The external completion gate is the contrast**:
    a push-stage resume that fails `staleStackEdgesFiltered` refuses with the shipped
    `Sync incomplete; stale stack edges remain:` output and **no** marker, because the shipped
    function owns it (§8.6.4a, §15.16l2 vi);
  - **every pre-seam shipped refusal keeps its shipped output and carries no marker — whatever its
    rank.** That includes the obvious rank 1-4 ladder (state cells, selection refusals, continuation
    gates, I19/I20, the dirty/detached/Git-op ladder, and the **new-mode**
    `sync modes require a stack; feature %q has no readable stack.yaml` literal) **and the rank 5
    cases a rank-based rule would have got wrong**: checkout's `head-ref-missing` and base-resolution
    failures raised *inside* `BuildCheckoutPlan` (`resolve branch %q`,
    `internal/checkout_sync.go:500-503`, and the base resolution below it) abort the whole plan build
    **before** the guard seam exists, so they are shipped refusals with shipped text and no marker,
    even though `head-ref-missing` is a kind the guard owns elsewhere. The previous draft's
    "ranks 5-12 carry the marker" was therefore false for a real, reachable cell; **origin** is the
    only rule that is true in every cell. **It also includes the shipped refusals a hoisted seam now
    runs *past*, which are re-evaluated rather than skipped**: `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s own arms —
    most visibly `sync guard held by live process %d; cannot reclaim`
    (`internal/sync_run_state.go:226-228`) — sit below the scoped-continuation seam in source order
    but are evaluated **before** the guard's plan and limits at that seam, and they keep their
    sentences and their marker-free output exactly as if the seam had never moved (§8.7.1, §8.7.5
    steps 1-3). The live-owner concurrency marker is for the cells where **no** shipped check
    refuses; it must never be printed over one that does. A consumer that needs a pre-seam refusal in structured form
    runs `--plan`, where it is projected as a blocker with the same sentence (§8.6.2, §8.6.4);
  - everything else on stderr is human prose and may change.

- **The mechanism, because "exactly one guard-written line" is not achievable by wishing.** The
  guard writes the marker **itself, directly, exactly once**, and the error it returns is
  **marker-free**:

  1. at the refusing seam, the guard calls a single helper — one call site per seam — that does
     `fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "plan-guard: %s: %s\n", kind, detail)`. It writes through
     `cmd.ErrOrStderr()`, not `os.Stderr`, so tests can capture it with Cobra's own plumbing and the
     plan path's stream discipline (§8.3.7) is respected;
  2. it then returns a plain error whose text is the **same sentence without the prefix** (and
     `cmd.SilenceUsage` is left alone — a usage block after a guard refusal is ugly but harmless,
     and suppressing it would be a shipped-behaviour change this feature has no licence to make);
  3. because the returned error never contains the literal `plan-guard: `, **no re-print can
     duplicate the marker**. This matters concretely: production `cli.Execute()` does **not** set
     `SilenceErrors`, and additionally prints the returned error itself
     (`internal/cli/root.go:53-56`), so a returned `RunE` error reaches stderr **twice**. A marker
     embedded in the error text would therefore appear twice in production while appearing once
     under the golden helper, which *does* set `SilenceErrors`
     (`syncExecute`, `internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go:1119-1126`) — a contract that passes its own
     tests and fails in the field;
  4. `kind` is a closed-enum token by construction, and `detail` is escaped so it **cannot open a
     second anchored marker line**: it goes through `ancestrySanitize`
     (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:551-570`) to one line with control characters removed, **`CR` and
     `LF` escaped rather than emitted** — so the detail can never start a new line at all — and any
     leading `plan-guard: ` ambiguity in the sanitized result explicitly neutralised, so the detail
     cannot be mistaken for the start of a marker even if the stream is re-wrapped. An
     attacker-chosen branch name or commit subject can otherwise reach `detail` (§11); it may still
     *contain* the substring mid-line, which is exactly why the published contract is an **anchored,
     guard-written line** rather than a substring count over a stream the guard does not own.

  **Test through production `cli.Execute()`, not the golden helper.** The single-line property is a
  property of the *whole* process stderr under the real error-printing path; asserting it through
  `syncExecute`, whose `SilenceErrors = true` suppresses exactly the second print, would prove
  nothing about what an operator sees. §15.16a fixes this: the marker assertions run the production
  entry point.

  Tests therefore assert exactly one **anchored** `^plan-guard: <kind>: ` line at **any position**
  in the stderr stream **under `cli.Execute()`**, assert the returned error text contains no marker,
  assert that an attacker-controlled branch name or commit subject carrying a literal `plan-guard: `
  into the detail still yields exactly one anchored guard line, and
  assert the marker's absence for the shipped pre-seam refusals — including the checkout
  in-`BuildCheckoutPlan`
  cases (§15.16a).
- **The marker carries no fingerprint at all**: an agent that needs the structured detail, the
  blocker rows, or a token **runs `--plan` with the same flags** and reads the document there
  (§8.7.7).
- **Success**: the run prints **exactly the ordinary shipped prose of the underlying route** — the
  `[+]`/`[-]`/`[?]` status lines, the mode header where the route already prints one, `Sync
  complete.` — and adds nothing. A guarded run that succeeded is indistinguishable on stdout from
  the same run unguarded, which is what keeps the guard from becoming an output contract of its own.
- **Token acquisition never happens here.** An executing invocation does not print, echo, embed or
  otherwise yield an `approval.fingerprint`, on refusal or on success. The supported workflows
  are fixed in §8.7.7.

**8.7.7 Token acquisition: the workflows, and the flag-identity rule.** A fingerprint exists only
inside a `--plan` document — as `approval.fingerprint` under `--json`, and as the labelled final
line of the human rendering (§8.3.5) — so obtaining one is always a `--plan` invocation, with or
without `--json`. Which
workflow an operator or agent is in depends only on whether they planned first.

**Flag-identity rule (binding for all of them).** Let `T` be the trigger flags of the run
(`--fetch/--no-fetch/--full/--local-only/--only/--from`), `L` its limit flags
(`--max-replay-per-entry`, `--max-replay-total`), `P` its `--push` presence and `V` its
validation-affecting flags (`--test`, checkout only — external ignores it, §3.11). Then:

```
plan     : tws sync <f> --plan [--json] T L P V
execute  : tws sync <f> T L P V --approve-plan <fp>
```

The executing invocation carries the **same `T`, `L`, `P` and `V`**, drops only `--plan`/`--json`,
and adds `--approve-plan`. **`L` is never empty on either side of a fresh guarded pair, and round 30
states the second half of that** (item 1): `--approve-plan` requires
at least one *effective* replay limit, so a fresh invocation that supplies a token and no limit flag
is a flag error before any document exists — **and the `--plan` invocation that carried no limit
minted no token to supply**, because a limitless document fails clause (b) of §4.4's usable-token
predicate and publishes `approval.fingerprint: null` (§8.5.1). So the "minted without `L`, replayed
with `L`" pair is not a mismatch, it is a pair that cannot be constructed, and no rule, workflow,
snippet or test may describe it. On a continuation the requirement is
met by the persisted values, which is why the workflows below drop `L` only where the state carries
it. `T` decides which run is described (§0.2); `L`, `P` and the validation
identity `V` produces are inside the
fingerprint tuple (§5.3), so changing any of them invalidates the token: a token minted **under one
effective limit** does **not** authorise a run guarded at a different value, or one that arms the
other limit key as well, a token minted with `--only pr2` does
not authorise a bare run, and — the case with teeth — **a token minted without `--push` does not
authorise a run that force-pushes every synced branch afterwards**. All of them surface as
`approval-mismatch`, not as a silent pass. The one shape that is **not** an `approval-mismatch` is
dropping `L` on the executing side: that is a flag error before any document exists, and its
`--plan` twin minted nothing in the first place (round-30 item 1, §8.5.1, §15.16g). On a continuation the rule is read against the
**effective** values of §8.7.4: on v2 routes `L`, `P` and `V` come from the state and the flags are
redundant (and, for `L`, refused when they disagree); on the legacy external route they must be
repeated on both invocations.

**Workflow A — proactive (two invocations, the recommended shape).**

```
1. tws sync <f> --plan --json --max-replay-per-entry 10      # exit 0; read approval.fingerprint
2. tws sync <f> --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan <fp> # guarded run
```

Step 1 always exits 0 and always publishes a token whenever all three clauses of §4.4's usable-token
predicate hold — there is a plan to approve, **a limit is in force** (both of which this workflow's
flags guarantee) and **`encoding_issues` is `[]`**, which is a property of the repository rather than
of the flags and is the one clause this workflow cannot guarantee — whether or
not `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` is `true`
(§8.3.5), so an agent decides from `runnable`, `guard.would_refuse` and `refusal.kind` and never has
to start a mutating run to learn anything. Dropping `L` from step 1 is the one way to make it publish
`Approval fingerprint: none` over a perfectly good plan — and the consequence is that **step 2 has
nothing to supply**, not that step 2 would be told `approval-mismatch` (round-30 item 1) — which is
why `L` appears on **both** lines
of every workflow here (§4.4, §8.5.1). Replaying the token with `--plan --approve-plan <fp>`
answers the sharper question directly:
`runnable && !guard.would_refuse && guard.execute_blocked_by == [] && refusal.kind == null`
means *this exact command line will be admitted and execute* (§0.2, §4.4) — all four conjuncts, since the third-listed
one is the only field that can report a controlled-path refusal the unguarded route would ignore
(§8.6.1 cause 3).

**Workflow A′ — proactive, human (three invocations, no JSON parser).**

```
1. tws sync <f> --plan --max-replay-per-entry 10             # exit 0; preview. Tail of stdout:
                                                             #   Plan runnable: yes
                                                             #   Guard would refuse: yes        <- legitimate here
                                                             #   Refusal kind: limit-per-entry
                                                             #   Configuration issues: none
                                                             #   Guarded execution blockers: none
                                                             #   Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>
2. tws sync <f> --plan --max-replay-per-entry 10 \
       --approve-plan <fp>                                   # exit 0; re-plan WITH the token:
                                                             #   Plan runnable: yes
                                                             #   Guard would refuse: no
                                                             #   Refusal kind: none
                                                             #   Configuration issues: none
                                                             #   Guarded execution blockers: none
                                                             #   Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>
3. tws sync <f> --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan <fp> # guarded run, same T/L/P/V
```

**The human is told to check the same four conjuncts an agent checks, round 31 stopped the human
workflow short of three of them, and round 32 fixes the step at which the four are demanded**
(round-31 item 6, round-32 item 6). The JSON predicate is
`runnable && !guard.would_refuse && guard.execute_blocked_by == [] && refusal.kind == null`
(Workflow A), and round 32 gives every conjunct a **labelled** human line rather than prose to
infer it from (§8.3.5): `Plan runnable:`, `Guard would refuse:`, `Refusal kind:` and the
**`Guarded execution blockers:`** block fixed immediately above the fingerprint line, with the
`Configuration issues:` block above that.

**The four-conjunct form may not be demanded of the first preview, and requiring it there was a
contradiction** (round-32 item 6). The whole reason an operator asks for a token is that the plan
exceeds a limit they have chosen to accept, so the **initial** over-limit `--plan` — the one that
mints the token, before any token is supplied — legitimately shows `Guard would refuse: yes` with
`Refusal kind: limit-per-entry`/`limit-total`. A rule that told the human "only proceed when all
four conjuncts hold on step 1" would have forbidden exactly the workflow it exists to serve, since
a plan that already satisfies all four needs no token at all. What step 1 must satisfy instead is
the **hard admission facts**, verified on its own labelled lines: `Plan runnable: yes`,
`Configuration issues: none`, `Guarded execution blockers: none`, and a `Refusal kind:` that is
either `none` or one of the **two waivable limit kinds**, `limit-per-entry` or `limit-total` — any
other kind, or a non-empty
blocker block, means no token can help and the run is not approvable (§5.3.1, §4.9).

**Step 2 is the verification step and is where the four conjuncts are required.** It re-runs the
**plan** with `--approve-plan <fp>` **and the identical trigger and limit flags** (the
flag-identity rule above: same `T`, `L`, `P`, `V`), and the operator then requires the full four-conjunct
form on the **displayed values** of that second document: `Plan runnable: yes`,
`Guard would refuse: no`, `Guarded execution blockers: none`, `Refusal kind: none`. That is the
document in which a matching token has actually moved the limit verdicts to `waived` (§5.3.1), so
it is the first document in which all four can hold, and reading them there is reading the answer
rather than predicting it. **Step 3** then executes with the same flags and the same token.

**Steps 2 and 3 can legitimately refuse with `approval-mismatch`, and the workflow says so out
loud** (round-34 item 6). On a **fetch-enabled** route — which is every legacy external run and
every new-mode run whose effective policy is `fetch` — step 2 is a *second plan*, so it **fetches
again**; if upstream moved between step 1 and step 2, the destination SHAs, tips and ranges move,
the fingerprint tuple moves with them, and the token minted over step 1's document no longer
matches. The second document then publishes `Guard would refuse: yes` with
`Refusal kind: approval-mismatch`, and the honest reading of that pair is **"the plan drifted"**,
not "the token failed to waive the limits": the token is intact and would still authorise the plan
it was minted over — that plan is simply no longer the plan in front of the operator. **The
recovery is to re-run the initial preview**, read the fresh document and take the fresh receipt;
re-running step 2 with the stale token cannot succeed, and a retry loop around it is a race, not a
workflow. **Step 3 can refuse the same way** — the refs may move between step 2's validation and
step 3's own re-resolution — and that refusal is the guard working exactly as designed: it is taken
**before** the first rebase, so nothing is partially applied and no recovery state exists (§5.2,
§5.3, §8.7.6, §12). Any diagnostic, doc, skill or example that attributes such a refusal to the
limit flags, or that tells the operator to re-supply the same token, is wrong and must be corrected.
**The deterministic alternative is a different route, chosen deliberately**: `--no-fetch` is a mode
trigger (§0.2), so `--plan --no-fetch` → `--no-fetch --approve-plan` previews and executes the
**new-mode** run and is stable because it is fully local — but no snippet, skill, agent instruction
or test may add `--no-fetch` to a legacy round trip to make it stable, because that silently
approves a different run (§5.3). A token
on its own is *not* the admission
signal: a document can mint a perfectly good token, publish `runnable: true` and still list
`live-owner-concurrency`, in which case the guarded run refuses at rank 3 while the
unguarded `tws sync` would have proceeded (§8.6.1 cause 3, §4.4 `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`). Both
blocks are printed on every document, so "I did not see a blockers section" is never a legitimate
reading — `none` is the literal that says the conjunct holds.

**The machine flow is unchanged and no impossible pair is implied** (round-32 item 6): Workflow A's
`--plan --json --approve-plan <fp>` replay answers the same four-conjunct question in fields, and
neither flow may describe a **limitless** token — a document with no effective limit mints nothing
(clause (b), §4.4), so "a token that authorises an unlimited run" is not a shape any workflow,
snippet, doc or skill may show.

The human rendering is a first-class token source (§8.3.5): the operator who just read the rows is
exactly the person entitled to approve them, and forcing a second `--json` invocation to obtain the
receipt would either train them to skip the reading or tempt the design into printing tokens from
places that never showed a plan. `--json` remains the agent contract; the human contract is the
labelled final line — **which is a line, not a token**. `tail -1` yields
`Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>` or `Approval fingerprint: none`; the token is the third field, and
`none` means the document minted no usable token, and it has **three** causes, exactly the three
clauses of §4.4's usable-token predicate: no approvable work, no effective limit, or a non-empty
`encoding_issues[]` — and under `--json` the three are read directly off
`approval.covers.has_work`, `approval.covers.requires_limits` and `approval.covers.encoding_safe`
rather than inferred (round-30 item 4, §8.6.3, §4.4). Any doc, skill, test or example
that pipes `tail -1` straight into `--approve-plan` is wrong and must be written as an explicit
extraction, and any that checks admission from the final line alone is wrong for the same reason —
three of the four conjuncts live above it (§8.3.5, round-32 item 6).

**Workflow B — reactive (three invocations, because a refusal yields no token).**

```
1. tws sync <f> --max-replay-per-entry 10                     # guarded; refuses: exit 1, marker line
2. tws sync <f> --plan --json --max-replay-per-entry 10       # exit 0; read approval.fingerprint
3. tws sync <f> --max-replay-per-entry 10 --approve-plan <fp> # guarded run
```

Step 1 is a refusal and nothing more: exit 1, one anchored `^plan-guard: ` line at any position on
stderr
carrying the `refusal.kind` chosen at the seam (§8.7.6), no JSON, **no token**. Step 2 must repeat
step 1's flags exactly — it is the same question asked in describing form — and step 3 repeats them
again with the token. **Three invocations total** when starting reactively; no shortcut collapses it
to two, and no documentation, skill, test or example may show a token being read out of step 1.

**Workflow C — continuation (§8.7.4).** An interrupted guarded run is Workflow A over the remaining
work: `--plan --continue` mints a `remaining-work` token, the approving `--continue` consumes it,
and on the legacy external route both repeat the limit flags. The initial full-run token is never
reusable here.

**Why not print the token on refusal.** It would make the refusal an output contract carrying an
authorisation value, tempt automation into "refuse → grep → re-run" loops that never look at the
plan, and produce a token for a document nobody read — the precise failure mode §5.3.1's narrow
waiver exists to prevent. The token is the *receipt of a description*, so it is issued only by the
command that describes — in either of that command's two renderings.

### 8.8 Validation identity is only stable where something freezes it

`intent.validation.command_digest` is inside the fingerprint (§5.3), and on one shipped route that
binding is currently **not true of the run**: the legacy external path resolves
`internal.LoadConfig().TestCommand` **fresh, inside `runValidation`, once per entry**
(`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:401-403`). Nothing freezes it. A config edit — by the operator, by a
concurrent process, by a `tws config` command, by a checked-in file being switched with the branch
that a rebase just moved — changes what entry *n+1* validates with, in the middle of a run whose
plan published one digest. The previous draft simply listed `config-per-entry` as a `source` value
and then asserted the digest binds an identity. Both cannot hold; this section fixes which.

**What the fingerprint actually binds, so plan and approval cannot disagree.** The tuple carries
`intent.validation.applies` and `intent.validation.command_digest` and **nothing else about
validation** — in particular **not** `source` and **not** `stability` (§5.3). That is not a
weakening; it is what makes the round trip possible at all. A `--plan` document describes the
**shipped** route (`source: config-per-entry`, `stability: per-entry-dynamic` on legacy external),
while the guarded invocation it authorises **freezes** that same command; if the labels were tuple
members, the token minted by the description could never match the run it describes, and the feature
would be self-refuting. The labels are descriptive, the **digest** is the identity, and the document
publishes both `stability` (what the route does unguarded, today) and `guarded_stability` (what a
guarded invocation does with it) so a reader gets both statements without either being softened
(§4.4).

**What is already frozen, and why nothing is required there.** New-mode external freezes the command
plus its `validation_source` into `SyncRunState` at start-up (`internal/cli/sync.go:180-186`), so a
resume cannot validate differently. Checkout takes it from `--test` into `CheckoutSyncOpts` and, on
a continuation, from the persisted `CheckoutTransaction`, so a checkout run has one command for its
whole transaction by construction. Those three routes publish `intent.validation.stability: frozen`
and their digest binds exactly what it says.

**Recommendation for the guarded routes.** A guarded invocation **freezes the exact digest the
approved document showed** and the executor consumes **that frozen command** for the duration of
**that guarded invocation**:

- the guard seam resolves the effective command once, computes its SHA-256, and compares it with the
  digest the token was minted against. **A changed digest invalidates the token** —
  `approval-mismatch` at the guard seam, `revalidation-mismatch` at a JIT seam — so a config edit
  between plan and execute stops the run instead of silently changing what it validates with;
- it then passes the frozen command down the same call path `runValidation` already uses — a value,
  not a re-read — so every entry of that invocation validates with the digest the operator approved.
  The guarded invocation **publishes nothing**: it emits no document and no token (§8.7.6), so the
  freeze is visible in the `--plan` document's `guarded_stability: frozen-at-plan`, never in output
  the executing run produces. The previous draft said the guard seam "publishes
  `source: frozen-at-plan`", which contradicted §8.7.6 outright; that wording is withdrawn;
- the JIT/revalidation seam (§5.2, §5.3) **confirms and follows** that frozen intent: it re-computes
  the digest of the command it is about to use and compares it with the approved one, and a
  disagreement is `revalidation-mismatch` (§4.9 rank 9) exactly as a drifted candidate identity is.
  It never re-reads config to pick a *different* command;
- **the raw command string is never published** on any surface — issue bodies and CI logs are where
  plan documents end up, and a `test_command` routinely carries a token or an internal hostname
  (§11). What is published is `source` plus the **full 64-hex SHA-256 digest**, which is sufficient
  to prove two invocations validate identically and insufficient to leak the command;
- **unguarded legacy behaviour is unchanged.** A bare `tws sync <f>` keeps re-reading config per
  entry, byte- and argv-identically (§10.1). The freeze is a property of the *guarded* invocation
  only, which is precisely the invocation that made an identity claim.

**And the fallback, if `define` declines the freeze.** Then the route stays dynamic and the document
must say so rather than over-claim: it publishes `intent.validation.stability: per-entry-dynamic`
**and `guarded_stability: per-entry-dynamic`**,
its digest is explicitly a **plan-time snapshot**, and **no text in the document, the flag help, the
skills or the tests may claim the token binds the validation command on that route**. The
fingerprint still includes the digest (a changed config between plan and execute is still worth
refusing on), but the guarantee published is "the command was X when I planned", not "the run will
use X". Under-claiming is the only safe direction here, and the `stability`/`guarded_stability` pair
is what makes the difference
machine-readable instead of a footnote.

**Push intent is bound the same way and is already total** (§3.11, §5.3): `--push` on a fresh run,
the persisted `Push` on a v2 external or checkout continuation, the invocation's flag on a legacy
external continuation, published as `intent.push` + `intent.push_source` and bound into the token —
so "replay this much" and "and then force-push it" are approved together or not at all.

---

## 9. Timing relative to fetch, locks, state, and mutation

Required order, per route, for a guarded run. Two rules govern every cell of it. **A refusal removes
only what that invocation created, and nothing else** — never a payload, legacy state, transaction
or guard it merely found (§8.7.5, §12). And **every state fact any seam of this section publishes or plans from
comes from the pre-acquisition snapshot** of §8.6.1 step 2 — read at the top of the route, before
this invocation creates, acquires or reclaims any guard, lock, transaction or sentinel, and carried
unchanged through plan derivation, blocker projection and the guard seam (§4.4 `state`). The single
carve-out — **normative in §8.7.5 step 1 and nowhere else, this sentence included** — is the
scoped-continuation seam's fresh re-evaluation of `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`'s **native**
conditions through the shared `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable` predicate, taken immediately before the
reclaim it gates: it publishes nothing, enters no
fingerprint and derives no `execute_blocked_by` member, and it exists so a shipped sentence about a
*live* owner is never printed for an owner that has already exited (§8.7.5 step 1). The two
rules are the same rule seen from both ends: an invocation neither refuses against, nor tears down,
anything but its own — and it can only tell the two apart because it looked **before** it took
anything. Where a route's own acquisition happens later in the pipeline (new-mode external
`setupSyncRunState`, checkout `AcquireCheckoutLock`/`forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, scoped
`ReclaimSyncRunGuard`), the artefacts it then writes are absent from the snapshot and carry
`self: true`, so they are excluded from the live-owner fact twice over (§8.6.1 cause 3).

**External, new-mode route** — current order is: selection → `verifySelectedBasesLocally` →
marker/token → **state + guard written** → header → fetch → rebase loop
(`internal/cli/sync.go:151-214`, `:559-577`). **The state snapshot is taken above all of it**, before
the marker/token write and before `setupSyncRunState`, so the `.sync-state.v2.yaml`, `.sync-run.lock`
and sentinel this invocation then writes are not in it; without that, the guard seam below would
read its own live `.sync-run.lock` and refuse the run against itself at rank 3 (§8.6.1 cause 3).
The plan must be computed **after the fetch** (or its
base SHAs are pre-fetch and wrong) and **before the first rebase**. That places the refusal *after*
this invocation wrote `.sync-state.v2.yaml`, `.sync-run.lock` and the legacy sentinel — **its own**
artefacts — so a pre-first-rebase refusal runs the same teardown the success path runs
(`clearSyncRunState`, `internal/cli/sync_modes.go:433-452`) and leaves no sentinel behind; otherwise
the next plain run hits `previous sync incomplete`. That teardown is licensed **only** because this
invocation created those files: it is never applied on a continuation, where the same three
artefacts belong to the interrupted run (§8.7.5). Alternatively the
spec may move state creation to just after the guard passes — an acquisition that happens **later
than the snapshot** is always sound, because the snapshot is what the seam reads (§4.4
`state.snapshot`), so this option costs nothing in correctness and removes the teardown entirely;
it is nonetheless a larger change to the
sync-modes contract and must be decided explicitly (§19.1). The same reading covers checkout's
`AcquireCheckoutLock`, which stays where it is: it too is taken after the snapshot, so the seam
below it never reads it as a neighbour.

**One step of the plan is deliberately hoisted on this route: the fetch-context enumeration**
(§8.6.1 step 5a, §8.6.9). The candidate set per `repo_token` — resolved through the `fetchQuiet`
ladder, canonicalized, and reduced by `(absolute common dir, effective fetch target)` equivalence —
is computed
**before** the fetch loop rather than alongside it, so an indeterminate token refuses with
`fetch-context-indeterminate` **before any network call and before `refs/remotes/**` moves in a
repository the guard could not name**. Three properties keep that safe and are binding:

- **It is a pure read moved earlier**, exactly like the `TopoSort` hoist of §8.6.1: `stat` on
  candidate worktree directories plus one `rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir` and
  one remote/refspec resolution per candidate root. It
  cannot add a mutation and can only remove one.
- **The teardown rule is unchanged, and it is the scoped one.** On a *fresh* new-mode run this
  refusal lands **after** the invocation created `.sync-state.v2.yaml`, `.sync-run.lock` and the
  sentinel, so it runs the same `clearSyncRunState` teardown a limit refusal at the same seam runs —
  **only those three artefacts, only because this invocation created them** — and touches no
  payload, legacy state, transaction or guard it merely found (§8.7.5, §12). A continuation never
  reaches this cell at all, because no continuation fetches (§8.6.4).
- **It is a controlled-path divergence, stated rather than implied.** The plan seam and the guard
  seam enumerate before fetching; the **unguarded** run does not change: it builds the same map in
  whatever order `TopoSort` produced and fetches wherever `fetchQuiet` lands, with its argv, its
  output and its `sync_noflag` goldens untouched (§18.12, §18.21). The guarded run therefore
  mutates strictly **less** than the unguarded one in the ambiguous cell, and identically in every
  other.

**External, legacy route** — the seam is inside `syncFeature` (`internal/cli/sync.go:535-553`), and
the plan/guard order is **not** the shipped one: the structural sort is hoisted above the fetch,
exactly as §8.6.1 step 5 requires on every route and as §15.15g asserts. The controlled order is

```
stack load (→ plan-unavailable, §8.5.5)
  → TopoSort                                   (hoisted above the fetch, §8.6.1 step 5)
  → fetch-context enumeration                  (§8.6.1 step 5a; one candidate per token here,
                                                because the legacy map follows stack.yaml order)
  → the legacy whole-stack fetch loop          (skipped by any suppression cause, §8.6.1 step 6)
  → **(guard here)**
  → syncWithStack
```

The **unguarded** legacy run keeps the shipped order — fetch loop, then `TopoSort` — with its argv,
its output and its goldens untouched (§10.1, §18.12); the hoist moves two pure reads on the plan and
guard seams only, and its entire observable effect is that a cycle refuses before the network rather
than after it. The previous draft's diagram here still showed the shipped order and therefore
contradicted §8.6.1, §8.6.3 and §15.15g; it is corrected, not re-decided.
No runtime state exists yet on this route — `.sync-state.yaml`
is written only by `saveIncompleteSync` on failure — so a refusal here leaves the feature exactly as
it found it, and there is nothing to tear down.

**Checkout, both routes** — the current order already has the ideal seam: preflight → lock → header
and (new-mode) fetch → `BuildCheckoutPlan` → **(guard here)** → `SaveCheckoutTransaction` → first
`git checkout` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:563-691`). A refusal here releases the lock **this
invocation acquired** and writes nothing; no transaction exists yet, so none is removed. **The
snapshot is taken in the preflight, above `AcquireCheckoutLock`** — at the same point as the shipped
`HasCheckoutTransaction`/`gitOperationInProgress`/`gitWorkingTreeDirty`/`gitCurrentBranch` reads at
`internal/checkout_sync.go:563-585`, which is where the executor already looks before it takes
anything. **The transaction and lock facts are read there through the plan's own `Lstat`-first
inspectors, not through `HasCheckoutTransaction`/`ReadCheckoutLock`** (§8.6.1 step 2a): the shipped
pair follows symlinks and reports *absent* for a path that exists but cannot be decoded, which is
the one answer the guarded route must never act on. The shipped calls stay exactly where they are on
the executing path (§10.1). The lock this run then acquires is therefore absent from the snapshot and carries
`self: true`, so the guard seam below it never mistakes it for a neighbour; a lock genuinely held by
another live process never reaches the seam at all, because `AcquireCheckoutLock` refuses first with
its own shipped sentence (`internal/checkout_sync.go:207-208`). **One cell of this route never
reaches the seam either**: an empty `BuildCheckoutPlan` returns at `len(plan) == 0` after releasing
the lock, writing no transaction and performing no restoration (`:651-654`) — the run the plan
describes with `restore.applies: false` and no token (§4.4, §8.6.4a).

**Plan-only route (`--plan`, non-mutating, §0.1)** — takes no lock, writes no state, and rewrites no
local branch, in either mode, so it has **nothing to tear down by construction**; it follows the
inspection order of §8.6.1 rather than the executor's
refusal ladder. It is **not** free of Git writes: under an effective `fetch` policy it performs the
route's fetch, updating remote-tracking refs, before it projects; under `--no-fetch` it is fully
read-only. It must run the fetch at the same point the executed run does, so the plan's base SHAs
are the ones the run would use, and it must publish the fetch outcome and freshness (§4.4) —
including the non-fatal-failure case both executors ignore. Consequence: it can
race a live run. It therefore *reports* an existing lock, guard or transaction as an observed fact — through the five
safe inspectors of §8.6.1 step 2a, which read the same paths the shipped
`HasCheckoutTransaction`/`ReadCheckoutLock`/`ReadSyncRunGuard` helpers read
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:173-178,290-301`; `internal/sync_run_state.go:236-251`) but `Lstat`
first, never following a symlink and never collapsing *absent* into *unreadable* — rather than
claiming the plan is authoritative. Reporting is not taking: `--plan` never acquires, steals, or
clears any of them, which is why its snapshot is pre-acquisition for free — the reason the
round-13 `state.snapshot.self_artefacts[]` field was withdrawn as unobservable: this route never
acquires anything, and the only route that could have published a non-empty list publishes no
document at all (§4.4, §8.7.6). Self-exclusion is published as the per-artefact `self` flag and is
proved by the unit/helper tests of §15.15f4.

**And when the pre-acquisition snapshot holds an artefact with a *pre-existing live foreign owner*,
the plan does not fetch at
all** (§8.6.1 step 6, suppression cause 3 of six). This is a
timing rule, not an optimisation: observation happens at step 2 and the fetch at step 6 precisely so
the fetch can be declined — and, on the plan-only route, the snapshot is trivially pre-acquisition,
because this route acquires nothing at any point. The hazard is **D3** — external passes `--onto <ref-name>` and re-resolves
it inside `git rebase` when each entry is reached (§2.4), so moving `refs/remotes/**` under a live
run changes the destination of entries that run has not yet reached. A preview that "only reads"
would have altered someone else's rebase. So: a **checkout lock or sync-run guard** that is
**present and readable in the snapshot** and whose recorded PID is **signalable and not ours** ⇒
`fetch.outcome: skipped`,
`freshness: not-refreshed-live-run`, and base SHAs that are as
old as the last fetch anyone performed — reported, not disguised. **A pre-existing foreign,
signalable PID on an owner-signalling artefact is
the whole
predicate**, defined once in §8.6.1 cause 3 and only cited here: it is computed from the raw
recorded PID rather than from `SyncExternalState.GuardLive`,
so a guard whose token does not match the payload still suppresses the fetch while its process runs,
and it does not additionally require the observation to be a `state-refused` blocker — the other
process moves refs whether or not our cell happens to refuse (§8.6.1 cause 3). **A checkout
transaction is not an owner-signalling artefact**: `tx.LockPID` is a persisted recovery field that
deliberately outlives its writer, so it never suppresses a fetch and never refuses a run, and a
transaction's concurrency question is answered by the checkout lock beside it or not at all — the
round-13 "or a transaction whose lock PID does" clause is withdrawn (§8.6.1 cause 3, §4.4 `state`).
**And "alive" means signalable**: `isProcessAlive` is `Signal(0)`, so an owner running under another
user reads as dead and a reused PID reads as alive; the wording here, in the document and in the
tests is the probe's, never a claim about process identity (§4.4 `state`, §19.21). Token ownership is
published beside liveness and changes nothing here; **this process's own PID does change it**, and
so does an artefact absent from the snapshot: neither is another process, so neither is a hazard,
which is the same conjunct `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` and `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` already apply
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:281`, `internal/sync_run_state.go:226`). The plan may still project a `state-refused`
blocker for the same observation where the shipped ladder implies one; suppression and refusal stay
independent facts (§8.6.2), and the plan document publishes the guarded twin's refusal as
`guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]` in **both** of those cells (§4.4). **The
suppression set is closed at six** (round-23 item 3 added the fifth, round-25 item 2 the sixth), and the other **five** share the
same shape: a `--continue` never reaches a fetch because no
continuation executor performs one (cause 1); a rows-less refusal established **before** step 6
(`plan-unavailable`, `selection-refused` and `stack-unsortable` — on **every** route, because the
plan/guard route hoists `TopoSort`/selection above the fetch as a deliberate non-mutating
reordering, §8.6.1) has no subject to fetch for — `freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`
(cause 2, §5.5, §8.6.3); and an **indeterminate fetch context** declines a fetch the route cannot
reproduce, enumerated at step 5a before any network call —
`freshness: not-refreshed-context-indeterminate` (cause 4, §8.6.9); and an **unbounded submodule
reach** declines a fetch whose *reach* the route cannot name — an effective
`fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse` of `yes` over a `submodule_recursion.reach` of
`unknown`, where the recursion is certain and the stores it would contact and rewrite are not
enumerable — `freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate` (cause 5, round-23 item 3,
§4.4, §4.9 rank 5.05, §8.6.9); and a **checked-out fetch destination** declines a fetch that would
write `refs/heads/**` in a store whose working tree is standing on one of those branches — a
positive refspec covering `refs/heads/**` over a non-empty
`local_branch_destinations.held[]`, where Git either dies at `refusing to fetch into branch …` and
leaves the run on stale refs or prunes the branch out from under that HEAD —
`freshness: not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out` (cause 6, round-25 item 2, §4.4, §4.9
rank 5.06). A **seventh** cell fetches nothing
without being a suppression at all: a fetching route whose
resolved context set is **empty** invokes no `git fetch` and reports
`freshness: not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets` (§4.4, §8.6.1). An **eighth** cell fetches, succeeds and
still refreshes nothing: a context whose **default** remote resolution resolves to nothing — with no
legacy `remotes/`/`branches/` file supplying a URL either (round-23 item 5) — or a
`fetch.all` whose every remote is `skipFetchAll`-suppressed — runs `git fetch`, contacts no remote
and exits 0, which is `fetch_effect.contacted: false`, `ok: true` and
`freshness: not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` (round-22 item 3, §4.4, §8.6.9). A **ninth** cell
fetches, succeeds, and cannot describe what it did: an attempted row with `fetch_effect: null`, or
with `submodule_recursion.reach: unknown` under `on-demand`, which is
`freshness: unknown-fetch-effect` and `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: null` (round-23 items 1
and 3). The precedence is §8.6.1's, in that
order — continuation, no plan subject, live owner, indeterminate context, unbounded submodule reach,
checked-out fetch destination, then the zero-target cell
below all six, and, among the cells where a fetch really ran, the total four-rule table of §4.4:
`possibly-stale`, then `unknown-fetch-effect`, then `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`, then
`fetched` — and the previous draft's "other two suppressions … a fourth cell" wording here
omitted cause 4 and mis-numbered the zero-target cell; it is corrected, not re-decided.
**Everything else fetches per policy**, including every `state-refused` cell with no pre-existing
live foreign owner — a
stale guard, a dead lock PID,
`previous sync incomplete`, a transaction with no live lock, an unreadable payload, **and every
artefact this invocation created, acquired or reclaimed** — and every
non-live blocker (dirty tree, detached HEAD, Git operation in progress, I19, row blockers), because
no other process is moving refs (§8.6.1). "The document refuses" and "the document fetched" are
independent facts and the schema publishes both.

**On the guarded execution seams the same observation is a *refusal*, not a suppression** (§8.6.1
cause 3, where the rule is defined). A guarded invocation that merely declined the fetch would go on
to rebase against refs it had deliberately left stale while the live process kept moving them, so at
every seam of this section **any pre-existing live foreign owner is a non-waivable `state-refused`
concurrency
blocker** and the invocation refuses before its first rebase — on a fresh run under the scoped
teardown rule above (only what this invocation created), on a continuation with nothing written and
nothing removed (§8.7.5). It is timing-relevant here for two reasons. The observation is the
**step 2
read**, so it precedes the fetch and the first mutation on every route, which is what makes the
refusal free of any teardown beyond the invocation's own artefacts. And that read is
**pre-acquisition**, which is what makes the refusal fire against neighbours only: a re-read at the
seam would see this run's own `.sync-run.lock` on the fresh new-mode external route, and this run's
own force-acquired lock on the checkout continuation route, and would refuse every guarded
invocation of both (§8.7.5). The **unguarded** run is
unchanged in this cell as in every other (§18.12), which is why this is recorded as a deliberate
controlled-path divergence rather than an executor behaviour change.

**Continuation routes (all of them)** — the seams are enumerated in §8.7.5. Four properties are
timing facts and belong here: a continuation seam sits **after** the route's state load, mismatch
checks and — in checkout — the forced lock reclaim, but on the external scoped route **before**
`ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, and always **before the first remaining rebase**, so a refusal leaves the
frozen state exactly as it found it; **the snapshot is taken above the reclaim on both routes**, so
the lock `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` re-takes and the guard `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` rewrites are never
read back as neighbours — a checkout `--continue` that re-read its own reclaimed lock at the seam
would refuse itself every time (§8.7.5); **no continuation applies the fresh-run teardown above**,
which
is licensed only for artefacts the refusing invocation created; and **no continuation fetches**, so
a continuation plan is computed over refs no invocation of this run refreshed (§8.6.4).

**Per-entry revalidation, and JIT resolution** — external pass 1 at
`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:117-135`, external pass 2 immediately before its
`git rebase <base> <git_branch>` call (`:196-201`, §5.4.4), checkout at
`internal/checkout_sync.go:1024-1030` plus the `resumeFromSwitched` arm that bypasses it
(`:933-939`, §8.7.5). Pass 1 and `processBranch` already re-resolve there, so for them the guard
adds a comparison and the resolution of that entry's deferred/conditional fields (§5.1), not a new
probe for values the executor already reads; pass 2 and `resumeFromSwitched` need the check
inserted. **What is re-probed at those seams is every *mutable* precondition of the row, not only
the ranges** (round-34 item 5, correcting the earlier "the extra probes are the candidate count and
bounded identity" reading, which left a guarded run authorising a rebase against a plan-time dirty
tree, a plan-time holder set and a plan-time rebase-directory answer). The set is: the **decision** SHA resolved as the executor resolves it, in `base_context`; the
destination, the head, the candidate count and the
full-sequence digest wherever the row's identity is revalidated, all in `execution_context`
(round-35 item 3); the `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`
operation-directory pair and the tracked-dirty status in `execution_context`; the branch/worktree
holds that decide `branch_checked_out_at`; untracked presence; and any other mutable fact the row's
own action depends on. **What is not re-probed** is the run-invariant half — the context identity
and the ordered configuration inventory of §13 — which is cached for the invocation. The
conservative ceiling is **twelve** Git processes per external JIT row — the ten of the re-probe set
plus the **one or two** `DefaultBranchIn` reads the seam's own re-resolution of a **literal** base
costs, round-37 item 3 — and **eight** per checkout row
(§13), of which the executor already issues one on pass 1.

Nothing above is atomic and the spec must not imply it is. Between the plan and the rebase, another
process can move any ref; the fingerprint check narrows the window to "between the last
re-resolution and `git rebase`", which is as tight as a non-transactional Git workflow allows.

---

## 10. Compatibility boundaries

1. **Frozen**: no-flag `tws sync <feature>` in both modes — stdout, stderr, exit code, argv
   sequence, and state-file shape. Enforced by `internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go` and
   `internal/cli/testdata/sync_noflag/**`.
2. **Frozen**: `--continue` / `--abort` semantics and the sync-modes mismatch refusals
   (`internal/cli/sync.go:435-466`; `internal/checkout_sync.go:767-814`), **including I20 and its
   gate**: no control flag joins `syncTriggerFlags`, so `newMode` — and therefore I20 and I8 — keep
   exactly their shipped operand sets and meanings (§8.5.2, §8.5.3). Every executing invocation
   still hits them at exit 1; `--plan` *projects* the same sentences as blockers instead, which adds
   a rendering, not a rule (§8.6.4). Persisted guard limits are subject to the *same* discipline —
   a supplied limit that contradicts a persisted one refuses (§8.7.4) — and nothing persisted ever
   re-opens the frozen axis decision (§8.5.4).
3. **Additive-only state**: any new key in `SyncRunState` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:38-63`) or
   `CheckoutTransaction` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:63-100`) must be `omitempty` so a legacy
   document round-trips unchanged — the rule sync-modes already established, with
   `CheckoutTransactionVersion` gating newer documents (`internal/checkout_sync.go:722-727`).
   The keys this feature adds are exactly **two**, `max_replay_per_entry` and
   `max_replay_total` (§8.7.4) — the **guard**, never an approval token, because a token authorises
   a plan the interruption has already invalidated (§5.3). **There is no `guard_enabled` key**: the
   previous draft's boolean is withdrawn as a third encoding of a fact the two values already carry
   (§8.7.4), and "this run was guarded" is read as *at least one key has a value*, which cannot
   drift out of step with the values themselves. **Both keys are pointer-backed
   (`*int` with `omitempty`) or carry explicit presence booleans; they are never plain `int` with
   `omitempty`.** With a scalar, an effective limit of `0` — a legal value meaning "refuse any entry
   that replays anything", §8.3.2a — marshals to *nothing*, so the resume reads the **strictest
   guard the CLI can express as no guard at all**: a silent safety inversion that only ever fires on
   the operator who asked for the most protection. `omitempty` on a pointer omits exactly `nil`,
   which preserves the additive round-trip this boundary requires while keeping `absent` and `zero`
   distinguishable on disk, in `guard.limits`'s per-key `{value, origin}` object, and in the
   fingerprint tuple (§5.3.2). A document written by a tws that had no such keys therefore reads as
   *unguarded* — both keys absent, both `value: null`, both `origin: none` — which is the correct
   degradation and needs no boolean to express it.
   They are written **only by the invocation
   that creates the state**: a continuation that arms a previously-unguarded run with flags
   (`origin: flags-persisted-continuation`, §8.7.4) guards itself and writes nothing, so a
   resume never mutates the frozen payload or transaction. They must **not** bump `state_version`:
   an older tws that ignores them resumes exactly as it does today, which is the correct degradation
   for an opt-in guard. Note the asymmetry §8.7.4 owns, and note that it is **not** the asymmetry
   the previous draft stated: `RunCheckoutSync` persists a transaction before the first
   `git checkout` on **both** checkout routes and sets `StateVersion` only under `opts.NewMode`
   (`internal/checkout_sync.go:652-681`), so a **newly started legacy checkout run persists the
   guard keys too**, with `state_version` still omitted; only the legacy *external* route, whose
   `.sync-state.yaml` has no version and no room, has nowhere to persist and repeats its limit flags
   instead. The withdrawn claim was "pre-v2 checkout persists nothing"; what is true is that a
   transaction **written before this feature existed** carries no guard keys, and a continuation over
   it is armable by flags like any other unguarded state.
4. **Runtime-state filters**: any new runtime file under a feature directory must be added to
   `isRuntimeState` in `internal/cli/importcmd.go`, or an imported archive can plant it. This is the
   same obligation sync-modes discovered. Prefer *not* creating a new file at all: the guard's
   persisted keys live in the existing payload/transaction, and nothing else is written.
5. **`tws status` / `tws doctor` / `tws stack status`** must be unaffected. If the plan is exposed
   anywhere else later, it must consume the same planner.
6. **Skill/doc contract**: user-visible flags are documented in `README.md:158`,
   `docs/cheatsheet.md:148-163`, `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces/SKILL.md:27,138-153`,
   **`assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces-orchestrator/SKILL.md:52-62,103-110,128-131`** (the
   third shipped skill, added to this ledger by round-37 item 5; it owns the pre-sync workflow step
   and must teach the plan/guard preview there, §14), and
   `assets/skills/copilot/tws.prompt.md:18,82`. The workflow requires updating them
   (`docs/engineering-workflow.md`, coding conventions). Seven statements are mandatory in each:
   `--plan` obeys the fetch axis (so it fetches by default in external and not in checkout, §0.1),
   and skips the fetch in exactly six cases (round-24 item 4 corrected this count where §14
   and §8.6.1's own header still said four; round-25 item 2 adds the sixth) — a `--continue`, a
   rows-less document with no
   plannable subject, an observed **checkout lock or sync-run guard** with a **signalable foreign
   PID** (whoever owns
   it, and whether or not it refuses this run; a checkout transaction's `lock_pid` is never such a
   signal), a new-mode fetch context the route does not
   determine, a context whose **unconditional submodule recursion** has an unbounded reach
   (round-23 item 3), or a context whose fetch would write a **local branch a worktree is holding**
   (round-25 item 2) — each named by its own
   `freshness` value
   (§8.6.1, §8.6.9); **`--approve-plan` requires at least one effective replay limit**, so the flag
   pair is always `<limit flags> --approve-plan <fp>` on a fresh run and the limits may be inherited
   from the interrupted run on a `--continue` (§8.5.1, §8.7.4);
   candidate counts are never applied counts (§4.2); `--plan` describes the run the *same*
   flags would perform — bare `--plan` describes the legacy no-flag run, `--plan` with an axis or
   scope flag describes **that** run instead, so adding `--no-fetch` previews a different run rather
   than the same one offline (§0.2, §5.3); `--plan --push` describes a pushing run and pushes
   nothing, and a token minted without `--push` never authorises a pushing run (§3.11, §8.7.7);
   guarded execution emits no JSON, so structured detail
   always comes from `--plan --json`, and its refusals are one **anchored, guard-written**
   `plan-guard:` line (`^plan-guard: <kind>: `) at any position on stderr — while **every refusal a
   shipped check owns** keeps its shipped text with
   no marker, whatever its rank (§8.7.6); and **a token is only ever read out of a `--plan` document
   — the human `Approval fingerprint:` final line or the `--json` field — and never out of any
   executing invocation** — so the reactive path is three
   invocations, an interrupted run needs a fresh `--plan --continue` token, and every invocation of
   a pair repeats the same trigger, limit, push and validation flags (§8.7.4, §8.7.7).
7. **New stdout contract, scoped to the new surface**: `--plan --json` emits the document and
   nothing else on stdout (§8.3.7). This is additive — it constrains only the new flag combination
   and must be implemented without altering the byte stream of any existing path, whose goldens are
   frozen by boundary 1.
8. **Trigger-flag set unchanged, and the presence map stays closed**: `syncTriggerFlags` keeps its
   six members, so the I8 operand list (`--abort cannot be combined with %s`,
   `syncChangedTriggerList`, `internal/cli/sync_modes.go:143-152`) and every message derived from it
   are untouched — and `syncPresenceFlags` keeps its seven, and `CheckoutSyncOpts.Changed` its seven
   keys. Control-flag presence lives in a separate `planGuardOptions` value with its own resolver
   (§8.5.1), so no continuation mismatch checker can ever see it.
9. **`TopoSort` order unchanged**: the plan canonicalizes its own document (§4.7); it does not make
   the shipped sort deterministic, because that would change execution order, persisted `Selected`
   lists, and the checkout plan array `--continue` indexes by position.
10. **No new config keys**: v1 ships no `sync.plan_guard.*` (or any other) configuration, so
