    `internal/config.go` is untouched and a bare no-flag run cannot become guarded by ambient state
    (§8.3.4).

## 11. Safety and security

- **Say what `--plan` does, exactly.** `--plan` must not rewrite any local branch, must not write
  `stack.yaml`, must not write or clear state, must not lock, must not push, and must not run any
  command outside **the context that row's executor would use** (`syncRepoContext`,
  `internal/cli/sync.go:593-602`; for a non-materialized entry that context is `entry.Repo` or, when
  it is empty, the **process cwd**, §5.4). The cwd is therefore a legitimate probe context, not an
  exception: the previous draft claimed the prunability mirror was "the only cwd-scoped command the
  plan issues", and that is false — an external **pass-2** row whose `Repo` is empty runs **every**
  probe there (base resolution, `rev-parse`, the candidate `rev-list` probes, the ref/worktree
  inventories and the `rebase.*` configuration read — one ordered `config --list --show-scope -z`
  plus the typed boolean interpretations §4.2 requires, never a per-key `--get` ladder, round-34
  item 4), because that is exactly what `RunSilent` does
  on that arm. Two cwd-scoped facts are published rather than hidden: the prunability mirror runs
  `git worktree list --porcelain` in the process cwd with no `-C`, published as
  `prunability.probe_context = cwd` (§3.7), and every row publishes the context it really used as
  `base_context` and `execution_context`, each `{context_id, repo_root, source}`, with `source: process-cwd` where that applies
  (§4.1, §4.4, round-33 item 1, round-34 item 1).
  **A probe may never be issued in a context because another context was *assumed* to be the same
  one** (round-35 item 2): a store fact is shared between a row's two contexts only after both
  canonical absolute common dirs have been read and compared byte-equal, and where they differ the
  row refuses rather than probing a repository the operator never named (§4.1 context-pair rule,
  §4.9 rank 5.15). **The push directory is a third context with its own identity**, published on
  every `push.targets[]` row (§4.4, round-35 item 5), so no rendered root anywhere in this document
  is a join key and no probe is attributed to a directory by its rendering.
  Both are read-only probes, and mirroring the executor is the point: a differently-scoped probe
  would desynchronise the plan from the run.
  Under `--no-fetch` it is **fully read-only**. Under an effective `fetch` policy it **does** run
  `git fetch` and therefore updates remote-tracking refs — that is a deliberate, documented,
  policy-obeying write, and the documentation must not describe `--plan` as read-only without that
  qualification (§0.1, §8.3.1). Three consequences the spec must state: a fetching `--plan` can
  change
  what a *subsequent* `--no-fetch` run sees; a fetching `--plan` inside CI performs network I/O;
  and — the one that is easy to miss — **the directory it fetches in is not always a repository of
  the workspace**. `fetchQuiet`'s last fallback is `internal.RunSilent` with **no `-C`**
  (`internal/cli/sync.go:604-635`), reached whenever `UniqueRepos` recorded no worktree for a token
  and the token is the empty default repo (`internal/stack.go:37-52`), so a bare external
  `tws sync <f> --plan` standing in an unrelated clone will move **that** clone's
  `refs/remotes/**`. The plan does not suppress this — suppressing it would desynchronise the
  preview from the run it previews — it **publishes** it, as a `fetch.repos[]` row with
  `context_source: process-cwd`, its resolved `context_root`, and the `fetch-context-divergent`
  warning where no entry row probes that directory (§4.4, §8.6.9). Any wording that implies a plan
  fetches only the repositories it is planning is wrong and must not appear in the analysis, the
  flag help, `README.md`, the cheatsheet or the skills (§14). **A fourth consequence is added by
  round 23, and it is the widest of them** (item 3): the fetch does not necessarily stop at the
  contexts `fetch.repos[]` names. `fetch.recurseSubmodules` defaults to **`on-demand`**, so a bare
  `git fetch` in a superproject can contact **submodule** remotes and rewrite refs in **their**
  stores — more network I/O, more repositories, and none of it visible in the row's own
  `context_common_dir`. The document answers that with the bounded
  `fetch_effect.submodule_recursion` value (§4.4): it publishes the reachable submodule stores with
  their own effects where it can, fails **closed** at rank 5.05 where recursion is unconditional and
  the reach is unknown, and publishes `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect` with
  `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs: null` where recursion is merely possible. **A fifth follows
  from round-23 item 5**: a legacy `$GIT_DIR/branches/<name>` remote fetches into
  **`refs/heads/<name>`**, so on such a repository a fetch can fast-forward a *local branch* — a
  write no text may exclude when describing what a plan's fetch can touch (§0.1, §4.3).
- **It never fetches under a live run — and liveness is the only *precaution* that suppresses it**
  (§8.6.1, §9). Moving
  `refs/remotes/**` while another tws
  process is rebasing changes what that process resolves for the entries it has not reached, because
  external re-resolves `--onto <ref-name>` inside `git rebase` (D3). A preview must not be able to
  alter someone else's run; when the **pre-acquisition snapshot** holds a **checkout lock or sync-run
  guard** — the two owner-signalling artefacts, never the checkout transaction, whose `lock_pid` is a
  persisted recovery field (§8.6.1 cause 3) — that is `presence: readable` and
  whose recorded PID is **signalable and belongs to another process**, the fetch is skipped
  and the document says `freshness: not-refreshed-live-run` instead of quietly showing fresher SHAs.
  "Signalable" is the honest word for what `Signal(0)` answers: an owner running under another user
  reads as dead (`EPERM`) and a reused PID reads as alive, and the residual window that leaves is
  documented rather than denied, with the portable birth-identity fix deferred to its own follow-up
  (§4.4 `state`, §19.21). An **unreadable or symlinked** guard is not "no owner": its liveness is
  unknown, so the plan publishes it as state and the guarded route fails closed on it (§8.6.1
  step 2a).
  **Token ownership and whether this cell happens to refuse are both irrelevant to the
  suppression** — a token-mismatched guard is still a live process — while **this process's own
  artefacts are excluded**, exactly as the shipped reclaim paths exclude them
  (`pid != os.Getpid() && isProcessAlive(pid)`), so a run never declines a fetch because of a lock it
  took itself. The predicate has exactly one
  definition, in §8.6.1 cause 3. The suppression is deliberately narrow in both directions: widening
  it to every `state-refused` cell would publish base SHAs staler than the run's own, and narrowing
  it below liveness would let
  a preview move refs under a running rebase. **A guarded execution goes one step further, and
  deliberately diverges from the run it guards**: declining the fetch and then rebasing would mean
  executing on refs the invocation knowingly left stale while the live process moved them, so a
  pre-existing live foreign
  owner at the guard seam is a non-waivable `state-refused` concurrency blocker and the invocation
  refuses (§8.6.1 cause 3, §9, §4.9 rank 3), which the plan document publishes as
  `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]` so the divergence is readable before it is
  hit (§4.4). The **unguarded** run is untouched — it fetches and
  rebases under another process's live guard exactly as it does today (§18.12) — which is what makes
  this a
  controlled-path safety divergence rather than a behaviour change. **The two other precautions are
  the indeterminate fetch context** (§8.6.9), which declines a fetch the guard cannot name, **and
  the unbounded submodule reach** (§8.6.1 cause 5, round-23 item 3), which declines a fetch whose
  *reach* it cannot name where recursion is unconditional; both are
  likewise not shared with the unguarded run; the remaining non-fetching cells are not precautions
  at all and must not be conflated with either: a `--continue` mirrors an executor that never
  fetches, and a rows-less refusal document had no subject to fetch for
  (`freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`, §8.6.1) — which now holds on **every** route,
  because the plan route sorts and selects before it fetches (§8.6.1 early structural validation).
  The zero-target non-fetching cell is not a decision at all: a policy-`fetch` route with **zero**
  resolved
  contexts invokes no `git fetch` because there is none to invoke, and says so with
  `freshness: not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets` (§4.4).
- **The collateral set is the honest one, not the flattering one** (§4.3). `--update-refs` moves any
  local branch whose tip is in the replayed range, so the plan lists **all** of them — including
  branches tws does not own — repo-qualified and labelled `stack_owned: false`. Reporting only stack
  refs, or only one repository's, would
  under-state a destructive blast radius, which is the one direction a safety surface must never
  err in. It is published as an **upper bound** (`summary.collateral_bound: upper`), because Git
  updates only the refs it puts in its actual todo, and the two filters differ: a candidate removed
  by the **preliminary clean-cherry-pick** filter never reaches the todo, so a ref pointing at it is
  left where it is and may be orphaned, while a candidate dropped for **becoming empty** keeps its
  `update-ref` step and its ref may still move onto the rewritten parent/base (§4.3). Over-listing
  here is the safe error; promising either movement or non-movement is not.
- **Validation commands are digested, not echoed** (§4.4 `intent.validation.command_digest`, §8.8).
  The
  plan document is a shareable artefact; a `test_command` may carry a token or an internal hostname.
  The published pair is `source` + full SHA-256 digest, never the string. And the digest only claims
  what it can prove: the document publishes `stability` for the shipped route (`per-entry-dynamic`
  on legacy external, where the unguarded run re-reads config per entry and no identity is claimed)
  and `guarded_stability` for what a guarded invocation does with the same command — freeze the
  approved digest and consume it, under §8.8's recommendation — so neither statement has to be
  softened to accommodate the other.
- **Never a rebase behind the operator's back.** Neither `--plan` nor a guarded run may execute a
  rebase the plan did not describe. The one shipped path that would — legacy external
  `syncFallback` — is intercepted structurally (§8.5.5), and a test asserts no `git rebase` process
  exists in that scenario (§15.18). This is the single most important safety property of the
  feature, because it is the one the routing decision could silently break.
- **Never a push behind the operator's back either.** `--push` **and the projected `push.targets[]`**
  are both inside the fingerprint (§5.3), so
  a token minted for a non-pushing plan cannot authorise a run that ends in
  `git push --force-with-lease` for every synced branch, **and a token minted for one push set
  cannot authorise a wider one** — a scoped push of `pr2` does not approve a `scope=all` push of the
  whole feature, in that repository or any other. That matters most in the one cell where the push
  is *all* that is left: a run interrupted at the push stage has no rebase rows, and binding only
  the boolean would have left its most destructive remaining operation unbindable (§4.4, §8.6.4a).
  `--plan --push` describes the intent and the targets while performing none of it (§8.3.1).
- **Never destroy another rebase behind the operator's back.** An external **pass-2** row rebases in
  a directory tws does not own, and the shipped failure handler answers Git's refusal with
  `git rebase --abort` **in that same directory** (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:200-206`). If a
  rebase was already in progress there — a colleague's, another tool's, or the operator's own in
  another terminal — the sync discards it as a side effect of failing. This is the only cell in the
  whole feature where the unguarded run *destroys* work rather than merely stopping, so the plan
  probes the **operation directory** (`rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply` via `rev-parse --git-path` +
  `os.Stat`, read-only, in the row's own execution directory) and blocks at rank 5.45 before the
  `git rebase`, at plan time and again at the pass-2 JIT seam (§4.1, §4.9, §5.4 consequence 7,
  §12). It deliberately does **not** use the shipped `isRebaseInProgress`, whose `false` at a
  `break` stop and on an unreadable context is precisely the answer that would walk into this cell
  (§8.6.4). The unguarded run keeps its shipped behaviour — the guard predicts and refuses, it does
  not repair the executor (§18.12).
- **Never a HEAD switch behind the operator's back either — and external does not switch it back.**
  An external **pass-2** row rebases with an explicit branch operand, which Git documents as
  "a shortcut for `git checkout topic && git rebase master`", in `entry.Repo` or, when that is
  empty, in the **process cwd**. On success HEAD is left on the rebased branch, and on this arm's
  own `git rebase --abort` it is reset to that same branch — external has **no** `restoreOriginal`
  path, unlike checkout's `StageRestoring` (§5.4.7). That is a real, previously undocumented
  mutation of the repository the operator is standing in, so the plan publishes it per row
  (`mutation.will_switch_head`, `mutation.will_leave_head_on`,
  `mutation.head_restored_by_run: false`) beside that row's `execution_context`, and refuses **before**
  it when the switch cannot happen safely: the branch is checked out in **another** worktree of that
  context (`branch-checked-out-elsewhere` — a **self** hold, where HEAD is already on that branch in
  the very directory the arm runs in, is the ordinary case and is never refused) or the context has
  **tracked** changes with `rebase.autoStash` false/unset — **or with it *true* on an arm the option
  does not reach, which round 26 separates out** (item 8): a checkout **continuation** issues a
  standalone `git checkout` before its rebase, which `rebase.autoStash` never reaches, so a
  tracked-dirty
  resume is refused there whatever the config says, while a fresh checkout run is already refused by
  the shipped whole-repo gate at rank 3 —
  (`context-dirty`), both §4.9 rank 5. Where an **untracked** file merely sits in that row's work
  tree — anywhere in it, since the enumeration is anchored at its top level and not at the cwd — the
  plan **states the residual instead of refusing**: `context.untracked_present: true` with
  `context.overwrite_risk: unknown` and one `untracked-present` warning, because the arm is about to
  write that working tree and Git **may** refuse to overwrite an untracked file — a question no
  static projection can decide, which is why round 18 withdrew round 17's rank 5.55 blocker and
  autostash cannot help either way, since it stashes tracked changes only (§4.1, §5.4.7, §19.26).
  Where `rebase.autoStash` **is** effectively true **and the arm is one it applies to — external
  pass 1
  or pass 2** (§4.1 `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`) —, Git will
  stash the operator's uncommitted **tracked** work and **attempt** to reapply it — in place on
  pass 1, **after**
  the implicit switch on pass 2 — which the
  `git config`
  manual itself warns "might result in non-trivial conflicts"; the plan states that rather than
  discovering it, as a **warning** that leaves `runnable: true` (settled in round-25 item 5; §19.18
  retains only the guarded-`--no-autostash` argv question). **Round 27 makes the residual explicit
  here too** (item 4): where that reapply conflicts, `git rebase` still **exits 0**, the working
  tree is left conflicted and the stash is **kept** in `refs/stash`
  (`sequencer.c` `apply_save_autostash_oid`, whose error `finish_rebase` discards, verified against
  Git 2.55.0), so the warning's detail names the residual and **no** surface of this feature may
  describe autostash as rescuing, protecting or restoring the tree
  (`context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`, §4.1, §5.4.7, §14). `--plan` performs none of this: the
  dirty probe is the tracked-only predicate of §5.4.7 — the single command
  `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 git -C <repo_root> status --porcelain --untracked-files=no
  --ignore-submodules=all`, whose
  in-memory index refresh mirrors `git rebase`'s own clean-work-tree check and writes nothing, and
  **not** the `diff-files`/`diff-index` pair, which reports stat-dirty content-identical files as
  modified — and the
  checked-out-elsewhere probe is the worktree inventory §4.3 already runs, compared after both
  sides are resolved with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` so a subdirectory of the row's own
  worktree reads as *self*, and the untracked-**presence** enumeration is a name-only `ls-files
  --others`, which opens no working-tree file and reads no blob (§5.4.7, §13).
- **Never a *local branch* rewritten by the plan's own fetch, and never a HEAD left dangling by it**
  (round-25 item 2). The fetch this route performs is the shipped one, and where a configured
  positive refspec covers `refs/heads/**` — the mirror `+refs/*:refs/*` is the common way a
  repository gets there — that fetch **writes local branches**: it fast-forwards them, a forced
  refspec moves them anywhere, and an effective prune **deletes** the covered ones the remote no
  longer has. The plan discloses the capability on every such context
  (`may_update_local_branches`, `may_delete_local_branches`, `local_branch_destinations`), and where
  one of those destinations is **held** by a worktree — HEAD, an in-progress rebase, or a bisect —
  it declines the fetch and refuses at rank 5.06 rather than performing it. That refusal covers both
  of Git's own outcomes: the `die` at `refusing to fetch into branch '<ref>' checked out at
  '<path>'`, which stops the fetch but leaves the shipped run continuing on **stale** refs, and the
  prune-only deletion of a held branch the remote no longer has, which Git does **not** refuse and
  which leaves that worktree's HEAD dangling. **Under the guard neither can happen**; on the
  unguarded route both can, and the document says so instead of implying the fetch is inert
  (§0.1, §4.4, §4.9 rank 5.06, §8.6.1 cause 6).
- **An approval may never be minted over an identity the document could not show** (round-27
  item 7). Git accepts bytes that are not valid UTF-8 in branch names, ref names, paths and config
  values; JSON does not, and every conforming Go encoder rewrites each invalid sequence to U+FFFD.
  The fingerprint's TLV pre-image binds the raw bytes and therefore separates such plans
  (§5.3.2a rule 6), but the *document* an operator reads before approving does not: two different
  runs render identically, and approving one would authorise the other. The controlled path
  therefore validates the raw bytes of every bound identity string with `utf8.Valid` **before**
  hashing and, on any failure, publishes the evidence and mints **no** token
  (§4.9, §5.3.2a rule 10). **Round 28 fixes where that evidence lives and how far the refusal
  reaches** (item 4). The evidence is the top-level **`encoding_issues[]`** array of §4.4 — closed
  rows of `{field_id, path_label_ascii, owner_entry_ascii_or_null, byte_length, raw_base64,
  sha256}`, deterministically sorted, every member ASCII — and **never** a sanitized `detail`
  string: this section's renderer is lossy by design, so putting raw invalid bytes through it would
  either destroy the evidence or defeat the sanitizer, and **no `detail` in this document may carry
  raw invalid text**. The non-waivable rank 5.08 `identity-not-utf8` blocker and `runnable: false`
  are published **only where the document would otherwise mint a token**; a limitless plan publishes
  the array, a `null` token and nothing else. Two properties make this a safety rule rather than a
  strictness: the check is on the
  bytes and never on the marshalled JSON, so a lossy renderer can never satisfy it; and the
  **unguarded** run is untouched — `tws sync` still replays those branches — so nothing is taken
  away except the ability to approve something that was never displayed.
- **The same evidence discipline binds the invalid-config rank, and round 30 moves it out of the
  blocker prose too** (item 2). A rejected Git config value is attacker-influenceable metadata of
  exactly the same shape — arbitrary bytes read out of a repository — so it follows the same rule:
  the machine-readable facts live in the top-level **`config_issues[]`** array of §4.4, closed rows
  of `{issue_id, context_id, repo_root, key, source, route_command, error_kind, raw_value_present,
  raw_value_base64, raw_value_sha256, sanitized_value}` whose only lossy member is
  `sanitized_value` — itself `null` where the occurrence carried no value at all, which the human
  line renders as the fixed literal `<valueless>` rather than as an omitted field (round-33 item 8,
  §8.3.5) — and the rank 5.07
  blocker's
  `detail` is a **sanitized string** carrying `config issue <issue_id> (<key>, <route_command>)` rather than
  reproducing the value. **`issue_id` and `context_id` disclose nothing**: each is a SHA-256 over a
  length-framed raw
  tuple, so they identify and join without publishing a byte of the offending value **or of the raw
  repository path** — which is what lets the identity be the *raw* context while every rendered
  surface stays sanitized, and what lets a `detail`, the `Configuration issues:` line and a human
  reading stay safe while remaining precise (round-31 item 2, round-32 item 1).
  **No `detail` anywhere in this document carries a raw or unsanitized value**, whatever its rank,
  and round 28's "the repository root, key and sanitized value are published as fields" on the
  blocker itself is withdrawn with the shape it assumed (§4.2 Part 3, §4.4, §4.9 rank 5.07).
- **Terminal-escape and injection hygiene.** Branch names, base refs, repo paths **and commit
  subjects** (§4.5) are attacker-influenceable metadata. Reuse `ancestrySanitize` /
  `ancestryCommandToken` / `ancestryDetail` (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:551-624`) for every
  rendered token, bound subjects to one sanitized line, and never interpolate an unsanitised ref
  into a suggested command.
- **No shell.** Plan probes must use `exec.Command` argv, never `sh -c` (checkout's validation is
  the one existing `sh -c` and is not a model to copy, `internal/checkout_sync.go:1296-1309`).
- **Ref/SHA confusion.** A ref name that looks like a SHA, or a tag shadowing a branch, must not
  change the plan's meaning: probe branches through `refs/heads/` as the evaluator does
  (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:389`) and validate full-SHA fields with the existing
  `ancestryFullSHA` guard.
- **Never destructive.** The guard must never `git reset --hard`, never abort someone else's rebase,
  and never delete state it did not create — the standing rule in
  `docs/engineering-workflow.md` (coding conventions).
- **Approval tokens are not secrets.** The fingerprint is integrity, not authentication: it prevents
  approving plan X and executing plan Y, nothing more. Document that.

## 12. Failure and recovery implications

- A plan refusal must be **idempotent and scope-correct**: re-running the same command produces the
  same refusal, and the invocation leaves behind exactly what it created and nothing else. For a
  *fresh* pre-rebase refusal that means the state, lock, guard and sentinel **this run wrote** are
  torn down (§9); for a *continuation* refusal it means nothing is written and nothing is removed —
  the interrupted payload, legacy state or transaction survives byte-identical (§8.7.5). "Clean"
  never means deleting another run's recovery record.
- **A refusal after the first successful rebase of the invocation is a failure, not a rollback.**
  Refs have already moved, so the guard stops before the refused entry and persists progress through
  the route's own failure path (`saveScopedSyncFailure` / `saveIncompleteSync` / the checkout
  transaction's persisted index), leaving a stale-but-recoverable guard exactly as a conflict would
  (§8.7.5). It never rewinds, aborts, or clears.
- **A refusal must never be mistaken for a conflict — and what it says about `--continue` depends on
  whether anything moved.** The message shape is distinct from a conflict's in every case, and the
  two cells are fixed:
  - **Pre-mutation refusals never suggest `--continue` as the way forward.** Every plan-only blocker
    and every guarded
    refusal taken at the plan/guard seam **before** the first rebase of this invocation — the
    projected ladder of §8.6.2, the limits, `approval-mismatch`, `guard-limit-mismatch`,
    `fetch-context-indeterminate`, `fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate` (round-23 item 3),
    `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` (round-25 item 2),
    `restore-blocked` — changed nothing, so there is no progress to
    resume. On a **fresh** run the invocation's own state was torn down (§9), and a `--continue`
    suggestion would point at a run that does not exist — on the external route, at a sentinel this
    invocation has just correctly removed. On a **continuation** the interrupted state is
    byte-identical (§8.7.5), so the remedy named is to fix the fact and re-issue the *same*
    invocation, stated in those words rather than as advice to "continue", which would imply this
    invocation advanced something. Neither form claims a recovery record was created, and neither
    carries the `state-preserved: ` marker token below. **On a continuation the refusal must
    nonetheless state that the interrupted run's recovery record is untouched**, because "nothing
    was preserved" and "this invocation preserved nothing of its own" are opposite readings of the
    same silence: the payload, legacy state and transaction it found are byte-identical, the guard
    was not reclaimed (the seam is above `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, and the native reclaim conditions
    that seam re-evaluates write nothing either, §8.7.5), and the operator's
    interrupted work is exactly where it was. The marker token is reserved for the cell where **this
    invocation** advanced or took ownership of something, so a consumer reading the marker alone
    still distinguishes the two, while the prose never leaves an operator believing a pre-resume
    refusal discarded their recovery record.
  - **A JIT/revalidation refusal taken *after* this invocation mutated something — or after it took
    ownership of an interrupted run's state — says so explicitly, and names the next step.** The
    cells are the ones §8.7.5 enumerates: a per-entry seam refusal (`revalidation-mismatch`, a
    newly-exceeded limit, a newly `indeterminate-entry` row) once at least one entry of this
    invocation has rebased, and a scoped external resume that has already reclaimed the guard. The
    refusal states three things in this order: **what refused** (kind, entry, field), **that the
    recovery state is preserved** — the payload/legacy state/transaction records the entries
    completed so far and the guard is left stale-but-reclaimable, exactly as a conflict leaves them,
    and nothing was deleted, rewound or aborted — and **the workflow to resume**: re-plan the
    remaining work with `tws sync <f> --plan --continue` (plus the same trigger, limit, push and
    validation flags), read the fresh `remaining-work` token, then resume with
    `tws sync <f> --continue` carrying the limits and, where a limit is really to be waived, that
    token (§8.7.4, §8.7.7). The full-run token of the interrupted invocation is dead and the text
    must not imply otherwise.
  - **The stable marker names the cell rather than leaving it to prose** (§8.7.6): a guarded refusal
    at or after the JIT seam writes its one anchored `^plan-guard: <kind>: ` line with a
    `<sanitized-detail>` that begins with the fixed, sanitation-safe token **`state-preserved: `**
    before the entry and field — e.g.
    `plan-guard: revalidation-mismatch: state-preserved: pr2 base moved (approved <sha>, now <sha>); continue with --plan --continue`.
    A pre-mutation refusal never carries that token, so a consumer can tell "nothing happened" from
    "something happened and is recoverable" from the marker alone, without parsing the prose that
    follows it. The token is part of the detail, not a second marker line, and the one-anchored-line
    rule of §8.7.6 is unchanged.
- **A guarded invocation never degrades into an unguarded one.** If the guard cannot compute a plan
  — unreadable `stack.yaml`, **an unusable repo context or a failed replay-critical probe** — it
  refuses (`plan-unavailable`, `repo-unavailable`, `probe-failed`) and rebases
  nothing; it does not "fall back" to the legacy behaviour it was asked to guard, and in particular
  never reaches `syncFallback` (§8.5.5, §8.7.5, §4.1). The same holds across an interruption: every
  route that persisted a guard — the v2 payload and **any** checkout transaction —
  resumes with the limits it persisted, including a persisted `0` (§10.3), so dropping the flags on
  `--continue` cannot silently
  un-guard it, and the legacy external route says so in the document instead of pretending
  otherwise (§8.7.4).
- **A continuation re-plans; it never revalidates a stored approval, because none is stored.** The
  remaining work is re-planned from live facts and re-checked against the effective limits, and a
  waiver requires a fresh `remaining-work` token from `--plan --continue` (§8.7.4). This is the
  "re-plan and re-approve" option of the earlier draft's pair, chosen deliberately: the alternative —
  "refuse when the stored plan changed" — presupposes a stored plan whose fingerprint could still
  match, and after an interruption it never can. The frozen-decision doctrine
  (`internal/cli/sync.go:435-466`) still governs the *axes* and now also the persisted *limits*
  (`guard-limit-mismatch`, §8.7.4); it simply has no approval to freeze.
- The guard **improves** one existing recovery defect for free: an unresolvable cutoff currently
  surfaces as a bogus "conflict" in external mode (§6.5). Pre-verifying the cutoff turns it into a
  pre-rebase refusal naming the entry and the SHA.
- **A guarded external run no longer aborts somebody else's rebase.** The sharpest recovery
  improvement this feature makes is not about tws state at all. A pass-2 row rebases in `entry.Repo`
  or the process cwd; if a rebase is already in progress there, `git rebase <base> <git_branch>`
  refuses, and the shipped handler answers that refusal with `git rebase --abort` **in the same
  directory** (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:200-206`) — discarding an unrelated rebase's HEAD
  position and conflict resolution as a side effect of a sync that never replayed a commit. The
  guard blocks that cell before the Git call, at rank 5.45, on both the plan and the JIT seam, with
  the marker line because no shipped check owns it (§4.1, §4.9, §5.4 consequence 7, §8.7.6). The
  unguarded run is unchanged, and the recovery note says which directory holds the other rebase so
  the operator finishes or aborts it deliberately rather than by accident.
- **A guarded external run no longer strands the operator on a branch they did not choose.** Today a
  pass-2 rebase switches HEAD to the rebased branch in `entry.Repo` or the process cwd and leaves it
  there — on success, on conflict, and after its own `--abort` — with no restoration path (§5.4.7,
  §11). The guard does not add one (that would be an executor behaviour change), but it **states the
  switch before it happens** and refuses the two cells where the switch fails outright: a branch
  already checked out in a **foreign** worktree of that context, and a context with **tracked**
  uncommitted changes and autostash off. Recovery advice
  therefore never has to begin with "find out which branch you are on now".
- A refusal that happened **after** the fetch must not claim the repository is untouched: the
  remote-tracking refs the fetch updated stay updated (§0.1). The refusal text should be silent
  about it rather than false about it. A **guarded** refusal says this in its prose only — it emits
  no document (§8.7.6); the `fetch.*`/`freshness` block belongs to `--plan`, where a refusal
  document carries exactly the same block as a successful one.
- The guard must not change what happens *after* a real conflict: the conflict message, state
  layout, and `--continue` path stay exactly as shipped.

---

## 13. Performance and process budget

Extra Git processes, **only on plan/guard paths**, per selected entry:

| Probe | Purpose | Already run today? |
|---|---|---|
| `rev-parse <base.ref>` | the strategy-decision SHA in `base_context` (`base.decision_sha`) **and** the destination/snapshot in `execution_context` (`destination.sha`/`destination.snapshot_sha`) — **one process where the row's two contexts coincide, and two on a split row**, since the same ref must be peeled in each store and neither answer may be reused for the other (round-35 item 3, counted honestly by round-36 item 3) | yes in checkout (`:495`), yes in external for the decision read (`GetBranchSHA`, `:122`); the **execution-context** read on a split row is new |
| `rev-parse --abbrev-ref origin/HEAD`, and on its failure `symbolic-ref --short HEAD` | the **default-branch read** `resolveBase` performs in `base_context` before `base.ref` exists at all — `DefaultBranchIn(repoCtx)`, or `DefaultBranch()` with no `-C` when the context is the cwd (`internal/exec.go:59-89`, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:342-356`). It is **one or two** processes, not zero and not always one: the second runs only when the first fails, and both failing yields the literal `main` with no third. It is **external-only** and **conditional**: `resolveEntryBase` short-circuits with **no** Git whenever the base names a same-repo stack entry (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:335-340`), and `BuildCheckoutPlan` never calls `resolveBase` at all, using `entry.Base` verbatim (`internal/checkout_sync.go:484-497`). The answer is **run-invariant for a context**, so the planner resolves it **once per base context that resolves at least one literal base** and reuses it for every row of that context — but it may not be dropped from the budget, which round-37 item 3 corrects: rounds 34-36 attributed the read to `base_context` in prose and counted **zero** processes for it | yes in external (the executor issues it inside `resolveEntryBase` for every such row, and again in the new-mode `--no-fetch` I14 preflight); **never** in checkout |
| `rev-parse --verify <cutoff>^{commit}` | cutoff resolvability (`cutoff.state`) | no (this is the new safety) |
| `rev-list --count --no-merges <upstream>..<branch>` | candidate count `N`, and the input every bounded identity probe below is derived from (§4.5) | no |
| `rev-list --count <branch>..<upstream>` | the **upstream-side** count that makes `may_drop_patch_equivalent` arm-aware (§4.2) — cheap, and the only honest way to answer it | no |
| `rev-list --skip=<N-1> --max-count=1 --no-merges --topo-order --format=…` | the **oldest** candidate for `first_candidate` (§4.5); skipped when `N == 0` | no |
| `rev-list --reverse --topo-order --no-merges` (streamed **to EOF**, hashed in full, capped in-process by retention only — never closed early) **or** `rev-list --skip=<max(0,N-cap)> --max-count=<min(N,cap)> --reverse --topo-order --no-merges` **plus** a second full-stream `rev-list --reverse --topo-order --no-merges` whose output is hashed and discarded | the bounded oldest-first candidate list (`--json`/verbose only) **and** `replay.candidate_digest`, which is computed over the **complete, uncapped** sequence and is therefore required on every countable row, in **both** renderings (§4.5, §4.6). The first shape answers both from one process **provided it consumes every line**: the rendering cap selects the oldest `cap` SHAs to publish and never bounds what the digest consumes. The second cannot see the tail, so it needs the extra full stream — which is what makes the probe-shape choice of §19.12 a real one | no |
| `rev-parse refs/heads/<branch>` | pre-SHA / fingerprint | yes in checkout (`:500`), no in external |
| `rev-parse --verify refs/heads/<branch>^{commit}` | `head.state` (§5.1 rule 6) — may be folded into the probe above when it already uses `--verify` | no (this is the new totality axis) |

Plus, **once per repository context** (not per entry) — where a *context* is the
`(repo, context_id)` row of §4.4, so the **process cwd is itself a context** whenever an external
pass-2 row has an empty `entry.Repo` (§5.4), and one `repo` token can therefore need two sets of
these probes when its arms resolve to two directories — **which since round 34 includes the ordinary
external pass-1 row whose `entry.Repo` is non-empty, whose `base_context` is that repository and
whose `execution_context` is the entry's worktree** (§4.1). Two rules bound the arithmetic of this
table. **Each probe is issued in the context whose fact it is, and round 35 corrects which context that is**
(item 3): `base_context` owns the default-branch read, the resolution of `base.ref` and the
`GetBranchSHA` behind `base.decision_sha` — **and nothing else**; `execution_context` owns everything
`git rebase` resolves (the destination `rev-parse`, the cutoff verification, the head
`rev-parse --verify`, the candidate `rev-list` probes and the `for-each-ref refs/heads/` inventory)
as well as the working-tree and operation-directory probes; and the `rebase.*` configuration read
belongs to `execution_context` **only** — a context that is nobody's execution
context pays **nothing** for configuration and publishes `status: not-evaluated` in all four slots
(§4.3, round-34 items 2 and 4). **A pass-1 split is two contexts and *may* be one object store, which
is measured rather than assumed** (round-35 items 2 and 8): the entry's worktree is normally a linked
worktree of the repository `entry.Repo` names, so the two normally share a canonical common dir even
though their roots — and therefore their `context_id`s — differ, but the sharing is a **fact to be
read**, not a property of the two `source` labels. Every probe that is a *common-dir* fact (the
branch inventory, the worktree inventory and its hold reads) may be answered once and reused for both
refs **only after both contexts' canonical absolute common dirs have been resolved and compared
byte-equal** (§4.1 context-pair rule); where they were not compared, or compare unequal, each ref
pays for its own and nothing crosses — and unequal is additionally the rank 5.15
`base-execution-store-divergent` refusal. Every probe that is a *directory* fact (the work tree's
status, the per-worktree `$GIT_DIR`'s operation markers, the untracked enumeration, and the
configuration, which Git resolves per worktree once `extensions.worktreeConfig` is in play) is
genuinely two probes because it has two answers. And **"once per context" is a statement about *run-invariant* facts
only**: the context identity, the ordered configuration inventory with its typed interpretations and
the other facts that cannot change under this run are computed once and cached, while every
**mutable** precondition in this table is re-probed at each JIT seam that gates on it, at the
per-row bound stated below (round-34 item 5, §5.2, §9):

| Probe | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `for-each-ref refs/heads/` | every local branch and its tip, via `BuildBranchRefInventory` — the candidate-range membership half of the collateral set (§4.3), issued in **`execution_context`**, where the candidate range is resolved (round-35 item 3). So a `--no-fetch` checkout run, a checkout continuation, a push-stage invocation and a `restoring` resume all pay the same single list read, evaluate **no** rebase-scope or fetch-only key, and still evaluate `submodule.recurse`, which is a string comparison over occurrences the list already delivered and costs no additional process. The **route scope never adds a probe and never removes one**: the list read is issued per repository context regardless, because it is what supplies the four *effective-value* keys of `repositories[].config`, the fetch keys and the submodule-recursion facts (§4.2 Part 2, §4.4). **What the route scope filters is the parsing and the evidence, not the reads** (round-30 items 2 and 3): only the occurrences of keys the described route will really hand to Git are parsed for validity, and only those produce a rank 5.07 blocker and a `config_issues[]` row — an out-of-scope invalid value is neither parsed nor published, and round 28's "the disclosure is published in and out of scope alike" is withdrawn as impossible, since nine of the thirteen keys have no value slot anywhere in the document. **The evidence costs one flag, not one process**: the same ordered per-context read carries **`--show-scope`** (`git -C <context_root> config --list --show-scope -z`, Git 2.26+), which is what supplies each `config_issues[]` row's `source` member, so the structured array is budgeted at **zero additional processes** over what round 28 already counted, and the base64/SHA-256 members are computed in-process from bytes the read already delivered. **Four *effective-value* keys** — `rebase.updateRefs`, `rebase.rebaseMerges`, `rebase.backend`, `rebase.autoStash`; `rebase.reapplyCherryPicks` does not exist in Git and is not probed. They are read **per execution context** and land in that context's `repositories[]` row — which is why the axis is a sorted array rather than one flat object: a multi-repo stack legitimately has different answers, and four probes × R repositories is the honest cost of not mis-attributing them (§4.4) |

A negative refspec that excludes the branch from fetching leaves the baseline outside every fetch, which the row records as `expected_sha_freshness: possibly-stale`. Issued **only when `intent.push` is true** — once per `(push context, remote)` for the refspecs, once per target for the value, and not at all for a branch the refspecs map nowhere, which is `expected_ref: null`/`expectation: absent` without a second process |

Plus, **once per invocation** in external mode:

| Probe | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `worktree list --porcelain` in the **process cwd**, no `-C` | the prunable verdict, mirroring `IsPrunableWorktree` exactly (§3.7, §5.4.3). The cwd does not change during an invocation, so one cached probe answers every pass-2 row — it is *not* the same probe as the repo-scoped inventory above and must not be merged with it, even when the cwd also happens to be a repository context in its own right (§5.4), because the two answer different questions |

**The arithmetic is stated as a formula over *contexts* and *rows*, not as a single number, because
round 34 made the context count a variable and round 35 makes the per-row set context-dependent**
(round-35 item 8; the earlier "roughly 35-45 extra processes for a 5-entry stack" is **withdrawn**,
having been computed when one entry meant one context). Let **N** be the number of selected rows and
**C** the number of **distinct** contexts the document establishes — distinct in the §4.4 identity
sense, so an external pass-1 row whose `entry.Repo` is non-empty contributes **two**, a pass-2 row
with an empty `Repo` contributes the process cwd, and a checkout run contributes exactly one. Let
**S** be the number of **distinct measured canonical common dirs** among those contexts; `S ≤ C`, and
`S < C` exactly where two contexts were **measured** to share a store — the ordinary pass-1
worktree-of-`entry.Repo` split. Let **D** be the number of **split rows** — external rows whose
`base_context` and `execution_context` are two different contexts, which after round-36 item 1 is
exactly the set of external pass-1 rows with a non-empty `entry.Repo`; `D = 0` in checkout, on every
pass-2 row and on every pass-1 row with an empty `Repo`, and `D ≤ N` always. (**`D` here is this
formula's variable and has nothing to do with the `D` in the quoted `stack-status` bound
"at most 2 + C + D Git processes" below, which is that helper's own.**) Let **B** be the number of
**base contexts that must resolve at least one literal base** — external only, since checkout never
calls `resolveBase`, and excluding every context all of whose rows name a same-repo stack entry,
which `resolveEntryBase` answers with no Git at all; `B ≤ C`. Let **K** be the number of **skip
rows**, which are counted separately because they are not per-row-table rows at all (below). Then
the plan-time cost is

> **≈ 6·N + D + (1..2)·B (external) or ≈ 5·N (checkout)  +  ≈ 5·C  +  ≈ 2·S  +  (0 or 1)·C  +  push and ancestry extras**,
> with the **N** in the per-row term counting only the **non-skip** rows and the **K** skip rows
> costing at most one process each (round-37 items 1 and 3)

with each term named rather than lumped: **6·N / 5·N** are the per-row probes of the first table (the
head-state probe folds into the existing `rev-parse` where that already uses `--verify`; the
full-sequence stream runs on every countable row because `replay.candidate_digest` is a fingerprint
member, while the *rendered* list it also yields is emitted only under `--json`/verbose). **`+ D`** is
the correction round-36 item 3 makes to an undercount round 35 shipped: a split row must peel
`base.ref` **twice** — once in `base_context` as the `GetBranchSHA` the executor issues anyway
(`base.decision_sha`) and once in `execution_context`, where `git rebase` peels its operand
(`destination.sha`/`destination.snapshot_sha`) — and the per-row table counted that ref resolution
once, which was right only for a coincident row. The second read is **not** optional and **not**
substitutable: the two answers are the two facts the rank 5.15/`base-execution-context-split` pair
exists to compare, so reusing one for the other would erase the very divergence the plan publishes.
**`+ (1..2)·B`** is the correction **round-37 item 3** makes to an undercount every round since 34
shipped: `resolveBase` cannot produce `base.ref` without first asking the context for its default
branch, and `DefaultBranchIn` is **one** `rev-parse --abbrev-ref origin/HEAD` plus, **only on its
failure**, a second `symbolic-ref --short HEAD` (`internal/exec.go:69-88`). Rounds 34-36 attributed
that read to `base_context` in prose while counting nothing for it, so every figure below was low by
between one and two processes per base context. It is a **per-context** term and not a per-row one
because the answer is run-invariant for a context and is cached for the invocation like the ordered
configuration inventory; it is `0` for a context whose rows all name same-repo stack entries, and
`0` for checkout on every route. **The `K` skip rows are budgeted explicitly rather than folded into
`N`** (round-37 item 1): a `skipped-anchor`, `skipped-archived` or `skipped-no-base` row issues
**zero** Git processes; a `skipped-updated-ref` row issues **exactly one** — its head
`rev-parse --verify refs/heads/<git_branch>^{commit}` in the established execution context — plus
**nothing** for the cwd prunability inventory, which is the single per-invocation probe two tables
below and is shared by every pass-2 row, and plus the route's own I14 preflight reads on the
new-mode `--no-fetch` route, which are the `(1..2)·B` default-branch term already counted and one
`rev-parse --verify <ref>^{commit}`. No skip row costs a cutoff verification, a `rev-list` of any
shape, a branch inventory, a dirty `status`, an untracked enumeration or an operation-directory
probe, so a document of nothing but skip rows is close to free.
**≈5·C** are
the genuinely per-*directory* probes — `rev-parse --path-format=absolute --show-toplevel`, the
absolute `--git-common-dir`, the tracked-dirty `status`, the untracked enumeration, and the two
`rev-parse --git-path rebase-*` reads on external execution directories (which is why an external
context runs slightly above the figure and a base-only context slightly below it, having no
working-tree question to ask). **≈2·S** are the **store** facts — `for-each-ref refs/heads/` and
`worktree list --porcelain` with its per-detached-worktree hold reads — and **`S`, not `C`, is the
multiplier only where the sharing was *measured***: §4.1's context-pair rule forbids answering both
refs from one process until their canonical common dirs have been read and compared byte-equal. An
implementation that measures pays `2·S` where the dirs are equal and `2·C` where they are not, and is
right in both cells; one that *assumes* a linked worktree shares its parent's store always pays `2·S`
and, in the cell where the assumption is false, publishes another repository's branches as this row's
collateral upper bound — the saving is two processes and the cost is a wrong blast radius, which is
why the cheaper term is conditional on a measurement rather than on a shape.
**(0 or 1)·C** is the configuration read: **one** ordered `config --list --show-scope -z` for each
context that some row uses as its `execution_context`, and **zero** for a context that is only ever a
base or push context (§4.3, §4.2 Part 2), **plus up to three conditional typed reads** —
`config --type=bool --get rebase.rebaseMerges`, `… rebase.updateRefs`, `… rebase.autoStash` — issued
only where their key is set at all, which is what resolves their effective value, while their
*validity*, their scopes and their value presence come out of the ordered list read rather than out
of any `--get`/`--get-all` ladder (round-26 item 7, round-27 items 1 and 3, round-32 item 4,
round-33 item 7, **round-34 items 2 and 4**). **No two-, three- or four-key `--get` ladder survives
anywhere in this document, and `rebase.backend` has no typed read at all**, its effective value being
a string the ordered list already carries (round-35 item 7). That ordered read's
**`--show-scope`** (round-30 item 2) costs no extra process and its scope names are what round 31
closes the `config_issues[].source` enum over — **`command` included**, which likewise costs nothing
because such occurrences are **inherited** command-scope configuration
(`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` and the supported `--config-env` mechanisms) that the
described route already passes to its children, not a `-c` this feature adds to the frozen argv
(round-31 item 2, round-32 item 2). The same single read, together with the absolute
`--git-common-dir` already counted in the `5·C` term, is what anchors fetch-context equivalence, and
it is the one that supplies `fetch.all`, the branch remote, every remote URL, every ordered fetch
refspec, each `skipFetchAll` and — from round 22 — each remote's effective prune/pruneTags/`tagOpt`,
the `insteadOf` rewrite rules and — from round 23 — the submodule recursion keys, replacing the
per-key ladder and staying constant as remotes are added (round-20 item 1, round-22 items 2-3,
round-23 item 3). Every per-context read named here answers **every row of that context** and no
row of any other. On top of the formula, and outside it because each is conditional: **only where a
context really has submodules**, one gitlink enumeration for it, **one ordered `.gitmodules` read where any of its three sources exists** (round-26 item 6 — the read rungs 2 and 4 of §4.4's ladder both come from, budgeted here for the first time; round-27 item 2 fixes *which* source it is: working tree, else index, else `HEAD`, and none at all in a bare context), and one probe pair per **present gitlink** submodule the
bounded reach reaches (round-23 item 3; round-24 item 2 replaces "active, present" — activity is not
what `git fetch` recurses on, so probing only active submodules would have under-enumerated the very
reach this budget exists to bound), plus, **only where a context or candidate's resolved effect
really covers `refs/heads/**` positively**, one `for-each-ref refs/heads/` and one
`worktree list --porcelain` (plus that store's per-detached-worktree hold reads) **per canonical
common dir, not per candidate** — nothing at all for the ordinary
`+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/<r>/*` clone, and nothing extra where a row already forced the same two
inventories in the same store (round-26 items 3 and 4), and **no process at all** for the two legacy remote-file
reads, which are `os.Stat`/reads under the common dir already resolved (round-23 item 5), plus **two per distinct external
execution directory** for the operation-directory probe and **one more per distinct work tree** for the untracked
enumeration (the first cached per directory and the second per canonical top level, so a stack whose rows share one `entry.Repo` pays for each
once, and rows standing in two subdirectories of one work tree pay for the enumeration once — its
anchor is the same `rev-parse --show-toplevel` already counted per context, and costs one extra
process only for a directory that is not a context, §5.4.7; a **fresh checkout** run now pays that
enumeration too, which is exactly **one** process, since checkout has one context, round-20 item 2 — and round 18 removes round 17's **two to three name-only `diff-tree` calls per external
row**, since the additions intersection they fed is withdrawn with the exactness claim it made,
§5.4.7, §19.26), plus one
cwd-scoped `worktree list` per external invocation, plus — **only on a run whose `intent.push` is
true** — one `config --get-all remote.<remote>.fetch` per `(push context, remote)` and one
`rev-parse --verify` per target for the implicit-lease baseline (§4.4, round-19 item 3), plus
the `StackEdge` evaluation if the
plan includes the ancestry verdict (already budgeted and documented by `stack-status`:
"at most 2 + C + D Git processes", `internal/stack_status.go:610-613`).

**A worked upper estimate for five entries, stated conservatively and with its assumptions visible**
(round-35 item 8, **recalculated by round-36 item 3 to include the split rows' second ref
resolution and by round-37 item 3 to include the default-branch read**). The honest answer now
depends on the shape, so two cells are given rather than one
number; both assume the worst case for the new term — every row's base is a **literal** ref, so
every base context pays the default-branch read, and both of its processes are needed because
`origin/HEAD` is unset. *(i) Five entries in one repository with no `entry.Repo`, cleanly stat-able worktrees —
`N = 5`, `C = 5` (each worktree is its own context), `D = 0` (an empty-`Repo` pass-1 row's two
contexts coincide, round-36 item 1), `B = 5` and, because those worktrees are linked
worktrees of one store **and the plan measured that**, `S = 1`:* ≈30 row probes + ≈25 per-directory
probes + ≈2 store probes + **0-10 default-branch reads** + 5 ordered config reads and up to 15 conditional typed reads + 1 cwd-scoped
`worktree list` ≈ **65-90** plan-time processes (round 36 published ≈65-80 here, which omitted the
`(1..2)·B` term). *(ii) The same five entries where each carries a
non-empty `entry.Repo`, so every row splits — `N = 5`, `C = 10`, `D = 5`, `B = 5` (only the five
**base** contexts resolve a base at all), and `S = 5` where each worktree was
measured to share its `entry.Repo`'s store:* ≈30 + **5 split-row destination reads** + ≈50 + ≈10 + **0-10 default-branch reads** + 5 ordered reads (only the five
**execution** contexts read configuration; the five base-only contexts read none) + up to 15 typed
reads + 1 ≈ **110-145** (round 35 published ≈105-130, which omitted the `+ D` term; round 36
published ≈110-135, which omitted the default-branch reads). **A stack of five `skipped-updated-ref`
rows is a third shape and costs almost nothing**: 5 head `rev-parse --verify` probes + the
per-directory and store probes of whatever contexts they establish + 1 cwd-scoped `worktree list`,
with **no** cutoff, range, digest, dirty, untracked or operation-directory probes at all
(round-37 item 1). All figures are **ceilings for an explicitly requested command**, all
exclude the conditional submodule, fetch-coverage, push-lease and ancestry extras above, and none
may be quoted as a typical cost. Where the store sharing is **not** measured — because a common-dir
read failed — the `2·S` term becomes `2·C` and cell (ii) rises by ten. Rows whose
`determinacy = unknown` are **cheaper**, not dearer: their range probes are skipped at plan time and
run once at the JIT seam instead.

**And the plan-time figure is not the whole cost, because the mutable facts are re-probed** (round-34
item 5, restated here as part of the arithmetic rather than as a rule elsewhere). A **guarded**
five-entry external run pays its plan-time figure **plus** up to **twelve** Git processes at each of its
five JIT seams — the ten of the re-probe set below plus the **one or two** the seam's own
re-resolution of the base ref costs where that base is a literal, since §5.4 consequence 4 requires
the guarded row to recompute its *resolved base ref* and `resolveBase` cannot do that without
`DefaultBranchIn` (round-37 item 3; a row whose base names a same-repo stack entry still pays ten) —
so at most **60** more, and cell (i) becomes ≈**125-150** and cell (ii) ≈**170-205** (round-36
item 3's recalculated plan-time base plus round-37 item 3's two corrections) —
and a guarded five-entry checkout run pays at most **eight** per seam, unchanged, because checkout
resolves no default branch anywhere. A **`--plan`** invocation pays
the plan-time figure alone, having no seams. The re-probe set and its per-row ceiling are fixed
below; what may **not** be done is to quote the plan-time number as the cost of a guarded run, or to
retire a seam probe on the ground that the plan already measured it. Rules to write into
the spec: **no `git log`, no working-tree `git diff` and no `diff-tree` in the plan at all** — round
17 carved out the bounded, name-only `diff-tree -r --name-only --diff-filter=A -z` for the
untracked-overlap probe, and round 18 removes both the probe and the carve-out, so the round-16
blanket rule stands unqualified again (round-18 item 1, §5.4.7); the **rendered** identity comes from bounded
`rev-list` probes derived from the count, never from an unbounded materialised list, and never from
`--reverse --max-count`, which reads from the wrong end of the range (§4.5); the **digest** is the
one place a full sequence is consumed, and it is consumed as a **stream read to EOF, hashed and
discarded** — never materialised and never truncated by closing the pipe, so memory stays O(cap)
while the read stays O(N) (§4.5); the human default
requests exactly
one identity and `--json`/verbose request at most the documented cap, with `commits_truncated`
derived from `N > cap` rather than from a cap-plus-one probe; commit **subjects** are sanitized and
one line;
per-context probes of **run-invariant** facts — the context identity of §4.4, the ordered
configuration inventory and its typed interpretations — are cached for the invocation and never
re-run per entry, while every **mutable** precondition is re-probed at the JIT seam that gates on it
and the blanket "never re-run per entry" of the previous rounds is **withdrawn as unsound**
(round-34 item 5): a cached dirty tree, a cached rebase-directory answer, a cached holder set or a
cached branch inventory is a *plan-time* observation being used to authorise a rebase that starts
seconds or minutes later, after this run's own earlier entries have moved refs and after any
neighbouring process has had its turn. The JIT re-probe set and its **conservative** per-row budget
are fixed here and cited by §5.2 and §9: at each seam, for the row about to run, at most
**two** ref resolutions — the `GetBranchSHA` read behind `base.decision_sha` in **`base_context`**,
which the executor issues anyway, and the head `rev-parse --verify` in **`execution_context`**
(round-35 item 3; on a coincident row they are two processes in one directory, on a split row two
processes in two) —, at most **two** range probes in **`execution_context`** (the candidate
`--count` and, where the row's identity is revalidated, the full `--reverse --topo-order
--no-merges` stream that recomputes `candidate_digest`), at most **one** branch inventory
(`for-each-ref refs/heads/`, where collateral is re-derived — a **store** fact, so it may answer
both refs only where their common dirs were measured equal, §4.1 context-pair rule), and in
`execution_context` **two** operation-directory probes
(`rev-parse --git-path rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`, external rows only), **one**
`status --porcelain --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all`, **one**
`worktree list --porcelain` for the branch/worktree holds, and **one**
`ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z` for untracked presence, **plus the one or two
`DefaultBranchIn` reads the seam's own re-resolution of `base.ref` costs in **`base_context`** where
that base is a literal ref** (round-37 item 3: §5.4 consequence 4 requires the guarded row to
recompute its resolved base ref, and `resolveBase` cannot answer without asking the context for its
default branch; a base that names a same-repo stack entry short-circuits and costs nothing) —
**twelve** Git processes per
external JIT row and **eight** per checkout row as an upper bound, of which pass 1 and
`processBranch` already issue one today, and **ten** per external row wherever the base needs no
default-branch read. Probes whose fact the seam does not consult are not issued,
so the bound is a ceiling and not a target; a 5-entry external stack therefore pays the plan-time
figure of the worked estimate above — ≈65-90 unsplit, ≈110-145 fully split (round-36 item 3,
round-37 item 3) — plus at most ~60 across
its five seams, on an explicitly requested guarded command. **The destination `rev-parse` the
executor performs in `execution_context` is not a separate seam probe**: it is the rebase's own
resolution of its operand and is counted in the row's two ref resolutions. **Two facts stay cached across seams on purpose**: the context identity, because a context
whose root moved mid-run is a different context and would refuse on identity anyway, and the
configuration inventory, because `git rebase` reads its configuration when it starts and the seam
sits immediately before that start. Everything else is measured as late as the executor measures it;
and
**zero** new processes on the unguarded no-flag path.
