## 14. Documentation and skills impact

Must be updated with the feature (user-visible behaviour changes):

- `README.md:64-101,158` — sync flag table and the sync-modes narrative.
- `docs/cheatsheet.md:148-163` — the sync block.
- `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces/SKILL.md:27,138-153`,
  `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces-orchestrator/SKILL.md:52-62,103-110,128-131` and
  `assets/skills/copilot/tws.prompt.md:18,82,138` — **all three** shipped embedded agent skills,
  and round-37 item 5 fixes the count: every earlier round named two and silently omitted the
  **orchestrator** skill, which ships under `assets/skills/**` like the other two
  (`skill-distribution`, §16), documents the `tws sync` flag set in its own command block and — the
  reason it cannot be treated as a copy of the worktree skill — owns the **pre-sync workflow step**
  an operator's agent actually follows (`6. Pre-sync check` → `7. Sync`), which is exactly where a
  plan/guard preview belongs. Its update is therefore **not** a duplicate of the worktree skill's:
  the worktree skill teaches an agent working *inside* one branch how to read a document and a
  token, while the orchestrator teaches the **pre-sync plan/guard workflow** — run
  `tws sync <feature> --plan --json` (with the same trigger and scope flags the sync will use)
  **before** `tws sync <feature>`, read `runnable`, `guard.would_refuse`,
  `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` and `refusal.kind` rather than the exit code, use the plan's rows to
  decide whether to broadcast a decision or narrow the run with `--only`/`--from`, and take the
  three-step token round trip only when a replay limit is in force. It must carry the same
  candidate-vs-applied distinction and the same collateral upper-bound wording as the other two, and
  it must **not** be given a shorter, "orchestrator-friendly" paraphrase of the four-conjunct
  admission predicate: a skill that teaches three conjuncts is wrong wherever it ships. **No
  normative sentence in this section says "both skills" any more** (round-38 item 4): every one
  names **all three**, so the count survives without depending on this interpretation clause, which
  remains only to fail closed on a sentence a future round might reintroduce. No doc, test or ledger
  may list two.
  The three must teach
  "run `--plan` (or `--plan --json`) before a wide sync", must state the candidate-vs-applied
  distinction so agents never report "N commits were applied", must state that `--plan` obeys
  the fetch axis — and that adding `--no-fetch` **previews a different run** (the new-mode one),
  so an agent that must not touch the network is choosing the new-mode route deliberately, while an
  agent reporting a base SHA quotes the plan's `freshness` alongside it — must state that
  `--plan` describes **the run the same flags would perform** (bare `--plan` = the no-flag run), and
  must state the exit-code contract: `--plan` exits 0 even when it refuses, so agents branch on
  `runnable` / `guard.would_refuse` / **`guard.execute_blocked_by[]`** / `refusal.kind`, never on the
  status code — and must state that
  `runnable` answers "can this plan execute at all" **over the unguarded route's own ladder**, so a
  limit violation or a token mismatch leaves
  it `true` and is read from `guard.would_refuse` / `refusal.kind` instead, while a
  **controlled-path** refusal the unguarded run would ignore — a pre-existing live foreign owner
  above all — leaves it `true` too and is read from `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` (§4.4, §8.6.1
  cause 3). The full "will this exact command run?" predicate the docs and all three skills must teach is
  `runnable && !guard.would_refuse && guard.execute_blocked_by == [] && refusal.kind == null`, and
  no snippet may teach the three-conjunct form. **Nor may any snippet teach it as a success
  oracle**: its scope is *admission* — "this command will be admitted, not refused by the guard or a
  projected gate" — and it says nothing about rebase conflicts, a checkout Git refuses, a failing
  validation command or a rejected push, none of which the planner can know (§0.2, round-18 item 1).
  **Two published warnings sit precisely in that gap and the skills must teach both the same way**
  (round-28 item 3): `untracked-present`, which says an untracked file may block a write the arm is
  about to make, and **`checkout-dirty-present`**, which says a checkout continuation's standalone
  `git checkout` may refuse where tracked dirt overlaps the switch. Both leave `runnable: true` and
  neither is covered by the four-conjunct predicate — a document carrying either can be admitted and
  still fail at Git — and no snippet, doc or skill may present the predicate as excluding them.
  The two supported
  round trips are per route (§5.3): `--plan --json` → `--approve-plan <fp>` for the legacy external
  run (both fetch; re-plan if the identities moved), and `--plan --no-fetch --json` →
  `--no-fetch --approve-plan <fp>` for the new-mode run, with `route` asserted — and in **both**,
  the executing invocation repeats the *same trigger, limit, push and validation flags* and adds
  only
  `--approve-plan` (§8.7.7). **The docs and all three skills must teach the drift window in the same
  breath** (round-34 item 6): on a fetch-enabled route *every* invocation of the round trip fetches,
  including the human flow's **verification** step, so an `approval-mismatch` at step 2 or step 3
  means **the plan drifted** — upstream moved between two previews — and **not** that the token
  failed to waive a limit. The taught recovery is "go back to the first preview, read it again, take
  the new receipt", never "re-run with the same token" and never "add `--no-fetch`", which would
  approve a different run (a mode trigger, §0.2). No user-facing text may call the round trip
  atomic, and none may promise that a token which validated will still execute. Guarded execution emits **no JSON and no token**: on refusal it is
  exit 1 plus exactly one **anchored, guard-written** line `^plan-guard: <kind>: <detail>` at **any
  position** on stderr — anchored because Git and Cobra passthrough is uncontrolled and may contain
  the substring mid-line, so a skill must teach a line-anchored parse with a known `<kind>`, never a
  substring grep over the stream — and the
  marker is decided by **origin, not rank**: every refusal a shipped check already owns (state
  cells, continuation gates, I19/I20, selection, **and checkout's in-`BuildCheckoutPlan` head/base
  failures**)
  keeps its shipped text with **no** marker, so a skill must not teach "parse the first stderr
  line" and must not assume "rank 5 and above means a marker" (§8.7.6). **Two guarded-run facts must
  be taught beside it.** First, whether the refusal happened before or after anything moved: a
  pre-mutation refusal never suggests `--continue`, while a refusal at or after the JIT seam carries
  the fixed `state-preserved: ` detail token, states that the recovery record was kept, and names
  the `--plan --continue` → guarded `--continue` workflow — so an agent branches on that token rather
  than guessing whether a resume is safe — and a **pre-resume** refusal, which changed nothing, still
  states that the interrupted run's recovery record is untouched while carrying no
  `state-preserved: ` token, so an agent never reads its absence as "my recovery record is gone"
  (§12, §8.7.5). Second, a **guarded run refuses under a pre-existing live foreign
  owner**: a checkout lock or sync-run guard that already existed, decoded, and whose PID is
  signalable and belongs to **another**
  process is a non-waivable `state-refused`
  refusal on the guarded route (it is only a fetch suppression on `--plan`, where it is published as
  `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]`, and the unguarded run is
  unaffected), so the advice on hitting it is to wait for the other process, never to retry with a
  token. The skills must not describe it as "a lock exists" or "a foreign token": an invocation's
  **own** lock, guard or reclaimed artefact never triggers it, a checkout **transaction** never
  triggers it (its `lock_pid` is a persisted recovery field, not an owner signal), and the wording
  must be the probe's — a **signalable PID**, never "the other process is definitely running", since
  `Signal(0)` misses an owner running as another user and can answer for a **reused** PID
  (§8.6.1 cause 3, §9, §11, §19.21). **A third state fact must be taught with them**: every
  `state.files.<artefact>` is always an object with `{applicable, presence, unreadable_reason}`, so
  an agent reads
  `presence` — `absent`, `readable`, `unreadable`, `symlink`, `not-applicable` — and never infers
  "nothing is running" from a missing value or from `alive: null`; an unreadable or symlinked guard
  is an artefact whose liveness is **unknown**, and the correct advice there is to inspect the named
  path (which `unreadable_reason` tells it how to read: a directory, an I/O failure, or bytes that
  **that artefact's own loader** refused), not to retry. The skill must teach the per-file rule
  explicitly, because the intuitive generalisation is wrong in three places: an **empty**
  `.sync-state.yaml` is `readable`, not broken; a **future** `state_version` on a checkout
  transaction is `readable` and means "upgrade tws", with the shipped continuation sentence carrying
  the number; and only `.sync-state.v2.yaml` turns a version it does not know into a decode failure
  (§8.6.1 step 2a, §8.6.4). An agent must not tell an operator a file is corrupt when the tool is
  merely older than it — and to read
  **`guard.execute_blocked_by: ["owner-artefact-undecodable"]`** as "the guarded run will refuse
  this, even though a plain `tws sync` would ignore the file" (§4.4 `state`, §4.4
  `guard.execute_blocked_by[]`, §8.6.1 step 2a). The skill must also teach that
  `state.files.*` is where file artefacts live and that `state.git_op`/`state.worktree`/
  `state.head` are **checkout-mode** facts carrying `applies: false` in external, so an agent never
  reads an external document's `state.git_op.in_progress: null` as "no operation in progress" (§4.4
  `state.git_op`). An agent that hit a refusal
  must run
  `--plan --json` with the same flags to obtain a token — **three invocations** for the reactive
  path, two for the proactive JSON one (Workflow A) and **three** for the proactive human one, whose
  middle step re-plans with the token (Workflow A′, round-32 item 6); a human may take the token from the labelled final line of a
  human `--plan` instead — which is `Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>` or
  `Approval fingerprint: none`, **a line containing the token, not the token**, so every documented
  snippet must extract the third field rather than piping `tail -1` into `--approve-plan` (§8.3.5).
  **The human approval flow the docs and all three skills teach is three steps, and round 32 fixes which
  step demands which check** (item 6, §8.7.7 Workflow A′): (1) **preview** — `--plan` with the
  trigger and limit flags, where an over-limit plan *legitimately* shows `Guard would refuse: yes`
  with a limit `Refusal kind:`, and what must hold is only the hard admission facts
  (`Plan runnable: yes`, `Configuration issues: none`, `Guarded execution blockers: none`, and a
  refusal kind that is `none` or one of the two waivable limit kinds); (2) **verify** — re-run the
  **plan** with `--approve-plan <fp>` **and the identical trigger and limit flags**, and require the
  full four-conjunct form on that document's displayed values (`Plan runnable: yes`,
  `Guard would refuse: no`, `Guarded execution blockers: none`, `Refusal kind: none`); (3)
  **execute** — the same flags plus the token. **No text may demand the four-conjunct form of the
  first preview**: that would forbid the very case a token exists for, since a plan that already
  satisfies all four needs no approval. **Nor may any text call a dropped limit flag an
  `approval-mismatch`** (round-33 item 13): changing a trigger, the scope or a limit *value* between
  steps is a mismatch on a real document, while dropping the limits altogether produces **no
  document** — a flag error on a fresh run, rank 7.5 `approval-without-limits` on a resume
  (§8.5.1, §8.7.4). The machine flow of Workflow A is unchanged, and **no doc,
  skill or snippet may show a limitless token**, which cannot exist (§4.4 clause (b)).
  **All three skills must also teach the bound *entry row*, because it is now the surface an agent
  quotes back to a human** (round-37 item 4, §8.3.5): the default human `--plan` prints one
  `Entries:` header and **exactly two lines per entry** —
  `  - <name> [<git_branch>] base <configured> → <resolved>@<destination> cutoff <recorded> upstream <effective> strategy <strategy>`
  and `    candidates <count> range <range> first <first>` — with every field present on every row
  and fixed literals for the absent cells (`<none>`, `<unresolved>`, `<unknown>`,
  `<not-executed>`, and the deferred destination's `post-rebase(<logical-parent-name>)` — the
  parent's logical name from `destination.depends_on`, rendered concretely as e.g.
  `post-rebase(pr1)`, which is the one spelling any skill may teach), so a skill may parse it **by position** and must not
  teach parsing it by prose. **Four** consequences must be taught with it: the SHAs on those lines are
  **12-character display truncations** of the `--json` twin's full SHAs, so an agent that needs a
  full SHA reads the JSON and never re-expands the human line; `<destination>` is the **destination
  commit** and never `base.decision_sha`, which has no human line at all; and `upstream` is the
  **effective** replay boundary, which on a pass-2 arm deliberately differs from the recorded
  `cutoff` (§5.4 consequence 1) — a skill that reports the recorded cutoff as the replay boundary is
  wrong on exactly the arm the operator is least likely to check. **And the fourth, added by round-38
  item 3**: `<resolved>` is a **mode** fact — external rewrites a base naming the repository's
  default branch to `origin/<default>` while checkout resolves it literally — so a skill must
  report `base master → origin/master@<D>` as the *same* configured base, never as a base that
  changed, and must never hard-code one mode's spelling into a check.
  `Entries: none` is a rows-less
  document, not a failure.
  **All three skills must also teach the `Configuration issues:` block, in its fixed grammar** (round-32
  item 5, the grammar settled by round-33 item 8): a rank 5.07
  document prints one line per `config_issues[]` row, exactly
  `  - <issue_id> <key> [<source>, <route_command>]: <value-field>` — the full 64-hex issue id, the
  key, the source scope, the route command and a **total** value field that is the literal
  `<valueless>`, the two characters `""` or the sanitized value, never omitted and never raw —
  immediately above the guarded-execution
  blocker block, and an agent joins a blocker to its evidence by the `issue_id` in the blocker's
  fixed `config issue <issue_id> (<key>, <route_command>)` substring, never by parsing the sentence
  and never by the displayed `repo_root`, which is a sanitized path that may collide; the array's
  own join to `repositories[]` is on **`context_id`** (§4.4, round-32 item 1). **`context_id` is the
  document's one context-identity function and the docs and skills must teach it as such** (round-35
  item 6): the same 64-hex identity keys an entry's `base_context`, an entry's `execution_context`, a
  `repositories[]` row, a `push.targets[]` row and a `config_issues[]` row, it is never
  execution-scoped, it never has an empty fallback, and it is the **only** legal join — a skill that
  joins any of them on `repo_root` or on the `repo` token is joining on a lossy rendering or on a
  non-key.
- **The two SHAs of a row, and the two contexts behind them, must be taught explicitly** (round-35
  items 2 and 3). A row publishes **`base.decision_sha`** — the SHA the executor reads in
  `base_context`, compares to the recorded cutoff to choose between the plain and `--onto` arms, and
  records afterwards — and **`destination.sha`** (or `destination.snapshot_sha` when the destination
  is deferred) — the commit the replay actually lands on, resolved in `execution_context`, where
  `git rebase` runs. **No doc, skill, help string or agent output may call the first one the
  destination**, and `base.sha` no longer exists in any surface. On the ordinary external pass-1 row
  whose `entry.Repo` is set, the two contexts are two directories of one repository and the document
  says so with the **`base-execution-context-split`** warning, whose detail names both roots and the
  shared object store; an agent must read that as "normal, and here is why two `repositories[]` rows
  appear for one `repo`", never as a problem. Where the two contexts are two **different** object
  stores the document publishes the **`base-execution-store-divergent`** blocker with
  `runnable: false`: the arm would be chosen from one repository and replayed in another. The skills
  must teach the honest consequence — a guarded run refuses, an **unguarded** `tws sync` still does
  it, and the fix is to repair the stack's metadata or its worktree, not to retry with a token.
  **A third shape must be taught beside those two** (round-36 item 4): on a **skip** row a context
  ref may be published as `{context_id: null, repo_root: null, source: not-applicable}`, which means
  "this row runs nothing there", **not** "the plan could not read that repository" — the failure
  shape keeps its directory `source` and carries a `repo-unavailable` blocker, while this one carries
  none and leaves `runnable` alone. An agent that reports a `not-applicable` ref as a broken
  repository is reporting a refusal the document did not make. **And it is a per-ref, per-route
  shape, not a per-row one** (round-37 item 1): a `skipped-updated-ref` row publishes a **real**
  `execution_context` — that is where its branch lives — and publishes a real `base_context` too on
  the new-mode `--no-fetch` route, whose preflight really resolved its base; a skill that teaches
  "skip rows have no contexts" is wrong on the arm most stacks actually hit. Two further facts must
  be taught with it, because both are counter-intuitive: a `skipped-updated-ref` row's `base.ref`,
  where present, is a **preflight** fact and **not** a destination the row rebases onto
  (`destination.sha` is `null` with a not-executed cause), and its `cutoff.state` is deliberately
  **`null`** where a cutoff is recorded, because the arm never reads it and the plan does not pay to
  verify a boundary nothing will use — `null` there means "not verified", never "unresolvable".
- **"`--plan` changes nothing" is a scoped claim and must never be taught unqualified** (round-35
  item 9, §0.1). What the docs, the skills and any agent may promise is that a plan invocation leaves
  HEAD, the index, the working tree, `stack.yaml`, every state/lock file and every `refs/heads/**`
  outside the fetch's own local-branch destinations untouched. A **fetch-enabled** `--plan` writes
  `refs/remotes/**` and that context's `FETCH_HEAD`, and may prune or clobber tags — which is exactly
  the mechanism behind the drift window above. Only the explicit new-mode `--no-fetch` route may be
  described as fully read-only, and choosing it is choosing a different run.
  A token is exactly 64 lowercase hex characters and is compared bytewise; `none`/JSON `null` means
  the document mints **no usable token**, which has exactly **three** causes — the three clauses of
  §4.4's usable-token predicate — and the document says which **in three published booleans, so no
  doc, skill or agent has to infer the cause** (round-30 item 4): the quadruple
  (`approval.usable`, `approval.covers.has_work`, `approval.covers.requires_limits`,
  `approval.covers.encoding_safe`) is total over the three clauses and all their combinations.
  **No approvable work** — `entries` empty, `push.targets` empty **and** `restore.applies` false
  (`has_work: false`) —, **no effective replay
  limit**, since `--approve-plan` requires one, so a plan run without `--max-replay-per-entry`/
  `--max-replay-total` describes the run fully and deliberately mints nothing
  (`requires_limits: true`, §8.5.1), **or a bound identity
  that is not valid UTF-8**, published as a non-empty `encoding_issues[]`
  (`encoding_safe: false`, §5.3.2a, §4.9 rank 5.08). **The docs and skills must state the pair-only
  reading as withdrawn**: `(usable, requires_limits)` alone reported "no work" and "encoding issue"
  identically, so any text that diagnoses from the pair is wrong. **And no text may describe a
  limitless plan's token being *rejected* later** (round-30 item 1): a limitless plan mints nothing,
  so there is no token to carry into an executing invocation and no `approval-mismatch` to report —
  dropping the limit flags on the *executing* side is a flag error before any document exists, and
  on a resume it is rank 7.5 `approval-without-limits` (§8.5.1, §8.7.7). The docs and all three
  skills must teach all three causes rather than "the token was null": the first case means there is nothing
  to approve, the second means the operator should re-run the same plan with the limits they intend
  to guard with, the third means the plan cannot be shown without loss and the operator must act on
  `encoding_issues[]`, and a limitless plan is **not** degraded — every row, aggregate and blocker in it is
  real. It is a rule about the work, the limits and the encoding, not a list of refusal kinds, not
  `entries == []`
  alone, and not
  the rebase-plus-push pair alone
  (§4.4). No skill text may tell an agent to read a fingerprint
  from an
  executing invocation. Agents must also be told the two guard booleans:
  `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` is the raw verdict and `guard.would_refuse` the effective
  one after a matching token, so `--plan --approve-plan <fp>` — read through the four-conjunct
  predicate above — answers "will this exact command
  execute?" without starting it (§4.4). A `--plan --continue` never fetches
  (`freshness: not-refreshed-continuation`,
  §8.6.4), reports its **effective**, state-derived route (§0.2), and is the **only** source of a
  token for an interrupted run — the original full-run token is dead (§8.7.4). A `--plan` that
  observes a checkout lock or sync-run guard with a **signalable foreign** PID reports
  `freshness: not-refreshed-live-run` and did not fetch (§8.6.1), so an
  agent must not read its base SHAs as current — while a **stale or dead** artefact does not
  suppress the fetch, so those documents are as fresh as the run would be; a rows-less refusal
  document reports `freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` **on every route** (unless it is a

  never a subject to fetch for; and a valid but empty stack under a `fetch` policy reports

  `fetched` and neither is ever `local-only` (§4.4, §8.6.1). Finally: collateral is an
  **upper bound** (`summary.collateral_bound: upper`) and repo-qualified, so a skill must say
  "these refs may be rewritten", never "these refs will move" — and never "these refs will stay"
  either: a candidate dropped by the **preliminary** filter leaves its ref where it was, while one
  dropped for **becoming empty** may still move it onto the rewritten base (§4.3). **When the
  movement comes from configuration rather than from the argv** — an effective `rebase.updateRefs`

  `collateral-update-refs-config` **warning** beside `collateral_mechanism: config`, and the docs

  as something the guard prevents: v1 refuses nothing for it and injects no `--no-update-refs`

  statements — **eight with round 22's two, on deletion and on a fetch that contacts nothing, and
  nine with round 25's, on a fetch that writes local branches** —
  are mandatory because each one corrects a reading an agent or an operator would

  choosing the **different** `--no-fetch` route; the unguarded command is unchanged (§4.9 rank 5.0,
  §8.6.9, §18.21);
  **a fetch can *delete* as well as add** (round-22 item 2): where the effect publishes

  `expectation: absent` — the docs and skills state this beside `freshness` rather than leaving

  **must state the precedence the way Git implements it** (round-25 item 1, extended by round-26
  item 6): a context mode, set by
  either config key's last occurrence **or — where the config chain sets nothing — by

  the per-submodule keys (config, then `.gitmodules`'s per-submodule section) are consulted only where no context mode is
  set at all, so no text may offer a per-submodule `no` as a way to stop a context-level `yes` — and
  no text may treat the two `.gitmodules` keys as one; **and the file is read the way Git reads it**

  mode unknown: Git falls through to `HEAD:.gitmodules` and resolves —
  and **may never describe the plan's
  fetch as reaching only the repositories the plan is about**;
  **a fetch can move — and delete — *local branches*, and a checked-out one makes Git refuse the

  **the set of causes that make a `--plan` decline a fetch it was told to perform is closed at

  **two configuration facts refuse the document outright, and both must be taught as configuration

  **Git's own parser rejects** is `invalid-git-config` (rank 5.07, `runnable: false`) — the docs and

  stops nothing on a route that attempts no fetch, and a `rebase.*` key stops nothing on a route that

  and joined by the 64-hex **`issue_id`**, and joined to its repository row by **`context_id`** —

  string that is not valid UTF-8** is
  `identity-not-utf8` (rank 5.08, no token, `runnable: false`) — where the skills must explain that

  produces no token to carry forward at all, rather than one the executing run would later call
  `approval-mismatch`** (round-30 item 1)
  (§4.4, §8.5.1, §8.7.4, §8.7.7); **a force-push with no remote-tracking ref is *stricter*, not weaker** — the
  document publishes `lease.expectation: absent`, meaning the push requires the remote branch not to
  exist and is rejected as stale info if it does, so no skill or doc may describe that cell as an
  unprotected force; the same cell is reached when the remote's **fetch refspecs map the branch
  nowhere** (`expected_ref: null`), and no text may name `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` as the lease
  baseline where the refspecs say otherwise (§4.4); and **a checkout run's restore is published work with its own
  executability** — `restore.applies`/`executable`/`blocked_by[]` say whether HEAD really will be
  put back, and `deletes_transaction`/`releases_lock` are effects **on success**, so an agent must
  not tell an operator their lock will be released when the restore is blocked; and **`applies` is
  not "this is checkout mode"** — a fresh checkout run whose plan is empty returns before it writes a
  transaction, so it publishes `applies: false` and mints no token, which is what makes "is there
  anything left?" answerable from the work triple alone (§4.4, §8.6.4a).
- `CHANGELOG.md` — Unreleased entry.
- `docs/roadmap.md` / `docs/engineering-workflow.md` — move rebase plan guard to shipped and name
  the next target, in the same style as the sync-modes entry.

## 15. Test strategy (real Git, no mocks)

Per `docs/engineering-workflow.md`, Git behaviour needs real temporary repositories and local bare
remotes. Existing harnesses to extend rather than reinvent:

- external: `newScopedFixture`, `createLinearStack`, `setupGitRepo`, `runSync`
  (`internal/cli/sync_scoped_test.go:18-62`);
- checkout: `checkoutModeFixture`, `saveTestStack`, `newModeOpts`, `captureRun`
  (`internal/cli/checkout_sync_modes_test.go:17-56`);
- deterministic interruption: `internal.StepHook` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:316`) and
  `internal.SyncStepHook` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:84`);
- argv capture: the `git` PATH wrapper and sidecar recorder in
  `internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go:44-120`.

Required cases:

1. **Frozen no-flag** — re-run the existing golden suite unchanged; committed goldens must not be
   re-baselined (`internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go:19-31`). This is the single most important test.
2. **Four customer topologies** (§6.1-§6.4) as real-Git fixtures, in **both** modes, asserting the
   printed plan fields, not just success.
2a. **The default human entry row is byte-exact, this item owns its tests, and the §6.4 topology is
   its acceptance case** (§8.3.5 row grammar, §4.5, §6.4, round-37 item 4, round-38 item 3).
   **Ownership is explicit so no assertion is written twice or in the wrong place**: the two
   **row** lines and their **eleven** fields are asserted *here*, and the four-part **tail** below
   them is asserted in §15.16a2 — neither item restates the other's assertions, and this one asserts
   only that the tail is undisturbed. Over the whole fixture matrix, assert the
   **default** human `--plan` output (no verbosity flag, no `--json`) prints one `Entries:` header
   and **exactly two lines per entry**, in the document's canonical row order, matching the bound
   grammar byte-for-byte:
   `  - <name> [<git_branch>] base <configured> → <resolved>@<destination> cutoff <recorded> upstream <effective> strategy <strategy>`
   and `    candidates <count> range <range> first <first>`. Assert **field totality** over all
   **eleven** fields, with one fixture per absent-value literal, so no cell may be blank or omitted:
   `<none>` for an unset base,
   an absent cutoff, a null range and a known-empty first candidate; `<unresolved>` for an unresolvable base ref
   and a failed destination peel; `<unknown>` for an unknown count, upstream and first candidate;
   the **concrete** deferred literal — a `pr2` row whose parent is `pr1` prints exactly
   `post-rebase(pr1)`, never a placeholder spelling and never `<destination.depends_on>`; and
   `<not-executed>` for the destination and the
   effective upstream of **every** `skipped-*` row; and the ` (unresolvable)`/` (unverified)`
   suffixes on the recorded cutoff. Assert every SHA on the two lines is the **first 12 lowercase
   hex characters** of the full SHA in the `--json` twin, that **no `rev-parse --short` process is
   spawned for the rendering** (argv sidecar), and that the human and JSON documents of the same
   invocation carry the identical `approval.fingerprint`, so the row grammar moves no token
   (§15.5a). The **acceptance case** is §6.4 built as a real repository (`master = A-B'-D`,
   `pr2 = A-B-C`, base `master`, cutoff `B` preserved), built **once per mode because the resolved
   base differs by mode and both variants are honest** (round-38 item 3): in **checkout** assert the
   destination cell is **`master@<D>`**, and in **external**, where `master` is the fixture's
   default branch and `resolveBase` rewrites it, assert **`origin/master@<D>`** — with
   `<configured>` the literal `master` in both, and with the `--json` twin's `base.ref` asserted to
   match the rendered `<resolved>` in each. Assert additionally an external fixture whose base is a
   deliberately **non-default** literal ref — the repository's default branch is `main` while the
   entry's base stays the literal `master` — which `resolveBase` leaves untouched and which prints
   `master@<D>` there
   too, so no test hard-codes one mode's spelling for the other. In every variant assert
   `<B>` as both the recorded and the effective boundary, `strategy onto`,
   `candidates 1`, and `first <C> "C"` — the customer's D and C stay visible on the default
   rendering whichever token names the base — and assert by grep over the rendered output that no line
   says `applies`, `applied` or `will be applied` (§4.2, §4.5). Assert finally that the four-part
   tail below the rows is **unchanged** byte-for-byte by the presence of these rows — asserted
   *there*, in §15.16a2, and merely required here — and
   that a rows-less document prints `Entries: none` and no row lines at all.
3. **Candidate vs applied, and *which* filter dropped** — assert the plan says
   `candidate_count: 1` for the exact-squash PR1 and
   that the run applies none; assert no plan field, human line, or JSON key ever states an applied
   count; and assert the **arm-aware** drop booleans of §4.2/§6.1. **Assert Git's own lines on
   stderr, never stdout**: `Rebasing (n/m)`, `dropping … patch contents already upstream` and
   `warning: skipped previously applied commit` are written by `git rebase` to stderr and reach the
   terminal through `runWithFilteredStderr`'s read loop (`internal/exec.go:142-185`), which is also
   where the `(skipped duplicate commit)` rewrite happens; a test that captures stdout will find
   none of them, and an earlier draft's prose implied it would (§2.1, §6.1, D9). Cases:
   (a) §6.1 (`--onto master A pr1`, cutoff `A` an ancestor of the head) →
   `may_drop_patch_equivalent: false`, `may_drop_becomes_empty: true`, and Git's own **stderr** is
   the
   `dropping … patch contents already upstream` (becomes-empty) line;
   (b) §6.2 (`git rebase master`, upstream holds `B'`) → `may_drop_patch_equivalent: true` and Git's
   **stderr** is `    (skipped duplicate commit)`, tws's rewrite of
   `skipped previously applied commit` (the preliminary drop) — assert the rewritten form, since
   that is what `RunDirClean` emits; assert the **checkout** run of the same topology prints neither,
   because `gitRebaseOnto` captures and discards `CombinedOutput()` on success (D9);
   (c) `may_drop_patch_equivalent` is computed from the `<branch>..<upstream>` probe, not from a
   config read and not from a literal — assert a fixture in which flipping only the *arm* flips the
   boolean; and assert **no `git config` process reads `rebase.reapplyCherryPicks` in any form — no per-key probe of that key is ever spawned, and the ordered list read is never filtered to it**
   (argv sidecar), because the key does not exist.
4. **Determinacy matrix** — the §5.1 rules, one case per row, in both modes:
   (a) recorded resolvable cutoff + deferred destination → `destination.deferred: true`,
   `depends_on: pr1`, `replay.determinacy: exact`, `upstream_provenance: recorded-cutoff`,
   non-null count, `strategy: conditional` with both argv shapes and the mode's **exact** predicate
   (external's includes the `currentBaseSHA != ""` conjunct);
   (b) **no** cutoff + deferred destination → `determinacy: unknown`,
   `reason: upstream-deferred`, `candidate_count: null`, **`strategy: plain` with non-null argv**
   (the correction of §5.1/§6.2 — assert it is *not* `conditional`), and no number rendered as
   exact;
   (c) no cutoff + frontier → `determinacy: snapshot`, `strategy: plain`;
   (d) recorded but unresolvable cutoff + resolvable destination → `cutoff.state: unresolvable`,
   **`strategy: onto` in both modes**, `blocking: true`, refusal before any rebase;
   (e) unresolvable `base.ref` → external models `strategy: plain` failing at `git rebase`,
   checkout models `strategy: unknown` failing while resolving the base, both
   `reason: base-ref-missing`.
   Plus: the per-entry JIT resolution turns (a)'s strategy and (b)'s count into determinate values
   using the real post-rebase parent SHA, and the guard's thresholds are enforced there too.
4a. **Deferral matrix** (§5.1 deferral rule) — deferral follows the route's **execution order**, so
   one fixture per cell, with the argv sidecar proving the order:
   (a) materialized child + materialized parent → `deferred: true`, `depends_on: <parent>`;
   (b) **materialized child + non-materialized parent** → `deferred: false`, `depends_on: null`,
   `destination.sha` populated from the live read, because the parent runs in pass 2 *after* the child —
   and, on an unscoped external run, that parent's own row is `skipped-updated-ref` (assert both
   rows, and assert the parent's per-row budget as **exactly** what its route issues — the shared
   cwd-scoped `worktree list --porcelain` prunability probe that precedes and gates the skip, one
   head `rev-parse --verify refs/heads/<git_branch>^{commit}` in its execution context and, on the
   **new-mode `--no-fetch`** route only, the preflight's own reads — with **no** rebase, **no**
   `GetBranchSHA` and **no** `rev-list` for it; "no Git process ran for the parent" is the withdrawn
   round-15-to-36 claim and no fixture may assert it, §4.1 skip-context rule, §15.10a, round-37
   item 1);
   (c) non-materialized child + materialized parent → `deferred: true`;
   (d) both non-materialized, parent will rebase → `deferred: true`; both non-materialized, parent
   `skipped-updated-ref`/anchor-skipped/unselected → `deferred: false`;
   (e) cross-repo parent that is not the resolved `base.ref` → `deferred: false`,
   `depends_on: null`, and no dependency claimed anywhere in the document;
   (f) checkout: a parent excluded from the plan array (archived, unselected, anchor under
   local-only, empty base) never defers its child.
4b. **Unset base** (§5.1 rule 5) — an entry with `base: ""`: in **checkout**, assert the row is
   published with `strategy: skipped-no-base`, `argv: []`, `determinacy: not-applicable`,
   `reason: not-executed`, the skip-rule candidate facts of §15.10a (`candidate_count: 0`,
   `commits: []`, `commits_listed: 0`, `commits_truncated: false`, the empty-sequence digest, and
   `null` for `range`/`upstream_*`/`first_candidate`), `collateral_refs: []`,
   `blocking: false`, and that the shipped run really does skip it — and assert the cause is still
   legible from `strategy` + `base.kind: none` without any extra key; in **external**, assert the row
   publishes the resolved token as the **empty string**, quoted, verbatim —
   and assert the argv sidecar shows `git rebase --update-refs ''` / `git rebase '' <branch>`,
   i.e. that no `origin/` token is ever produced, since `DefaultBranchIn` cannot return an empty
   default (`internal/exec.go:59-88`) — with `reason: base-unset`, `blocking: true`, a `base-unset`
   entry in `blockers[]`,
   `runnable: false`; assert a guarded external run refuses **before** any `git rebase` (argv
   sidecar) while `--plan` exits 0 with the document.
5. **Candidate identity and replay order** — assert `replay.range`,
   `replay.first_candidate.{sha,short,subject}` and
   the bounded `replay.commits` list match `git rev-list --reverse --topo-order --no-merges
   <upstream>..<branch>` computed
   independently in the fixture, i.e. **oldest-first**; on a range of `N > cap` commits assert the
   published list is `C1..Ccap` — the **oldest** cap, not the newest — and that
   `first_candidate` is `C1`; assert this against a real rebase's todo order by interrupting a
   rebase of the same range and comparing `.git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo`'s pick order to
   `replay.commits`; assert **no probe uses `--reverse --max-count`** (argv sidecar), which would
   return the newest end (§4.5); assert truncation metadata (`commits_listed`, `commits_truncated`)
   is correct at the cap boundary and derived from the count;
   assert a control-character/escape-bearing subject is sanitized;
   assert the §6.4 reparent fixture names **C** and not merely `1`.
5a. **The candidate digest is over the full sequence, not the rendering** (§4.5, §4.6, §5.3.2) —
   the property the previous draft's "a digest of `replay.commits`" would have broken:
   (a) **independent recomputation**: on a range of `N` commits assert `replay.candidate_digest`
   equals the SHA-256 the fixture computes itself over
   `git rev-list --reverse --topo-order --no-merges <upstream>..<branch>` with one `\n` after each
   full 40-hex SHA, for `N < cap`, `N == cap` and `N > cap`;
   (b) **same token, human vs JSON**: plan the identical fixture as `--plan` (human, no list) and as
   `--plan --json` (capped list) and assert `approval.fingerprint` is **byte-identical**, and that
   both documents publish the same `candidate_digest` even though only one publishes
   `replay.commits`; repeat with the verbose human rendering, and — if the cap is made
   configurable — with two different caps, asserting the token never moves;
   (c) **same oldest-cap prefix, different tail ⇒ different token**: build two fixtures whose first
   `cap` candidates are byte-identical (same SHAs, same order) and which differ only **beyond** the
   cap, with the **same** `candidate_count` in one variant and a different one in another. Assert
   `replay.commits` is identical in both, `candidate_digest` **differs**, and the tokens differ —
   i.e. a token minted over one cannot approve the other. A digest taken over the rendered list
   would pass this test's negation, which is why it is asserted explicitly;
   (d) **order matters**: two ranges with the same SHA *set* in a different topological order mint
   different digests;
   (e) **known-empty is not unknown, and a skip row is known-empty**: a resolvable range with zero
   candidates publishes
   `candidate_count: 0`, `replay.commits: []` and the digest of the **empty sequence** (not `null`),
   and **every `determinacy: not-applicable` skip row publishes exactly the same three values**
   (`skipped-anchor`, `skipped-archived`, `skipped-updated-ref`, `skipped-no-base`), because
   the row runs no rebase and that is counted, not unmeasured (§4.1 skip rule). Only an
   `unknown` row publishes `candidate_digest: null`. Assert the three pairwise distinctions —
   known-empty vs unknown mint **different** tokens; a skip row and a resolvable empty range mint the
   **same** replay sub-tuple; and no fixture, table or prose asserts `null` candidate fields for a
   `not-applicable` row (§4.8, §8.3.2a);
   (f) **probe shape, and the stream is consumed to the end**: assert via the argv sidecar that
   whichever shape §19.12 picks really reads
   the **whole** range — shape 1 as a single streamed `rev-list`, shape 2 as the capped window
   **plus** a full-stream hash probe — and that no shape publishes a digest computed from fewer
   than `candidate_count` SHAs. For shape 1, assert the pipe is **not closed early** on a range with
   `N > cap`: wrap `git` so the child writes the full list and then observes its own stdout write
   result, and assert it completes without `EPIPE`/`SIGPIPE` and exits 0 — the observable form of
   "the cap bounds retention, not consumption" (§4.5). Assert in the same fixture that
   `commits_listed == cap`, `commits_truncated: true` and the digest still equals the independent
   full-sequence recomputation of (a);
6. **Canonical ordering and fingerprint stability** (§4.7) — a two-root stack (two independent
   anchors, each with a child) planned repeatedly across **separate processes**: assert the
   `--plan --json` bytes are identical every time and that `approval.fingerprint` is identical,
   despite `TopoSort`'s map-seeded queue (`internal/stack.go:157-163`) being free to order the roots
   differently; assert `depends_on` — not row position — carries the parent relation; assert that
   swapping two independent entries' order in `stack.yaml` does not change the fingerprint, while
   changing a parent relation does. Assert no test asserts a row order that claims to be execution
   order.
   **6a. The fingerprint's *bytes* are asserted, not only its stability** (round-25 item 4, replaced
   by round-26 item 2, §5.3.2a). The implementation must expose the tuple's canonical pre-image to
   tests (a debug accessor and its annotated dump, not a published field), and the suite asserts:
   the pre-image is **byte-identical**
   across processes and across renderings — human, `--json`, `--json` with a different
   `replay.commits` cap, and the guard seam's own computation — and that
   `sha256(pre-image) == approval.fingerprint`, computed independently in the test rather than by
   calling the same helper; that the pre-image **begins with the 16-byte header** `tws-plan-fp\0`
   plus **encoding version** `0x0001` plus **tuple schema version** `0x0004` — the value round-35
   items 3 and 5 bump it to, and the suite asserts the literal bytes rather than "whatever the
   constant says", so a suite still asserting `0x0003` (or `0x0002`, or `0x0001`) fails —, and that
   changing either version byte changes the fingerprint; that the entry struct carries
   **thirty-eight** members whose ids are exactly `1..38`, that **field 4 carries
   `execution_context.context_id`, field 5 `execution_context.source`, field 36
   `base_context.context_id` and field 37 `base_context.source`** (round-34 item 3), that **field 12
   carries the `execution_context` destination SHA and field 38 the `base_context`
   `base.decision_sha`** (round-35 item 3) — asserted as two distinct payloads on a divergent
   fixture and as two equal payloads on a coincident one, and asserted *by position*, so an
   implementation that filled 12 from the base read fails here —, and that **no** entry member
   carries either rendered `repo_root` (scan the pre-image for the fixture's root path bytes and
   require their absence as a standalone `BYTES` payload, while the same bytes are provably inside
   the `context_id`s the test recomputes from §4.4's pre-image). **Assert the push struct with the
   same discipline** (round-35 item 5): a `push_targets[]` element carries the ids
   `{1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11}` — **ten** members with a permanent hole at **2**, whose
   absence the walk asserts explicitly — `11` is the target's `context_id` and is never `NULL`, the
   array is ordered by `(context_id, git_branch)`, and the fixture's push `repo_root` bytes do not
   appear as any standalone `BYTES` payload; two push contexts whose §11 renderings collide but
   whose identities differ must produce two elements, two orders and two tokens. **Assert the split discriminates**, on
   two real fixtures: an external pass-1 entry with a **non-empty** `entry.Repo`, whose worktree and
   whose `Repo` are two different repositories, publishes **different** bytes at fields 4 and 36 and
   mints a token that a fixture in which the two coincide does **not** match; and a pass-2 or
   checkout row publishes **identical** bytes at 4 and 36, which the test asserts positively rather

   whose *execution* context failed mint **different** tokens, the `NULL` tag sitting at 36 in the
   first and at 4 in the second; **and that neither header field is the document's
   `schema_version`** (round-27 item 6) — asserted in both directions with two fixtures: a document
   whose `schema_version` is rendered under a *bumped* constant while the tuple is unchanged mints
   the **same** token, and a build whose tuple schema version is bumped while `schema_version` is
   unchanged mints a **different** one, so no implementation can wire the two numbers together; that the top-level value is a `STRUCT` whose members appear in
   **ascending field-id order** with **every** whitelisted id present exactly once — the decoder in
   the test walks the pre-image and asserts the id set equals the §5.3.2a tables, so a silently
   dropped member fails here rather than in a token mismatch a year later; that every composite's
   declared byte length and every array's declared element count match what the walk actually
   consumes, with **no trailing bytes**; that unknowns are the `NULL` **tag** and are
   distinguishable from `BOOL 0x00`, from `UINT 0` (8 zero bytes), from a zero-length `BYTES` and
   from a zero-count `ARRAY` — asserted as four distinct pre-images and four distinct fingerprints

   carriers; that array elements are **bare values** carrying no field id; and that a
   `repositories[]` element carries its **eleven** ids — `1 repo`, `2 context_id` (**in place of the
   rendered `repo_root`**, round-32 item 1), the four `.value`s at 3-6, `7
   config.rebase_merges.interpretation` and the four `.status`es at 8-11, which is the struct
   §5.3.2a defines; round 31's four status members made the count eleven and this assertion was left
   saying seven (round-33 item 7) — including
   `config.rebase_merges.interpretation` (round-26 item 7) while carrying **no** `.source` bytes

   Git fixture where Git allows the name**, in three families (§5.3.2a):
   **separator injection** — entries and
   branches named `a","b`, `a\",\"b`, `a"b` and `a\"b`; a repo path containing `","`; a detail
   string containing `}{`; a ref name containing a tab and one containing a raw newline;
   **Unicode** — a non-ASCII name beside its percent-escaped
   spelling; the precomposed `é` (U+00E9) against the decomposed `e`+U+0301; and an ASCII `a`
   against a Cyrillic `а` (U+0430); and **invalid UTF-8**, the family the withdrawn JSON pre-image

   holding the truncated `0xE2 0x82`, and each of those against the same name spelled with the three

   while each single value produces the **same** digest across processes and

   **The repository-path cells are asserted through the context identity, not as bound members**

   appears in no `BYTES` payload of either struct, so the positive byte-faithfulness assertion for
   those cells is made over the identity's pre-image rather than over a tuple member that no longer
   exists.
   **Round 27 rewrites what the invalid-UTF-8 cells assert about *approval*, and the round-26 form
   of these assertions is removed rather than weakened** (item 7): those documents mint **no**

   Assert the document is still **valid JSON** and still complete
   (`json.Unmarshal` succeeds, every §8.3.6 top-level key is present, `encoding_issues` among them)
   and that the offending string
   field itself renders as the lossy U+FFFD spelling, so the two representations are asserted to
   coexist. **Assert the limitless split** (round-28 item 4): plan the *same* fixture with **no**
   limit flag and require `encoding_issues[]` published identically, `approval.fingerprint: null`
   and `approval.usable: false`, together with **no** `identity-not-utf8` blocker,
   `runnable: **true**` and `refusal.kind: null`; then run the real `tws sync` over that fixture and

23. **Operational checklist for advancing *this artifact*, not the product** (round-37 item 6,
    **its content proof corrected by round-38 item 5, its recovery step added by round-39
    item 5 and every step below made to *abort* — nonzero exit, no later command — by round-40
    item 2**, and the one item of this section that
    describes the tpatch lifecycle rather than `tws` behaviour —
    see the Path B note below §20). **`git diff --stat` is not a content proof here and must not be
    used as one**: before the first landing `analysis.md` is **untracked**, so `git diff`,
    `git diff --stat` and `git diff --check` are all silent over it whatever happens to its bytes —
    including a full provider overwrite — and round 37's "`git diff --stat` on it is empty" would
    therefore have passed in exactly the failure case it was written to catch. The proof is a
    **content digest taken by this checklist itself, over bytes the index also holds**, in this
    order:
    (1) assert `tpatch status` reports this feature's state as **`requested`** — an assertion that
    **fails the sequence**, never a bare command whose output is read by eye: `tpatch status` prints
    the whole dashboard and exits 0 on every state, so the check matches this feature's own line
    (`- rebase-plan-guard [requested]`) and aborts when it does not;
    (2) compute and keep the **SHA of `.tpatch/features/rebase-plan-guard/analysis.md`** —
    `git hash-object -- <path>`, which is Git's own digest of exactly the bytes `git add` would
    stage and is therefore the one digest comparable with the index (an out-of-band `shasum -a 256`
    is a legitimate second witness, never a substitute for the comparison in (4));
    (3) **stage the artifact before advancing**: `git add -- .tpatch/features/rebase-plan-guard/analysis.md`.
    Staging **changes no byte of the working file** — it copies those bytes into the index — and it
    is what turns an untracked, unrecoverable artifact into one with a **recoverable copy** behind
    it; without it, step (7) has nothing to restore from;
    (4) assert the **index blob SHA equals the worktree SHA** —
    `git rev-parse ":.tpatch/features/rebase-plan-guard/analysis.md"` equals (2) — so the copy that
    would be restored is provably the reviewed artifact and not a stale one;
    (5) advance with **exactly** `tpatch analyze rebase-plan-guard --manual`;
    (6) compute the worktree SHA **again** and require **exact, bytewise equality** with (2) — any
    difference at all is artifact loss, not a formatting detail;
    (7) **on mismatch, recover first and stop**: run
    `git restore --worktree -- .tpatch/features/rebase-plan-guard/analysis.md`, which rewrites the
    working file from the index copy staged in (3); assert the restored worktree SHA now equals (2);
    and **abort before any further action** — no commit, no re-run, no further tpatch phase — until
    it does. A mismatch that cannot be restored to (2) is artifact loss and must be reported as
    such, not worked around;
    (8) on success only, assert `tpatch status` now reports this feature as **`analyzed`**, in the
    same failing form as (1);
    (9) and assert the **only** changes the advancement made are the intended lifecycle metadata — this
    feature's own `status.json` (`state`, `updated_at`, `last_command`, and `compatibility` where
    the phase sets it) and the regenerated `.tpatch/FEATURES.md` row — and that **no**
    `artifacts/analysis.json` or other provider output appeared and no other feature's `status.json`
    moved, since either is the signature of a provider run; the intended-diff check is a filter over
    `git status --porcelain -- .tpatch` that **fails on any path outside those two plus this
    artifact** (staged at (3), so it appears as `A`, not `??`), not a listing to be eyeballed.
    **Every step above is an abort, not a report** (round-40 item 2): the sequence runs under
    `set -e` with an explicit `|| exit 1` on each check, and any failure — the wrong state at (1) or
    (8), index ≠ worktree at (4), a digest mismatch at (6), a failed or unverified recovery at (7),
    a provider artifact or a stray `.tpatch` path at (9) — ends it with a **nonzero exit before the
    next command runs**. The round-39 spelling printed and continued, which advanced the feature
    after a detected mismatch; no restatement of this item may reintroduce a check whose only effect
    is output. The snippet after §20 is the exact, `sh`- and `bash`-parseable form.
    Round 38's "nothing is staged until every check passes" is **withdrawn as false** (round-39
    item 5):
    it made the digest the *only* line of defence, so a provider overwrite was detectable and
    **unrecoverable** in the same breath. The artifact stays staged from (3) through the whole
    checklist; the tpatch metadata (`status.json`, `.tpatch/FEATURES.md`) is reviewed, staged and
    committed **after** (8)-(9) pass, in its own `chore(tpatch)` commit, per the Path B ordering of
    `docs/engineering-workflow.md` and `.tpatch/steering/local.md`. Staging is not committing: a
    failed advancement still leaves nothing half-committed to
    unwind. The provider-mode form
    `tpatch analyze rebase-plan-guard` — without `--manual` — remains **forbidden for this feature**: it
    runs the provider analysis phase and can overwrite the authored artifact, which is the one
    failure this checklist exists to prevent. A run whose (6) digests differ is handled by (7) and
    by nothing else: restore from the index copy staged in (3), verify, and stop — the "working
    copy's own backup where the file is still untracked" of earlier rounds is withdrawn, because
    (3) now guarantees a copy Git itself holds (round-39 item 5).

## 16. Dependencies

The three declared hard parents are **necessary and, for the code this feature touches, sufficient**:

- `sync-modes` — owns the axes, the selection model, the frozen-decision persistence, the scoped
  argv, and the golden harness this feature must not break. Its own hard closure already pulls in
  `branch-name-decoupling`, `multi-repo-workspaces`, `archive-worktree`, `checkout-stack-safety`,
  `fix-default-base-branch`, `fix-sync-continue-descendants`, `push-branches`, `cobra-migration`,
  and `agent-work-status-dashboard` (`.tpatch/features/sync-modes/status.json`).
- `stack-status` — owns the projection/`null`-honesty conventions **and `BuildBranchRefInventory`
  (`internal/stack_status.go:424-447`), which §4.3's all-branches collateral set consumes
  unchanged**, and hard-depends on
  `stack-ancestry-doctor`, which is where `StackEdge` lives
  (`.tpatch/features/stack-status/status.json`).
- `amend-aware-rebase` — owns `LastBaseSHA` and the `--onto` strategy the plan describes
  (`.tpatch/features/amend-aware-rebase/status.json`).

Recommended additions, decided by which files the implementation actually edits:

- **`stack-ancestry-doctor:hard`** — add **only if** the change edits `internal/stack_ancestry.go`
  (e.g. to export a helper). Otherwise the transitive edge through `stack-status` is enough and an
  extra edge would be noise.
- **`agent-work-status-dashboard:hard`** — same rule for `internal/agent_status.go`: §4.3 reuses
  `BuildWorktreeInventory` for the `--update-refs` exemption set, and **extends** it only if the
  checked-out-branch set is not directly available. Consuming it unchanged needs no new edge (it is
  already in `sync-modes`' hard closure); editing it does.
- **`skill-distribution:soft`** — the embedded skills under `assets/skills/**` must be updated
  (§14). **All three ship**: `claude/tesseraworkspaces/SKILL.md`,
  `claude/tesseraworkspaces-orchestrator/SKILL.md` and `copilot/tws.prompt.md` (round-37 item 5).
- **`fix-missing-completions:soft`** — if a new entry-valued flag registers completion, mirroring
  `--only`/`--from` (`internal/cli/sync.go:144-145`).

Run `tpatch feature deps --validate-all` after define/explore, per `.tpatch/steering/local.md`.

**One shipped-code refactor is in scope, and it is deliberately the smallest possible one**: the
extraction of `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable` out of `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`
(`internal/sync_run_state.go:207-232`, §8.7.5 step 1). It adds no dependency edge — the file is
already inside `sync-modes`' ownership — and it is behaviour-preserving byte-for-byte: the same
**single** `os.ReadFile`, the same order, the same four error strings, with `os.MkdirAll`, the
`reclaim sync guard: %w` wrapper and the two writes left in the caller. Its signature is
`checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable(featurePath, ownerToken string) (syncGuardReclaimCheck, error)` with
`syncGuardReclaimCheck` carrying `{absent, originalBytes, guard}`: the caller needs *which* arm
succeeded and *over which bytes* in order to reproduce `main`'s absent-vs-stale branch and to anchor
`removeLockIfUnchanged`'s compare-and-swap to the judged bytes, and an `error`-only predicate could
supply neither without a second read that would defeat the CAS (round-17 item 1). The `ownerToken`
parameter exists for call-shape parity and is consulted by no arm. The extraction exists so the
hoisted precheck and the reclaim cannot diverge, which is a property no
amount of prose can hold (§15.16c e3a). If `define` also takes the optional checkout hoist of
§19.24, `checkForceAcquireCheckoutLockReclaimable` is lifted out of `forceAcquireCheckoutLock`
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:262-288`) in the identical shape — one read, `{absent, originalBytes,
info}`, no token — and that is the only circumstance in which a second file is restructured.
Nothing else in `internal/` is restructured by this feature.

## 17. Alternatives considered and rejected

- **Say that "pre-v2 checkout persists nothing"** — the previous round's §8.7.4 item 2, and false:
  `RunCheckoutSync` writes a `CheckoutTransaction` before the first `git checkout` on **both**
  checkout routes and sets `StateVersion` only under `opts.NewMode`
  (`internal/checkout_sync.go:652-681`). A newly started guarded **legacy** checkout run therefore
  has somewhere to persist its guard and does so additively, with `state_version` still absent.
  Rejected in §8.7.4/§10.3: only the legacy *external* route has nowhere to persist, and the real
  no-persistence cell is a transaction written **before this feature existed**, which a
  continuation's flags may arm.
- **Persist the limits as scalar `int` with `omitempty`** — the previous round's §10.3 shape, and a
  silent safety inversion: `0` is a legal limit meaning "refuse any entry that replays anything",
  and a scalar `omitempty` marshals it to nothing, so the resume would read the strictest guard the
  CLI can express as **no guard at all** — failing exactly the operator who asked for the most
  protection. Rejected in §10.3: pointer-backed values (or explicit presence booleans), which keep
  `absent` and `zero` distinguishable on disk, in the document and in the fingerprint tuple.
- **State the fingerprint's membership as two prose lists "closed in both directions"** — the
  previous round's §5.3, and not closable: a field named in neither paragraph had no defined status,
  and every schema addition silently reopened the question. Rejected in §5.3.2: an **exhaustive
  inclusion whitelist** plus the rule that anything not listed is excluded, including future fields,
  so adding a member is an explicit edit to one table. The same round drops `route_triggers[]` in
  favour of the effective policy, because binding the raw flag list would make a redundant, legal
  flag repeat on a continuation mint a different token for the same resume.
- **Publish `fetch.repos[]` as `{repo, attempted, ok}`** — every earlier round's shape, which
  asserted that a fetch happens in the repository the token names. `UniqueRepos` fixes the context
  from the **first entry** of the token — its worktree if it exists, else the `Repo` directory, else
  **no `-C` at all**, i.e. the process cwd (`internal/stack.go:37-52`,
  `internal/cli/sync.go:604-635`). Rejected in §8.6.9: the row carries
  `{repo_token, context_root, context_common_dir, context_source, fetch_effect,
  context_candidates[], attempted, ok}` — the single shape of §4.4/§8.6.9/§15.21 —, `freshness` is
  scoped to those
  contexts, and a divergent context raises `fetch-context-divergent` instead of letting `fetched`
  imply a repository was refreshed that never was.
- **Treat external pass 2 as "a rebase like any other"** — every earlier round's framing, and it
  hid a real mutation: `git rebase <base> <branch>` is "a shortcut for `git checkout topic &&
  git rebase master`" (`git rebase` manual), so the arm switches HEAD in `entry.Repo` or the
  **process cwd**, leaves it there on success, and leaves it there after its own `--abort` too —
  and external has no `restoreOriginal`. Rejected in §5.4.7: the plan publishes `mutation.*` per
  row, probes the dirty state and the checked-out-elsewhere condition **in the row's real context**,
  and blocks the two cells where the implicit checkout cannot happen (`context-dirty`,
  `branch-checked-out-elsewhere`), with `rebase.autoStash` added to the per-context config because
  it decides which of those two answers is correct.
- **Report "every aggregate `null`" on a rows-less document, and claim `repositories[]` can never be
  `[]`** — the previous round's §5.5 and §4.4, which contradicted each other and both contradicted
  the count-of-published-rows fields (`entries_with_unknown_candidates` and its two siblings are
  `0`, not `null`) and the constants (`total_candidates_lower_bound` was "always present";
  `collateral_bound` was "always `upper`"). Rejected in §4.4: one `summary.plannability`
  discriminator and one two-column profile table, with `repositories[]` legitimately `[]` when no
  context was ever probed.
- **Let any `unknown` evaluation row set `guard.would_refuse*`** — the previous round's §4.4
  wording, which contradicted §8.3.2's own recommendation that a deferred unknown is benign and
  JIT-checked: taken literally it refused every cold stack's second entry the moment a limit was
  supplied. Rejected in §8.3.2a: `unknown_kind` splits `deferred-resolvable` from `not-resolvable`,
  the published `guard.indeterminacy_policy` says which policy was applied, and only
  `not-resolvable` refuses under the recommended default.
- **Leave the threshold comparison and the aggregate's unknown remainder to the implementation** —
  the previous rounds' silence, which left `count == limit` and "lower bound fits but rows are
  uncountable" undefined. Rejected in §8.3.2a: strict `>` (equality passes), one evaluation row per
  entry per supplied limit whether or not anything is exceeded, and a three-way aggregate rule where
  `B <= L` with an unknown remainder is `unknown`, never `within-limit`.
- **Leave "the remaining entries" as an unstated primitive** — every earlier round, in which the
  persisted `Pending` list, the persisted selection and a recomputation were all defensible
  readings. They disagree in real cells: `Pending` is written from the failing run's `sorted` slice
  and goes stale across a stack edit, and it is read only to print a count
  (`internal/cli/sync.go:347`, `:417`). Rejected in §8.6.4a: one shared `RemainingRebaseEntries`,
  external = current `TopoSort` ∩ selection minus `Completed ∪ {FailedBranch}`, checkout = `Plan`
  cursored by `CurrentIndex` with `Stage` deciding whether the current index is still owed a rebase.
- **Make a repo-context or probe failure a `null` fact like any other** — the previous rounds'
  implicit position, which would have let a guard publish a runnable plan it could not measure.
  Rejected in §4.1/§4.9: replay-critical failures fail closed as rank 5 `repo-unavailable` /
  `probe-failed` with `runnable: false`, while enrichment failures (ancestry, notes, subjects,
  collateral inventories on non-switching rows, config reads) stay `null` and non-blocking — and the
  cwd prunability probe keeps the executor's own fail-open answer rather than inventing a failure.
- **Make `--plan` a seventh `syncTriggerFlags` member** — the shortest implementation, and the one
  the previous draft recommended. Rejected (Finding 5, §8.5): a trigger flag *selects new-mode
  execution*, so a bare `tws sync <f> --plan` would preview a run with a different fetch set (R1), a
  header, v2 state, and two refusals (duplicate `GitBranch`, checkout cross-repo) that the run the
  operator is about to perform does not have. It would also change the I8 operand list and the I20
  gate for invocations that merely asked for a description, and it would *still* not make
  `syncFallback` unreachable for a **guarded** legacy run. Orthogonal control flags plus an explicit
  `plan-unavailable` interception (§8.5.5) give the same protection without lying about the run.
- **Let `--plan` fall through to the legacy `syncFallback` when the stack is unreadable** — never
  considered acceptable, and named here so no future edit reintroduces it: the fallback rebases
  every directory under the worktrees root (§2.1 step 3). Rejected in favour of the structured
  `plan-unavailable` refusal.
- **Make `TopoSort` deterministic so plan rows are the execution order** — attractive, and rejected
  in §4.7: it would change execution order, the persisted `Selected` lists, and the checkout plan
  array `--continue` indexes by position, for every existing run. The document is canonicalized
  instead, and row order is declared non-semantic.
- **Exclude base/head snapshots from the approval fingerprint to make tokens stable across
  fetches** — rejected in §5.3: a token that survives a moved base authorises a rebase onto a commit
  nobody previewed. The stable path is the explicit new-mode no-fetch round trip
  (`--plan --no-fetch --json` → `--no-fetch --approve-plan`); a legacy external approval fetches on
  both invocations and must be re-planned when the identities move, which is the honest cost of
  previewing a route that fetches.
- **Recommend `--plan --no-fetch` as the universal preview** — rejected this round: `--no-fetch` is
  a mode trigger, so it does not make a legacy preview local, it swaps the previewed run for the
  new-mode one (R1-R11). There is intentionally no fully-local preview of the legacy external route
  (§0.1, §5.3, §14).
- **Ship config defaults (`sync.plan_guard.*`) with v1** — rejected in §8.3.4: a config default arms
  the guard on the bare no-flag path that §8.1 freezes, and makes "is this run guarded?" depend on
  ambient state the goldens do not capture. Limits are flags only in v1; config defaults are a
  possible follow-up with their own no-flag analysis.
- **Emit a JSON refusal document from a guarded execution** — rejected in §8.3.5/§8.7.6: `--json`
  is valid only with `--plan` in v1, so an executing invocation has no document surface, and adding
  one would create a second, half-populated schema whose relationship to the plan document nobody
  could pin down. Guarded refusals are exit 1 plus one anchored, guard-written `^plan-guard: ` line;
  structured detail
  and fresh tokens come from `--plan`.
- **Promise the guarded refusal as the *first* stderr line** — the earlier drafts' contract, and
  rejected this round as unimplementable: Cobra prints a returned `RunE` error itself, the root
  command and (under `--verbose`) `git fetch`'s own stderr write before the guard seam is reached
  (`internal.RunDir`, `internal/exec.go:126-134`), and a shipped pre-seam refusal may have written
  the only line there is. A position promise would have been either false or a constraint on code
  this feature does not own. The replacement is stronger where it matters and weaker only where it
  was fictional: **exactly one anchored, guard-written `^plan-guard: <kind>: ` line, at any position
  on stderr, only for
  guard-generated refusals** (§8.7.6).
- **Promise that the substring `plan-guard: ` occurs exactly once in the whole stderr stream** — the
  previous round's replacement, and still an over-promise: the stream also carries Git's own output,
  a `--verbose` fetch, Cobra's usage block and shipped refusal text, none of which this feature
  owns, and any of them may echo an attacker-chosen branch name or commit subject containing the
  literal. Rejected in §8.7.6 and narrowed to what the guard can actually guarantee: **one
  guard-written line**, anchored at line start, with a `<kind>` from the closed §4.9 enum, and a
  detail that escapes `CR`/`LF` and any leading marker ambiguity so it cannot open a second one.
  Consumers parse the anchored line; the substring count over a stream nobody owns is not a
  contract.
- **Decide the marker by refusal *rank* ("ranks 5-12 carry it")** — the previous round's rule, and
  wrong in a reachable cell: checkout raises the rank 5 `head-ref-missing` **inside**
  `BuildCheckoutPlan`, before the guard seam exists, so a rank rule would have demanded a marker on
  a refusal the guard never generated and whose shipped sentence must be preserved. Replaced by an
  **origin** rule — the guard marks what the guard writes (§4.9, §8.7.6).
- **Put the marker inside the returned `RunE` error** — the obvious implementation, and rejected:
  production `cli.Execute()` does not set `SilenceErrors` and re-prints the error itself
  (`internal/cli/root.go:53-56`), so the marker would appear **twice** for real users while
  appearing once under the golden helper, which does set it
  (`internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go:1119-1120`). The guard writes the marker itself to
  `cmd.ErrOrStderr()` and returns a marker-free error (§8.7.6).
- **Publish the invalid-config evidence as extra members of the rank 5.07 blocker** — round 28's
  shape ("each blocker of this kind carries `repo_root`, `key` and the sanitized `value` as members
  of its own detail object"), and rejected in round 30 (item 2): `blockers[]` is a closed
  `{kind, entry, detail}` tuple with one canonical sort and one de-duplication rule (§4.4, §4.7), so
  giving one kind a wider row makes the array heterogeneous, gives every consumer two shapes to
  parse, and leaves the base64/SHA-256 evidence with nowhere safe to live — while the alternative of
  putting the raw value into `detail` is barred outright by §11. Replaced by the top-level, closed-row
  **`config_issues[]`** array, sorted and de-duplicated on its own `issue_id`,
  with `detail` left a sanitized string that points at it — the same split `encoding_issues[]`
  already makes for rank 5.08 (§4.2 Part 3, §4.4, §4.9 rank 5.07, §11, §15.21).
- **Key the invalid-config evidence on the raw `(repo_root, key, source)` triple** — round 30's
  shape, and rejected in round 31 (item 2): the triple is not an identity a consumer can *carry*.
  A `detail` cannot quote a raw repository root (§11 bars the bytes), so the "join by the raw triple"
  rule asked every reader to reassemble a key out of members two of which are lossy in the only
  rendering they ever see, and it left the `source` member doing double duty as both a fact and a
  key component while §4.2's occurrence rule was making at most one row per `(context_id, key)`
  anyway. Replaced by a single opaque **`issue_id`** — a SHA-256 over a length-framed raw tuple that
  additionally covers `route_command`, the value presence byte, the value bytes and `error_kind` —
  which sorts, de-duplicates, joins to the blocker one-to-one, prints safely in a sanitized `detail`
  and in the human rendering, and discloses nothing (§4.2 Part 3, §4.4, §4.7, §11, §15.21).
- **Key the repository axis and the issue/blocker join on the rendered `repo_root`** — every round
  through 31, in the `repositories[]` sort `(repo, repo_root)`, in the `status: invalid`
  biconditional, in the "one row per `(repo_root, key)`" rule and in the surviving raw
  `(kind, repo_root, key)` blocker identity, and rejected in round 32 (items 1 and 4): `repo_root`
  is the **sanitized** rendering §11 produces, which is lossy by construction, so two distinct
  contexts can render to one string. Every use was therefore unsound in the same way — a sort key
  that is not total, a biconditional that can match the wrong slot, a row rule that can merge two
  contexts' issues, and a second de-duplication key that can only disagree with `issue_id`. Replaced
  by **`context_id`**, a SHA-256 over the domain-separated, length-framed **raw** canonical context
  identity (raw repo-root bytes, `root_source`, raw common dir), published on every `repositories[]`
  and `config_issues[]` row, carried in the `issue_id` pre-image, and used for every join, sort and
  de-duplication; `repo_root` stays as display only (§4.2 Part 3, §4.4, §4.7, §4.9 rank 5.07,
  §15.16e, §15.21).
- **Keep one context per entry row** — every round through 33, and rejected in round 34 (item 1):
  a single `repo_context` had to be either the directory the base resolves in or the directory the
  rebase runs in, and on an external pass-1 row whose `entry.Repo` is non-empty those are **two
  different repositories** — `resolveEntryBase(stack, entry, syncRepoContext(layout, entry))` and
  `GetBranchSHA(entry.Repo, base)` on one side, `RunDirClean(<worktree>, "git", "rebase", …)` on the
  other (`internal/cli/sync.go:593-602`, `internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:116-152`). Whichever the
  single field named, the other half of the row was published against a directory it was never
  probed in, and the `rebase.*` configuration — which decides collateral movement, the backend and
  the autostash precondition — was read from the wrong repository whenever the two diverged.
  Replaced by the two closed refs `base_context` and `execution_context`, each joined to
  `repositories[]` by `context_id`, each bound in the fingerprint, and each nulled independently on
  a `repo-unavailable` row; the tuple schema version is bumped `0x0002` → `0x0003` because adding
  and re-pointing bound ids must move every token (§4.1, §4.3, §4.4, §5.3.2a, §5.4, §7.3, §13,
  §15.8b′).
- **Cache every per-context probe for the invocation and never re-run it per entry** — the §13 rule
  as every round through 33 stated it, and rejected in round 34 (item 5): it is right for
  run-invariant facts and unsound for mutable ones. A cached dirty tree, rebase-directory answer,
  holder set or branch inventory authorises a rebase against observations taken before this run's
  own earlier entries moved refs and before any neighbouring process had its turn — the precise
  window the JIT seam exists to close. Replaced by the explicit split: the context identity and the
  ordered configuration inventory stay cached, every mutable precondition is re-probed at the seam
  that gates on it, and the cost is bounded at **twelve** Git processes per external JIT row —
  **ten** only where the row's base names a same-repo stack entry and no `DefaultBranchIn` runs
  (round-37 item 3) — and eight per
  checkout row (§5.2, §9, §13, §15.16 (d2)).
- **Diagnose a step-2 `approval-mismatch` as "the token did not waive the limits", and stabilise the
  round trip by adding `--no-fetch`** — round 33's snippet, and rejected in round 34 (item 6): the
  verification step is a *second plan* that refetches on any fetch-enabled route, so the ordinary
  cause of a mismatch there is **plan drift**, and a message about limit flags sends the operator to
  inspect the one thing that did not change. Adding `--no-fetch` would "fix" it by approving a
  different run, since the flag is a mode trigger (§0.2). Replaced by an explicit `approval-mismatch`
  arm that names plan drift, a fallback message that points at the published `Refusal kind:`, a
  documented step-3 window with the same cause, and the explicit new-mode `--no-fetch` route kept as
  a deliberate, separately chosen pair (§5.3, §8.3.5, §8.7.7, §14, §15.16a2).
- **Bind the rendered `repo_context.repo_root` into the fingerprint's per-entry tuple, and publish
  the entry's context without an identity** — every round through 32, and rejected in round 33
  (items 1 and 4): the entry row named its repository row in prose while binding a **display**
  string that §11 renders lossily, so two materially different contexts could project one tuple
  member and a consumer had no key to join on but a path it was told not to trust. Replaced by the
  closed `repo_context = {context_id, repo_root, source}` — the shape round 34 then split into
  `base_context` and `execution_context`, both of which keep it — and by binding **`context_id`** at
  the entry struct's field 4, with the tuple schema version bumped `0x0001` → `0x0002` because
  re-pointing a bound id must move every token; the raw root bytes still enter the pre-image, once,
  inside the identity's own digest, so nothing is weakened and the display root is bound nowhere
  (§4.1, §4.4, §5.3.2, §5.3.2a, §15.6a, §15.21).
- **Define `context_id` with an empty-string fallback for a context that resolved no common dir, and
  allow an issue row to name a `repo-unavailable` context that has no repository row** — round 32's
  shape, and rejected in round 33 (item 2): a fallback member gives two *different* unestablished
  contexts one identity, and an issue over such a context claims a config parse that never happened,
  because nothing there was safely probed. Replaced by: the pre-image is defined **only** for a
  successfully established context (raw canonical root, root source, raw absolute common dir, no
  fallback); a context that cannot be established is `repo-unavailable`/`probe-failed` with
  `context_id: null`, no repository row, no citation and **no** `config_issues[]` row; and the
  `config_issues[].context_id → repositories[].context_id` map is total in both directions, an
  unmatched id being a schema failure (§4.1, §4.4, §4.9 rank 5.1, §15.9b, §15.21).
- **Print the configuration-issue value only "where `sanitized_value` is non-`null`"** — round 32's
