  human block, and rejected in round 33 (item 8): an optional field makes two documents with
  different evidence render identical lines and leaves the block unparsable by position, which is
  exactly what a byte-exact human contract may not do. Replaced by the fixed line grammar
  `  - <issue_id> <key> [<source>, <route_command>]: <value-field>` with a **total** three-cell
  value field — the literal `<valueless>`, the two characters `""`, or the sanitized value — every
  row always rendered and no raw byte ever printed (§4.4, §8.3.5, §15.16a2, §15.21).
- **Demand all four admission conjuncts of the *first* human preview, and treat a dropped limit flag
  as an `approval-mismatch`** — the §8.3.5 snippet that survived round 32's own correction of the
  surrounding prose, and rejected in round 33 (items 11-13): the preview that mints a token is by
  construction the one that exceeds a limit, so `Guard would refuse: yes` is correct there and a
  check demanding `no` rejects every run the workflow exists to serve; and dropping the limit flags
  produces **no document at all** — a flag error on a fresh run, rank 7.5
  `approval-without-limits` on a resume — so no `refusal.kind` can be asserted for it. Replaced by
  the three-invocation snippet whose step 1 checks the hard-admission facts (`Plan runnable: yes`,
  `Configuration issues: none`, `Guarded execution blockers: none`, and a waivable
  `Refusal kind:`), whose step 2 replays the identical flags plus `--approve-plan <fp>` and requires
  all four conjuncts, and whose step 3 executes (§8.3.5, §8.7.7, §15.16a2, §15.16g).
- **Budget the `rebase.*` configuration as a per-key `--get` ladder** — every round through 32 in
  §4.3 and §13, which kept `config --get --type=bool rebase.updateRefs`, `config --get
  rebase.backend` and a two-, three- or four-read count beside the ordered list read that had
  already replaced them, and rejected in round 33 (item 7): a per-key read names no scope, cannot
  separate a valueless occurrence from an empty one, and pays a process for a value the list already
  carries. Replaced by **one ordered `config --list --show-scope -z` per repository context** plus
  the three explicitly required typed boolean reads (`rebase.rebaseMerges`, `rebase.updateRefs`,
  `rebase.autoStash`), each only where its key is set, with the config facts referenced by
  `context_id` and never by the `repo` token (§4.2, §4.3, §13, §15.16e (vi), §15.21).
- **Produce `source: command` by having tws add `-c key=value` to the argv it builds** — the reading
  round 31's wording invited, and rejected in round 32 (item 2): the argv of §2.1/§2.2 is frozen and
  this feature adds nothing to it (§4.3), so a plan that injected `-c` would be describing a run
  other than the one it previews. The member is real for a different reason — **inherited**
  command-scope configuration (`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` with its key/value pairs, `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS`,
  and the environment mechanisms Git's supported `--config-env` form writes) that the tws process
  was started with and passes to every child Git process, which `--show-scope` labels `command`. The
  enum is unchanged; only the cause, and the fixtures that produce it, are (§4.4, §13, §15.16e (v3)).
- **Publish "no value" as an empty string** — the shape round 30's `sanitized_value`/
  `raw_value_base64` pair implied, and rejected in round 31 (item 2): Git distinguishes a
  **valueless** occurrence (`rebase.backend` with no `=`, which dies at `missing value for
  'rebase.backend'`) from an **explicitly empty** one (`key =`, which parses as the empty string and
  is *true*/*false* depending on the key), and a schema whose only encoding of both is `""` publishes
  two different repository states as one — the same class of error round 27 fixed for
  `rebase.rebaseMerges`'s two empty spellings. Replaced by the total triple
  `raw_value_present` + nullable `raw_value_base64`/`raw_value_sha256`/`sanitized_value`, with the
  biconditional asserted in both directions (§4.4, §15.16e (vii2), §15.21).
- **Report a `repositories[].config` slot with no value as a bare `null`** — every round through 30,
  and rejected in round 31 (item 4): four materially different runs reach `value: null` — the key is
  unset, this route never parses the key, the probe failed, or Git rejects the value — and a bare
  `null` reports them identically, which is the same defect the `(usable, requires_limits)` pair had
  for the token. The alternative of **adding a general per-key slot** for all thirteen keys was
  rejected with it, as a partial enumeration of Git's config surface presented as total (§4.8's false
  completeness rule, and the same objection that keeps the domain closed at thirteen). Replaced by
  the closed per-field object `{status, value, source}` over the closed status enum
  `valid`/`absent`/`not-evaluated`/`probe-failed`/`invalid`, with `status` bound into the fingerprint
  precisely because `value` alone is no longer discriminating (§4.4, §5.3.2, §5.3.2a, §15.21).
- **Leave `source: null` under `status: invalid`, and keep an `unset` member for `absent`** — round
  31's trio, and rejected in round 32 (item 3): the one status in which the document *knows* exactly
  where the offending occurrence came from was the one publishing no provenance, while `absent`
  spent a member restating its own status. Replaced by: `source` is `probed` under `valid`, `null`
  under `absent`/`not-evaluated`/`probe-failed`, and the occurrence's **scope** under `invalid`,
  byte-equal to the matching `config_issues[].source` — and `interpretation` gains an `invalid`
  member so the never-`null` `rebase_merges` reading stays total on that slot (§4.2, §4.4, §15.21).
- **Guarantee that every out-of-scope invalid config key is "still published" somewhere** — round
  28's "scope narrows the blocker, never the disclosure", and rejected in round 30 (item 3) as a
  promise no schema could keep: `repositories[].config` has four members, so nine of §4.2's thirteen
  keys have no value slot in it whether or not the route parses them, and the two alternatives were
  both worse — a **general per-key value slot** would publish a partial enumeration of Git's config
  surface as though it were total (the false completeness §4.8 forbids, and the same objection that
  keeps the domain closed at thirteen), and **parsing out-of-scope keys anyway** would spend the
  work on values the run never reads and invite a consumer to treat an empty array as a
  clean bill of health. Replaced by: parse and publish the route-applicable invalid values in
  `config_issues[]`, disclose nothing about the rest, and say so — an absent row is not a claim of
  validity (§4.2 Part 2, §4.4, §13, §14).
- **Diagnose the `null` token from the `(usable, requires_limits)` pair** — every round from 12 to
  29, and rejected in round 30 (item 4): once round 27 added the encoding clause the pair became
  ambiguous, reporting "no approvable work" and "an identity that cannot be shown" identically as
  `(false, false)`, so §4.4's own totality sentence was wrong in the cell it had just added.
  Replaced by the quadruple `(usable, has_work, requires_limits, encoding_safe)` over an
  eight-member `approval.covers`. The alternative of leaving the two new clauses to be *inferred* —
  work from `entries`/`push.targets`/`restore.applies`, encoding from `len(encoding_issues)` — was
  rejected with it: it makes every consumer re-derive a predicate the document already evaluated,
  across fields that live in three different places (§4.4, §14, §15.21).
- **Publish a single flat `git_config` object** — the previous rounds' shape, and rejected this
  round: a plan can span repositories, `rebase.updateRefs` can differ between them, and one object
  can hold only one answer, so the document would attribute a collateral blast radius to the wrong
  repository. Replaced by the sorted `repositories[]` axis, with every collateral tuple
  repo-qualified and the fingerprint binding repo-qualified facts (§4.3, §4.4, §5.3).
- **Key `repositories[]` by the `repo` token alone, and treat the process cwd as a probe exception**
  — the previous round's shape, and wrong in the divergent-cwd cell: external pass 2 runs
  `RunSilent`/`resolveEntryBase(stack, entry, "")` with **no `-C`** when `entry.Repo` is empty, so
  every probe for that row belongs to the **process cwd**, not to the workspace repo root, and one
  `repo` token can legitimately resolve to two directories in one document. Rejected in
  §5.4/§4.4/§11: rows publish the closed `{context_id, repo_root, source}` context refs — one in
  round 33, and since round-34 item 1 **two**, `base_context` and `execution_context` — and cite
  their repository row **by `context_id`** (round-33 item 1), `repositories[]` is keyed by
  `(repo, context_id)` with a `root_source` label and a display-only `repo_root`, and the claim that prunability is "the only
  cwd-scoped command the plan issues" is withdrawn.
- **Say a collateral ref whose candidate Git drops is simply "left where it is"** — the previous
  round's single sentence, and false for one of the two filters. A candidate removed by the
  **preliminary clean-cherry-pick** filter never enters the todo, so no `update-ref` step exists and
  the ref may be orphaned; a candidate that reaches the todo and is dropped for **becoming empty**
  keeps its `update-ref` step and may still move onto the rewritten parent/base. Rejected in §4.3:
  the upper bound is stated per filter, and the tests assert the two cases as a matched pair
  (§15.13 b3/b3′).
- **Give skip rows a blanket `collateral_exposed: false`** — the previous round's rule, and it
  erased the one exposure that matters most: a `skipped-updated-ref` row exists precisely because an
  earlier entry's `--update-refs` is expected to move its tip. Rejected in §4.1/§4.8:
  `collateral_refs` is `[]` (the row moves nothing), while `collateral_exposed` is computed from the
  earlier rows exactly as for any other row and may be `true`, `false` or `null`.
- **Classify an effective limit against a `merge-recreation` row as a hard blocker
  (`config-blocking`)** — the previous round's hard-blocker table entry, contradicting the same
  round's §4.2/§4.4, which made it `indeterminate-entry` on a `runnable: true` plan. Rejected in
  §4.9/§5.3.1: it is a **rank 10 guard verdict**, non-waivable because a token clears only ranks
  11-12 and because there is no number to compare — and round 19 removed the `config-blocking` kind
  itself as memberless, so there is no configuration refusal left for it to be misfiled under
  (§4.9, §19.4).
- **Bind `intent.validation.source` and `stability` into the fingerprint** — the previous round's
  tuple, and self-refuting: a `--plan` document describes the shipped route
  (`config-per-entry`/`per-entry-dynamic` on legacy external) while the guarded invocation it
  authorises freezes the command, so the labels necessarily differ and no token could ever match.
  Rejected in §5.3/§8.8: the tuple binds `intent.validation.applies` plus `command_digest`, the
  labels stay descriptive, and the document publishes `stability` **and** `guarded_stability` so
  both statements are made without contradiction. The related claim that a **guarded invocation
  publishes** `source: frozen-at-plan` is withdrawn too — a guarded invocation emits no document at
  all (§8.7.6).
- **Compute the fingerprint over the canonical document** — the previous round's §4.7 wording,
  which contradicted §5.3's tuple and would have made a supplied token change the token: with
  `approval.*` and the guard verdicts inside the hash, `--plan` and `--plan --approve-plan <fp>`
  could never agree, and waiving a violation would mint a different fingerprint than the document
  that authorised it. Rejected in §5.3: the hash is over a **canonical invariant tuple projected
  from** the document, with a closed exclusion list.
- **Null the token only for the three rank 1-2 rows-less kinds** — an early rule, which
  left a rank 3 rows-less document (`nothing to continue`, an empty remaining set, an empty stack)
  claiming a token over no rows. Rejected in §4.4/§4.9/§8.6.3.
- **Null the token whenever `entries == []`** — the correction that replaced it, and itself now
  rejected: it is right about every workless document and wrong about exactly one cell, a
  **push-stage** continuation, whose rebase set is empty and whose remaining work is a
  force-push of every synced branch. Under that rule the most destructive operation a sync performs
  was the one operation no token could bind, and a supplied `--approve-plan` was silently ignored
  there.
- **Null the token whenever `entries == [] && push.targets == []`** — the next correction, and
  itself now rejected for the same class of reason, one cell further along: a checkout transaction
  resumed at `stage: restoring` has neither rebase rows nor push targets and still switches HEAD in
  the operator's one physical checkout, deletes the transaction and releases the lock. Under that
  rule the one resume whose *entire* content is a HEAD mutation was unbindable. The rule is now
  stated over the **work, the limits and the encoding**: `null` **iff** (`entries == []` **and**
  `push.targets == []`
  **and** `restore.applies == false`) **or** no `guard.limits` key carries an effective value **or**
  `encoding_issues != []` — the
  three-clause usable-token predicate, whose second clause round 12 added because `--approve-plan`
  requires an effective limit, so a limitless document's token could never be supplied to anything,
  and whose third round 27 added because a plan that cannot be shown without loss is a receipt for a
  run nobody read; **round 30 repairs this restatement, which round-29 item 3 missed** (item 4)
  (§4.4, §4.9, §5.3.2a, §8.5.1, §8.6.3, §8.6.4a).
- **Mint a token on a plan with no effective limit** — the previous rounds' behaviour, and the third
  correction in the same family: `--approve-plan` requires at least one effective limit (§8.5.1), so
  such a token could not be consumed by any invocation — supplying it on a fresh run is a flag error
  before any document exists, and on a resume it is `approval-without-limits`. Publishing it hands the operator a receipt no
  command accepts and makes `Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>` mean two different things. **Note what
  the rejection does *not* license anyone to say** (round-30 item 1): because the token is never
  minted, no rule, workflow, snippet, doc, skill or test may describe a limitless plan's token being
  carried into an executing invocation and answered with `approval-mismatch` — that pair cannot be
  constructed, and the mismatch cases that *can* be are the ones between two real tokens minted
  under different effective limits (§5.3.2, §8.7.7, §15.16g). Rejected in
  §4.4/§8.5.1: the limitless plan stays a complete, useful document and publishes
  `approval.fingerprint: null` with `approval.usable: false`,
  `approval.covers.requires_limits: true` and `approval.covers.has_work: true`. The two rejected repairs are also recorded: **adding a
  blocker** for the missing limit (looking is not an error, and it would make the ordinary `--plan`
  refuse) and **implying a default limit** so a token could be minted (a config- or default-armed
  guard is non-goal 14, §8.3.4).
- **State push executability in prose beside the targets** — the previous round's shape ("the
  document carries the blocker and states that these targets are not executable"), which gave a
  consumer no field to read and asked it to re-derive executability from `blockers[]` on the one
  operation that force-pushes branches. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.4a: `push.executable` and
  `push.blocked_by[]` are published, derived, and outside the fingerprint.
- **Derive `push.targets[]` from the run's `completed` list** — the reading the shipped
  `pushScoped` signature invites, and wrong at plan time on a fresh run, where `completed` is empty
  by construction and the array would be `[]` for every `--push` preview — hiding the whole blast
  radius the flag creates. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.4a: the array is a projection **conditional on the
  described rebase and validation succeeding**, derived per arm from the shipped loops
  (`pushEntries` over `stack.Branches`, `pushScoped` over the selection minus anchors,
  non-materialized rows and `payload.Pushed`, `finalizeCleanup` over `tx.Plan`), and it reads the
  persisted `Completed`/`Pushed` state only on a continuation.
- **Leave the guard-limit-mismatch document undefined** — the previous rounds' dash in the §8.7.4
  table, which left "what does the plan evaluate against?", "is a token minted?" and "can a token
  clear it?" unanswerable. Rejected in §8.7.4/§4.9 rank 7: the **persisted** limits stay effective
  and published, the attempted value is published in `guard.limit_conflicts[]`, `runnable` stays
  `true`, a real token is minted over the persisted plan, and no token can clear the mismatch.
- **Digest the *published* candidate list** — "a digest of `replay.commits`, so truncation cannot
  weaken it", which does not survive contact with the cap: the published list is capped at 50, so
  two ranges sharing their oldest 50 commits and differing only in the tail would hash identically
  and one token would authorise the other — the "same count, different commits" hole of Finding 4,
  moved from the count to the list — while the same plan rendered with a list, without one, or with
  a different cap would hash *differently* and no `--plan` → `--approve-plan` round trip could hold.
  Rejected in §4.5/§4.6: `replay.candidate_digest` is taken over the **complete, uncapped**
  oldest-first sequence from the plan object, `replay.commits` is an explicit fingerprint
  non-member, and the cap becomes a pure rendering choice.
- **Block every non-null `branch_checked_out_at`** — the previous round's rank 5.4 predicate, and
  wrong in the common case: a checkout row after the first `gitCheckout`, and a pass-2 row in a
  repository the operator already has on that branch, are both *self* holds, which Git accepts
  because the arm's implicit `git checkout <branch>` is a no-op. The rule would have refused runs
  that work today — a guard stricter than the executor, which §8.1 forbids. Rejected in
  §4.1/§4.9/§5.4.7: the field is always published, and only a **foreign** holder blocks — the
  holding worktree and the row's own command directory each resolved through
  `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and then canonicalized, so a subdirectory of the row's own
  worktree is *self*.
- **Read holders from `git worktree list --porcelain`'s `branch` lines alone** — the obvious
  inventory, and incomplete in the direction that matters: a worktree that is mid-rebase or
  mid-bisect on a branch is reported as `detached` and holds the branch anyway, so `git checkout`
  and `git rebase <base> <branch>` still fail with Git's holder refusal. The rule would have
  published `branch_checked_out_at: null` for exactly the situation stacked workflows produce most
  often — an interrupted rebase — and authorised a run that dies at Git. Rejected in §4.1/§5.4.7:
  the inventory adds the `rebase-merge/head-name`, `rebase-apply/head-name` and `BISECT_START`
  reads, at no extra Git process.
- **Treat a `rev-parse --show-toplevel` failure as a `null` enrichment fact** — tempting, since the
  field it feeds is only a comparison input. Rejected in §4.1/§4.9 rank 5.9: on a `will_switch_head`
  row it is the *left-hand side* of the self-vs-foreign test, and either default is wrong in one
  direction — self authorises a run that fails, foreign refuses a run that works. It is
  replay-critical there and never probed elsewhere.
- **Compare fetch contexts by worktree root** — the previous round's equivalence, and wrong on the
  ordinary multi-worktree external stack: two worktrees of one repository are two directories with
  one object store, so a `git fetch` in either refreshes the same refs. Root comparison would have
  produced a `fetch-context-indeterminate` refusal for the most common topology this feature
  previews, and a `fetch-context-divergent` warning for an `entry-repo` fallback that refreshed
  exactly the refs the rows read. Rejected in §8.6.9: the equivalence key is the pair
  `(canonical absolute --git-common-dir, effective bare-fetch effect)`, candidates collapse when
  **both** match, and only genuinely independent stores, genuinely different fetch effects, or an
  unresolvable one refuse.
- **Enumerate fetch-context candidates as "every selected entry that is not a descendant of
  another"** — the previous round's rule, which admits entries `TopoSort` can never place first.
  `TopoSort` is Kahn's algorithm over a FIFO queue on a forest, so it emits strict BFS level order:
  only minimum-depth entries of a token can be first. The broader rule manufactures candidates, and
  with them refusals the shipped code cannot produce. Rejected in §8.6.9: the candidate set is one
  entry per **root component** — round 22 narrows the replacement rule again, since only the root
  seed is randomized (item 5, and the separate entry below).
- **Enumerate the fetch contexts after (or during) the fetch** — the shape the shipped
  `for repo, wtPath := range repos` loop suggests, and rejected in §8.6.1/§9: on the new-mode
  external route it would refuse `fetch-context-indeterminate` *after* `refs/remotes/**` had already
  moved in one of the candidate repositories the guard could not choose between. The enumeration is
  hoisted above the fetch on the plan and guard paths only, it is pure, and its refusal tears down
  only what the refusing invocation created.
- **Null every fact of a `repo-unavailable` row** — the previous round's probe-failure rendering.
  Most of a row is stack- and route-derived and needs no directory, so the rule erased `name`, the
  branch and repo tokens, the role, the materialization, the recorded cutoff and the frozen
  `mutation.*` facts — leaving rows that could not be told apart, a canonical sort with nothing to
  sort on, and a fingerprint that could not discriminate two different broken entries. It also
  forced `head.state` to claim `missing` for a ref nobody probed. Rejected in §4.1: only
  Git-probe-dependent facts are `null`, `head.state` is `null` with
  `replay.reason: repo-unavailable`, and no `head-ref-missing` blocker is fabricated.
- **Use the full-porcelain dirty verdict for the per-row rebase precondition** — reusing
  `probeDirty`'s argv unchanged. `git rebase` refuses only on **tracked** modifications; untracked
  files never block it. The rule would have refused runs Git performs happily and would have implied
  that `rebase.autoStash` protects untracked work, which it does not (`git stash` without `-u`).
  Rejected in §4.1/§5.4.7: the per-row predicate is the single command
  `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 status --porcelain --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all`, which is
  also what makes a moved or dirty **submodule** a non-blocker, exactly as `git rebase`'s own
  `require_clean_work_tree` treats it, while checkout's shipped
  whole-repo gate keeps full
  porcelain — untracked files and submodules included — and is published separately as
  `state.worktree.dirty`. **Round 17 added a boundary this rejection must not be read past, and
  round 18 corrects how that boundary is expressed**: it remains true that untracked files never
  make a row `context-dirty`, and that this is not the same as "they never stop a run". What
  changed is the answer: the untracked-overwrite question is a *separate* fact with a separate
  predicate, but it is **not decidable by the planner**, so it is published as the non-blocking
  `context.untracked_present`/`context.overwrite_risk` pair and the `untracked-present` warning
  rather than as round 17's rank 5.55 blocker (§4.1, §5.4.7, §19.26). The reason it stays separate
  is still precisely this rejection: folding it back into the dirty verdict would again refuse the
  untracked-but-unrelated runs Git performs — and refusing on the withdrawn intersection would have
  done the same thing by another route.
- **Call `diff-files --quiet` + `diff-index --quiet --cached HEAD` "equivalent" to that probe** —
  the previous round's parenthetical, offered as a free-choice alternative. It is not equivalent:
  the plumbing pair compares recorded stat data, so a **stat-dirty but content-identical** file
  reads as modified, while `git status` — and `git rebase`'s own clean-work-tree check — refreshes
  the index in memory first and reads it clean. Taking the pair would have invented a
  `context-dirty` refusal for a run that starts fine, i.e. a guard stricter than the executor.
  Rejected in §4.1/§5.4.7/§13: the argv is fixed to `status --porcelain --untracked-files=no
  --ignore-submodules=all` under
  `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` — read-only, because the refresh never reaches disk — and no document,
  test or skill may emit the diff pair for this fact (§15.8c d3).
- **Emit no `guard.evaluation[]` rows on any rows-less document** — the previous round's blanket
  `[]`. It conflated two opposite facts: a valid empty stack really was measured and really replays
  `0` (which a total limit passes), while an unreadable or unsortable one was never measured at all.
  Rejected in §8.3.2a/§4.4: `plannability: empty` emits one `total`/`value: 0`/`within-limit` row
  for a supplied total limit and no per-entry rows; `plannability: unavailable` emits `[]`.
- **Sort where each route's executor sorts** — keeping the plan's `TopoSort` *after* the fetch on
  the legacy external route, to mirror the executor step for step. It bought exact mirroring of an
  ordering that has no observable effect and paid for it with a rows-less document that fetched on
  one route and not on the other three, so no consumer could read the fetch block without first
  branching on the route. Rejected in §8.6.1/§5.5: the plan and guard seams hoist the sort above the
  fetch on every route — a reordering of two pure reads that can only prevent a network write —
  while the unguarded no-flag path keeps the shipped order and its goldens.
- **Resolve continuation limits as one all-or-nothing operand** — the previous round's table, which
  left every mixed cell undefined: inheriting one key while supplying the other, or supplying a key
  the interrupted run never persisted. Rejected in §8.7.4: limits resolve **per key**
  (inherit / confirm / conflict / arm), `guard.limits` becomes a per-key `{value, origin}` object
  — the *single* encoding, with the parallel `guard.limits_source` field withdrawn — a conflict
  names the key, and the fingerprint binds each key's effective **`value`**, with `origin`
  published beside it as a descriptive label and excluded from the tuple (§5.3.2).
- **Bind each key's `{value, origin}` pair into the fingerprint** — the previous round's rule, and
  self-contradictory in its own sentence, which bound the pair while arguing that the source label
  was immaterial. It also had a real cost: a resume that inherited `--max-replay-total 20` from
  persistence and one that repeated the identical flag guard the identical remaining work, yet
  would have minted different tokens, sending an operator to re-plan a run nothing had changed
  about. The same table introduced a second origin domain (`persisted` / `supplied` / `null`)
  beside the published enum. Rejected in §5.3.2/§8.7.4: the tuple binds the effective **value**
  (with `0` distinguishable from absent), `origin` is an explicit non-member, and the only origin
  vocabulary anywhere is the closed enum of §4.4 (§15.16c c6).
- **Promise a byte-identical new-mode fetch context** — the previous round's "the plan mirrors
  whichever applies to the route it describes, and publishes the resolved `context_root`". On the
  new-mode route that value is not reproducible: `UniqueRepos` is built over a `TopoSort`-ordered
  selection whose independent-root order is unspecified, so two runs of one command can resolve two
  contexts and the "canonical, byte-stable document" guarantee (§4.7) would be false. Rejected in
  §8.6.9: each row publishes a deterministic, sorted `context_candidates[]` — one entry per **root
  component** of the token (round-22 item 5), since Kahn/FIFO `TopoSort` emits strict BFS level
  order and randomizes only its root seed; candidates sharing
  one canonical absolute `--git-common-dir` **and one effective fetch target**
  collapse safely to the one context and fetch as before; **two or more** candidates with differing
  (or unresolvable, and therefore unprovably equal)
  common dirs publish
  `context_root: null`, refuse with the rank 5.0 `fetch-context-indeterminate` blocker and skip the
  fetch on the plan/guard route only — while a **single** candidate is determinate and fetches
  however broken it is (round-21 item 7) — the unguarded run, the legacy route and checkout are
  untouched (§18.12, §15.15h4″).
- **State the push rule as `intent.push` ⇔ non-empty `push.targets[]`** — the previous round's
  biconditional. The forward direction holds; the converse is false in four shipped cells: every
  selected entry archived or worktree-less, every branch already in `payload.Pushed`, an empty
  `tx.Plan`, and the checkout `restoring` resume, which reaches `finalizeCleanup` with
  `Stage != completed` and drops the persisted push outright. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.4a: only
  `intent.push: false ⇒ targets == []` is asserted, `intent.push: true` with `[]` is a legal and
  tested document, and the approval token follows the **work** rather than the intent boolean
  (§15.16l, §15.16l2 vii).
- **Close the candidate `rev-list` pipe once `cap` lines are read** — the previous round's shape-1
  wording, which contradicted the digest defined three paragraphs below it: `replay.candidate_digest`
  is taken over the *complete* sequence, so a closed pipe would hash a prefix while claiming to bind
  the range, and two ranges differing only beyond the cap would mint the same token. Rejected in
  §4.5/§13: the stream is read to EOF and hashed in full, the cap bounds **retention** only, and
  §15.5a(f) asserts the child process completes without `EPIPE`.
- **Report an empty plan as unconditionally `runnable: true`** — the previous round's §8.6.3
  wording, already inconsistent with §4.4's own profile table, whose `refusal.kind` row admitted an
  independent rank 3-6 fact. It would have told an operator with a dirty tree, a live guard or an
  I19 failure that a command which exits 1 was runnable. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.3: emptiness is not
  itself a blocker and never suppresses one, so `runnable` is `true` on an empty document **only**
  when no independent non-waivable fact applies — ranks 3, 4, 4.5 and 6 being the reachable ones, since
  rank 5 needs a row or a multi-candidate fetch token (§15.18b b2).
- **Report `guard.would_refuse: true` together with `approval.accepted: true` as the executing
  shape** — the previous round's contract, and rejected: it made the one field a consumer reads to
  answer "will this run?" say `true` when the answer was "yes, it runs". Replaced by the raw/effective
  pair `guard.would_refuse_without_approval` / `guard.would_refuse`, with waived violations kept
  observable as `verdict: waived` rows (§4.4, §5.3.1).
- **Treat the human final line as the token** (`tail -1 | xargs tws sync ... --approve-plan`) —
  rejected: the line is `Approval fingerprint: <64-hex>` or `Approval fingerprint: none`, so piping
  it whole would pass a label and a `none` sentinel as a token. Every documented snippet extracts the
  field explicitly (§8.3.5).
- **Hide the fingerprint from the human `--plan` rendering** — the earlier drafts' shape, where only
  `--json` published a token. Rejected in §8.3.5/§8.7.7: it forced the person who had just read the
  plan to re-run it as JSON to obtain the receipt, which trains operators to skip the reading and
  pushes them toward wanting a token from the refusal instead. The human form prints it as a
  labelled final line; the invariant that matters — *tokens come only from an invocation that
  described a plan* — is preserved exactly.
- **Print the approval fingerprint on a guarded refusal** — the shape the earlier drafts implied.
  Rejected in §8.7.7: it makes an authorisation value part of a refusal's output contract, invites
  "refuse → grep → re-run" automation that never reads the plan, and issues a token for a document
  nobody saw. The cost is one extra invocation on the reactive path (three instead of two), which
  is the correct price for keeping the token a receipt of a description.
- **Persist the approval so a `--continue` can reuse it** — the previous draft's design, with the
  token in `SyncRunState`/`CheckoutTransaction`. Rejected in §8.7.4: the plan a resume executes is
  the *remaining* plan, whose entry set, tips and destinations differ from the approved full-run
  plan, so a persisted token could only be honoured by loosening what the fingerprint binds — the
  one thing that makes it worth anything. What persists instead is the **guard** (enabled flag plus
  limits), so a resume cannot silently become unguarded, and every continuation waiver comes from a
  fresh `--plan --continue` token.
- **Let `--plan` refuse `--push`** — the previous draft's rule. Rejected in §8.3.1: it made the runs
  with the largest blast radius — the ones that end in `git push --force-with-lease` for every
  synced branch — the only runs that could not be previewed or approved. `--plan --push` describes
  the push and performs none of it, and `intent.push` inside the fingerprint stops a non-push token
  from authorising a pushing run.
- **Treat every guard verdict as `runnable: false`** — the previous draft's conflation. Rejected in
  §4.4: it made "this plan cannot execute" and "the guard is refusing this plan" the same signal, so
  an agent could not tell a broken stack from an over-limit one, and `--approve-plan` appeared to
  waive unrunnability rather than a threshold. `runnable` is now exactly a rank 1-5 fact, plus
  rank 6 only under the explicitly selected blocking rendering of `selection-hazard`.
- **Answer prunability from the repository-scoped worktree inventory** — the previous draft's
  recommendation, and wrong: the executor calls `IsPrunableWorktree` in the **process cwd**, so an
  inventory answer would make the plan disagree with the run in exactly the multi-repo case that
  matters. Rejected in §3.7: mirror the cwd-scoped verdict, publish
  `prunability.probe_context`, and record the scoping defect as its own follow-up (§18.16).
- **Derive deferral from stack topology** — rejected in §5.1: external executes materialized entries
  before non-materialized ones, so a materialized child's non-materialized parent runs *after* it
  and cannot defer its destination — while the child's `--update-refs` may retro-mark that parent
  `skipped-updated-ref`. Deferral is computed from the route's real execution order or it is wrong.
- **Guard as a separate command (`tws sync plan <feature>`)** — a cleaner story for the fetch
  question (a separate command could plausibly be defined as never fetching), but it would resolve
  axes and layout independently of `tws sync` and drift. Rejected: `--plan` on `sync`
  guarantees the preview and the run share one code path and one flag parse — and the fetch question
  is answered honestly instead, by obeying the axis and publishing the outcome (§0.1, §4.4).
- **Force `--plan` to imply `--no-fetch`** so that it is unconditionally read-only — tempting, and
  it would make §0.1 a one-liner. Rejected: in external mode the *run* fetches by default, so a
  never-fetching preview would routinely show a different new base than the run uses, which is the
  one failure mode a plan guard cannot have (§7.2 makes the same argument about base resolution).
  The chosen contract is: obey the axis, document the write, publish `fetch.*`/`freshness`, and let
  `--plan --no-fetch` be what it actually is — the fully-local preview of the **new-mode** run.
- **Fetch unconditionally in `--plan`, even under a live run** — the previous draft's silent
  behaviour. Rejected in §8.6.1/§9: external re-resolves `--onto <ref-name>` inside `git rebase`
  (D3), so a preview's fetch can change the destination of an entry a *concurrently running* sync
  has not reached yet. A description must not be able to alter the thing it describes for someone
  else. The plan observes state before it fetches, skips the fetch when a **checkout lock or
  sync-run guard** has
  a **signalable foreign** PID — ownership and blocking are both irrelevant, so a live *foreign* guard
  suppresses it too, while a checkout transaction's persisted `lock_pid` is not an owner signal at
  all (§8.6.1 cause 3) — and reports `freshness: not-refreshed-live-run`
  rather than quietly showing SHAs it
  obtained at another run's expense. The symmetric over-correction — **suppressing the fetch for
  every refusing state cell**, which an earlier §15.20b assertion implied — is rejected too: a stale
  sentinel or a dead-PID guard harms nobody, and declining to fetch there would publish base SHAs
  staler than the run's own. And the opposite over-correction — **reading liveness off
  `SyncExternalState.GuardLive`**, which reports a live foreign guard as not live — is rejected in
  §8.6.1/§4.4: it answers "is *this run* still running?", not "is a process moving refs?".
- **Probe `rebase.reapplyCherryPicks` "defensively"** — the previous draft's recommendation.
  Rejected in §4.2/§4.3: Git 2.55.0 defines no such key (verified with `git help -c` and the
  `git config` manual), so the probe would read unset on every machine, could never flip
  `may_drop_patch_equivalent`, and would document a knob that does not exist. The boolean is derived
  from the *arm and the range* instead, which is what actually decides whether the preliminary drop
  can fire.
- **Treat `rebase.backend = apply` as incompatible with `--update-refs`** — the previous draft's
  claim, and factually wrong: the `git rebase` manual lists `--update-refs` as incompatible with
  `--apply`, `--whitespace` and `-C`, the *command-line* selectors of the apply backend, while
  `rebase.backend` is documented as the **default** backend. Neither executor passes any of the
  three, so the merge backend simply wins. Rejected in §4.2; the plan publishes the derived
  `effective_backend` per row and raises no backend-based refusal.
- **List candidates with `--reverse --max-count=<cap>`** — rejected in §4.5: commit limiting is
  applied *before* ordering (`git rev-list` manual), so that shape returns the **newest** `cap`
  commits reversed — the opposite end of the rebase todo list from the one the operator is about to
  replay first. The corrected shapes are count-first with an implementation-side cap, or a
  count-derived `--skip`/`--max-count` window, both `--reverse --topo-order`.
- **Report only stack-owned refs as collateral** — the previous draft's set, and too narrow:
  `--update-refs` force-updates *any* local branch whose tip is inside the replayed range, so a
  maintainer's `wip/foo` moves exactly like `pr1`. Rejected in §4.3: compute over all of
  `refs/heads/*` via `BuildBranchRefInventory`, minus worktree-checked-out refs, and **label**
  `stack_owned` instead of filtering. Under-reporting a destructive blast radius is the one error a
  guard must not make.
- **Reuse `tws stack status` as the guard** — rejected in §7.2: its base resolution deliberately
  differs from both executors.
- **Infer patch equivalence with `git cherry` / `--cherry-mark` patch-ids** to predict drops —
  technically available (verified: `git cherry master pr1` marks the squashed commit `-`), but it is
  an explicit non-goal, it is a heuristic that context/rename changes defeat, and it would create a
  second equivalence truth competing with the future tesserapatch contract
  (`docs/roadmap.md`, non-goals: "Reimplementing tpatch patch identity … inside tws").
- **Simulate the whole run in a scratch worktree/`--dry-run` clone** to make every destination
  knowable — genuinely resolves §5, including the `determinacy = unknown` rows of §5.1 rule 3, but
  costs a full replay of the stack per plan, can itself
  conflict, and would need its own recovery story. Rejected for v1; worth recording as a future
  option if deferral proves too weak in practice.
- **Report a single `--max-replay` number and leave its scope implicit** — rejected in §8.3.2: on a
  broad stack, per-entry and aggregate limits refuse different runs, and an implicit choice makes
  the guard's refusals unpredictable exactly where the stack is widest.
- **Resolve the fetch effect as one remote, always** — every round through 19, and false in a
  configuration Git ships: with `fetch.all` set (honoured since Git 2.44), a bare `git fetch`
  updates every **configured** remote, minus the `skipFetchAll` ones. Publishing `origin` there names one of five stores the run is
  about to write and hides the rest, which is the same class of error `remote.pushDefault` was
  removed for. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9 (round-20 item 1): the effect is
  `{all, contacted, may_delete_refs, may_delete_tags, may_clobber_tags, may_update_local_branches, may_delete_local_branches, local_branch_destinations, remotes[], submodule_recursion}` (round-22 items 2 and 3), the
  remote rows are canonically sorted, the whole value is the collapse key, and an unresolvable
  **read** is `null` rather than a guess.
- **Drop `origin` in favour of the branch remote alone, and call the sole-remote fallback
  “no rule of Git's”** — round 19's phrasing, and wrong on the second half: `remote_for_branch`
  answers the branch's remote, then **the single configured remote when there is exactly one**, then
  `origin`, and a detached HEAD enters that ladder at its second step. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9
  (round-21 item 5): the published effect named `origin` for every single-remote clone whose remote
  is called something else — a remote the run never contacts — while `remote.pushDefault` and
  `remotes.default` stay correctly out of the ladder.
- **Treat an unknown fetch effect as a refusal wherever it appears** — rounds 19-20 published
  `fetch_effect: null` **and** a rank 5.0 blocker for a *single* context whose remote was missing,
  URL-less or unreadable. Rejected in §4.9/§8.6.9 (round-21 item 7): with one candidate there is no
  choice to be indeterminate about, the shipped `fetchQuiet`/`RunSilentDir` call runs and ignores
  the failure, and refusing there would refuse a run the executor performs — so those cells attempt
  the fetch and publish `ok: false`/`failed`/`possibly-stale`, and rank 5.0 is reserved for a
  nondeterministic choice among two or more candidates.
- **Call the sole-configured-remote step older than any Git that matters** — round 21's phrasing
  when it restored the step, and wrong about its age: the fallback was added by commit `8a649be7`
  ("push: default to single remote even when not named origin") and ships from **Git 2.37**, so on
  2.36 and earlier an unset `branch.<name>.remote` resolves to `origin` and the published effect
  would name a remote the run never contacts. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9/§13/§19.27 (round-22 item 1):
  the step is version-gated exactly like `fetch.all` (2.44) and unlike `skipFetchAll` (ungated), the
  three are stated independently, **no minimum supported Git is assumed anywhere**, and §19.27's
  options are applied **per capability** rather than once for the feature.
- **Publish one URL per remote** — every round through 21, and one field short of the behaviour:
  `url.<base>.insteadOf` rewrites what Git really contacts, so a row showing only the configured
  value describes a fetch that may not happen and hides one that does. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9
  (round-22 item 3): each row publishes `url_configured` **and** `url_effective`, both are members
  of the collapse comparison, and `pushInsteadOf` stays out for the same reason
  `remote.pushDefault` does.
- **Say a URL-less remote always fails the fetch, and that an unresolvable default remote fails it
  too** — round 21's single answer to two different questions. Git treats a name as a URL (and
  rewrites it through `insteadOf`) **only when the name was given**: under `fetch.all` each remote
  is fetched by explicit name, so a URL-less member may be rewritten into something reachable and
  succeed, while a **default**-resolved name that resolves to nothing makes `git fetch` contact
  nothing and exit **0**. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9 (round-22 item 3): the three cells are stated
  separately, the third publishes `contacted: false` with `ok: true` and the new
  `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` freshness rather than `fetched`, and no cell is described by
  the outcome of another.
- **Say a `pruneTags` fetch "clobbers" local tags** — round 22's wording, and half wrong on every
  Git since 2.20: an unforced tag update is **rejected**, not applied ("any updates will be rejected
  without `+` in the refspec (or `--force`)", `git fetch` manual, verified against Git 2.55.0), so
  pruneTags **deletes** tags the remote no longer has while leaving a differing existing tag exactly
  where it was. Rejected in §0.1/§4.4/§14/§15.15h4b3 vi-b (round-23 item 2): deletion and clobbering
  are two members with two preconditions, each written as the single predicate §4.4 fixes —
  `may_delete_tags` is `prune && (prune_tags || a positive refspec whose destination covers
  `refs/tags/**`)`, `may_clobber_tags` is a **forced** refspec whose destination covers
  `refs/tags/**` — and no prose may merge them or restate either with a narrower conjunction
  (round-25 item 7 restored the `prune_tags` disjunct this bullet had dropped).
- **Test the tag members with `pruneTags` and a literal `refs/tags/` destination prefix** —
  round 23's own predicates, and both too narrow. Pruning is a function of the *refspec*, not of
  `pruneTags` ("if the refspec for the remote includes e.g. `refs/tags/*:refs/tags/*` … it won't be
  stale remote tracking branches that are deleted, but any local tag that doesn't exist on the
  remote", `git fetch` manual, PRUNING; `pruneTags` merely appends `TAG_REFSPEC` to that list,
  `builtin/fetch.c` `fetch_one`), and a destination that *covers* `refs/tags/**` need not start with
  it — the mirror `+refs/*:refs/*` covers tags, and under round 23's rule published
  `may_delete_tags: false`/`may_clobber_tags: false` for a fetch that really deletes and really
  clobbers them. Rejected in §0.1/§4.4/§14/§15.15h4b3 vi-b/§15.21 (round-24 item 3): one
  pattern-coverage predicate decides both members, `tagOpt` is excluded from it ("We only prune
  based on refspecs specified explicitly … we don't care whether `--tags` was specified",
  `builtin/fetch.c` `do_fetch`), and the tests assert coverage with a pattern table rather than a
  prefix check.
- **Publish the fetch effect as if a bare `git fetch` stopped at the context it runs in** — every
  round through 22. `fetch.recurseSubmodules` **defaults to `on-demand`**, so an ordinary
  superproject's bare fetch can contact submodule remotes and rewrite `refs/remotes/**` in stores
  the row's `context_common_dir` does not name, and a document that implies otherwise under-reports
  exactly where §0.1 forbids it. Rejected in §0.1/§4.4/§8.6.9/§11/§13/§14 (round-23 item 3): the
  effect carries `submodule_recursion`, the reachable stores are published **bounded** with their
  own effects, an unconditional `yes` over an unknown reach **fails closed** at rank 5.05, an
  `on-demand` unknown reach publishes `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect`, and no text may call the
  listed contexts the run's full reach. **The alternative of publishing nothing and marking every
  submodule-bearing context unknown was also rejected**: it would have made the default
  configuration of every superproject undescribable, which is a shrug rather than a fact.
- **Resolve the recursion mode as `fetch.recurseSubmodules` else `submodule.recurse`** — round 23's
  reading of the manual's "Defaults to on-demand, or to the value of `submodule.recurse` if set",
  and a precedence `git fetch` does not implement: `git_fetch_config` (`builtin/fetch.c`) assigns
  **both** keys into the same `fetch_config->recurse_submodules` field as the ordered config is
  parsed, so the **last occurrence wins** — a later `submodule.recurse` overrides an earlier
  `fetch.recurseSubmodules` in the same file, and a repository-local key of either name overrides a
  global one. Under the withdrawn rule the document would have published `mode: yes` for a context
  that really recurses not at all (and vice versa), taking the rank 5.05 refusal and the
  candidate-equivalence key with it. Rejected in §0.1/§4.4/§8.6.9/§13/§15.15h4b3 vi-f/§15.21
  (round-24 item 1): the effective mode is the last writing occurrence across both keys,
  `mode_source` is a closed enum naming it — **three values as round 24 left it, four values plus
  `null` as it stands** since round 26 added the `.gitmodules` context-level rung
  (`fetch.recurseSubmodules`, `submodule.recurse`, `gitmodules-fetch.recurseSubmodules`,
  `default-on-demand`, or `null` where the `.gitmodules` read failed while the config chain set
  nothing; §4.4, §15.21) —, and the ordered `config --list -z` this row
  already issues is what resolves it at no extra cost. **Making `mode_source` part of the
  candidate-equivalence key was rejected with it**: two contexts that resolve the same mode from
  different keys fetch identically, and comparing provenance would refuse a run for a difference
  that has no effect.
- **Gate the submodule reach on `submodule.<name>.active`/`submodule.active`** — round 23's
  activity/presence test, and the wrong question for a *fetch*: for a populated gitlink, `git fetch`
  decides on the index entry, the submodule store and the effective mode alone (`submodule.c`
  `get_fetch_task_from_index` → `fetch_task_create` → `get_fetch_recurse_config`, none of which
  calls `is_submodule_active`), so an inactive-but-populated submodule is fetched under `yes` while
  round 23's rule published `may_recurse: false`/`reach: none` for it — an under-report in exactly
  the direction §0.1 forbids, and one that would have let such a context slip past the fail-closed
  rank 5.05 cell and fetch into stores the document could not name. Rejected in §0.1/§4.4/§4.9/§8.6.1/§8.6.9/§13/
  §15.15h4b3 vi-f/§15.21 (round-24 item 2): the gate is gitlink-and-presence, `active` survives as
  an **informational** member describing the one arm that does consult it (the unpopulated-but-
  changed scan, `get_fetch_task_from_changed` → `is_tree_submodule_active`), and no operator exit
  anywhere offers deactivation as a way to stop a recursion it does not stop.
- **Resolve remotes from `git config` alone** — every round through 22, and a resolution Git does
  not perform: `remotes_remote_get_1` consults `$GIT_DIR/remotes/<name>` and then
  `$GIT_DIR/branches/<name>` whenever the config remote has no URL, and both can turn an apparently
  unresolvable default into a real, contacting fetch — the `branches/` form into
  `refs/heads/<name>`, a **local branch**. Rejected in §0.1/§4.4/§8.6.9/§13/§14/§15.15h4b3 vi-g
  (round-23 item 5): both files are read (from the **common** dir, at no process cost), each row
  publishes its `source`, `insteadOf` applies to legacy URLs as to configured ones, an unreadable
  legacy file makes the effect **unknown** rather than empty, and round 22's contact-free cell (iii)
  is now conditioned on those reads coming back empty.
- **Spell an unresolvable URL as the remote's name** — round 22's `url_effective` fallback ("else
  the name verbatim"), which put a *name* in a *URL* field, made an unreachable row look configured,
  and contradicted §15.21's own assertion that `url_effective` is `null` "only where no URL and no
  rewrite exist". Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9/§15.21 (round-23 item 1): `url_effective` is nullable and
  the name fallback is modelled separately as `url_source: name-verbatim`, whose transport target is
  the row's own `name`.
- **Decide `freshness` by existential clauses over the attempted rows** — the shape every round
  through 22 carried ("`fetched` requires at least one attempted row with `contacted: true`, and no
  failure"), which left a mixed run — one context contacting a remote, another contacting none —
  satisfying `fetched` and `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote` at once, and had no spelling at all
  for an attempted row whose effect was unknown. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.1/§9/§15.15g3 (round-23
  item 1): the verdict is a **total, ranked** table — any failure, else any unknown effect or reach,
  else any no-contact, else `fetched` — with `unknown-fetch-effect` added as the missing member and
  the mixed cell settled as `not-refreshed-no-resolved-remote`.
- **Publish `fetch.mutated_remote_tracking_refs` as "`true` whenever `attempted`"** — the round-13
  form, kept through 22, and an assertion of a write for a fetch that provably performed none: a
  default remote that resolves to nothing exits 0 having touched only `FETCH_HEAD`. Rejected in
  §0.1/§4.4/§15.15g3a (round-23 item 1): the field is tri-state — `true` only where a contacted,
  successful, ref-writing effect exists, `null` where an attempted effect, a mid-transfer failure or
  a possible submodule recursion leaves it undecidable, `false` otherwise — and the `FETCH_HEAD`
  write stays in §0.1's inventory, where it always was. **Round 24 rejects the converse
  over-report too** (item 5): §8.6.1's rule-1 restatement said a failing row yields `null` unless
  another row wrote, which spells a *known zero* as unknown — a row that failed while its resolved
  effect contacted nothing, with no possible recursion, moved no ref at all and publishes `false`;
  `null` is for the **contacted**, possibly mid-transfer failure and for the unknown effect or
  reach.
- **Treat pruning as invisible to the plan** — every round through 21 published an effect that
  could only add refs. It can remove them: `fetch.prune`/`remote.<name>.prune` deletes
  remote-tracking refs and `fetch.pruneTags`/`remote.<name>.pruneTags` deletes local
  tags, per-remote keys overriding the globals (round 22 said "deletes and clobbers"; the clobbering
  half is corrected by round-23 item 2 and is now the separate `may_clobber_tags`, which needs a
  **forced** tag refspec). Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9 (round-22 item 2): each
  remote row publishes its effective `prune`/`prune_tags`/`tag_opt`, the effect publishes
  `may_delete_refs`/`may_delete_tags`, all of it is compared by the collapse rule, and the
  implicit-lease baseline says plainly that the plan's own fetch may flip it to `absent`.
- **Call `FETCH_HEAD` a common-dir file, and let the equivalence rule rest on it** — the wording
  every round carried. `FETCH_HEAD` is a **per-worktree** pseudo-ref written into each worktree's
  own `$GIT_DIR`; only `refs/`, `objects/` and `packed-refs` are shared. Rejected in §0.1/§8.6.9/§13
  (round-22 item 4): collapse rests on the shared refs, tags and objects plus equivalent remote
  effects, the planner reads `FETCH_HEAD` nowhere, and it stays in the mutation inventory only as a
  write the run performs.
- **Enumerate one fetch-context candidate per minimum-depth entry** — round 21's rule, which read a
  tie at a BFS level as a draw. Only the zero-in-degree **root seed** is drawn from a Go map;
  children are appended in `stack.yaml` order and a FIFO queue preserves them, so a component's own
  first entry is a fact. Rejected in §8.6.9/§4.9 (round-22 item 5): candidates are enumerated one
  per **root component** (minimum depth across components, deduplicated on the resolved context),
  same-root siblings and different parents produce one candidate, and rank 5.0 therefore needs a
  token spanning two or more root components with materially different effects — the earlier rule
  manufactured refusals for stacks the shipped code resolves deterministically.
- **Sort fetch refspecs for canonicalization** — the previous draft's rule, and a semantic change
  dressed as formatting: the configured sequence is itself the published fact, and the implicit
  `--force-with-lease` baseline is read off the **first matching non-negative** entry, so a byte
  sort can move which remote-tracking ref that lease reads. Rejected in §4.4/§4.7 (round-20
  item 3): refspec lists are published in configured order, remote rows are the sorted part, and
  negative refspecs are published but excluded from the lease mapping — with a negative-excluded
  branch labelled `possibly-stale` rather than `fetched`.
- **Describe the fetch itself as “first-match”** — round 20's rationale for preserving refspec
  order, and a misstatement of `git fetch`: a fetch applies **every** matching positive refspec, in
  configured order, writing each mapped destination. Rejected in §4.4/§4.7/§13 (round-21 item 6):
  the order is preserved because it is the configured sequence the row publishes and because the
  *lease query* is separately first-match, not because Git stops at the first hit — the earlier
  wording would have under-reported a remote whose two refspecs write two destinations.
- **Let the shipped dirty gate stand in for the untracked-presence fact on a fresh checkout run** —
  round 18's exemption, which assumed the gate refuses "for any untracked file". It does not: it is
  `git status --porcelain`, and `status.showUntrackedFiles=no` silences exactly the files the fact
  is about, so the plan would publish `null` for a run that writes the work tree with untracked
  files present. Rejected in §4.1/§5.4.7 (round-20 item 2): the presence probe runs on those rows
  too, warning-only, while the shipped gate keeps its own behaviour and its own rank 3 projection.
- **Derive `push.blocked_by[]` by copying every kind in `blockers[]`** — round 18's totality rule,
  which made the array a restatement of the array it was supposed to explain and had two wrong
  cells: a **waived** limit violation (which stops nothing) and any future kind whose fact sits
  *after* the push in the shipped arm. Rejected in §4.4 (round-20 item 6): membership is the
  effective, unwaived **unreachability** predicate, evaluated against the shipped control flow —
  which is also what puts `restore-blocked` into `push.blocked_by[]` in checkout, where the restore
  precedes the push, and keeps `push-dropped-restoring` out of `restore.blocked_by[]`.
- **Name "one example entry context" in the `fetch-context-divergent` warning** — the previous
  draft's detail, and an arbitrary choice inside a document that promises byte-stability across
  processes. Rejected in §4.4/§8.6.9 (round-20 item 7): the warning is `entry: null` with a
  canonically derived detail over the sorted, deduplicated diverging contexts, and every warning
  kind's `entry` is fixed by a total mapping rather than by the emitter.
- **Automatic guard on every run with a generous default** — rejected in §8.1/§8.2 (goldens).

---

## 18. Non-goals (explicit)

1. No reparent/restack mutation: this feature never edits `base` or `last_base_sha` to retarget a
   branch. That is `safe reparent/restack`.
2. No patch-id, tpatch, or any other change-equivalence **inference**; no prediction of which
   commits Git will drop, and no `B ≡ B'` claim. The plan publishes the candidate upper bound and
   the two drop mechanisms by name (§4.2), and stops there.
3. No multi-parent composition or implicit merges.
4. No PR/remote retargeting (GitHub/ADO API calls).
5. **No hidden fetch — and no denied fetch either, beyond a closed set of six causes.** The plan
   performs
   exactly the fetch the run's
   resolved input-ref policy prescribes: none under `no-fetch`, the run's own fetch under `fetch`,
   and **none at all on a `--continue`, because no continuation executor fetches** (§0.1, §8.6.4).
   The suppression set is closed at six (§8.6.1, round-23 item 3 adding the fifth, round-25 item 2 the sixth): a `--continue`; a **rows-less document with no
   plannable subject**, where `plan-unavailable`, `selection-refused` or `stack-unsortable` leaves
   nothing to fetch for — **on every route**, since the plan/guard seams sort and select before they
   fetch (`freshness: not-refreshed-no-plan-subject`); a **pre-existing, readable** checkout lock or
   sync-run guard
   whose recorded PID is **signalable and belongs to another process** — token ownership and cell are
   irrelevant, the checkout transaction is not an owner signal, and this invocation's own artefacts
   are excluded, §8.6.1 cause 3 — where fetching
   could move
   refs under another process's rebase (§8.6.1, §9); and an **indeterminate fetch context**, where
   the new-mode route's `TopoSort`-ordered map could resolve two different directories for one
   token and the plan declines to fetch in a directory it cannot reproduce
   (`freshness: not-refreshed-context-indeterminate`, §8.6.9); and an **unbounded submodule
   reach**, where an effective `fetch.recurseSubmodules`/`submodule.recurse` of `yes` would
   recursively contact and rewrite refs in submodule stores the document cannot enumerate
   (`freshness: not-refreshed-submodule-reach-indeterminate`, §8.6.1 cause 5, §4.9 rank 5.05 —
   Git's `on-demand` default never reaching it); and a **checked-out fetch destination**, where a
   positive refspec covering `refs/heads/**` meets a local branch some worktree holds, so the fetch
   either dies before doing anything and leaves the run on stale refs or prunes that branch out from
   under its HEAD (`freshness: not-refreshed-local-branch-checked-out`, §8.6.1 cause 6, §4.9
   rank 5.06 — an ordinary `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/<r>/*` clone never reaching it). Each is published as
   `fetch.outcome: skipped`
   with its own `freshness` value, never disguised as a policy decision, and none of them
   extends to stale, dead-PID, self-owned or otherwise ownerless state cells, which fetch per policy.
   **A pre-existing live foreign
   owner additionally *refuses* a guarded execution** (§8.6.1 cause 3, §9): that is a refusal
   decision, not a fetch decision, and it is stated here only so the two are not read as one — the
   plan-only route still describes that cell in a complete document, publishing the guarded twin's
   refusal as `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]` (§4.4), and the unguarded run
   still fetches and rebases through it. A **seventh**
   cell publishes the same block without being a suppression at all — a fetching route whose
   resolved context set is **empty** has no `git fetch` to run and says
   `freshness: not-refreshed-no-fetch-targets` (§4.4); round-27 item 5 corrects the number, which
   had stayed at "fifth" while the list above it grew to six causes (§8.6.1, §9).
   It never fetches a repository the run would not fetch, never suppresses a fetch for any other
   reason, and never presents a fetch-enabled `--plan` as read-only — **including** the shipped
   external fallback that fetches in the **process cwd**, which the plan discloses through
   `fetch.repos[]` rather than declining to perform (§0.1, §8.6.9, §11). Enumerating *which*
   remote-tracking refs the fetch moved is also out of scope: the plan states that it fetched and
   whether the fetch succeeded, not a ref-by-ref diff.
6. No destructive recovery: no `git reset --hard`, no force push beyond the existing
   `--force-with-lease`, no auto-abort of a foreign rebase.
7. No change to conflict handling, validation, or push semantics — the plan **describes** push and
   validation intent (§3.11, §4.4) and changes neither; `--plan --push` performs no push, and no
   route gains, loses or re-resolves a validation command because a plan was requested.
8. No new workspace mode, no change to external multi-worktree behaviour.
9. No applied-commit count, anywhere, in any output shape (§4.1, §4.2).
10. No unbounded commit listing: identity is capped and the truncation is declared (§4.5, §13).
11. **No change to the mode-trigger set, the I8 operand list, the I20 gate, or the frozen axis
    decision** (§8.5). The control flags describe and guard; they never re-route.
12. **No change to `TopoSort`'s global ordering** and no claim that plan row order is execution
    order (§4.7).
13. **No change to the unguarded rebase argv**, including no `--no-update-refs` and no destination
    pinning on a path the goldens cover (§4.3, §5.3 option 3).
14. **No configuration surface in v1**: no `sync.plan_guard.*` keys and no config-armed limits.
    Limits are flags on a fresh run, and on a continuation only the values that run itself persisted
    (§8.7.4), so a bare no-flag run is unguarded by
    construction (§8.3.4, §10.10).
15. **No structured output from an executing invocation**: `--json` requires `--plan`, and a guarded
    run's machine contract is one anchored, guard-written `^plan-guard: <kind>: ` line plus exit 1
    (§8.7.6) — with uncontrolled Git/Cobra passthrough explicitly outside that guarantee. It also
    emits **no
    approval token**: tokens come only from a `--plan` document, human or JSON (§8.7.7).
16. **No fix to `IsPrunableWorktree`'s cwd scoping.** The planner mirrors the shipped, cwd-scoped
    verdict exactly and publishes `prunability.probe_context = cwd` so the scope is visible
    (§3.7, §5.4.3). Correcting the probe to a `-C`-scoped one would change *which runs stop* — an
    executor behaviour change with its own compatibility surface — and is recorded here as a
    separate follow-up, not smuggled in behind a plan feature. The same mirroring discipline, and
    the same refusal to "improve" it, applies to every other probe an external pass-2 row issues in
    the process cwd when `entry.Repo` is empty (§5.4 consequence 6): the plan follows the executor's
    context, publishes it as that row's `base_context`/`execution_context` pair, and changes nothing.
17. **No new refusal kinds beyond the §4.9 enum**, and no second precedence: the same closed order
    produces `refusal.kind` for the JSON document and for the guard's marker line — the guard simply
    ranks only the facts available at its seam (§4.9, §8.7.1).
18. **No prediction of which filter Git will apply to a given commit.** The plan states *whether*
    each filter can fire — `may_drop_patch_equivalent` from the arm and range, `may_drop_becomes_empty`
    always — and never which commits they will drop (§4.2, non-goal 2).
19. **No restoration of the operator's original branch in external.** The plan **states** that an
    external pass-2 row switches HEAD and leaves it there (§5.4.7, §11) and refuses the cells where
    the switch cannot happen, but it does not add a `restoreOriginal` path to external, does not
    pass `--no-autostash`, and does not change what the unguarded run does with a dirty tree.
    Correcting the executor's behaviour there is its own change with its own compatibility surface;
    this feature makes it visible and refusable, not different.
20. **No repair of the checkout `restoring` push loss.** A `--push` transaction resumed at
    `stage: restoring` reaches `finalizeCleanup` with `tx.Stage != StageCompleted`, so its
    `tx.Stage == StageCompleted && opts.Push` guard is false and the requested push is **dropped**
    before the transaction is deleted (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1010-1017`, `:1239-1247`). That is
    a shipped defect and it is **recorded here as an explicit follow-up**, not fixed behind a plan
    feature: making the resume push would change what an existing `--continue` does to a remote,
    which is exactly the class of change §10 freezes. What this feature does instead is make the
    loss **legible** — the document states the intent that was requested (`intent.push: true`,
    `intent.push_source: persisted-transaction`) alongside the effective targets (`push.targets:
    []`) and the explicit **`restore.push_dropped: true`** (§4.4). It does **not** conclude that the
    resume is workless: the same resume switches HEAD back to the original branch, deletes the
    transaction and releases the lock, so the document publishes the `restore` object and a **real**
    approval token over it. The earlier "mints no token over work that will not happen" reading is
    withdrawn — the push will not happen, the restore will (§4.4, §8.6.4a, §15.16l2 vii). The
    follow-up itself is unchanged: repairing `finalizeCleanup`'s stage condition is its own change,
    with its own compatibility surface.
21. **No fix for the new-mode fetch-context nondeterminism.** `UniqueRepos` over a `TopoSort`-ordered
    selection can resolve two different directories for one token between two runs of the same
    command — and, when those directories are different **repositories** rather than two worktrees
    of one, a different object store (§4.7, §8.6.9). This feature neither sorts `selectedRealEntries`, nor changes
    `UniqueRepos`, nor makes `TopoSort` deterministic — all three would change which repository an
    existing unguarded run refreshes. It enumerates the candidates, refuses to *authorise* an
    ambiguous fetch (`fetch-context-indeterminate`), and leaves the unguarded behaviour exactly as
    shipped. Making the choice deterministic is a separate executor change with its own
    compatibility surface.

---

## 19. Open questions for `define`

Resolved by this revision and **no longer open**: whether the control flags are mode triggers (they
are not, §8.5); whether they join the presence map (they do not — separate `planGuardOptions`,
§8.5.1); which run a bare `--plan` describes (the legacy no-flag run, because that is the run
the same flags perform, §0.2/§8.5); which run `--plan --no-fetch` describes (the **new-mode** run,
so there is no fully-local preview of the legacy route, §5.3); whether `--plan` inherits the
fresh-run refusal ladder (it does not — dedicated inspection route, §8.6, with the hard-error set
and both dispatch positions fixed in §8.6.6-§8.6.8); whether `syncFallback` is reachable (it is, and
is intercepted, §8.5.5); the JSON version key spelling (`schema_version`, §8.3.6); plan row ordering
(canonicalized document, unchanged `TopoSort`, §4.7); whether v1 ships config defaults (it does
not — flags only, §8.3.4);
whether a guarded execution emits a document (it does not — exit 1 plus one anchored, guard-written
`^plan-guard: ` line, §8.7.6); what an approval waives (only the limit violations shown in
the approved document, never hard blockers or newly-resolved JIT excesses, §5.3.1); **how multiple
blockers collapse to one `refusal.kind`** (the closed precedence and canonical blocker sort of §4.9,
identical in JSON and on the guard's marker line for every kind the guard produces); **what an
unknown fact looks like** (`null`,
never `[]`/`false`/`0`, §4.8); **head-ref state** (a first-class totality axis with its own
`head-ref-missing` kind, §5.1 rule 6); **an unsortable stack** (a rows-less `stack-unsortable`
document, exit 0 plan-only and exit 1 guarded, §5.5); how deferral is computed (from the
route's real execution order, §5.1); whether a continuation fetches (it never does, §8.6.4); what
`--plan --continue` describes (the remaining work only, with **every** continuation gate projected
as a blocker carrying the shipped sentence, and the effective route/policy read from the state,
§8.6.4/§8.5.3); **what a refusal may delete** (only what
that invocation created; a continuation refusal preserves the interrupted state and refuses above
`ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, §9/§8.7.5/§12); and **how prunability is probed** (mirroring the executor's
cwd-scoped `IsPrunableWorktree`, with the scoping defect deferred to its own follow-up, §3.7).

**Settled by earlier rounds, and likewise no longer open:** what `runnable` means (ranks 1-5,
plus rank 6 only under the explicitly selected blocking rendering of `selection-hazard`;
guard verdicts and approvals never move it, §4.4/§4.9); **where a token comes
from** (any `--plan` document that describes an approvable plan under an effective limit — the
`--json` field or the human
final line — and never an executing
invocation, §8.3.5/§8.7.7; the limit clause was added in round 12, §4.4); **that push and validation intent are plan facts bound into the
fingerprint**, that
`--plan --push` is legal and pushes nothing, and that external ignores `--test` exactly as shipped
(§3.11, §4.4, §8.3.1); the **collateral set** (all local branch refs in range minus
worktree-checked-out ones, labelled `stack_owned`, §4.3); **arm-aware clean-cherry semantics** and
the removal of the non-existent `rebase.reapplyCherryPicks` probe (§4.2); **`rebase.backend` as a
default, not a constraint**, published per row as `effective_backend` with no backend-based refusal
(§4.2, §4.9); the **candidate list's end and order** (oldest-first, count-derived, never
`--reverse --max-count`, §4.5); the existence and rank of `selection-hazard`,
`guard-limit-mismatch` and `revalidation-mismatch` (§4.9); and the **external unset-base token**
(the empty string; the `origin/` alternative is unreachable, §5.1 rule 5).

**Settled by earlier rounds of review, and no longer open:** the **fetch-suppression predicate for a
live owner** — an owning PID that answers the liveness probe independently, computed from the raw recorded
PID rather than from `SyncExternalState.GuardLive` (which folds token ownership into liveness), so a
**token-mismatched** live guard suppresses the fetch and a payload-owned but dead one does not;
ownership is
published separately as `state.files.external_run_guard.token_matches_payload`, and the round-10 second
conjunct — "and the observation is a non-waivable `state-refused` blocker" — is **withdrawn**, since
another process moves refs whether or not our cell refuses; every stale, dead-PID or
ownerless cell fetches per route policy; and the same predicate, defined once in §8.6.1 cause 3,
also decides the **guarded** seam, where it is a non-waivable `state-refused` concurrency
refusal rather than a fetch skip (§8.6.1 cause 3, §9, §15.15f/f2, §15.20b). **Round 13 completed
that predicate rather than reopening it**: liveness is evaluated over the **pre-acquisition
snapshot** and excludes this process's own PID, so the settled sentence reads "a *pre-existing live
foreign process*" — three conjuncts, of which the round-11 wording stated only one; **round 14 adds
the remaining two** (the artefact must be one of the two owner-*signalling* lock files, never the
checkout transaction, and its `presence` must be `readable`) and restates "alive" as *signalable*
(§8.6.1 cause 3, §4.4 `state`); the **token's lexical form** — 64 lowercase hex
characters compared bytewise, with the human final line a *line containing* the token, never the

per-key limit-origin enum, including `flags-persisted-continuation` for arming a previously-unguarded v2
resume without writing state (§8.7.4, §10.3); the **marker contract by origin rather than rank**,

replacing flat `git_config`, repo-qualified `{repo, ref, sha, stack_owned}` collateral tuples sorted

**Settled by an earlier round, and no longer open:** the **collateral drop split** — the preliminary
clean-cherry-pick filter removes a candidate *before* the todo, so a ref pointing at it is not
updated and may be orphaned, while a becomes-empty drop keeps the `update-ref` machinery and the ref

§10.3, §15.16c c5); **the exact remaining-work derivation** — one shared `RemainingRebaseEntries`,
external = current `TopoSort` ∩ persisted selection minus `Completed ∪ {FailedBranch}` with

`CurrentIndex` with a stage table that includes the current index only for `planned`/`switched`/
`rebasing`, excludes it for `conflict`/`rebased`/`validating`, and yields none for
